Brazil pauses presidential vote count after Supreme Court extends hours
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
05:39:00 UTC
14:39:00 KST

BRASILIA, Brazil (Reuters) -- Brazil's Supreme Court allowed some polling stations to extend voting in the country's presidential election by two hours on Sunday, leading the electoral authority to pause a vote count that had already started publishing early-stage results.
The Supreme Court's decision and the subsequent pause of the vote count add confusion to a tense contest between two opposing political forces: leftist President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva versus right-wing Sen. Flavio Bolsonaro, son of convicted former President Jair Bolsonaro.
A victory for Bolsonaro, 45, would extend a wave of right-wing victories for Latin American candidates friendly to U.S. President Donald Trump, while a fourth mandate for Lula would be a bulwark against Washington's influence in the region as his government has pushed back on U.S. trade and security policies.
Supreme Court Justice Cristiano Zanin accepted a request by Lula's campaign to extend voting, pointing to public transportation issues in three cities in the state of Bahia.
Zanin's decision landed right around the election's 5 p.m. Brasilia time (2000 GMT) cutoff, creating confusion as some polling stations had already closed.
In a subsequent ruling, Zanin said those stations would remain shut, allowing authorities to begin tallying those votes, but that polling stations that had not closed after the official cutoff could keep receiving voters for an additional two hours.
The electoral court, or TSE, had already started publishing results that showed Lula leading Bolsonaro with 0.25% of ballots counted. Lula had 57.66% of votes, compared with 42.34% for Bolsonaro, the early count showed.
After the Zanin ruling, the TSE said it would pause the vote count to allow for the extended voting window to close.
The pause in the vote count injects uncertainty into a Brazilian electoral process still grappling with the fallout from 2022, when Jair Bolsonaro refused to concede defeat to Lula. His supporters later invaded government buildings in protest against the result, and Bolsonaro received a 27-year prison sentence for plotting a coup.
The candidate's brother Eduardo Bolsonaro, speaking on a livestream on his YouTube channel, questioned why the Supreme Court had ruled in a process overseen by the country's federal electoral court: "Strange, isn't it?" he said. "It's hard to imagine what the legal basis for this could possibly be. It doesn't inspire credibility."
Two legal experts told Reuters the extension of voting hours and allegations around disrupted public transportation could draw legal challenges.
"Depending on the election result, there is a possibility that the losing side might attempt to contest the outcome, arguing that many people were unable to vote even with the extended deadline," said Vera Chemim, a constitutional lawyer in Sao Paulo.
Lula had asked electoral authorities to extend voting in at least nine states after his campaign alleged some officials reduced election day public transportation, impacting voters' ability to get to the polls.
Earlier on Sunday, a court in Bahia, a Lula stronghold in the Northeast, ordered the arrest of a top transportation official in the city of Salvador over allegations that he directed a reduction in the city's bus fleet.
In comments before Zanin's decision, Lula said "something abominable is happening" in this election.
Flavio Bolsonaro had also asked for voting to be extended in at least three states, citing bad weather.
Lula and his allies see Sunday's runoff as a chance to stem Latin America's conservative drift.
Reuters on Saturday revealed a campaign within Trump's State Department to help get the Bolsonaros back in power.
Trump has so far declined to endorse a candidate. Asked on Sunday who he hoped would win, Trump declined to say.
"I don't want to get into that, but we are watching," he told reporters in Washington.

Saint Demetrius protects Bulgaria in times of trouble and hardship

Saint Demetrius protects Bulgaria in times of trouble and hardship
The church bearing the name of the saint in Pancharevo is a symbol of the desire for freedom and unity
Monday 26 October 2026 06:25
Monday, 26 October 2026, 06:25
PHOTO facebook.com/hramsvetidimitarpancharevo
Font size
St. Demetrius of Thessalonica is one of the most revered saints in Bulgaria. There are many churches in this country, built in honor of the saint who died a martyr's death in the 4th century, because of his refusal to persecute and punish the Christian believers. During the Second Bulgarian State (1185-1396), the Bulgarians regarded Saint Demetrius as the heavenly protector of the capital city of Tarnovo.
According to historical records, in 1185 an icon of St. Demetrius miraculously arrived in Tarnovo. The icon came from a basilica that was looted during the Norman invasion in Thessaloniki where the relics of the saint were kept. The icon's arrival was a sign for the Bulgarian rulers that the saint will protect the recently restored Bulgarian state. In honor of the saint, a magnificent church was built at the foot of the Trapezitsa fortress. Until the third decade of the 13th century, it served as the leading church of the Bulgarian state. It was there that Archbishop Basil I became the head of the restored independent Bulgarian Church following Byzantine rule. All Bulgarian rulers who reigned between 1186 and 1241 received the insignia of their royal dignity in the Church of St. Demetrius.
The Church of St. Demetrius the Great Martyr of Thessaloniki in Pancharevo district
PHOTO bg-patriarshia.bg
The tradition of building churches dedicated to St. Demetrius continues to this day, reinforcing the saint’s enduring role as a protector of Bulgaria. The beautiful white church of St. Demetrius in the Pancharevo district of Sofia is one such example. The local residents did not have their own church for many years, but even before Bulgaria became a free state, large-scale construction of a church began in the then village of Pancharevo, situated near Sofia. The building was finally completed in 1882 and solemnly consecrated on October 26, St. Demetrius Day. The church is located in the historical center of Pancharevo and is designated a cultural monument of local significance.
Archpriest Krastin Apostolov
PHOTO facebook.com/HramRojdestvoHristovoMladost
"The church was built through the efforts of the entire Pancharevo community, embodying the dream of a free and united Bulgaria", Archpriest Krastin Apostolov says. In the 17th-19th centuries, at the end of the Ottoman Empire, Pancharevo was a remarkably diverse place, inhabited by refugees from Macedonia and Thrace, as well as Circassians. The settlers gave the name of the settlement, which is believed to derive from the old Bulgarian word "panitsa”, meaning a bowl and the Turkish word “çare”, meaning "resort", in reference to the healing mineral springs in the area, which have been known since antiquity.
"Many of the Bulgarians who fled from Macedonia had ties to Thessaloniki, the center of the geographical region of Macedonia, so choosing St. Demetrius as the patron saint was a natural decision. In a way, this church heralded the emergence of a free Bulgaria, not only because of its beautiful appearance but also because it became a gathering place for the people who would go on to build modern Bulgaria. One of the first hydroelectric power plants, not only in this country, but in the entire Balkan Peninsula, was built here. This happened a few decades after the church was built, but the people who constructed the power plant came from France and Italy and some of them settled in the small village of Pancharevo. In the beginning of the 20th century the population rapidly increased and the church became the gathering place for both newcomers and long-time residents."
"Today, the situation in Pancharevo is not much different from what it was 140 years ago, when the temple was built", Archpriest Krastin Apostolov adds.
"The church was built in a multicultural environment. That is why, I personally feel responsible for continuing the work of those who managed to build such a majestic and iconic temple before the Liberation and within the framework of the Ottoman Empire - a true symbol of a new and free Bulgaria."

Russia is escalating its confrontation with the West in orbit. Its satellites are pursuing spacecraft from companies helping Ukraine — and Starlink has been put on notice.
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
05:30:27 UTC
14:30:27 KST

Russia is escalating its confrontation with the West in orbit. Its satellites are pursuing spacecraft from companies helping Ukraine — and Starlink has been put on notice.
There has long been talk of “hunter” satellites and an intensifying confrontation in space between Russia and the United States. But this week brought an unprecedented escalation in the new “star wars.” On October 18, a Russian inspector satellite came closer than ever to a spacecraft operated by the Finnish-American company ICEYE. The company openly helps Ukraine, giving its armed forces access to satellite images of Russian military facilities, including airfields, naval ports, and oil refineries. Here’s what we know about the exceptionally close encounter, how Moscow is describing it, and why independent experts are alarmed.
Russian Kosmos satellites have pursued this spacecraft before, but never like this
Overnight into October 18, the Russian satellite Kosmos-2612 approached the radar imaging satellite ICEYE-X36 after a series of maneuvers that began four days earlier. The Ukrainian military uses data from the ICEYE satellite.
This was not their first close encounter. In the spring, four Russian spacecraft were “hunting” this same satellite: Kosmos-2612, 2610, 2611, and 2613 all approached it. Earlier, in February, news outlets reported on maneuvers by Luch spacecraft pursuing telecommunications satellites operated by Intelsat and Eutelsat.
This time, Kosmos-2612 came exceptionally close to its target: hundreds or even tens of meters away, rather than tens of kilometers as before. Observational astronomer Marco Langbroek estimates that at their closest approach, at 1:35 a.m. GMT on October 18, the spacecraft were between 26 and 470 meters apart. Measurement errors make a more precise estimate impossible. Bart Hendrickx, an independent researcher of Russia’s space program, told Meduza that he knew of no previous encounter at such close range in low Earth orbit. In earlier encounters, he said, satellites had remained at least several dozen kilometers apart.
He said the complexity and methodical persistence of the maneuvers by Kosmos-2612 and its fellow satellites, numbered 2610, 2611, 2613, and 2614, were also surprising. All these spacecraft, along with satellite 2609, were launched aboard a single rocket from the Plesetsk Cosmodrome on April 16.
“The satellites used a considerable amount of fuel on these maneuvers. By May, it was already clear that these weren’t ordinary Earth-observation and communications satellites, which generally conserve their fuel. Perhaps [through this latest escalation] Russia is demonstrating its ability to change orbits quickly and unpredictably to threaten enemy satellites,” Hendrickx said.
Moscow calls these maneuvers “a tool of strategic deterrence” and a warning to commercial companies
The Russian military previously acknowledged launching inspector satellites but said their sole purpose was “monitoring the condition of Russian satellites” — and said they had carried out such monitoring. Now, following Kosmos-2612’s dangerous maneuvers, the government newspaper Rossiyskaya Gazeta has published an article by Yuri Knutov, a military expert, retired colonel, and director of the Air Defense Forces Museum in Balashikha, outside Moscow. The article says Russia’s actions “do not violate international law” and that the inspector satellites themselves are “a tool of strategic deterrence.”
“Russia is demonstrating its ability to ‘blind’ or at least identify sources of threats. The approach to ICEYE-X36 sends a clear signal: Any commercial company making its capabilities available for intelligence gathering against Russia must recognize that its spacecraft may be subjected to forced inspection in orbit,” Knutov wrote. He said both ICEYE satellites and the Starlink constellation, which is critical to Ukrainian military command and communications, had effectively become part of NATO’s intelligence apparatus.
Like analyst Georgy Trishkin, whose views we quoted here, Knutov believes the Kosmos maneuvers were intended to force the ICEYE satellite to take evasive action to avoid a collision and quickly use up its fuel, turning it into “a useless piece of metal that will eventually burn up in the upper atmosphere.”
Knutov said the Russian satellites were less vulnerable to such a tactic because modern inspector spacecraft have much larger fuel reserves than their predecessors. Earlier models could perform only two or three orbital maneuvers before running out of fuel, he said, whereas newer satellites can remain in orbit for extended periods, carry out complex close approaches, and track other spacecraft over long stretches.
This latest episode in the space cold war was clearly visible from Earth. On Monday, Spaceweather.com asked whether the close encounter between Kosmos and ICEYE would be visible through binoculars or a backyard telescope. By Tuesday, it had its answer: yes.
This image, taken by the Swiss company s2a systems, shows the encounter. The bright object in front is the ICEYE-X36 radar satellite. Its apparent magnitude is about 7, making it invisible to the naked eye but easy to see through binoculars or an amateur telescope. The fainter object behind it is Kosmos-2612.
Russia isn’t the only country with space programs like these
Other countries, particularly the United States and China, have their own programs to develop inspector satellites. These spacecraft are designed to approach other objects in space that aren’t built for such encounters — those without docking ports, for example. These approaches can have various purposes: intercepting radio transmissions, inspecting another spacecraft, diagnosing problems, or even destroying it.
Militaries initiated and funded nearly all of these programs, so the public first learned they existed from amateur astronomers tracking the strange behavior of uncataloged satellites. Since 2011, when these observers identified an American satellite nicknamed Prowler this way, dozens more inspector satellites and many cases of pursuit have been detected, most involving Russian spacecraft.
Russian satellite maneuvers are easier to track because of censorship in the Pentagon’s main space catalog
Unequal access to information partly explains this pattern of observations. The U.S. military maintains Space-Track, the main publicly accessible catalog of artificial objects in space. It withholds the full orbital parameters of some U.S. military and intelligence satellites or publishes them with a delay. Until 2018, the Pentagon even classified data on civilian spacecraft launched as secondary payloads alongside military ones.
The U.S. military does not conceal Russian satellites’ orbital data, so anyone with the relevant skills can use the available data to plot their movements rather than track them through a telescope.
In 2018, the State Department protested the “very abnormal behavior” of Russian satellites. The U.S. military has protested their “threatening” maneuvers and anti-satellite weapons tests (we wrote about these nesting-doll satellites). Then, in 2024, Washington accused Moscow of preparing to deploy nuclear weapons in space.
Yet the United States has operated GSSAP satellites since 2014. These are essentially the same kind of inspector satellites, used to monitor satellites in geostationary orbit. And in June 2026, the U.S. military launched Jackal, built by True Anomaly, and Puma, made by Rocket Lab, as part of the Victus Haze exercise to practice space “hunting” scenarios.
In September of this year, the Pentagon acknowledged for the first time that it had deployed weapons in space — both kinetic and nonkinetic. The next few years in Earth orbit will clearly be tense.
Inspector satellites are also being developed for entirely civilian purposes. One example is LINK, a spacecraft meant to attempt a rescue of the Swift space telescope, but its mission ended in failure.
It’s hard to predict what the Kosmos satellites will do next
What happens next depends largely on how much fuel the Russian satellites have left. They may continue maneuvering around ICEYE spacecraft. According to Langbroek, as of midday on October 21, Kosmos-2612 had stopped moving away from its target and was holding at a distance of 480 kilometers. Hendrickx cautioned that the pursuit might not be over: Kosmos-2612 could return if it had enough fuel. He also pointed to four other Russian satellites launched alongside it — Kosmos-2610, 2611, 2613, and 2614 — that operate in similar orbits and probably have the same mission. Both ICEYE-X36 and ICEYE-X37 could be targets, he said.

Trump Administration backs Orbán for UN Secretary-General – media
Ukrinform reports this, citing The Wall Street Journal and The Jerusalem Post.
According to the reports, U.S. officials have already approached Orbán with the proposal. He has expressed interest but has not yet made a final decision on whether to enter the race for UN Secretary-General.
Washington believes Orbán’s previous contacts with Moscow and Beijing could help secure their support for the Hungarian politician, who is seen as pro-Russian. This could make Orbán a joint candidate backed by three permanent members of the UN Security Council.
A State Department official estimated that Orbán could secure the support of at least eight of the Security Council’s 15 members, and potentially as many as 10 if circumstances are favorable.
It remains unclear, however, whether the United Kingdom and France, which hold veto power on the Security Council, would be prepared to block his candidacy.
A State Department official described Orbán as a “MAGA conservatives' dream candidate,” citing his positions on mass immigration, liberal nongovernmental organizations, and established centers of influence in Hungary’s judiciary and media.
Orbán has repeatedly clashed with EU leaders while strengthening ties with China. His relations with Moscow and Beijing, as well as his domestic policies, could come under particular scrutiny if he is nominated.
U.S. President Donald Trump supported Orbán in Hungary’s parliamentary election in April, while Vice President JD Vance personally took part in his election campaign.
Another informal vote is scheduled for Wednesday at the UN Security Council to gauge support for the candidates. It remains unclear whether Orbán’s name will be included in the ballot.
António Guterres’s term as UN Secretary-General ends on December 31. The next Secretary-General will be elected by the General Assembly following a recommendation from the Security Council.

Aleksandar Vucic, the Serbian leader brought down by students
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
05:24:59 UTC
14:24:59 KST

Aleksandar Vucic, the Serbian leader brought down by students
Serbia’s longtime leader concedes defeat to a student-led protest movement in parliamentary elections.
Aleksandar Vucic, who has shaped Serbia’s political life for more than a decade, has lost snap parliamentary elections to a student-led movement that led protests against him for almost two years.
After a heated race, Vucic conceded defeat to the Student List in Sunday’s elections, which saw voter turnout reach its highest level in more than 30 years.
“It is clear that we have lost these elections,” the leader of the Serbian Progressive Party (SNS) told supporters after a sample of votes showed his electoral list was expected to win 105 seats in Serbia’s 250-member parliament, compared with 135 to 140 for the Student List.
The student movement emerged after 16 people were killed when a train station canopy collapsed in the city of Novi Sad on November 1, 2024.
The youth-led protests grew into a broader wave of social unrest and evolved into the Student List political platform, which promised to tackle corruption, depoliticise public institutions and restore citizens’ rights.
During the election campaign, the movement was led by Ilija Srdanovic, a professor at the Faculty of Medicine in Novi Sad.
Vucic referred to the demonstrators, who included university professors, doctors and workers, as “blockaders” and accused them of seeking to destabilise Serbia.
A former ultranationalist, Vucic cultivated an image of a pragmatic leader who maintained ties with the European Union, Russia and China as well as, increasingly, with Israel in recent years.
Born in Belgrade in 1970, the nearly 2-metre-tall (6.5ft-tall) Vucic graduated from the University of Belgrade’s faculty of law. He entered politics in 1993, joining the ultranationalist Serbian Radical Party led by Vojislav Seselj.
His political record during the 1990s was marked by nationalist rhetoric. One of his most remembered statements came in Serbia’s parliament in July 1995, nine days after the Srebrenica genocide: “Kill one Serb, and we will kill 100 Muslims.” Vucic made the comments during a debate on possible NATO strikes against positions held by the Army of Republika Srpska in Bosnia and Herzegovina.
Vucic’s political mentor at the time, Seselj, was sentenced in 2018 to 10 years in prison by the Appeals Chamber of the International Residual Mechanism for Criminal Tribunals for persecution, deportation and forcible transfer of non-Serbs during the wars in the Balkans in the 1990s.
Aleksandar Seselj, the son of Vojislav Seselj, was on Vucic’s electoral list in Sunday’s elections.
After a split within the Serbian Radical Party, Vucic and Tomislav Nikolic founded the SNS in 2008. The new party sought to move closer to mainstream European politics.
Safeta Bisevac, a Serbian journalist who has long followed Vucic’s political career, believes he was initially less popular than Nikolic, who appeared closer to common citizens.
“Vucic lagged far behind in popularity at the time and was essentially the organiser of the newly formed party,” Bisevac told Al Jazeera.
In 2012, the SNS came to power promising to fight corruption, organised crime and abuses committed under previous governments.
One of the most prominent cases was the December 2012 arrest of businessman Miroslav Miskovic and his son Marko on suspicion of financial irregularities and tax evasion. After years of legal proceedings, both were acquitted and the state paid them compensation.
Bisevac said the results of the fight against corruption remained modest while the authorities expanded their control over institutions, the media and political life.
Vucic served as first deputy prime minister from 2012 to 2014 before ascending to the post of prime minister in 2014. Three years later, he became president of Serbia and won re-election in 2022. His term was due to run until 2027.
Under pressure from the student-led protests, he resigned in September and called early elections. Although the Serbian presidency is constitutionally limited, Vucic has retained a dominant influence over his party and state policy.
“He made many promises and fulfilled few of them, but in the meantime, he established almost complete control over the state apparatus,” Bisevac said.
Economic growth and the debate over living standards
The Serbian economy has expanded significantly since Vucic took Serbia’s political centre stage in 2012. Unemployment dropped from 26 percent to 8 to 9 percent while nominal gross domestic product nearly tripled, reaching about 90 billion euros ($101bn), according to official data cited by the Reuters news agency.
Annual foreign direct investment inflows rose from about 800 million euros ($896m) in 2012 to a record 5.2 billion euros ($5.8bn) in 2024.
A network of modern motorways has also been built.
However, rising wages have not necessarily translated into a proportional improvement in living standards. The rising cost of living and public debt remain important elements of the debate over the government’s economic record.
Political scientist Dusko Radosavljevic said “the students simply gave a voice to the justified anger of citizens.”
Speaking to Al Jazeera about Vucic’s policies, Radosavljevic said the past decade was characterised by “systematic pressure and the destruction of social institutions”.
“State intelligence services have spent less time on their actual duties and more time monitoring political opponents while critical thinking has been pushed out of the public media,” Radosavljevic said.

The Gambia’s first blind magistrate tests a system built for the sighted
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
05:18:00 UTC
14:18:00 KST

The Gambia’s first blind magistrate tests a system built for the sighted
For a decade, Muhammed Krubally has shown what is possible and what still needs to change.
Banjul, the Gambia – It is still early when Magistrate Muhammed Krubally arrives at the Banjul Magistrates’ Court.
Before the first case, his clerk goes over the day’s proceedings, running through the files and making sure everything is in place. Krubally listens, asks questions, and prepares to preside.
Then he enters a packed courtroom, where lawyers, witnesses and relatives have gathered for a criminal case.
The room falls quiet.
Krubally cannot see the people before him, but he can hear them. A lawyer rises. A witness speaks. Papers move across the room. His clerk is nearby.
At his desk, his computer speaks back to him.
Krubally uses JAWS, or Job Access With Speech, a screen reader that allows him to navigate his computer and read documents and judgements.
“This makes my job very easy,” he tells Al Jazeera.
He also uses AI-enabled smart glasses to access information and carry out tasks independently.
But technology is only part of how he works.
He listens for voices, remembers details and follows the rhythm of proceedings, building a picture of the courtroom through sound. When necessary, he relies on his clerk.
At 41, Krubally says he has presided over more than 1,000 civil and criminal cases since joining the bench.
In 2016, he became the Gambia’s first visually impaired magistrate. The Gambia Organisation of the Visually Impaired (GOVI) identifies him as the country’s first person with a visual impairment to hold the position.
For Krubally, this is not an experiment in what a visually impaired person might be capable of doing.
It is his profession.
And he has spent a decade doing it.
A determination shaped early
Long before he took his place on the bench, Krubally grew up in a village in the Gambia’s Central River Region, the second of nine children.
From an early age, he wanted to become a lawyer. Part of that ambition was personal: he wanted to defend his own rights. But he also wanted to advocate for others.
He wanted, he says, “to be the voice for the voiceless”, particularly people with disabilities.
The path was not straightforward.
From primary school through university, Krubally encountered limited resources and an education system that often left visually impaired students like him facing obstacles their sighted classmates did not.
He remembers being discouraged by fellow students and some teachers from pursuing the education he wanted.
Instead of making him abandon his ambition, he says, their doubts only strengthened it.
“Their discouragement kept me going. I knew what I wanted, and see where I am now,” he says.
Those experiences later shaped his decision to enter the judiciary.
“I became a magistrate to change the system, to make it inclusive,” he says.
But joining one of the country’s most important public institutions did not make those barriers disappear.
Rights on paper, barriers in practice
The Gambia’s Persons with Disabilities Act, passed in 2021, sets out principles including independence, non-discrimination, full participation, equality of opportunity and accessibility.
The law also contains provisions covering employment, public buildings and services, information and access to justice.
Yet putting those rights into practice remains a challenge.
The National Human Rights Commission has identified barriers affecting people with disabilities, including discrimination and difficulties accessing services, education and employment.
Al Jazeera contacted the Ministry of Gender, Children and Social Welfare for a response on implementation of the act, including measures to improve accessibility, education and employment opportunities for people with disabilities. The ministry did not respond.
Krubally encounters those challenges not only as a judicial officer, but also as an advocate.
As president of the Gambia Federation of the Disabled, he speaks at events in the Gambia and beyond, pressing for greater recognition of the rights and potential of people with disabilities.
“I want to see a world for all; inclusion matters,” he says.
For Krubally, inclusion is not simply about opening the door. It is about having the means to participate once inside.
The barriers begin at school
For many people with disabilities, working towards full inclusion begins long before they enter a courtroom or parliament.
It begins at school.
Today, GOVI’s Resource Centre for the Blind provides specialist education for children with visual impairments before they transition into mainstream schools.
Forty-nine pupils aged between four and 14 currently attend the centre, Lamin Colley, its head of school, told Al Jazeera.
After completing their studies there, pupils are expected to enter mainstream schools, where special-needs teachers stationed across school clusters are meant to support them.
But that support is stretched.
Colley told Al Jazeera that limited learning materials and the size of the school clusters are putting pressure on the support available to students. A single special-needs teacher, he said, cannot maintain regular contact with all students across those clusters.
“The reality on the ground is that not much has changed after the disability act has been passed,” Colley says.
He attributes this partly to what he describes as insufficient government funding for disability issues in the national budget.
Colley remembers Krubally as a pupil who loved to read and could often be found in the library. He also remembers his determination to participate in activities alongside his sighted classmates.
Years later, Krubally’s journey carries a message beyond the school gates.
“Disability does not mean inability.”
But one person’s achievement does not erase the obstacles facing those coming behind him.
Entering an institution is not enough
Ndey Yassin Secka-Sallah knows what it means to enter a public institution without having the tools to participate independently.
She was nominated to the Gambia’s National Assembly and has long advocated for the rights of people with disabilities. GOVI describes her as the country’s only visually impaired parliamentarian.
She was also involved in advocacy around disability rights and the push for stronger legal protections.
Yet taking a seat in parliament did not make the institution accessible.
“I used to depend on my fellow colleagues to know what was being discussed,” she told Al Jazeera.
What she wanted was not special treatment, but independence.
“I would have loved to be independent, without depending on people for help.”
Five years after the disability law was passed, Secka-Sallah says implementation remains a major challenge.
She sees Krubally’s appointment to the bench as significant, but not as the end of the struggle.
“Inclusion is all we wish for,” she says.
Musa Barrow, another visually impaired professional, teaches media law and ethics to journalism students.
Like Krubally, Barrow has encountered assumptions about what a visually impaired person can do. Some students have questioned whether he can meet the standards they expect from a lecturer.
Technology has helped him work independently. He uses digital tools to read, write and prepare lecture notes.
“Technology has broken that barrier for me,” he says.
But students’ assumptions have not disappeared.
His response is direct.
“I can do more than what sighted people can do,” he says.
Barrow’s visual impairment has also shaped how he teaches journalism, particularly when discussing the media’s portrayal of disability.
The experiences of Krubally, Secka-Sallah and Barrow all point to the same gap: entering an institution is not the same as being equipped to participate fully in it.
What does the law look like in practice?
The scale of the challenge is difficult to measure.
The Gambia’s 2013 Population and Housing Census recorded a disability prevalence of 1.2 percent, representing 21,873 people, according to later analysis of the census data.
But that figure may understate the scale of disability in the country. The census used a narrower set of questions and did not use the Washington Group questions commonly used to measure functional difficulties.
The Gambia has since conducted a new population and housing census, with preliminary results released in September 2024. But the preliminary report did not include detailed updated national disability data.
That leaves an incomplete picture of how the country’s disability landscape may have changed over the past decade.
What is clearer is the experience of people navigating institutions that were not designed with them in mind: a parliamentarian depending on colleagues to follow proceedings, a lecturer being questioned about his ability to teach, or children entering mainstream schools with limited specialist support.
Krubally knows that journey personally.
He now mentors young people, many of them visually impaired. One is Modou Lamin Dampha, who describes Krubally as someone who encourages him to keep pursuing his ambitions.
“He advises and encourages me to keep going, that things are possible,” Dampha says.
For Dampha, Krubally is more than a magistrate.
He is evidence that professional ambition does not have to end with disability.
Has the courtroom changed?
Back inside the Banjul Magistrates’ Court, the case continues.
Krubally listens as the proceedings unfold, using voices, memory, technology and experience to follow what is happening before him.
His career raises a harder question: how much has the system itself changed?
The judiciary was asked what accommodations are available to Krubally, what accessibility measures are in place for judicial officers and court users with disabilities, and what changes it has made since the Persons with Disabilities Act was passed.
It did not respond by the time of publication.
Krubally has spent a decade adapting to the demands of the courtroom.
Whether the institution around him has also adapted remains an open question.
Asked what he sees when he looks to the future, Krubally says it is not about the obstacles he has overcome.
“All I see is possibility.”

'You won't hear us coming': Police surveillance is ramping up across Australia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
05:16:59 UTC
14:16:59 KST

in brief
- WA Police has expanded its automated drone response program in Perth.
- Rights groups say better legal protections are needed to ensure individual privacy.
WA Police is expanding Australia's first automated Drone as First Responder (DFR) fleet, aiming to fill the sky with remote aircraft dispatched from Perth's CBD to emergency scenes within seconds.
While the police promote the rapid-response technology as a vital tool to catch criminals and protect officers, civil liberties advocates warn the rapid rollout risks allowing Australian aerial policing to outpace laws meant to protect individual privacy.
WA Police is also trialling artificial intelligence-assisted facial recognition cameras, and while its drone program is the most advanced in the country, similar programs are being used across Australia.
It's "pretty scary, dystopian stuff", Tom Sulston, head of policy at the digital human rights charity Digital Rights Watch, told SBS News about the direction policing technology is moving in Australia.
In announcing an extension of the drone program, WA Police commissioner Col Blanch said unmanned aircraft will not be patrolling or hovering passively.
News that makes sense
Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
"We don't do patrol, we simply do response," he told ABC News. "You ring 000, we come to help."
However, the commissioner also said that he hopes the program will expand: "The aim is to have as many as possible out there so we cover maximum distance throughout the state," he said.
WA Police Minister Reece Whitby went further, saying criminals "won't see us coming ... won't hear us coming, but we'll be there in the air watching your every move".
The DFR X program, which will initially operate across the southern Perth suburbs of Baldivis, Kwinana, and Rockingham, is the latest move by Australian police who are increasingly experimenting with drones.
Sulston said it is "inevitable" their use will increase among police forces and it's therefore essential Australia has the frameworks to ensure they are used responsibly.
"If you don't have good transparency legislation over the police to know what they're doing, then how are we holding them accountable?"
How does the WA police drone program work?
Many police forces across Australia have been using drones for years for operations from search and rescue to monitoring unfolding incidents. Their small size, rapid response, and low cost make them particularly convenient.
Unlike traditional approaches, where drones are launched manually by officers at the scene, WA's DFR X system houses drones in docking stations atop police stations, ready to launch remotely from a central command centre in Perth.
Flying "beyond visual line of sight", the drones are designed to arrive on the scene of a Triple Zero call in less than a minute, feeding high-quality video back to headquarters before officers can arrive.
Police drones spreading across Australia
In north-west NSW, the state's police force has been conducting its own controversial and high-profile automated drone trial in the regional centre of Moree.
Officers stationed more than 600km away in Sydney have been piloting the aircraft to respond to property crime, break-ins, and vehicle theft.
In August, the Minns government moved to expand the trial, saying police surveys reported strong community support. However, the operation has drawn criticism from national human rights organisations and legal advocates.
Australian Human Rights Commissioner Lorraine Finlay warned NSW should halt any wider rollout until the civil liberties impacts of automated aerial policing can be properly addressed.
"While existing surveillance laws regulate some aspects of these activities, they leave important questions about permissible uses, data handling, transparency and independent oversight unresolved," she said.
"Effective policing and human rights should never be treated as competing priorities. We should expect both."
Deploying automated drones over regional towns, particularly ones with a significant First Nations population like Moree, risks establishing a regime of persistent overhead surveillance of already over-policed demographics, civil rights groups say.
Can police drones film in your backyard?
The shift from police helicopters to manually operated drones and automated suburban fleets raises legal questions, as it's unclear what happens when drones film private property while travelling to a callout.
Under Australian common law, property owners have limited rights to the airspace above their land.
"Aeroplanes can fly overhead, helicopters can fly overhead, but they are constrained by no damage or nuisance being caused," Sulston said.
"If a police drone flies over your house and you want to go out and sunbathe in the garden, and it's videoing you doing that, that could count as a nuisance."
Modern aerial imaging makes distinctions about private space unclear, as Sulston said most people will be completely unaware they have been filmed from above.
"If you're in private from street level, but you're publicly viewable from 200m up, is that a private or a public place?" he said. "Those are largely legally untested questions.
"We have to have pre-existing transparency and reporting regimes so that we collectively can see what the police have been looking at and make a call on whether this is a reasonable thing for them to be doing."
What happens to police drone footage?
The operation of drones beyond line of sight is regulated by the Civil Aviation Safety Authority (CASA), which told SBS News it has "approved emergency service operators" for such use.
"CASA has worked closely with police and emergency service operators over many years to support the safe use of drones," a spokesperson said.
However, CASA does not regulate how drones are used or what footage they can collect, only their aviation safety.
Privacy protections are left to state and federal legislation, which often predates the use of autonomous robotics.
State police forces are largely exempt from the federal Privacy Act 1988 when carrying out law enforcement roles.
In WA, there is no comprehensive public-sector privacy regime and surveillance device laws are designed for much more primitive technology.
When asked about the retention of footage, WA Police told SBS News that video captured during drone flights is "retained in accordance with agency retention policy".
Asked what protections are in place to prevent private residences being recorded, SBS News was told that "all DFR X flights are in accordance with CASA Regulations and endorsed Operations Manual".
"This requires a pilot to navigate remotely whilst transiting to an incident, using the aircraft camera to scan to the horizon for aircraft and hazards.
"Only once a DFR X aircraft has arrived at the incident will the pilot use the camera to record information relating to the incident."

Israel’s election: Five key things to know
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
05:16:38 UTC
14:16:38 KST

Israel’s election: Five key things to know
High-stakes vote comes as Israel is mbroiled in multiple years-long conflicts, faces growing international criticism and grapples with deepening domestic polarisation.
Israelis will head to the polls on Tuesday for legislative elections.
The vote, the first since the Hamas-led attacks on Israel on October 7, 2023 and the subsequent genocidal war against Palestinians in the Gaza Strip, is being called one of the most important in its history.
It will determine the direction of Israel’s government as the country remains embroiled in multiple years-long conflicts, faces growing international criticism and grapples with deepening polarisation at home.
Here are five things to know about the upcoming election:
Which are the main parties and what do opinion polls suggest?
Any party clearing an electoral threshold of 3.25 percent enters parliament, whose term lasts four years.
There are two main blocs vying to lead the next government.
The first is the pro-Netanyahu coalition, led by Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s Likud party and joined by several far-right and ultra-Orthodox parties. These include United Torah Judaism (UTJ) and Shas – both conservative religious parties – and Otzma Yehudi and Religious Zionism-Zehut, led respectively by far-right ministers Itamar Ben-Gvir and Bezalel Smotrich.
The main opposition coalition comprises four Jewish-led opposition movements – the Yashar party, led by former Israeli military chief Gadi Eisenkot, the Democrats, led by former deputy military chief of staff Yair Golan, the Yisrael Beiteinu party, led by former Finance Minister Avigdor Lieberman and the Together alliance, led by former Prime Minister Naftali Bennett and joined by Knesset opposition leader Yair Lapid.
The latest opinion polls published before a ban on new surveys took effect on Friday showed that neither bloc was on course to secure a parliamentary majority of 61 seats.
A poll by public broadcaster KAN projected that the opposition alliance would win 52 of the Knesset’s 120 seats, compared with 50 for Netanyahu’s bloc, with the remaining seats going to unaffiliated parties, including the country’s two main Arab-majority political lists – Ra’am, also called the United Arab List, and the Joint List, an alliance of Hadash, Balad and Ta’al parties.
However, both the pro-Netanyahu and anti-Netanyahu blocs have effectively ruled out joining forces with the Arab-led parties for now.
The fractured landscape means Israeli parties could be in for tough post-election negotiations to cobble together a governing majority. If those efforts fail, Israel could end up with a minority government reliant on support from parties outside the governing coalition – or potentially head to another round of elections.
What are the key issues?
Israelis are grappling with a series of domestic and international crises this election cycle.
On the domestic front, there is growing demand for accountability for reported security failures, including those leading up to the October 2023 attacks, anger over the growing ultra-Orthodox community’s military exemption and concern over Netanyahu’s repeated efforts to push judicial reforms that critics say undermine Israel’s liberal democratic order.
“The secular and liberal opposition factions in Israel feel this election is the last chance to save Israeli democracy and restore the institutions that have eroded over Netanyahu’s successive terms,” Mairav Zonszein, an Israeli-American commentator who is a senior analyst at the International Crisis Group, told Al Jazeera.
A war-weary public is also weighing how Israel should proceed with its multiple military conflicts, with many voters seeking security and economic stability while remaining resistant to perceived concessions in Gaza, the occupied West Bank and Lebanon.
What makes this election so important?
It is Israel’s first election since the October 2023 attacks and comes amid a surge in far-right attitudes and growing divisions over the direction of the country.
“Strains of Israeli society had always been given to violence and right-wing rhetoric, but the trends that had always been present had accelerated under the current government,” prominent Israeli sociologist Yehouda Shenhav-Shahrabani told Al Jazeera.
The election also comes as Israel’s international standing has deteriorated, with a host of Israel’s allies sanctioning its illegal settlements in the occupied West Bank, and many other nations denouncing the country’s continued attacks in Gaza and Lebanon.
When Netanyahu addressed the United Nations General Assembly on September 24, dozens of envoys from around the world walked out, some jeering and booing.
The outcome of the upcoming vote could determine whether Israel’s next government maintains its approach to the international community or seeks to repair ties.
What does it mean for Netanyahu’s political future?
Netanyahu, Israel’s longest-serving prime minister who has led the country for more than 15 of the last 17 years, and a total of 19, faces growing scrutiny at home and abroad over alleged security failures leading up to the October 7 attack, as well as corruption charges he has been battling since 2019.
An electoral defeat would also leave Netanyahu more exposed to his ongoing corruption trial, which could ultimately result in a prison sentence if he is convicted.
A new government could also affect the prospects of a potential commission of inquiry into the October 2023 attacks and Netanyahu’s political standing as he faces an arrest warrant for war crimes issued by the International Criminal Court.
What about Palestinian citizens of Israel?
About 7.3 million Israeli citizens are eligible to vote in Tuesday’s election, including Palestinian citizens of Israel, who number about 1.2 million.
Meanwhile, roughly three million adult Palestinians in Gaza, the occupied West Bank and occupied East Jerusalem have no say in the government that controls their borders, movement and legal status.
Recent polling suggested that the turnout among the Palestinian citizens of Israel could reach 60 percent, with the majority of the votes expected to go the Arab lists, which are the principal representatives of Palestinian citizens of Israel. If turnout reaches 65 percent, these parties could potentially win as many as 15 seats in the Knesset. Campaigners are aiming for 70 percent turnout, which would be the highest in decades and raise the threshold, keeping smaller parties out of parliament.
Last month, Israel’s Central Elections Committee voted to bar the Joint List and Ra’am from the election.
Israel’s top court quickly reversed that decision, enabling the Arab parties to stay in the race. However, the court did force Balad leader Sami Abu Shehadeh to withdraw from the race over an article in which he described the October 7 attacks as “an important historical event”.
The role of Arab parties is going to be significant. Both major coalitions have ruled out joining forces with them for now, but without them, neither coalition might be able to form a majority.
Netanyahu has repeatedly sought to portray his opponents as potential partners of the Arab parties, claiming that an opposition-led government will seek their support and that only his Likud party can prevent this.
Joseph Mansour, a former aide to Israeli Knesset member Ayman Odeh, said politically alienating Arab parties is part of Netanyahu’s political strategy, which could allow him to remain in office as a caretaker prime minister if neither coalition forms a majority.
“If Palestinian-led party support becomes politically toxic and the opposition falls short of 61 seats, the deadlock itself becomes the latest win for Netanyahu,” wrote Mansour for the Arab Center Washington DC.

‘We built this land’: descendants of enslaved people are reclaiming their history across South Africa’s vineyards
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
05:00:23 UTC
14:00:23 KST

At Groot Constantia, the oldest wine farm in South Africa, the 450,000 visitors who pass through its gates annually can admire the picturesque vineyards sloping towards a bay ringed by mountains or enjoy a glass of sweet Grand Constance, reputed to have been Napoleon’s favourite wine.
Unusually among the region’s old vineyards, there is also a museum that includes the history of slavery, run by state body Iziko Museums. Panels display information about enslaved people – about 30 of whom lived on the estate at any given time from its founding in 1685 until slavery was abolished in 1834 by the British colonial government – detailing everything from their work to what they ate.
Two plaques list the names of people forcibly taken from Mozambique, Madagascar, India, Sri Lanka and Indonesia. “Today we pay tribute and acknowledge the enormous contribution of these men, women and children in the success of Groot Constantia and also acknowledge their oppression and suffering under slavery and their resilience and courage,” the plaques read.
“We have accepted that it’s part of our history and we are actually grateful for what they have done,” said Groot Constantia CEO, Jean Naudé. “It’s sad that it was built on that unsound foundation, but the foundation is there and the least we can do today is to build something proper on that foundation.”
Although there is no complete data, historians agree that only a handful of estates explicitly acknowledge their history of enslavement, in an industry that sold R36.3bn (£1.65bn) of wine last year. Groot Constantia is also unusual in having been owned by the South African government from 1885 to 1993, then transferred to a not-for-profit trust.
Jan van Riebeeck established a colony for the Dutch East India Company in what is now Cape Town in 1652, and the first enslaved people were brought there within a few years to work in houses and on farms. By the 19th century, the 21 most prominent wine industry families owned 3,557 enslaved people between them, according to Wayne Dooling, a School of Oriental and African Studies lecturer.
“The wine industry was very dependent on enslaved labour,” said Kate Ekama, a historian at Stellenbosch University. By the 1820s, according to her research, about 80% of “coerced” workers were enslaved, with the remainder dispossessed Indigenous people.
“People don’t want to sully their legacy,” Linda Mbeki, the Iziko Museums curator at Groot Constantia, said of the absence of slavery memorials from most historic wine farms. “To acknowledge slavery history; to acknowledge culpability, if not directly, comes with privilege and generational wealth.”
Nonetheless, Groot Constantia still faces criticism from unions and workers’ rights groups who draw a line from slavery, through colonialism and apartheid, to the present conditions of wine farm workers, many of whom are descended from enslaved people.
At least 10 families, mostly of former workers, have been evicted from the farm since July, according to the Trust for Community Outreach and Education (TCOE), an NGO, and the Commercial, Stevedoring, Agricultural and Allied Workers Union (CSAAWU).
“You may want to claim the history of being the oldest wine farm, but at the same time those that have given their labour and that have built the sector can be easily dispensed of,” said Mercia Andrews, a TCOE director.
Naudé said that evictions did not take place without a court order and referred to comments he made about previous evictions in 2024, when he said: “As a responsible and progressive employer, Groot Constantia upholds fairness and complies with all relevant laws at all times for all employees … ensuring all policies are implemented consistently and equitably.”
Rico Basson, CEO of South Africa Wine, an industry body, acknowledged that slavery had “left deep social and economic inequalities”.
“These are serious issues that cannot be separated from broader conversations about dignity, opportunity and fair treatment in the workplace. Acknowledging our history and improving the circumstances of those who contribute to our industry today are both important,” he said.
One farm that has tried to acknowledge its history and redress inequality is Solms-Delta, in Franschhoek, 40 miles east of Cape Town. “It’s not just some abstract historical principle,” said neuropsychology professor Mark Solms, who bought the estate in 2001. “You live in a big house on a farm with a whole lot of poor people, who are there as a direct result of that history and are impoverished as a direct result of that history.”
Nico Jansen is the third generation of his father’s family living on Solms-Delta, which was founded in 1690. When he was appointed as estate manager in 2001, he initially didn’t believe Solm’s promises to renovate their houses or raise wages above those of neighbouring farms.
“I wanted to exploit him as much as possible … so he can’t take the houses back to the old days, so if he wants to leave, then we are already in a better place,” said Jansen, who identifies his heritage as indigenous Khoikhoi.
In 2005, Solms helped the workers set up a trust and take out a loan to buy a neighbouring farm for themselves. From 2004 to 2016, the farm employed a historian, Tracey Randle, who carried out excavations, set up a history museum and helped the workers bring their musical traditions back to life.
However, the farm is not currently operating. According to Solms, in 2016 the government stepped in to take over the workers’ shares, but did not put in the promised financial contribution, pushing the indebted estate into a business rescue process.
A spokesperson for the department of rural development and land reform did not respond to a request for comment. A 2018 statement blamed Solms-Delta’s problems on “accumulated debt and poor management” at the time of the government takeover, adding: “The challenges that have arisen have forced the department to cease the continued funding of Solms-Delta in its present form.”
Tommy Hall, an American technology executive, has pledged to buy back the government’s shares for the workers and invest in the business. Negotiations with the government are ongoing, Solms and Jansen said, and they hope to reopen the farm and sell wine again in about a year.
Jansen noted that many other wine farms were evicting workers whose families had lived there for generations, often since the time of slavery. “We built this land with our blood and tears and sweat,” he said. “And now it’s being taken away.”

Could Europe’s autumn of discontent threaten the survival of the EU? | Catherine De Vries
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
05:00:23 UTC
14:00:23 KST

Europe is living through an autumn of unusual discontent. What protesters from Paris to Milan to Madrid share is a deepening anxiety about the future and a growing anger at the gap between what they expect from their governments and what they feel governments are delivering, whether the issue is unaffordable housing, stagnant wages, the spiralling cost of living or failing schools.
The electoral consequences of the failure to get a grip on this public anger are already with us. Spain goes to the polls next month in a snap election called after parliament voted down key housing reforms. France begins the process of electing a new president in April, while Poland, Italy and a string of smaller states will vote before the end of 2027. The stakes could not be higher.
At the same time, national leaders face mounting pressures from abroad. Issues such as Ukraine, uncertainty over US security guarantees and economic competition with China demand more European cooperation, even as national politics makes this increasingly difficult. Governments face popular demands to deliver security and prosperity, just as their capacity to do so independently is shrinking. This leaves Europe with a difficult question: how can countries whose leaders are increasingly struggling at home find the common ground needed to act together abroad?
If the EU did not exist, Europeans would have every reason to invent it. Together, its members form a market of 450 million people and an economy of almost €19tn, the third largest after the US and China. No individual EU country comes close to that weight on its own. Germany, the largest, has 84 million people and an economy about a sixth the size of the US’s. Twenty of the 27 member states have fewer than 12 million inhabitants, less than half of Shanghai’s. In a world of tariffs and export controls, it is scale that secures a seat at the table.
But this rationale for cooperation does not make the EU’s survival inevitable. This political project has often been declared on the brink of collapse; the most recent crises include Brexit, the pandemic and energy shocks. Yet it has proved remarkably durable, responding with improvised solutions that previously seemed impossible.
The very traits that infuriate Eurosceptics – slow decision-making, endless negotiations and messy compromises – are, counterintuitively, sources of strength for Europe. The dispersion of power between governments, parliaments, courts and EU institutions makes the system hard to capture and compromises tend to stick.
The EU’s staying power lies in its capacity to adapt despite disagreements, while helping countries achieve what is termed “effective sovereignty”. Nominal sovereignty is the right to decide alone, even when deciding alone – as the UK has discovered to its cost since it left the club supposedly to regain its sovereignty – changes little. Effective sovereignty is the capacity to shape outcomes on energy, trade, migration or defence that no European state can control by itself. And the EU has itself adapted: its fully paid-up members remain the core but non-members such as Norway and Switzerland participate on defence, security, energy and economic policy. The EU has an interest in bringing Britain back into closer cooperation too, even if not exactly as it looked pre-Brexit.
But the EU’s resilience should not be taken for granted. Negotiations over the next seven-year budget, worth almost €2tn, show just how hard it is to achieve consensus. While everyone agrees on the need for greater European security and economic competitiveness, countries can’t agree on who should foot the bill. France, for example, is pushing for new EU-wide taxes, which others resist.
Even so, growing domestic political instability does not necessarily mean there will be paralysis in Brussels. Quite the opposite – it creates an impetus to act. With France’s presidential election approaching, Emmanuel Macron has urged fellow leaders to strike a budget deal by Christmas, warning that political room for manoeuvre would shrink in the new year if Marine Le Pen succeeds him.
Le Pen no longer talks about taking France out of the euro or a Brexit-style referendum. But her platform would undermine the union from within, turning the EU into a “Europe of Nations” and threatening cuts to France’s contribution to the EU budget.
Whether political change comes through elections, protests or new compromises in Brussels, public discontent cannot simply be negotiated away. This brings us back to the streets. French, Italian and Spanish citizens want functioning public services, affordable housing, economic and national security, and a sense that they have some control over their futures.
Younger Europeans, in particular, face growing uncertainty about their economic prospects, from finding affordable housing to securing stable employment. So far, this pessimism has not translated into widespread rejection of the EU. Recent polling suggests that young Europeans remain among the EU’s strongest supporters, with 90% favouring greater unity among member states and 78% wanting the EU to have more resources to act.
This gives Europe an opportunity, but also a responsibility, to turn that support into tangible improvements in their lives. That is the real test in the years ahead. Decisions about defence, industrial policy and social protection will involve difficult trade-offs, and not everyone will benefit equally. But if European cooperation becomes better at preserving institutions than at responding to citizens’ concerns, the discontent now spilling on to the streets could increasingly turn against the EU itself. The EU has repeatedly shown that it can survive political crises. Now it must ensure that the people living through them can do more than merely get by.
- Catherine De Vries is professor of political science at IE University in Madrid. She is the co-author with Alexandros Kentikelenis of How Europe Survives

I saw a drone suddenly descend towards me. My heart started pounding and I thought, ‘Is this the end of my life?’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
05:00:22 UTC
14:00:22 KST

It was mid-April and after a month of deadly airstrikes across Lebanon, Israel agreed to a ceasefire. Much of the bombing had focused on southern Lebanon, where entire villages had been demolished. But with the truce, people were hopeful of being able to return to their homes or to see what remained.
Zeinab Faraj, a 21-year-old photojournalist, decided to join Amal Khalil, 42, a newspaper reporter in Lebanon, on a trip to an area in the south of the country to document the aftermath of war. The two had worked together on a number of assignments after Khalil had seen Faraj’s work on social media and contacted her.
“I expected it to be like every other time. Amal and I would go out, take some footage and then leave. I had absolutely no sense of fear. We could hear some gunfire and artillery, but as a videographer, you find those things important to document and capture,” says Faraj, who was freelancing alongside finishing her degree in radio and TV.
By the time they reached the village of al-Tiri on the afternoon of 22 April, Faraj began to look out the window and reminisce. She was born and grew up in the nearby city of Bint Jbeil. “My whole life revolved around this area. As we say, a fish suffocates when it’s taken out of water. That’s how we feel whenever we leave Bint Jbeil.”
Ahead of them was a car carrying Ali Nabil Bazzi, 27, a municipal official in Bint Jbeil, and Mohammed Hourani, 37, a friend of the mayor. They had met them by chance earlier in the day at Tebnine governmental hospital, which had become a gathering point because people considered it relatively safe and would base their movements from there. Bazzi was due to sign a marriage contract that evening, but was still keen to join the trip.
Faraj says she did not hear the missile coming, just the sound of Khalil screaming and then the sight of the car in front of them on fire. The two women got out of their car.
“I do not know how I managed to stay so calm. The only thing I could think was: if I come closer, I will be able to see Ali. Maybe I will be able to pull him out.”
Khalil kept repeating: “Oh God, they’re gone.” Slowly, Faraj began to understand what was going on. “I could see their bodies torn apart.”
Then the drones appeared.
“When the drones came, my heart started pounding in a terrifying way. The drone started coming very close to my face. I tried to cover my face, but whenever I did, it would fly back up. That was when I really felt the real danger.”
The drones flew low and close as Khalil and Faraj frantically made phone calls to emergency services who repeatedly assured them that help was on its way. Faraj says the assurances were “like an anaesthetic”, something that briefly numbed the reality that no one was rescuing them.
One of the paramedics on a call told them to get into their car and try to drive back up the road, as ambulances were being preventing from driving to where they were. But as they tried to get into the car, it was struck by a missile.
Both of them were thrown backwards, with Khalil wrapping her arms around Faraj. As the drone continued to circle overhead, Khalil said she hoped it would “think we were dead”.
With the nearby car engulfed in flames, they decided to take shelter in a nearby house. Khalil had visible injuries, with blood on her face, hand and leg. Faraj says she sent her sister a last message before her phone died: “There’s no hope left. Forgive me.”
Inside, they sat on a bathroom floor. Khalil was unable to move, so Faraj says she crawled to a position from where she could watch the road. Suddenly a drone descended towards her.
“It had been high up and suddenly it came down. The way it descended was terrifying. My heart stopped.” Soon after this, Faraj says she came back inside and began to feel tired and detached from what was happening. “I felt alone.”
Then came the sound of a missile falling. “I’ve never heard anything like it in my life. I’ve heard so many strikes and drones, but this was completely different. It was terrifying and Amal was screaming,” she says.
She does not remember what happened next, but when she opened her eyes an enormous weight was pressing down on her body. Everything was black and she could barely breathe. She was trapped underneath rubble. “I couldn’t bear the weight. It felt like something was pushing me down, crushing me. All I cared about was being able to breathe.”
Faraj says she then heard a voice and thought it was her father, but it was a paramedic who had managed to reach the scene of the attack. As he held her by the shoulders, Faraj says she instinctively clung to him and refused to let go. “I told him: ‘Don’t leave me. I’m afraid to stay alone.’” He stayed beside her while a second paramedic cleared the rubble.
As the sound of drones returned once more, the paramedics quickly pulled Faraj free as she screamed from the pain. At about the same time, Faraj says she heard a stun grenade dropped by the drone. As they drove away in the ambulance, she repeatedly mistook the sound of the vehicle for a drone. “They’re going to hit us. We’re not going to make it,” she says she kept repeating.
After they got to a hospital, Faraj says she started to ask about Khalil. At first the nurses tried to reassure her. But eventually, she says, they fell silent. “That’s when I knew she was gone.” Khalil is believed to have died about an hour before the paramedics had been allowed to return to the area again after rescuing Faraj.
The Israeli military justified their attack saying they had identified saboteurs violating the ceasefire. However, human rights groups called it a war crime. As Khalil and Faraj took refuge in the building the Israeli military received repeated messages urging them to allow a rescue operation. A week before the attack, an Israeli military spokesperson shared a video of Khalil published by her newspaper and described it as “terrorist media”. Khalil had also received death threats from Israeli numbers.
Today, as Faraj prepares to return to university, she still struggles to walk properly and has visible injuries to a hand. An injury to her face has affected the movement of one eyebrow; others are hidden by her clothes and hijab. Her limp is especially hard to bear. “I was always on the move. I lost that. Even climbing stairs can be hard,” she says.
At first she was in shock, she says, but now more symptoms are starting to appear. She wakes at night screaming and buries herself in the pillows as if a missile is going to strike. The sound of drones and warplanes put her on edge.
Returning to frontline journalism feels uncertain and she says she is repeatedly haunted by the image of Hourani lying on the ground after the first missile attack. “His head was turned towards me. His eyes open and looking at me. That is something I will never get out of my head.”

Labour urged to plug predicted £400m shortfall in overseas aid funding in 2027
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
05:00:22 UTC
14:00:22 KST

The UK is on course to miss its target of spending 0.3% of national income on international aid by an estimated £400m by the end of next year.
Calculations from the Center for Global Development (CGD) found the UK was on course for a large shortfall in promised official development assistance at the end of 2027.
The researchers said the central forecast from the Treasury’s comparison of independent experts implied UK aid would be £410m less than anticipated – at only 0.29% of national income.
However, they said it was “very plausible” that the shortfall would be £580m, at only 0.28% of national income. Even the most conservative forecast implies a £250m shortfall, according to the estimates.
Ian Mitchell, a senior fellow at the CGD and co-director of its Europe programme, described these as “material shortfalls in the spending power of UK aid”.
Making up a shortfall of even £400m would be enough to halve cuts to Africa that are likely to cost thousands of lives and mean the UK’s de facto exit from the south and east of the continent, he said.
The CGD attributed the shortfall to higher than expected inflation, which means national income will be higher than forecast at the spending review, and a 2025 policy change around the Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office (FCDO) budget.
The researchers called on ministers to consider allocating additional funds to international aid in this week’s budget, to avoid the embarrassment and criticism from missing a target.
The 0.3% spending target for 2027 is far below the 0.7% promised in Labour’s election manifesto, having been downgraded by Keir Starmer to boost spending on defence.
Fleur Anderson, a former minister who sits on the foreign affairs select committee, said she would like to see higher spending on development aid in the budget.
She said: “I’d like to see this government going further and reversing these cuts altogether in time, but at the very least we should be hitting the reduced target that was set.
“Falling short isn’t an abstract accounting issue. It means communities not having clean water, girls pulled out of school, vaccines that don’t get delivered, peace programmes in war zones cut.
“The upcoming budget presents real opportunity for the Treasury to address this and for the government to show that its words on Britain’s place in the world are matched by action.”
Charities have repeatedly said that the government’s deep aid cuts will hit children’s education and increase the risk of disease and death in some African countries.
The latest figures released by the FCDO in September showed that British aid cuts under Starmer’s government hit the world’s poorest countries the hardest, while higher-income countries’ share of aid increased. The data showed a 6.7% decrease in funding to the least-developed and low-income countries, amounting to cuts of £118m.
The UK’s overall official development assistance (ODA) budget in 2025 decreased to 0.44% of gross national income, compared with 0.5% in 2024, a drop of £987m.
The government has prioritised spending through multilateral agencies such as the World Bank’s development arm, the International Development Association, and the global vaccines initiative Gavi. It has also continued to fund humanitarian support.
The Conservative party and Reform UK have pledged to slash aid even further, from about £9bn a year to £1bn – a level that would leave the UK unable to cover existing contributions to the UN and World Bank.
An FCDO spokesperson said: “The publication of the FCDO multi-year ODA allocations in March 2026 set out our spending plans and priorities for the next three financial years based on GNI [gross national income] at the time of the 2025 spending review.
“Moving to a fixed budget reduces volatility and provides the necessary stability to deliver high-impact aid programmes.”

Roca releases innovative all-in-one Avant toilet
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
05:00:00 UTC
14:00:00 KST

Roca releases innovative all-in-one Avant toilet
Spanish bathroom brand Roca has rethought conventional toilet design with Avant, integrating the cistern within the toilet itself.
For the Avant toilet, Roca designed the cistern to sit within the bowl, removing the external cistern on its floor-standing model and the concealed cistern and flush plate on its wall-hung version.
Avant’s cistern uses flushing technology based on the Venturi effect. Here, fluid pressure drops when liquid is funnelled from a larger pipe section to a smaller one.
This creates a powerful suction in the tank, which is needed for the flush. As the components are concealed within the wall, this gives Avant a more minimalist appearance but also offers benefits in space, aesthetics, installation and maintenance.
The integrated aesthetic also makes bathrooms more adaptable and practical for different design needs and interiors.
“The removal of an external cistern or the flush plate further enhances the overall aesthetic of the bathroom, and its neutral, minimalist design blends seamlessly into any bathroom style, adding a touch of modernity,” said Roca.
Another innovative element is that the Avant is also powered without electricity, but if water pressure or flow is insufficient in a building, the Avant-E model is best suited – an electric version suitable for a wider range of plumbing systems.
The Avant also features dual-flush options, side-mounted flush buttons, a soft-close seat and cover and Roca Rimless Vortex. According to Roca, it meets the highest hygiene standards and operates with splash-free, low-consumption flushing, reducing water consumption.
The toilet is also covered in Supraglaze, a custom finish that mitigates the build-up of dirt, germs and residue, making cleaning simple and further increasing hygiene.
The result is an efficient, minimalist toilet ideal for compact spaces, easy to install and maintain.
“Avant not only brings a modern aesthetic to the bathroom, but it also reduces flush noise, providing a quieter, more comfortable experience than conventional toilets,” said Roca.
Founded in Spain in 1917, Roca now operates in 170 countries, with a special focus on sustainability and craftsmanship.
The company produces high-end, design-forward bathroom appliances, including everything from toilets to sinks, hardware and faucets.
It recently released modular bathroom furniture that can be adjusted to fit different scales and colourful taps in collaboration with designer Inma Bermúdez, in bright green, blue and yellow finishes.
To learn more about the Avant toilet, visit Roca’s website.
The photography is courtesy of Roca.

Drone reportedly strikes business center in Russia's Voronezh as fires break out across city
Editor's note: This is a developing story.
A drone reportedly struck a business center in the Russian city of Voronezh early on Oct. 26, as explosions and fires were reported across the city amid an ongoing drone attack, independent Russian media outlet ASTRA reported.
Footage published by ASTRA appears to show a drone exploding at the Chizhov Gallery business center, a 25-story building in central Voronezh.
Ukrainian monitoring channel Exilenova+ also published imagery of the reported attack.
ASTRA further reported fires in residential areas, having received eyewitness photographs and videos that identified locations near apartment buildings where explosions occurred.
Voronezh Oblast Governor Aleksandr Gusev confirmed that Russian air defenses responded to a drone attack over Voronezh and its surrounding areas on the morning of Oct. 26.
According to ASTRA, a drone threat was announced at approximately 3 a.m. local time, followed by a missile warning about two hours later.
Reports mentioned numerous explosions across the city and thick smoke rising from several locations. Some residents told ASTRA that they had not heard air raid sirens despite the ongoing attack.
The Kyiv Independent could not verify the extent of the damage or whether the explosions near residential buildings were caused by direct drone impacts or falling debris. There were no immediately confirmed reports of casualties.
Voronezh Oblast directly borders eastern Ukraine, with the regional capital located about 200 kilometers (nearly 120 miles) from the nearest Ukrainian-held territory in Kharkiv Oblast. The areas has repeatedly been targeted by Ukrainian long-range strikes against Russian military and industrial infrastructure.
On June 22, Ukrainian forces struck the Voronezh Semiconductor Plant, a facility producing electronic components used in Russian missile and air defense systems, according to Ukraine's General Staff.
