Jordan arrests three suspects in deadly church attack, state media says
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
05:56:31 CET
13:56:31 KST

By Yomna Ehab
Oct 26 (Reuters) - Jordanian security forces have arrested three suspects in connection with an attack on a church in the US-allied country that killed nine people, state television reported on Monday.
The attack, in which gunmen opened fire during a funeral at a Greek Orthodox church on Friday in the village of Hamoud in Karak governorate, about 120 km (75 miles) southwest of the capital Amman, also wounded 40 others. The shooting lasted several minutes, witnesses said.
Jordan’s Public Security Directorate said security forces located the three suspects early on Monday hiding in an abandoned house in Karak. The suspects refused to surrender and opened fire on security forces, who returned fire and arrested all three after they were wounded, the directorate said in a statement carried on state media.
No security personnel were injured, and a number of firearms and ammunition were found in the suspects’ possession after their arrest.
”Terrorism has no place among us,” the directorate said, adding that the suspects had met their “just fate”.
The Public Security Directorate did not identify the suspects’ affiliation or say whether they belonged to any militant group.
Jordanian authorities have said the attack was carried out by “extremist terrorists”, but it was too early to determine whether they had links to known groups inside or outside Jordan. There has been no claim of responsibility.
Interior Minister Mazen al-Faraya said on Monday authorities were reviewing the circumstances that led young people towards extremism and would hold accountable anyone found to have participated in the attack.
King Abdullah, a US partner in the fight against Islamist militant groups, has ordered security forces to respond with an “iron fist” to the rare attack on Jordan’s Christian minority.
Such violence is highly unusual in Jordan, a relatively stable state in the Middle East, though authorities say they have foiled several Islamist militant plots over the years.
(Reporting by Yomna Ehab, Additional reporting by Eman Abouhassira; Editing by Clarence Fernandez, Raju Gopalakrishnan and Michael Georgy)

Taiwan startup develops rapid gene sequencing test for infections
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
04:54:06 UTC
13:54:06 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Biotech startup Asia Pathogenomics has developed gene sequencing technology that can identify infectious pathogens in as little as 24 hours, CNA reported Monday.
The company, also known as APG, said a clinical study found its technology detected pathogens at more than three times the rate of conventional testing, helping doctors identify causes of infection and make treatment decisions faster. Since its founding in 2020, the company said it has helped clinicians diagnose and treat more than 10,000 patients with infections.
APG CEO Li Ting-huan (李定寰) said conventional tests require doctors to suspect a pathogen and test for possible causes one by one, while culture results can take days or weeks. Gene sequencing compares samples against thousands of pathogens at once, without requiring doctors to predict the cause in advance.
In a clinical study provided by APG, gene sequencing detected pathogens in 88% of patients with bloodstream infections, compared with 26% using conventional blood cultures. The Taiwan Society of Infectious Diseases incorporated gene sequencing into its clinical recommendations for identifying infectious pathogens in July last year.
APG was selected for the Industrial Development Administration’s Corporate Venture Capital Accelerates Innovation and Entrepreneurship Program this year, receiving about NT$19 million (US$580,000) in government-approved funding. TCI Co., Ltd. is its corporate venture capital partner, and the program aims to facilitate NT$200 million in investment.
The company plans to link sequencing results with clinical information using the health ministry’s data exchange standard and apply AI to help identify pathogens. It also plans to introduce a lower-cost test covering more than 100 common pathogens at prices 30% to 50% below those of existing tests, which cost NT$30,000 to NT$50,000 out of pocket.
Li estimated the annual market for tests related to severe infections could reach NT$1 billion. APG is expanding in Japan, where it plans to complete clinical validation within one to two years before seeking public health insurance coverage.

PROFILE - From prison to historic 4th term: Brazil's Lula extends extraordinary political career
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
04:51:32 UTC
13:51:32 KST

Brazilian President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva secured an unprecedented fourth presidential term Sunday, defeating challenger Flavio Bolsonaro in a closely contested runoff that marked another chapter in Latin America's largest country.
Lula won 51.78% of valid votes against 48.22% for Bolsonaro, according to Brazil's Superior Electoral Court (TSE), with 99.98% of polling stations counted.
The victory extends the political longevity of the 80-year-old leader, who rose from poverty to become Brazil's first working-class president and later returned to power after serving time in prison on corruption convictions that were subsequently annulled.
Lula, the candidate of the Workers' Party (PT), entered the runoff after finishing second in the Oct. 4 first round, receiving 45.16% of valid votes against 47.03% for Bolsonaro, a senator.
His comeback made him the first candidate since Brazil's return to democracy to win a presidential election after finishing second in the first round, adding another historic distinction to his political career.
Speaking after his victory in Sao Paulo, Lula pledged to govern for all Brazilians despite the country's political divisions.
"Nobody is obliged to like the elected president, but he was elected to govern for everyone," he said, emphasizing respect for the Constitution.
Lula’s reelection followed a campaign dominated by concerns over living costs, public security, corruption and the direction of Brazil's foreign relations, particularly its increasingly strained relationship with the US under President Donald Trump.
Born on Oct. 27, 1945 in the northeastern state of Pernambuco, Lula grew up in poverty before moving with his family to Sao Paulo, where he worked from an early age.
He received vocational training as a metalworker and lost a finger in an industrial accident, an experience that became part of his political identity as a representative of Brazil's working class.
Lula became involved in organized labor during the country's military dictatorship and rose to lead the metalworkers' union in Sao Bernardo do Campo, an industrial center outside Sao Paulo.
His leadership of major strikes in the late 1970s brought him national prominence. He helped establish the Workers' Party in 1980, combining trade union activists, leftist intellectuals and other groups opposed to military rule.
Elected to Congress in 1986, Lula made unsuccessful presidential bids in 1989, 1994 and 1998 before winning the presidency in 2002.
He took office in January 2003, promising to combat poverty while maintaining economic stability.
During his first two terms, which ended in 2010, Brazil benefited from rising commodity exports and economic growth, while social programs including Bolsa Familia provided financial assistance to millions of low-income households.
Poverty declined substantially, although his administration also faced corruption scandals involving senior officials and lawmakers.
Lula left office with high approval ratings and was succeeded by his political ally Dilma Rousseff, who was later impeached in 2016.
Lula's political career suffered a major setback during the sweeping Operation Car Wash corruption investigation, which implicated politicians and business executives in bribery and money laundering.
He was convicted on corruption and money laundering charges and imprisoned in April 2018, preventing him from contesting that year's presidential election.
He spent 580 days in prison before being released in November 2019.
In 2021, Brazil's Supreme Court annulled his convictions, ruling that the court which handled his cases lacked jurisdiction. The court also found that former judge Sergio Moro had been biased in one of the proceedings.
The decisions restored Lula's eligibility to seek public office.
He returned to the presidency after narrowly defeating incumbent Jair Bolsonaro in the 2022 election, winning approximately 50.9% of valid votes.
His inauguration in January 2023 was followed a week later by an assault on Congress, the Supreme Court and the presidential palace by Bolsonaro supporters seeking to overturn the election result.
During his third presidency, Lula prioritized poverty reduction, social spending, public investment and environmental protection while seeking to maintain fiscal stability.
His administration expanded social assistance programs and pursued measures to strengthen wages and employment, but concerns over living costs, government spending and violent crime weighed on his popularity.
The government also faced difficulties advancing legislation in a Congress where centrist and conservative parties held considerable influence.
For his fourth-term campaign, Lula promised to maintain Bolsa Familia, expand affordable housing and strengthen public health care and education.
His economic proposals included higher taxation of high incomes, continued infrastructure investment, support for domestic manufacturing and further increases in the minimum wage.
Lula also championed legislation to reduce the standard workweek from 44 to 40 hours without cutting wages, a constitutional amendment enacted on Oct. 16 that will be implemented gradually over 14 months.
Environmental protection remained another priority, with Lula pledging to eliminate deforestation by 2030 while supporting continued oil and gas development.
However, his victory does not guarantee control of Congress, where conservative parties strengthened their influence in the October elections.
The composition of the legislature could complicate his efforts to advance tax reforms, social spending, public security measures and environmental legislation, forcing his administration to negotiate with parties outside his political coalition.
Internationally, Lula has pursued closer cooperation with emerging economies through BRICS, strengthened relations with China and advocated a larger diplomatic role for Brazil.
He has criticized Israel's military operations in Gaza, supported Palestinian statehood and called for negotiated solutions to international conflicts.
His relationship with Washington frayed as Trump imposed tariffs on Brazilian goods and publicly supported former President Jair Bolsonaro, although Trump stopped short of formally endorsing Flavio Bolsonaro in the 2026 election.
Lula criticized what he viewed as US interference in Brazilian affairs, making national sovereignty a central theme of his reelection campaign.
His latest victory comes amid a broader shift to the right across Latin America, where conservative governments have taken power in several countries including Chile, Colombia and Peru, some seeking closer ties with Trump.
The result leaves Brazil among the region's largest governments maintaining an independent diplomatic approach toward Washington and seeking increased cooperation with the Global South.
Lula's new four-year term will begin on Jan. 5, 2027, extending his presidential career across nearly three decades.

How purchases of sanctioned Iranian jet fuel were disguised by Myanmar
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
04:41:20 UTC
13:41:20 KST

In December 2025, the US-sanctioned tanker Reef arrived in Myanmar waters with some 113,000 barrels of fuel backed by sham paperwork.
Myanmar-based energy broker Dynamic Wave ordered the shipment, agreeing in a sales contract inked with Thailand’s Tawan-Oil Trading to supposedly take delivery of a similar amount of South African diesel. But the $15.8 million agreement, which Reuters viewed, was a charade: there was no such trade between South Africa and Myanmar in 2025, according to data from the United Nations and Vortexa, a shipping and energy data provider.
In reality, Reef carried jet fuel from Iran to Myanmar, according to records of fuel shipments to Myanmar, as well as satellite images and analysis by SynMax Intelligence, which tracked the tanker’s journey from the Iranian port of Bandar Abbas to Southeast Asia.
The deception was needed because the US in 2023 imposed targeted sanctions on Myanmar’s jet-fuel industry. The US did so citing the deadly bombing campaign waged by the Southeast Asian country’s military on civilian targets as part of an effort to crush a rebel-led insurgency. All purchasers of Iranian oil and fuel are also exposed to sweeping American sanctions.
Details of how Myanmar disguised purchases of Iranian jet fuel, as well as the entities involved in the transactions, are reported here for the first time.
Myanmar’s military junta was involved in the ruse. Days before Reef arrived, Myanmar’s foreign exchange regulator told the client of Dynamic Wave that it would issue import documentation that labeled the delivery as diesel “instead of jet fuel,” according to a copy of the agency’s November 30 letter seen by Reuters. The document, which was provided to Reuters by the activist group Justice for Myanmar, did not explain the purpose of the mislabeling.
The letter from the regulator also authorized Dynamic Wave and its client, National Energy Prime Aviation Services Company, to pay Tawan for the shipment.
Neither Dynamic Wave nor its client, which is part-owned by Myanmar’s military-backed government, responded to questions about the fuel shipment.
Spokespeople for Myanmar’s military-backed government and foreign exchange regulator, as well as the Iranian foreign ministry, also did not return requests for comment.
Tehran was the Myanmar military’s primary supplier of jet fuel between October 2024 and December 2025, with much of the trade carried out by the tankers Reef – since renamed Maris – and Noble, a Reuters report revealed in January.
The scheme uncovered by Reuters underscores both the reach and limits of Washington’s power. The lengths taken to disguise the trade suggest US sanctions are biting. But Iranian jet fuel has continued to flow, earning Tehran valuable foreign currency and providing Myanmar with the means to conduct both commercial aviation and air raids.
The US Treasury did not respond to questions about jet-fuel shipments between Iran and Myanmar.
Jet fuel, airstrikes, and civilian casualties
Myanmar’s generals seized power in 2021 from the democratically elected government of Aung San Suu Kyi. The coup sparked a civil war, during which the military has killed thousands – including many civilians – in aerial assaults, the United Nations said in August.
Myanmar’s foreign ministry said in response to the UN allegations that the military “exercises maximum restraint to avoid civilian harm.”
Justice for Myanmar, which also shared the fuel sales contract with Reuters, published a report on Monday concluding that Myanmar’s junta was importing jet fuel mislabeled as diesel.
The organization, which supports further sanctions on Myanmar's jet fuel imports, said it obtained the documents from a junta-run server that was briefly publicly accessible.
Reuters found a dead link to one of the documents on the DuckDuckGo search engine, indicating it had once been hosted on that server. Delivery dates and fuel quantities in the documents also match Iranian jet fuel shipment records that were separately reviewed by the news agency.
Thai bank connection
The sales contract for Dynamic Wave's fuel shipment stipulated that the payment be transferred into Tawan’s account at Siam Commercial Bank (SCB), Thailand’s oldest bank.
Tawan was identified by UN experts in a 2024 report as a jet-fuel supplier to Myanmar’s military. The firm has not commented on those allegations.
SCB was described as a major facilitator of Myanmar military procurement in that report.
The bank said after the report’s release that it adheres to anti-money-laundering laws and that its Myanmar-related transactions were legitimate and not connected to the arms trade.
Reuters could not determine whether SCB was aware of the nature of Tawan’s business.
Thai regulators in 2024 ordered banks to closely scrutinize transactions involving Myanmar in order to comply with sanctions and anti-money-laundering laws.
SCB did not respond to repeated requests for comment about its commercial relationship with Tawan.
Tawan and the Bank of Thailand, which supervises the kingdom's financial industry, also did not respond to questions.
The December shipment was not the first time jet fuel arrived in Myanmar disguised as diesel.
Dynamic Wave in May 2025 agreed to buy from Tawan 202,000 barrels of what a second contract, also obtained from the junta server, described as South African diesel. The agreement stipulated that the diesel should arrive at Yangon within a month and that Dynamic Wave would pay $26 million into Tawan’s SCB account.
The invoice for that contract contained discrepancies suggesting the tanker actually contained jet fuel.
The density of the fuel listed in the document matched the specifications for jet fuel rather than diesel sold in Southeast Asia, according to Joshua Heyne, a jet-fuel expert at Washington State University, and data from Platts, the energy-industry information provider. In addition, the price of the fuel was more than 50% higher than a global diesel benchmark.
Noble called at Yangon on June 17 carrying just under 200,000 barrels of jet fuel earmarked for Dynamic Wave, shipment records show.
Like Reef's December shipment, Noble’s cargo was loaded at Iran’s Bandar Abbas according to SynMax’s analysis of satellite imagery. As it made its way to Myanmar’s commercial capital, Noble transmitted location signals that made it appear as though its destination was the port of Chittagong in Bangladesh, according to SynMax.
The manager of the Reef and Noble tankers did not respond to questions sent via its listed website.
Shipments of jet fuel between Iran and Myanmar have continued this year, Reuters reported in October, citing SynMax analysis and satellite imagery.

Jordanian security forces have arrested three suspects in connection with an attack on a church in the US-allied country that killed nine people, state television reported on Monday.
The attack, in which gunmen opened fire during a funeral at a Greek Orthodox church on Friday in the village of Hamoud in Karak governorate, about 120 km (75 miles) southwest of the capital Amman, also wounded 40 others. The shooting lasted several minutes, witnesses said.
Jordan's Public Security Directorate said security forces located the three suspects early on Monday hiding in an abandoned house in Karak. The suspects refused to surrender and opened fire on security forces, who returned fire and arrested all three after they were wounded, the directorate said in a statement carried on state media.

Authorities say attack was carried out by terrorists
Jordanian authorities have said the attack was carried out by "extremist terrorists," but it was too early to determine whether they had links to known groups inside or outside Jordan. There has been no claim of responsibility.
Interior Minister Mazen al-Faraya said on Monday authorities were reviewing the circumstances that led young people towards extremism and would hold accountable anyone found to have participated in the attack.
King Abdullah, a US partner in the fight against Islamist terror groups, has ordered security forces to respond with an "iron fist" to the rare attack on Jordan's Christian minority.
Such violence is highly unusual in Jordan, a relatively stable state in the Middle East, though authorities say they have foiled several Islamist militant plots over the years.

For Russia’s sanctions-busting A7 payment service, international transfers start with bags of cash at Moscow markets. At its peak, it processed at least 58 metric tons in a single month.
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
04:40:10 UTC
13:40:10 KST

For Russia’s sanctions-busting A7 payment service, international transfers start with bags of cash at Moscow markets. At its peak, it processed at least 58 metric tons in a single month.
What A7 is and how it became the largest player in the shadow payments market
Sanctions against Russian banks and payment systems, along with their disconnection from SWIFT after Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, gave rise to shadow intermediaries offering Russians cross-border money transfers. Many have offices in the capital’s Moscow City business district, the investigative outlet Proekt reported in spring 2026.
The largest is A7, a company owned by Moldovan businessman Ilan Shor, who was convicted of fraud and embezzlement in Moldova. Shor owns a controlling stake; the remaining 49% belongs to Russia’s state-owned Promsvyazbank (PSB). In late 2019, PSB officially became the designated bank for Russia’s Defense Ministry and defense industry.
The state development corporation VEB.RF, headed by Igor Shuvalov, “provides support” to A7. Proekt’s journalists suggest that Roman Abramovich may play “an important but secret role in the company.” A source in the cross-border payments business described Abramovich to Proekt as A7’s “protector and sponsor.” In the source’s view, Abramovich began working with Shor because he valued Shor’s ability to “devise financial schemes.” Abramovich’s representatives deny that he is involved in A7.
How Abramovich is connected to A7
According to Proekt, Shor’s first flight to Russia after a Moldovan court ordered his arrest in absentia was aboard Abramovich’s plane, suggesting that the two knew each other well.
Igor Shuvalov, the head of VEB.RF, the state corporation that “provides support” to A7, is a longtime acquaintance of Abramovich’s.
In 2024, A7 rented offices in Abramovich’s Belye Sady and Skolkovo Park business centers. Two A7 subsidiaries still occupy offices owned by Abramovich.
“Another indication of the oligarch’s involvement is the enormous financial support A7 receives from businessman Viktor Kharitonin, whom the press has long called ‘Abramovich’s protégé,’” Proekt reported.
A business partner of Abramovich’s, who spoke to Proekt on condition of anonymity, estimated that A7 handles about 15% of all cross-border transfers in Russia. The company puts its share even higher, at 19%. “No one else even comes close to A7,” a source working in the market told Proekt. The outlet’s other sources agreed that A7 is the largest player in the industry.
Proekt obtained a list of all of A7’s clients. They included at least 25 Russian companies already under U.S. and EU sanctions. Five manufacture or supply combat drones used by the Russian army in its war against Ukraine.
Other A7 clients include Arkady Rotenberg’s tour operator Biblioglobus, the online marketplace Wildberries, cigarette manufacturer International Tobacco Group, the Sunlight jewelry chain, and industrial companies including Leonid Mikhelson’s natural gas producer Arctic LNG 2, AAEM Turbine Technologies, and S7 Engineering.
In late October, journalists from the International Consortium of Investigative Journalists (ICIJ) expanded on Proekt’s investigation. After reviewing internal company documents and speaking with sources, they found that most payments entering A7’s network are funded by hundreds of metric tons of rubles in cash collected from individuals and companies at several Moscow wholesale and retail markets, including the largest, Sadovod.
Sadovod is known as a market where most transactions are conducted in cash, and many of its shop employees and owners are migrant workers from countries in the Commonwealth of Independent States. “Sadovod is simply a big client base,” a source familiar with the situation told ICIJ, explaining A7’s choice of location.
How the scheme works
Before 2022, intermediaries at Sadovod were already converting cash into ordinary bank transfers or into cryptocurrency, which most often went to China. Western sanctions later disrupted this system by cutting Russian companies off from SWIFT.
A7’s improved system allowed a group of brokers at Sadovod to keep operating. They now accept bags of cash brought in by vendors and count the money, according to the documents. A7’s records refer to these initial cash collection points as “departments”; there are at least eight.
The brokers then pack the rubles into numbered bags. The bags are loaded into vans along with customers’ payment orders and sent to an A7 payment processing center elsewhere in Moscow. About 50 cashiers work there, recording the cash in A7’s counting system. The cash is then delivered to Promsvyazbank, which places it in a vault and credits A7’s accounts.
A7 then uses its shell companies registered abroad. Intermediary companies in Kyrgyzstan buy cryptocurrency through Grinex, a crypto exchange linked to A7. By this point, the money is no longer identified as originating in Russia, thanks to Kyrgyzstan’s permissive policies on cryptocurrency transactions.
PSB provides the banking infrastructure for transferring money to Kyrgyzstan, along with loans and guarantees when needed. From Kyrgyzstan, the money goes to intermediary companies linked to A7 in third countries, most often in the Middle East and Southeast Asia. They convert the cryptocurrency into local currencies and send the money to the end recipient.
“By the time [an A7 payment] is received, nobody in the chain, from the U.S. clearing bank to the Chinese supplier, knows where it came from,” said illicit finance expert Zachary Tvarozna, who co-authored an investigation into A7 conducted with the British nonprofit Open Source Centre. “Washington essentially created a market for A7 [by restricting legitimate transactions] and then did nothing about it,” he concluded.
The risks this scheme poses to the global financial system
From November 2024 to July 2025, A7 processed at least 283 metric tons of rubles in cash worth more than $14 billion, ICIJ and Proekt reported. The journalists were unable to trace the cash’s origins, but it is clear that most of it went to China, as before.
A registry of A7 promissory notes that leaked online and was reviewed by ICIJ shows that A7’s cash deposits at PSB rose in 2025, reaching 195 billion rubles ($2.3 billion) a month by April and 250 billion rubles ($3.1 billion) in June. At its peak, A7 processed at least 58 metric tons of cash a month.
On October 1, 2026, the U.S. Treasury Department designated A7 a “significant transnational criminal organization.” This means U.S. financial institutions will no longer be able to process transfers involving A7’s “Sub-Agents” — foreign shell companies through which the network routes payments for clients in Russia.
A7 “uses a modern, multilayered system of controls” and “was established to ensure uninterrupted payments in the Russian market, which has been subjected to unlawful restrictive measures,” the company said in a press release issued after the Treasury Department’s announcement. “All clients are screened to identify risks and prevent us from serving individuals or organizations whose activities violate regulatory requirements,” the company insisted.
Just two years earlier, when it launched, A7 presented itself as a “sanctions-proof payment system.”
George Voloshin, a financial crime expert at the Association of Certified Anti-Money Laundering Specialists, told ICIJ that A7 “not only helps Russia circumvent Western sanctions and export controls” but “is also likely to facilitate cash-based money laundering by effectively legitimizing potential proceeds of crime.”
International intermediary banks and beneficiaries effectively become complicit in these activities even though they do not know where the money comes from. The reason lies in the cash itself, Voloshin added:
Cash is considered one of the highest-risk payment methods because it is anonymous, can move across borders, and is not tied to a specific person or company.
The entire scheme “depends on trusted intermediaries, established relationships and confidence that money will arrive,” said Ilya Shumanov, managing partner of TriTrace Investigations, a Russian company specializing in financial market due diligence. “Its international reach can be extensive, while outsiders have limited visibility into the underlying transactions.”
According to documents reviewed by ICIJ, A7 received 314 payment requests totaling $76 million from brokers working at Sadovod in late 2024. All of the money was intended for the Hong Kong export company Yiton Trading Ltd.
A7 representatives did not respond to ICIJ’s request for comment.

US appeals court sceptical of Trump’s lawsuit over California voter rolls
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
04:32:48 UTC
13:32:48 KST

US appeals court sceptical of Trump’s lawsuit over California voter rolls
Judge questions the Trump administration’s efforts to exert greater influence over elections process ahead of the upcoming midterm vote.
A United States appeals court has expressed doubt over the Department of Justice’s lawsuit against California, which seeks to force the state to throw out mail-in ballots it has deemed likely to go to noncitizens.
Circuit Judge Mark Bennett said on Sunday the three-judge panel would issue a decision as soon as possible, following a rare weekend oral argument.
But Bennett, an appointee of Republican President Donald Trump, voiced concern that the lawsuit would not hold up to scrutiny.
He pointed to the Elections Clause in the US Constitution, which allows states — not the federal government — to administer elections.
“It seems to me that you want us to issue an injunction that is entirely inconsistent with the law that the California legislature has adopted pursuant to the Elections Clause,” Bennett told Justice Department lawyer Matthew Donnelly. “How can we do that?”
The case is part of a larger effort under the right-wing Trump administration to crack down on alleged noncitizen voting ahead of the crucial November 3 midterm elections.
On October 15, less than three weeks before the midterm races, the Justice Department issued a complaint targeting California, a left-wing stronghold.
It asked the federal court system to set aside thousands of mail-in ballots that the government says were sent to “likely noncitizens”.
The lawsuit indicates the Trump administration sent California officials a list of 20,000 names it believes are not eligible to vote, based on citizenship.
Trump has often pushed the discredited claim that the Democratic Party is benefitting from widespread voting by noncitizens.
California has long been one of the targets of his election misinformation.
Earlier this year, Trump denounced the state’s primaries after right-wing candidates like Los Angeles mayoral hopeful Spencer Pratt felt short of his expectations.
“There’s BIG cheating by the Dumocrats in California,” he wrote on social media at the time.
He then announced that the state would be under investigation by the US Attorneys’ Office.
Trump’s efforts have caused alarm, with critics accusing him of seeking to dampen voter turnout through intimidation and confusion.
The midterms will decide which party controls the US Congress, as well as key state and local positions.
Polls, however, predict steep odds for Republican candidates, given Trump’s souring approval ratings and dissatisfaction with issues like the cost of living and the US-Israel war on Iran.
Voting rights advocates have warned that the Trump administration has not publicly revealed how it has compiled its list of noncitizen voters, and whistleblower reports have cast doubt on the accuracy of such lists.
In response to the October 15 lawsuit, California has countered that it has strong safeguards to prevent noncitizens from voting.
It also said the Justice Department’s claims are based on dubious data.
“This is a sad, desperate attempt by Trump to use his politicized Justice Department to try to suppress California voters just three weeks before Election Day,” California Governor Gavin Newsom said in a statement earlier this month.
“We will continue to carry out free and fair elections in the Golden State — and call out this authoritarian as he tries every play in the dictator’s playbook.”

Israel must listen to its friends, not dismiss their warnings - editorial
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
04:21:47 UTC
13:21:47 KST

When one of Israel’s most outspoken American supporters says two ministers are damaging the country’s standing, the government should listen. Bill Ackman’s Sunday warning about Itamar Ben-Gvir and Bezalel Smotrich deserves attention because it comes from someone who wants Israel to succeed, has defended it publicly, and has praised Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.
The Jewish-American billionaire investor made clear in his post on X/Twitter that Israelis must decide who becomes their prime minister. But from his vantage point in America, the national security minister and finance minister, respectively, have caused Israel “enormous reputational damage,” their statements and actions presented internationally as expressing the will of all Israelis.
A government without them, Ackman argued, would signal a new beginning, help restore credibility, improve relations with Democrats and Republicans, and increase the prospects of expanding the Abraham Accords, which normalized relations between Israel and several Arab states.
His warning should not be dismissed as another intervention by someone hostile to the government. Ackman has praised Netanyahu’s leadership since October 7 while identifying the two ministers as a serious liability. His criticism cannot credibly be reduced to opposition to Netanyahu or indifference to Israel’s security.
That makes it politically uncomfortable and valuable. It asks government supporters to consider whether loyalty to particular coalition partners serves the country they intend to defend.
US Ambassador Mike Huckabee offers another example. A longstanding supporter of Israel appointed by President Donald Trump, Huckabee told The Jerusalem Post in September: “I wish that they understood the damage they’re doing to the country they claim to love because it is not helpful.”
He was referring to violence against Palestinians in the West Bank, which he warned was damaging Israel’s reputation, including among Republicans. He also argued that condemning Palestinian violence while refusing to condemn Israeli violence would be hypocritical. His support for Israel did not prevent him from demanding accountability.
There is a moral obligation here, before any question of reputation. Violence and humiliating treatment deserve scrutiny because of the harm they inflict, regardless of the headlines they generate. Israel should demand standards of its representatives that it can defend openly before its citizens and its allies.
Recognizing that friendship doesn’t require silence when Israelis harm Israel’s interests.
These interventions differ in scope. Huckabee’s criticism of specific conduct is not an endorsement of Ackman’s proposed coalition arrangement. What connects them is the recognition that friendship does not require silence when Israelis damage Israel’s interests.
Jerusalem should be capable of hearing that distinction. Criticism must be judged on its merits, whoever delivers it. But when people who regularly defend this country describe the difficulties created by its ministers, their warnings deserve attention. They understand Israel’s arguments abroad because they have made those arguments themselves.
Nor can every damaging image be explained away as hostile coverage. Ministers hold public authority. Their words carry weight because of their offices, and the government cannot expect foreign audiences to treat them as private citizens whenever their conduct becomes embarrassing.
There are limits to Ackman’s prescription. Removing two ministers would not automatically restore Israel’s standing, resolve disagreements over the Palestinians, or secure additional normalization agreements.
Those outcomes require policy, diplomacy, and decisions by other governments. Changing ministers alone would not substitute for responsible policy and leadership.
The people entrusted with power nevertheless help define a government’s priorities and credibility. A prime minister who promises responsible leadership abroad must exercise it within his cabinet.
Coalition calculations cannot be the only measure of whether a partnership serves the national interest. That responsibility belongs to whoever forms the next government and chooses its senior ministers.
The test for any coalition should be whether it can protect the country while governing responsibly at home and maintaining credibility abroad. That requires leaders willing to confront damaging conduct among their allies, rather than dismiss every warning as disloyalty or leave accountability to those watching Israel from overseas.
Israel needs leadership that puts security, responsible government, and national cohesion first. Israelis alone will choose that leadership. They should do so with an honest accounting of the costs of political partnerships, including those identified by friends who remain committed to the country.
Listening to those friends is an act of responsibility. Their support should give their warnings weight, not excuse ignoring them.

Attackers kill nurse, injure health worker responding to DRC Ebola case
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
04:21:26 UTC
13:21:26 KST

Attackers kill nurse, injure health worker responding to DRC Ebola case
The attack in eastern DR Congo is the latest on health workers and responders to the deadly Ebola outbreak.
A nurse has been killed and another health worker severely injured after they were attacked while responding to an Ebola alert in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC), according to the World Health Organization.
It was the latest in a series of attacks on health workers and responders that authorities say is hampering efforts to slow the fastest-growing Ebola outbreak in the world.
The attack took place on Saturday in the town of Bafwasende in the DRC’s eastern Tshopo province, WHO Director-General Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus said in a post on X on Sunday.
“Everyone working to protect communities from this deadly disease must be able to work in dignity and safety. Healthcare must always be protected,” he said.
The WHO’s regional director for Africa, Dr Mohamed Yakub Janabi, also condemned the attack on X.
“Health is NOT a target,” he said. “Those responding to the Ebola outbreak must be protected. Misinformation and fear must never fuel violence.”
Local authorities have not yet commented on the attack or the suspects.
Widespread distrust
Data from the DRC’s Ministry of Health indicate that more than 9,800 cases, including more than 4,700 deaths, have been recorded since the start of the outbreak in May, making it the deadliest Ebola outbreak in the country’s history.
The government’s handling of the outbreak, combined with chronic corruption, has sown widespread distrust, with some even dismissing Ebola as a hoax.
Responders say scepticism about the disease among communities has complicated their efforts, including in remote areas and emerging hotspots already facing shortages of medical supplies and healthcare workers.
Last month, a DRC politician was beaten to death in North Kivu after publicly defending the government’s response to Ebola. He had called on the public to obey response measures, particularly social distancing and hand-washing, on a radio show.
In May, at the start of the outbreak, angry residents set alight two tents at health centres in two separate attacks in just one week.
Responders say some residents have held captive or threatened team members in designated health zones.
Spreading to other countries
The current outbreak has now been reported in four countries across eastern, central and western Africa, giving it the widest geographic spread of any Ebola outbreak on the continent to date.
On Sunday, Uganda’s Minister of Health Chris Baryomunsi announced that all citizens returning to the country with a history of travel to the DRC will be quarantined for 21 days.
Uganda says it is Ebola-free after declaring an end to its latest outbreak in July. But health experts remain on alert after two people who had recently passed through the country later tested positive in Kenya and Nigeria.
Ebola spreads through direct contact with the bodily fluids of infected people.
The strain responsible for the current outbreak, known as Bundibugyo, has no approved vaccine or specific treatment.
Symptoms can take up to 21 days to appear, according to the WHO. In an October 23 update, it urged stronger monitoring and cooperation across borders, while advising against restrictions on travel or trade with affected countries.

Xinhua Commentary: Raising the bar for CPC's self-governance
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
12:17:46 CST
13:17:46 KST

BEIJING, Oct. 26 (Xinhua) -- The Fifth Plenary Session of the 20th Communist Party of China (CPC) Central Committee has drawn close attention for its core agenda: strengthening full and rigorous Party self-governance, with a landmark document tabled for deliberation.
As China enters the 15th Five-Year Plan period (2026-2030), a critical stage in laying the groundwork for basically achieving socialist modernization by 2035, the CPC faces severe challenges: strengthening its governing capacity, staying connected with the people, guarding against complacency and resolutely combating corruption.
Only through strong Party leadership and unwavering commitment to full and rigorous self-governance can central leadership decisions be fully implemented and the country's long-term development stay on course.
For more than a decade, the Party has emphasized advancing this effort, calling for higher standards and more concrete measures to strengthen full and rigorous Party self-governance.
In the implementation of the major decisions and plans of the CPC Central Committee, there must be no resort to empty rhetoric. Words must be matched by deeds.
Oversight must be enhanced in a more targeted, precise and regular manner on applying the new development philosophy, promoting high-quality development, and accelerating the efforts to create a new development pattern, among other strategic imperatives. It should also target key tasks, including developing a modern industrial system and fostering new quality productive forces in line with local conditions.
More scientific and effective efforts are required to confine power to an institutional cage. It is essential to both refine institutional rules and regulations to close loopholes and strengthen safeguards, and ensure their effective implementation through rigorous enforcement and binding constraints.
Compliance brooks no privilege, and enforcement permits no exceptions. The Party has made clear that laws and regulations must be strictly enforced, serving as high-voltage lines that must not be touched.
The fight against corruption remains arduous and complex, demanding greater sobriety and resolve. This high-stake struggle cannot be lost and requires sustained and uncompromising pressure.
Few observers can doubt the resolve and intensity of the CPC's anti-corruption drive, as shown by years of consistent action targeting senior officials, grassroots misconduct, and cross-border corrupt fugitives alike. Beyond investigating individual cases, the drive combines institutional fixes and education campaigns to demonstrate that the Party's self-governance is sustained and systematic, not a flash in the pan. This approach targets root causes to ensure officials dare not, cannot and do not want to commit corruption.
For global investors and policymakers, this signals greater predictability. By steadily tackling these problems, China is also creating a more transparent environment for international cooperation. The "rigorousness" in official documents must be translated into a level playing field where merit and the rule of law prevail over connections and bribery. It is hardly surprising that many foreign observers said the CPC's ability to reform itself is a key factor in its success.
The message is clear: Party self-governance is a continuous endeavor, with no finish line, only new starting points. The CPC will continuously strengthen its capacity to serve the people better. ■

From Budapest to New York: Trump eyes ousted Hungarian PM Orbán for UN chief, report says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
04:13:39 UTC
13:13:39 KST

After 16 years in power and an election defeat, Viktor Orbán could be headed for a new position, this time in New York. The Trump administration is promoting the former Hungarian prime minister's candidacy for UN secretary-general and is even considering putting him forward as a joint candidate of the United States, Russia and China. The White House is weighing the possibility of handing leadership of the organization to a politician who spent years clashing with the international establishment.
According to The Wall Street Journal, U.S. officials have already approached Orbán and invited him to enter the race. He has expressed interest but has yet to make a decision.
The move would mark a significant development in the race to succeed António Guterres, whose term ends Dec. 31. A State Department official acknowledged that the idea initially sounded almost far-fetched, but said previous discussions with Russian and Chinese representatives suggested that both Moscow and Beijing might support Orbán. The administration has even begun counting votes. The official estimated that he could secure eight votes on the UN Security Council relatively easily, and possibly as many as 10 of the 15. A candidate needs at least nine votes and no veto from any of the five permanent members. The question would then be whether Britain and France would agree to his appointment. Both have traditionally been cautious about exercising their veto power, but either could block the move independently.
The unusual proposal reflects Trump's search for a conservative leader capable of confronting the international establishment, prompting his aides to approach Orbán directly. U.S. officials described him as "the dream candidate for MAGA conservatives," noting that, unlike candidates whose careers have largely unfolded in diplomatic circles, Orbán has extensive experience leading a country and confronting political opponents. According to a source familiar with the discussions, a possible announcement of his candidacy has been postponed until after the U.S. midterm elections in November, in part because Orbán is unwilling to enter the race without assurances that he can win.
Orbán, 63, is one of the most prominent figures on Europe's nationalist right. During his 16 consecutive years in power in Hungary, from 2010 to 2026, he pursued hard-line policies on immigration, civil society organizations and liberal institutions, repeatedly clashing with the European Union over judicial independence, press freedom and the rule of law. Critics accused him of undermining democratic institutions and tightening his grip on the political system and media. Orbán, however, portrayed himself as a defender of national sovereignty and conservative values against what he called liberal interference from Brussels. His close relationship with Russian President Vladimir Putin, even after Russia's invasion of Ukraine, drew fierce criticism across Europe, while he was also regarded as one of China's most prominent allies on the continent.
Orbán's time in power ended in a crushing defeat in April. His Fidesz party lost to Péter Magyar's Tisza party, which secured a two-thirds majority in parliament. Trump, who publicly endorsed Orbán during the election campaign, also sent Vice President JD Vance to Hungary to support his reelection bid. The effort failed, and Magyar was sworn in as prime minister in May. Orbán remained leader of Fidesz but found himself in opposition.
Orbán is well known in Israel. Throughout his years in power in Budapest, he cultivated close personal and political ties with Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and supported Israel during sensitive discussions within the European Union. He was among Netanyahu's closest European allies and, during the war in Gaza, backed him in his confrontation with the International Criminal Court. In April 2025, Orbán hosted Netanyahu in Budapest despite an arrest warrant issued against him by the court and announced that Hungary would withdraw from the institution. The court later ruled that Hungary had violated its obligations by failing to arrest Netanyahu, while Magyar's new government reversed the withdrawal plan. Orbán also blocked European sanctions for months against settlers and Israeli organizations accused of violence against Palestinians. Those sanctions were approved following the change of government. His appointment, if it materializes, would therefore carry particular significance for Israel, whose relationship with Guterres deteriorated sharply during the war.
The idea is not entirely new. In May, Hungarian media reported that figures in the MAGA movement were considering securing a senior UN position for Orbán, partly because of the possibility of diplomatic immunity amid threats of corruption investigations by the new government. In September, The Guardian reported that his name was being mentioned as a possible candidate for secretary-general, although there was no public indication that he intended to run. What is new now is the claim that the U.S. administration has approached him directly and is holding discussions based on the support it believes it can secure.
Meanwhile, the race itself remains deadlocked. None of the candidates has secured sufficient support in six rounds of secret, informal straw polls held by the Security Council. In the latest round, on Oct. 16, Costa Rica's Rebeca Grynspan received nine votes in favor but also six against, including two from permanent members with veto power. Grynspan, who is Jewish and the daughter of Holocaust survivors, is still considered the frontrunner. She serves as secretary-general of the United Nations Conference on Trade and Development and previously served as Costa Rica's vice president. She has close family ties to Israel, including a sister who lives in Mevaseret Zion and nephews who served in the IDF. Nevertheless, Republican officials in the United States have expressed reservations about her candidacy, arguing that she is too critical of Israel and too accommodating toward China. Other prominent candidates include Rafael Grossi of Argentina, director general of the International Atomic Energy Agency, and Carolyn Rodrigues Birkett of Guyana.
The lack of a clear outcome prompted the White House to seek new names beyond the existing field of candidates. According to a Politico report, the Trump administration does not want another veteran diplomat who would continue running the UN as it has been managed until now, but rather someone who would lead a sweeping transformation of an organization facing both budgetary and political crises. Among the names considered was Feridun Sinirlioğlu, Turkey's former foreign minister and secretary-general of the Organization for Security and Cooperation in Europe. He previously served as Turkey's ambassador to the UN and accused Israel of war crimes. Yet he was also the official who signed the 2016 reconciliation agreement with Israel on Turkey's behalf following the Mavi Marmara crisis.
Last week, a new official candidate entered the race: Lana Nusseibeh of the United Arab Emirates, the country's former ambassador to the UN. Nusseibeh, 48, comes from a longstanding Palestinian family in Jerusalem, speaks Hebrew and holds a master's degree in Israeli and Jewish Diaspora studies. Her grandfather, Anwar Nusseibeh, held talks with Moshe Dayan after the 1967 Six-Day War, while her uncle, Sari Nusseibeh, partnered with Ami Ayalon on an Israeli-Palestinian peace initiative. She condemned the Oct. 7 massacre and the abduction of Israelis by Hamas, but later criticized IDF operations in Gaza and opposed the annexation of territory in the West Bank. As ambassador, she played a central role in advancing a resolution to expand humanitarian aid to Gaza. Her candidacy has the backing of Gulf states but has drawn criticism over allegations that the UAE provided support to a militia implicated in atrocities in Sudan, allegations that Abu Dhabi denies. On Tuesday, Nusseibeh is scheduled to formally present her candidacy at a public UN hearing and answer questions from representatives of member states. The Security Council is expected to hold another round of straw polls afterward.

Incumbent President of Brazil Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva won in the second round of presidential elections and was re-elected as the president of the country for the fourth term, the Brazilian Superior Electoral Court (TSE) reported.
 
According to the TSE, after 97.69% of the ballots in the runoff election were counted, Lula da Silva secured 51.74% of the votes, while his opponent, a right-wing opposition candidate Senator Flavio Bolsonaro, was backed by 48.26% of the votes.
 
Lula da Silva is now the first politician in the present-day Brazilian history to win the presidential election after trailing in the first round of voting. The elected head of state will assume the office on January 1, 2027.
 
The voter turnout in the second round was reported at 80.79%, with 127,807,732 citizens participating in the voting. The rate of abstainers was reported at 19.21%, which corresponds to 30,081,854 voters. The share of blank ballots was at 1.12% (1,426,055 votes), while the share of invalid ballots was amounted to 2.12% (2,713,225 votes).

Lula's triumph bucks a regional trend of victories for right-of-center presidential candidates allied with Trump. It also means Latin America’s largest economy will likely continue defying Trump’s demands, despite the pressure of increased tariffs.
Brazil’s President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva pulled off a dramatic comeback on Sunday as he clinched a re-election victory with a lead of nearly 4.4 million votes over opponent Flávio Bolsonaro, giving him 51.8% of the total vote.
The 81-year-old leftist defied projections to win an unprecedented fourth term, staving off a conservative wave that has seen numerous South American countries, such as Argentina, Chile, Colombia, and Peru, all shift right, backed by US President Donald Trump.
Bolsonaro quickly refused to concede defeat and asked for the election results to be annulled after an evening of chaos at some polling places that followed a last-minute decision to extend voting by two hours.
The senator is the son of former far-right president Jair Bolsonaro, who is serving a 27-year jail term for attempting a coup after his loss to Lula in the country's last election in 2022.
Lula had requested the extension after he complained that buses had been pulled from circulation in various cities, barring citizens from voting.
Flavio Bolsonaro also requested an extension in some regions due to heavy rains, but he described the decision as "unacceptable" and a "dirty trick".
"It is impossible to recognise the results. I am going to request the annulment of these elections," he said in a brief speech in Brasília.
Comeback after first round defeat
After a first-round defeat, the left swung into action with massive rallies, declaring "Never Again Bolsonaro" and revamped their social media strategy.
No candidate who lost the first round has gone on to win the second in Brazil since 1989, the first direct election after the end of the country's military dictatorship.
The abstention rate decreased from the first round, falling from 21 percent to 19 percent.
"People went to vote because we managed to convince them that voting was very important for ensuring democracy in the country," Lula said in his first comments after the win.
Fireworks and vuvuzelas rang out in Rio de Janeiro, while thousands of people dressed in red, the color of Lula's Workers' Party, streamed into the streets of Sao Paulo to celebrate.
Lula's campaign leaned heavily on the theme of sovereignty in the face of commercial and diplomatic pressure from Trump's United States.
“Either the homeland remains free, or we die for Brazil,” he said. “This country will not accept being anyone’s backyard," he said as he addressed his supporters.
In Rio de Janeiro, cars beeped their horns and a woman dressed in red — the color of Lula supporters — shouted “You lost! Cry harder!” to four men in yellow and green sipping beers, Bolsonaro's signature colors. A huge roar echoed in the street as the result was confirmed.
Lula heads into a fourth term with almost half of the nation having rejected him, desperate for change.
He rose from poverty to become president in 2003 and was re-elected in 2006.
Lula made a dramatic return to office in 2022 elections after a corruption scandal saw him jailed for over 18 months. The charges were annulled on procedural grounds.
In his third term, Lula oversaw a drop in inflation and unemployment, and lifted millions out of hunger, but many voters felt gloomy about the high cost of living and crime.
Already one of the world's oldest leaders, Lula will be 85 by the end of his new term in 2030.

Gray zone tactics are defined as “an effort or series of efforts beyond steady-state deterrence and assurance that attempts to achieve one’s security objectives without resort to direct and sizable use of force.”

France works with 10 European nations to increase strength as nuclear deterrent - report
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
04:06:16 UTC
13:06:16 KST

France is working with 10 other European nations to expand its capacity as a nuclear weapons power on the continent and a deterrent to Russian aggression as Europe's faith in the US's commitment to its security wanes, the Wall Street Journal reported on Monday morning.
The 'forward deterrence' plan involves the creation of new infrastructure, communications, early-warning and intelligence-sharing links with France's allies as well as deployments of French nuclear-enabled Rafale jet fighters across Europe.
The UK, Germany, Poland, the Netherlands, Belgium, Finland, Norway, Sweden, and Denmark have all joined the project with varying degrees of involvement since French President Emmanuel Macron announced it in March.
“We don’t have any plans to put nuclear weapons on Finnish soil in peacetime. But we do have plans for creating a strategic dilemma for Russia,” said Finnish President Alexander Stubb.
“We felt it would be useful for our security to get information, to be involved in it. We don’t know where this is going to end, it’s probably a 10- to 15-years process.”
Instead of the countries all gathering together to work on the plan, France has been holding individual talks, leading European partner nations to constantly communicate with each other to compare what the French have told them, WSJ cited senior defense officials as saying.
European countries doubt US reliability
The plan comes as faith in the US's willingness to defend Europe wanes. Doubts over if the US would risk nuclear war over the defense of a European ally have increased as US President Donald Trump strikes energy deals with Russian President Vladimir Putin and puts increasing pressure on Ukraine, WSJ wrote.
France claims that the French program is more credible as the safety of European countries is of far more direct importance.
“There is one difference between France and the US–we share the same geography, we are part and parcel of the same continent, we have economic and sociological continuity with our neighbors writ large,” Chatel, Macron’s adviser, said at the Warsaw Security Conference.
In his speech announcing the initiative in March, Macron emphasized that France's vital interests were directly affected by its allies.
“Could we consider that the survival of our closest partners may be put at risk without it affecting our vital interests?” Macron said.
Norwegian Foreign Minister Espen Barth Eide said that the plan was not intended to "replace anything. It supplements the nuclear guarantees that were already there" from the US.
Program under French control
Macron also announced that France would resume making nuclear devices for the first time in decades and that the size of its stockpile would become confidential. Despite the involvement of other countries, the nuclear force will be entirely under French control, WSJ wrote.
“The French will let us participate in their nuclear deterrence as much as the Americans,” one government minister of another European nation said.
According to the WSJ report, the decision was made to make the forward deterrence strategy acceptable across the political spectrum, including to the far-right party of Marine LePen who is polling ahead in the race for the presidency in next spring's elections.

The FBI is investigating whether to pursue economic espionage charges against former OpenAI engineer Abdulrahman Alfozan, who was arrested earlier this month for allegedly planting a recording device in a restricted conference room at the artificial intelligence company, the Wall Street Journal reported Saturday.
Investigators are examining whether Alfozan obtained confidential information to offer to the Saudi government, even without being recruited to do so, according to a law enforcement official cited by the WSJ.
Authorities are also considering potential trade secret theft charges, although the investigation may not result in additional prosecution.
Alfozan, 35, a Saudi national and US permanent resident, allegedly concealed a small circuit board and microphone behind a television in a conference room primarily used by OpenAI executives.
He currently faces a federal charge of unlawfully intercepting communications, punishable by up to five years in prison. His next court appearance is scheduled for November 6.
His attorney, William Pernik, said he had received no indication that additional charges were being considered.
“We made it very clear that Mr. Alfozan will fight these charges and allegations in court, not in the press,” Pernik said.
Prosecutors examine ties to Saudi royal family
Prosecutors say Alfozan exchanged frequent WhatsApp messages with an unidentified member of the Saudi royal family in 2025 and 2026.
The royal family member allegedly sought to recruit him for a Saudi artificial intelligence initiative, writing, “Saudi needs you more then [sic] the US!”
Alfozan reportedly responded, “100,” but indicated he intended to remain at OpenAI until his company shares had vested.
Prosecutors said their last known exchange occurred on October 5, the same day Alfozan allegedly returned to the conference room to retrieve the recording device. OpenAI security personnel had already discovered and removed it, subsequently notifying the FBI.
Planned departure, Saudi consulate involvement raise concerns
Prosecutors also disclosed that Alfozan purchased one-way tickets to Saudi Arabia via Istanbul for himself, his wife, and their three-month-old son. He was arrested three days before their planned departure.
His wife and son subsequently traveled to Qatar on business-class tickets purchased by a Saudi military official, according to prosecutors.
Defense attorneys said the official was the wife's brother-in-law, that no military funds were used, and that Alfozan frequently booked one-way flights.
During an October 19 detention hearing, US Magistrate Judge Alex G. Tse questioned a letter from the Saudi Consulate in Los Angeles offering to cover Alfozan's entire bail bond.
“Even if I set it at $10 million?” the judge asked. “I find that problematic. Seems like a blank check. ‘We’re gonna pay whatever the court wants to make sure he gets out.’ ”
Alfozan was denied bail after the judge determined he posed a significant flight risk.
OpenAI is examining what information the recording device may have captured and whether the incident involved corporate espionage or potential state-sponsored intelligence gathering, according to a person familiar with the investigation.

US military says it helped Gulf states export 1.5 billion barrels of oil
US Central Command says more than 3,000 commercial vessels have transited the Strait of Hormuz with its support.
US military forces have helped Gulf countries export more than 1.5 billion barrels of oil since June, despite Iran’s efforts to control the critical waterway, according to US Central Command (COMMAND).
The US military command said on Sunday that more than 3,000 commercial vessels had transited the Strait of Hormuz with its support over the past six months.
It added that more than 95 percent of ships navigating the channel had sailed through safely in recent months despite Iranian threats, “clearly demonstrating that the United States and regional partners control the international waterway”.
CENTCOM announced the figures as Commander Admiral Brad Cooper made a visit to the region, during which he observed the “current operational environment” in the strait while flying in a US Army helicopter.
“We continue to stand shoulder to shoulder with our Gulf partners and the shipping industry,” Cooper said in a statement.
“This visit underscores our strong commitment to continued freedom of navigation through the Strait of Hormuz.”
Cooper said the primary transit routes for vessels in the strait were free of Iranian mines due to the “incredible efforts” of personnel who conduct mine clearance operations.
“We remain intensely focused on keeping commercial traffic flowing as we work with our teammates in the US interagency, Gulf Cooperation Council, and shipping industry,” he said.
Crude oil flows have largely returned to levels seen before the US and Israel launched their war on Iran in late February, despite the ongoing threat of attacks on commercial vessels by Iranian forces.
At least 16.5 million barrels of oil per day left the region in September, equal to the pre-war average, excluding Iran, according to market intelligence firm Kpler.
Analysts have attributed the rebound to a combination of offshore ship-to-ship transfers, US military escorts, and increased use of oil pipelines.
However, oil prices remain far higher than before the start of the war.
Brent crude futures stood at about $114.50 a barrel on Sunday, after easing about 2 percent from last week’s nearly six-month high.
Brent settled at $72.48 per barrel on February 27, the day before the US and Israel began strikes on Iran.

Top officials from the Mecca Pact countries, Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan, are set to meet Iranian officials in Tehran on Monday to discuss regional coordination, two people with knowledge of the matter said.
Saudi Arabia will be represented by Defense Minister Prince Khalid bin Salman, and Pakistan by army chief Field Marshal Asim Munir, the people said on condition of anonymity.
The Turkish head of intelligence will also join, one of the people said.
The Saudi government media office, Pakistan's military media wing, and Turkey's foreign ministry did not immediately respond to Reuters' requests for comment.
The planned talks would be the first high-level contact between Iran and all members of the three-nation bloc since Saudi Arabia came under escalating attacks from Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthis.
Munir visited Tehran last week, where he met Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian and other senior officials. During the visit, Iranian officials told him there would be no talks with Washington until Tehran's demands were met, according to Iranian media.
Pakistan has been a key intermediary between the United States and Iran. Earlier mediation efforts helped produce an interim peace agreement in June, but the deal quickly unraveled as fighting between Iran and the United States resumed weeks later.
Saudi Arabia intercepted another wave of missiles and drones on Sunday as fighting with the terror group continued unabated.
Ministers from the Mecca Pact countries held an emergency meeting in Riyadh earlier this month and agreed to ensure the "rapid deployment" of military forces and capabilities in Saudi Arabia.
The conflict has become an increasingly destabilizing element in the US-Israeli offensive against Iran, turning US ally Saudi Arabia into a pressure point in the wider war.
Joint Defense Agreement signed in August, has yet to be ratified by Turkey
Turkey, Pakistan and Saudi Arabia signed the Mecca Joint Defense Agreement in August, under which an armed attack on one member is considered an attack on all.
The agreement's first article says the parties shall use "all necessary means" to eliminate threats to one another's territorial integrity, sovereignty or internationally recognized borders, according to a text seen by Reuters.
Efforts by Turkey’s parliament to ratify the agreement began last week and are still underway, while Pakistan approved the pact last week.

North Korea-South Korea tensions high as letters lodged with UN, howitzer spotted
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
05:03:58 CET
13:03:58 KST

By Hongji Kim, Kyu-seok Shim and Joyce Lee
SEOUL, Oct 26 (Reuters) - Tensions between North Korea and South Korea are running high this week after Pyongyang sent a letter to the UN Security Council, repeating accusations that Seoul fabricated a September landmine incident, and after a North Korean howitzer was spotted close to the border.
A Reuters witness at an observatory in South Korea overlooking the heavily armed border on Monday confirmed the presence of a North Korean artillery piece positioned in clear view near the frontier.
South Korea’s Yonhap news agency on Sunday identified the weapon as a self-propelled 122-mm howitzer, saying its deployment near the border marked a rare public display of such artillery.
Reuters also observed three North Korean armored vehicles with their gun barrels pointed south, as well as about 20 to 30 North Korean soldiers carrying out fencing work inside the Demilitarised Zone (DMZ).
“It is highly unusual (for North Korea) to expose its self-propelled artillery so conspicuously,” said Lim Eul-chul, a professor at Kyungnam University in Seoul.
“By deliberately displaying it, North Korea is signalling through action, not words, that it intends to enforce its border policy through force rather than dialogue or negotiation.”
It is also warning South Korea to exercise caution about escalating border friction, with the intention to prevent an accidental clash, he added.
North Korean state media KCNA reported that in the letter sent on Sunday, the country’s UN representative said Seoul was using the landmine incident to depict Pyongyang’s border construction as a military incursion.
North Korea warned in the letter that violations of its sovereignty could trigger self-defence measures and that South Korea would be “wholly accountable for all the ensuing consequences.”
PHOTOS ALSO SHOW NORTH KOREAN DRILLS
The letter is a response to a South Korean letter to the Security Council last week, which said a September 21 blast in the DMZ was planted by North Korean troops and constituted a violation of the Korean War Armistice Agreement.
The UN Command, which oversees the DMZ, has said a North Korean mine across the line violated the armistice. Pyongyang has denied responsibility.
A spokesperson for South Korea’s Unification Ministry said on Monday that the North Korean letter appears to repeat North Korea’s existing position and seeks to justify its so-called border line marking work.
The ministry had no separate comment on the placement of the howitzer. Seoul has proposed dialogue with North Korea to defuse border tensions.
North Korea’s letter also repeated accusations that South Korea had opened fire on North Korean personnel, calling that a violation of the UN Charter, which bars the threat or use of force against another state’s territorial integrity.
Seoul has said its military issues warning broadcasts and fires warning shots to send North Korean soldiers back across the line when they cross the military demarcation line (MDL), which bisects the DMZ.
North Korean troops have been building tactical roads and fences and laying mines near the MDL in recent years.
The Yonhap report cited photographs taken from an observatory in the South Korean border city of Gimpo that appeared to show the howitzer as well as North Korean troops conducting drills on the coast of Kaepung county, about 1.5 km (1 mile) from the observatory.
In 2015, there was a similar incident in which South Korean troops were injured by North Korean mines. Then, Seoul resumed anti-North Korea loudspeaker broadcasts across the DMZ, triggering a military standoff. After North Korea expressed regret, the standoff ended with a high-level inter-Korean agreement.
(Reporting by Kyu-seok Shim and Joyce Lee; Editing by Bill Berkrot and Edwina Gibbs )
