Trump dials up Islamophobia against Abdul El-Sayed at Michigan Senate rally
Al Jazeera looks at the key takeaways from the US president’s campaign event in Michigan ahead of the midterm vote.
Port Huron, Michigan – United States President Donald Trump has sharpened his anti-Muslim attacks against Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed, going so far as to suggest that Christmas would be cancelled if the progressive doctor won.
Trump visited Michigan on Sunday to shore up support for Republican candidates in the Midwestern state ahead of the midterm elections on November 3.
But from his podium, he levelled unfounded allegations against El-Sayed, including calling him a “jihadist”.
“He would be the only senator that will have to go through a metal detector before he’s allowed to go into the Senate,” Trump said of El-Sayed.
“I want him to have a metal detector.”
The president, whose popularity has been slipping in part due to the US-Israel war on Iran, spoke for nearly two hours to hundreds of supporters.
His remarks largely focused on Michigan’s Senate election, which is one of only about seven toss-up races for the upper chamber of Congress.
El-Sayed faces Republican candidate Mike Rogers for the state’s open Senate seat, and the race is considered crucial for Republicans to retain control of the 100-member Senate.
If Rogers wins, he would flip a seat currently held by retiring Democratic Senator Gary Peters, leaving Democrats with the difficult task of flipping five other seats to regain control of the chamber.
Currently, Republicans have a 53-seat majority in the Senate. Only 35 Senate positions are up for election in 2026.
Here are five key takeaways from the Republican event.
Trump doubles down on anti-Muslim attacks
While Trump has repeatedly targeted El-Sayed’s Muslim identity in recent weeks, including by misrepresenting the Democrat’s name as “Mohammed”, the US president took his rhetoric to new heights on Sunday.
Throughout the speech, Trump returned to themes related to El-Sayed’s Muslim faith, falsely accusing the candidate of wanting to impose Islamic law in the US.
“So Abdul… also wants our country to go to Sharia law, and if he ever pulls that off, he should be the first one that’s tried. I’ll be a witness,” Trump said, apparently imagining El-Sayed being tried in a religious court.
Several times during the rally, some attendees blurted out “traitor” when El-Sayed’s name was mentioned.
“I’m here to keep a jihadist Muslim Brotherhood member from becoming a United States senator,” Trump said.
El-Sayed is a US-born citizen and former public health official who has pledged to uphold the Constitution. There is no evidence that he was ever a member of the Muslim Brotherhood or any foreign organisation.
Since Trump first ran for president during the 2016 election cycle, he has weaponised anti-Muslim bigotry for political gain.
In 2015, for instance – near the beginning of his first successful campaign – Trump said he would support “a total and complete shutdown of Muslims entering the United States”.
Less than two years later, Trump used the presidency to sign a short-lived executive order barring travel from multiple Muslim-majority countries, what became known as the “Muslim ban”.
In Sunday’s speech, Trump appealed once more to fears of Muslim immigration.
“If Abdul and the Democrats win, they will open the floodgates and invite hordes of jihadists to our shores, creating a nightmare of violence and terror until you cannot even have a Christmas,” Trump said.
El-Sayed has previously largely dismissed the anti-Muslim rhetoric against him as an attempt to create “distractions”, saying he is focused more on domestic issues, including lowering the cost of living and expanding access to healthcare.
Rogers embraces Trump
With Trump’s approval ratings plummeting, some Republican candidates in tight races have kept their distance from the president.
Rogers has previously called for an end to the Iran war and expressed reservations about Trump’s tariff campaign, urging an end to the trade war with Canada, which borders Michigan.
But Rogers attended Sunday’s rally and took the stage alongside Trump in a display of mutual support.
A survey by the research firm Marketing Resource Group suggested earlier this month that only 35 percent of voters in Michigan view Trump positively.
Rogers set the tone for the anti-Muslim attacks against El-Sayed earlier in the rally, also claiming the Democrat is connected to the Muslim Brotherhood, a political movement in Egypt designated as a “terrorist” group by the US this year.
As a congressman, however, Rogers voted in 2012 to continue US aid to Egypt under Muslim Brotherhood President Mohamed Morsi.
In Sunday’s speech, Rogers also tried to paint El-Sayed as part of the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA), but unlike other progressives, El-Sayed is not a member of the left-wing group.
“This DSA-affiliated candidate is also taking a lot of money from organizations that support the Muslim Brotherhood, Hamas and Hezbollah,” Rogers said, without offering evidence.
All three groups are designated as “terrorist” organisations in the US, making it illegal to provide any material support to them.
Trump unapologetic about Iran
On Sunday, the average price of a gallon (3.8 litres) of petrol in Michigan was $4.83, up from $2.91 before the start of the war on Iran.
Tehran has restricted passage through the Strait of Hormuz in response to the war, sending energy prices soaring.
Trump initially promised the conflict would only last four to six weeks.
But nearly eight months after the US and Israel launched the war on February 28, the conflict is showing no signs of concluding.
On Sunday, Trump said he has no regrets about the war.
“I made that decision, and I have no second guess,” Trump told the crowd.
He added that he thought petrol prices would have increased by much more than they had. He also defended his decision by referencing the threat of nuclear warfare.
“The number one state sponsor of terror is Iran by far, and we had to make sure they didn’t have a nuclear weapon,” Trump said.
Iran has denied seeking a nuclear weapon. It has long argued its uranium enrichment programme is for civilian energy production.
Before the war, Trump also argued that US strikes against Iran’s uranium enrichment facilities in June 2025 had completely “obliterated” the country’s nuclear programme.
‘We’re making a freaking fortune’
Despite the economic anxiety related to the cost of living and skyrocketing petrol prices, Trump bragged about the amount of profit US oil companies are making from the war.
Demand for energy products has increased globally in recent months, as supply chains tighten.
“Our country is making hundreds of billions of dollars because of what’s happened in the Middle East, because they’re coming to Texas, and they’re coming to Oklahoma, and they’re coming to Louisiana, and they’re taking that oil,” Trump said. “They’re making hundreds of billions of dollars.”
Trump added that his advisers asked him not to bring up this issue because “people are paying a little higher” for petrol and gas.
“I could just see the fake headline: ‘President Trump is talking about all the money they’re making while people are suffering at the pump.’ That’ll be the headline. I said, ‘I don’t give a damn. I’m going to say it. We’re making a freaking fortune,'” the US president said.
Trump can still mobilise Republican base
A line of Trump supporters stretched several blocks outside the rally on Sunday.
Attendees, dressed in Make America Great Again (MAGA) gear, filled the hockey arena where Trump spoke.
The crowd roared and laughed with Trump, with attendees frequently blurting out expressions of admiration for the president and insults against his opponents, especially El-Sayed.
Trump may appear politically on the back foot amid dwindling popularity and mounting anger over inflation and the Iran war.
But the president has highlighted his continued ability to mobilise his core MAGA base, often pointing to his crowd size as a metric for his success as a campaigner.
The audience remained engaged and seated throughout the speech on Sunday.
At one point, the address took a bizarre turn as the president spoke about the backside of Jon Husted, a Republican incumbent from Ohio competing in another tight Senate race.
“I looked at his a**, and I’ve never done that with a man before. Women? Yes. Men? No,” Trump said.
The US president also complimented the derriere of the rapper Nicki Minaj, one of his prominent supporters in attendance.
“By the way, I looked at one hell of a beautiful a** before: Nicki Minaj. That’s hard to miss,” Trump said.
The crowd cheered.

How Beijing’s Africa ambitions, financed by China’s mega banks, triggered a crisis in Zambia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
04:01:17 UTC
13:01:17 KST

As Kanangwa Newlove walked through her 10-acre farm just outside Lusaka, Zambia, one day in October 2025, she felt as if her dreams were withering away in front of her. The spinach, lettuce and mustard wilted in the heat. Tomatoes shriveled on their vines. She uprooted entire rows of organic vegetables — once sought-after by discerning customers, now rotting in the sun — and fed them to her pigs. “The crops that suffered the most without water were our mainstay,” she told a reporter for the International Consortium of Investigative Journalists. “There was nothing we could do. There was no water for the crops because there was no electricity.”
Every few days, she needed nearly 8,000 gallons of water from borehole pumps to keep her farm going. The pumps required a reliable supply of electricity, but since March 2024, Zambia’s rolling blackouts had left swathes of the country without power, turning everyday tasks into Herculean struggles. Sometimes she had only four hours of power a day.
The blackouts had a “cascading effect,” Newlove said. Without electricity she couldn’t refrigerate the few meager vegetables she could harvest. She stopped breeding and slaughtering animals. She was unable to sell to many of her regular customers, like local “mom and pop shops.” She had to drastically reduce the area she farmed and cut back on planting, and she couldn’t hire seasonal workers.
The rolling blackouts affecting Newlove’s farm were a result of “load shedding,” scheduled power cuts meant to reduce demand on the grid. ZESCO, the state-owned power company supplying almost all of Zambia’s energy needs, alerted its customers to the load shedding schedule, but these schedules weren’t consistent or reliable, Newlove told ICIJ, making it hard to plan how to maintain — or save — her crops. “One week you’d get a schedule from, say, morning to midday and you’d make a plan based on that,” she said. “Then, without prior notice, it would change.”
She couldn’t run a farm on four hours of electricity. For the first time since she’d started the farm over a decade earlier — a labor of love she launched while working for a social enterprise — she began to wonder if she’d need to shut it down. “Farmers are optimistic people until that is obliterated entirely by reality. … It’s a mammoth thing to fathom, that you’re going to kill a business that you’ve worked so hard for for so many years,” she said.
Newlove and other small-business owners across Zambia faced collapse amid a perfect storm in which environmental and economic shocks were exacerbated by the country’s deep-seated financial problems. Zambia — where roughly 60% of the population lives in poverty — is overwhelmingly dependent on hydropower, but a severe drought in 2024 left dams empty and forced ZESCO to ration electricity usage. While Zambia is drought-prone, ZESCO’s financial woes left it uniquely ill-prepared for the drought, the worst in decades.
The company was sinking financially. Among its biggest expenses was a long-term loan of nearly $285 million from the Industrial and Commercial Bank of China (ICBC) with tough repayment terms. The loan was signed more than a decade before, in 2011, and in the following years, ZESCO had taken on more and more debt from ICBC and other Chinese lenders. Beholden to Chinese creditors, the power utility mirrored Zambia, one of the world’s most indebted countries and the first in Africa to default on its sovereign debt during the COVID-19 pandemic. As the country’s largest state-owned company, ZESCO was a significant contributor to Zambia’s overall debt.
Now, newly revealed documents show how Chinese lenders, working with Chinese contractors in Zambia, piled loans onto the country and its ailing state-owned enterprises. When it came time for ZESCO to pay, ICBC adopted what analysts see as a hardball stance to recover debt from a struggling borrower.
These documents form part of China Capital, an ICIJ-led investigative collaboration with 23 media partners. Based on a trove of 4.8 million documents, including client dossiers, due diligence reports, loan agreements, meeting minutes and internal emails in English and Chinese, China Capital exposes the inner workings of ICBC’s U.K. subsidiary and London branch, and the crucial role ICBC London has played in advancing Chinese interests in Africa.
China Capital lays bare what experts describe as the bank’s muscular lending tactics, which burdened some of Africa’s most economically vulnerable states — claims the Chinese Embassy in Zambia denied. The project reveals the complex picture of Zambian debt arrangements and the role played by lenders such as ICBC, which presents itself as a commercial bank but acts as a foreign policy tool of the Chinese state, advancing Chinese strategic interests in resource-rich countries like Zambia.
Although China became a vital lender for Zambia and helped the country fill an enormous infrastructure gap, Chinese objectives were not always aligned with Zambia’s best interests. Chinese lenders like ICBC were willing to make onerous and high-risk loans to a country that could not afford them. Meanwhile, Chinese companies seeking infrastructure contracts urged Zambian state entities to take on new debt to fund those projects. Zambia’s government, eager for easily accessible credit to fund its infrastructure plans, needed little encouragement. These factors combined to push Zambia into a disastrous debt spiral in which it was unable to service its debt, followed by years of sluggish recovery.
A $285 million loan
Zambia’s economic outlook was positive in 2011, the year ZESCO signed its $285 million loan agreement with ICBC.
The country had emerged from successful debt relief programs involving the World Bank, the International Monetary Fund and other international lenders years before. Relatively debt-free, it began to focus on funding new infrastructure projects, such as power lines, highways, stadiums and airports. To do so, it turned to the international financial market. Between 2012 and 2015, Zambia issued three international bonds worth $3 billion to foreign investors chasing high yields in the developing world.
At the same time that Zambia was eagerly courting foreign infrastructure investment, China was rapidly expanding its interests in Africa. In 2013, Chinese President Xi Jinping announced China’s Belt and Road Initiative, a strategy to bolster the country’s connectivity with the rest of the world through infrastructure and development. Chinese companies were encouraged to invest abroad, accompanied by a surge in Chinese foreign lending. To poor, landlocked countries like Zambia, China portrayed itself as an alternative to Western funders, untainted by accusations of paternalism and willing to engage developing nations as equals. It offered fewer economic policy conditions on its loans than its Western counterparts, whose legacies were associated with painful economic reforms forced onto indebted African countries.
Chinese investors were also willing to go where others were not. For Western companies, Zambia came with a risk premium that drove up the cost of capital and meant that they would invest only if high returns made up for the perceived risk. Barbara Dutzler, an economist with Germany’s main development agency and head of the agency’s Good Financial Governance in Zambia program, told ICIJ that, with China, there was “an alignment between state and industry” and an overarching geostrategic plan. That meant China could direct investment where it wanted and fund projects that would not hold up in purely commercial terms.
Although it presents itself as a commercial bank, ICBC remains majority state-owned and is driven not only by the profit-maximizing interests of shareholders but also the political prerogatives of the party-state. Documents from China Capital show that ICBC bankers routinely weighed Chinese strategic policies like the Belt and Road Initiative when considering loan decisions around the world.
In response to written questions from ICIJ, the Chinese Embassy in Zambia denied that China pursues political interests through lending: “Strictly following market rules and international norms, China respects the will of all partner countries,” embassy officials said in a statement. “It never forces borrowing, presses for repayment, attaches political conditions to loan agreements, or seeks political interests.”
The bank’s $285 million loan to ZESCO gave it a foothold in Zambia alongside other Chinese lenders. At a July 2012 groundbreaking ceremony for the ZESCO electrification project that the loan was meant to fund, China’s Ambassador Zhou Yuxiao referred to several Chinese loans to Zambia that were either in effect or being sought.
For Zambia, Africa’s second-largest copper producer, these were years of high growth driven by the commodities boom and China’s demand for metal. The growth in Zambia’s gross domestic product averaged 7.4% in the decade from 2004 to 2014, 1.6 percentage points higher than the average for rapidly growing sub-Saharan Africa.
It was an optimistic time for Newlove, who began farming commercially in 2012. “When I started selling, the opportunities were quite astonishing,” she told ICIJ. What began as a small experiment to feed friends and family turned into a booming business: Soon she quit her day job to focus on her new venture, supplying organic fruit and vegetables to supermarkets and to an in-flight caterer serving major airlines at Lusaka’s international airport.
As Newlove’s business took off, so did Gerald Soko’s. In 2011, Soko rented a modest property to start a butchery in Mtendere Compound, a high-density neighborhood in the capital city where tiny, tin-roofed shops and kiosks cling to the dusty roadside. Business thrived, he recalled. The shop heaved with customers buying meat for their families or in bulk for the many local bars and restaurants. “Everything would sell,” he told ICIJ, yielding impressive profits for a small business.
For the poorest Zambians, however, the years of growth didn’t translate into productive jobs and improved livelihoods. Zambia’s Parliament acknowledged that growth skewed toward urban centers and mining, and did not address the structural weaknesses in the economy.
The Chinese-funded infrastructure projects, frequently awarded without competitive bids, were also often wasteful and led to inflated prices, fuelling debate in Parliament. Critics, including opposition-party members of Parliament, said such projects were often detached from development priorities and failed to boost the economy. That view is shared by Zambian financial analyst Trevor Hambayi, who cited the example of two “questionable” airport expansions at Lusaka and Ndola. “With infrastructure we needed to plan and see what was feasible within our budget,” he told ICIJ.
Newlove recalled “shoddy” roads and other infrastructure projects that were quickly rolled out across Lusaka before elections as showpieces for voters, and how those seemed to rapidly deteriorate and now need repair.
Some Zambian officials tried to slow the rate of borrowing, according to a former Finance Ministry official, but the finance minister at the time “was calling [that] fiscal conservatism,” saying that you have to borrow to develop. “Our reaction was that you can borrow,” but not without a plan, the former official told ICIJ.
Propelled by political interests, ZESCO played a key role in the country’s debt-funded infrastructure spree. A World Bank report determined that the power company’s management was “swayed by political decisions on investments.”
After Edgar Lungu became president in 2015, Zambia “ratcheted up borrowing” from China even further, wrote Deborah Brautigam, founding director of the China Africa Research Initiative (CARI) at Johns Hopkins University’s School of Advanced International Studies. Unfortunately for the country, the borrowing spree coincided with a steady drop in the price of Zambia’s main export: copper.
Rating agencies soon began sounding the alarm by downgrading Zambia’s sovereign rating. In September 2015, S&P Global noted subdued copper prices and foresaw a widening deficit and “increased external indebtedness.”
Once again, Zambia was straining under the weight of its loans, yet Chinese creditors continued to aggressively lend millions to the country, which had limited capacity to account for all the borrowing.
The Chinese Embassy in Zambia said that “in recent years, debt risks in developing countries have notably increased due to various external challenges,” which it said “some parties” have used to “spread false narratives” about China.
“Based on individual national development needs, China focuses its foreign investment and financing cooperation on infrastructure, energy and essential public sectors. These efforts help developing countries build independent and sustainable development capacity,” the embassy said.
Debt frenzy
In Zambia in the 2010s, Chinese companies seeking work on infrastructure projects helped drive the frenzied acquisition of government-backed loans to fund projects they then profited from. In the case of the $285 million ICBC loan, TBEA, a Chinese firm based in the Xinjiang region specializing in power transmission and renewable energy projects, arranged the financing for a project it was contracted by ZESCO to undertake: construct power transmission lines and infrastructure to supply electricity to Zambia’s Northern Province on the border of the Democratic Republic of Congo and Tanzania, and Eastern Province bordering Malawi and Mozambique.
This sort of “contractor-facilitated lending” became institutionalized in Zambia, where the government found it convenient to start “outsourcing much of the financing and mobilization process directly to Chinese contractor partnerships,” according to a paper by researcher Tianyi Wu at the Global China Initiative, part of Boston University’s Global Development Policy Center. Besides ICBC, the funds came from an array of Chinese financial institutions that were all too willing to provide high-risk loans. In these transactions, China benefited on both ends — as lender and contractor — while Zambia assumed the repayment obligation and much of the financial risk.
The former Finance Ministry official told ICIJ the ministry was supposed to oversee borrowing, but “a lot went on outside the Ministry of Finance, and they’d find out that ministry X had signed with Y company from China and organized the finance. It was a bit of a free-for-all for a while.”
Researchers at CARI found that among African countries with Chinese loans, Zambia had the highest number of lenders and the second-largest number of Chinese contractors securing Chinese-financed infrastructure projects. “Only Angola, which has borrowed four times as much from Chinese lenders, has more contractors, and even Angola has fewer Chinese lenders,” the researchers found.
Many analysts agree that widespread corruption, patronage and institutional weaknesses helped fuel Zambia’s debt spiral. The country’s bureaucracy lacked capacity to negotiate, evaluate and monitor its high levels of debt, while politicians had perverse incentives to keep accumulating it. The money was easily available for large infrastructure projects from which political elites could derive kickbacks and other illicit gains: “Patronage is part of the political landscape of Zambia,” the former Finance Ministry official said. “People were seeing things like roads being built, a new airport and stadium. Things were getting better in terms of infrastructure but at a very high price because of rent-seeking behavior.”
Chinese banks loan billions to Zambia
The debt-ridden African nation has used Chinese money to finance major infrastructure projects, defense contracts and more.
An IMF report noted both that “large public investment projects were often transformed into vehicles for political patronage and rent seeking opportunities,” and that “embedded governance weaknesses cannot be overestimated in accumulation of sovereign debt and the subsequent crisis.”
Zambia was an increasingly risky prospect, but ICBC continued expanding its interests there. In 2016 and 2017, ICBC committed to finance three other ZESCO electricity supply projects worth over $100 million and, together with the Export-Import Bank of China (known as China Eximbank), was a joint lender in the $1.5 billion syndicated loan for the 750 megawatt Kafue Gorge Lower Hydropower Station, for which ICBC claimed $15 million in management fees from ZESCO. It also signed six additional loans with the central government between 2016 and 2018, committing over $1 billion to a range of projects, from police and defense force housing to the construction of a hospital and an international airport, not all of which were fully implemented. Borrowing “mushroomed during the [Lungu] administration … to the degree they couldn’t even disburse the loans,” said Dutzler — a view backed by findings of Zambia’s auditor general. This led to growing alarm among Zambian opposition politicians and civil society groups over alleged Chinese predatory lending, as well as international headlines warning of “debt-trap diplomacy” — where a creditor country overloads a borrower with debt with the intention of extracting concessions.
Meanwhile, Gerald Soko, the butcher, was still trading on Zambia’s good years and focusing on expanding his business, unaware of an approaching debt cliff and the years of economic strain ahead.
ICBC comes knocking
The first installment of ZESCO’s $285 million loan was due to ICBC in June 2018: a $20 million payment. But by that time, the utility was in deep financial trouble. It was saddled with debt and in arrears to power suppliers, and ICBC had already committed hundreds of millions of dollars to another ZESCO power project involving TBEA just months before.
Internal ICBC records in the China Capital documents show that the bank flagged concerns about ZESCO’s financial health. They noted that reduced rainfall had curtailed electricity revenue and that the company was already struggling under the weight of the $1.5 billion syndicated loan commitment with China Eximbank and ICBC for the hydropower plant. ZESCO had just paid $15 million to ICBC in “management fees” for that loan, the documents note, which “put some pressure on the company’s financial situation.”
In a sign of ICBC’s hardball attitude to recovering its debt, the bank’s headquarters pressured ICBC London to transfer the $20 million from a reserve account it held on behalf of ZESCO. This caused a stir among ICBC London staffers when they “later learned that [head office] had pushed [the London branch] to make the payment” without the necessary documentation being in place, according to an internal ICBC report in the China Capital documents.
The reserve account was firmly under ICBC’s control. “What this means is a bank doesn’t have to go to a separate bank, to ask for permission to touch the money in the [debt service reserve account]. They’re like, ‘I am the escrow account bank, I can do whatever the hell I want with this money,’ ” said Bradley Parks, executive director of AidData, a research center at the College of William & Mary that has tracked Chinese lending globally.
Later that year, S&P Global again downgraded Zambia “on rising fiscal deficits and debt burden.” In its analysis, it referred to mounting government arrears “to contractors involved in the construction of new roads and to ZESCO … which had to import emergency power to replace a shortfall of hydro-generated power.” It added that “the increase in debt accumulation has also been accompanied by rising debt service payments.” Between 2014 and 2019 the government’s debt to foreign creditors as a percentage of GDP more than quadrupled.
The effects of a severely strained economy soon reached ordinary Zambians. Zambia’s currency, the kwacha, depreciated, inflation rose and high interest rates made borrowing more expensive. “This has affected the ordinary person, this high inflation without GDP growth that can match the cost of living,” said Hambayi, the Zambian financial analyst.
By 2019, ICBC was “reportedly reluctant” to release funds because Zambia began defaulting on payments to other creditors, according to an AidData analysis. In 2020, a ZESCO subsidiary defaulted on its repayment obligations for the $1.5 billion China Eximbank-ICBC hydropower loan. ZESCO — which had guaranteed higher electricity prices from independent power producers than the tariffs it charged its customers — was insolvent. So was the country, after defaulting on its debt that year. Lungu’s government had run out of options and had begun talks to restructure its debt.
Among other measures to recover costs and reduce losses, the government began cutting subsidies, including for fuel, and increasing electricity tariffs. The escalating cost of living weighed heavily on Soko’s butchery business. “People complain about the cost of electricity … and are struggling to make ends meet. They keep asking for meat on credit, the same people who used to spend a lot,” he said, before listing the many neighboring businesses that had closed in recent years: barbers and salons, welders and fast-food franchises.
Zambia’s weakened fiscal position left it extremely vulnerable to the worst drought in four decades, which began in 2023 and led to the relentless power cuts that nearly ended Newlove’s farming business. During the most intense period of cuts, as her crops wilted, she and the farm supervisor scrambled to find a generator and eventually found someone willing to rent them an old one. It sputtered and shook and looked as if it would give out, but it got her through those difficult days. The generator’s high costs ate into her dwindling margins, though, forcing Newlove to use her personal savings to keep the business afloat. “If we didn’t have that reserve of money, we would have sunk,” she told ICIJ.
The electricity crisis also dealt a heavy blow to Soko’s butchery, leaving fridgefuls of rotting meat. Customers stopped buying in bulk, worried that they would face the same problem, what Soko called the “trickle-down effects” of load shedding. He said that burglars twice took advantage of the darkness during power cuts to target his shop. To get through the worst of the outages, Soko too had to fork out for a generator he could barely afford to run. Sales from the butchery these days is less than half of what it was before load shedding, and he has had to put all his plans for expanding his business on hold. “There is no profit,” he told ICIJ.
Negotiating the future
After China became the world’s largest source of bilateral official lending to developing countries, it faced a critical test in Zambia: How would it negotiate to restructure an unusually complex mountain of debt? How would it work with other external creditors? As a creditor nation, China has not joined the Paris Club — an informal group of mostly high-income lending countries that coordinates solutions to heavily indebted developing countries — and Chinese creditor loan agreements often contain provisions to exclude them from collective debt-restructuring initiatives. Chinese lenders also had a reputation for taking a hard line and refusing to accept markdowns on their loans, “a core Chinese position,” said Dutzler of Good Financial Governance in Zambia. “They don’t give a haircut.” Among those at the negotiation table, she said, “China was the big unknown.”
The restructuring efforts began on shaky ground, as the negotiating parties — numerous governments and private lenders — went through back-and-forth talks that dragged on for years, hamstringing Zambia’s development and economic recovery.
The true scale of the country’s debt remained hidden, adding to the tension. Researchers at CARI, which had been tracking Chinese lending to Africa for almost a decade, found that “Zambia’s outstanding external debt to all Chinese financiers, official and commercial, was approximately $6.6 billion in August 2021.” This was nearly double the highest figure cited by the Zambian government. Part of the problem stemmed from the structure of the Chinese loans, which were cloaked in confidentiality clauses.
A study by AidData and three other international research organizations published in March 2021 found that Chinese loan contracts typically contained “unusual” and “far-reaching” confidentiality clauses imposed on borrowers that were not normally found in agreements from other lenders. It pointed to the link between such confidentiality conditions and “hidden debt [that] can impede debt restructuring.” At the time, holders of Zambia’s bonds were “refusing to proceed with debt renegotiation, citing insufficient information about China’s claims on the country.”
In an email to ICIJ, the Chinese Embassy in Zambia said that claims about opaque lending were “baseless” and that China’s “overseas financing cooperation is fully open and transparent.”
Ultimately, the worst fears of Chinese predatory lending, rumors of China seizing national assets like ZESCO and screaming international headlines about debt-trap diplomacy turned out to be alarmist. China agreed to co-chair Zambia’s official creditors’ committee alongside France, signaling a willingness to work with others rather than go it alone. An important milestone came in 2024, when Zambia reached agreements in principle to restructure debt with Chinese commercial lenders, including ICBC. As of 2026, debt-restructuring negotiations were largely concluded, with most of the talks occurring under the government of Lungu’s rival and successor, Hakainde Hichilema.
Ordinary Zambians still feel the lingering effects of years of intersecting crises that battered the economy and shifted perceptions of China’s role in Zambia. At Soko’s spartan butchery, the long queues of customers have been reduced to a trickle. Turnover is less than half of what it was, he said, leaning against a mostly empty display cabinet. Survey data shows that Zambians have grown increasingly skeptical of China’s role in their country. In 2014, 72% of those polled by Afrobarometer — an independent public opinion research network — viewed China’s economic and political influence positively. By 2022, that figure was down to 42%. China too was burnt by the debt troubles of developing nations; that’s part of the reason it has shifted focus to what it calls a “small and beautiful” approach to infrastructure projects, with smaller loans and shorter repayment windows.
Newlove, the farmer, told ICIJ that she feels she has made it out of the crisis intact. Her farm is fully operational, and she avoided laying off any of her 14 full-time staff. They have begun replanting on portions of the land they were forced to abandon. The chickens, goats, rabbits and pigs survived, and she has since crisis-proofed her farm with large solar panels that soak up energy from Zambia’s mostly sunny skies. But on the other side of Newlove’s stone perimeter wall is dry, dusty scrubland — a graveyard for failed farms and a constant reminder of her close brush with disaster. “Our resilience was tested,” she said. “I knew a lot of farmers who shut down or changed business. … They were very lucrative, and I thought, ‘We’re next.’ ”
Contributing reporters: Scilla Alecci, Denise Ajiri, Jelena Cosic and Delphine Reuter (ICIJ)

Yemen's Houthis say they targeted Riyadh airport and Saudi oil pipeline
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
03:59:04 UTC
12:59:04 KST

Muhammed Emin Canik and Gizem Nisa Demir
26 October 2026•Update: 26 October 2026
Yemen's Houthi group said early Monday that they targeted King Khalid International Airport in the Saudi capital Riyadh and launched attacks on pumping stations along the East-West crude oil pipeline.
Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree said on the US social media platform X that the group targeted the airport with a ballistic missile.
Saree also said the Houthis carried out drone attacks targeting crude oil pumping stations along the East-West Pipeline.
Saudi Arabia's Civil Defense Directorate earlier announced that the early warning system had issued a danger alert for Riyadh.
Major General Turki Al-Maliki, spokesman for the Saudi-led coalition, said a Houthi ballistic missile targeting Riyadh had been intercepted.
Yemen has been embroiled in a civil war since September 2014, when the Houthis seized control of the capital, Sanaa, and several provinces.
The East-West Pipeline is one of Saudi Arabia's most important crude oil transportation routes.
Operated by the state-owned oil giant Saudi Aramco, the pipeline stretches approximately 1,200 kilometers (745 miles) from the Abqaiq area in eastern Saudi Arabia to Yanbu on the Red Sea coast.
Located entirely within Saudi Arabia, it transports crude oil from production and processing facilities in the east to refineries and export terminals along the Red Sea.
The pipeline provides Saudi Arabia with an overland alternative for transporting oil to the Red Sea without relying on maritime shipments through the Strait of Hormuz.
The Saudi-led coalition has supported Yemen's internationally recognized government since March 2015.
Clashes between Yemeni government forces and the Houthis have intensified in recent months. The group has targeted Saudi Arabia with ballistic missiles and drones, accusing the kingdom of being responsible for attacks against it.

The election results have drawn reactions across the world with leftist global figures celebrating Lula’s victory.
Here’s how the world reacted:

US officials and politicians

Peruvian President Keiko Fujimori

Bolivian President Rodrigo Paz

Panamanian President Jose Raul Mulino

Jordan arrests three over Karak church attack, state TV says
- Jordanian security forces arrested three suspects over the Oct 23 church attack in Karak that killed nine people and wounded 40, state TV said.
- The suspects were found hiding in an abandoned house, refused to surrender, and exchanged fire with police before being wounded and detained.
- Authorities seized firearms and ammunition. No group has claimed responsibility, and officials have not confirmed any militant link.
AI generated
Jordanian security forces have arrested three suspects in connection with an attack on a church in the US-allied country that killed nine people, state television reported on Oct 26.
The Oct 23 attack during a funeral at a Greek Orthodox church in the village of Hamoud in Karak governorate, about 120km south-west of the capital Amman, also wounded 40 others. Witnesses said the shooting lasted several minutes.
Jordan’s Public Security Directorate said the suspects were located while hiding in an abandoned house in Karak.
They refused to surrender and attacked security forces, who returned fire and arrested all three after wounding them, the directorate said in a statement published on state media.
No security personnel were injured, and a number of firearms and ammunition were found in the suspects’ possession after their arrest.
“Terrorism has no place among us,” the directorate said, adding that the suspects had met their “just fate”.
Jordanian authorities have said the attack was carried out by “extremist terrorists”, but it was too early to determine whether they had links to known groups inside or outside Jordan. No group has claimed responsibility.
King Abdullah, a US partner in the fight against Islamist militant groups, has ordered security forces to respond with an “iron fist” to the rare attack on Jordan’s Christian minority.
Such violence is highly unusual in Jordan, a relatively stable state in the Middle East, though authorities say they have foiled several Islamist militant plots over the years.
The Public Security Directorate did not name the suspects or publicly identify possible affiliations with any Islamist militant groups.
Interior Minister Mazen al-Faraya said on Oct 26 the authorities were reviewing the circumstances that led young people towards extremism and would hold accountable anyone found to have participated in the attack. REUTERS

Tarek Chouiref
26 October 2026•Update: 26 October 2026
Israeli forces continued bulldozing farmland in southern Syria on Sunday to extend a military barrier that Damascus has condemned as a violation of the 1974 disengagement agreement, the official SANA news agency reported.
The work west of al-Hanout Farm in southern Quneitra province involves building an earth berm across privately owned agricultural land as part of the “Sufa 53” fortification project, according to the agency.
Residents fear the work will affect extensive farmland west of the berm, SANA said.
On Oct. 18, Israeli forces bulldozed around 13 dunams (1.3 hectares) of olive groves in al-Hanout, near Saida village, and prevented farmers from reaching their remaining fields to harvest olives, the agency reported.
Syria’s Foreign Ministry has called for the project to stop, describing it as a breach of the disengagement agreement and international resolutions.
Sufa 53 comprises a military road, trenches and earth berms. Israel began construction in mid-2022 near Hadr in northern Quneitra before extending the project south through the province along the separation line with the occupied Syrian Golan Heights.
Separately, Israeli troops entered northern Quneitra on Sunday and set up a temporary checkpoint on the road between Jubata al-Khashab and Ain al-Bayda, SANA said.
The force, comprising several military vehicles, stopped and searched passersby before withdrawing. Israeli forces carried out a similar incursion near Jubata al-Khashab on Saturday, according to the agency.
Since the fall of Bashar al-Assad’s regime in December 2024, Israel has carried out repeated incursions into southern Syria after declaring the 1974 disengagement agreement void and occupying the demilitarized buffer zone.

Probiotics may help protect against early signs of Alzheimer’s
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
03:39:41 UTC
12:39:41 KST

Probiotics may help protect against early signs of Alzheimer’s
A daily probiotic supplement improved some cognitive test scores and lowered a blood marker linked to Alzheimer’s disease in older adults with early cognitive impairment, according to a clinical trial published in the Journal of Alzheimer’s Disease, Qazinform News Agency correspondent reports, citing Science Alert.
The 24-week trial involved 87 participants in South Korea. Researchers compared a daily probiotic supplement with a placebo, without telling participants or researchers who received which treatment.
The probiotic group showed a significant reduction in blood levels of pTau181, a marker associated with Alzheimer’s-related changes in the brain. The group also showed improvements in some cognitive tests, including tasks involving visual memory and the ability to understand spatial relationships.
The supplement, called KL-P301, contained 3 bacterial strains. Participants took it daily for 6 months, either as a powder or mixed with water.
The findings suggest that probiotics could help address some early changes associated with Alzheimer’s disease. However, the researchers stressed that the results remain preliminary and do not prove that probiotics reduce harmful tau protein buildup in the brain.
The study also examined signs of inflammation. Most inflammatory markers changed only slightly, although levels of one marker, IL-1β, fell more in the probiotic group than in the placebo group.
Researchers believe that gut bacteria may influence brain health through the body's immune system and inflammatory processes. However, scientists still do not fully understand how probiotics affect the brain or whether they can restore a healthy balance of gut bacteria.
The trial builds on earlier research linking probiotics to changes in blood markers associated with brain health. However, the researchers said larger and longer studies are needed to confirm the benefits and determine whether they last.
Earlier, Qazinform News Agency reported that Saudi Arabia sent biological samples into space to study Alzheimer’s disease.

Three-game Bledisloe Cup series looms as new deal struck

Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26

The Wallabies will play New Zealand at the MCG in both 2027 and 2029 under a deal between Rugby Australia and the Victorian government.
There is no confirmation that the Bledisloe Cup will permanently expand to a three-game series, but the Test in 2029 will be an additional game in the series.
Next year's MCG Test in July will come ahead of the Rugby World Cup, where Australia and New Zealand will also meet in the group stage.
The Wallabies are set to play two Bledisloe Cup Tests at the MCG in a matter of years, fuelling hopes that one of rugby union's biggest rivalries could be permanently returning to a three-game series.
Rugby Australia struck a multi-year deal with the Victorian government which secures Melbourne to host the Wallabies and New Zealand in the Rugby Championship in 2027 and an additional Bledisloe Cup Test in 2029.
It comes as Lang Park in Brisbane is set to stage the first Anzac Day Bledisloe Cup Test next April, which sets up a three-match series between the bitter rivals for the first time since 2021.
Whether a three-game series would persist beyond next year has been a hot question exercising pundits.
But Monday's announcement of an additional Test in Melbourne in 2029 will very much boost optimism that a permanent three-game Bledisloe Cup series could return.
That is because Brisbane has also secured the rights for the 2029 Anzac Day Test along with the 2031 instalment.
RA officials were coy on whether the announcement was a signal for a return to full-time three-Test series, and were unsure if 2028 would be similar to 2027 considering no Anzac Day Test has been announced.
An extra Bledisloe Cup Test would favour the Wallabies, who haven't held the trophy since 2002 and have been unable to win both Tests since it became a two-game duel in 2022.
In 2026, they were utterly humiliated by the All Blacks, conceding a mammoth 93 points across the two games, which dealt coach Les Kiss a harsh reality check ahead of next year's home Rugby World Cup.
Regardless of the three-Test speculation, having a Bledisloe Cup Test at the MCG next July is set to be a stellar moment for the sport in Australia as it ramps up preparations for the World Cup.
The Wallabies last played the All Blacks at the MCG in 2023, where a crowd of 83,944 filled the historic ground, which was the largest rugby attendance in more than 20 years at the time.
Last year, 90,307 watched the Australians' second Test against the British & Irish Lions, breaking the Lions' all-time crowd record.
"The Melbourne Cricket Ground is one of the world's great stadiums — and a jewel in Australia's sporting crown — and the Wallabies are proud to be hosting the All Blacks at the iconic venue in 2027," RA chief executive Phil Waugh said.
"The Wallabies and All Blacks have played only four previous Test matches at the MCG, and this Bledisloe Cup encounter will mark 30 years since both teams took to the hallowed turf for the first time.
"The Wallabies and All Blacks have won two Tests apiece at the 'G and another enthralling contest awaits next year."
Australia will also meet the All Blacks at least one more time in 2027 when they face off in their second Pool A match of the Rugby World Cup at Sydney's Olympic stadium.

Lula vows to govern for all Brazilians after historic reelection victory
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
03:34:53 UTC
12:34:53 KST

Gizem Nisa Demir
26 October 2026•Update: 26 October 2026
Brazilian President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva pledged to govern for all Brazilians, bolster the country’s international standing and advance an ambitious climate agenda after securing reelection late Sunday.
"No one is required to like the president-elect, but he must govern for everyone," Lula said as he addressed supporters, expressing gratitude to the Brazilian people and promising to respect citizens regardless of their political allegiances.
He also criticized his opponent Flavio Bolsonaro’s political camp, declaring "this was a defeat for denialism and lies."
Promising an ambitious agenda for his next term, Lula said: "I want to make a commitment: I will deliver the best term any president has ever served. I will dedicate myself 24 hours a day to making this the country that everyone dreams of."
He also emphasized national sovereignty, saying "in this election, we defeated the interference that was coming from the outside in."
"This country will not accept being anyone's backyard," he added.
Outlining his vision for Brazil's place in the world, Lula said the country should play a central role in international affairs and lead by example on climate policy.
"We want to be a central country, not a peripheral one. We are going to show the world how climate policies are handled in this country," he said.
Lula's victory marked a historic comeback after he finished second in the Oct. 4 first round, when Bolsonaro led with 47.03% of valid votes against Lula's 45.16%.
Lula became the first candidate in Brazil's democratic history to finish second in the first round and win the presidency in the runoff, according to Brazil's Chamber of Deputies.
His campaign mobilized supporters through street rallies and social media.
The victory gives Lula a fourth, nonconsecutive presidential term following his wins in 2002, 2006 and 2022. He is the first Brazilian president elected to four terms by popular vote, according to the G1 news portal. His new term is scheduled to begin on Jan. 5, 2027.
The runoff recorded an abstention rate of 19.22%, down from 21.08% in the first round, according to reported figures from Brazil's Superior Electoral Court. Blank ballots accounted for approximately 1.12% of ballots cast and null ballots for 2.12%, bringing their combined share to 3.24%.
Lula's next administration is expected to face congressional opposition and pressure to balance public finances while expanding social programs.

Visitors look at exhibits themed on Greenwich Mean Time at the Royal Observatory in Greenwich, London, Britain, on Oct. 25, 2026. The Royal Observatory in Greenwich was founded in 1675 to improve navigation at sea through astronomical observations and help ships determine their longitude. As the home of Greenwich Mean Time, it holds an important place in the history of astronomy, precision timekeeping and navigation. In 1884, the meridian passing through the observatory was adopted as the international Prime Meridian, establishing a common reference for measuring longitude worldwide. This historic line is still marked at the observatory today. (Xinhua/Li Mangmang)

RLWC quick hits: Big crowds and bigger scorelines in week two
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
03:28:38 UTC
12:28:38 KST

Fri, 11 Sept, 7:50 pm, Final score, Rabbitohs 10, Knights 20
Rugby League World Cup quick hits: Big crowds and bigger scorelines in week two
The second week of the Rugby League World Cup was short on genuine contests as the tournament's haves and have-nots collided.
Aside from Australia's win over Fiji, where the gallant Bati gave the Kangaroos a hell of a scare, it was big scorelines across the board.
But with fans across three Australian states and two other counties voting with their feet, there are still plenty of quick hits from the second round of matches.
1. Tongan wall holds yet again
For the second week in a row, Tonga's opponent enjoyed plenty of field position and for the second week in a row Tonga's scrambling defence proved more than up to the challenge.
After holding England to 12 points last week, despite the English enjoying 34 tackles inside the red zone to Tonga's 18, they repeated the dose against Lebanon on Friday night.
The Cedars came in with an offload-heavy game plan and had some success moving the ball up the field. By the end, they had 29 tackles inside the attacking 20 to Tonga's 30, but that was where they stalled.
Some of it was due to a lack of creativity but there were plenty of last-gasp Tongan efforts to deny Lebanese players who looked tryline bound, and it means Tonga carry a strong form line into Sunday's blockbuster against Samoa.
2. Samoa running riot over PNG is a sign of the times
Rarely will you see two halves of a single game more different than what Samoa and Papua New Guinea dished up in Port Moresby.
The Kumuls held the gloves up well through the opening 40, trailing just 14-6 at the break and could have been even closer had Robert Derby successfully grounded the ball for their second try.
But what followed was a procession: Samoa scored 50 unanswered points in the second half, as their size and athleticism totally overwhelmed PNG, who had just four sets in the entire stanza.
Of all the blowout results this weekend, this more than any other was a sign of the times. Rugby league's embrace of the set restart rule and the increased speed of the game makes it almost impossible for an underdog team to stay in the fight beyond a certain point and when things break they can break badly.
Samoa only had to make 36 tackles through the entire second and the Kumuls only got over halfway for two tackles.
They finished the game conceding six tries in 15 minutes against a side they had held their own against for the whole first half.
There were plenty of less-extreme examples of the same through this year's NRL season, most notably when a top eight side conceded the third-most points in a game ever, but it's been turned up to greater levels through this World Cup given the talent and fitness disparity and it stacks the deck even further against the underdogs.
3. France's woes continue in England smash-up
England beat the clock against their old rivals in Perth, running out 82-0 winners in a result that means France have conceded 160 points in as many minutes through their two matches.
It's hard to find any silver lining for Les Chanticleers and ahead of their tournament finale against Lebanon, the French game finds itself in a strange position.
The potential for growth or a return to the glory days when France were one of Test football's true powers is always the dream, and with two Super League clubs in Catalans Dragons and Toulouse — giving France more professional teams than New Zealand — they seemingly have the ingredients and infrastructure for improvement.
All but two of this year's squad were home-grown players and since 2020 they have won nine of the 16 Tests they have played, with all seven losses coming against England or Samoa.
Problem is, across those seven games they have been outscored by a cumulative total of 394-44, with this England loss the worst of them.
There's greater pathways to the top for French talent than ever before but they can't seem to close the gap between them and the big dogs.
If anything, the gap has become wider. Nine years ago, in the 2017 World Cup, they played England at the same ground and lost 36-6 a week after losing to Australia 52-6.
Those scorelines aren't exactly a good time, but they're not a point-a-minute for two straight weeks either.
The Southern Hemisphere racing ahead of the north is a wider issue for the sport, but France are the collateral damage and they don't have a contingent of heritage NRL players to paper over the cracks.
4. Christchurch puts its best foot forward
Despite Esom Ioka's first-half hat-trick that briefly gave the Cook Islands the lead, few would have ever expected the Aitu to trouble New Zealand for long in their match at Te Kaha in Christchurch.
That didn't stop a sell-out crowd of 26,800 coming through the gates, marking the fifth biggest Test attendance of the past century in New Zealand and the highest ever for a game outside of Auckland.
It was a strong week of crowds throughout the tournament — Tonga and Lebanon pulled in more than 25,000 and Australia topped 40,000 for the second week in a row despite taking on Fiji.
But with the NRL expansion race heating up as the league prepares to hand out a licence for a 20th team, Christchurch showing up in droves did their chances of winning the bid no harm at all.
5. Fiji take Australia to the brink
Speaking of that Australian-Fiji crowd, the 41,108 punters who packed into Lang Park didn't just push the attendance past that of the 2017 World Cup final at the same venue, they were treated to easily the best clash of the weekend.
On the back of an inspired display by five-eighth Kurt Donoghoe and a hat-trick to Castleford winger Semi Valemei, Fiji pushed Australia all the way before a late Jacob Preston try wrapped up a 36-22 win for the green and golds.
Consider the previous margins between the two (42-8, 54-6 and 64-0 in their last three meetings) and it's a measure of how far the Bati have come and how this World Cup is more up for grabs than one might think.
A couple of contentious calls and some killer instinct in key moments got the Kangaroos home.
But on what they've shown through two weeks, Samoa, Tonga and New Zealand will all fancy their chances of springing an upset should they meet Australia, who have wrapped up a semi-final berth in surprisingly shaky fashion.

Top officials from the Mecca Pact countries Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan are set to meet Iranian officials in Tehran on Oct 26 to discuss regional coordination, two people with knowledge of the matter said.
Saudi Arabia will be represented by Defence Minister Prince Khalid bin Salman, and Pakistan by army chief Field Marshal Asim Munir, the people said on condition of anonymity.
The Turkish head of intelligence will also join, one of the people said.
The Saudi government media office, Pakistan’s military media wing, and Turkey’s foreign ministry did not immediately respond to Reuters’ requests for comment.
The planned talks would be the first high-level contact between Iran and all members of the three-nation bloc since Saudi Arabia has come under escalating attacks from Yemen’s Iran-aligned Houthis.
Munir visited Tehran last week, where he met Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian and other senior officials. During the visit, Iranian officials told him there would be no talks with Washington until Tehran’s demands were met, according to Iranian media.
Pakistan has been a key intermediary between the United States and Iran. Earlier mediation efforts helped produce an interim peace agreement in June, but the deal quickly unravelled as fighting between Iran and the United States resumed weeks later.
Saudi Arabia intercepted another wave of missiles and drones on Oct 25 as fighting with the militant group continued unabated.
Ministers from the Mecca Pact countries held an emergency meeting in Riyadh earlier in October and agreed to ensure the “rapid deployment” of military forces and capabilities in Saudi Arabia.
The conflict has become an increasingly destabilising element in the US-Israeli offensive against Iran, turning US ally Saudi Arabia into a pressure point in the wider war.
Turkey, Pakistan and Saudi Arabia signed the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement in August, under which an armed attack on one member is considered an attack on all.
The agreement’s first article says the parties shall use “all necessary means” to eliminate threats to one another’s territorial integrity, sovereignty or internationally recognised borders, according to a text seen by Reuters.
Efforts by Turkey’s Parliament to ratify the agreement began last week and are still underway, while Pakistan approved the pact last week. REUTERS

Bolsonaro refuses to concede as would-be Ukraine peace mediator Lula wins Brazil election
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
03:23:18 UTC
12:23:18 KST

Bolsonaro refuses to concede as would-be Ukraine peace mediator Lula wins Brazil election
Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva won reelection on Oct. 25, securing a fourth, nonconsecutive term in office, as his opponent, right-wing Senator Flávio Bolsonaro, refused to concede defeat and vowed to challenge the election results.
The election ended with Lula receiving 51.79% of votes compared with Bolsonaro's 48.21%, according to Brazil's electoral authorities.
Bolsonaro said he would seek to annul the election, calling a decision by Supreme Court Justice Cristiano Zanin to extend voting by two hours "unacceptable."
The extension was introduced following transportation disruptions and severe weather that affected voting in parts of the country, according to the Associated Press.
The electoral court has recognized Lula's victory, and Bolsonaro's refusal to concede does not invalidate the result.
Lula had expressed the view in 2024 that Brazil should remain neutral and not interfere in Russia's war against Ukraine, but in the years that followed had been engaging in diplomacy, including efforts to position Brazil as a potential mediator between Kyiv and Moscow.
In June of this year, President Volodymyr Zelensky accepted Lula's offer to assist efforts to negotiate an end to the war, Ukrainian presidential communications adviser Dmytro Lytvyn said, according to Reuters.
The leaders held a bilateral meeting on during the G7 summit in France on June 17, discussing ways to revive stalled diplomatic negotiations, including potential outreach to permanent members of the United Nations Security Council.
While Ukraine maintains close diplomatic ties with three of the five permanent members — France, the United Kingdom and the United States — Brazil has maintained diplomatic relations with Russia and China.
Lula spoke with Russian President Vladimir Putin by telephone in August, discussing the war in Ukraine and bilateral relations, CNN Brasil reported.
Brazil has maintained diplomatic and economic ties with Russia since the beginning of the full-scale invasion in February 2022, opting out of Western sanctions and expressing a wish to have a role in a negotiated settlement to the war.
Lula has also rejected suggestions that Brazil supports Russia's invasion, saying in an April interview that his government has never recognized Moscow's right to occupy Ukrainian territory.
The Brazilian president's victory comes after a closely fought campaign against Bolsonaro, the son of former President Jair Bolsonaro, who is serving a prison sentence for his role in an attempted coup following his 2022 election defeat.
The elder Bolsonaro also refused to concede defeat after losing to Lula in 2022. He was subsequently convicted for his role in a plot to overturn that election.
The victory makes Lula, 80, the first Brazilian president to win four terms and the first candidate since the country's return to democracy to win a presidential runoff after finishing second in the opening round.
While Bolsonaro refuses to concede and asks for the vote to be annulled, election officials have expressed "absolute" confidence in the proceedings and the result, as reported by Reuters.

Albania plans new legal measures as student protests continue
Unknown

Dzihat Aliju and Gizem Nisa Demir
26 October 2026•Update: 26 October 2026
Albanian Prime Minister Edi Rama announced plans Sunday for new legal measures targeting protests as demonstrations by university students demanding improved education conditions continued in the capital Tirana.
The protests, which began on Oct. 13, entered their 13th day, drawing support from high school students, citizens, faculty members from several universities and various trade unions. Some demonstrations turned violent.
Protesters marched through streets and squares across the capital, first gathering outside the Education Ministry, where they threw stones at the building. They later moved to the prime minister's office, where tensions escalated between demonstrators and security forces.
Protesters threw stones at police and public institutions while officers responded with tear gas. Some demonstrators were injured during clashes in which Molotov cocktails were occasionally used.
Rama reiterated his calls for dialogue, as he had in previous days, but protesters rejected the appeals. Students said they would continue their demonstrations.
Rama said the current law governing demonstrations dates back to 2001 and contains no provisions addressing digital technology tools, which have become a fundamental part of protests today.
The proposed legislative package includes compensation for businesses affected by demonstrations, fines for participants in violent protests, measures to address calls for violence on social media and amendments to the Criminal Code.
The planned regulations would introduce fines for organizing unauthorized demonstrations, failing to comply with orders to disperse, wearing masks during protests and obstructing traffic.
The package also aims to require the removal of social media posts calling for violence and initiate legal proceedings against those responsible.

Automated aged care algorithm needs a human override, ombudsman finds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
03:08:00 UTC
12:08:00 KST

Aged care funding algorithm neither fair or consistent, ombudsman finds
In short:
Use of automation in Australia's aged care system lacks safeguards and has led to unfair outcomes for elderly patients, the Commonwealth Ombudsman has found.
The ombudsman released his findings after an investigation into the Department of Health, Disability and Ageing's classification algorithm.
What's next?
Of the 10 recommendations made, six were accepted by the government and a further two, including instating a human override, were noted.
The Commonwealth Ombudsman Iain Anderson has issued a damning report on the aged care algorithm, saying the government should amend the law to allow senior assessors to override its decisions when it gets it wrong.
In a scathing report of more than 100 pages, the ombudsman says the actions of the Department of Health, Disability and Ageing, in its administration of the assessment scheme and the algorithm, "have been unreasonable".
The report says the department put the classification algorithm in place "without any meaningful risk assessment, evaluation or analysis, despite the obvious risks that would arise with deterministic automated decision-making".
The classification algorithm was launched on November 1 last year as part of the government's "once in a generation" reforms to aged care and is used to assign people a level of funding to stay at home with support rather than go into a nursing home.
But it has been mired in controversy since its introduction, with hundreds of people appealing its decisions, a more than five fold increase on appeals in the previous year.
In his report released today, Mr Anderson said: "A reasonable person would, in my view, lack confidence that the system is in fact fair and consistent."
In a response to the draft report, the department said it "does not accept this characterisation" that it didn't test the algorithm or validate it.
However, as revealed by Four Corners and by the ombudsman, tests were conducted on an original version of the algorithm created by a consultancy. The algorithm in place today was modified by the department and there was no external validation.
Audit recommended
Mr Anderson also recommends the Australian National Audit Office consider doing an audit of the implementation of the Single Assessment System and the Independent Assessment tool, which is the questionnaire which drives the algorithm, "and in doing so, assesses whether the Department's use of public resources was efficient, economical and ethical".
The ombudsman made a total of 10 recommendations, with six being accepted by the government. The first two recommendations, that legislation be introduced to allow override by a human and amending the aged care rules, have not been accepted by the department, and have only been noted.
However, the department has accepted the recommendation for a comprehensive review of the Aged Care Act in relation to the assessment process and algorithm to "identify legal defects, inconsistencies, ambiguities or unintended consequences" and address these issues in a timely way.
It has also accepted the recommendation that any amendment to the act be "preceded by and informed by meaningful consultation with the public".
Department 'incorrectly advising' assessors
Mr Anderson said the department had been wrongly telling assessors that the algorithm outcomes could be changed right up until the new legislation took effect.
This is despite the fact that there was no mechanism in the act or the rules to change outcomes.
"The Department did not, and may still not, understand key components of the legal framework it created, nor did it understand what legal framework it was meant to create,"
Mr Anderson said.
The government has resisted calls to give blanket permission for delegates for assessment agencies to override the classification algorithm.
It instead passed legislation last week to allow an "escalation pathway" for appeals in exceptional circumstances.
In return for the Coalition's support in passing the legislation, it has commissioned a review into the assessment system and algorithm, with a report due in the first half of next year.
In a statement, Minister for Health and Ageing, Mark Butler, and Minister for Aged Care, Sam Rae, said: "The Government will consider the Ombudsman's report carefully as we continue to improve our aged care system, including the assessments system."
"We're already acting on many of the recommendations to ensure our aged care system is transparent and reliable, and we'll examine what further action we can take to give every Australian confidence in the system."
Over a million people, or 85 per cent of those using aged care, receive services through the home support system.

'Our motherland needs us': The Israeli expats flying home to vote
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
03:04:29 UTC
12:04:29 KST

Thousands of Israeli expats, including Australians, fly home to vote in election
In short:
Political activists have mobilised to bring thousands of overseas Israeli citizens to the country to vote.
As many as 67,000 voters are returning to Israel, according to one non-profit organisation, with some estimating up to 1,000 could be coming from Australia.
Some travelling from Australia said they felt Israel's PM Benjamin Netanyahu had contributed to "division amongst the people".
Tens of thousands of Israeli citizens abroad, including estimates of hundreds from Australia, are travelling to Israel to vote in the country's most consequential election in decades.
Polling indicates Israel's Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu could face a stiff challenge to hold onto power in a vote largely seen as a referendum on his leadership and handling of Hamas's October 7 attacks.
His main challenger is Gadi Eisenkot, a former Israeli military chief who leads the newly established Yashar opposition party.
Political activists mobilised around the world to bring Israeli citizens overseas to the country to vote, given ballots can only be cast in person on election day, with exceptions for serving soldiers and diplomats.
The AID Coalition, a US-based non-profit that describes itself as non-partisan, estimates that as many as 67,000 voters are returning to Israel, based on surveys of expatriates and registration data gathered for its Fly&Vote initiative.
It says about half are flying in from the United States, with others from Europe, Canada, Australia and New Zealand.
Among those who have travelled to Israel is Anat Dror, who has been living in Melbourne for almost five years and recently became an Australian citizen.
"The sentiment for us is that right now, voting is absolutely essential. It's something that absolutely comes from the heart and no-one would be able to talk me out of it," she told the ABC.
"I'm coming here at the very expensive cost of missing out on work days and paying for a very expensive ticket and missing my kids at home … all of these are not deterring any of us from coming here to vote.
"This is our motherland and our motherland needs us right now."
In September, the Likud party tried to block the AID Coalition's Fly&Vote initiative by lodging an appeal with the elections committee, but withdrew the case after reaching an agreement.
'I don't trust any of them'
The most recent data from Israeli television networks Channel 12 and Channel 13, released on Thursday, put Mr Eisenkot's Yashar a few seats ahead of Mr Netanyahu's Likud.
After Tuesday's vote both parties will need to embark on complicated coalition negotiations to secure the 61-seat majority required to form government.
Ms Dror said Israel was still reeling from the trauma of Hamas's deadly assault on October 7, 2023, and the legacy of that day cast a long shadow over this election.
But she argued the broader societal challenges Israel is facing began emerging before the terrorist attacks, including intense cost-of-living pressures.
She said Mr Netanyahu's government needed to go, but did not want to publicly back a particular candidate in the so-called "change" camp: the anti-Netanyahu parties, including Yashar, trying to end his tenure.
"What one single politician, do I trust his words or her words? The answer is none of them. I don't trust any of them, nor should anyone ever trust politicians' words before elections," she said.
"They will say everything because they are indeed politicians.
"What I'm counting on isn't any one individual. I'm counting on the change bloc to have the ability to oversee differences, oversee personal gain for the sake of actually building a coalition that is diverse."
Ms Dror said she believed anywhere between 500 and 1,000 Israeli citizens from Australia were making the journey.
"We have a really big Israeli WhatsApp group in Australia, and we made a joke that maybe we should meet for coffee here in Tel Aviv instead of in Melbourne," she said.
Another Israeli citizen travelling to the country to vote, Guy Marom, moved to Australia with his family during the COVID-19 pandemic.
As he packed his bags in Sydney's north-east, he was also undecided on which candidate to back, but insisted one of the "change" parties would get his vote.
"Most of them, at least, have leaders that I consider trustworthy, and I hope they will shape Israel differently than what it is today," he told the ABC.
"I think [Netanyahu is] maybe not the single cause, but I think he's contributing to the division amongst the people."
ABC/Associated Press

Ukraine accuses Google of providing Russian search results
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
03:02:27 UTC
12:02:27 KST

Ukraine accuses Google of providing Russian search results
Ukrainian language ombudswoman Elena Ivanovskaya has accused Google of not doing enough to promote the national tongue in the global digital environment. The US tech giant’s search engine often provides results to Ukrainians in Russian even when the queries are typed in Ukrainian, she told a local media outlet.
The government has been cracking down on the use of the Russian language in Ukraine since the 2014 Western-backed Maidan coup, using what Moscow has repeatedly denounced as discriminatory practices.
Former Ukrainian President Pyotr Poroshenko introduced restrictions on the import of books from Russia and Belarus in 2016, which became an outright ban in 2023. Kiev also purged Russian literature from state curricula and systematically removed cultural monuments, memorials, and inscriptions to remove historical links to Russia.
Kiev seeks to block access to Russian music on international streaming platforms inside Ukraine and prevent its performers from appearing in domestic popularity charts, according to Ukrainian Sanctions Policy commissioner Vladislav Vlasiuk. More than 100 Russian performers have been blacklisted in Ukraine, and the list will be expanded, according to the official.
In an interview with the outlet Censor.net, Ivanovskaya stated that her office had filed a formal complaint with Google over its search algorithms. “For example, when a user enters a search query in Ukrainian, the system returns results in Russian – solely because of the user’s geographic location,” she stated, adding that her office asked the company to address the supposed lack of “accuracy of their search result algorithms.”
The Ukrainian authorities have banned the use of any language other than Ukrainian in the public sphere, including government, education, media, and customer service. Violations can result in administrative fines of up to $270.
Ivanovskaya has previously suggested increasing the fines tenfold and demanded Russian-speaking children and parents use Ukrainian during breaks and in conversations with teachers, arguing that both instances fall under the “public sphere rule” and could be punished with fines.
Despite the concerted persecution campaign, Russian remains widely used in Ukraine. According to Ukrainian polling data, as many as 46% of country’s nationals spoke Russian in everyday life before the conflict escalated in 2022. Another survey last year showed the number of Russian speakers had fallen to 30% since four former Ukrainian territories, including the Donbass republics and Kherson and Zaporozhye Regions formally joined Russia after a series of referendums.
Ukrainian Culture Minister Tatyana Berezhnaya said earlier this year that 71% of Ukrainians regularly consume Russian-language content, with nearly a quarter doing so every day.
Moscow has repeatedly denounced the discriminatory measures as “Russophobic censorship,” warning that attempts to “cancel” Russian culture will ultimately fail.
