Lula, Brazil’s political titan, defies the passage of time
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
01:40:00 UTC
10:40:00 KST

Brazil election: Lula, Brazil’s political titan, defies the passage of time
- Lula won an unprecedented fourth term after losing the first round, beating Flavio Bolsonaro in a run-off and keeping Brazil as a leftist stronghold.
- His career spans poverty, union work, prison and a major comeback, with supporters praising his “love for the poor” and defence of democracy.
- He faces criticism over crime, corruption and debt, but his Bolsa Familia welfare plan and social gains remain central to his legacy.
AI generated
RIO DE JANEIRO – Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva, Brazil’s president granted an unprecedented fourth term in office, once likened the events of his life to a miracle.
The titan of the political left made history by becoming the first person to win a presidential run-off after losing the first round in Brazil.
His shock win follows a long and storied political career, beginning in the bowels of a metalworkers’ trade union and even including stints behind bars.
He charted a rocky road to his fourth election victory.
Questions about his ability to do the job at almost 81 encouraged Lula to do squats and jog along the campaign trail to prove that he was fitter than ever.
Initially startled by his second-place finish to Flavio Bolsonaro earlier in October, Lula dusted himself off and launched into an energetic run-off campaign.
He upped his social media game at the eleventh hour, posting selfie videos and buying a cellphone for the first time.
The shift highlighted a certain disconnect with his country’s extremely online, deeply polarised population, 14 years after he was first elected.
His victory preserves Latin America’s largest country as a leftist stronghold amid a regional lurch to the right championed by US President Donald Trump.
Poverty, presidency, prison
Lula, a defining figure in Brazilian politics over four decades, rose from poverty to the presidency, fell into disgrace and was jailed, before once again rising from the political ashes when he returned to power almost four years ago.
His first-round campaign focused heavily on his life story and legacy, which critics said was a misreading of what weary Brazilians wanted to hear.
The president grew up in deep poverty, the seventh of eight children in a family of illiterate farmers in the arid north-eastern state of Pernambuco.
He worked as a shoeshine boy and peanut vendor before becoming a metalworker and trade unionist. In the 1960s, he lost a finger in a workplace accident.
After losing three presidential bids, Lula finally entered the presidential palace in Brasilia in 2003 and was re-elected in 2006.
He left office in 2010 as a blue-collar hero who presided over a commodity-based economic boom that helped lift 30 million people out of poverty.
Massive corruption scandals haunted Lula and his party, fuelling a wave of disgust that propelled Jair Bolsonaro into the presidency in 2018.
Lula was jailed before the election until the charges were annulled on procedural grounds and the lead judge on the case was found to be biased.
However, Lula was not exonerated and the scandal contributed to enduring polarisation in Brazil.
Bolsonaro’s presidency brought more division, and by the 2022 election, Lula pulled off a dramatic comeback by a razor-thin margin.
‘Love for the poor’
In his third term, Lula is credited with restoring social programmes eroded by his predecessor, curbing the destruction of the Amazon rainforest, and putting Brazil’s democracy back on a more secure footing.
But the father of five still triggers fierce rejection among voters frustrated by crime and corruption.
He has also faced criticism over Brazil’s mounting public debt, which, with high interest rates, costs the government around US$18 billion (S$23 billion) a month in interest alone.
Lula came under fire for an election-season spending push, including an increase to the Bolsa Familia social welfare benefits which, launched 20 years ago, remains his most significant legacy.
“He has that love for the poor. That’s all it is,” fisherman Antonio Carlos Lima Ferreira told AFP at his home in the interior of Maranhao state, recalling times when he had to send his son to bed hungry.
“Today, at my table, I can choose what I want to eat.”
Lula said recently he did not want to be remembered as “just the Bolsa Familia president”.
No successor
Lula, who has not cultivated a potential successor, campaigned on a pledge to stop the far right from returning to “destroy” the country.
His improbable victory on Oct 25 awed his supporters, many of whom feared an erosion of rights under a theoretical Flavio Bolsonaro presidency.
Lula “will always remain a symbol of the defence of democracy”, civil servant Gustavo Monteiro, 58, told AFP at a leftist rally.
“He represents the fight against political repression.”
The leftist veteran has already spent more time in office than any other democratically elected leader in Latin America’s biggest country.
“There is no one in this country with more experience as president than me,” Lula told foreign media, including AFP, in an interview. AFP

BRASILIA, Oct. 25 (Xinhua) -- Brazilian incumbent President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva, candidate of the ruling Workers' Party, won Sunday's presidential runoff, according to results released by Brazil's Superior Electoral Court on Sunday night.
With 99.96 percent of the votes counted, Lula received 51.78 percent of the valid votes, compared with 48.22 percent for Flavio Bolsonaro, the Liberal Party's presidential candidate and son of former Brazilian President Jair Bolsonaro, according to the official tally.
Lula will be sworn in on Jan. 5, 2027, for a four-year term, marking his fourth election as Brazil's president.
Brazil's presidential election follows a two-round majoritarian system. To win in the first round, held on Oct. 4, a candidate must secure more than half of the valid votes. Flavio Bolsonaro finished ahead of incumbent Lula, winning about 47 percent of the valid votes against Lula's roughly 45 percent. As neither candidate crossed the 50-percent threshold, the two advanced to a runoff, which Lula won. ■

KATHMANDU, Oct. 26 (Xinhua) -- The Nepali government has unveiled plans to expand flood early warning systems across six major river basins and lower water levels in four high-risk glacial lakes as part of efforts to strengthen disaster preparedness amid growing climate-related risks in the Himalayan region.
The initiatives are part of a broader strategy to improve flood forecasting, reduce the risk of glacial lake outburst floods (GLOFs) and modernize weather forecasting through advanced technologies, according to separate documents issued by the Center for Hydrology and Water Resources Research and the Department of Hydrology and Meteorology, the secretariat of Nepal's Ministry of Energy, Water Resources and Irrigation said in a press statement on Sunday.
The plans come in the wake of devastating floods on Aug. 26 that claimed around 1,500 lives, while more than 5,000 people remain missing. The floods also caused 1.81 billion U.S. dollars in physical damage, according to the Nepali government's preliminary Rapid Damage and Needs Assessment (RDNA).
Rising temperatures have accelerated glacier melting in the Himalayas, increasing concerns over glacial lake instability, avalanches and potentially destructive floods downstream.
Under the proposed Glacial Lake Outburst Flood (GLOF) Sanjeevani Project, the government plans to lower water levels in four high-risk glacial lakes: Thulagi in Manang district, Lower Barun in Sankhuwasabha district, and Lumding Tsho and Hongu-2 in Solukhumbu district.
The project is scheduled to run from 2026 to 2033, with an estimated budget of 49.9 million dollars.
The initiative builds on previous efforts to reduce risks at Tsho Rolpa in Dolakha district and Imja Lake in Solukhumbu district, where water levels were successfully lowered to mitigate the threat of glacial lake outburst floods.
Meanwhile, the Center for Hydrology and Water Resources Research plans to install flood early warning systems across six river basins under the Priority River Basins Flood Risk Management Project, which runs from 2022 to 2028, with an investment of 7.54 million dollars.
The center will also provide round-the-clock flood forecasting and early warning services from mid-May to mid-October, covering the country's main monsoon season.
In a separate initiative to improve weather forecasting, the Department of Hydrology and Meteorology plans to prioritize artificial intelligence, machine learning and high-performance computing systems to enhance the accuracy and reliability of forecasts. ■

Advance voting opens in New Zealand ahead of Nov. 7 election

WELLINGTON, Oct. 26 (Xinhua) -- Advance voting opened across New Zealand on Monday, allowing voters to cast their ballots nearly two weeks before the Nov. 7 general election, as political parties vie for support in a closely contested race.
A total of 207 voting places opened on the first day of advance voting, with more locations to become available in the days leading up to election day, according to the Electoral Commission. More than 2,300 voting places are expected to operate nationwide on election day.
Voting locations include community halls, shopping centers, schools, tertiary institutions and marae, or Maori meeting grounds. More than 220 dedicated Maori community voting places are also available, including 67 where voters can cast their ballots in either Maori or English, according to the commission.
Prime Minister Christopher Luxon's center-right National Party is seeking a second term after taking office in 2023, while Labor, led by former prime minister Chris Hipkins, is campaigning to return to power amid public concerns over the cost of living, economic growth, jobs and public services.
Poll results suggested that neither major party could secure a parliamentary majority on its own, leaving smaller parties potentially pivotal in forming the next government.
New Zealand uses a mixed-member proportional electoral system to elect its parliament. Under this system, the government is usually formed by two or more parliamentary political parties.
The electoral system makes the party vote particularly important. Voters cast two ballots, one for a political party and another for their local electorate candidate. A party generally needs at least 5 percent of the party vote or to win an electorate seat to qualify for proportional representation in parliament. This allows smaller parties to enter parliament and potentially hold the balance of power when neither major bloc commands a majority.
Under changes to electoral law, voters in this year's election are required to enroll or update their details by midnight Sunday. Those who missed the deadline can no longer enroll during the voting period.
Official election results are scheduled to be declared on Nov. 27. New Zealand citizens or permanent residents aged 18 or above, who have lived in New Zealand continuously for 12 months or more at some time in their life, are eligible to vote in the election, according to the commission. ■

Zou Jingyuan of China celebrates during the men's parallel bars final at the Artistic Gymnastics World Championships 2026 in Rotterdam, the Netherlands, Oct. 25, 2026. (Xinhua/Weng Xinyang)
ROTTERDAM, the Netherlands, Oct. 25 (Xinhua) -- China claimed men's parallel bars gold through Zou Jingyuan and women's balance beam silver through Zhang Qingying on Sunday, as five apparatus finals brought the World Artistic Gymnastics Championships to a close.
Zou successfully defended his title with 15.733 points, finishing 0.833 ahead of Croatia's Illia Kovtun. Russia's Daniel Marinov claimed bronze with 14.866.
The two-time Olympic champion combined a difficulty score of 6.000 with an execution mark of 9.633 and a 0.100 bonus. Kovtun matched his difficulty but posted an execution score of 8.900.
The victory gave the 28-year-old his fifth world parallel bars title, extending his record after winning his fourth in Jakarta last year.
The women's balance beam final was decided by an execution tiebreak, with Algeria's Kaylia Nemour edging defending champion Zhang after both scored 14.566.
Zhang, competing last, performed a routine with a difficulty score of 6.500, compared with Nemour's 6.300. However, Nemour's execution mark of 8.266 put her ahead of Zhang's 8.066.
Brazil's Flavia Saraiva took bronze with 14.300, while China's Qiu Qiyuan finished seventh with 13.633. Nemour's victory completed a golden double following her uneven bars triumph on Saturday.
Armenia's Artur Davtyan won men's vault gold with a two-vault average of 14.850. Britain's Jake Jarman took silver with 14.650, ahead of Norway's Sebastian Sponevik on 14.366.
Chinese Taipei's Tang Chia-hung captured the men's horizontal bar title with 14.966. Japan's Oka Shinnosuke and Russia's Sergei Naidin both scored 14.800, with Oka taking silver on execution.
The United States secured a one-two finish in the women's floor exercise. Claire Pease won with 13.866 ahead of teammate Reese Esponda's 13.566. France's Maiana Prat earned bronze with 13.466, edging Britain's Abigail Martin on execution after the pair finished level on total points.
China ended the championships with three golds, two silvers and two bronzes. Its women reclaimed the team title for the first time since 2006, while Lan Xingyu won rings gold on Saturday. Yang Haonan took men's all-around silver, while the men's team and women's all-around gymnast Ke Qinqin contributed bronze medals.
Japan retained the men's team crown, while Daiki Hashimoto won his fourth consecutive world all-around title. American Skye Blakely captured the women's all-around championship before adding bronze medals on vault and uneven bars.
The championships also awarded the first artistic gymnastics team berths for the Los Angeles 2028 Olympic Games. Japan, Russia and China qualified in the men's competition, while China, the United States and Japan secured women's team berths.
Next year's World Championships will be held in Chengdu, China. ■

Five economic challenges facing Brazil’s re-elected President Lula
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
02:32:53 CET
10:32:53 KST

By Marcela Ayres and Bernardo Caram
BRASILIA, Oct 25 (Reuters) - Brazil’s economy has beaten expectations in recent years, but mounting debt and entrenched structural problems could complicate leftist President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva’s fourth term, which begins in January.
Here are the five main economic challenges he faces:
SOARING DEBT
Brazil’s public debt has surged more than 10 percentage points during Lula’s current term to over 82% of GDP, driving up borrowing costs.
The root cause is years of rising mandatory spending, leaving under 8% of the federal budget adjustable.
Lula has sent mixed fiscal signals, at times dismissing debt worries as “nonsense,” while arguing strong economic growth would fix the problem.
His team has pledged to keep the government’s current budget rules, which cap spending growth and set primary balance targets — revenues minus expenditures, excluding interest payments on public debt — and hinted at tightening them.
Hitting those targets will be harder given Lula’s promise to raise the minimum wage faster than inflation, which also lifts pension costs, after already raising welfare benefits and promising new spending.
HIGH INTEREST RATES AND STICKY INFLATION
Even with interest rates at 13.75%, Brazil’s annual inflation of 4.6% remains above the central bank’s tolerance range of 1.5% to 4.5%.
The central bank delivered its fifth straight rate cut last month on growing signs of an economic slowdown, but markets expect inflation to remain above the official 3% target until as late as 2029.
Lula’s platform promises lower interest rates through fiscal discipline that spares social programs, but most economists say rates will only fall faster if Brazil cuts spending, and it’s unclear how he will square the two.
DEBT-LADEN HOUSEHOLDS AND BUSINESSES
A record nearly 84 million Brazilians and 9.3 million businesses are behind on debt payments, according to credit bureau Serasa, as high interest rates bite.
That has fueled public dissatisfaction despite strong indicators such as record-low unemployment and wage growth outpacing inflation.
Lula plans a new round of debt relief, this time through discounted purchases of distressed household loans from banks, plus tax debt forgiveness for some small business owners. Analysts say such measures offer only temporary relief.
The government has also discussed with the central bank ways to rein in heavy use of easy but expensive credit, such as credit cards and unsecured consumer loans, though it has not detailed any proposals.
SCARCE POLITICAL CAPITAL FOR REFORMS
Lula will likely struggle to push his economic agenda through Congress after voters elected the most conservative legislature since Brazil’s return to democracy in the 1980s.
Although he defeated right-wing Senator Flavio Bolsonaro in Sunday’s runoff, Bolsonaro’s Liberal Party and its allies are set to control both chambers.
Lula’s aides have signaled he will keep pushing to curtail tax breaks, but lawmakers have repeatedly resisted measures that raise the effective tax burden.
During his current term, Lula has struggled to name nominees and win Senate approval for them at key institutions, including the Supreme Court, central bank, securities regulator and antitrust watchdog, and that is likely to be even more difficult ahead with the rightward shift of Congress.
TAX REFORM UNCERTAINTIES
Lula won congressional approval in 2023 for a sweeping overhaul of Brazil’s consumption taxes, and a new value-added tax is set to take effect in January.
With under three months to go, the government has still not disclosed the effective rate, which independent analysts estimate will be around 28%.
Fearing a backlash during the campaign, the administration has also held off on sending Congress a bill to regulate a new tax on products considered harmful to health or the environment, such as cigarettes and alcohol.
That delay could push back revenue from the tax and has fueled criticism of the government’s handling of tax policy.
(Reporting by Marcela Ayres and Bernardo Caram, Editing by Rosalba O’Brien)

Venezuela opposition leader Machado returns home after fraught year away

By Vivian Sequera, Sarah Kinosian and Keren Torres
CARACAS/BARQUISIMETO, Oct 25 (Reuters) - Venezuelan opposition leader Maria Corina Machado was greeted by tens of thousands of cheering supporters as she made her way by car to Caracas on Sunday night, after she arrived home following several failed return attempts which have strained her ties with US President Donald Trump’s administration.
“This country is giving lessons to everyone,” she shouted as her convoy entered the capital, leaning out of the sunroof to shake hands and hug raucous supporters
Nobel Peace Prize laureate Machado, who was prevented from challenging deposed leader Nicolas Maduro for the presidency in 2024, has been out of the country for 10 months and spent the previous year in hiding following the disputed election.
On Sunday morning, Machado appeared at a church in western Lara state and was greeted by bystanders who sang the national anthem and shouted “liberty!” as she left in an SUV, a Reuters witness said.
She then traveled to the capital in a journey that took eight hours because of crowds. By the time she neared Caracas, festooned in rosaries handed to her by followers, the highway was all but blocked by cheering supporters.
“For the reunion of every family, for freedom of every political prisoner, for the freedom of Venezuela,” she wrote on social media.
Machado’s return was coordinated with the US, Panamanian and Colombian governments, according to a person briefed directly on her movements, who added Trump approved her return and was kept informed about it.
At the White House on Sunday, Trump said he did not know anything about Machado’s return and suggested the US would continue to back Venezuelan interim President Delcy Rodriguez.
“She’s a very nice woman,” he said, referring to Machado. “But we’re doing really well in Venezuela.”
The White House and the State Department did not respond to Reuters questions on the matter.
RETURN PREVIOUSLY DELAYED
Machado’s efforts to return have tested her relationship with the Trump administration, which she sought to cultivate as an ally even before it captured Maduro in January and took him to New York for trial.
Trump has repeatedly expressed support for Rodriguez, a former deputy to Maduro, and hailed deals on oil production and other business ventures by US companies in the South American country. Trump said in September it was too soon to consider democratic elections in Venezuela.
US officials have asked Machado at least once to delay her return, Reuters reported in June, and she has made several failed attempts to enter the country. Her team did not disclose details of how she returned.
Machado traveled in a private plane from Panama to Colombia and crossed overland on Sunday to Venezuela, four people familiar with her trip told Reuters.
One person briefed on her movements said the flight took place late last week and US security contractors guarded her during the journey. Rodriguez and the country’s authorities were warned by the US not to interfere or threaten her safety, the person said.
“The conditions allowing for the safe return of Ms. Machado to Venezuela are the direct result of the US-supported reconciliation talks which have already seen hundreds of political prisoners freed and hundreds of political opposition figures return from exile,” US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said in a statement on Sunday.
“We expect all political actors to support these talks which represent the best chance Venezuela has had in thirty years to peacefully achieve not just a free and fair election but an enduring democracy.”
A faction of the opposition and the interim government held a round of talks this month, with the aim of remaking the top court and electoral council, among other goals, ahead of eventual elections. The talks have not included Machado’s political movement.
The Venezuelan Communications Ministry, which handles all press queries for the government, did not immediately respond to requests for comment on Machado’s return.
SUPPORTERS CHEER MACHADO ON ROUTE
“Maria Corina Machado will achieve liberty and democracy in Venezuela,” said Hernan Adames, 69, as he celebrated with other supporters in Barquisimeto.
Zuleima Granadillo, 61, an employee at the Ministry of Education, waited for Machado at a point on the highway in Aragua state, closer to Caracas.
“What does Machado’s arrival mean? All paths are opening up for us, the future is opening up, we have a light, and we are going all the way to the end,” she said.
“This dictatorship is already over with the arrival of our leader.”
Machado plans to meet victims of the deadly earthquakes that struck Venezuela in June, as well as the families of political prisoners, the international community and various leaders from the democratic movement in Venezuela, David Smolansky, her top foreign affairs adviser, told Reuters.
“She will work proactively for a date for free and fair elections,” he added.
International energy firms committed last month to expanding projects in the country in a signing ceremony overseen by Rodriguez and US Energy Secretary Chris Wright.
Machado has said that only a “serious, democratic government” can provide the stability needed by investors.
She had been barred by Maduro’s government from exiting Venezuela but she secretly left in late 2025 to receive the Nobel Peace Prize, after spending more than a year living mostly in hiding.
Machado’s Vente Venezuela movement released an app on Saturday to collect voter registration information from Venezuelans abroad. The group hopes eventually to share data from the app, which was built by 15 staff over the last 18 months, with a reformed electoral council so users can be officially added to voter rolls.
Edmundo Gonzalez, a former presidential candidate for Machado’s movement who has been living in Spain, said on X he would soon join her in Venezuela.
(Reporting by Vivian Sequera and Sarah Kinosian in Caracas, Keren Torres in Barquisimeto, Mircely Guanipa in Aragua, and Matt Spetalnick and Trevor Hunnicutt in Washington; Editing by Julia Symmes Cobb, Laura Gottesdiener, Edmund Klamann and Kate Mayberry)

Pentagon plans to keep US military bases running for 90 days without outside support: Report
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
01:32:40 UTC
10:32:40 KST

Gizem Nisa Demir
26 October 2026•Update: 26 October 2026
The Pentagon is preparing US military bases to operate independently for at least 90 days during a major war, securing essential services and supplies against disruptions to civilian infrastructure and global supply chains, according to a report.
The plans are part of FORTRESS, an initiative detailed in documents reviewed by Fox News Digital on Sunday.
"We don't want to rely on standard civilian municipal infrastructure to run our national defense. We just simply can't. It's an intolerable risk," Pentagon chief spokesperson Sean Parnell told Fox News Digital.
Parnell said US homeland defense planning must adapt to threats that could reach the American mainland.
"I realized that a lot of the way we think about homeland defense was built around the antiquated assumption that two oceans would protect us," he said, adding that President Donald Trump had advanced a new approach through initiatives such as Golden Dome and a renewed focus on the Western Hemisphere, Greenland and Panama.
FORTRESS envisions portable nuclear reactors, large-scale battery storage and microgrids to keep bases operational during power outages. It also calls for strategic reserves of munitions, fuel, critical minerals, electronics, spare parts and medical supplies, alongside at least two qualified supply or production pathways for critical defense needs.
"The next conflict will likely be fought on multiple fronts. Look at the geopolitics behind any major war. When that happens, global supply chains will break," Parnell said.
The initiative also aims to prepare civilian factories to switch to defense production through the Civil Reserve Manufacturing Network, with advance planning for contracts, cybersecurity and conversion procedures as well as regular industrial stress tests and mobilization exercises.
FORTRESS further seeks to protect military communications, navigation and satellite capabilities against interference, including GPS jamming and disruptions to space-based assets.
"Power is combat now. Without electricity, you lose communications, water, logistics, assembly lines and just basic military command structures," Parnell said. "You don't want to be making these decisions in the middle of a global multi-front conflict. We have to have a plan."
He described FORTRESS as an insurance policy to keep US forces operational if a major conflict disrupts the infrastructure and supply chains on which they depend.

However, Zelenskyy has repeatedly said Kyiv will only stop the strikes if Moscow stops hitting Ukraine’s power infrastructure, or if the US allows Ukraine to use of Starshield over Russia to detect launch places of its ballistic missiles, or if it supplies Ukraine with Patriot missiles.
- Zelenskyy on Sunday said Russia had launched nearly 2,300 drones targeting Ukrainian cities over the past week, renewing his call on western allies to speed up deliveries of interceptors. “This week alone, Russia has launched about 1,600 guided bombs, 48 missiles of various types, including ballistic missiles, and almost 2,300 strike drones at Ukraine,” he wrote in an online post.
- Russia’s defence ministry said on Sunday its drones had struck a cargo vessel bound for the Black Sea port of Chornomorsk in an overnight attack and another cargo vessel en route to the port of Odesa during the day. The ministry said the vessels were being used to supply the Ukrainian army. Russian forces also hit a logistics centre, a distribution centre and a logistics terminal in the Ukrainian city of Kharkiv overnight. Reuters could not confirm the reports.
- A Ukrainian drone attack overnight on the Russian border city of Belgorod killed three people and injured 13, local authorities said on Sunday, while a separate drone strike later in the day killed another person. The overnight attack on Belgorod damaged 30 apartment buildings, regional governor Alexander Shuvayev said.
- The presidential election in Bulgaria on Sunday ended inconclusively, with the next head of state to be picked in a runoff. In a surprisingly strong performance, the candidate of the pro-western reformist opposition, Andrey Gyurov, will face the incumbent leftist president, Iliana Yotova. Iotova opposes military aid to Ukraine and favours dialogue with Russia, while Gyurov has often expressed firm support for Kyiv. The vote was held amid security concerns after a series of drone attacks on ships in the Black Sea.

Under-fire aged care tool offers no public information on how it works, Ombudsman says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
01:13:27 UTC
10:13:27 KST

IN BRIEF
- The Commonwealth Ombudsman has highlighted the "serious consequences" of the government's automated assessment tool.
- Government staff and health advocates previously raised concerns about inability to override IAT assessments.
A Commonwealth Ombudsman investigation has revealed that the government's aged care tool has led to unfair outcomes and undermined public confidence and safety.
The Department of Health, Disability and Ageing uses a Single Assessment System (SAS) which includes the Integrated Assessment Tool (IAT) introduced on 1 November 2025. The legislatively prescribed tool is used for home care assessments and is automated to determine the level of aged care services an older individual requires.
However, the Ombudsman found that the IAT lacks safeguards and capacity to override incorrect assessments.
"Currently, under the law, automated decisions made by the IAT's algorithm cannot be overridden and changed, even if they are clinically inappropriate," Commonwealth Ombudsman Iain Anderson said on Monday.
"The IAT and its associated decision-making framework do not merely have the potential to undermine public confidence — rather, a reasonable person would, in my view, lack confidence that the system is in fact fair and consistent."
News that makes sense
Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
'Serious consequences'
Around 1.1 million older Australians access aged care services through the home support system.
The SAS has attracted several complaints, particularly about contracted assessment providers using the IAT and its algorithm, the ombudsman said.
Complaints about the SAS detailed poor communication, long wait times, slow review processes, insufficient assessors, and assessors lacking appropriate training and qualifications.
Complaints about the IAT detailed the underassessment of care needs, inability to change automated decisions and limited clinical expertise and algorithmic transparency.
The Ombudsman found no publicly available information on how the IAT determines an outcome — which is "inconsistent with the intentions of the Robodebt Royal Commission recommendations about transparency of government automated decision-making".
Anderson said he believed the department "did not and may still not, understand key components of the legal framework it created".
He said it also did not "understand what legal framework it was meant to create".
The investigation also revealed that the department has been stating assessments automated by IAT could be changed — which is untrue.
"Up until the introduction of the legislation in October 2025, the Department had been incorrectly advising assessment providers and the public that automated IAT outcomes could be changed," he said.
"This had serious consequences."
The Ombudsman also found that the SAS assessment provider performance has been "falling short" of KPIs.
It also found the department has taken a "limited role" in checking training requirements and compliance of assessors using the IAT, and that there are no safeguards protecting the "integrity of the online training".
Prioritise 'meaningful consultation'
The Ombudsman investigation made 10 recommendations to the department, including amending the legislation to allow overrides of automated IAT decisions and conducting a comprehensive review of both the legislation related to the needs assessment process and the business rules underpinning the algorithm.
It also recommended that any changes be "preceded by meaningful consultation with the public" and that the Australian National Audit Office consider a performance audit of the department's use of public resources.
In a statement, Health, Disability and Ageing Minister Mark Butler and Aged Care and Seniors Minister Sam Rae said the government will consider the Ombudsman's report "carefully".
"We’re already acting on many of the recommendations to ensure our aged care system is transparent and reliable, and we’ll examine what further action we can take to give every Australian confidence in the system," they said.
They said the government "accepts or accepts-in-principle all remaining recommendations and will work with other agencies to support responses to recommendations directed outside the portfolio".
In September, The Guardian reported that department staff had warned the Aged Care Minister Sam Rae and Health Minister Mark Butler about removing the IAT's human override function — three days before it was rolled out.
At the time, Motor Neurone Disease Australia CEO Clare Sullivan said the organisations had been "raising serious concerns".
"For months, MND Australia has been raising serious concerns about a system where an algorithm can determine the level of care someone receives without an assessor being able to intervene when the outcome is clearly inappropriate," she said.
"People living with MND do not have the luxury of waiting indefinitely for answers."
She said there needed to be a "clear pathway for experienced assessors to apply clinical judgement when the system gets it wrong".
At the time, the National Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Ageing and Aged Care Council said it had "consistently raised" that the issues with the IAT were "simply not implementation issues" and rather reflect a "failure in national system design".
"Recognising the failures in the IAT is one thing. The real test is what the government does about it," CEO and Warramunga woman Kim Whiteley said.
"The answer cannot simply be another tool built on the same system assumptions. What comes next must deliver assessments that uphold dignity and respect, are culturally safe and appropriate and genuinely understand the person and their circumstances."

Lula clinches historic fourth presidential term in dramatic Brazilian runoff
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
01:01:36 UTC
10:01:36 KST

Brazilian President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva has clinched a historic fourth term in office following a razor-thin runoff triumph over conservative Senator Flavio Bolsonaro, with official results confirming an unassailable lead.
With 100 percent of ballots counted, Brazil's electoral court announced that the veteran leftist leader secured 51.7 percent of the vote against 48.2 percent for Bolsonaro, the son of former president Jair Bolsonaro.
The declaration sparked jubilation among supporters gathered inside and outside the Sao Paulo hotel where the soon-to-be 81-year-old president tracked the tally alongside First Lady Rosangela da Silva, key allies, and close friends.
Lula's triumph marks the first time since Brazil's military dictatorship ended in 1985 that the runner-up in a first-round election went on to capture the presidency.
Bolsonaro had led the October 4, opening round with 47 percent against Lula's 45 percent—a gap of 2.2 million votes—before Lula overhauled the deficit in the decisive second-round showdown.
His new term commences on January 5, 2027.
Historic comeback
The victory caps an extraordinary trajectory for the veteran trade union leader who helped establish the Workers' Party in the 1970s.
After three unsuccessful presidential bids, Lula won his first mandate in 2002 and secured re-election in 2006.
In 2018, he was barred from running and served 580 days in prison before Brazil's Supreme Court annulled his convictions after evidence surfaced proving judicial bias.
He returned to power in 2022 after defeating Jair Bolsonaro.
Following his setback in the opening round this month, Lula overhauled his campaign machinery.
He actively mobilised young voters, urged millions of citizens onto the streets to safeguard democratic institutions, raised public concerns over another Bolsonaro administration, and championed domestic sovereignty.
The announcement followed an evening of heightened tension at polling stations across the nation after a last-minute Supreme Court decision extended voting hours by two hours, a measure that may provoke legal challenges from the Bolsonaro campaign.
Sunday's milestone triumph is widely seen as the crowning victory of Lula's lifelong political journey.
Bolsonaro challenges result
The milestone victory was immediately contested late on Sunday when Bolsonaro announced that his Liberal Party (PL) legal team will formally petition to annul the election.
Addressing supporters following the TSE declaration, Bolsonaro launched a scathing attack against the Federal Supreme Court (STF) over its last-minute ruling extending polling hours nationwide by two hours until 7 pm Brasilia time.
"We will engage our legal team and seek to have these elections annulled," Bolsonaro said.
"I will not accept that the rules of the game have been arbitrarily changed—once again—by Lula's friends on the Federal Supreme Court."
Bolsonaro directed his criticism at STF Justice Cristiano Zanin, who issued the blanket extension following emergency petitions regarding transport blockades and severe weather, pointing out that Zanin previously served as Lula's personal defence lawyer prior to his bench appointment.
The PL challenge is set to trigger intense legal battles in Brasilia as electoral authorities prepare to certify the results.

====================================================================================================

Xi Jinping’s corruption crackdown in the spotlight as China prepares for meeting of top leaders
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
00:58:25 UTC
09:58:25 KST

When Xi Jinping came to power in 2012, he pledged to stamp out corruption all through the ranks of the Communist party. More than a decade later, the pace of investigations has not slowed. Last year, China’s disciplinary authorities opened investigations into more than 1 million people, including more than 100 officials at or above ministerial or provincial level.
As Chinese Communist party (CCP) officials kick off an important meeting this week, discipline – and party loyalty – is high on the agenda. For those who try to read the tea leaves of elite Chinese politics, concern about the apparent lack of discipline is dominating CCP discussions.
The “fifth plenum” began on Monday and is set to focus on “major issues on advancing the party’s full and rigorous self-governance”, according to a Chinese state media. In party-speak, “governance” is a byword for discipline, loyalty and anti-corruption.
As Xi continues to crack down on corruption, the fact that investigations nearly always result in a conviction begs the question over whether targets are truly guilty of corruption, or are they just political rivals to the people in charge.
Kerry Brown, director of the Lau China Institute at King’s College London, explained that in Xi’s worldview, which is obsessed with discipline and loyalty, there may not be much difference between the two. “If you’re corrupt, you’re not politically loyal. If you’re politically loyal, you’re not corrupt,” Brown said.
He added that in the CCP system, “corruption is not just material things”, but also “spiritual corruption”, which includes political disloyalty.
Some analysts argue that the reason that the anti-graft drive is so enduring is because corruption is a feature rather than a bug of an authoritarian, top-down political system with a sprawling bureaucracy that governs 1.4 billion people.
Neil Thomas, a senior fellow at the Asia Society thinktank, said: “Xi has made the party less corrupt and strengthened his control, but he knows that tougher punishment cannot fully resolve the problem of officials putting their own interests ahead of the party’s.
“Xi’s answer is to keep tightening discipline, making anti-corruption a permanent method of governing with no obvious point at which he can declare the job done,” Thomas said.
The job may be never ending, but the plenum is an opportunity to refocus the party’s energy on discipline. The fifth plenum is the fifth of seven gatherings that normally happen in every five-year cycle between CCP congresses. The plenums bring together more than 300 members of the CCP’s Central Committee, the most senior officials in the party hierarchy.
The meeting is particularly significant because it is likely to be the last substantive meeting before next year’s 21st Party Congress, where a new Central Committee will be chosen, and where Xi is expected to be anointed for a fourth term as the head of the CCP.
Eliminating anyone who poses a risk to his authority or to the party’s credibility is a key priority for Xi. And potential threats are everywhere. Nearly 15 years after Xi took office, according to CCP proclamations and a host of recent investigations, the problem is still not stamped out. “It is a deeply ingrained part of [Xi’s] worldview,” said Brown. “Everyone else is corrupt”.
In the past, Xi has warned that the party could “lose its ruling status and inevitably be eliminated by history” if it could not get its house in order. “This is by no means an exaggeration,” he said.
The current focus on party governance comes amid a host of high-profile investigations against senior party and military leaders.
In January, Zhang Youxia, China’s top general and a man second only to Xi in the military hierarchy, was placed under investigation; he was expelled from party last month, having already been removed from the military’s top ruling body, the Central Military Commission (CMC)
A host of other purges means that the CMC, which normally has seven members, has been reduced to just two: Xi and Zhang Shengmin, the CMC’s head of discipline.
Other recent scalps include Ma Xingrui, the former party secretary for Xinjiang, and Huang Qifan, the former mayor of Chongqing.
Huang had long been known as the ultimate survivor in Chinese politics because of his connections to the scandals in the early 2010s in which Xi’s political rival, Bo Xilai, the former Party boss for Chongqing, was embroiled in the death of the British businessman Neil Heywood. Bo was ultimately convicted of bribery and embezzlement, for which he is serving a life sentence, but Huang survived. No longer.
Some China analysts have asked whether the recent purges, which have reached the highest echelons of the Party and military ranks, indicate instability in the regime. But Xi likely sees it differently. Corruption investigations demonstrate who is in charge. Plus, Brown added, they are “the most easy and natural tool by which to enforce unity and discipline”.

Republican Congressman Mike Rogers, who is running in a tight race against Democratic rival Abdul El-Sayed, has tried to distance himself from the president’s tariff policy on the auto sector.
Rogers on Oct 25 hailed Trump’s tariffs for securing manufacturing investments for Michigan by Chevrolet and Detroit Diesel, but said “the automobile portion of these Canadian tariffs worries me a little bit”.
“There’s some good and there’s some things we have to work on,” he told NBC programme Meet The Press. REUTERS

The Trump administration has encouraged former Hungarian Prime Minister Viktor Orban to consider running for UN secretary-general, with Russia and China said to be receptive to the idea, The Wall Street Journal reported Sunday.
According to the newspaper, officials from three countries confirmed that Washington had raised Orban's potential candidacy, which could make him a joint candidate backed by the US, Russia and China. The proposal is awaiting a final decision.
A US State Department official acknowledged that the idea might initially sound far-fetched but argued that the three powers could secure sufficient support in the UN Security Council.
The official estimated that eight of the council's 15 members would "comfortably" support Orban, with 10 votes potentially within reach. Britain and France, both permanent members with veto power, could oppose the proposal, although the editorial noted that they have generally been cautious about using their vetoes.
The newspaper reported that Orban's name repeatedly surfaced in discussions among US, Chinese and Russian officials about potential candidates. According to the editorial, American officials eventually began asking "Why not Mr. Orban?"
The proposal reflects the Trump administration's ideological alignment with Orban, whom the editorial described as "the dream MAGA-conservative candidate." It cited his opposition to mass migration, liberal nongovernmental organizations and Hungary's left-leaning courts and media, as well as his frequent clashes with the European Union.
Despite his close alignment with China, Orban has maintained an image as a defender of Western civilization, the editorial said.
US President Donald Trump endorsed Orban in Hungary's April 2026 election, while Vice President JD Vance campaigned for him. A third source familiar with the process told the newspaper that both were expected to support Orban again if he entered the UN race, although an announcement was being held back until after the US midterm elections.
US officials initially contacted Orban to gauge his interest in the position. He was reportedly receptive but remained cautious, with the nationalist politician unwilling to run unless he believed he had a strong chance of winning. Orban declined to comment.
The editorial contrasted Orban with other potential candidates, describing the field as dominated by figures with international bureaucratic or diplomatic experience.
One official from another country characterized Orban as a "general" rather than a "secretary," a view shared by the US official, who argued that Orban possessed the ideological convictions and political resolve to challenge the UN establishment.
Lana Nusseibeh, a diplomat from the United Arab Emirates (UAE), entered the race the previous week.
The editorial said the UAE's alleged support for a paramilitary force involved in Sudan's civil war could weigh against her candidacy, although it described her as qualified and gaining momentum. Nusseibeh was scheduled to answer questions Tuesday, followed by a new Security Council straw poll Wednesday.
Additional candidates could still enter the contest.
Current UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres' term ends on Dec. 31, 2026. The editorial criticized his leadership and argued that Orban's potential candidacy would expose the extent of the institution's decline.

What challenges await Brazil's Lula in his fourth term as president?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
00:52:54 UTC
09:52:54 KST

What challenges await Brazil's Lula in his fourth term as president?
President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva will have to wrestle with a divided Brazil, an unfriendly Congress, feeble public finances and a Donald Trump-shaped menace during his unprecedented fourth term.
Days before his 81st birthday, the former union leader won Sunday's runoff with 51.7 percent of the vote over 48.2 percent for his right-wing challenger Flavio Bolsonaro.
The narrow result confirms the political divide that has split Brazil for a decade and shows that Bolsonarism remains strong, despite its far-right leader's 27-year prison sentence for attempting a coup.
Here are the main challenges awaiting Lula in his next mandate.
Governability
As in his current term, Lula will not have a majority in Congress.
Legislative elections earlier this month bolstered the right, making Bolsonaro's Liberal Party the leading force with 121 out of 513 deputies and 28 out of 81 senators.
To get his proposals through, Lula will depend heavily on the so‑called "Centrao," a bloc of center-right parties that usually backs whoever is in power in exchange for benefits.
But negotiating with them is becoming increasingly difficult, according to political scientist Mayra Goulart of the Federal University of Rio de Janeiro.
Lawmakers now decide the fate of an ever larger share of the federal budget, she told AFP, giving them "more independence from the executive."
Money
Economically, "Brazil's three big problems are the fiscal problem, the fiscal problem, and the fiscal problem," economist Mauro Rochlin of the Getulio Vargas Foundation (FGV) told AFP.
The state spends more than it collects, public debt exceeds 80 percent of GDP, and Brazil's central bank maintains one of the world's highest interest rates to contain inflation.
The situation "could very quickly turn into an economic crisis," said Rochlin.
Adjustment is inevitable but difficult since it involves "unpopular measures" and confronting "very powerful lobbies within Congress," he said.
The challenge is likely going to clash with Lula's flagship welfare programs, which have lifted millions out of poverty, and which he expanded during the campaign to win voters -- drawing fierce criticism from the opposition.
Insecurity
The election campaign was dominated by security concerns, with violence a huge worry for many Brazilians.
Accused by the opposition of having a soft touch, Lula will be under pressure to show results, particularly by tackling criminal groups and militias that control territory in several cities.
On the campaign trail, he said he would support lowering the age of criminal responsibility from 18 to 16 for heinous crimes, while the political right wants to reduce it to 14 years.
Trump
Lula campaigned on a pledge to protect Brazilian sovereignty as concerns grow about the broadening interventions of the United States across Latin America.
Trump slapped tariffs on Brazil last year in retaliation for legal proceedings against his ally Jair Bolsonaro, followed by another 25 percent tariff on some products this year.
Brazil's president will have to manage relations with Washington without relaxing his anti-imperialist tone, all while the Trump administration increasingly asserts itself in the region.
Right-wing leaders across Latin America have meanwhile aligned with Trump in a trend dubbed the "Orange Wave," in reference to the US leader's complexion.
Although ideology "matters for symbolic encounters," it is "not that relevant" in practice, according to Oliver Stuenkel, an international relations professor at the FGV.
He points to Brazil-Argentina relations as an example.
"Deep down, the substance of the relationship hasn't changed that much" despite Argentine leader Javier Milei's insults toward Lula, Stuenkel told AFP.
(FRANCE 24 with AFP)

Lula’s Surprise Brazil Victory Sends Assets Lower

Lula’s Surprise Brazil Victory Sends Assets Lower

====================================================================================================

Brazil election drama: anti-Israel Lula takes lead over Bolsonaro's son in vote count
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
00:38:48 UTC
09:38:48 KST

Brazil's left-wing President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva scored a dramatic and unexpected victory overnight Sunday into Monday in the country's fiercely contested presidential election, defeating far-right candidate Flávio Bolsonaro, son of jailed former President Jair Bolsonaro. With 99.9% of the votes counted, Lula secured 51.77%, compared with 48.23% for Bolsonaro. Although relatively narrow, the margin was clear and decisive, defying polls that had predicted a razor-thin victory for Bolsonaro.
Bolsonaro's defeat is a blow to U.S. President Donald Trump, who did not explicitly endorse him but would have seen his growing influence in Latin America expand further with a right-wing victory. Lula, by contrast, has frequently clashed with Trump. His victory is also unwelcome news for Israel. The incumbent president, who at 80 will begin his fourth nonconsecutive term, is one of Israel's fiercest critics worldwide and has repeatedly accused it of "genocide."
Brazil uses electronic voting machines, allowing results to be counted rapidly overnight. Polling stations were originally scheduled to close Sunday at 5 p.m. local time (10 p.m. in Israel), but Lula's campaign petitioned to extend voting following reports of public transportation disruptions in several areas, including São Paulo. Brazil's Supreme Court subsequently extended voting nationwide by two hours. Bolsonaro's campaign also requested an extension, citing rainy weather in the country's south.
Bolsonaro's defeat came as a surprise after he entered the decisive runoff as the favorite. In the first round earlier this month, when several other candidates were also competing, he finished first with 47% of the vote, compared with 45% for the incumbent. That result had surprised pollsters, who predicted Lula would finish first by a relatively comfortable margin. In the 2022 election, when Lula defeated his current rival's father, Jair Bolsonaro, his margin of victory was also much narrower than polls had forecast, prompting speculation that surveys were once again underestimating the younger Bolsonaro's support. Historical precedent had also favored Bolsonaro: Never before had a candidate who finished second in the first round of a Brazilian presidential election gone on to win the decisive runoff. That changed overnight with Lula's victory.
The ideological divide between the two candidates could hardly have been greater. Bolsonaro, 45, and Lula, 80, hold sharply opposing views on a range of issues, from Brazil's relations with the United States to climate change and welfare policy. Lula's victory also dashed hopes among Latin America's right-wing movements that the conservative wave sweeping the region over the past year, with election victories in Chile, Peru and Colombia, would reach its most populous country and largest economy. Instead, Lula's reelection leaves Brazil and Mexico, Latin America's second-most populous country, led by President Claudia Sheinbaum, under center-left leadership.
A victory visit to the Western Wall?
As noted, incumbent President Lula secured his fourth nonconsecutive term overnight. He previously served as Brazil's president from 2003 to 2010 and won the presidency again in 2022. He was released from prison in 2019 after spending more than 500 days behind bars, and his corruption convictions were annulled in 2021. In recent months, he faced an increasingly difficult election campaign amid public dissatisfaction over the cost of living and concerns about personal security. His rival, Bolsonaro, made a tough stance on crime the cornerstone of his campaign and pledged to lower food prices. Bolsonaro, who has served as a senator since 2019, also promised judicial reform, which he planned to pursue in part through the next president's power to appoint at least three of the Supreme Court's 11 justices, with several retirements expected in the coming years.
Bolsonaro and Lula also differ sharply in their attitudes toward Israel. Flávio Bolsonaro, like his father Jair, is a staunch supporter of Israel, and their political movement is known in Brazil for its support for Israel and the Jewish people. Israeli flags are traditionally displayed at rallies held by both father and son. At his final campaign rally Saturday in Barra da Tijuca, in Rio de Janeiro state, Flávio himself was filmed waving an Israeli flag.
Earlier this year, the younger Bolsonaro made his fourth visit to Israel alongside his brother Eduardo. He toured Samaria in the northern West Bank, prayed at the Western Wall and pledged to move Brazil's embassy to Jerusalem. "We appreciate and love Israel," he said at the time. "We support Israel's right to defend itself in every way."
Estevam Hernandes, Bolsonaro's personal pastor and one of his closest associates, who has accompanied him throughout the campaign, told ynet's Itamar Eichner in an interview Sunday that if Bolsonaro wins, he could make a victory visit to Israel as early as next month.
"Flávio Bolsonaro is a man who loves Israel with all his heart. We agreed that we would celebrate his victory in Jerusalem. We will visit Israel in November and bring Brazil's future economy minister with us, and Flávio may join us as well. In any case, the plan is to bring Flávio to the Western Wall to celebrate the victory," Hernandes said.
Lula, by contrast, has become one of Israel's fiercest critics worldwide during his current term, particularly since the October 7 massacre and the war in Gaza. In February 2024, he accused Israel of committing genocide, comparing its actions to those of Hitler. Two months later, he incorrectly claimed that more than 12 million children had been killed in the Gaza war. That same year, he recalled Brazil's ambassador from Israel, and in 2025 refused to approve the appointment of a new Israeli ambassador to Brasília. In his address to the UN General Assembly this past September, although he condemned Hamas, he also accused Netanyahu's government of "the genocide of women and children in Gaza."
$12 million for a movie and a promise to pardon his father
Both candidates have faced allegations of corruption involving family members and political allies. Bolsonaro himself is currently embroiled in a sprawling investigation into corruption, money laundering and tax evasion. As part of the affair, he acknowledged seeking approximately $12 million from Daniel Vorcaro, a former banker, to finance a film about his father's life.
His father, Jair Bolsonaro, is still serving the 27-year prison sentence imposed after he was convicted of attempting a coup following his defeat to Lula in the 2022 election, although he is currently under house arrest for medical reasons. In the run-up to the vote, Lula repeatedly portrayed the younger Bolsonaro as a threat to democracy, while Bolsonaro pledged to pursue a pardon for his father if elected.
Since his defeat in the first round, Lula has attempted to woo undecided voters with costly economic incentives. His government approved a debt-relief program for small businesses, among other measures, and promised free public transportation on weekends. But those efforts appeared to have fallen short. At a polling station in Rio de Janeiro, Elba Marques, a 75-year-old retiree, said her vote for Bolsonaro was a vote against Lula's Workers' Party rather than an endorsement of Bolsonaro himself.
"I can't stand hearing the same man say for 40 years that he's going to fix Brazil. It's the same promise over and over again," she said.
Bolsonaro, speaking after casting his ballot at a polling station in Rio de Janeiro earlier Sunday, said the time had come for change. "Brazil can’t take another four years the way things are ... Everyone’s life has got worse," he warned, as supporters nearby chanted, "Lula, thief, you belong in jail!"
Lula: It's either our flag or the US flag
Lula, meanwhile, once again sought to frame the election as a referendum on Brazil's independence, portraying his opponent as a proxy for U.S. President Donald Trump. Speaking to reporters after casting his ballot in his political stronghold of São Bernardo do Campo, near São Paulo, he accused Bolsonaro of wanting to "govern under the U.S. flag." Lula said Brazilians had to choose between someone who would defend their national flag and someone who would defend the American flag. Perhaps to reinforce that message, Lula also posed for photographs holding up the Brazilian flag inside the polling station.
The remarks came against the backdrop of Lula's sharp criticism of Trump throughout the campaign and his warnings about attempted U.S. interference in Brazil's election. The Trump administration imposed steep tariffs on Brazilian exports, announced sanctions against the Supreme Court justice who oversaw the investigation that led to Jair Bolsonaro's conviction, and designated drug trafficking organizations as foreign terrorist organizations. Some experts suggested the latter move may have been intended to portray Lula as soft on crime.
Flávio Bolsonaro, for his part, has boasted of his close ties to White House officials and insisted that Brazil must negotiate better deals with the Trump administration, including in the rare-earth minerals sector. Brazil's reserves are estimated at up to 21 million metric tons, second only to China's. Politically, however, Bolsonaro denies receiving assistance from the U.S. administration.

Brazil election: Lula, iconic working class president, wins historic fourth term in dramatic comeback
- Lula won an unprecedented fourth term, beating Flavio Bolsonaro in a shock comeback that defied polls and slowed a right-wing shift in Latin America.
- The 80-year-old campaigned on lower poverty, less inequality and welfare gains, while warning Bolsonaro would cut social spending and weaken Brazil’s sovereignty.
- He now faces a hard term with a more conservative Congress, weak growth, high debt and pressure for spending cuts, which could limit his power and spark unrest.
AI generated
SAO PAULO – Brazilian President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva won an unprecedented fourth term on Oct 25, the country’s electoral court said, in a shock result that defied polls, precedent and global anti-incumbent sentiment to put the brakes on a wave of right-wing election victories across Latin America.
Lula, an icon of the global left and the most dominant force in Brazilian politics in this century, defeated Senator Flavio Bolsonaro, the eldest son of former president Jair Bolsonaro.
The senator had finished first in the election’s first round but lost in the runoff by over four million votes, said he would ask for the result to be annulled due to a Supreme Court ruling on Oct 25 that extended voting for two hours.
Bolsonaro’s refusal to concede defeat has echoes of his father’s reaction after losing to Lula in 2022. Former president Jair Bolsonaro never accepted his loss and was later given a 27-year sentence for plotting a coup to remain in power.
The scale of Flavio Bolsonaro’s loss to Lula – by more than twice his father’s losing margin – and the fact his campaign also asked for an extension due to rains in the south, make any annulment unlikely, analysts said.
Mario Braga, a Latin America analyst at the risk consultancy RANE, said there could be right-wing protests in coming days, but “it’s very improbable that it will lead to the reversal of the result”.
Comeback king
For Lula, his victory marks another comeback in a career full of them. The 80-year-old was jailed from 2018 to 2019 on corruption charges that were later overturned, paving the way for him to beat Jair Bolsonaro in the 2022 election.
“He is a statesman, a giant,” leftist federal lawmaker Erika Hilton, who was with Lula in Sao Paulo during the vote count, told Reuters.
At times, Lula’s re-election looked like a long shot, as voters soured on him and his Workers’ Party after years of corruption scandals and rising prices.
Sweeping societal changes also left the former metalworker and union leader looking out of touch with an increasingly app-based economy and its growing ranks of informal workers.
A Tokyo-listed exchange-traded fund tracking Brazil’s Bovespa index fell nearly 15% in Asia trade on news of Lula’s victory.
Pollsters said better-than-expected turnout had powered Lula to victory. Leonardo Barreto, the co-founder of consultancy Think Policy, said voters had chosen Lula’s familiar embrace over Bolsonaro’s novelty.
“People today are choosing between change, with some apprehension, and a known path, which guarantees certain rights,” he said.
During the campaign, Lula pointed to a track record of falling poverty and inequality, while unemployment, illiteracy and deforestation hit record lows during his third term.
He warned that Bolsonaro would cut welfare spending, backslide on social advances and hand over Brazil’s sovereignty to US President Donald Trump, whose State Department led a campaign to get the Bolsonaros back to power.
Lula’s win deprives Trump of a major addition to what has been a growing bloc of friendly right-wing Latin American governments that have embraced Washington’s agenda on security and migration.
Celso Amorim, a former Lula foreign minister, told Reuters the leftist “would be very important for establishing a point of balance in Latin America. Lula is that balance”.
Late-campaign boost
Lula becomes the first candidate since Brazil’s return to democracy in the 1980s to be elected after finishing second in the first round.
Lula, who was president between 2003 and 2011, campaigned on a potent mix of pragmatism and populism that has shaped his career in national politics for half a century, rolling out a slew of reforms aimed at improving the lives of workers and poor Brazilians.
These gained steam with late-campaign pledges that ranged from free nationwide weekend public transport, which has to be formally submitted to Congress, to a 15% increase in his trademark welfare programme that is already being implemented.
Lula also championed a constitutional amendment that became Brazil’s biggest labour reform in decades, which passed with wide support in Congress.
Challenges ahead
Still, Lula’s fourth term could be his most difficult yet, after Brazil elected its most conservative Congress since returning to democracy in the 1980s.
Combined, Bolsonaro’s Liberal Party (PL) and allied parties could control over 280 seats in the Lower House and up to 50 seats in the Senate, enough for comfortable opposition majorities in both chambers.
That may deepen recent trends of presidents ceding power to Congress on the budget, major legislation and key nominations.
Lula faces an economy that his government forecasts will grow a meager 2.3% in 2027, adding to fiscal concerns tied to high interest rates and public debt that has risen past 82% of GDP, the highest since the pandemic.
The President’s critics blame spending, though borrowing costs have driven most of the increase in debt.
Goldman Sachs said it expects Lula to make modest progress at most to contain spending in a fourth term, as he stays committed to a state-led growth model.
Surging household debt also concerns economists. Trying to address the issue, Lula rolled out a provisional ban on online betting and unveiled a new debt relief program during the campaign.
The incoming right-wing Congress will try to pass structural reforms that favor businesses, experts say, prompting spending cuts that could trigger popular backlash.
Challenging legislative reality
Still, Lula’s fourth term could be his most difficult yet, after Brazil elected its most conservative Congress since returning to democracy in the 1980s.
Combined, Bolsonaro’s Liberal Party (PL) and allied parties could control more than 280 seats in the Lower House and up to 50 seats in the Senate, enough for comfortable majorities in both chambers.
“He is likely to be a lame duck from the start,” said Oliver Stuenkel, a professor of international relations at the Getulio Vargas Foundation in Sao Paulo.
The incoming legislature will likely deepen recent trends of presidents ceding power to Congress, Stuenkel said, predicting Lula will face waning influence over Supreme Court nominations, unwieldy party coalitions, and even the threat of impeachment.
Economic headwinds
Lula faces an economy that his government forecasts will grow a meagre 2.3% in 2027, adding to fiscal concerns tied to high interest rates and public debt that has risen past 82% of gross domestic product, the highest since the Covid-19 pandemic.
The President’s critics blame spending, though interest costs have driven most of the increase in debt.
Goldman Sachs said it expects Lula to make modest progress at most to contain spending in a fourth term, as he stays committed to a state-led growth model.
Surging household debt also concerns economists. Trying to address the issue, Lula rolled out a provisional ban on online betting and unveiled a new debt relief programme during the campaign.
The incoming right-wing Congress will try to pass structural reforms that favour businesses, experts say, prompting spending cuts that could fuel social upheaval. REUTERS

Kharkiv establishes first anti-drone corridor
This was reported by a Ukrinform correspondent.
The work was recently completed. The corridor is seven meters high. As Oleh Syniehubov, head of the Kharkiv Regional State Administration, confirmed to journalists, there are plans to cover other sections as well. The current priority is the section of the ring road from the “Losk” car market to the Oleksiyivka residential area. This is approximately 14 km. The corridor will be constructed using funds from the regional budget.
“This is what will happen in the near future. This is what we see as critically necessary to do. We will allocate about 10 million hryvnias for this,” said Syniehubov.
As reported by Ukrinform, on the morning of May 21, Russian troops used an FPV drone to attack a truck traveling on the Kharkiv Ring Road, killing the 40-year-old driver. Following this, a section of the ring road (the M-03 highway between km 491 and km 501, from Feldman Ecopark to the Lyptsivske Intersection) was closed to traffic.
In July, the installation of anti-drone nets was completed on this section, but the road remained closed to traffic.

Said Amori and Tarek Chouiref
26 October 2026•Update: 26 October 2026
Israel placed eight Palestinian prisoners in solitary confinement for making a cake to celebrate the possible departure of National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir from the government, Israel Hayom reported Sunday.
The prisoners at Lavi prison had saved food over several days to make the cake, hoping the Oct. 27 election would end Ben-Gvir’s tenure, according to the newspaper.
Prison staff found the cake in a cell, prompting officials to order disciplinary proceedings against the eight and send them to solitary confinement.
Ben-Gvir, whose ministry oversees the Israel Prison Service, has tightened restrictions on Palestinian prisoners, including cutting food allocations and prison amenities.
Whether he retains his post will depend on the election results and coalition negotiations involving his Jewish Power party.
Palestinian rights groups accuse Israeli authorities of systematic abuses against prisoners including torture, starvation, solitary confinement and denial of medical care.
