Brazil elections: Lula wins another term, beating Flavio Bolsonaro
Published October 25, 2026last updated October 26, 2026
What you need to know
- Left-wing incumbent Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva defeated Flavio Bolsonaro, the son of the far-right former President Jair Bolsonaro
- It was a tight runoff, with Lula winning 51.7% of the vote against Bolsonaro’s 48.2%, official results showed
- In his victory speech, Lula urged more regulation of big tech platforms after allegations that Meta interfered in the race
- Several Latin American leaders congratulated Lula on win
- Bolsonaro refused to concede, calls for election results to be annulled
- Brazilians voted in the final round of the presidential election
Keep reading for the latest updates from the second round of Brazil's presidential election on Sunday, October 25.
Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click here to add us as a Preferred Source on Google. Then tap the "Star" or "Preferred" to keep DW News at the top of your feed.
Flavio Bolsonaro rejects defeat, seeks annulment of Brazil election
Right-wing presidential candidate Flavio Bolsonaro has rejected his defeat to incumbent Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva in Brazil’s presidential run-off, calling for the election to be annulled over a two-hour extension of voting hours.
Speaking to reporters after the electoral court declared Lula the winner, Bolsonaro said he could not accept the result. He criticized a decision by Supreme Court judge Cristiano Zanin to extend voting hours nationwide, arguing that it had changed the rules of the election.
"What happened today was not normal. It was unacceptable," Bolsonaro said, arguing that the nationwide extension had undermined equal treatment between states. He said he would take legal action against the result.
Lula’s campaign had requested the extension, citing difficulties transporting voters to polling stations in several states. Bolsonaro’s campaign had also sought extra voting time, but only in municipalities across five states, citing heavy rain, flooding and power outages.
Lula says Brazilians voted to defend democracy, vows to resist US influence
Brazilians voted to "guarantee democracy," President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva said Sunday after beating Flavio Bolsonaro to win an unprecedented fourth term.
In a post on X, Lula thanked Brazilians, particularly young people who took to the streets in defense of democracy, saying: "This victory belongs to a people who believe, who fight, and who never give up on building a more just, sovereign, and democratic Brazil."
In his victory speech, Lula reiterated that Brazil would "not accept being anyone’s backyard," a recurring campaign message defending the country’s sovereignty against US influence. The stance may have helped him win votes, with some voters viewing Washington’s actions as interference.
Relations between the two countries deteriorated in 2025, when the US imposed tariffs on Brazil in retaliation for legal proceedings against former president Jair Bolsonaro, who was later convicted of coup-plotting.
Speaking in a hoarse voice, Lula thanked his campaign team and Brazilians, particularly young people who took to the streets to defend democracy. He described the result as a "loss for negativity, lies."
The re-elected president also promised better regulation of big tech platforms, after Meta was the subject of legal complaints over alleged "interference" throughout the polarizing campaign.
Latin American leaders congratulate Lula on election victory
Several Latin American leaders congratulated leftist President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva on his victory.
Chilean President Jose Antonio Kast said he had spoken to Lula and congratulated him, adding that "Chile and Brazil have a lot of shared future ahead."
Mexico’s left-wing President Claudia Sheinbaum congratulated Lula on his victory, writing on X: "Long live democracy, the people of Brazil won. Congratulations, President Lula!"
The presidents of Uruguay, Paraguay, Panama and Bolivia also congratulated Lula in posts on X.
Cuba’s president congratulated Lula on X, calling him "dear brother" and praising his victory as a win for peace, sovereignty and social justice.
IN PICTURES: Lula supporters celebrate, while Bolsonaro's fans disappointed
Brazil's Lula defeats conservative Flavio Bolsonaro in presidential election
Brazilian leftist President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva has won a fourth term in office, defeating right-wing challenger Flávio Bolsonaro in a presidential runoff, electoral authorities said.
Lula overcame his first-round defeat to Bolsonaro to secure victory in the runoff. The nearly 81-year-old leader won 51.7% of the vote, compared with 48.2% for Flavio Bolsonaro, the son of former president Jair Bolsonaro.
The campaign was marred by scandals and mudslinging. Sunday’s vote was thrown into confusion after a last-minute Supreme Court ruling extended voting by two hours, following Lula’s claim that buses had been taken off the roads in several cities, preventing some voters from reaching polling stations.
Pollsters said higher-than-expected turnout appeared to have benefited Lula. Conservative candidates in Brazil typically lead early in the count, while left-wing candidates gain ground as votes from poorer, more populous northeastern states come in.
In regards to foreign policy in his next term, Lula will have to manage relations with Washington while maintaining his anti-imperialist stance, as the Trump administration increasingly asserts its influence across the region. Flavio Bolsonaro had campaigned on a promise of closer cooperation with Washington.
Around 159 million Brazilians were eligible to vote. Under Lula’s left-wing Workers’ Party, unemployment fell to a record low, poverty declined, the minimum wage rose and deforestation in the Amazon decreased. Congress also approved the gradual introduction of a five-day working week with two days off.
However, rising living costs, high public debt, Lula’s spending policies and a scandal involving alleged pension fraud weighed on his government. The economic challenges left many voters dissatisfied with his record and open to a return of the Bolsonaro family to power.
Lula finished the first round with 45% of the vote, two percentage points behind Flavio Bolsonaro. He became the first candidate since Brazil restored direct presidential elections in 1989 to overcome a first-round deficit and win the runoff.
The former trade unionist, who served as president from 2003 to 2010 before returning to office in 2023, now faces a challenging fourth term with a strong right-wing opposition.
Votes tallied in Brazil's presidential election after polls close
The electronic voting system used in the country means that a final result could be determined within a matter of hours, although that final result is expected to be tight.
Here's a DW infographic on where the results stand:
Voting extended after complaints by both sides
Brazil's Supreme Court has moved to extend voting time in the presidential election until 7 p.m. local time (2200 GMT), giving voters an additional two hours.
The decision comes amid complaints from Lula's team that public bus services had been hampered, blocking people from getting to polling stations.
At the same time, Bolsonaro's team complained of weather conditions in certain regions making it more difficult for people to get out and vote.
Lula asks for polls to stay open longer after people 'barred from voting'
President Lula has requested an extension to poll opening hours after buses were taken out of circulation in Sao Paolo, the country's largest city, which he said prevented many people from voting.
"We are asking the Supreme Court to extend the electoral process so that those who were effectively barred from voting, due to the dirty tactics of mayors, can still cast their votes," Lula said, according to AFP.
Lula said 40% of buses in the city had been prevented from going into service, a claim that matched local media reports saying 75 buses had been blocked from leaving garages.
"I've never complained about anything in any election before. Whether I won or lost, I'd just accept it and get ready for the next one. But this time, something abominable is happening," he said.
"No one should give up on voting just because some scoundrel of a business owner or some crooked, criminal mayor tried to stop the people from casting their ballots."
Results show Brazilian voters in Germany back Lula
Brazilians in Germany have voted overwhelmingly for Lula, according to figures posted by Brazilian Embassies across the country and seen by DW's Portuguese service.
The left-wing incumbent, Lula, won 79.09% of the ballots cast by the 20,923 voters across Germany. This marks an increase on the 71.9% he won in the first round.
Brazilian voters in Germany could vote at embassies in Berlin, Hamburg, Cologne, Frankfurt and Munich.
The German capital saw the greatest support for Lula, with 88.77% of the votes going his way. Frankfurt was the city with the greatest support for Bolsonaro, but on 29.03% he still trailed his opponent by some margin.
The turnout also increased in the second round in comparison to the first round when it stood at 19,322. However, for both rounds, only around half of the 41,552 eligible voters turned out to vote. Across the world, there are some 918,900 eligible voters for Sunday's election.
IN PHOTOS: Almost 160 million called out to vote
What role is Trump playing in Brazil's election?
Although he hasn't endorsed either candidate, US President Donald Trump is close to the Bolsonaro family.
Not only did the senior Bolsonaro imitate Trump's rhetoric and policies, he also refused to concede defeat after losing to Lula in 2022, leading to his imprisonment for an attempted coup, provoking comparisons with Trump's own defeat to Joe Biden in 2020.
On the other side, Lula has presented himself as a defense against US interference.
The right "wants to govern with the American flag," Lula said after casting his ballot on Sunday.
A Bolsonaro win would mark a further move in Latin America toward pro-US far-right leaders, following in the footsteps of countries such as Colombia, Chile and Peru.
Results expected within hours of polls closing
The president of Brazil's Superior Electoral Court, Kassio Nunes Marques, has said he expects the winner of Sunday's vote to be announced officially between 8.30 p.m. and 9 p.m. (2330 and 0000 GMT), according to A Folha de Sao Paolo.
Brazil uses an electronic voting system meaning that ballots can be tallied quicker than in elections where paper votes are counted by hand.
However, the gap between the winner and loser is expected to be small, with the two running head-to-head in pre-election polls.
Supreme Court president urges candidates to accept result of vote
The head of Brazil's Supreme Federal Court, Edson Fachin, has called for the candidates to respect the result of Sunday's vote.
"It's important to remember that all authority and power comes from the people and, thus, it is fundamental that the choices that derive from the manifestation of popular sovereignty are respected," he said as he left his local polling station, according to A Folha de Sao Paulo.
"Brazil needs peace and calm to, from tomorrow, be able to confront the major challenges in many areas that demand the presence of the state."
Some observers have posited that Flavio Bolsonaro could refuse to accept a Lula victory, like his father before him, with the potential for violence to erupt.

Lula wins fourth term as Brazil president after historic upset over far-right Flávio Bolsonaro
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
00:19:05 UTC
09:19:05 KST

Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, the Brazilian president, has staged a dramatic election fightback, defeating his far-right opponent, Flávio Bolsonaro, to claim a historic fourth term in power.
With 100% of votes counted the 80-year-old leftist received 4.4m votes more than Bolsonaro, with a 51.79% share to his 45-year-old rival’s 48.21%. However, soon after Brazil’s electoral authority confirmed Lula’s victory, Bolsonaro refused to concede defeat and asked for the results to be annulled.
Lula narrowly lost the first round of the election to Bolsonaro in early October, casting his political future into doubt and plunging progressive Brazilians into three weeks of despair. Never, since the return of democracy in the 1980s, has the first round runner-up won the second vote.
But Lula did precisely that on Sunday, prompting joyous scenes on the streets of São Paulo, where he had been following events, and at the hotel where he was watching the count.
Addressing a packed crowd of ecstatic supporters in a São Paulo conference hall, Lula said: “We are going to change the way that this country is governed … This election was a defeat for denialism … I want to thank God and to thank you, Brazilian men and women of this country … it was democracy that made this happen.”
After the result was confirmed, Alexandre Padilha, Lula’s health minister, said: “This is a huge victory for the Brazilian people who in the second round had the chance to think about what President Lula means for the environment, for the defense of our national health service and our education system and the Brazilian constitution. And the risks that the extreme right candidate entailed.”
“It’s a massive victory – not just for Brazil. It’s also an important signal to the rest of Latin America and to the world,” Padilha added.
The 8o-year-old appears to have made up much of the difference through what his allies had identified as his main opportunity: persuading his voters to turn out. After a record abstention rate of 21.08% in the first round, which disproportionately affected Lula voters because they tend to live further from polling stations, the rate fell to 19.21%.
Speaking during Lula’s victory speech, Bolsonaro said it was “impossible to concede the election result” and that his legal team would seek to have the election annulled.
Following in the footsteps of his father, former president Jair Bolsonaro, who four years ago also refused to acknowledge his defeat to Lula – before attempting a coup and being convicted for it – the senator cited a supreme court justice’s decision to extend voting hours as the alleged reason.
His speech made no mention of the fact that his campaign had also asked the electoral court to extend voting hours, but he nevertheless said Justice Cristiano Zanin’s decision to extend voting by two hours to 7pm “was not normal, it was unacceptable” and amounted to “changing the rules of the game while the game was being played”.
For Lula, who turns 81 on Tuesday, the victory represents a sensational final chapter in a storied political career that began when he emerged as a union leader in São Paulo’s industrial suburbs in the late 1970s.
After entering politics, the former factory worker who was born in rural poverty made three unsuccessful presidential bids, in 1989, 1994 and 1998, before finally becoming Brazil’s first elected working-class president in 2002.
Lula stepped down after the maximum two consecutive terms allowed by the constitution but returned to power after winning the 2022 election against Bolsonaro’s father, then the incumbent president Jair Bolsonaro, who was subsequently jailed for plotting a coup.
Lula’s win is bad news for Jair Bolsonaro who is serving a 27-year sentence for that botched power grab and was hoping to be freed and given a role in government had his son prevailed.
It is also a blow for Donald Trump, the Bolsonaro clan’s most important international ally. The US president had been hoping Bolsonaro would become the latest in a series of pro-Trump leaders to take power in Latin America, including Abelardo de la Espriella in Colombia, Daniel Noboa in Ecuador, José Antonio Kast in Chile and Javier Milei in Argentina.
Confirmation of Lula’s victory was greeted with anger and bewilderment in Brasília, where Bolsonaro is living under house arrest and where his son watched the count.
On Sunday night, political leaders applauded Lula. Mexican president Claudia Sheinbaum said: “Long live democracy, the people of Brazil won. Congratulations, President Lula!”, while Paraguayan president Santiago Peña said “I salute the Brazilian people for this great democratic journey.”
Lula’s victory came after his supporters staged two massive shows of support on Saturday, with more than a million people flocking to Rio’s Copacabana beach and an even larger number marching on Paulista Avenue.
Many people on the streets of São Paulo were angry at an apparent attempt by pro-Bolsonaro politicians to derail the election by sabotaging public transport in Lula-leaning voting areas across the country.
“I think it’s another coup attempt that the extreme right is trying in Brazil. But we need to really fight so we can win,” said Lucas Lopes, a 32-year-old from São Paulo who works with public relations.
But that alleged attempt to scupper a Lula victory failed.
“I’ll be sincere: in the first round the left failed. But in the second round they woke up,” said Caio Marques, a 40-year-old photographer from Franca, a city in the interior of São Paulo state. “And there is no coup that will take this away from us.”
“I feel so, so happy … There’s not enough room in my chest for all this joy. Lula’s victory represents so much. It means life for those who believe in love and in life,” said Maicon Douglas Bento, a 34-year-old photographer, as he joined tens of thousands of jubilant Brazilians on Paulista Avenue at the heart of São Paulo.

S. Korea to expand international flights in winter season
South Korea will increase international passenger flights for the winter season, with more services to Japan and China amid strong travel demand, the transport ministry said Sunday, Yonhap reports.
5,353 weekly international flights are scheduled on 264 routes connecting 44 countries during the winter season from Oct. 25 to March 27, 2027, according to the Ministry of Land, Infrastructure and Transport.
The flights will be operated by 84 airlines, including 11 South Korean carriers and 73 foreign airlines.
The weekly total marks a 7.6 percent increase from 4,973 flights during last year's winter season, surpassing the pre-pandemic level of 4,980 in the winter of 2019.
The expansion will be driven mainly by additional services to Japan and China, with weekly flights increasing by 314 and 232, respectively, amid robust inbound and outbound travel demand.
As reported earlier, South Korea renewed its offer Friday to hold military talks with North Korea to discuss their conflicting views on where the inter-Korean border sits, seeking to ease tensions sparked by last month's land mine blast inside the Demilitarized Zone (DMZ)

Lula holds off far right with victory in Brazil presidential election
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
00:16:29 UTC
09:16:29 KST

Lula holds off far right with victory in Brazil presidential election
Leftist president mounts stunning comeback after unexpected first-round loss galvanised supporters of Flavio Bolsonaro.
Leftist President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva has defeated right-wing Senator Flavio Bolsonaro in Brazil’s contentious presidential race, pulling off a remarkable comeback after a first-round loss that galvanised the country’s political right.
Shortly after 9pm Brasilia time on Sunday (00:00 GMT), Brazil’s Superior Electoral Court called the race for Lula, who had earned more than 51 percent of the vote. More than 64 million ballots were cast for the incumbent.
Bolsonaro, meanwhile, netted 48 percent, or north of 59 million ballots. More than 4 million votes separated the two candidates, with the final votes still being counted.
Coughing and audibly hoarse, Lula took to a flag-draped podium shortly after to give his victory speech. He acknowledged clashes ahead, including with his legislative agenda.
“I do not choose the Congress,” he said, citing the legislature’s rightward tilt. “It was the people who chose it, and it is with them that I will vote, work and get things approved.”
He also thanked the voters who cast their ballots “to secure democracy in the country”.
With his victory, Lula has made history. No other politician in modern Brazilian history has lost the first round of a presidential election only to win the second.
“A historic turning point for democracy,” Edinho Silva, the head of Lula’s Workers’ Party, posted on social media, along with a video of supporters chanting, “Ole, ole, ole, ole, ola! Lula, Lula!”
But Bolsonaro has so far refused to concede, teeing up a likely court battle over the legality of a Supreme Court decision to extend the voting time by two hours.
“It is impossible to acknowledge the result,” Bolsonaro said in a short speech, accusing the Supreme Court of having “changed the rules of the game mid-game”. He added that he would seek an annulment of the results.
Tumult in the voting process
Leaders across the Western Hemisphere, particularly on the left, applauded the result. “Long live democracy, the people of Brazil have won,” Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum wrote in the wake of the results. “Congratulations, President Lula!”
United States Senator Bernie Sanders likewise offered his felicitations, calling Lula’s re-election “extraordinary”.
“Lula has stood up for Brazilian workers & democracy — and will continue to do so in the next four years,” Sanders said in a statement.
Still, the vote process was marred by allegations of voter suppression after reports emerged that public transport in some areas had been suspended.
Lula’s allies accused Bolsonaro’s supporters of reducing bus availability in an attempt to dampen the president’s working-class base.
Heavy rains, meanwhile, affected southern areas considered to be Bolsonaro strongholds.
The campaigns of both Lula and Bolsonaro ultimately petitioned the Supreme Court for a voting extension. Polls across the country were kept open two hours later than expected, until 7pm Brasilia time (22:00 GMT), following a ruling from Supreme Court Justice Cristiano Zanin.
Bolsonaro, however, has argued that some polling stations were not able to reopen in time, harming any additional votes he may have earned.
A left-wing victory
Sunday’s victory means Lula will retain the presidency of Latin America’s largest country, denying a crucial victory to the region’s right wing.
In recent years, right-wing leaders have swept presidential races in nearby countries like Peru, Colombia, Argentina, Bolivia and Ecuador. Many have ridden a wave of anti-incumbent energy and enjoyed support from US President Donald Trump, who returned to office in January 2025.
A former union leader for metalworkers, Lula – at age 80 – will be sworn in on January 5, 2027, when he will beat his own record as the oldest Brazilian president to take the oath of office since the country’s return to democracy.
His victory has earned him an unprecedented fourth non-consecutive term.
Lula came into Sunday’s run-off as an underdog. While he narrowly led pre-election, the first round of voting on October 4 showed him trailing Bolsonaro.
He earned 45 percent of the first-round vote, compared with the right-wing senator’s 47 percent, both tallies short of the 50 percent needed to avoid a run-off.
But in the weeks since, Lula has rallied supporters around cost-of-living issues. He championed a constitutional amendment passed this month that shortened the Brazilian workweek, and floated the possibility of providing free public transport on weekends.
Having entered politics in the 1980s, during the twilight of the country’s military dictatorship, Lula has run for president seven times.
He won two consecutive terms from 2002 through 2010, as well as a third term in 2022, in what was the tightest race in modern Brazilian history up to that point.
His rival in that election, former far-right President Jair Bolsonaro, is the father of Senator Bolsonaro, Lula’s adversary in this race.
Jair Bolsonaro has since been sentenced to 27 years in prison for his role in plotting a coup following his loss to Lula.
Despite overseeing a decline in poverty and low unemployment during his third term, Lula has faced questions about his advanced age, his ability to combat crime, and the country’s polarised political landscape.
An explosion of household debt has also left many Brazilians feeling their economic circumstances have worsened.
In September, Lula banned online gambling and sport betting apps to address the issue.
Uncertainty ahead
While the victory over Bolsonaro cements Lula’s status as one of the most significant and influential figures in Brazil’s modern history, efforts to advance legislative priorities during his fourth term could be stymied by the most right-wing Congress in recent memory.
There are also questions about how Bolsonaro’s right-wing base and the Trump administration might react to Lula’s re-election.
Already, Bolsonaro has suggested he would seek to nullify the election, citing the prolonged voting hours.
“What happened today was not normal. It was, in fact, unacceptable,” Bolsonaro told his supporters.
Trump’s eldest son, Donald Trump Jr, also suggested there had been judicial malpractice as a result of the extension.
“If a conservative government in Brazil did this, everyone in the mainstream press in America would lose their minds, but I guess they’re just choosing to be silent because it’s all for the cause,” Trump Jr wrote on social media.
The Trump White House has been openly supportive of the Bolsonaro family, issuing 50-percent tariffs last year on certain Brazilian products in a push to end the prosecution of Jair Bolsonaro.
Judges involved in the case were also subjected to US sanctions, most notably Supreme Court Justice Alexandre de Moraes.
Lula has framed such manoeuvres as an attack on the sovereignty of Brazil’s judicial system.
One of Trump’s critics, US Representative Ro Khanna, suggested the US president could take further actions against Brazil in response to Sunday’s vote.
“People all across the world are fighting back against extremism. With Lula in Brazil, they just won,” Khanna wrote.
“Trump must respect the results and not undermine Brazil’s elections.”

Lula thanks voters for his victory, Flavio Bolsonaro does not recognize the results
It is the first time in the country’s history since the return of democracy that a candidate who lost in the first round manages to come back and win in the runoff. The left-wing president obtained 51.7% of the votes, compared with the 48.2% received by right-wing Senator Flavio Bolsonaro.
Veteran pro-union President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva suddenly found himself the underdog after right-wing challenger Flavio Bolsonaro took 47% compared to 45% for the incumbent in the October 4 first round.
A combative, three-week run-off campaign turned the political atmosphere electric. The left threw all its energy into securing a comeback, taking to the streets and mobilising on social media – notably with a WhatsApp channel dubbed "Lula’s Army" that now boasts 8.5 million subscribers. Finally, Lula, a former labor leader, sought and won a fourth (non-consecutive) term in what he has framed as his final battle.
Thank you to all our readers who followed our live coverage of Brazil’s presidential election. This live blog was coordinated first by our team in Paris and then by María Clara Calle and Léa Hurel from our Spanish-speaking newsroom in Bogotá.
Lula’s victory reverses the trend of the right’s rise in Latin America
For more than a year, right-wing candidates had won every election held in the region, as happened in Chile with Jose Antonio Kast, in Peru with Keiko Fujimori, in Ecuador with Daniel Noboa, and in Colombia with Abelardo de la Espriella. Once in office, these countries also joined the U.S. military cooperation initiative known as the Shield of the Americas.
In this way, Washington has been consolidating a bloc favorable to Donald Trump’s policies. Nevertheless, Brazil’s elections represent a setback for the U.S. president, after the Republican supported the Bolsonaro family and the victory of Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva breaks this streak.
In his speech, he defended his country’s sovereignty and stressed that Brazil needs to develop its own artificial intelligence so as not to depend on the United States. “We had to overcome the external interference of digital platforms, which we are going to have to regulate,” he said.
Thus, he continues as one of the few left-wing leaders in the region, alongside Claudia Sheinbaum in Mexico.
Even so, Brazil remains split in two: those who support Lula’s progressive ideas and those who want change with the Bolsonaros.
“It is impossible to recognize this election; we are going to request its annulment”: Bolsonaro
Brazilian presidential candidate Flavio Bolsonaro of the Liberal Party (PL) arrives to speak after losing the presidential runoff election, in Brasilia, Brazil October 25, 2026. REUTERS/Agustin Marcarian
From Brasilia, candidate Flavio Bolsonaro delivered his speech after the results were announced. He spoke briefly and said it was difficult to acknowledge the results given the current context.
The Supreme Court ordered the voting period to be extended by two more hours after Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva’s campaign filed an appeal alleging delays in voter transportation.
“This country will not accept being anyone’s backyard”: Lula
He also stood up for Brazil’s sovereignty. Donald Trump has supported several candidates in Latin America, as he did with Abelardo de la Espriella in Colombia and Daniel Noboa in Ecuador. The Republican also backed the Bolsonaro family during the campaign.
The Workers' Party candidate also said “I am going to deliver the best term that any president has ever had in this country” and he added that he will govern for all Brazilians, despite the polarization.
Lula delivers his first victory speech after reelection
Brazil's President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva, the Workers' Party (PT) candidate for re-election, smiles as he gathers with supporters after winning the presidential runoff in Sao Paulo, Brazil, October 25, 2026. REUTERS/Amanda Perobelli
“Thanks to the Brazilian people for their generosity, to the youth who took to the streets to defend democracy.” This is what Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva said in his victory speech from São Paulo. He also thanked those who helped convince others that “voting was very important to protect the country’s democracy.”
He referred as well to the controversy involving Meta that reached the courts. “We had to overcome the external interference of digital platforms, which we are going to have to regulate,” Lula said. And he added that digital communications will be very important in his government—an essential point, since during the reelection campaign he doubled down on his efforts on social media.
Leftist former presidents congratulate Lula on his victory
Contrary to the trend set by recent elections in Latin America, the right did not win in Brazil. Various leftist former presidents from the region celebrated the victory of Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva.
"Thank you, dear old friend, for never stopping the fight, for upholding the hope of a world," said Gabriel Boric of Chile. Meanwhile, Bolivian leader Evo Morales posted: "Your triumph renews the hope of the peoples who fight for social justice, dignity, and sovereignty."
Former Colombian president also congratulated Lula.
Abstention decreased in Brazil’s second round
Lula’s campaign focused over the last three weeks on winning new votes in order to come back from Flavio Bolsonaro’s first-round victory.
In that effort, securing votes from those who had abstained was essential. In the end, abstention was three million votes lower than in the first round. Although not all of those can be attributed directly to Lula, the difference between the president and Flavio Bolsonaro was just over four million votes in the runoff.
According to the Superior Electoral Court, 33.4 million people abstained from voting on October 4, compared with 30.4 million abstentions in the runoff.
Lula surprises in the runoff and wins Brazil’s presidential election
Supporters of Brazil's President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva, the Workers' Party (PT) candidate for re-election, react to early result during the presidential runoff election, in Sao Paulo, Brazil, October 25, 2026. REUTERS/Amanda Perobell
President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva went from losing in the first round with 45.16% of the votes to winning the runoff with a total of 51.79%, while right-wing Senator Flavio Bolsonaro obtained 48.21%, according to the official count from the Superior Electoral Court.
It is the first time in Brazil’s history since the return of democracy that a candidate who lost in the first round manages to win the runoff and become president.
Lula widens his lead over Bolsonaro with 70% of the votes counted
Supporters of Brazilian President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva, the Workers' Party (PT) candidate for presidential re-election, gather to wait for the results of the presidential runoff election, on the outskirts of Brasilia, Brazil, October 25, 2026. REUTERS/Diego Herculano
At this point, President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva has 50.92% of the votes, while Flavio Bolsonaro has 49.08%.
During the count, the difference between both candidates did not exceed one percentage point, but that gap has now been surpassed and continues to grow in favor of the left-wing president.
This is how Lula’s surge in the vote count was experienced in Rio de Janeiro
Lula retakes the lead in the vote count with a minimal difference
When half of the votes have been tallied, President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva has 50.14% of the vote. Senator Flavio Bolsonaro has 49.86%, according to the Superior Electoral Court.
The difference between both candidates has not exceeded one percentage point during the count.
Lula to win Brazil election runoff, AtlasIntel CEO says
Although in the vote count President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva is trailing by a narrow margin, the CEO of pollster AtlasIntel, Andrei Roman, predicts that Lula will be re-elected.
Roman spoke to Reuters and made his predictions based on the ongoing vote count in the presidential runoff against Senator Flavio Bolsonaro.
A slight lead for Flavio Bolsonaro with 20% of the votes counted
The senator has 50.41% compared to Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva’s 49.59%, as the TSE reports 20% of the votes counted. It is a difference of less than one percentage point.
As in the first round, the states in northern Brazil support the outgoing left-wing president, while those in the south back the far-right candidate.
Flavio overturns the results and takes the lead over Lula
Opposition presidential candidate Sen. Flávio Bolsonaro waves as he arrives in Brasilia, Brazil, on the day of the presidential runoff election, Sunday, Oct. 25, 2026. (AP Photo/Eraldo Peres)
Although President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva began ahead in the Superior Electoral Court’s count, Senator Flavio Bolsonaro now has 50.04% of the votes.
He began to lead the count from 13% of the votes tallied.
Lula holds a slight lead with 5% of the votes counted
Incumbent President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva has 51.16% of the votes, which is just over two percentage points more than his runoff rival Flavio Bolsonaro.
The Superior Electoral Court begins by counting votes cast abroad, where Lula won in the first round.
Voting officially ends in Brazil and the counting resumes
At 7:00 p.m. Brasilia time (10:00 p.m. GMT), the polling stations that were still operating closed.
Now, the Superior Electoral Court is resuming the vote count that it had suspended after the Supreme Court ordered voting to be extended by two more hours.
The extension of voting in Brazil causes confusion at the polls
The Supreme Court’s decision came at around 5:00 p.m. Brasilia time (8:00 p.m. GMT), when the polls were supposed to close. Local media report that several polling stations had already shut down.
In response, the Superior Electoral Court stated that “the election continues in progress only in the locations where voting had not been concluded by 5 p.m.” Meanwhile, the Workers’ Party (PT) and the Liberal Party called on its supporters to keep voting.
Supreme Court approves extending voting by two hours across Brazil
Cristiano Zanin is the Supreme Court justice who decided to extend voting in Brazil’s runoff on October 25. (AP Photo/Eraldo Peres)
At the last minute, Brazilian Supreme Court Justice Cristiano Zanin ordered that voting in the country’s presidential runoff on Sunday be extended by two hours, until 7:00 p.m. Brasilia time (10:00 p.m. GMT).
The decision grants a request from President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva’s campaign. A similar petition was sent to the Superior Electoral Court, but it has not made any decision.
Meanwhile, the Superior Electoral Court has paused the counting of votes following the Supreme Court’s decision.
Flavio Bolsonaro’s campaign also asked to extend the closing of the ballot boxes
Their request is to extend the voting period by two hours, so that it ends at 7:00 p.m. Brasilia time. The appeal was submitted to the president of the Superior Electoral Court, Kassio Nunes Marques, and they are asking for the extension to apply in 17 municipalities in the states of São Paulo, Paraná, and Santa Catarina.
Just like Lula’s Workers’ Party, the Liberal Party that supports Bolsonaro denounced delays in transportation. However, Flavio Bolsonaro’s campaign says that the transportation delays are due to the rains and flooding affecting those states.

Brazil's Lula overtakes Bolsonaro in runoff, with half of votes counted
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
00:12:06 UTC
09:12:06 KST

Brazilian President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva won an unprecedented fourth term on Sunday, the country's electoral court said, in a shock result that defied polls, precedent and global anti-incumbent sentiment to put the brakes on a wave of right-wing election victories across Latin America.
Lula, an icon of the global left and the most dominant force in Brazilian politics this century, defeated Senator Flavio Bolsonaro, the eldest son of former President Jair Bolsonaro. The senator had finished first in the election's first round and hoped to revive his father's far-right movement.
At times, Lula's reelection looked like a long shot, as voters soured on him and his Workers' Party after years of corruption scandals and rising prices, while sweeping societal changes left the former metalworker and union leader looking out of touch with an increasingly app-based economy and its growing ranks of informal workers.
Lula's victory marks another comeback in a career full of them. The 80-year-old was jailed from 2018 to 2019 on corruption charges that were later overturned, paving the way for him to beat Jair Bolsonaro in the 2022 election.
"He is a statesman, a giant," leftist federal lawmaker Erika Hilton, who was with Lula in Sao Paulo during the vote count, told Reuters.
Unlikely path to victory
Pollsters said better-than-expected turnout had powered Lula to victory. Leonardo Barreto, the co-founder of consultancy Think Policy, said voters had chosen Lula's familiar embrace over Bolsonaro's novelty.
"People today are choosing between change, with some apprehension, and a known path, which guarantees certain rights," he said.
During the campaign, Lula pointed to a track record of falling poverty and inequality, while unemployment, illiteracy and deforestation hit record lows during his third term.
He warned Bolsonaro would cut welfare spending, backslide on social advances and hand over Brazil's sovereignty to US President Donald Trump, whose State Department led a campaign to get the Bolsonaros back to power.
Lula's win deprives Trump of a major addition to what has been a growing bloc of friendly right-wing Latin American governments that have embraced Washington's agenda on security and migration.
Celso Amorim, a former Lula foreign minister, told Reuters the leftist "would be very important for establishing a point of balance in Latin America. Lula is that balance."
Comeback King
Lula becomes the first candidate since Brazil's return to democracy in the 1980s to be elected after finishing second in the first round.
Lula, who was president between 2003 and 2011, campaigned on a potent mix of pragmatism and populism that has shaped his career in national politics for half a century, rolling out a slew of reforms aimed at improving the lives of workers and poor Brazilians.
These gained steam with late-campaign pledges that ranged from free nationwide weekend public transport, which has to be formally submitted to Congress, to a 15% increase in his trademark welfare program that is already being implemented.
Lula also championed a constitutional amendment that became Brazil's biggest labor reform in decades, which passed with wide support in Congress.
Challenging legislative reality
Still, Lula's fourth term could be his most difficult yet, after Brazil elected its most conservative Congress since returning to democracy in the 1980s.
Combined, Bolsonaro's Liberal Party (PL) and allied parties could control over 280 seats in the lower house and up to 50 seats in the Senate, enough for comfortable majorities in both chambers.
"He is likely to be a lame duck from the start," said Oliver Stuenkel, a professor of international relations at the Getulio Vargas Foundation in São Paulo.
The incoming legislature will likely deepen recent trends of presidents ceding power to Congress, Stuenkel said, predicting Lula will face waning influence over Supreme Court nominations, unwieldy party coalitions, and even the threat of impeachment.
Economic headwinds
Lula faces an economy that his government forecasts will grow a meager 2.3% next year, adding to fiscal concerns tied to high interest rates and public debt that has risen past 82% of GDP, the highest since the pandemic.
The president's critics blame spending, though interest costs have driven most of the increase in debt.
Goldman Sachs said it expects Lula to make modest progress at most to contain spending in a fourth term, as he stays committed to a state-led growth model.
Surging household debt also concerns economists. Trying to address the issue, Lula rolled out a provisional ban on online betting and unveiled a new debt relief program during the campaign.
The incoming right-wing Congress will try to pass structural reforms that favor businesses, experts say, prompting spending cuts that could fuel social upheaval.

Polling station committee members and observers representing parties and candidate lists may not relay information about the number of voters who have actually cast ballots at a particular polling station to their parties. Bulgaria's presidential election heads to Nov. 1 runoff

Unknown Publisher

Dzhanan Mehmed Ismail and Gizem Nisa Demir
26 October 2026•Update: 26 October 2026
Bulgaria’s presidential election will proceed to a runoff, as no candidate ticket secured more than 50% of the vote.
According to unofficial results from polling agency Alpha Research released by Bulgarian National Television (BNT), incumbent President Iliana Yotova and her vice presidential running mate Kiril Valchev received 34.6% of the vote, while former Prime Minister Andrey Gyurov and his running mate Georgi Kandev secured 32.7%.
Voter turnout stood at 22.5%.
Unofficial results from polling agency Myara put Yotova at 35% and Gyurov at 31.9%, with turnout reported at 22.2%.
Yotova and Gyurov will face each other in the runoff scheduled for Nov. 1.
Speaking to the media after polls closed, Yotova expressed concern over the low voter turnout, thanking Bulgarian citizens who voted and those who supported her.
"Thinking that we can change anything in the country without voting is an illusion," she said.
Yotova said her campaign would continue with a renewed effort to engage more decisively with all Bulgarian citizens. She also stressed that Bulgaria needed stable governance rather than alliances formed between political parties.
Gyurov challenged Yotova to take part in a public debate ahead of the runoff, saying Bulgaria needed an active president who united citizens rather than divided them.
"I invite Yotova to an open, honest and civilized debate to present our views on how we would exercise our powers and how we would act when Bulgaria faces difficult choices," he said.

Brazil elections: Lula wins another term, beating Flavio Bolsonaro

- In his victory speech, Lula urged more regulation of big tech platforms after allegations that Meta interfered in the race
- Several Latin American leaders congratulated Lula on win
- Bolsonaro refused to concede, calls for election results to be annulled
- Brazilians voted in the final round of the presidential election
Keep reading for the latest updates from the second round of Brazil's presidential election on Sunday, October 25.
Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click here to add us as a Preferred Source on Google. Then tap the "Star" or "Preferred" to keep DW News at the top of your feed.
Flavio Bolsonaro rejects defeat, seeks annulment of Brazil election
Right-wing presidential candidate Flavio Bolsonaro has rejected his defeat to incumbent Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva in Brazil’s presidential run-off, calling for the election to be annulled over a two-hour extension of voting hours.
Speaking to reporters after the electoral court declared Lula the winner, Bolsonaro said he could not accept the result. He criticized a decision by Supreme Court judge Cristiano Zanin to extend voting hours nationwide, arguing that it had changed the rules of the election.
"What happened today was not normal. It was unacceptable," Bolsonaro said, arguing that the nationwide extension had undermined equal treatment between states. He said he would take legal action against the result.
Lula’s campaign had requested the extension, citing difficulties transporting voters to polling stations in several states. Bolsonaro’s campaign had also sought extra voting time, but only in municipalities across five states, citing heavy rain, flooding and power outages.
Lula says Brazilians voted to defend democracy, vows to resist US influence
Brazilians voted to "guarantee democracy," President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva said Sunday after beating Flavio Bolsonaro to win an unprecedented fourth term.
In a post on X, Lula thanked Brazilians, particularly young people who took to the streets in defense of democracy, saying: "This victory belongs to a people who believe, who fight, and who never give up on building a more just, sovereign, and democratic Brazil."
In his victory speech, Lula reiterated that Brazil would "not accept being anyone’s backyard," a recurring campaign message defending the country’s sovereignty against US influence. The stance may have helped him win votes, with some voters viewing Washington’s actions as interference.
Relations between the two countries deteriorated in 2025, when the US imposed tariffs on Brazil in retaliation for legal proceedings against former president Jair Bolsonaro, who was later convicted of coup-plotting.
Speaking in a hoarse voice, Lula thanked his campaign team and Brazilians, particularly young people who took to the streets to defend democracy. He described the result as a "loss for negativity, lies."
The re-elected president also promised better regulation of big tech platforms, after Meta was the subject of legal complaints over alleged "interference" throughout the polarizing campaign.
Latin American leaders congratulate Lula on election victory
Several Latin American leaders congratulated leftist President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva on his victory.
Chilean President Jose Antonio Kast said he had spoken to Lula and congratulated him, adding that "Chile and Brazil have a lot of shared future ahead."
Mexico’s left-wing President Claudia Sheinbaum congratulated Lula on his victory, writing on X: "Long live democracy, the people of Brazil won. Congratulations, President Lula!"
The presidents of Uruguay, Paraguay, Panama and Bolivia also congratulated Lula in posts on X.
Cuba’s president congratulated Lula on X, calling him "dear brother" and praising his victory as a win for peace, sovereignty and social justice.
IN PICTURES: Lula supporters celebrate, while Bolsonaro's fans disappointed
Brazil's Lula defeats conservative Flavio Bolsonaro in presidential election
Brazilian leftist President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva has won a fourth term in office, defeating right-wing challenger Flávio Bolsonaro in a presidential runoff, electoral authorities said.
Lula overcame his first-round defeat to Bolsonaro to secure victory in the runoff. The nearly 81-year-old leader won 51.7% of the vote, compared with 48.2% for Flavio Bolsonaro, the son of former president Jair Bolsonaro.
The campaign was marred by scandals and mudslinging. Sunday’s vote was thrown into confusion after a last-minute Supreme Court ruling extended voting by two hours, following Lula’s claim that buses had been taken off the roads in several cities, preventing some voters from reaching polling stations.
Pollsters said higher-than-expected turnout appeared to have benefited Lula. Conservative candidates in Brazil typically lead early in the count, while left-wing candidates gain ground as votes from poorer, more populous northeastern states come in.
In regards to foreign policy in his next term, Lula will have to manage relations with Washington while maintaining his anti-imperialist stance, as the Trump administration increasingly asserts its influence across the region. Flavio Bolsonaro had campaigned on a promise of closer cooperation with Washington.
Around 159 million Brazilians were eligible to vote. Under Lula’s left-wing Workers’ Party, unemployment fell to a record low, poverty declined, the minimum wage rose and deforestation in the Amazon decreased. Congress also approved the gradual introduction of a five-day working week with two days off.
However, rising living costs, high public debt, Lula’s spending policies and a scandal involving alleged pension fraud weighed on his government. The economic challenges left many voters dissatisfied with his record and open to a return of the Bolsonaro family to power.
Lula finished the first round with 45% of the vote, two percentage points behind Flavio Bolsonaro. He became the first candidate since Brazil restored direct presidential elections in 1989 to overcome a first-round deficit and win the runoff.
The former trade unionist, who served as president from 2003 to 2010 before returning to office in 2023, now faces a challenging fourth term with a strong right-wing opposition.
Votes tallied in Brazil's presidential election after polls close
The electronic voting system used in the country means that a final result could be determined within a matter of hours, although that final result is expected to be tight.

Voting extended after complaints by both sides
Brazil's Supreme Court has moved to extend voting time in the presidential election until 7 p.m. local time (2200 GMT), giving voters an additional two hours.
The decision comes amid complaints from Lula's team that public bus services had been hampered, blocking people from getting to polling stations.
At the same time, Bolsonaro's team complained of weather conditions in certain regions making it more difficult for people to get out and vote.
Lula asks for polls to stay open longer after people 'barred from voting'
President Lula has requested an extension to poll opening hours after buses were taken out of circulation in Sao Paolo, the country's largest city, which he said prevented many people from voting.
"We are asking the Supreme Court to extend the electoral process so that those who were effectively barred from voting, due to the dirty tactics of mayors, can still cast their votes," Lula said, according to AFP.
Lula said 40% of buses in the city had been prevented from going into service, a claim that matched local media reports saying 75 buses had been blocked from leaving garages.
"I've never complained about anything in any election before. Whether I won or lost, I'd just accept it and get ready for the next one. But this time, something abominable is happening," he said.
"No one should give up on voting just because some scoundrel of a business owner or some crooked, criminal mayor tried to stop the people from casting their ballots."
Results show Brazilian voters in Germany back Lula
Brazilians in Germany have voted overwhelmingly for Lula, according to figures posted by Brazilian Embassies across the country and seen by DW's Portuguese service.
The left-wing incumbent, Lula, won 79.09% of the ballots cast by the 20,923 voters across Germany. This marks an increase on the 71.9% he won in the first round.
Brazilian voters in Germany could vote at embassies in Berlin, Hamburg, Cologne, Frankfurt and Munich.
The German capital saw the greatest support for Lula, with 88.77% of the votes going his way. Frankfurt was the city with the greatest support for Bolsonaro, but on 29.03% he still trailed his opponent by some margin.
The turnout also increased in the second round in comparison to the first round when it stood at 19,322. However, for both rounds, only around half of the 41,552 eligible voters turned out to vote. Across the world, there are some 918,900 eligible voters for Sunday's election.
IN PHOTOS: Almost 160 million called out to vote
What role is Trump playing in Brazil's election?
Although he hasn't endorsed either candidate, US President Donald Trump is close to the Bolsonaro family.
Not only did the senior Bolsonaro imitate Trump's rhetoric and policies, he also refused to concede defeat after losing to Lula in 2022, leading to his imprisonment for an attempted coup, provoking comparisons with Trump's own defeat to Joe Biden in 2020.
On the other side, Lula has presented himself as a defense against US interference.
The right "wants to govern with the American flag," Lula said after casting his ballot on Sunday.
A Bolsonaro win would mark a further move in Latin America toward pro-US far-right leaders, following in the footsteps of countries such as Colombia, Chile and Peru.
Results expected within hours of polls closing
The president of Brazil's Superior Electoral Court, Kassio Nunes Marques, has said he expects the winner of Sunday's vote to be announced officially between 8.30 p.m. and 9 p.m. (2330 and 0000 GMT), according to A Folha de Sao Paolo.
Brazil uses an electronic voting system meaning that ballots can be tallied quicker than in elections where paper votes are counted by hand.
However, the gap between the winner and loser is expected to be small, with the two running head-to-head in pre-election polls.
Supreme Court president urges candidates to accept result of vote
The head of Brazil's Supreme Federal Court, Edson Fachin, has called for the candidates to respect the result of Sunday's vote.
"It's important to remember that all authority and power comes from the people and, thus, it is fundamental that the choices that derive from the manifestation of popular sovereignty are respected," he said as he left his local polling station, according to A Folha de Sao Paulo.
"Brazil needs peace and calm to, from tomorrow, be able to confront the major challenges in many areas that demand the presence of the state."
Some observers have posited that Flavio Bolsonaro could refuse to accept a Lula victory, like his father before him, with the potential for violence to erupt.

Brazil is heading back to the polls, but the impact could be felt worldwide.
With the Amazon vital to the health of the planet, the election could help shape its future.

Aleksandar Vucic: Serbia’s veteran ruler felled by student-led movement

Aleksandar Vucic: Serbia’s veteran ruler felled by student-led movement
- Aleksandar Vucic, Serbia’s dominant leader for 14 years, conceded defeat in the Oct 25 snap poll after a student-led protest movement won support.
- He rose from Milosevic’s camp to found the pro-European SNS, but critics saw him as increasingly authoritarian and tied to corruption and nationalist politics.
- Anger grew after a station canopy collapse killed 16 in 2024, and mass protests forced snap elections after demands for transparent investigations and political change.
AI generated
Belgrade - The dominant force in Serbian politics for over 14 years, Aleksandar Vucic, who conceded defeat in a snap parliamentary poll on Oct 25, rose from the wreckage of strongman Slobodan Milosevic’s cabinet to the centre of power using his brand of populist nationalism.
For supporters, the 56-year-old represented stability, development and patriotism in a country scarred by the bloody wars of the 1990s and ensuing international isolation.
But opponents saw him as an increasingly authoritarian figure, twisting between the Kremlin and Brussels and leading a government accused of endemic corruption.
Vucic conceded his party had lost after voters cast ballots in record numbers in the vote on Oct 25, defeated by a new political force that emerged from a years-long protest movement.
“Based on a stratified sample, it is clear that we lost these elections,” Vucic told supporters at his party headquarters in Belgrade.
Political turnaround
Vucic rose to prominence in the 1990s as an ultra-nationalist ally of Milosevic, serving as his information minister in 1998.
After protests ousted the Yugoslav strongman in 2000, Vucic became a senior figure in the far-right Serbian Radical Party.
He was then a vocal supporter of Bosnian Serb political and military leaders Radovan Karadzic and Ratko Mladic, both later sentenced to life for genocide and other crimes committed during the Bosnian war.
But Vucic underwent a dramatic rebrand in 2008, co-founding the conservative, pro-European Serbian Progressive Party (SNS), which won parliamentary elections in 2012 and has dominated Serbian politics since.
He served as deputy prime minister, defence minister and prime minister before becoming president in 2017.
Even after polishing his image, Vucic has been reluctant to distance himself from nationalist leanings and far-right associates.
He has stopped short of condemning Serbs convicted of atrocities during the 1990s conflicts and looked the other way as pro-government media and political allies openly praised war criminals.
Despite trying to deny state involvement in a large funeral gathering for Mladic in the Serbian capital in September, several of his ministers attended, drawing sharp criticism from Brussels.
‘Land of cranes’
A relentless campaigner, he maintained a near-constant presence on pro-government television channels, embracing locals in tiny rural villages and chastising critics during lengthy news conferences.
He has cultivated the image of a tireless leader criss-crossing Serbia, attracting investment and creating jobs.
At the same time, he has juggled the competing interests of European Union aspirations and Serbia’s close ties to Russia.
Supporters praised him as a brave defender of Serbian sovereignty, spending billions of euros on defence – as he warned of foreign influence and pressure from NATO-member neighbours.
He often cited Serbia’s infrastructure and improved living standards as proof of his success, once pledging to make the country a “land of cranes”.
From the gleaming waterfront district to the numerous projects unfolding in preparation for Expo 2027, his party’s slogan “United Serbia” is plastered on billboards across the capital.
Rail station tragedy
But when a concrete canopy collapsed at a newly renovated train station in 2024 killing 16 people, the accusations of corruption which had dogged many of his signature projects caused an outpouring of anger.
Student-led demonstrations calling for transparent investigations drew hundreds of thousands to the streets in the largest protests since the Milosevic era.
As demands grew into calls for snap elections, Vucic and his supporters pushed back.
Students manning university blockades were labelled tools of foreign powers.
In September, nearly two years into the protests, Vucic finally called snap elections for October, citing “major turbulence on the domestic political scene”, thus meeting a key student demand.
“All of this will end on Oct 25,” Vucic said, referring to the protests, at a major pre-election rally in Novi Sad, the city where the canopy had collapsed. AFP

Voting ends in Brazil's presidential runoff after 2-hour extension
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
07:55:17 CST
08:55:17 KST

BRASILIA, Oct. 25 (Xinhua) -- Voting in Brazil's presidential runoff ended at 7 p.m. Brasilia time (2200 GMT) on Sunday, two hours later than originally scheduled, following a Supreme Federal Court (STF) ruling extending voting hours amid disruptions caused by public transportation problems and heavy rains in several parts of the country.
Results of the closely contested runoff were expected within hours of the close of voting.
STF Justice Cristiano Zanin issued the ruling earlier Sunday, with the Superior Electoral Court (TSE) responsible for its implementation.
TSE President Kassio Nunes Marques notified regional electoral courts of the decision at 5:49 p.m. Brasilia time, instructing polling stations that were still open to continue operating until 7 p.m.
As some polling stations had already closed when the decision was communicated, Zanin later clarified that the extension would apply only to those that remained open, while stations that had already closed would not reopen.
Earlier Sunday, the campaign of incumbent President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva of the Workers' Party requested an extension of voting hours until 7 p.m., citing difficulties faced by voters in reaching polling stations due to reduced bus services and other public transportation problems in at least nine states, including Sao Paulo, Rio de Janeiro and Pernambuco.
The campaign of his rival, Flavio Bolsonaro, candidate of the Liberal Party and son of former President Jair Bolsonaro, also sought extended voting hours in Belo Horizonte, capital of Minas Gerais state, and other areas affected by power outages, as well as parts of Rio Grande do Sul state affected by heavy rains.
In the first round of voting on Oct. 4, Bolsonaro secured 47.03 percent of valid votes, ahead of Lula's 45.16 percent. Neither secured more than 50 percent of valid votes, the threshold required to win outright, sending the two candidates into Sunday's decisive runoff. ■

IDF veteran completes Hawaii Ironman race three years after losing leg in Gaza combat
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
23:55:17 UTC
08:55:17 KST

Three years after being injured and losing his right leg while in Gaza, IDF veteran Boris Baruch Shtonda completed the Ironman World Championship in Hawaii on October 10.
Shtonda competed in the long-distance triathlon consisting of a 3.8-kilometer swim, a 180-kilometer bike ride, and a full marathon in a division for athletes with disabilities while wearing a custom-fitted specialized running prosthetic.
Shtonda lost his right leg while serving in the IDF’s Duvdevan as a reservist after Hamas’s October 7 massacre. A month after being deployed, he was severely wounded by an explosive device in the northern Gaza city of Beit Hanoun.
He underwent multiple surgeries before his leg was amputated above the knee and made athletic challenges a central goal for his recovery.
Since starting his recovery, Shtonda climbed Mount Kilimanjaro twice, swam across the Sea of Galilee, and finished a half Ironman race in Spain before deciding to train for the Hawaii Ironman.
Shtonda completed the race after a year and a half of training and support from Friends of the Israel Defense Forces (FIDF).
Shtonda dedicates Ironman achievement to wounded soldiers in rehabilitation
Shtonda dedicated his race to wounded soldiers and others undergoing rehabilitation, encouraging them to draw on their inner strength, believe in themselves, and become their own heroes.
“I want to share a message with all wounded soldiers and anyone going through a rehabilitation process: you are your own compass,” Shtonda said. “Sometimes, we have to be our own heroes and pull ourselves out of the predicaments we find ourselves in. Keep the faith, and always–always–believe in yourselves.”
Shtonda also received support from FIDF supporter Mike Hochstein of Dallas, who was moved by his aspirations, determination, and mental resilience after meeting him during a visit to Israel.
“I first met Boris during an FIDF bike ride through Israel last year, and from that first meeting, Boris’s determination and spirit made a lasting impression,” Hochstein said. “His dedication, perseverance, and commitment to pushing his limits are truly inspiring. I'm so proud to support Boris on this extraordinary journey.”
FIDF helps wounded IDF soldiers rebuild their lives through sports and rehabilitation
FIDF's support for Shtonda is part of the organization's broader efforts to assist wounded IDF soldiers and their families through rehabilitation programs, sports, and adventure activities designed to build physical and mental resilience. These initiatives aim to help wounded veterans regain their independence, return to everyday life, and pursue new goals beyond their initial medical treatment.
“Boris’s achievement reflects the determination wounded soldiers bring to the long process of rehabilitation,” said FIDF CEO Maj. Gen. (Res.) Nadav Padan. “Recovery does not end when medical treatment is over. It takes continued support, opportunities to rebuild strength and confidence, and the chance to set new goals. Through the commitment of FIDF supporters in the United States, we help wounded soldiers and their families navigate that process and continue moving forward.”
Shtonda's journey highlights the inner strength and resilience of wounded IDF soldiers, demonstrating how rehabilitation extends beyond medical treatment and how sports, personal determination, and community support can help wounded soldiers regain confidence, overcome challenges, and rebuild their lives after injury.

====================================================================================================

Brazil’s Lula overtakes Bolsonaro in runoff, with half of votes counted
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
00:55:13 CET
08:55:13 KST

By Lisandra Paraguassu, Brendan O’Boyle and Luciana Magalhaes
SAO PAULO, Oct 25 (Reuters) - Brazilian President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva won a historic fourth term on Sunday, the country’s electoral court said, in a shock result that defied polls, precedent and global anti-incumbent sentiment to put the brakes on a wave of right-wing election victories across Latin America.
However, his opponent Senator Flavio Bolsonaro, the eldest son of former President Jair Bolsonaro, refused to accept defeat and said he would ask for the result to be annulled due to a Sunday ruling from a Supreme Court justice that extended voting for two hours.
Bolsonaro led the election’s first round but lost in the runoff by over 4 million votes, rattling Brazilian financial markets which had bet on his victory. His refusal to concede defeat has echoes of his father’s reaction after losing to Lula in 2022. Jair Bolsonaro never accepted his loss and was later sentenced by the Supreme Court to 27-years in prison for plotting a coup to remain in power.
The scale of Flavio Bolsonaro’s loss to Lula — by more than twice his father’s losing margin — and the fact his campaign also asked for an extension due to rains in the conservative-leaning south make any annulment unlikely, analysts said.
Mario Braga, a Latin America analyst at the risk consultancy RANE, said there could be right-wing protests in coming days, but “it’s very improbable that it will lead to the reversal of the result.”
COMEBACK KING
Investors expect recent bets on a change of government to unwind in a volatile week ahead on financial markets. A Tokyo-listed exchange-traded fund tracking Brazil’s Bovespa index dived nearly 15% in Asia trade on news of Lula’s victory, while the Brazilian real was set to fall sharply against the US dollar.
The victory marks another comeback in a career full of them for Lula, an icon of the global left and the most dominant force in Brazilian politics this century. The 80-year-old was jailed from 2018 to 2019 on corruption charges that were later overturned, paving the way for him to beat Jair Bolsonaro in the 2022 election.
“He is a statesman, a giant,” leftist federal lawmaker Erika Hilton, who was with Lula in Sao Paulo during the vote count, told Reuters.
At times, Lula’s reelection looked like a long shot, as voters soured on him and his Workers’ Party after years of corruption scandals and rising prices, while sweeping social changes left the former metalworker and union leader looking out of touch with an increasingly app-based economy and its growing ranks of informal workers.
Pollsters said better-than-expected turnout had powered Lula to victory. Leonardo Barreto, the co-founder of consultancy Think Policy, said voters had chosen Lula’s familiar embrace over Bolsonaro’s novelty.
“People today are choosing between change, with some apprehension, and a known path, which guarantees certain rights,” he said.
During the campaign, Lula pointed to a track record of falling poverty and inequality, while unemployment, illiteracy and deforestation hit record lows during his third term.
He warned Bolsonaro would cut welfare spending, backslide on social advances and hand over Brazil’s sovereignty to US President Donald Trump, whose State Department led a campaign to get the Bolsonaros back to power.
Lula’s win deprives Trump of a major addition to what has been a growing bloc of friendly right-wing Latin American governments that have embraced Washington’s agenda on security and migration.
There was no immediate comment from Trump or the US State Department, while Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney and Latin American leaders were quick to offer their congratulations.
Celso Amorim, a former Lula foreign minister, told Reuters the leftist “would be very important for establishing a point of balance in Latin America. Lula is that balance.”
LATE-CAMPAIGN BOOST
Lula becomes the first candidate since Brazil’s return to democracy in the 1980s to be elected after finishing second in the first round.
His campaign this year mixed the kind of pragmatism and populism that has shaped his career in national politics for half a century, rolling out a slew of reforms aimed at improving the lives of workers and poor Brazilians.
These gained steam with late-campaign pledges that ranged from free nationwide weekend public transport, which has to be formally submitted to Congress, to a 15% increase in his trademark welfare program that is already being implemented.
Lula also championed a constitutional amendment that became Brazil’s biggest labor reform in decades, which passed with wide support in Congress.
CHALLENGES AHEAD
Still, Lula’s fourth term could be his most difficult yet, after Brazil elected its most conservative Congress since returning to democracy in the 1980s.
Combined, Bolsonaro’s Liberal Party and allied parties could control over 280 seats in the lower house and up to 50 seats in the Senate, enough for comfortable opposition majorities in both chambers.
That may deepen recent trends of presidents ceding power to Congress on the budget, major legislation and key nominations.
Lula faces an economy that his government forecasts will grow just 2.3% next year, adding to fiscal concerns tied to high interest rates and public debt that has risen past 82% of GDP, the highest since the pandemic.
Goldman Sachs said it expects Lula to make modest progress at most to contain spending in a fourth term, as he stays committed to a state-led growth model.
Surging household debt also concerns economists. Trying to address the issue, Lula rolled out a provisional ban on online betting and unveiled a new debt relief program during the campaign.
The incoming right-wing Congress will try to pass structural reforms that favor businesses, experts say, prompting spending cuts that could trigger popular backlash.
(Reporting by Oliver Griffin, Luciana Magalhaes and Lisandra Paraguassu in Sao Paulo; Ricardo Brito, Bernardo Caram and Brendan O’Boyle in Brasilia; Marta Nogueira in Rio de Janeiro, Trevor Hunnicutt in Washington; Writing by Brendan O’Boyle and Oliver Griffin; Editing by Brad Haynes, Gabriel Stargardter, Alistair Bell, Christina Fincher, Andrew Heavens, Nick Zieminski, Aurora Ellis and Lincoln Feast.)

Israel fuel prices could top NIS 9 per liter as tax cut expires after elections
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
23:55:12 UTC
08:55:12 KST

Fuel prices in Israel are expected to rise sharply immediately after the elections, as a temporary NIS 1 per liter fuel tax reduction introduced by Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich is set to expire on November 3.
Combined with rising global oil prices amid expectations of renewed fighting involving Israel, the US and Iran, the expiration of the tax cut could push the price of 95-octane gasoline above NIS 9 per liter, up from its current price of NIS 7.77.
Smotrich introduced the temporary reduction in the state's excise tax on gasoline last month to prevent fuel prices from soaring ahead of the elections.
The original order, signed a month earlier, reduced the tax by half a shekel per liter. However, rising oil prices prompted Smotrich to double the reduction.
Under normal circumstances, taxes account for more than 60% of the price of gasoline in Israel, generating approximately NIS 20 billion in annual state revenue.
According to the Finance Ministry's Budget Department, the tax cuts introduced over the past two months are expected to reduce state revenue by approximately NIS 467 million, at a time when the ongoing war has driven defense spending to record levels.
Election outcome could determine fate of fuel tax relief as fuel prices could top NIS 8
Following the elections, Smotrich will have to decide whether to extend the tax reduction. However, if it becomes clear the current government will not remain in office, he could let fuel prices surge, leaving the next government to deal with the economic consequences.
Regardless of whether the tax cut is extended, the first fuel price increase is expected as early as Saturday night.
Expectations of a third round of fighting involving Israel, Iran and the US have already pushed oil prices up by approximately 10% compared with late September, when the Energy Ministry's Fuel Administration set gasoline prices for October.
As a result, even if the tax reduction remains in effect, gasoline prices are currently expected to rise by approximately 30 agorot per liter, bringing the price to just over NIS 8.
The final price will be determined toward the end of the week, based on oil prices in the Mediterranean basin at that time. However, the new price could remain in effect for only a few days.

Trump repeats endorsement of Netanyahu, calls for Israel, US to 'finish the job'

Netanyahu pressures Trump for additional endorsement

“If Israel has the wrong leader, meaning anyone other than Bibi, America will have to do this job itself, and I’m not inclined to do that,” he wrote, referring to the confrontation with Iran.

Zelenskiy says US fully resumes warnings on ballistic strikes
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
00:55:04 CET
08:55:04 KST

KYIV, Oct 25 (Reuters) - Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy said US warnings about imminent Russian ballistic missile strikes, critical to Ukraine’s air defences, had been fully restored after recent issues.
Speaking to Ukraine’s TSN television channel, he said SpaceX’s Starshield satellite internet had been working at speeds of up to 420 kilometres per hour since early on Saturday morning, after it had been throttled earlier in October amid diplomatic pressure on Kyiv from Washington.
Zelenskiy said he discussed both issues in a meeting with US special envoy Steve Witkoff in Oslo, casting the changes as results of that meeting.
The US has pressed Ukraine to suspend strikes on Russian oil refineries, which it argues added to high energy prices, a sensitive issue for the Trump administration amid its war on Iran and US midterm elections next month.
Zelenskiy said that in order for Kyiv to halt the strikes, Moscow must stop hitting Ukraine’s power infrastructure, or the US should allow the use of Starshield over Russia to detect launch places of its ballistic missiles, or supply Ukraine with Patriot missiles.
Speaking about the upcoming technical talks between Kyiv, Moscow and Washington in November, Zelenskiy said Ukraine would not discuss limits to its armed forces, or enforced post-war neutrality. Kyiv has long sought entry into NATO despite the reticence of some members.
Zelenskiy also renewed his push for a trilateral US-brokered meeting between him and Vladimir Putin.
The Ukrainian leader has long argued Putin is the only person in Russia who can make major decisions to end the war or meaningfully discuss core issues, such as the fate of the nearly 20% of Ukraine that Russia occupies.
“The issue of territories is a red line that can be discussed exclusively at the level of leaders,” Zelenskiy said.
(Reporting by Max Hunder, Bogdan Kochubey and Jekaterīna Golubkova; Editing by Chris Reese)

Antonelli misses out on clinching F1 title despite dominant US Grand Prix win
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
23:54:57 UTC
08:54:57 KST

Efe Ozkan
26 October 2026•Update: 26 October 2026
Mercedes driver Kimi Antonelli moved closer to his maiden Formula One world title with a dominant victory at the United States Grand Prix on Sunday.
The 20-year-old Italian finished ahead of Red Bull's Max Verstappen and Ferrari's Charles Leclerc but narrowly missed the opportunity to clinch the championship in Austin, Texas.
Antonelli now leads Mercedes teammate George Russell by 123 points with the championship set to continue in Mexico City next weekend.
He will be crowned world champion if he does not lose more than 23 points to Russell or 24 points to Ferrari's Lewis Hamilton in Mexico.
A ninth-place finish would therefore be enough for Antonelli to secure the title even if Russell wins the race, while 10th place would be sufficient if Hamilton takes victory.
If neither Russell nor Hamilton wins in Mexico City, Antonelli will become world champion regardless of where he finishes.
Antonelli dominated Sunday's race in the same fashion as he has controlled much of the 2026 season, pulling clear of the field from the opening corner as his rivals battled behind him.
The victory was Antonelli's first since the Spanish Grand Prix last month and his ninth of the season.
The main battle of the race was for second place, with Verstappen and Leclerc engaged in a race-long contest.
Despite missing the chance to seal the championship in the US, Antonelli now has a clear opportunity to complete his title-winning campaign in Mexico City next weekend.
