Rania Abushamala
26 October 2026•Update: 26 October 2026
Sri Lanka has repatriated 40 Iranian sailors who were brought ashore from stranded merchant vessels for medical treatment, the Daily Mirror reported Sunday.
Foreign Minister Vijitha Herath told the newspaper that all 40 received medical attention before returning to Iran on Saturday morning.
The sailors were aboard merchant vessels approximately 24 nautical miles off Galle when authorities received distress calls concerning their medical conditions, according to the Foreign Ministry.
The Iranian Embassy in Colombo arranged the evacuation while Sri Lankan authorities coordinated their transfer through Galle port.
“We have coordinated the transfer and carried out our humanitarian obligations,” ministry spokesman Thushara Rodrigo said, according to the report.
Nearly a dozen empty Iranian oil tankers reportedly remain anchored off Galle, unable to return home because of a US blockade.
Sri Lankan authorities say the vessels are in international waters, beyond the country’s 12-nautical-mile territorial limit. Reconnaissance aircraft and naval patrol boats have been deployed to monitor them, the newspaper reported.
In March, Iran’s army said 104 crew members of the Iranian warship IRIS Dena were killed and 32 others injured in a US attack off Sri Lanka.
According to Iran’s state news agency IRNA, the vessel was attacked on March 4 while returning from the Milan Peace 2026 naval drills in India. Washington confirmed that an American submarine carried out a torpedo attack on the ship.
Sri Lanka said it launched a joint rescue operation after receiving a distress call from the vessel off Galle, taking 32 wounded crew members to a local hospital.

Flavio Bolsonaro rejects defeat, seeks annulment of Brazil election
Right-wing presidential candidate Flavio Bolsonaro has rejected his defeat to incumbent Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva in Brazil’s presidential run-off, calling for the election to be annulled over a two-hour extension of voting hours.
Speaking to reporters after the electoral court declared Lula the winner, Bolsonaro said he could not accept the result. He criticized a decision by Supreme Court judge Cristiano Zanin to extend voting hours nationwide, arguing that it had changed the rules of the election.
"What happened today was not normal. It was unacceptable," Bolsonaro said, arguing that the nationwide extension had undermined equal treatment between states. He said he would take legal action against the result.
Lula’s campaign had requested the extension, citing difficulties transporting voters to polling stations in several states. Bolsonaro’s campaign had also sought extra voting time, but only in municipalities across five states, citing heavy rain, flooding and power outages.
Lula says Brazilians voted to defend democracy, vows to resist US influence
Brazilians voted to "guarantee democracy," President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva said Sunday after beating Flavio Bolsonaro to win an unprecedented fourth term.
In a post on X, Lula thanked Brazilians, particularly young people who took to the streets in defense of democracy, saying: "This victory belongs to a people who believe, who fight, and who never give up on building a more just, sovereign, and democratic Brazil."
In his victory speech, Lula reiterated that Brazil would "not accept being anyone’s backyard," a recurring campaign message defending the country’s sovereignty against US influence. The stance may have helped him win votes, with some voters viewing Washington’s actions as interference.
Relations between the two countries deteriorated in 2025, when the US imposed tariffs on Brazil in retaliation for legal proceedings against former president Jair Bolsonaro, who was later convicted of coup-plotting.
Speaking in a hoarse voice, Lula thanked his campaign team and Brazilians, particularly young people who took to the streets to defend democracy. He described the result as a "loss for negativity, lies."
The re-elected president also promised better regulation of big tech platforms, after Meta was the subject of legal complaints over alleged "interference" throughout the polarizing campaign.
Latin American leaders congratulate Lula on election victory
Several Latin American leaders congratulated leftist President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva on his victory.
Chilean President Jose Antonio Kast said he had spoken to Lula and congratulated him, adding that "Chile and Brazil have a lot of shared future ahead."
Mexico’s left-wing President Claudia Sheinbaum congratulated Lula on his victory, writing on X: "Long live democracy, the people of Brazil won. Congratulations, President Lula!"
The presidents of Uruguay, Paraguay, Panama and Bolivia also congratulated Lula in posts on X.
Cuba’s president congratulated Lula on X, calling him "dear brother" and praising his victory as a win for peace, sovereignty and social justice.
IN PICTURES: Lula supporters celebrate, while Bolsonaro's fans disappointed
Brazil's Lula defeats conservative Flavio Bolsonaro in presidential election
Brazilian leftist President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva has won a fourth term in office, defeating right-wing challenger Flávio Bolsonaro in a presidential runoff, electoral authorities said.
Lula overcame his first-round defeat to Bolsonaro to secure victory in the runoff. The nearly 81-year-old leader won 51.7% of the vote, compared with 48.2% for Flavio Bolsonaro, the son of former president Jair Bolsonaro.
The campaign was marred by scandals and mudslinging. Sunday’s vote was thrown into confusion after a last-minute Supreme Court ruling extended voting by two hours, following Lula’s claim that buses had been taken off the roads in several cities, preventing some voters from reaching polling stations.
Pollsters said higher-than-expected turnout appeared to have benefited Lula. Conservative candidates in Brazil typically lead early in the count, while left-wing candidates gain ground as votes from poorer, more populous northeastern states come in.
In regards to foreign policy in his next term, Lula will have to manage relations with Washington while maintaining his anti-imperialist stance, as the Trump administration increasingly asserts its influence across the region. Flavio Bolsonaro had campaigned on a promise of closer cooperation with Washington.
Around 159 million Brazilians were eligible to vote. Under Lula’s left-wing Workers’ Party, unemployment fell to a record low, poverty declined, the minimum wage rose and deforestation in the Amazon decreased. Congress also approved the gradual introduction of a five-day working week with two days off.
However, rising living costs, high public debt, Lula’s spending policies and a scandal involving alleged pension fraud weighed on his government. The economic challenges left many voters dissatisfied with his record and open to a return of the Bolsonaro family to power.
Lula finished the first round with 45% of the vote, two percentage points behind Flavio Bolsonaro. He became the first candidate since Brazil restored direct presidential elections in 1989 to overcome a first-round deficit and win the runoff.
The former trade unionist, who served as president from 2003 to 2010 before returning to office in 2023, now faces a challenging fourth term with a strong right-wing opposition.
Voting extended after complaints by both sides
Brazil's Supreme Court has moved to extend voting time in the presidential election until 7 p.m. local time (2200 GMT), giving voters an additional two hours.
The decision comes amid complaints from Lula's team that public bus services had been hampered, blocking people from getting to polling stations.
At the same time, Bolsonaro's team complained of weather conditions in certain regions making it more difficult for people to get out and vote.
Lula asks for polls to stay open longer after people 'barred from voting'
President Lula has requested an extension to poll opening hours after buses were taken out of circulation in Sao Paolo, the country's largest city, which he said prevented many people from voting.
"We are asking the Supreme Court to extend the electoral process so that those who were effectively barred from voting, due to the dirty tactics of mayors, can still cast their votes," Lula said, according to AFP.
Lula said 40% of buses in the city had been prevented from going into service, a claim that matched local media reports saying 75 buses had been blocked from leaving garages.
"I've never complained about anything in any election before. Whether I won or lost, I'd just accept it and get ready for the next one. But this time, something abominable is happening," he said.
"No one should give up on voting just because some scoundrel of a business owner or some crooked, criminal mayor tried to stop the people from casting their ballots."
Results show Brazilian voters in Germany back Lula
Brazilians in Germany have voted overwhelmingly for Lula, according to figures posted by Brazilian Embassies across the country and seen by DW's Portuguese service.
The left-wing incumbent, Lula, won 79.09% of the ballots cast by the 20,923 voters across Germany. This marks an increase on the 71.9% he won in the first round.
Brazilian voters in Germany could vote at embassies in Berlin, Hamburg, Cologne, Frankfurt and Munich.
The German capital saw the greatest support for Lula, with 88.77% of the votes going his way. Frankfurt was the city with the greatest support for Bolsonaro, but on 29.03% he still trailed his opponent by some margin.
The turnout also increased in the second round in comparison to the first round when it stood at 19,322. However, for both rounds, only around half of the 41,552 eligible voters turned out to vote. Across the world, there are some 918,900 eligible voters for Sunday's election.
IN PHOTOS: Almost 160 million called out to vote
What role is Trump playing in Brazil's election?
Although he hasn't endorsed either candidate, US President Donald Trump is close to the Bolsonaro family.
Not only did the senior Bolsonaro imitate Trump's rhetoric and policies, he also refused to concede defeat after losing to Lula in 2022, leading to his imprisonment for an attempted coup, provoking comparisons with Trump's own defeat to Joe Biden in 2020.
On the other side, Lula has presented himself as a defense against US interference.
The right "wants to govern with the American flag," Lula said after casting his ballot on Sunday.
A Bolsonaro win would mark a further move in Latin America toward pro-US far-right leaders, following in the footsteps of countries such as Colombia, Chile and Peru.
Results expected within hours of polls closing
The president of Brazil's Superior Electoral Court, Kassio Nunes Marques, has said he expects the winner of Sunday's vote to be announced officially between 8.30 p.m. and 9 p.m. (2330 and 0000 GMT), according to A Folha de Sao Paolo.
Brazil uses an electronic voting system meaning that ballots can be tallied quicker than in elections where paper votes are counted by hand.
However, the gap between the winner and loser is expected to be small, with the two running head-to-head in pre-election polls.
Supreme Court president urges candidates to accept result of vote
The head of Brazil's Supreme Federal Court, Edson Fachin, has called for the candidates to respect the result of Sunday's vote.
"It's important to remember that all authority and power comes from the people and, thus, it is fundamental that the choices that derive from the manifestation of popular sovereignty are respected," he said as he left his local polling station, according to A Folha de Sao Paulo.
"Brazil needs peace and calm to, from tomorrow, be able to confront the major challenges in many areas that demand the presence of the state."
Some observers have posited that Flavio Bolsonaro could refuse to accept a Lula victory, like his father before him, with the potential for violence to erupt.

Brazil is heading back to the polls, but the impact could be felt worldwide.
With the Amazon vital to the health of the planet, the election could help shape its future.

Serbia's Vucic concedes election defeat as student-led movement claims victory
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
06:12:33 CST
07:12:33 KST

Former Serbian President Aleksandar Vucic speaks at his campaign headquarters in Belgrade, Serbia, Oct. 25, 2026. Former Serbian President Aleksandar Vucic conceded defeat in Sunday's snap parliamentary election, as independent projections and leaders of a student-backed movement born out of anti-corruption protests confirmed an outright parliamentary majority that ends the Serbian Progressive Party's (SNS) 14-year grip on power. (Photo by Predrag Milosavljevic/Xinhua)
BELGRADE, Oct. 25 (Xinhua) -- Former Serbian President Aleksandar Vucic conceded defeat in Sunday's snap parliamentary election, as independent projections and leaders of a student-backed movement born out of anti-corruption protests confirmed an outright parliamentary majority that ends the Serbian Progressive Party's (SNS) 14-year grip on power.
Initial projections released by polling agencies Ipsos and CeSID showed the "Student List -- Students Win" winning 52 percent of the vote, well ahead of Vucic's SNS-led coalition, "Aleksandar Vucic -- United Serbia," which stood at 39.3 percent.
Speaking at his campaign headquarters in Belgrade before final official results were available, Vucic said a stratified sample indicated that the student-backed list would win between 135 and 140 of the 250 parliamentary seats, compared with around 105 for his coalition.
"I want to inform you that based on the stratified sample, it is clear that we have lost these elections," Vucic said. "The student-backed list has won. They will have between 135 and 140 seats, and we will have around 105."
According to Vucic's projections, the student-backed list received approximately 2.2 million votes, while his coalition secured roughly 1.72 million.
As victory celebrations erupted at the Student List's headquarters, prominent candidate Radomir Saicic, a University of Belgrade professor and member of the Serbian Academy of Sciences and Arts, declared a historic triumph for Serbian citizens.
"Tonight the voice of the people is heard," Saicic said, noting that preliminary results showed the Student List convincingly leading across polling stations.
"This is a victory of courage over fear, a victory of hope over apathy, a victory of faith that Serbia can and must be different ... This victory is no one's personal trophy. It belongs to all of us," he said.
Stressing that the electoral will of the public "must be respected without exception," Saicic called on supporters to celebrate peacefully and with dignity, urging citizens not to fall for provocations or enter into conflicts.
Sunday's vote determined all 250 seats in Serbia's unicameral parliament, with 126 needed for a majority.
About 6.45 million voters were eligible to cast ballots at 8,392 polling stations, with 18 electoral lists competing. Polling stations closed at 8 p.m. (1900 GMT), though voters already in line at that hour were permitted to cast their ballots.
The outcome marks a major shift in Serbian politics, where Vucic and the SNS have held a dominant position since 2012. Vucic resigned as president on Sept. 27 to take part in the parliamentary election, with a new presidential vote required by the end of December.
The student-backed movement emerged from nearly two years of anti-corruption protests and university blockades following the November 2024 collapse of a railway station canopy in Novi Sad that killed 16 people. The tragedy became a focal point for public anger over corruption and demands for accountability.
The movement's electoral list, formally headed by Novi Sad university professor Ilija Srdanovic, campaigned on institutional reform and anti-corruption measures. It challenged not only the ruling bloc but also established opposition parties, including the Socialist Party of Serbia and other pro-European and right-wing groups.
In his concession address, Vucic said he had chosen to announce the projections before official results were released to spare supporters uncertainty and counter claims that he would refuse to acknowledge an electoral defeat.
He attributed his bloc's projected defeat to foreign support for the protest movement, describing the result as a "verification of a revolution".
Vucic thanked his supporters and pledged that his political movement would remain united and continue its work from the opposition benches.
The projections represent the most significant electoral setback for the SNS since it came to power in 2012 and place the student-backed movement in a position to form a single-party parliamentary majority. ■

A voter verifies his identity at a polling station during the second round of Brazil's 2026 presidential election in Brasilia, Brazil, on Oct. 25, 2026. (Photo by Lucio Tavora/Xinhua)

Nigeria identifies 53 contacts linked to confirmed Ebola case
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
06:12:10 CST
07:12:10 KST

ABUJA, Oct. 25 (Xinhua) -- Nigerian public health authorities on Sunday said they had identified and followed up on 53 contacts linked to the country's only confirmed Ebola case.
Jide Idris, director-general of the Nigeria Centre for Disease Control and Prevention (NCDC), told a media briefing Sunday evening that the contacts include healthcare workers, domestic staff, and the patient's spouse.
The confirmed case involves a 42-year-old woman who returned to the Nigerian capital of Abuja from Uganda via Addis Ababa on Oct. 3. She developed symptoms, including fever, diarrhea, generalized body aches and sore throat, on Oct. 7.
Idris said contact tracing and monitoring were underway, with public health teams working to identify people who might have been exposed to the confirmed case and monitor them for 21 days after their last possible exposure.
The NCDC director-general said the index case had "improved remarkably" and was receiving medical care in isolation in Abuja.
The woman first presented at a private health facility on Oct. 10 and was admitted to another private facility on Oct. 11. The NCDC was notified of the case on Oct. 19, after which samples were collected and an investigation conducted, Idris said. Laboratory tests conducted by the NCDC confirmed the case on Oct. 20.
According to Idris, a suspected case reported by Rivers State on Friday tested negative for Ebola, with the result communicated to state authorities.
"Assessments of infection prevention and control capacity have been conducted across states and healthcare facilities ... and enhanced surveillance at the country's points of entry is continuing, alongside public awareness activities and monitoring of rumors and misinformation," he added.
Meanwhile, authorities in Nigeria's most populous city, Lagos, have dismissed reports of a suspected Ebola case in the southwestern state.
In a statement, the Lagos State government reassured residents of its readiness to prevent, detect and respond to potential Ebola threats following the confirmation of an imported case of Ebola virus disease caused by the Bundibugyo virus in Abuja.
Ebola virus disease is transmitted through direct contact with the blood, secretions, other bodily fluids or organs of infected people or animals. Its incubation period ranges from two to 21 days.
Symptoms may include fever, intense weakness, muscle pain, headaches, sore throat, vomiting, diarrhea and rashes. In severe cases, the disease can cause impaired kidney and liver function as well as internal and external bleeding. ■

Voting opens in New Zealand for November 7 election with no clear frontrunner
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
23:12:01 CET
07:12:01 KST

By Lucy Craymer and Renju Jose
WELLINGTON, Oct 26 (Reuters) - New Zealand Prime Minister Christopher Luxon said the national election on November 7 would be decided on economic issues, as early voting opened on Monday in a race that polls suggest will be closely contested.
With voters frustrated by a sluggish economy and persistently high inflation, the cost of living has emerged as a key election issue, prompting competing policy solutions from across the political spectrum.
Luxon said his National Party had “the best plan” to help the economy to grow and improve affordability.
“We’ve worked incredibly hard over the last three years … the plan is working, but we need more time,” Luxon said after casting his vote.
Opposition leader Chris Hipkins said he hoped to form a Labour-led government before Christmas and would move swiftly to ease cost-of-living pressures.
Ballot boxes will be open for nearly two weeks at shopping centres, transport hubs and community halls across the country ahead of election day.
Recent polls show no clear frontrunner under New Zealand’s mixed-member proportional system, where coalition deals are often needed to form governments.
A 1News-Verian poll published on October 20 put the ruling centre-right National Party at 32% and opposition Labour at 27%, while a Post/Freshwater Strategy poll published a day earlier had Labour narrowly ahead at 28.7% to the National Party’s 27.6%.
In both surveys, the smaller Opportunity Party was polling around or above the 5% threshold needed to enter Parliament, making it a potential kingmaker.
New Zealand’s Electoral Commission said 207 voting places were open on Monday, with that number rising to more than 2,300 on election day. Overseas voting opened earlier, on October 21.
UNCERTAINTY FACTORS CONVERGE
Political commentator Gareth Hughes said the level of uncertainty surrounding the outcome of a New Zealand election at this stage was unprecedented.
“Multiple factors are converging to contribute to the uncertainty,” Hughes told Reuters.
These include the possibility that both left- and right-wing parties could face an overhang - where a party wins more electorate seats than its share of the party vote entitles it to, increasing the total number of seats in Parliament, he said.
Hughes added that the emergence of the centrist Opportunity Party had compounded the uncertainty, amid the unpopularity of the two main legacy parties - National and Labour.
Voting began just hours after enrollment closed at midnight on Sunday, a deadline that has become one of the campaign’s most contentious issues.
Critics say the earlier cutoff could deter participation, particularly among harder-to-reach groups. The Human Rights Commission said last year that ending election-day enrolment was likely to unjustifiably restrict participation and would disproportionately affect underrepresented groups.
(Reporting by Lucy Craymer and Renju Jose; Editing by Bill Berkrot and Thomas Derpinghaus)

SOFIA, October 25. /TASS/. Bulgarian’s incumbent President Iliana Iotova is winning in the first round of the presidential election with 35.3% of votes, according to exit polls.
Her rival, the former prime minister of the technical government Andrey Gyurov, who was supported by the opposition, is garnering 32.2% votes. The two will face each other in the runoff election on November 1.
The record-low voter turnout came as a surprise. According to polls, about 22.3% of took part in the voting.

News Analysis: Five challenges facing Netanyahu ahead of Israeli election
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
06:11:49 CST
07:11:49 KST

JERUSALEM, Oct. 25 (Xinhua) -- Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who has served 19 years in office across several terms since 1996, is fighting for his political survival in Tuesday's parliamentary election.
Analysts say Netanyahu is seeking to turn military gains into electoral support while facing public anger, economic isolation and a shortage of potential coalition partners.
The vote, Israel's first since the Hamas-led Oct. 7, 2023 attack, comes after three years of wars in Gaza, Lebanon and Iran that have reshaped Israeli politics and deepened divisions over the country's future.
LEGACY OF OCT. 7 AND PROLONGED WARS
Analysts note that Netanyahu's central challenge is persuading voters to judge him by Israel's military achievements rather than the failures that allowed the Oct. 7 attack, which the Israeli authorities said killed about 1,200 people and took 251 hostages.
He has refused to accept personal responsibility or establish an independent state commission of inquiry, instead campaigning on Israel's military achievements against Hamas, Hezbollah and Iran.
Political scientist Ilana Shpaizman at Bar-Ilan University told the Jewish Telegraphic Agency (JTA) that Netanyahu's campaign sought to avoid discussing the Oct. 7 attack and instead emphasize subsequent military successes.
But victims' families dispute the narrative. On Oct. 20, relatives representing 17 hostages who died in Gaza accused Netanyahu of exploiting their deaths in his campaign.
"Do not use their deaths to ask the public for another term in office," they said.
A Channel 12 poll on Oct. 5 found that 65 percent of respondents held Netanyahu largely responsible for the failures, yet 75 percent of coalition voters attributed him at least some responsibility.
Tamar Hermann, a public opinion expert at the Israel Democracy Institute, said the Oct. 7 attack had reinforced existing political loyalties.
"Most of the facts are already on the table, and it is the interpretation of the events that influences people's decisions," Hermann said.
CHALLENGE FROM EISENKOT
Netanyahu faces an unusual challenger in Gadi Eisenkot, a former military chief who served in his wartime cabinet before resigning in 2024. Eisenkot's son and two nephews were killed fighting in Gaza.
Eisenkot questions Netanyahu's ability to turn military operations into strategic gains.
"Never has an Israeli government been given so much room to maneuver and so much legitimacy, from the public and the world, and suffered such a resounding strategic failure," Eisenkot said earlier this month.
He promises an independent Oct. 7 inquiry, broader conscription and restored confidence in state institutions.
Yet their differences on Palestinian policy are narrower. Both oppose Palestinian statehood and demand Hamas's disarmament. Eisenkot criticizes settler violence and some settlement expansion, while Netanyahu governs with parties advocating West Bank annexation.
The contest is therefore less about competing visions of peace than about leadership, accountability and the conduct of war.
ECONOMIC PRESSURE, INTERNATIONAL ISOLATION
Netanyahu faces a growing economic dilemma: military policies presented as essential to security have deepened Israel's international isolation and increased the threat of sanctions.
In a Friday interview with Channel 10, he acknowledged concerns over possible banking sanctions.
"Of course I'm concerned," Netanyahu said, suggesting blockchain technology as a possible workaround.
The Bank of Israel rejected the proposal, while 109 economists, business leaders and former officials warned Sunday that sanctions could cause severe economic damage, according to the Israeli Hebrew-language business newspapers Calcalist and Globes.
The controversy highlights a broader challenge to Netanyahu's security doctrine: military gains may come at an economic and diplomatic cost Israel cannot sustain indefinitely.
DOMESTIC DIVISIONS, ULTRA-ORTHODOX DRAFT
Netanyahu also faces opposition over his corruption trial, attempts to weaken judicial oversight and exemptions from military service for ultra-Orthodox Jewish men.
He denies bribery, fraud and breach-of-trust charges, accusing the justice system of political persecution.
The conscription dispute has intensified after three years of wars and repeated reserve deployments.
An August survey by the Dialog Institute for Ynet and Yedioth Ahronoth found that about 70 percent of 509 reservists said the government's handling of ultra-Orthodox conscription would significantly influence their vote. Only 34 percent of former Likud voters surveyed said they would definitely vote for the party again.
Netanyahu risks alienating reservists by protecting his ultra-Orthodox allies, but enforcing broader conscription could jeopardize those alliances, analysts say.
THE BATTLE FOR A MAJORITY
Netanyahu's coalition support collapsed after the Oct. 7 attack and has only partially recovered. Final polls by Kan, Channel 12 and Channel 13 project 50 seats for his bloc in the 120-seat parliament, against 52 to 56 for the opposition and 14 to 16 for Arab parties.
Netanyahu relies on ultra-Orthodox and far-right allies, including Bezalel Smotrich and Itamar Ben-Gvir, whose demands for West Bank annexation further strain Israel's relations with Western allies.
Opposition parties, including right-wing factions, refuse to join a Netanyahu-led government, citing his corruption trial and responsibility for the Oct. 7 attack.
In an interview with Radio 103FM, Eisenkot said that he "will not serve under Netanyahu, not even in a rotation agreement," further narrowing Netanyahu's options.
Gideon Rahat, a political scientist at the Hebrew University of Jerusalem, told JTA that Netanyahu's bloc had lost support since winning 64 seats in 2022, but the opposition still lacked a majority.
The paradox is that while many opposition parties agree on replacing Netanyahu, their divisions could prevent them from forming an alternative government, leaving Israel facing another electoral deadlock. ■

RIYADH, Oct. 25 (Xinhua) -- The localization rate of military spending in Saudi Arabia rose to 27.30 percent by the end of 2025, up from 24.89 percent in 2024, the General Authority for Military Industries (GAMI) said on Sunday.
GAMI made the announcement during the Military Industries Forum held in Riyadh, adding that local content accounted for 40.91 percent of military spending, while the military industries sector contributed 7.468 billion Saudi riyals (about 1.99 billion U.S. dollars) to gross domestic product.
The figure marks further progress toward the kingdom's target of localizing more than 50 percent of military spending by 2030, the authority said.
GAMI Acting Governor Bandar Alkhorayef said Saudi Arabia is building an industrial base capable of meeting domestic demand, serving regional markets and supporting exports.
Alkhorayef added that GAMI is working to strengthen the sector's regulatory and legislative framework, facilitate investment, expand international partnerships and support technology and knowledge transfer.
The forum also saw the signing of four memoranda of understanding between GAMI and Saudi banks to strengthen financing solutions for the military industries sector. ■

North Korea tells UN South fabricated landmine incident, KCNA says
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
23:11:33 CET
07:11:33 KST

By Hongji Kim, Kyu-seok Shim and Joyce Lee
SEOUL, Oct 26 (Reuters) - Tensions between North Korea and South Korea are running high this week after Pyongyang sent a letter to the UN Security Council, repeating accusations that Seoul fabricated a September landmine incident, and after a North Korean howitzer was spotted close to the border.
A Reuters witness at an observatory in South Korea overlooking the heavily armed border on Monday confirmed the presence of a North Korean artillery piece positioned in clear view near the frontier.
South Korea’s Yonhap news agency on Sunday identified the weapon as a self-propelled 122-mm howitzer, saying its deployment near the border marked a rare public display of such artillery.
Reuters also observed three North Korean armored vehicles with their gun barrels pointed south, as well as about 20 to 30 North Korean soldiers carrying out fencing work inside the Demilitarised Zone (DMZ).
“It is highly unusual (for North Korea) to expose its self-propelled artillery so conspicuously,” said Lim Eul-chul, a professor at Kyungnam University in Seoul.
“By deliberately displaying it, North Korea is signalling through action, not words, that it intends to enforce its border policy through force rather than dialogue or negotiation.”
It is also warning South Korea to exercise caution about escalating border friction, with the intention to prevent an accidental clash, he added.
North Korean state media KCNA reported that in the letter sent on Sunday, the country’s UN representative said Seoul was using the landmine incident to depict Pyongyang’s border construction as a military incursion.
North Korea warned in the letter that violations of its sovereignty could trigger self-defence measures and that South Korea would be “wholly accountable for all the ensuing consequences.”
PHOTOS ALSO SHOW NORTH KOREAN DRILLS
The letter is a response to a South Korean letter to the Security Council last week, which said a September 21 blast in the DMZ was planted by North Korean troops and constituted a violation of the Korean War Armistice Agreement.
The UN Command, which oversees the DMZ, has said a North Korean mine across the line violated the armistice. Pyongyang has denied responsibility.
A spokesperson for South Korea’s Unification Ministry said on Monday that the North Korean letter appears to repeat North Korea’s existing position and seeks to justify its so-called border line marking work.
The ministry had no separate comment on the placement of the howitzer. Seoul has proposed dialogue with North Korea to defuse border tensions.
North Korea’s letter also repeated accusations that South Korea had opened fire on North Korean personnel, calling that a violation of the UN Charter, which bars the threat or use of force against another state’s territorial integrity.
Seoul has said its military issues warning broadcasts and fires warning shots to send North Korean soldiers back across the line when they cross the military demarcation line (MDL), which bisects the DMZ.
North Korean troops have been building tactical roads and fences and laying mines near the MDL in recent years.
The Yonhap report cited photographs taken from an observatory in the South Korean border city of Gimpo that appeared to show the howitzer as well as North Korean troops conducting drills on the coast of Kaepung county, about 1.5 km (1 mile) from the observatory.
In 2015, there was a similar incident in which South Korean troops were injured by North Korean mines. Then, Seoul resumed anti-North Korea loudspeaker broadcasts across the DMZ, triggering a military standoff. After North Korea expressed regret, the standoff ended with a high-level inter-Korean agreement.
(Reporting by Kyu-seok Shim and Joyce Lee; Editing by Bill Berkrot and Edwina Gibbs )

Ukraine is stalling EU-required reform of bureau that can raid any official, risking European money it badly needs
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
22:11:10 UTC
07:11:10 KST

Whoever controls Ukraine’s State Bureau of Investigation wields enormous influence over law enforcement, judges, and government officials. The EU wants Ukraine to reform it, and Ukraine’s government is likely to pass changes that satisfy monitoring requirements on paper while leaving the body effectively under the President’s Office’s control, the investigative outlet Texty reports.
The stakes are money and power at once. The State Bureau of Investigation, known by its Ukrainian initials DBR, investigates officials, judges, prosecutors, and soldiers. So choosing an independent director is one of the rule-of-law conditions the EU has tied to Ukraine’s 2026 and 2027 budget aid.
Yet the version the government may pass would change how the director is chosen only for the one after next, in 2032. Brussels wants the model used at the anti-corruption bureau NABU, where the chief cannot be confirmed without the votes of independent foreign experts.
Who picks the watchdog
Today a nine-member commission selects the director:
- three named by the president
- three by a parliament his party dominates
- three proposed by the government on international partners’ suggestion.
That leaves the foreign experts without a decisive vote and the President’s Office effectively choosing the winner. Ukrainian leader Volodymyr Zelenskyy promised in January that a reform bill would reach parliament within a month.
It is now October, and there is none.
Director Oleksii Sukhachov’s term ends this year, so his successor will be picked under the old rules.
Sukhachov has publicly argued that overhauling the bureau during the war would threaten the state.
The deadline to adopt the reform was October. To carry it out, the end of 2026. Miss it, and Ukraine risks reputational damage and the European funding it needs amid a budget deficit, money the EU has frozen before when anti-corruption guarantees slipped.
A factory of “procedural nightmaring”
What makes the fight so bitter is that the bureau’s searches, seizures, and summonses are levers over individuals and whole institutions.
For example, NABU’s Operation Midas tapes, from the $100 million kickback case at the state nuclear company Energoatom, mention the bureau’s entire leadership. In March 2025, its investigators searched the commission that vets and appoints Ukraine’s judges, itself reformed with international experts, in what the commission called pressure that could stall the courts.
Cases against the bureau’s own officials, meanwhile, are handled by a unit inside the bureau. And its director sits under his own cloud: the outlet Slidstvo.Info reported that his brother bought 143 apartments cheaply from a developer. Nevertheless, a court banned publication, and eight newsrooms jointly ran the story.

Trump goes on the attack against El-Sayed in Michigan as midterms loom
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
22:08:23 UTC
07:08:23 KST

President Donald Trump escalated his attacks against Democratic Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed of Michigan on Sunday with rhetoric that questioned the Muslim candidate’s loyalties to the U.S. and repeatedly tried to tie him to extremism, claims the Democrat has repeatedly denied and denounced.
“Over the past three weeks, I’ve traveled all over the country. But I’m here today in Michigan for a very important reason,” Trump told the crowd in Port Huron. “I’m here to keep a jihadist Muslim Brotherhood member from becoming a United States senator.”
The Republican president has been attacking El-Sayed’s faith throughout the campaign and claiming his past statements and background show a sympathy for extremists. El-Sayed, a former public health official, has repeatedly said he is loyal to the U.S. and disavowed the Muslim Brotherhood, an Islamic movement with branches that the U.S. government has designated as terrorist organizations.
The claims by Republicans have been denounced by Democrats as attacks on El-Sayed’s faith and his Egyptian heritage. El-Sayed would be the first Muslim senator if elected.
Trump’s return to Michigan reflects the importance of the race. Republicans see an opening to flip a Senate seat as they try to hold onto the majority in the chamber. El-Sayed faces Republican Mike Rogers, a former congressman backed by Trump, in the November 3 race to succeed retiring Democrat Gary Peters.
The race has taken on significance beyond Michigan, with Republicans casting El-Sayed as a symbol of a Democratic Party moving further to the left. Progressives, meanwhile, see his candidacy as a test of whether their agenda can win in a battleground state ahead of the 2028 presidential election.
Trump invokes 9/11 when talking about El-Sayed
Trump on Sunday invoked the Sept. 11, 2001, terrorist attacks, drawing a comparison between stopping El-Sayed from entering the Senate and the passengers who fought back against the hijackers aboard United Flight 93.
“Twenty-five years later, Michigan needs to stand up and fight, just like Todd did, to stop a jihadist from walking into the Capitol,” Trump said, referring to Todd Beamer, a Michigan native who died aboard the flight. Trump then invited Beamer’s parents onto the stage.
Trump’s visit to Port Huron follows former Democratic President Barack Obama’s appearances Saturday in Michigan and Ohio for his party’s candidates. It is Trump’s latest stop on a packed campaign schedule to bolster Republicans on the midterm ballot as the GOP is weighed down by voters’ frustration with the economy and the war with Iran.
Port Huron, about 60 miles (96.56 kilometers) northeast of Detroit, sits across the St. Clair River from Canada, where Trump’s tariffs have strained trade relations between the longtime allies.
Unlike Trump’s earlier trips to Republican-controlled states where his party is on defense, the GOP has not won a Senate race in Michigan for more than three decades. Rogers unsuccessfully ran for Senate in 2024, losing to then-Rep. Elissa Slotkin.
El-Sayed has taunted Trump, encouraging him to come to Michigan in the belief that a visit would backfire on Rogers. “Donald, if you’re watching, don’t wuss out, man,” El-Sayed said. The progressive, who won a divisive primary in August, has said the country needs to “turn the page on Donald Trump.”
The campaign has been one of the most contentious this year
During their second and final general election campaign debate, Rogers questioned El-Sayed’s loyalty to the United States. “Are you for America, or are you for these terrorist groups overseas?” Rogers asked.
El-Sayed said that questioning was “shameful.”
“I’m proud of our Constitution that guarantees all of us the right to pray as we choose to pray,” he said.
Speaking before Trump’s appearance Sunday, Rogers repeated his allegations linking El-Sayed to the Muslim Brotherhood. “The Muslim Brotherhood celebrated exactly one victory in the United States in the primary this year,” Rogers said on stage. “Abdul El-Sayed’s.”
El-Sayed has faced criticism for his own rhetoric, particularly when he said “hurt people hurt people” after an attack on a synagogue in the Detroit area. The attacker had lost four relatives in an Israeli airstrike on Lebanon the week earlier. El-Sayed later apologized, saying he was not trying to justify what happened.
“To anyone who feels like my comments might have been hurtful, I’m really sorry,” he said. “That was not my intention.”
El-Sayed has struggled to unite Democrats following a contentious primary against Rep. Haley Stevens. Appearing Sunday on CNN, Stevens declined to explicitly say whether she was “still fully behind” El-Sayed, instead saying she was “on the team” and naming other Michigan Democratic candidates but not the party’s Senate nominee.

Political and legal developments

RIO DE JANEIRO, October 25. /TASS/. Voting in the runoff presidential election in Brazil has been extended for two more hours amid reports on serious logistics problems, the Brazilian Superior Electoral Court (TSE) decided after voting officially finished at 5:00 p.m. local time (8:00 p.m. GMT).
Earlier, the campaign headquarters of the country’s incumbent president, Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva, stated that voters in several cities were unable to reach polling places due to a lack of free public transportation. The situation was further exacerbated by weather conditions: heavy rains have been falling in southeastern Brazil since early morning, causing road flooding and traffic gridlock.
Voters are to choose between Lula da Silva and his rival, a right-wing opposition candidate Senator Flavio Bolsonaro. According to the results of the first round of voting on October 4, Bolsonaro took the lead with 47.03% of the vote, while Lula da Silva was second with 45.16%. The margin between the candidates was less than two percentage points.
The winner will take office on January 1, 2027.

Songs of praise: An emotional Greek-German musical collaboration at Berlin Cathedral
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
22:01:57 UTC
07:01:57 KST

Thirty-eight students from the Chios Music School joined forces with choirs and ensembles from Berlin’s Song Academy as part of German Unity Day.
German Unity Day may well have been celebrated earlier this month but the sounds of the songs sung to mark the occasion are still reverberating from Berlin to Athens.
Some 240 Greeks and Germans joined their voices in a festive service at Berlin Cathedral on Saturday 3 October. The Greek participants were 38 pupils from the Chios Music School, who performed alongside choirs and ensembles from Berlin’s Sing-Akademie (Sing-Akademie zu Berlin).
Together they performed works by Mendelssohn, Poulenc, Britten, Lewandowski and Holst, as well as "Ora kali" by Michalis Adamis and "Messa Latina" by Yannis Christou. The result of this remarkable musical encounter was deeply moving.
Kai-Uwe Jirka, the artistic director of the Sing-Akademie zu Berlin, was the conductor of the concert given at the Berliner Dom:
"Today we celebrate the reunification of the two parts of Germany. For the past three years we have held a ceremony in the cathedral. After the service inside, we go outside with the congregation and we all sing together on the church steps for Europe. There is a special story behind this, because this event for Europe was our own idea. Three years ago, after the service, we came out of the cathedral and there was another event taking place in the Lustgarten, organised by the far-right party in our society.
And we all said that this could not be allowed to happen. We had just come out of the service and we wanted to be together without hatred, without racism. So for three years now we have been reserving this space for our choirs and saying: 'All right, we cannot celebrate only Germany. Because what is Germany without Europe? And what is Europe without Greece?' This year, for me, everything that happened was perfect. We have young people from all over Europe coming together, singing side by side and sending a very strong message for Europe."
This was not the first collaboration between the Greek choir and the German choral ensembles. As part of the 10th Chios Music Festival last August, more than 50 young choristers from the Sing-Akademie zu Berlin spent a week on the island, giving concerts at various venues across Chios.
Conductor Friederike Stahmer founded the Berlin Sing-Akademie Girls’ Choir 20 years ago. She was on Chios this summer and shared her experience with Euronews:
"What really makes this exchange programme special is that we come together and create music. A short while ago my choir travelled to Chios for the island’s Music Festival. There we learnt some Greek songs, mainly from Chios but also from the wider region. The pupils of the Chios Music School learnt German songs. Of course, at the beginning such musical collaborations are always challenging: the musical style is different, the language is different and you really have to work hard. At the same time you realise that you are learning so much about another musical culture.
And now it is very rewarding that the Chios Music School is in Berlin and we have the chance to revisit all the repertoire we had already performed on Chios. You can see how it develops and blossoms. And I think it is not only about getting to know one another; creating art together, making music together has an even deeper impact on them. I am sure it will be an unforgettable experience in their lives."
The Chios Music Festival and the Sing-Akademie zu Berlin have set up this special cultural exchange, bringing the island’s Music School together with German choirs, with the support of the Greek-German Youth Foundation (ΕΓΙΝ/DGJW). The Greek group stayed for eight days in the German capital and took part in three concerts in total.
Olga Holdorff Myriagou and Lefteris Veniadis shared the artistic direction of the highly successful Chios Music Festival:
"For the Chios Music Festival it is very important to offer opportunities to young people, to the new generation, because the choir that is here in Berlin taking part in the exchange programme has many more opportunities than the children on Chios, which lies on the edge of Europe. It is therefore a great chance for the children of Chios to come to Berlin and join such a project. Suddenly we have 100 children on stage. So we want to create opportunities on Chios as well, when the children from Berlin come through this programme, and ensure that they too have high-quality experiences there. We want to bring similarly significant activities to the island, but also to have the chance to take our children abroad, so that they can learn and discover new things, to open their ears," explains Olga Holdorff Myriagou.
Lefteris Veniadis adds: "Through the common language of music, we witnessed a miracle. German children sharing the stage with the children of Chios, singing German and Greek songs. There was, in other words, a kind of osmosis, a common goal. We managed to stage all these concerts as part of the Chios Music Festival in different parts of the island, in wonderful landscapes that took on a new dimension through music. And now something similar is happening in Berlin. We are very pleased with the outcome and the children from Chios are truly impressed by what is taking place here."
Four young people who took part in the exchange programme and sang in the service and the concerts shared their experience with us:
Orfeas Kirythras, who is from the Chios Music School said: "First of all, the experience is absolutely unique. Nothing like this has ever happened before in my life, or anything similar. I believe this exchange is extremely valuable, because we learn to live alongside people from another culture, another mindset, and overall they teach us a great deal. Greeks and Germans share this desire to create, this longing for creativity and for music. We want to build this beautiful thing called music."
Chrysa Noka is also a student at the Chios Music School: "At first I had doubts, but then I agreed to come, because I thought I would never have this experience again. When the children came to Chios, of course we faced quite a few difficulties because of our differences, but in the end we were able to coexist and we adapted our daily lives so that everyone felt comfortable."
Louise Castellani from the Berlin Girls’ Choir noted: "The experience on Chios was so wonderful, because I made many friends there. In the morning we would go to the beach and play volleyball, so it was really fantastic, and here in Berlin it is also just perfect. I enjoy it very much and I hope we can repeat this collaboration next year. We had a great time."
Elsa Kriegenburg from the Berlin Girls’ Choir said: "What brings us together is the common language of music. It makes everything much easier. Singing together creates a very different sense of companionship and community. Communication in general was not that difficult either, because I think that, especially as young people, we all speak English to some extent, so we could really talk, have conversations with one another. So we became friends very quickly. And it is wonderful that we are now meeting again here in Berlin."
After the service ended, the musical encounter continued outside Berlin Cathedral, on the steps overlooking the Lustgarten, with the initiative "Sing for Europe!", where the choirs and the large crowd sang together.

Alibaba Cloud founder says open-source, closed-source AI philosophies not at odds, calls for more Chinese cloud competition to strengthen industry
Long before artificial intelligence became the next big thing in the tech industry, Wang Jian was crafting the foundational infrastructure that would eventually power it. Today, Wang’s purview has expanded considerably. As an academician at the Chinese Academy of Engineering and the director of Zhejiang Lab, a research institution backed by the Zhejiang provincial government, his focus has turned to a new frontier: space computing.

Russian-friendly Vucic concedes defeat to student protest movement in Serbian election
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25

06:57:28 KST

Russian-friendly Vucic concedes defeat to student protest movement in Serbian election
Former Serbian President Aleksandar Vucic conceded defeat in parliamentary elections on Oct. 25 to the student-led protest movement that has gripped the nation for months.
“Based on a stratified sample, it is clear that we have lost this election. The student blockade list won,” Vucic said in a press briefing.
According to Vucic, the Students' List party, backed by the protest coalition, is projected to take between 135 and 140 seats in Serbia's Parliament. Vucic's Serbian Progressive Party appears to have come in second in the elections, and will have 105 seats in Parliament.
For almost two years, student-led demonstrations in Serbia rallied against Vucic's right-wing incumbent Serbian Progressive Party. Protesting against alleged corruption in the government, the movement was triggered when a train station canopy in the city of Novi Sad collapsed in 2024, killing 16.
Vucic previously announced his resignation as Serbia's president on Sept. 27, allowing him to run as prime minister in the nation's October parliamentary elections.
Vucic, having served as either Serbia’s prime minister or president since 2014, was known as a right-wing populist leader with authoritarian tendencies and warm ties with Russia.
The elections saw Serbia's highest voter turnout, 70%, since the dissolution of Yugoslavia in 1992, according to Reuters.
The election results are being hailed as a momentous political shift for Serbia, potentially turning the Balkan country away from ties with Russia and Vladimir Putin, who endorsed Vucic.
The defeat of Serbia's right-wing government echoes recent elections in Hungary. In April, populist leader Viktor Orban, also endorsed by Putin, was defeated in a landslide election.
Hungarian Prime Minister Peter Magyar drew an explicit parallel between this election and that in his country which saw him rise to power, celebrating the Serbian opposition's victory in an Oct. 25 post on X.
"In Serbia, @avucic has conceded defeat. The Students’ List has won an absolute majority in the elections. Celebrations have begun in the streets across Serbia. Sound familiar?" Magyar wrote.
The Guardian also reported that Magyar subsequently spoke with the Students' List leadership and offered Hungary's support, saying his own electoral victory in April had encouraged the Serbian movement during its struggle.

Marine Le Pen vows a French ‘renaissance’ as far right eyes seat of power
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
21:50:36 UTC
06:50:36 KST

Marine Le Pen vows French ‘renaissance’ as far right eyes seat of power
National Rally’s Le Pen launches presidential campaign against the backdrop of mass protests and social and economic discontent.
Orleans, France – Marine Le Pen took to the stage with a clear message: She would lead France’s “renaissance” as the country sank into crisis – and she would do so soon.
The far-right figure’s words were met with cheers from thousands of supporters gathered in Orleans in central France on Sunday, as she launched her presidential campaign against a backdrop of mass demonstrations and widespread social and economic discontent.
“Marine présidente!” the crowd chanted, waving French flags beneath a sea of red and blue lights. Organisers said 8,500 supporters had gathered in a venue transformed into a fort for the event.
Standing tall on stage in a pink blazer, her hair impeccably coiffed, Le Pen spoke with the confidence of a leader who believes the presidency is within reach.
Riding high in the polls, with candidates from the right, left and centre trailing behind her, she presented the election as a historic opportunity to restore France’s past glory.
“This is a story to be written, a destiny to be fulfilled,” she told the crowd, which erupted in cheers.
Her pitch was a promise to restore authority and security in a country she portrayed as having lost control.
“We are going to re-establish the rule of law,” she said, drawing loud applause from supporters wearing “Marine présidente” T-shirts.
Manon Funeau, 21, a business school student, was among the supporters.
“What they propose are values that resonate with me, that vibrate within me,” she said. “Honestly, I feel at home here.”
Le Pen’s speech comes as the country is at a crossroads. France has been shaken by a wave of protests since mid-September, a movement sparked by high school students in a Paris suburb that grew into a nationwide mobilisation tapping into widespread discontent.
Over the past two weekends, largely peaceful protests have been accompanied by episodes of violence on a scale rarely seen in recent years.
On October 17, shops were looted and ransacked, and more than 2,000 people were arrested as hundreds of thousands took to the streets of French cities. A similar dynamic unfolded the following weekend, though on a smaller scale. The protests show little sign of abating, with calls for further demonstrations already circulating.
The unrest has given Le Pen’s National Rally (RN) an opportunity to play one of its favourite cards: presenting itself as the guarantor of law and order. It has fuelled criticism of President Emmanuel Macron over his handling of public security, allowing Le Pen to accuse him of incompetence and the far-left leader Jean-Luc Melenchon – a contender in the coming elections – of encouraging the violence.
‘My country is drifting off course’
“I believe that my country is currently drifting off course,” said Nadede, a 56-year-old who began voting for RN in 2024 over what she said was the country’s growing lack of security. She did not spell out any specific event.
“I think that the only person capable of setting it back on the right track is Marine Le Pen – especially since, up until now, everyone else who has run for office has struggled to do so,” she said.
Outside the convention hall, the scale of the security operation offered a glimpse of the tensions surrounding the event. Police checks began at departure stations in Paris and continued on arrival, while officers in full gear moved through train carriages during the journey.
Orleans itself had been brought to a near standstill. All businesses were shut and public transport suspended.
Standing almost alone in the city’s main square was the statue of Joan of Arc, surrounded only by fences. A day earlier, about 3,000 police officers had been deployed to prevent unrest as anti-RN protesters gathered against what they say is a xenophobic and racist party.
Orleans was no casual choice. For a party that has long sought to cast itself as the guardian of French identity and national sovereignty, the city is inseparable from the story of Joan of Arc, the 15th-century heroine who helped lift the English siege of Orléans in 1429 and became a symbol of France’s resistance and liberation.
For decades, the far right has claimed her as an emblem of national pride, invoking the image of a warrior who came to save France from foreign domination. Le Pen herself has drawn parallels between Joan’s mission and her political ambitions.
The crowd at the RN Congress offered a glimpse of how the party has expanded its appeal to a wider section of society: from young people from urban centres to middle-class workers who used to vote for the centrist party.
Only a few years ago, the party was still considered on the fringes of French politics. Its growth has been driven in part by a carefully crafted strategy known as dédiabolisation, or de-demonisation, developed over the past two decades to broaden the party’s base while tempering its rhetoric and distancing it from positions that had made it toxic to many voters.
The party has long been associated with racism, xenophobia and anti-Semitism. Le Pen’s father, Jean-Marie Le Pen, was convicted of hate speech, including for describing Nazi gas chambers as “a detail of history”. He was expelled from the party in 2015.
Far right ‘gaining ground’
Marine Le Pen has sought to broaden RN’s appeal, combining restrictive immigration policies with promises of social protection. The party has gained ground in working-class areas traditionally associated with the left, including former Communist strongholds, by presenting itself as a defender of public services and the purchasing power of everyday people.
While RN has long abandoned some of its most radical proposals, including leaving the Eurozone and pursuing a fully fledged “Frexit”, the election of such a eurosceptic to the helm of the European Union’s second-largest economy would send shockwaves. She has pledged a referendum to challenge the primacy of EU law over migration policy, as well as an annual 11-billion-euro ($12.3bn) reduction in France’s contribution to the bloc.
The party’s membership has nearly tripled, with approximately 112,000 members now paying their dues, up from fewer than 37,000 in 2022.
“The party has been gaining ground at every level: mayors, deputies, senators. Usually, when a movement seems on the rise, people join,” said Baptiste Roger-Lacan, a historian and political analyst with a focus on far-right parties in Europe. “It also shows how it is less and less socially damaging to be a member of the RN.”
But the party’s programme “is still fraught with fiscal absurdity”, Roger-Lacan said. “They still want to implement racist laws, which are bound to provoke widespread anger, and their diplomatic agenda is still pro-Russian and anti-EU – even if they don’t advocate Frexit any more.”
Jordan Bardella, Le Pen’s second-in-command and Le Pen protégé – an impeccably dressed 31-year-old who looks like a cross between the Wolf of Wall Street and Superman’s alter ego, Clark Kent – also spoke at the event.
“No one should be intimidated by their political opinions,” he said, speaking ahead of his mentor.
Some observers say the October 17 protests and their aftermath have proved a gift to RN, allowing the party to not only reinforce its law-and-order message but also to shift attention away from recent difficulties.
In September, investigative outlet Mediapart published allegations that Bardella had expressed anti-Semitic views in private messages dating back to his teenage years. He denied the allegations and announced legal action against the journalists.
The episode posed a challenge for a party that has spent years trying to shed its xenophobic image and recast itself as a supporter of Israel.
Bardella has also reportedly differed with Le Pen over the party’s economic agenda and whether to make her proposed ban on the wearing of the Islamic headscarf in public spaces a central campaign issue.
Yet, at the Congress, those tensions appeared to have been set aside, at least publicly.
“Marine president – a Bardella government” was the slogan, projecting unity as Le Pen launched her presidential bid and Bardella positioned himself as her prospective head of government.

Lula defeats Trump ally in Brazil’s presidential election: LIVE UPDATES
Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva has won reelection as Brazil’s president, defeating right-wing challenger Flavio Bolsonaro, the son of jailed former President Jair Bolsonaro and an ally of US President Donald Trump.
Lula secured 51.79% of valid votes against Bolsonaro’s 48.21%, according to the completed count published by the Superior Electoral Court (TSE), winning a historic fourth term by more than 4.4 million votes.
The victory means Latin America’s largest economy is set to maintain its prominent role in BRICS rather than shift closer to Washington under the Bolsonaro political dynasty. The defeated challenger had openly questioned Brazil’s membership in the bloc, accusing Lula of using it to antagonize the United States.
Addressing jubilant crowds in Sao Paulo, Lula thanked Brazilians for his reelection and singled out young people who had taken to the streets during the campaign.
“Today, my remarks are about gratitude,” he declared, pledging to give citizens a greater say in government decisions. “We are going to change the way this country is governed.”
However, Bolsonaro has refused to concede defeat and vowed to seek the annulment of the election, accusing the Supreme Court of improperly interfering in the vote.
“Brazil cannot accept this dirty trick,” he declared, denouncing the last-minute decision to extend voting hours nationwide by two hours as “unacceptable” and equivalent to “changing the rules of the game while the game was being played.”
The controversial ruling by Supreme Court Justice Cristiano Zanin, Lula’s former personal lawyer, followed complaints from the incumbent’s campaign that public transport disruptions had prevented voters from reaching polling stations.
However, Bolsonaro did not mention that his own campaign had also requested extended voting hours in several cities affected by severe weather.
The decision came shortly after the original 5 PM deadline, when many polling stations had already closed and sealed their electronic voting machines. Senior judges have reportedly acknowledged procedural errors in handling the extension but ruled out annulling the election, according to Folha de S.Paulo.

NCERT has developed a 20-hour introductory module for Classes IX-XII, which CBSE has earmarked for school-based assessment.
NEW DELHI: From spotting deepfake to questioning a chatbot’s confident but incorrect answers, artificial intelligence (AI) is moving from being an optional subject towards becoming a basic skill for CBSE schoolchildren. Taking a step towards more formal AI teaching in schools, NCERT has developed a 20-hour introductory module for Classes IX-XII, which it has earmarked for school-based assessment. Separate AI textbooks are also being prepared for students pursuing the subject at a more advanced level.The move is part of a wider effort to make AI literacy accessible to students, irrespective of whether they study computers or choose AI as an elective. The idea is to first familiarise children with how the technology works, its uses and limitations, before moving towards more structured teaching through textbooks.NCERT developed the module on computational thinking (CT) and AI in consultation with IIT Madras and IIT Jodhpur.
In an April-9 circular, CBSE had announced that NCERT would provide modules for Classes IX-XII for internal assessment during the 2026-27 academic session.
Under the board’s revised scheme, CT and AI modules are compulsory for Class IX, while Class X continues under the existing scheme.A senior education ministry official said AI had become an important part of everyday activities, from education and research to content writing and career guidance. “AI tools are being used for studies, research, content writing and even career advice. Students will be taught how to use AI tools correctly and fact-check information,” they said.

US Attorney General Todd Blanche defends Alaska Senate election lawsuit
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
21:41:10 UTC
06:41:10 KST

US Attorney General Todd Blanche defends Alaska Senate election lawsuit
The Department of Justice has faced criticism that its lawsuit is aimed at blocking a Democratic victory in a key race.
United States Attorney General Todd Blanche has defended the Department of Justice’s decision to sue to prevent the certification of a Republican loss in Alaska’s tight Senate race.
On Sunday, Blanche did a tour of the morning political shows in the US, making stops at CNN’s State of the Union TV programme and CBS’s Face the Nation.
In each appearance, he faced pointed questions about the legality of the Justice Department’s efforts, responding, in some cases, with open frustration.
“ Why is this controversial?” Blanche asked CNN host Dana Bash at one point. He proceeded to accuse one of the candidates in the Senate race of intentionally trying to confuse voters.
“We’re going to try to create a situation where that can be remedied,” he said. “That shouldn’t be something that is causing this shock and horror.”
But the Justice Department’s lawsuit, filed on October 22, has been the subject of bipartisan criticism.
Many have accused the administration of President Donald Trump of laying the groundwork to block a Democratic win in the race. Trump himself claimed to have authorised the lawsuit.
“I’m the one who said do it,” he told reporters on Friday.
Inside the Alaska Senate race
During the midterm elections on November 3, citizens in Alaska will vote in one of the closest Senate races in the country, which will help decide whether Republicans maintain their majority in the chamber.
Senator Dan S Sullivan, the Republican incumbent, is seeking to defend his seat in the US Senate. But he faces fierce competition from former US Representative Mary Peltola, a Democrat.
Also in the running is another candidate named Dan J Sullivan, a former Forest Service employee.
The second Sullivan’s decision to run has raised concerns that he is a spoiler candidate, whose presence on the ballot is designed to draw votes away from the incumbent.
But the Forest Service worker has denied any such intent. Such allegations, he said, are “entirely false”.
“I am not a registered Democrat, and I have had no conversations whatsoever with the Peltola campaign about my candidacy,” the second Sullivan wrote in a letter to Alaska’s lieutenant governor before the state’s primaries.
“I have considered running for political office for over a decade. I made the decision to formally run for the United States Senate in the upcoming primary election because Senator Sullivan has routinely failed the people of Alaska, and they deserve a better representative. It is my right to do so.”
Four candidates advanced to the final round of voting after Alaska’s August primaries. They included Peltola and both Sullivans. The two men are running as Republicans.
A controversial lawsuit
The Justice Department has argued that its lawsuit – filed less than two weeks before the midterm elections – is necessary “to protect the integrity” of the election.
Any result in the Senate race, it argues, would be “tainted by the inclusion on the ballot of Daniel J Sullivan”.
The department has therefore called on the US District Court in Alaska to issue an order declaring the race’s certification “unlawful” and barring the state from “allowing such a certification to occur”.
Under the US Constitution, only states have the power to administer elections, though Congress has the right to pass regulations concerning federal votes.
It is highly unusual for a presidential administration to inject itself into issues of state election certification, and experts say such a move is likely to be deemed illegal.
Already, in June, Alaska’s Supreme Court ruled that both Sullivans could compete in the Senate race. The state’s Division of Elections has also taken steps to reduce voter confusion.
The November 3 ballot, for instance, will list Dan S Sullivan as the incumbent and as a “registered Republican”.
Dan J Sullivan, meanwhile, will have the suffix “Jr” added to his name, and his party affiliation will be left blank, despite the candidate identifying as Republican.
But in Sunday’s television appearances, Blanche — who leads the Department of Justice and formerly served as Trump’s personal lawyer — argued that merely having two Sullivans on the ballot is a recipe for confusion.
“It is wrong,” Blanche told CNN. “Putting aside whether we’re going to win or lose in the courts, putting aside what the Alaskan Supreme Court has done, in our system, we should not have a candidate who has to worry about another candidate being on the ballot for no other reason than to confuse voters.”
Blanche also denied any impropriety in Trump saying he ordered the lawsuit.
“He’s supposed to make sure that everything in this country is running right, including elections,” Blanche said.
The race for the Senate
Historically, the Justice Department has embraced a norm of judicial independence, though critics have accused the Trump administration of wielding its prosecutorial powers for political gain.
Bash, the CNN host, raised some of those concerns, pointing to Trump’s comments accusing Democrats of cheating, as well as his history of election denialism.
The president has long denied his loss in the 2020 presidential race, and his supporters sought to block the certification of that election, notably by storming the US Capitol on January 6, 2021.
When Bash pointed to that incident, Blanche chided her: “Oh, you’ve got to stop it with that.”
“Why are you yelling at me?” Bash responded as the two talked over each other.
“You are not being a real person. Come on, man,” Blanche continued. “That is crazy.”
He also denied that Trump was setting the stage for a contested election if the Democrat Peltola were to win. Instead, he framed the lawsuit as setting the stage for further investigations into any eventual results.
“The relief that we’re seeking – which, again, isn’t to determine who the senator is, it’s not to try to overturn something the state is going to do – it’s just to make sure that the ballots that come in are kept in a way that may allow a court to investigate further,” Blanche said.
Speaking to CBS, Blanche also dodged a question about whether Trump personally asked him to file the lawsuit.
“I will never, ever, ever talk about communications that I have with the president of the United States. I never have, and I never will,” Blanche said.
The race to control the US Senate is expected to be a nail-biter, with Republicans holding a slim majority at present: They have 53 seats in the 100-member chamber.
Only a third of the Senate’s seats – 35 in total – will be up for grabs in the midterm races, as terms in the chamber last six years and are staggered across different election years.
Trump’s Republican Party is projected to face an uphill battle to protect its congressional majorities, amid backlash against the rising cost of living and Trump’s own withering poll numbers.
Roughly seven Senate elections are considered toss-ups, including the Alaska race.
In early October, The New York Times and Siena College released a poll finding Peltola leading the incumbent Sullivan by nearly 7 percentage points, one of the widest margins of any of the toss-up states.

Musk warns military use of Starlink could spark space war. Kyiv’s ex-disinformation chief says he’s building alibi after Starshield scandal
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
21:35:44 UTC
06:35:44 KST

SpaceX founder Elon Musk says that if Ukraine fires through Starlink, Russia would be entitled to shoot the network down. That is why Starlink must remain a civilian operation and cannot be used for outright offensive strikes that would put its very existence at risk.
The warning lands in the middle of a fight over Musk’s own hand on that network. Weeks ago, his company unexpectedly throttled the service Ukraine’s drones depend on amid US President Donald Trump diesel deal with Russia, which led to the disruption of a few operations on the front.
The US Treasury authorized the sale, delivery, offloading, and import of Russian-origin diesel fuel, effectively suspending sanctions on that trade until 7 April 2027, the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) said on its website on 9 October.
The diesel deal combining intelligence halt and military Starlink, with pressure on Ukraine to make a quick peace deal, has angered both Democrats and Republicans ahead of the US elections on 3 November, where Democrats could win.
Meanwhile, a Ukrainian official interprets Musk's talk of strikes as an attempt to build an alibi before a possible investigation into that decision.
A civilian network, or a target
Musk was responding to a post warning that if Starlink shifted from a civilian network into a military system, Russia could treat it as a target for retaliation, and that destroying satellites in orbit could scatter enough debris to make space unusable for years or centuries.
“An adversary blowing up Starlink satellites would create a domino effect of destruction that would generate a vast field of debris, making space unusable," he writes.
When the shield and the warnings failed together
Overnight into 14 October, SpaceX quietly capped the speed of Starshield, the military version Ukraine’s drones run on, without telling Kyiv. Ukrainian units said the limit broke a series of missions, with connections dropping mid-flight and leaving drones hard to control.
At the same time, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Ukraine relies on the network for air defense, not attack, to intercept the Russian drones Moscow sends to its cities, and that once the speed was cut, his forces could no longer stop some of them as effectively as before.
Simultaneously, Ukraine's other American lifeline also went dark: for about three days, the US stopped passing the intelligence that warns of Russian ballistic launches. On 12 October, Russian ballistic missiles hit Kyiv before the air-raid alert reached people, with no advance data from partners. In a strike during that window, three people were killed in the capital, the sirens sounding only after the blasts.
A Ukrainian official sees alibi-building
Meanwhile, Andrii Kovalenko, the ex-head of Ukraine’s Center for Countering Disinformation, read Musk’s statement as self-protection rather than physics
“Musk, having taken responsibility for the restrictions on Starlink and Starshield for Ukraine, is now trying to build himself an alibi before a possible investigation into that decision,” he wrote.
He said that regardless of who was behind the idea of restricting Starlink and Starshield access for Ukraine, it represents a strategic setback for the US in the long run, as it risks portraying the country as an unreliable partner that may fail to honor its commitments.
"Europe purchases around 60% of its imported weapons from the US. Trust in the US as a security guarantor directly supports sales for American defense companies. Moves like this only undermine that trust and encourage European countries to develop their own systems," he said.
The US has sent a message that its guarantees may not be reliable and that even paid-for services can be subject to political decisions, Kovalenko stressed.
