stepped timber platforms and operable textiles shape circular düsseldorf home by urselmann interior
urselmann interior renovates a 1939 apartment in düsseldorf using reversible dry joinery, nine manufacturer take-back agreements, and flexible multi-tiered platforms to achieve a circular residential interior.
prefer designboom on google
[FEATURED]
URSELMANN INTERIOR DESIGNS CIRCULAR DÜSSELDORF APARTMENT
Located within a 1939 residential building in Düsseldorf, Germany, this apartment renovation by local practice Urselmann Interior is engineered entirely for circular disassembly. The studio established take-back agreements with nine manufacturers: Pfleiderer, Granorte, Shards, Søuld, ClayTec, STRAMEN.TEC, Tarkett, Bosch, and Vitra, ensuring that interior building products can be reclaimed and reprocessed into new materials at the end of their lifecycle. All joinery relies on mechanical dry joints, screws, and reversible adhesives to facilitate sorting by material category, while major kitchen appliances are leased rather than purchased. The material palette prioritizes biogenic, carbon-sequestering matter such as straw, cork, wood, and seagrass, allowing the project to achieve a net-negative carbon balance of minus 577 kg CO₂e under circular assessment standards (DIN SPEC 91606).
STEPPED TIMBER PLATFORMS DOUBLE FUNCTIONAL USABLE SPACE
To optimize the apartment’s compact footprint, Urselmann Interior studio removes two internal walls and a door to combine the entryway, kitchen, dining, and living zones into a continuous open-plan volume. Multi-tiered spatial interventions and operable textiles subdivide programmatic functions without rigid permanent partitions. In the living area, a heavy curved perimeter curtain deploys around a sleeper sofa to form a private guest room. The bedroom incorporates a tiered timber platform integrating a desk, a meditation space, and an elevated bed, all concealed behind a full-height curtain during the day. The color strategy draws inspiration from the architecture of Luis Barragán, featuring a vibrant Mexican Pink entrance corridor that transitions into green-blue living quarters detailed with glossy turquoise tiles and integrated houseplant arrangements.

Iranian doc ‘Ameneh’s Golden Blood’ screened simultaneously in Toronto, Tehran
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

Iranian doc ‘Ameneh’s Golden Blood’ screened simultaneously in Toronto, Tehran
TEHRAN- Iranian writer and filmmaker Habib Ahmadzadeh’s documentary “Ameneh’s Golden Blood” was screened simultaneously at York University in Toronto, Canada and Tehran’s Tarikh Café on Friday, October 23, bringing audiences in the two countries together to explore a story of medical urgency, human solidarity and the search for an exceptionally rare blood type.
The screening at York University was organized at the invitation of Claudia Chaufan, a professor at the university’s School of Health Policy and Management. The event was held in person and online for faculty members and students, followed by a 90-minute question-and-answer session with Ahmadzadeh.
The documentary follows Ameneh, a young girl from the southern Iranian port city of Bushehr, whose urgent need for an extremely rare blood type triggers an international search for a potentially life-saving transfusion.
The screening and discussion were organized by York University’s West Asia Research Cluster, with the event also examining the human consequences of sanctions and their effects on healthcare and medical decisions.
Meanwhile, the documentary was screened for Iranian audiences at Tehran’s Tarikh Café. The program was hosted by documentary filmmaker and Iranian history researcher Hossein Dehbashi, with film critic Abbas Yari also in attendance. A discussion with Ahmadzadeh followed the screening.
The film recounts the efforts of physician Mostafa Moqaddam to find compatible blood for Ameneh, whose blood type is identified in the documentary as Rh-null, an exceptionally rare type sometimes referred to as “golden blood.” The search highlights the importance of international cooperation and the challenges medical professionals face when a patient requires a blood type available from only a handful of known donors worldwide.
Through a suspenseful cinematic narrative, Ahmadzadeh’s documentary presents the medical complexities of the case alongside the efforts of people and organizations working across national borders to locate the needed blood.
The film has been prepared with subtitles in 55 languages, according to information released by its organizers, with the aim of raising public awareness about rare blood types and making the story accessible to international audiences. It is also available to watch free of charge on the Iranian video-sharing platform Aparat.
The York University screening forms part of the documentary’s international outreach, using a personal medical story to encourage discussion about healthcare, access to treatment and the role of international solidarity in life-threatening situations.

‘Yellow Letters’ goes on screen at Tehran cultural center
Unknown

‘Yellow Letters’ goes on screen at Tehran cultural center
TEHRAN- German-Turkish filmmaker İlker Çatak’s 2026 political drama “Yellow Letters” went on screen at the Arasbaran Cultural Center in Tehran on Sunday.
Film critic Kourosh Jahed attended a screening of the film followed by a review session.
“Yellow Letters” won the Golden Bear at the 76th Berlin International Film Festival in February 2026, bringing international attention to a story about political persecution, artistic freedom and the personal cost of dissent.
The film, which premiered in the festival’s main competition, follows Derya Tufan, played by Özgü Namal, and Aziz Tufan, portrayed by Tansu Biçer, a married couple of Turkish theater artists whose lives take a dramatic turn after they lose their jobs following the premiere of their play.
As professional opportunities disappear, the couple must confront the consequences of political pressure while trying to preserve their relationship and protect their family. Their marriage begins to unravel as the loss of their livelihoods exposes differences in how they respond to the circumstances surrounding them.
Çatak directed the film and co-wrote its screenplay with Ayda Çatak and Enis Köstepen. The cast also includes Leyla Smyrna Cabas, İpek Bilgin, Aydın Işık, Aziz Çapkurt and Yusuf Akgün.
An international co-production of Germany, France and Turkey, “Yellow Letters” was developed over several years with support from European film institutions. The project received a €10,000 grant from the German-Turkish Co-Production Development Fund in 2021 and participated in the Berlinale Co-Production Market in February 2022.
In November 2022, the project received €65,000 in funding from MOIN Filmförderung, the film funding organization for Hamburg and Schleswig-Holstein. Eurimages, the Council of Europe's fund supporting independent European cinema, awarded the production a further €368,000 in November 2023. International sales were handled by Be For Films.
Principal photography took place in Hamburg and Berlin, which served as stand-ins for the Turkish cities of Ankara and Istanbul. Filming wrapped in July 2024. One of the locations was the Berliner Ensemble's main auditorium, where a scene involving approximately 250 extras was filmed.
Following its Berlin premiere, the film was released theatrically in Germany by Alamode Film on March 5, 2026. It was also selected for the Horizons section of the 60th Karlovy Vary International Film Festival, where it screened from July 3 to 7. The production was subsequently included in the official selection of the 71st Valladolid International Film Festival for its Spanish premiere.
The Golden Bear was not the film's only recognition in Germany. It also won the Prize of the Guild of German Arthouse Cinemas. At the 2026 German Film Awards, “Yellow Letters” received nominations for Best Fiction Film, Best Director for Çatak, Best Screenplay for Çatak, Ayda Meryem Çatak and Köstepen, Best Actress for Namal, Best Actor for Biçer, Best Cinematography for Judith Kaufmann, Best Editing for Gesa Jäger and Best Production Design for Zazie Knepper. Marvin Miller won the award for Best Original Score.
The film received generally favorable reviews from critics. Its reception reflects the continuing interest in political dramas that explore how restrictions on freedom of expression affect not only public life but also the private relationships and everyday decisions of those caught in their consequences.
Through the story of two theater professionals confronting the loss of their careers, “Yellow Letters” examines the intersection of political pressure, artistic expression and family life. Its international production and festival journey have helped bring these themes to audiences beyond Turkey and Germany.
SAB/

Vucic concedes defeat in Serbia's parliamentary election
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
21:30:57 UTC
06:30:57 KST

Aleksandar Vucic concedes defeat in Serbia's parliamentary election, marking political shift
The long-serving strongman leader of Serbia, Aleksandar Vucic, conceded defeat on Sunday in an election that pitted him and his right-wing party against a diverse student-led opposition movement that spent two years protesting his government.
It was a seismic political shift in the Balkan country where Vucic, who had been endorsed by Russian President Vladimir Putin and who denounced the student movement as a foreign-led attempt to unseat him, led with virtually absolute power for 14 years.
High turnout and gathering tensions marked the highly contested parliamentary election that was a showdown between Vucic and his right-wing Serbian Progressive Party and university students who, accusing the government of corruption and dismantling democracy, had built a popular following across the country.
Serbia's 6.4 million voters were electing lawmakers to the 250-member Parliament. In conceding the election, Vucic said his party projects that his opponents, the youth-backed Students' List, will take between 135 and 140 seats while his SNS party will have around 105.
"The Students' List has won," Vucic told supporters at his party's election night event, though he blamed Serbia's independent media as well as alleged interference by unnamed European countries and an "American deep state" for the loss.
Vucic said that his SNS party won around 1.7 million votes compared to the Students' List, which he said took around 2.2 million.
Supporters of the Students' List immediately flooded onto the streets of Belgrade and other cities, honking horns, shouting and chanting: "Aleksandar is gone," referring to Vucic.
The outcome, which Vucic announced only around an hour and a half after polls closed, came after tensions had built as voting progressed during the day.
Police in anti-riot gear cordoned off an area in central Belgrade around the election commission headquarters. Special police vehicles could be seen near a Belgrade park where Vucic's loyalists have been camping for over a year, and large groups of black-clad men had congregated at various points throughout the city.
Vucic was seeking to become Serbia's prime minister after serving two near-full terms as president. He resigned the presidency last month to lead the campaign.
Support for the populist had eroded since 16 people were killed in 2024 when a concrete canopy collapsed at a train station in Novi Sad. That set off a wave of youth protests that blamed the collapse on high-level corruption, cronyism and rampant graft during renovation work at the station.
Despite the protests, Vucic retained considerable support among many of Serbia's voters. Admirers viewed him as a capable leader who can steer the nation through global uncertainties - the image that was carefully crafted by the mainstream media.
While the increasingly authoritarian Vucic has routinely outplayed Serbia's fractured opposition in the past, the leaderless youth movement proved to be a tough opponent that rattled his firm grip on power in Serbia like no one else in the 14 years since his party took office.
The newly formed Students' List movement was shaped by university students, but none actually appeared on the election list. Instead, its candidates are little-known experts, athletes, farmers and artists.
This approach was meant to counter Vucic's one-man rule and restore a sense of community and solidarity. The students' message during the campaign focused on a non-partisan effort to rebuild Serbia's economy and restore its democracy.
The students have used youthful energy to attract voters who are disillusioned with local politicians. Vilified by pro-government media, they cycled and walked through the country to reach voters in rural areas — Vucic's traditional strongholds.
The student victory echoed the recent electoral defeat of a Vucic ally in Hungary, where youth participation helped oust the autocratic Viktor Orbán after 16 years and bring in a new pro-European government. It was likely to resonate beyond Serbia as countries across Europe have faced angry youth and student protests.
Monitors predicted that total turnout in the election could reach around 70%, unseen in Serbia since 2000. During the day, long queues formed at polling stations in Serbia and in cities around the world. Some in the Serbian diaspora were made to vote in the middle of the night after authorities tied voting hours to local Serbian time.
Recent Serbian elections had been marred by irregularities, and the EU was closely watching the conduct of Sunday's vote in a candidate nation for the bloc's membership.
Independent election monitors reported dozens of cases of irregularities on Sunday such as photographing of ballots that suggested pressure on voters and attempted vote buying.
Both international and local election monitors had expressed concern about the safety and fairness of an election campaign marked by detentions, near-total government control over the media and reports of surveillance and cyberattacks against activists.
Local elections earlier this year in 10 municipalities in Serbia saw violent attacks on journalists and activists. The previous parliamentary vote in 2023 was followed by opposition protests alleging fraud.

Peak lighting outcry spotlights the trouble with fast-track governance
The backlash over the Hong Kong tourism project should raise a red flag where it concerns consulting stakeholders in policymaking
3-MIN READ3-MIN
3
 Listen
Alice Wu is a political consultant and a former associate director of the Asia Pacific Media Network at UCLA. 
It’s common knowledge that Hong Kong has a spectacular skyline, especially at night. And given our current obsession with boosting tourism and other value-adding objectives, it shouldn’t come as a surprise that our tourism authorities are actively adding more light to our night skyline.
The Tourism Board tried holding monthly firework and drone shows in 2024, but had to scale back after a budget cut – and amid questions of whether more frequent displays, costing the public HK$1 million (US$127,537) a pop, were really making a bigger impression on visitors. They weren’t. Regular firework shows diminished the novelty factor of the experience and heightened the likelihood of disappointment; effectively, public money was being thrown at unimpressed visitors. And this is not to mention the environmental costs associated with all that smoke and fire.
Yet, the tourism authorities seem not to have learned, or remembered, the lesson that less is more. This year, they tried to roll out a lighting project along a walking trail on The Peak, and have succeeded in causing quite the outrage. Going by the images shared online, it is not difficult to see why the lighting installations along the narrow Lugard Road and Harlech Road trail encircling The Peak have drawn such a negative response from residents.

Turkey warns Washington against renewed strikes on Iran
TEHRAN– Turkey has warned the United States against launching fresh military strikes on Iran, saying a new attack would widen the conflict across West Asia and that diplomacy remains the only viable path toward ending the war.
Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan delivered the message on October 23 after meeting with his counterparts from Germany, France, Britain, Italy, Egypt, Pakistan and Saudi Arabia in Istanbul. He said the eight countries shared the view that renewed military action against Iran would further destabilize the region.
“We are all in agreement that a new attack on Iran would expand the war in the region,” Fidan said at a joint press conference.
“A military intervention on Iran is not in any way a solution. Nobody approves this at the moment,” he added, stressing that diplomacy and dialogue were the only way to bring the conflict involving the United States, Israel and Iran to an end.
The meeting brought together foreign ministers from the so-called Regional Four (R4) and the European Union’s E3, alongside Italy, in the first collective gathering of the group in this format.
Discussions focused on the war involving Iran, the risk of further regional escalation, attacks on Saudi Arabia attributed to Yemen’s Ansarallah movement, and the conflict in Ukraine.
The meeting came amid growing reports that Washington was considering renewed military action against Iran following the November 3 US midterm elections, raising concerns among regional and European governments about the prospect of a wider confrontation.
European powers call for de-escalation
British Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband also underscored the need for a diplomatic solution, saying the conflict had continued for too long and imposed an excessive burden on the British public.
 
“The very clear message” is that “diplomacy, dialogue and de-escalation has to be the answer to this conflict,” Miliband told broadcaster ITN. “Frankly, this conflict has gone on too long, the British people have suffered too much from it and we cannot afford months more of it.”
French Foreign Minister Jean-Noël Barrot warned that further escalation would leave all sides worse off and push oil prices higher, highlighting the potential consequences of a prolonged conflict for global energy markets.
German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul said Germany, France and Britain were prepared to engage in talks with Tehran to address concerns over Iran’s nuclear program.
The statements reflect mounting concern among European governments that renewed hostilities could deepen instability across West Asia, disrupt energy supplies and carry significant economic consequences beyond the region.
The diplomatic push came after The New York Times reported on October 21 that US and Israeli military officials had drawn up detailed plans for renewed strikes against Iran following the US midterm elections.
Citing US officials, the newspaper reported that potential targets could include Iran’s energy infrastructure, nuclear facilities, and missile and drone capabilities.
The report intensified concerns over the possibility of another military campaign against Iran and the risk that attacks on critical infrastructure could trigger a broader cycle of retaliation.
Iranian media citing officials that a possible Iranian response to renewed US-Israeli attacks could extend beyond conventional military targets to include undersea cables, data centers and artificial intelligence infrastructure in West Asia owned wholly or partly by US investors and commercial interests.
Such scenarios underscore the potential for a wider conflict to affect critical digital infrastructure and economic assets, alongside its more immediate military and energy consequences.
According to Reuters, Fidan said the Istanbul meeting had also addressed possible parameters for preventing the conflict from spreading further, although he did not disclose details of the discussions.

Serbia’s Vučić concedes defeat after tense parliamentary elections
Unknown

Aleksandar Vučić, the Serbian Progressive Party (SNS) candidate for prime minister, delivers a speech and concedes defeat in the Serbian parliamentary elections in Belgrade on October 25, 2026. | Pedja Milosavljevic/AFP via Getty Images
BELGRADE — Aleksandar Vučić announced the end of his 12-year reign as the most powerful man in Serbia on Sunday following a pivotal election that swept the Student List protest movement to victory.
“I want to inform you that, based on a stratified sample, it is clear that we lost these elections,” Vučić said in an address to journalists and party members at the headquarters of his Serbian Progressive Party in the capital.
Vučić said the Student List had secured a majority of between 135 and 140 mandates in the country’s 250-seat parliament, while his own party won 105.
Advertisement
As the minutes ticked by after the polls closed at 8 p.m. local time, the Central Election Commission and election observers remained silent instead of publishing their customary exit results. An hour later, Vučić’s abrupt statement was carried simultaneously on all TV channels in Serbia.
The moment the news landed, euphoric residents started streaming into central Belgrade, dancing, hugging and chanting Gotov je! (“He’s finished!”), a refrain popularized a quarter century ago, the last time the country saw this level of voter participation. That October 2000 ballot toppled Serbian strongman Slobodan Milosević following a punishing decade of wars in the Balkans.
“Never again to tyranny in our country!” said the leader of the Student List candidates roster, Ilija Srdanović. “We are moving toward a civilized and better Serbia,” he told journalists in an address at the party’s headquarters.
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen also released a statement after Vučić’s concession, noting that “today, the people of Serbia turned out in record numbers to shape their country’s future” and congratulating the Student List on its victory.
“We stand ready to support reforms on the rule of law, media freedom, the fight against corruption and strong democratic institutions, and to work together to advance Serbia’s future in the European Union,” she added.
While Serbia has been an official EU candidate country since 2012, its candidacy remains frozen over rule-of-law and democracy concerns and Belgrade’s refusal to join EU sanctions on Russia.
Advertisement
Tense hours precede euphoria
Turnout hit a near-record 67.8% by 7 p.m., according to independent election monitors CRTA, up from 58.8% in the 2023 general elections.
Voters queued for hours on Sunday, including diaspora voters in cities across the world with large Serb populations such as Chicago, Toronto, Vienna and Zurich.
Tensions were particularly high in Belgrade after the main street leading to the Central Election Commission was closed off by metal police barriers before noon and armored riot control vehicles rolled into the center.
“For the first time in Serbia, access to the CEC by voters was blocked. Average citizens were denied the right to report any kind of irregularity, or even approach the building,” Raša Nedeljkov, program director at CRTA, said after polling stations closed.
After the vote ended, the main thoroughfares in front of City Hall and the parliament were also barricaded, and groups of hooded men in dark clothing appeared in front of key institutions along with black police vans. The Student List called on voters not to gather in the center and to avoid physical confrontation.
Election observers from the OSCE, the Council of Europe and the European Parliament were on the ground to provide an independent assessment of the electoral process, with the latter being escorted by police.
Advertisement
“We’re sad that it’s come to a point where European Parliament representatives need police protection while going around Belgrade and Serbia,” Nedeljkov added.
“Imagine what it’s like for voters.”
Vučić served as prime minister from 2014 to 2017 and then held the presidency until resigning in September to lead the progressives into the election. Under his rule Serbia was classed as an electoral autocracy by the Sweden-based V-Dem research institute and only “partly free” by the Washington-based Freedom House advocacy NGO.
Reporters Without Borders, which named Vučić a “press freedom predator” in 2025, now ranks Serbia 104th in the world for press freedom, last among the 40 countries in the EU and the Balkans.
Sunday’s elections capped two years of protest in Serbia, in which the largest movement in the country’s modern history drew unprecedented support nationwide. The trigger for the unrest was the collapse of a railway station canopy in the northern Serbian metropolis of Novi Sad in November 2024 that killed 16 people.
A group of university students announced in May last year that they would run in Sunday’s elections and put forward a list of experts to lead the ballot, largely doctors, engineers and other professionals.
Vučić’s right-wing populist Serbian Progressive Party has repeatedly been criticized by independent watchdogs for overseeing a significant democratic decline in Serbia, including limiting press freedoms and the operation of an independent judiciary.

Nothing will be the same as it was before 40-day war: Araghchi
TEHRAN – Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi has reaffirmed Iran’s readiness to cooperate with all countries in the region, particularly those bordering the Persian Gulf, stressing that lasting peace, security and stability in West Asia can be achieved only through regional cooperation and without foreign interference.
Speaking on Sunday at a ceremony marking the inauguration of the Martyr Kamal Kharrazi Museum and Document Center at the Foreign Ministry, Araghchi said, “Allow me to look beyond the war. We and the countries of the region must live together in peace, without foreign interference. This is the only way to achieve peace, security and stability in our region.”
Kharrazi served as Iran’s permanent representative to the United Nations from 1989 to 1997 and as foreign minister from 1997 to 2005. He subsequently chaired the Strategic Council on Foreign Relations, an advisory body on Iran’s foreign policy. He died on April 9, 2026, from injuries sustained in a US-Israeli airstrike on his home in Tehran on April 1.
“Our relations and communications with all these countries in the Persian Gulf region remain in place, and we are working to reach a common approach and understanding on a new security structure for the region. This is the only way to establish peace and stability in our region,” he said.
Regional countries must take responsibility for their own security
At the gathering, Araghchi recalled Kharrazi’s remarks at an Iranian-Arab dialogue in Doha in May 2025, in which the late diplomat emphasized that regional prosperity and security depended on cooperation among regional countries rather than reliance on foreign military forces.
“The policy outlined by the late Dr. Kharrazi before the past two wars remains the Islamic Republic of Iran’s fundamental position: regional security must be ensured by the countries of the region themselves, without relying on or allowing the presence of foreign forces. The Islamic Republic of Iran stands ready to help achieve this goal and is prepared to engage in dialogue on the matter,” he said.
“Our neighborhood policy is based on peaceful coexistence with our neighbors. We have been, are, and will remain neighbors. Therefore, we must find a common solution to ensure our own security and that of the region, with all regional countries involved and no foreign forces interfering,” Araghchi added.
The foreign minister argued that the two wars against Iran since 2025 had demonstrated the shortcomings of regional security arrangements built around a foreign military presence.
According to Araghchi, US military bases in the region had failed to provide the security expected by their host countries and had instead contributed to instability.
“These wars have shown that the security structures of some countries in the region, which relied on a foreign military presence and interference, have failed to deliver the desired results. US bases in the region have not brought peace and security to the countries hosting them. On the contrary, their presence has itself become a source of insecurity,” he said.
Araghchi added that these bases had been involved in attacks against Iran and had subsequently come under Iranian retaliatory action, arguing that their presence had intensified insecurity rather than prevented it.
He further maintained that foreign military forces were deployed in the region primarily to protect Israel, a principal source of instability and conflict in West Asia.
Iran calls for a new regional security order
Araghchi said the experience of the recent wars had prompted a reassessment of existing security arrangements and created an opportunity for regional countries to pursue new approaches based on their own capabilities and cooperation.
He said Iran welcomed initiatives that would enable countries in West Asia to take greater responsibility for their collective security without depending on external military powers.
The foreign minister also stressed that the war against Iran had fundamentally changed the regional landscape, including the situation in the Strait of Hormuz.
“Nothing will be the same as it was before the 40-day war,” he said, emphasizing that regional countries would need to recognize the new realities.
“The current war has changed everything. We must accept that new realities have emerged. Shipping routes through the Strait of Hormuz will no longer be the same as before, and the strait will no longer be managed as it was in the past. There are issues we have discussed in negotiations, and those talks will continue,” Araghchi said.

A total of 82 polling stations have been opened across the United Kingdom and Northern Ireland, including 24 in London. Voter turnout among Bulgarians living there has also been low in today’s presidential election. The highest turnout among Bulgarians in the UK has been recorded in the final hours of the day. There have been no queues outside polling stations, even in the afternoon, when Bulgarians who work on Sundays and plan to vote are heading to the polls, BNR’s correspondent Veselin Paunov reports.
The only exceptions are polling stations set up in smaller premises. “There was a larger gathering of people at a café in London’s Wood Green neighbourhood, for example, but it would be difficult to call it a queue. Election commissions at many polling stations report that not even half of those who submitted applications in advance have turned up yet. Although the weather in London is sunny, there is a fairly strong, chilly wind. Weather conditions caused problems during the first half of the day in Scotland, Northern Ireland and northern England, which were affected by Storm Boelo. By the afternoon, however, the winds had eased and the rain had stopped, which may help increase turnout.”
PHOTO bgben.co.uk
There are 27 voting machines across the country, and no problems with their use have been reported. Voting is due to close at 20:00 GMT (22:00 Bulgarian time).
By the afternoon of election day, around 200 people had cast their ballots at the polling station in Reading, a town on the outskirts of London, its chair, Viktoria Vlahovska, reported.

“People voting at our polling station want change. They want Bulgaria to have a stable leader who can serve as commander-in-chief and someone we can be proud to have representing us on the world stage.”

“Typically, between 600 and 800 people vote at this polling station, but by midday today, only 45 people had cast their ballots. Voters are reluctant to share their expectations, and the mood is subdued. It seems they have simply come to cast their votes.”

Serbia's long-standing leader Aleksandar Vučić has admitted defeat to the student-led protest movement in snap parliamentary elections.
"We still do not have final results... it is clear that we have lost these elections," the right-wing populist leader said as he conceded late on Sunday.
Preliminary figures from Serbia's election commission indicated a record high turnout, which commentators had suggested would favour the student movement. Celebrations erupted after Vučić conceded.
Vučić called the snap elections after two years of protests triggered by the collapse of a train station canopy in the city of Novi Sad, which killed 16 and was seen as emblematic of corruption and negligence.
Vučić had spent two terms as president and could not seek a third term, so was leading his Serbian Progressive Party (SNS) with the aim of returning to the post of prime minister, which he left in 2017.
The Student List's lead candidate Ilija Srdanović told BBC Serbian: "This will be a free state."
He said the anti-corruption movement, which had attracted anti-government voters across Serbia, hoped to "free the country from tyranny".
There were celebrations on the streets of the city, with people dancing and chanting "victory", cars honking, and fireworks set off. "Serbia is free," one student told the BBC. "It's a miracle."
During a celebration speech, Student List candidate Radomir Saicic said Serbians had shown "no obstacle was greater than their will", Reuters reported. "No force can forever overpower a people who have decided to take their destiny into their own hands," he added.
Amid scenes of people dancing in the streets Belgrade, Selena Lebovic said the result was "really fabulous".
"We are all crying, and what to say. We couldn't believe that it would be so easy," she told Reuters.
Vučić made his announcement at the headquarters of his Serbian Progressive Party (SNS) in the capital Belgrade.
The centre of Novi Sad - the northern city that triggered the student-led protests - was crowded. "Everything is going to get better now," David Vasić, one of those celebrating, told the BBC Serbian.
The Student List - which has no obvious leaders and whose members are not used to politics - had attracted anti-government voters across Serbia.
It decided to field candidates to the 250-member parliament from across Serbian society including doctors, actors, academics and sports personalities.
The anti-corruption movement campaigned on a manifesto that included purging officials who broke rules cracking down on protesters, stopping party loyalists from leading public enterprises, and freeing the public broadcaster of political control.
Vučić and the SNS party have repeatedly denied corruption.
Vučić, who backs Serbia's candidacy for the European Union while refusing to impose sanctions on Russia over its full-scale invasion of Ukraine, had pledged to increase pensions and public sector salaries, and investment in state healthcare.
Preliminary figures provided by Serbia's election commission suggested a record high turnout, with 64.9% having cast their vote by 18:00 local time (17:00 GMT), two hours before polls were set to close.
Earlier in the day, long queues were seen outside polling stations in cities and towns across Serbia.
This was also the case outside booths in a number of countries with sizeable Serbian communities - including Slovenia's capital Ljubljana, Germany's Munich, and Los Angeles and Chicago in the US.
In France, Serbian voters waited in line in heavy rain in Paris.
The election was held amid high tensions across Serbia, with police sealing off streets around the Republic Electoral Commission (RIK) in Belgrade.

Zelensky details expectations for upcoming trilateral peace talks with Russia, US
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
21:07:07 UTC
06:07:07 KST

President Volodymyr Zelensky outlined his expectations for upcoming trilateral peace negotiations, and discussed air defenses and the planned ceasefire in the Russian-occupied town of Oleshky in an interview on Oct. 25.
In an exclusive interview with Alla Mazur, host of "TSN The Week," Zelensky detailed Ukraine's readiness to meet with Russian and American teams for peace negotiations scheduled for early November.
Above all, Zelensky stressed the need for robust security guarantees for Ukraine in any deal aimed at ending the war.
"Our security guarantees are our guarantees, and they cannot be dictated by the Russian side," Zelensky said. "Restrictions on our army and Ukraine's neutrality are not up for discussion."
The question of NATO's involvement in Ukrainian security will "undoubtedly" come up in the negotiations, Zelensky said. The president suggested that if Ukraine is not allowed to join NATO, European countries and the U.S. should agree to extend the body's Article 5 defensive pact to Ukraine. Ukraine would also need to maintain a strong army after a peace deal is reached. 
"The best, in my opinion, is NATO plus a strong Ukrainian army, as part of the alliance," Zelensky said. "If I have enough finances, I want to keep the army of 800,000 people. We decide for ourselves what our army will be. If we are in NATO, the number can be 800,000 or less. But it will be a question of who is willing to finance or co-finance with us."
Before a meeting between Zelensky, Russian President Vladimir Putin, and U.S. President Donald Trump can take place, technical talks among the three countries' negotiating teams must be held first, said Zelensky.
"The issue of territory is a red line that can only be discussed at the level of leaders," Zelensky said. "Everyone should understand: first, we are not exchanging anything for anything. We are ready to discuss. If it's a territorial issue, then at the level of leaders. Other issues can be discussed at the level of technical groups."
As part of the negotiations, Zelensky said he was prepared to discuss an energy ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine, establishing a new deal to protect grain shipments in the Black Sea, and prisoner exchanges.
"Energy, grain, and people – these are the specifics," Zelensky said. "A meeting at the level of leaders is an opportunity to achieve those specifics after our trilateral meeting. That's what we are asking for and offering."
Zelensky said that by offering these points for negotiation, a refusal by the Russian team to engage on the items will help expose whether the Kremlin is serious about peace with Ukraine or not.
"We are not demanding, but rather offering this to the American side," Zelensky said. "That would demonstrate seriousness. But if it's just a political maneuver and Putin is simply saying, 'Yes, I'm ready,' because he doesn't want to escalate tensions with America before the [midterm] elections, we will very quickly see in November whether it was a trick or not."
The president also warned that loosening sanctions on Russia before the negotiations would weaken Ukraine's leverage. This follows Trump waiving sanctions on Russian oil exports in October in an attempt to ease oil prices heightened by his war with Iran.
"I don't want us to be left without tools – without sanctions, without money, or without frozen assets – at the meeting with Putin," Zelensky said. "Because then, as Mr. Trump said, we will really have very few cards in our hand."
Turning his attention to the Russian-occupied town of Oleshky, Zelensky said that the planned Oct. 27 ceasefire would need to last several days and include Russian assistance.
Oleshky has been under Russian occupation since the early days of the full-scale invasion. Residents face severe shortages of food, water, and electricity, while mined roads and constant drone attacks make safe evacuation virtually impossible.
"Of course, Russia will do everything it can to clear the roads in a way that encourages people to go towards Russia and stay there; they won't simply let people go," Zelensky said. "Some people will be evacuated to Ukraine – to the part that we control – in one format or another. The most important thing is to unblock the people so they can live. Ideally, they should be able to reach their destination and evacuate here, to us, to Ukraine, where they will receive everything they need and be supported."
Zelensky also detailed his conversations with U.S. envoy Steve Witkoff in Oslo, Norway, in October that set the stage for the planned round of trilateral negotiations. In meeting with Witkoff, Zelensky said they discussed limits placed on Ukraine's Starlink military systems, restrictions on intelligence the U.S. shares with Kyiv, and air defense shortages.
While the issues plaguing Ukrainian forces' use of Starlink systems and the matter of American intelligence sharing have been resolved for now, Zelensky stressed that Kyiv still lacked key air defense assistance.
"There is progress; it's just very slow," Zelensky said. "It's not enough to simply say, 'Yes, we will give [Patriot missiles] to you,' and then not deliver them for a month or two. That simply doesn't work."

She also said she did not want to see foreign flags waving in the country’s squares and streets.
Yotova pledged to maintain a positive campaign and said she did not want to be governed by “makeshift coalitions” (sglobki).
She also pointed to the non-participation of the second-largest political force, GERB, as one factor affecting voter turnout.
Gyurov, meanwhile, invited Yotova to take part in an open presidential debate before the November 1 runoff. He proposed that they face the Bulgarian public without their respective vice-presidential running mates. He made the invitation at a briefing at his campaign headquarters after the polls closed.
“I would like to call upon Ms. Yotova to join me in an open, honest, and civilized debate before the Bulgarian people. Let us present our positions and our visions regarding how we intend to exercise our powers and how we will act when Bulgaria faces difficult choices,” Gyurov said.
He expressed hope that Yotova would accept, allowing “Bulgarian citizens may make an informed decision.”
Gyurov said the debate was owed to everyone who had voted, particularly those who had stayed home and would now have to decide whether to participate in the runoff and whom to support.
He said his team had held no discussions with political party headquarters and would not negotiate with them during the week before the second round. Gyurov stressed that he was relying exclusively on support from Bulgarian voters.
At the start of his statement, Gyurov thanked those who had voted and those who had backed his presidential ticket. “I want to thank every single Bulgarian citizen who exercised their right to vote. Bulgaria is one, and we must not divide ourselves into 'us' and 'them.' I thank everyone who supported our presidential ticket. This represents a tremendous show of trust, which compels us to continue the fight for a new direction for Bulgaria,” he said.
Gyurov said his candidacy had gained substantial support but acknowledged that further work was needed before the decisive second round.
“This is no time for back-slapping; there is a lot of work ahead of us. Next week, Bulgaria must once again choose between two individuals, two directions, and two different approaches to exercising presidential powers,” he said.
Gyurov said Bulgaria needed a president capable of counterbalancing the concentration of power, explaining decisions regardless of whether they were good or bad, and bringing citizens together instead of dividing them.

Vucic Concedes Serbia Election Defeat as Student List Claims 135-140 Seats
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
21:01:05 UTC
06:01:05 KST

Aleksandar Vucic conceded defeat in Serbia’s snap parliamentary election, saying the opposition Student List had won an absolute majority with an estimated 135 to 140 seats in the 250-member National Assembly, potentially ending 14 years of rule by the Serbian Progressive Party (SNS).
“We do not have the final results yet. Many will be surprised, and you will realize just how much some have lied. Based on a representative sample, it is clear that we have lost this election,” Vucic told reporters at the ruling party’s election headquarters.
The former Serbian president acknowledged that the Student List, which emerged from mass student protests following the deadly collapse of a canopy at Novi Sad railway station in November 2024, had won the largest number of parliamentary seats.
“The Student List will hold between 135 and 140 mandates,” Vucic said.
He estimated that the coalition named Aleksandar Vucic – United Serbia would win about 105 seats. With 126 of the 250 seats required for an absolute majority, the projected result would allow the student-led movement to govern without support from other political forces.
Vucic put the Student List’s preliminary vote total at approximately 2.2 million, compared with around 1.72 million for the ruling coalition, a difference of nearly half a million votes. The estimates were based on a stratified sample of polling stations intended to reflect the nationwide result, rather than a full count. The figures are not official final results.
The projections differed sharply from the Republic Electoral Commission’s initial figures, which showed the ruling coalition with 54.69% of the vote and the Student List with 36.04% after results from just 203 polling stations had been processed. The commission is publishing results as polling-station protocols arrive, while Vucic’s estimates relied on a sample designed to represent the country as a whole. The final distribution of seats remains subject to confirmation by the commission.
Vucic said the Serbian Progressive Party would continue its work in opposition. “We will fight, and we will show them what it means to be the opposition,” he declared.
He also expressed pride in his party’s record and said its political structure remained united.
The snap election, called by Vucic in September, came after nearly two years of student-led demonstrations against perceived corruption and growing authoritarianism. The protests began after 16 people died when a concrete canopy collapsed at the railway station in Novi Sad in November 2024.
The Student List brought together candidates from academia, civil society, culture and sports, attracting support from a significant part of the traditional opposition. The election was widely viewed as a test of Vucic’s political dominance and the system that has shaped Serbia for more than a decade. Vucic first became prime minister in 2014 and president in 2017.
Turnout was unusually high. According to the Center for Research, Transparency and Accountability (CRTA), 67.8% of eligible voters had cast ballots by 7 p.m., one hour before polling stations closed, compared with 55.5% at the same time during the 2023 parliamentary election.
Celebrations broke out in Belgrade and other Serbian cities after Vucic acknowledged the projected defeat, with crowds singing, chanting, lighting flares and sounding car horns.
By around 9:40 p.m. local time, hundreds of people had gathered along central streets in the capital. Motorists greeted the crowds with prolonged horn blasts as demonstrators lit flares. According to Serbian magazine Vreme, celebrations began around 9 p.m. at the intersection of Kralja Milana and Kneza Miloša streets.
People jumped, sang and chanted “Pump it! Pump it!”, a prominent slogan of the student protest movement. Other cries included “It’s over!” and “Vucic is leaving, Vucic is leaving!” Many of those celebrating believed the country was experiencing a historic political shift.
British newspaper The Guardian also reported jubilant scenes, describing people embracing in the streets, with some still finding it difficult to believe what was happening.
Celebrations spread beyond Belgrade. Serbian newspaper Danas reported songs, car horns and cheers in several parts of the country, with residents coming onto their apartment balconies to join in.
In Kragujevac, in central Serbia, people gathered near polling stations and sang popular songs, including “Three Kisses” (Tri celuvki), as well as songs featuring the refrain “Vucic is leaving.” Drivers responded by honking their horns.
Celebrations also took place at the Student List’s election headquarters, where candidates and students sang together and chanted “Victory!” Red and white balloons had been arranged at the headquarters earlier, and the candidates had expressed optimism before the first reliable projections emerged.
Despite the festive atmosphere, security remained heightened in central Belgrade. Additional police, gendarmerie units and specialized riot-control vehicles were deployed near the Serbian Presidency, the National Assembly and the Republic Electoral Commission. Metal barriers and police lines blocked sections of streets around key state institutions.
Dozens of men, most dressed in black, gathered throughout the evening in Pioneer Park, where a camp for ruling-party supporters known as “Chatsiland” had been established. At around 9:45 p.m., some began leaving the fenced-off site.
Serbian media had repeatedly warned during election day of possible provocations and clashes. Student List representatives called on supporters to remain calm and avoid areas with a heavy police presence or groups of people in plain clothes. The movement also urged citizens to stay in their own towns and cities and help monitor the vote count.

Brazil's Federal Supreme Court Justice Cristiano Zanin has issued an urgent ruling extending voting hours across the entire country by two hours until 7 pm Brasilia time, following separate emergency petitions lodged by both presidential candidates.
The decision comes after incumbent President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva and conservative Senator Flavio Bolsonaro cast their ballots early on Sunday morning in a fiercely contested runoff election that opinion polls indicate is locked in a statistical tie.
President Lula initially petitioned the Superior Electoral Court and the Supreme Court to extend voting in crucial metropolitan strongholds, including Salvador, the capital of Bahia with nearly 2 million registered voters, and Sao Paulo, home to more than 9 million voters.
"What we want is an election done honestly and with everyone having their right to vote," Lula said in a public address, urging voters to remain in queues.
"Wait, and vote, because democracy must win."
Transit arrests
The left's legal filing followed severe transit bottlenecks in Salvador, where municipal authorities reported that at least 75 public buses were prevented from leaving depots.
Salvador City Hall alleged that union workers affixed stickers featuring the Workers' Party (PT) logo and candidate number 13 onto public buses, breaching federal election advertising statutes.
The Bahia Regional Electoral Court issued an immediate arrest warrant for Salvador's Secretary of Mobility Pablo Souza over an electoral crime linked to the fleet reduction; however, Federal Police could not execute the warrant as Souza is currently in Paris on an official trade mission.
Shortly after Lula's filing, Flavio Bolsonaro's Liberal Party (PL) submitted a parallel motion requesting polls remain open until 7 pm across 17 municipalities in Sao Paulo, Parana, and Santa Catarina, where torrential rain and flooding severely disrupted voter access.
Justice Zanin unified the competing claims, granting a blanket nationwide extension to guarantee uniform voting conditions.

Kenya bus crash kills at least 24 as government vows road safety crackdown
Church mourners die on Kenya’s Nairobi-Mombasa Highway weeks after another crash killed 17 people.
A bus carrying mourners has collided with a truck on a major highway in southeastern Kenya, killing at least 24 people, police say.
The crash happened in the Kanga area near Mtito Andei, on the road linking the capital, Nairobi, to the coastal city of Mombasa, at about 7:45am (04:45 GMT) on Sunday, October 25.
Another 24 people were injured, hospital officials said.
The deaths came just over three weeks after another crash on the highway killed 17 people, prompting fresh government promises to improve road safety.
The bus belonged to Power of the Word Church International in Mombasa and was taking passengers home from their pastor’s funeral in western Kenya.
They had stopped for breakfast shortly before the collision, according to one survivor.
The other vehicle was a truck transporting cement.
Violet Mwandonyi, who survived the crash, told the Associated Press on Sunday that she remembered passengers crying out for passing motorists to help.
She said she did not know what had happened to her two children, who had been travelling on the bus.
The cause of the crash remains under investigation.
Makueni County Commissioner Abdullahi Khalif, the government’s senior administrator in the area, told Kenyan newspaper The Standard that the bus driver had tried to overtake several vehicles before colliding with an oncoming truck.
Kenya’s National Transport and Safety Authority (NTSA) also identified dangerous overtaking as a possible cause. Another survivor said the truck struck the bus from behind.
On October 3, a crash involving several vehicles killed 17 people, most of them Catholic pilgrims travelling to a prayer site, near Salama on the same highway.
Police said a truck driver had tried to overtake another truck before the collision.
The NTSA had identified that stretch of road as an area with a history of crashes.
President William Ruto offered condolences on Sunday and ordered inspections of vehicles used for public transport.
Transport Minister Davis Chirchir said the government would step up enforcement against speeding and unsafe overtaking, improve dangerous sections of road and strengthen training and checks for commercial drivers.
In a statement on Sunday, Chirchir said the government would work with police, local authorities and lawmakers on the measures, including closer oversight of buses and heavy goods vehicles.
“We cannot continue treating road safety as business as usual,” he said, calling for stronger action to reduce deaths.
Figures from the NTSA, reported by Kenyan media, show that 5,009 people died in road crashes in 2025, with 2,150 deaths recorded in the first half of 2026.
The authority estimates that about 20,000 crashes occur across Kenya each year.
Following Sunday’s collision, it called for road crashes to be declared a national disaster.

Serbian leader Aleksandar Vučić concedes defeat in fiercely contested parliamentary election
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
20:58:57 UTC
05:58:57 KST

The long-serving leader of Serbia, Aleksandar Vučić, has conceded defeat, ushering in a seismic political shift after a historic election that saw the increasingly authoritarian leader pitted against a student-led movement that had spent two years protesting against his government.
Vučić pointed to preliminary results that suggested voters had overwhelmingly backed the students, potentially giving them a majority in the country’s 250-seat parliament.
“We still do not have final results,” Vučić told supporters at his party headquarters in Belgrade. “On the basis of a sample … it is clear that we have lost these elections, the Student List has won, they will have between 135 and 140 seats and we will have 105.”
A representative sample by the CeSID-IPSPS pollsters suggested that the Student List’s candidate list will have 138 deputies, while Vučić’s rightwing Serbian Progressive party (SNS) garnered 104 seats. The remaining seats were likely to be shared between ethnic national minority parties, said the pollsters.
As news broke that Vučić’s 12 years in power had come to an end, celebrations erupted on the streets of Belgrade and other cities.
In the capital, Ivana, 43, was ecstatic. “This feels like New Year’s Eve to me, like three New Year’s Eves all at once, really,” she said. “We can finally breathe again.” She added that she was hoping for swift accountability for top members of the ousted regime, a key campaign pledge from the Student List.
Others offered handshakes, high fives and hugs to police officers in the streets, while a chorus of honking horns rang out from passing cars.
At the headquarters of the Student List, supporters chanted “Victory, victory!” as they applauded, cried and traded hugs. “Dear Serbia, tonight the voice of the people is being heard,” said Radomir Saičić, a professor at Belgrade University, speaking on behalf of the students at their headquarters. “Tonight we celebrate victory, tomorrow we build the future.”
The scenes of joy came hours after a record number of voters turned up to cast their ballot on Sunday. Across the country, long lines snaked out of polling stations, with some reporting wait times of up to two hours. By 7pm local time pollsters and monitors CeSID and Ipsos put the turnout at 67.6%, the highest since the breakup of Yugoslavia in 1992.
The high turnout, along with the estimated 150,000 people who flocked to the students’ final pre-election rally last week in Belgrade, fuelled early speculation that the students may have rallied enough support to launch a new political era in the Balkan country.
In the lead-up to the vote, opinion polls had varied wildly, with analysts pointing to the high degree of uncertainty at play as the candidates representing the grassroots student movement went up against Vučić’s SNS.
The results were watched across the world as part of 10 pivotal days of elections across the globe in which the authoritarian right is facing off against pro-democracy forces. The victory for the student-led movement in Serbia is also likely to reverberate across Europe, adding momentum to the youth and student protests that have rocked cities across the continent.
As people waited for the election results to come in, speculation had begun to swirl online about whether Vučić would seek to hold on to power regardless. His swift admission of defeat, however, was reminiscent of his ally, Viktor Orbán, in neighbouring Hungary six months ago, fuelling hopes of a democratic resurgence to central Europe.
The high-stakes election in the EU-candidate country traces back to November 2024, when a concrete canopy collapsed at the Novi Sad railway station, killing 16 people. The tragedy set off protests among students, snowballing into a broad anti-government movement as evidence suggested that slipshod construction, fraud and corruption were to blame for the roof collapse.
As Vučić, the increasingly authoritarian leader who has dominated Serbian politics for more than a decade, grappled with mounting pressure from the students, he resigned the presidency last month to gamble on snap elections.
The students seized on the chance to transform the movement into political power. They announced a slate of 250 candidates for the 250-seat parliament, ranging from academics to athletes and farmers, as they called on voters to back their push to rebuild Serbia’s economy and restore its democracy.
The campaign pitted them against the political monolith of Vučić’s SNS party, leaving them in an uphill battle against a ruling party that had taken over almost all of the broadcast channels and which wielded ministries and other state institutions as political tools.
Vučić had repeatedly sought to undermine the students by accusing them of being stooges of foreign powers, a charge that the students have dismissed. As he pledged to increase pensions and public sector salaries, Vučić sought to present himself as a leader capable of walking the diplomatic tightrope between the country’s ties with the west, and Russia and China to steer Serbia through global uncertainties.
Undaunted, the students took to the streets, staging rallies, turning up in the rural areas that had long been Vučić strongholds and going door-to-door as they sought to pitch themselves as the anti-establishment candidates and to rally voters behind their slogan of “Serbia or Mafia?”
The message was reiterated on Sunday as Dejan Bodiroga, a candidate on the Student List and the Euroleague Basketball president, cast his ballot in Belgrade.
“Today, above all, Serbia is fighting for freedom and for the return of a country that has been hijacked,” Bodiroga told reporters. “Serbia is voting today to decide which direction it will take – towards the future or the past.”
In the lead-up to Sunday’s vote, both international and local election monitors expressed concerns about detentions and reports of surveillance and cyber-attacks against activists.
On Sunday, independent monitoring groups warned of recorded cases of photographing of ballots that suggested pressure on voters, attempted vote-buying and carousel voting.
Among them was Raša Nedeljkov of the election monitory CRTA, who said that “a large number of irregularities continue to be recorded, while violent incidents outside polling stations are also becoming increasingly frequent”.

This, he said, “troubled him the most” as the case was assigned years ago and was taken away all of a sudden.Reacting to the claims, Justice Chandrachud said, “There was never even a dissent by any member of the collegium over any name during discussions for appointments to the SC.”
‘DYC asked if he should call government on collegium picks’
Sources said resolutions passed by the collegium for appointments to the SC during Justice Chandrachud’s tenure were unanimous and signed by all members of the collegium without recording a single dissent.In this case, a bench of Justices Kaul and Sudhanshu Dhulia had pulled up govt for its alleged pick-and-choose policy in clearing names sent by the collegium and had on Nov 20, 2023, asked why Centre was not transferring four judges from Gujarat HC and not appointing two Sikh lawyers for Punjab and Haryana HC as recommended by the collegium.

That is why it troubles me,” he said, adding that there was nothing wrong in holding consultations with govt, but it should happen only after the collegium’s decision and not before.Asked whether Justice Chandrachud was too deferential to govt, Justice Kaul said, “There is a judicial side and there is an administrative side of the Chief Justice of India. I wouldn’t be concerned with the judicial side. I believe he had both the intellectual heft and the capacity and hard work to do so. But in consultations with govt and collaboration, I felt he was more deferential than necessary to carry it forward.
”Justice Kaul said he tried to discourage Justice Chandrachud from discussing everything with govt beforehand as it could create its own problems. Asked whether Justice Chandrachud failed to live up to the high expectations from him, Justice Kaul said, “I would say that expectations were higher from him.”TOI has reported how Justice Kaul had vigorously and successfully pushed many names for judgeship as part of the SC and HC collegiums and three of his proposals had met with resistance from other members of the panel. The then CJI had tactically refrained from holding collegium meetings to avoid embarrassing situations.In reply to the TOI article, Justice Kaul had sent a rejoinder and said, “There was no question of insistence of appointment of those suggested by me and all recommendations have been made by consensus. That other collegium members had reservations and I pushed the names, thus, seem to be a flight of your imagination.”

Israel fears copycat attacks ahead of election after deadly West Bank terror shooting
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
20:55:23 UTC
05:55:23 KST

Security forces have heightened their alert across the West Bank amid fears of copycat attacks following a deadly shooting near Hebron on Friday, stepping up arrests, patrols and counterterrorism operations less than two days before the national election.
The military said Sunday that troops had arrested a suspect believed to be planning an imminent attack on Highway 60, a major highway used daily by Israeli motorists in the West Bank. The arrest came as security forces continued a large-scale operation in Hebron, where approximately 50 suspects have been detained and more than 500 locations searched.
The heightened security measures follow Friday's shooting near the West Bank city, which killed Staff Sgt. Ron Yonatan Roytman and Sgt. Yuval Shai Svilem and left three other soldiers lightly wounded.
Defense officials are particularly concerned that the attack could inspire additional assaults in the days leading up to Tuesday's election, prompting the military to expand its operational presence across the territory.
Alongside the security operations, the IDF launched a major military exercise Sunday involving four divisions and the air force, aimed at strengthening readiness across several regions.
Suspect arrested over alleged imminent attack
In the Binyamin area of the central West Bank, soldiers from the Paratroopers Brigade's 202nd Battalion arrested a suspect believed to be preparing an attack on Highway 60.
The operation followed specific intelligence provided by the Shin Bet domestic security agency.
Acting on the information, troops established a checkpoint along the highway and detained the suspect.
No weapons were found in his possession at the time of the arrest, and he was transferred to security authorities for further questioning.
Highway 60 is one of the West Bank's main north-south highways, connecting several major Palestinian cities and Israeli settlements. It is heavily traveled by Israeli motorists and has been the site of previous attacks.
The arrest was part of a broader effort to prevent further violence following Friday's shooting.
Security forces have intensified raids, patrols and arrests at several locations across the West Bank, seeking to identify suspects involved in terrorist activity and prevent additional attacks inspired by the Hebron incident.
Homes of two gunmen sealed ahead of demolition
Israeli troops also sealed the homes of the two terrorists responsible for Friday's attack, following an order signed by the head of the military's Central Command authorizing their seizure and temporary closure.
The military intends to proceed with demolishing the properties.
Both gunmen were killed in exchanges of fire with Israeli security forces during the attack.
Israel has long used punitive home demolitions against Palestinians who carried out deadly attacks, a practice authorities defend as a deterrent.
New footage released Sunday showed the confrontation at Yehuda Junction, near Hebron, where the two terrorists exchanged fire with the command group of the deputy commander of the 755th Battalion.
According to the military's account, command teams from the battalion and paratrooper forces rushed to the scene and engaged the attackers in a gunbattle that ended with both gunmen dead.
The military said the soldiers' response prevented the attackers from reaching a nearby road used by Israeli motorists, potentially averting a more serious attack.
Hebron operation continues with no end date
Israeli forces continued their operation in Hebron overnight, with troops from the Paratroopers Brigade and the elite Maglan commando unit arresting 12 additional suspects.
The troops also confiscated vehicles described by the military as illegal and located weapons.
Since the operation began, approximately 50 suspects have been arrested and security forces have searched more than 500 locations throughout the city.
The military has not announced when the operation will end, saying its duration will depend on ongoing security assessments.
Israeli forces are also maintaining an expanded presence outside Hebron, conducting raids and arrests aimed at disrupting terrorist networks and preventing attacks elsewhere in the West Bank.
The military said its efforts are intended both to apprehend suspects involved in terrorist activity and to prevent the establishment of infrastructure that could support future attacks.
With the election approaching, defense officials are particularly concerned about attempts to imitate Friday's shooting or carry out attacks inspired by the incident.
Alongside the raids, the military has instructed soldiers stationed along roads, at intersections, checkpoints and security posts to tighten operational procedures.
The measures are intended to improve the identification of threats in real time, stop attacks before they develop and reduce risks to troops operating in the area.
The Hebron operation also includes the removal of structures the military considers illegal and efforts to reshape parts of the operational environment to make it easier for troops to maneuver and identify threats.
Four divisions and air force join major military drill
Meanwhile, a large-scale military exercise began Sunday involving the IDF's West Bank Division, the 98th, 96th and 210th divisions, along with the Israeli Air Force.
The exercise is taking place in areas under the responsibility of the participating regional divisions.
According to the military, the drill was planned as part of the Operations Directorate's 2026 training program and is intended to strengthen operational readiness, rehearse military procedures and incorporate lessons learned from the war.
The military said the exercise also aims to improve the defense of Israeli communities and strengthen coordination with air forces supporting ground operations.
Increased movement of troops, military vehicles and aircraft is expected Sunday and Monday in areas under the military's Central and Northern commands.
The IDF emphasized that the exercise had been scheduled in advance and that the increased military activity was not an indication of a new security incident.
The drill comes amid heightened alert levels ahead of the election, with the military seeking to maintain readiness for threats across several fronts.
Security forces reinforce West Bank olive harvest
The military also provided an update Sunday on security arrangements during the annual olive harvest in the West Bank, which has been accompanied by tensions and incidents of nationalist violence.
According to IDF figures, approximately 220,000 dunams, or 54,400 acres, of olive groves have been harvested so far this season.
Security forces have coordinated protection at approximately 100 harvesting locations.
The military estimated that about 22,500 metric tons of olives have been collected, producing approximately 5,500 liters of olive oil.
Despite recent incidents of nationalist violence, including attacks connected to the harvest, Israeli defense officials said confrontations had affected only a small percentage of the areas being harvested.
They maintained that the overwhelming majority of coordinated harvesting activities conducted under security protection had proceeded without unusual incidents.
To facilitate the harvest and prevent confrontations, violence and attacks, the military has reinforced its Central Command with additional forces.
The reinforcements include the headquarters of the 98th Division, a task force headquarters from the Paratroopers Brigade, a regular infantry battalion and Border Police companies.
The forces have been deployed throughout the West Bank to provide security, prevent attacks and reduce the risk of clashes during the harvest.
The olive harvest is an important source of income for many Palestinian families, and access to agricultural land has frequently been a source of friction between Palestinian farmers and Israeli settlers.
The additional deployments come as the military balances several security priorities, including protecting civilians, preventing attacks and maintaining a heightened operational presence before Tuesday's election.
For Israeli security officials, the immediate concern remains the possibility that Friday's deadly shooting could trigger further attacks.
With no announced end date for the Hebron operation and troops continuing arrests and patrols across the West Bank, the military is seeking to prevent another deadly incident during the final days of the election campaign.

Ukraine-US-Russia Talks May Resume in November as Trump Eyes Business With Both Sides
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
20:55:15 UTC
05:55:15 KST

The Kremlin is prepared to resume trilateral negotiations with Ukraine and the United States after November 4, Russian President Vladimir Putin’s foreign policy aide Yuri Ushakov told state-controlled outlet Vesti on October 25, as U.S. President Donald Trump said Washington could do business with both Moscow and Kyiv after the war ends.
Ushakov’s remarks followed Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky’s statement on October 23 that another round of trilateral talks was expected in the first half of November, with Abu Dhabi among the possible venues.
“The next deadline is now Nov. 4, our major holiday. After that, we will be ready to resume negotiations,” Ushakov said, referring to Russia’s National Unity Day.
The Kremlin has repeatedly dismissed ceasefire proposals, insisting that Kyiv surrender the parts of the Donbas region in eastern Ukraine that Russian forces have not captured. The territory is strategically important, and handing it over would give Moscow land its military has been unable to take on the battlefield. Ukraine, meanwhile, has accepted several ceasefire proposals put forward by Washington.
Ushakov said he did not anticipate major progress at the first trilateral meeting after the pause, describing it as a “trial run.” He added that a peace agreement between Russia and Ukraine “still needs work.”
On October 20, U.S. envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner met with Zelensky and European partners, including Finnish President Alexander Stubb and Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Store.
Witkoff met Putin in St. Petersburg the following day for three hours. Afterward, the Kremlin said it was prepared to restart trilateral negotiations in November. Witkoff said on October 21 that discussions involving Ukrainian, American and Russian representatives would “continue at the technical level.”
Putin has long avoided direct talks with Zelensky. Instead, the Russian leader is reportedly seeking a meeting with Trump in China next month in an effort to secure a favorable peace agreement without Ukraine’s participation.
In recent weeks, Trump has criticized Zelensky, announced an energy ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine without agreement from both sides that ultimately failed, threatened to halt intelligence-sharing with Kyiv and eased restrictions on Russian oil exports. Trump has defended the sanctions relief, arguing that it could encourage Moscow to negotiate with Ukraine.
Trump said on October 24 that he expected the United States to resume commercial dealings with both countries once the war was over, despite criticism of efforts to restore business ties with Russia.
The remarks came as the first tanker carrying Russian diesel under a supply agreement announced by Trump on October 9 was heading from the Baltic port of Primorsk to New York. The vessel is due to deliver 40,000 metric tons of fuel.
Following the announcement of the deal, Moscow partially relaxed restrictions on diesel exports, allowing 500,000 metric tons to be sold.
“Certainly, we'll do business with Ukraine and with Russia after this war ends, I would think,” Trump said. He added that he wanted to “get back to life where Russia and Ukraine make a deal, and then we'd be able to do business with both.”
The U.S. president also argued that Washington should have obtained greater financial compensation for the billions of dollars in assistance provided to Kyiv during Joe Biden’s presidency.
“I feel foolish because all you had to do is ask them, and they would have paid. Meaning the EU would have paid,” Trump said.
Plans to import about 900,000 metric tons of Russian diesel over the coming months have drawn criticism from European allies, Ukraine and members of Congress. Critics say the shipments would circumvent sanctions imposed on Moscow over its war against Ukraine.
The delivery would be the first shipment of Russian diesel to the United States since 2022, when then-President Joe Biden prohibited imports of Russian oil and petroleum products in response to the invasion of Ukraine.
The agreement comes as tensions between Washington and Kyiv deepen, with Ukraine facing restrictions on Starlink access and reported delays in deliveries of Patriot air defense interceptors.
Trump has intensified his attacks on Zelensky, accusing the Ukrainian president of refusing to end the war and calling for him to be replaced.
The resumption of Russian diesel imports also comes as Republicans face a difficult political environment ahead of the November 3 U.S. midterm elections, with recent polling showing declining support for Trump.
A Reuters/Ipsos poll published on October 19 found that only 31% of Americans approved of Trump’s performance, the lowest rating of either of his presidential terms. Meanwhile, 47% of registered voters said they would support Democrats if congressional elections were held that day, compared with 35% who favored Republicans, giving Democrats a 12-point lead, their largest of the current election cycle.
