IDF chief pushed back on Netanyahu order for ‘action’ against Iran, fearing political motives
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
20:54:38 UTC
05:54:38 KST

Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and IDF Chief of Staff Lt.-Gen. Eyal Zamir clashed over a military action that could renew the conflict with Iran days before Israel's elections, N12 News reported Sunday evening.
Recently, Zamir received a directive from the political echelon to carry out an action, which security officials told N12 would "trigger a rapid escalation into a confrontation with Iran."
Due to the sensitive nature of the action, N12 reported that Zamir requested an in-depth discussion and formal authorization before moving forward with the action.
Sources familiar with the details told N12 that Zamir and additional IDF leadership are concerned that the political echelon may be trying to exploit the front with Iran ahead of elections for political gain.
Netanyahu denied the report late on Sunday night, saying on Channel 14’s The Patriots that “there is no confrontation” and that “someone is trying to obscure the fact that Zamir himself had said Iran was attempting to interfere in the elections.”
US President Donald Trump and Zamir have, at different points during the election season, acted as constraints on Netanyahu’s approach regarding aspects related to a potential renewed conflict with Iran.
It remains unclear how far Netanyahu would have been willing to go if he had not anticipated that certain figures would place the brakes on certain actions.
The prime minister would have welcomed a US return to war with Iran in August, earlier in October, and again more recently. In some of those scenarios, Israel would have been prepared to join the US.
Netanyahu may also have played with the possibility of Israel taking a leading, ‘first-attacker’ role, or serving as a spoiler to prevent versions of an Iranian nuclear deal which he would view as a bad deal.
In all of these discussions, Trump, while vacillating, has ultimately, to date, come out in trying to continue to stare down Tehran with a mix of military threats and economic pressure.
Likewise, in all of these decisions, Zamir has had Israel on a war footing versus Iran if necessary, but has viewed the meaning of "necessary" before Election Day in a limited fashion.
To avoid interfering with the election, and given that Iran poses no immediate existential threat since prior Israeli attacks have pushed back its nuclear and ballistic missile threats, Zamir has only been ready to attack Iran if two conditions were met: If Iran were preparing to strike Israel, or if Trump initiated a new round of fighting and Israel had full US backing for both offensive and defensive operations.
Generally, Zamir's instinct has been that he is ready to strike Iran if it starts recovering its threat capabilities too fast, which it has not yet done, or if such a strike would be part of a well-thought-out and considered strategy to finally push Tehran into making key nuclear concessions to the US.
More broadly, Zamir has viewed military action as potentially justified if Iran rapidly rebuilt its nuclear and ballistic missile capabilities or if a strike formed part of a carefully considered strategy to compel Tehran to make significant nuclear concessions to Washington. Previous Israeli attacks have set back Iran’s capabilities, reducing the immediate urgency for another round of strikes, according to this assessment.
The requests for formal authorization and an in-depth discussion, as reported by N12, could serve to clarify the government’s intentions and ensure that any military action had a clear legal and strategic basis.
The report further described ‘new lows’ in the Netanyahu-Zamir relationship.
Netanyahu selected Zamir to lead the military because he was his personal military secretary, and for the latter’s known aggressive approach to warfare. The prime minister partially alienated the IDF chief by refusing to draft haredi (ultra-Orthodox) men into the IDF and allowing Defense Minister Israel Katz to politicize certain key military appointments.
Zamir has likewise partially alienated Netanyahu even before this point, by slowing the Gaza war in late 2025 and by pressuring him over the haredi conscription issue.
Eisenkot warns Netanyahu against using IDF as political tool
Yashar party chairman Gadi Eisenkot on Sunday night said he supports Zamir's decision to be cautious, warning Netanyahu against putting his political interests above the state's.
"Netanyahu, my eyes are on you," stated Eisenkot. "The man, on whose watch the greatest disaster in the nation’s history occurred, refuses to grasp that Israel’s security is not a political plaything; that the lives of Israeli citizens and IDF soldiers are not to be treated with reckless disregard; and that the State of Israel is not his private property."
"I have full confidence in IDF Chief of Staff Eyal Zamir and the IDF commanders, who act with professional responsibility and an absolute commitment to the nation’s security. We will not allow the IDF to be turned into a tool for Netanyahu’s political survival campaign."
"Do not dare to place your own political interests above the security of the State," Eisenkot warned the prime minister.
He added that holding elections according to the set schedule is a "cornerstone of Israel’s national resilience," stating that he "will not let you [Netanyahu] jeopardize Israel’s future just to preserve your own rule."
"In two days, the citizens of Israel will put an end to this era of reckless, lawless governance and restore responsibility, a sense of statehood, and the security of Israel," Eisenkot said. "I give you my word."
Betrayal of state, security
The Democrats party chair Yair Golan echoed Eisenkot's support for Zamir's caution in a Sunday night post on X/Twitter, saying that he wholeheartedly backs Zamir for "standing firm on his professional duty."
"It is forbidden to allow any military action that lacks a clear security need, a strategic purpose, and a responsible action plan behind it," Golan wrote. "When Israeli citizens go to the polls next Tuesday, they must remember this: Netanyahu constitutes a security threat to Israel. He does not hesitate to sacrifice the lives of our children for his survival on the eve of elections, and this is what the IDF is trying to thwart."
"Israel's security is in the hands of a corrupt political echelon, unfit and deranged people who do not hesitate to sacrifice Israel's security in order to cling to their seats."
Yisrael Beytenu head Avigdor Liberman called Netanyahu's attempt to "drag Israel into military action in order to prevent the elections" an act of "betrayal of the state and its security."
"The duty of the chief of staff is to prevent the political use of the IDF and to safeguard the lives of IDF soldiers, not endanger them because of the prime minister's fear of losing the elections."

‘Rings of Revenge’: Tehran Women Rise for Vengeance
Iranian women donate wedding rings and gold to avenge martyred Leader as revenge vow enters ninth month
TEHRAN – Since February 28, Iranians have pledged to avenge the blood of their martyred Leader and other martyrs of the war, and in the latest step, groups of women are offering their wedding rings and gold to pursue that revenge.
This is part of the first message by Ayatollah Seyyed Mojtaba Khamenei on March 12, 2026, in which the issue of avenging the blood of the war martyrs was raised for the first time:
"I assure everyone that we won’t forgo avenging the blood of your martyrs. The revenge we have in mind is not just because of the martyrdom of the illustrious Leader of the Revolution. Every member of the nation who is martyred by the enemy constitutes a separate case that demands seeking revenge. A limited portion of this seeking revenge can already be seen. But until we completely take revenge, this file will remain on top of all the others. We’re even more sensitive with regard to the blood of our children and infants. The crime deliberately committed by the enemy against the Shajarah-Tayyibah School in Minab and other similar cases will receive particular attention in this process of taking revenge."
The demand for revenge has since become one of the most serious public demands in Iran. Red flags of revenge have been present at nightly gatherings that began at the start of the war and have now passed more than 240 nights, with their largest presence at the vast, multi-million funeral of the martyred Leader of the Revolution.
Multiple rewards for avenging the assassins of the martyred Leader have so far been announced. For example, a campaign for revenge against Trump was launched from the early days of the war. The campaign’s website states:
Following the hostile actions of Zionist terrorist regimes and the United States of America in violating the sacred soil of Iran and assassinating the Leader of the Islamic Ummah, Grand Ayatollah Imam Khamenei (may his soul rest in peace), we, the free nations of the world, unanimously express our outrage against the perpetrators of these crimes. In light of the jihad decree issued by the supreme religious authorities in response to the assassination of the Supreme Leader of the Islamic Republic of Iran, Seyyed Ali Khamenei, and the oppression of the Iranian people, the campaign “Kill Trump” has been launched with the aim of providing financial rewards for the assassin of Donald Trump, the criminal president of the United States. By submitting the required information, you can join this international movement.
According to organizers, more than 665,000 people have so far joined this campaign, and more than $116 million has been allocated for it.
Rings that become a noose
In the latest move for revenge, groups of Iranian women have formed a separate campaign. A popular women’s group called “Madari” (Motherhood) is behind the initiative.
On Thursday night, October 22, hundreds of women held a gathering called “Rastakhiz of Tehran Women” (The Uprising of the Women of Tehran) in front of the main gate of the University of
Tehran in the city center. Women from different walks of life, including wives and daughters of martyrs of the two recent wars, volunteers and students, took part in the gathering, which featured speeches by women activists, choir performances and elegies, with “revenge” as the common thread and soul of the program.
Alongside the gathering, registration began for donating wedding rings to the avenger of Trump. A group of women under the name “Madaraaneh” (Maternal) has launched the “Rings of Revenge” campaign. These women have declared their wedding rings as the prize for revenge, and in a symbolic visualization, it was shown that each of the women’s rings will become a hangman’s noose around Trump’s neck.
The revenge-seeking women also joined the “Golden Retribution” drive by donating gold and money to share in every bullet spent for revenge. Notably, the “Nehzat-e Madari” movement, which runs the drive, gifted gold donors a bracelet with a bullet plaque as a reminder of this revenge and blood-seeking. The bracelets are a sign that these women consider retribution for the murderer of the martyred Leader as their mission.
Zahra, 36, an engineer and mother of three, said as she joined the drive: "This gold necklace is the only keepsake I have from my mother, and I am certain that if she were alive, she too would have prioritized avenging the Leader just as we do. So I donate it to share in every bullet fired in retribution against Trump."
Reyhaneh, 25, a graduate student who joined the drive by donating her bracelet, said: "The Iranian woman will not let these aggressor murderers go until we have taken retribution for each and every one of our martyrs. Gold is nothing; we will give our lives to eliminate these child-killers who bereaved us of our martyred Leader."
Marzieh, 45, a tailor and mother of four, explained why she joined the drive. "I had struggled to save this money to buy a new sewing machine; but if the spilled blood of my martyred Imam goes unanswered and I cannot see my young Imam [Ayatollah Seyyed Mojtaba Khamenei], I want nothing. Punish the murderers so severely that they will never again dare to insult our Imam."
Ayatollah Seyed Mojtaba Khamenei had stressed in a message issued on July 9, coinciding with the funeral of the martyred Leader:
"Now, I offer these words to our martyred Leader: O unjustly slain Leader! O you who’ve been oppressed but are exalted! O righteous servant of God! As we bid farewell to your body with tearful eyes and broken hearts, we pledge to safeguard your legacy, to steadfastly traverse the straight path you laid out, to fear no hardships along the way, and to attach our hearts to divine promises and glad tidings as you did. We pledge to avenge your pure blood and the blood of all the martyrs of these two wars by taking revenge against the criminal, disgraceful murderers.
This vengeance is what our nation is demanding, and this must definitely be done. These criminals, whose names are fully documented from the highest to the lowest ranks, will carry their dream of a peaceful death in bed to the grave. They must know that this action doesn’t depend on my presence or that of any other official. Whether we are here or not, this will be done. Soon, free-spirited people throughout the world will each carry out a part of this divine mission."
Justice, not emotion
Some American media and analysts try to portray the issue of revenge as emotional, while such a demand must be seen through the lens of “justice.” If criminals do not face justice, they see the way paved for repeating their crimes.
The shadow of revenge weighs so heavily on Trump that his exit from Turkey after the NATO summit in July turned into a historic scandal for the U.S. president. In an unprecedented move, after waving to cameras and reporters and boarding Air Force One, Trump secretly exited through another door of the plane, boarded a catering truck and was transferred to another aircraft to head to Britain.
After the incident, Trump said his life is always in danger. It seems he will likely now also fear the wedding rings of Iranian women.

Vučić concedes defeat in pivotal Serbian elections, says Student Movement has won
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
20:51:39 UTC
05:51:39 KST

The election was seen as a referendum on Vučić’s political dominance and the political system that had been in place in Serbia for more than a decade.
Serbia has entered a new political era. The Student List has won the country's parliamentary election, marking a dramatic breakthrough for a movement that emerged from months of student protests and rapidly transformed itself into the country's most important political force.
In a brief statement to the nation, outgoing Serbian President Aleksandar Vučić conceded defeat and declared that the Student List has won the majority in parliament.
Vučić said that “based on the stratified sample, it is clear that we have lost the election,” adding that “the Student List has won and will have between 135 and 140 seats, while we will have around 105.
“No one else has entered parliament. The Alliance of Vojvodina Hungarians (SVM) has won three seats, the Albanians one, and I think the SDA has also secured a seat,” he added.
The Serbian Progressive Party received around 1.72 million votes, admitted Vučić. The Student List won 2.2 million, giving it a majority of 52% to 32.3 %.
It is still too early to assess the final results and determine whether any other smaller parties have crossed the 3% electoral threshold, but it is clear that this would not affect the final outcome of the election or the identity of the winner.
The result represents far more than a change in the distribution of parliamentary seats. It is a profound rejection of the political model that has dominated Serbia for more than a decade.
From protest movement to political force
The Student List's victory is particularly significant because it was not created as a conventional political party. Its origins lie in the student protests that became a powerful expression of dissatisfaction with the country's political institutions, the government, corruption allegations, media conditions and what many protesters described as a lack of accountability.
What began as a protest movement has therefore achieved something considerably more difficult - it has translated street mobilisation into electoral legitimacy.
The result suggests that the movement managed to attract voters far beyond the university campuses where the protests began. Young people were its most visible supporters, but the electoral coalition appears to have extended to parts of the urban middle class, opposition-minded voters and citizens who had previously been reluctant to support established opposition parties.
A defeat for the old political establishment
For the ruling establishment, the result is a major political setback.
For years, President Aleksandar Vučić and the Serbian Progressive Party dominated Serbian politics through a combination of strong electoral organisation, extensive political influence, control over a large part of the media environment and a highly personalised political strategy centred on Vučić himself.
The election result indicates that this model has reached a critical limit.
What happens next?
The transition from protest movement to government could therefore prove much harder than winning the election for the Student List.
Running a country requires decisions on the economy, foreign policy, relations with the European Union, Kosovo, security, energy, public finances and Serbia's relations with Russia and China. The students will now have to demonstrate that their political legitimacy can be transformed into effective state governance.
What does the result mean for Serbia?
There are several possible consequences.
First, it represents a generational change in Serbian politics. A movement dominated by young people has succeeded in challenging a political establishment that has shaped the country for years.
Second, it could lead to a major institutional reset. The new government is likely to face strong expectations concerning the independence of institutions, the judiciary, corruption, public media and electoral conditions.
Third, Serbia's foreign policy could enter a new phase. The new political leadership will face immediate questions about the country's EU accession process, relations with Brussels and Washington, and its traditionally close relationship with Moscow and Beijing. Whether the Student List seeks a clear pro-European orientation or attempts to maintain a more balanced foreign policy will be closely watched.
Fourth, Aleksandar Vučić's political future becomes uncertain. Even if he remains president, an electoral defeat would fundamentally change the political balance in Serbia. His ability to dominate the political agenda would be significantly reduced, while his party would have to rebuild itself in opposition.
A new political test
The Student List has won the election. But its real political test begins now.
Winning an election requires mobilisation, a powerful message and the ability to unite voters around the desire for change. Governing requires something different: institutions, experienced personnel, economic policy, compromise and the ability to take responsibility for difficult decisions.
For Serbia, the election therefore represents both a political rupture and a moment of uncertainty.
The central question is no longer whether the students can challenge the established political order.
They have already done that.
The question now is whether they can replace it - and what kind of Serbia they intend to build in its place.

EPFO considers Rs 25,000cr war chest to stabilise interest payouts
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
20:48:10 UTC
05:48:10 KST

File photo: Employees Provident Fund Organisation- EPFO
NEW DELHI: Employees’ Provident Fund Organisation is discussing a dedicated Rs 25,000-crore Interest Stabilisation Reserve, designed to insulate the annual interest payouts of its nearly 30 crore members from the turbulence caused by corporate bond defaults and forced-exit losses.Officials said EPFO and government want a stable regime for its subscribers and wish to avoid any sharp fall or spike in rates due to market conditions or defaults.Under existing regulatory frameworks, credit losses and exit haircuts, resulting from downgraded securities, directly impact EPFO’s interest account and depress the annual interest rate for members.
Report on ISR sent to panel studying EPFO investment framework
A proposal submitted by IIM Kozhikode, which among other things studied the feasibility of creating an Interest Stabilisation Reserve (ISR), was discussed in detail by EPFO’s investment committee (IC) Thursday, TOI has learnt.The report has now been sent to a high-poweredJ panel constituted to examine the agency’s investment framework and recognise non-performing investments.The report suggested building the stabilisation reserve progressively via surplus ETF capital gains and excess interest income and investing it strictly in liquid govt securities (G-Secs) to ensure absolute capital safety, sovereign backing, immediate liquidity, and risk-free yield, said persons familiar with the deliberations.
The reserve will not only shield subscribers but will also back active exit policies and empower portfolio managers to execute disciplined, multi-year exits from troubled assets without hesitation.The report took into account the current realities of India’s over-the-counter (OTC) corporate bond market, which remains shallow and illiquid, such that when institutional holders such as EPFO are forced to exit distressed assets, thin market depth results in severe haircuts.Historically, EPFO relied heavily on equity ETF capital gains to offset credit stress.The report, however, noted that the volatile market downturn of FY 2019-20 coincided with major credit events like the IL&FS default, which exposed a critical vulnerability.“Credit stress and equity market crashes are highly correlated. Relying solely on ETF gains is dangerous; a standalone prudential reserve is a structural necessity,” it said.The study evaluated absolute worst-case liquidation scenarios across the portfolio netted against available ETF gains, pinpointing a cumulative baseline shortfall of approximately Rs 23,837 crore.“To account for incomplete market data and ensure a bulletproof prudential buffer, the report recommends formalising an ISR Fund of Rs 25,000 crore,” it said.
The study also ran a historical back-testing simulation which modelled portfolio returns from 2010-11 to 2023-24, demonstrating that a Rs 25,000-crore baseline successfully absorbs annual shortfalls and stabilises declared interest rates across typical economic cycles.The only exception was 2019-20, where portfolio deficit spiked to Rs 55,640 crore, leading to deep drawdown from the reserve.“However, the subsequent recovery in investment performance in later years indicates that such a shortfall would likely have been temporary in nature.In such a scenario, EPFO could have bridged the temporary deficit through a short-term advance or loan mechanism, which could subsequently be repaid from future surpluses generated during recovery years,” the study said.

If Democrats win the House, and possibly the Senate, a result nonpartisan analysts call plausible, they would gain the power to bring new Ukraine aid to a vote and to push back on President Donald Trump’s deals easing pressure on Russia, Reuters reports in an analysis of how US foreign policy could shift.
The stakes are concrete. Trump has largely halted direct US aid to Ukraine, which lawmakers of both parties had backed, and its current supplies run from packages passed under his predecessor.
Weeks ago, he also waived the sanctions on Russian energy that Congress had written into law and struck a deal to bring Russian diesel back to the market, angering Republicans and Democrats alike.
What a Democratic Congress could do for Ukraine
With both chambers, Democrats could put new Ukraine aid on the floor, and given the bipartisan support such aid has drawn, it could pass with the two-thirds majorities needed to override a Trump veto.
Other steps could be taken, too. Representative Gregory Meeks of New York, in line to chair the House Foreign Affairs Committee if his party wins control, has already introduced bipartisan legislation to block Trump’s plan to return Russian diesel to the global market.
Democrats are also readier than Trump’s Republicans to rein in military spending. They blocked his request for an unprecedented 67% rise in the military budget, to $1.5 trillion, in the Senate, and many say they will try to restore the foreign aid he has withheld or canceled.
The limits of a slice of power
The leverage has limits. Even with both chambers, Democrats would still face a president who can veto, and overriding him would require two-thirds of each chamber. The pattern has already been visible in Iran: Trump launched that war on 28 February without congressional approval, and when a War Powers resolution passed with a handful of Republican votes, his administration ignored it.

Serbia's Vucic concedes defeat to student led movement in parliamentary election

Serbia’s Aleksandar Vucic concedes defeat in historic election win for student protest movement
- Aleksandar Vucic conceded defeat as the student-led Student List won Serbia’s historic election, ending his long hold on power after nearly two years of protests over corruption and authoritarianism.
- Voter turnout was close to 70%, the highest since 1992, and crowds in Belgrade celebrated as students won about 135 to 140 of 250 seats, according to Vucic.
- The result may reshape Serbia’s politics and foreign policy, but key questions remain over the next prime minister, anti-corruption plans, and ties with the EU, Russia and China.
AI generated
BELGRADE – Serbia’s Aleksandar Vucic conceded defeat to a student-led protest movement in a historic election on Oct 25 that ends his long grip on power and heralds a new political era in the Balkan country.
Vucic, a populist and nationalist, has dominated Serbian politics as prime minister or president since 2014.
But he called snap elections in September after almost two years of student-led demonstrations against perceived corruption and creeping authoritarianism triggered by the deaths of 16 people when a train station canopy collapsed in the city of Novi Sad in 2024.
“It is clear that we have lost these elections, the Student List has won,” Vucic said in a televised speech.
Within moments of his announcement, the streets of Belgrade erupted in celebration. Tens of thousands of people thronged along the city’s main boulevards, with cars honking, people dancing and students shouting “victory” and “he’s done”.
The students’ win marks a profound political shift in the country of some six million people and is reminiscent of the defeat of Hungary’s Viktor Orban in April.
It may also offer a blueprint for other student movements across Europe, which have taken to the streets in recent weeks to protest, in some cases violently, against poor education standards and a lack of prospects.
Vucic said the students would have between 135 and 140 seats in the 250-seat Parliament and that his Serbian Progressive Party (SNS) would have 105, based on preliminary results.
“Dear Serbia, tonight the voice of the people is being heard,” said Radomir Sajcic, a professor at Belgrade University, speaking on behalf of the students at their headquarters.
“Tonight we celebrate victory, tomorrow we build the future.”
European leaders and officials congratulated the Student List on its victory, among them President of the European Commission Ursula von der Leyen and European Commissioner for Enlargement Marta Kos.
“We stand ready to... work together to advance Serbia’s future in the European Union,” von der Leyen wrote on X.
Hungarian Prime Minister Peter Magyar assured the students of his country’s support.
Record turnout spurs students to victory
Lines snaked from polling stations in cities and towns across the country earlier in the day, and even Vucic waited for nearly two hours to vote in Belgrade. Pollsters and the election commission put turnout close to 70%, the highest since the break-up of Yugoslavia in 1992.
“(The turnout) did not surprise me because there was a large and strong mass that has formed throughout the past two years,” said voter Katarina Petrovic.
Vucic, who resigned from his second term as president to run again for prime minister, was a strong incumbent and few in the student protest movement dared believe he would concede so fast.
Supporters credit him with modernising Serbia’s economy and building new highways, railways, schools and hospitals.
“Some businessmen, some people will leave us but our structure is firm, we are very united, very strong, we are used to being in the opposition,” Vucic said.
Uncertainty over the students’ candidates
Much remains unclear about how the student-backed candidates will fare.
Their list of 250 largely unknown candidates includes university professors, actors and farmers, and is led by cardiologist Ilija Srdanovic, who was in tears after Vucic’s announcement.
However, it is unclear who will be prime minister and enact the students’ domestic agenda, which aims to root out graft and improve schooling.
Political analysts predict some kind of purge of Vucic allies in the police, security services and ministries. But the students have been quieter on their international ambitions.
As Vucic did for years, they will have to juggle relations with China, a major investor, Russia, Serbia’s traditional ally and principal supplier of natural gas, and the European Union, Serbia’s largest trading partner.
“The biggest uncertainty is... who is going to lead the government, who will be the key ministers, and how they will operate based on the promises they made to fight corruption, to reintroduce the rule of law, but also to re-establish Serbia’s position in foreign policy,” said Radivoje Grujic, a Warsaw-based election consultant.
Protest movement increased pressure
The student-led street protests sparked by the station disaster started small but quickly became the biggest in a generation, calling for Vucic to step down. Rights groups and activists say repression worsened in the period since.
Vucic and the SNS repeatedly denied accusations of repression, corruption and spying on their opponents. He has said the students are funded by foreign agents in Croatia and Montenegro, a charge the students dismiss.
Meanwhile, on the streets of Belgrade, a traditional brass band struck up, and a group including a man in a “students are champions” jumper floated balloons in the shape of the number three, representing the number of the students’ list of candidates.
“We will drink a beer to celebrate, we will get drunk, we are so happy, I have no words to describe how much,” said Andjela, a student who was with a group of friends.
Dejan Soskic, a former central bank governor and a candidate of the Student List, called on people to maintain order and peace, and thanked voters for their civilised conduct during the electoral process. REUTERS

Serbia votes in historic election as students seek to unseat Vucic
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
20:36:26 UTC
05:36:26 KST

Serbia's Aleksandar Vucic conceded defeat to the student-led protest movement in parliamentary elections on Sunday.
"We still do not have final results, on the basis of a sample ... it is clear that we have lost these elections, the Student List has won, they will have between 135 and 140 seats and we will have 105, no one else has entered parliament," Vucic said.
The snap elections, called by Vucic in September, came after almost two years of student-led demonstrations against perceived corruption and creeping authoritarianism triggered by the deaths of 16 people when a train station canopy collapsed in the city of Novi Sad in 2024.
The students have since gained widespread support to become the greatest threat to Vucic since he first became prime minister in 2014 and then president in 2017.
Serbia saw record-breaking voter turnout
Long lines snaked from polling stations in cities and towns across the country, and even Vucic waited for nearly two hours to vote. Pollsters and monitors CeSID and Ipsos put turnout at 67.6% by 7 p.m., the highest since the breakup of Yugoslavia in 1992.
A student victory would is a profound political shift in the Balkan country of some 6 million people, reminiscent of the defeat of Hungary's Viktor Orban in April. It could also offer a blueprint for other student movements across Europe, which have taken to the streets in recent weeks to protest, in some cases violently, against poor education standards and a lack of prospects.
"(The turnout) did not surprise me because there was a large and strong mass that has formed throughout the past two years," said voter Katarina Petrovic.
Opinion polls predict tight race
Vucic has pledged higher pensions and public sector salaries, and investment in state healthcare. Internationally, he has sought closer ties with China, a major investor, and remained close to Russia, Serbia's traditional ally and principal supplier of natural gas. At the same time, he still says he wants to join the European Union, Serbia's largest trading partner, but the bloc has become increasingly frustrated with a lack of reform.
"I voted for our children, our young people...our children deserve peace and work, only Vucic can bring that," said Hatidza, a Roma woman.
The students' domestic agenda aims to root out graft and improve schooling, but they have been quieter on their international ambitions. Their list of 250 largely unknown candidates includes university professors, actors and farmers, and is led by cardiologist Ilija Srdanovic, although it is not clear who would be prime minister should they win.
"I hope that today will pass in a democratic atmosphere, in peace, and that we will legitimately elect a new government in Serbia," Srdanovic said after casting his vote in Novi Sad early in the morning.
After casting his vote, Vucic said he would respect the result.
"If we lose we will acknowledge the will of the electorate, if we win no one will take it (from us)," he said.
Opinion polls ahead of the vote had predicted a tight race to win the 250 seat parliament. The head of the Election Commission, Vladimir Dimitrijevic, said voting had passed without incident, but police cordoned off the road leading to the state commission building. Monitoring bodies CeSID and CRTA pointed to incidents related to the electoral roll and secrecy of voting.
Student protests increase pressure on Vucic
The student-led street protests sparked by the station disaster quickly became the biggest in a generation, calling for Vucic to step down. Rights groups and activists say repression has worsened in the period since.
"For decades the people have been waiting for this time, something to bring hope that we can live freely and by the rules of democracy," said actor Jelena Stupljanin, 48, at a Belgrade polling station.
Vucic and his Serbian Progressive Party (SNS) have repeatedly denied accusations of repression, corruption and spying on their opponents. He says the students are funded by foreign agents in Croatia and Montenegro, a charge the students dismiss.
"This has been one of the most difficult but the most emotional campaigns," Vucic told his supporters on Thursday. "We stood against those who wanted to destroy Serbia."

Eisenkot might have said the same about Churchill in 1933. History proved that the danger then was not imaginary and that Churchill was right. Very, very right.

Hard-hitting Ali G is back, leading new group of idiots in 'Ali G: Who Iz I?'
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
20:36:11 UTC
05:36:11 KST

For once in his life, Ali G, Sacha Baron Cohen’s iconic white guy who thinks he’s black character, did something quietly.
Ali G snuck into theaters in Israel and around the world for the new movie Ali G: Who Iz I?, which was set for a two-day release on Friday and Saturday.
It will come to Amazon’s Prime Video later, but the good news for fans in Israel is that certain theater chains, including Planet, Cinema City, Movieland, Rav-Chen, and Hot Cinemas, have extended the release until Wednesday.
For those who can roll with Baron Cohen and his often sophomoric humor, it could be the perfect movie to see on Election Day on Tuesday, especially because most of the participants, from both the Left and Right of the political spectrum, were not “in on it”: they were duped into taking part in what they thought was a serious political documentary, a guerrilla tactic that Baron Cohen has been pulling off for decades.
The movie starts with a quote from Voltaire, “Those who can make you believe absurdities can also make you commit atrocities,” and it’s key to understanding the movie.
Baron Cohen handles lawsuits over pranks in the movie
Even though the movie says that only Baron Cohen and Morgana Robinson, who plays his pregnant girlfriend, Julie, were in on the joke, while watching it, I had a hard time believing that this was true. It’s hard to imagine that anyone who is not mentally ill or drugged could have gone along with the pranks that Baron Cohen pulls in this movie.
But they did, and he is currently dealing with a few lawsuits from participants who don’t find it funny and regret that they gave their permission for him to use the segments he filmed with them.
It’s an insane piece of performance art that functions as a critique of our absurd political climate, and it will hit harder than a thousand op-eds, mainly because it is designed to be not only entertaining but a teaching moment aimed at those who would never read an op-ed.
As the movie opens, it’s tough times for Ali G, who has had trouble adjusting to life as a regular guy since his HBO series was canceled over 20 years ago. He is back at home in a quiet British suburb and reeling from the news that Julie is pregnant.
As he sells various relics from his former life as a celebrity to support her and their soon-to-be-born child, an ancient fax machine spits out one more page that says that HBO has agreed to pay him an additional $3 million. So it’s off to Los Angeles and back to the high life for Ali and Julie.
You can guess the reception he gets in Hollywood (HBO says the offer is null and void), but at the same time, an ultra-left, straight, white Berkeley professor who hates himself, Dr. Nira Cain-N’Degeocello (an utterly unrecognizable Baron Cohen, using one of several characters he introduced in the series Who Is America?) decides that Ali G is a menace who must be stopped because he is a cultural appropriator.
Baron Cohen's critique of the left
He recruits a few young, woke, useful idiots to help in his pursuit of Ali.
These recruits don absurd faux-Rastafarian costumes and a sequined bodysuit with strategically placed black hands in a plot to deceive and entrap Ali G by collecting his DNA to prove he is white – and if you’ve ever seen a Baron Cohen movie, you can guess what bodily substance they end up getting.
These characters are the main source of Baron Cohen’s critique of the Left, and it’s the more restrained part of the movie. At the heart of his satire of the Right, Baron Cohen gets a similarly clueless band of useful idiots from the other side of the spectrum involved, in his guise as a poker-faced Mossad agent, Erran Morad.
I won’t give away the main joke, but the sequence gives him the chance to use a little Hebrew.
Hearing these all-American good old boys reciting Israeli slang terms for certain body parts got the biggest laugh and even applause from the mostly 20-something and younger audience in the auditorium where I saw the movie.
Unlike in the Borat movies, where Baron Cohen speaks Hebrew when Borat is supposedly conversing in Kazakh, there isn’t nearly as much Hebrew in this movie.
Those laughing away may not have known or cared that Baron Cohen duped a baker’s dozen of right-wing media and political figures into taking part in the movie, including disgraced former congressman George Santos and Jacob Chansley, aka the Qanon Shaman.
Ali G is tapped to host a show on a right-wing network called The Free Speech Show with Ali G. It shouldn’t surprise anyone at this point that he gets the studio audience for this show to imitate Elon Musk and has them all doing a “Heil Hitler” salute.
Celebrity features in the film
A couple of celebrities from the entertainment industry appear in the movie, including Rihanna and A$AP Rocky. While they may not technically have been “in on it,” they were smart enough to know that Baron Cohen was playing the Ali G character.
How entertaining you will find the movie depends on how much of Baron Cohen’s bathroom and sex humor you can stomach. In addition to the verbal jokes, the movie has some of the funniest costumes Baron Cohen has ever come up with, from a giant puffy jacket to the return of some of the FUBU (“For Us, By Us”) outfits he has sported in the past.
All jokes aside, Baron Cohen has said in interviews that he returned to the comedy of Ali G for a serious reason: “Because I’m terrified of where our society is headed, and the way I can comment on that is through my comedy. I wanted to show the extremism on both sides of the political spectrum and the danger of virtuous violence,” he told The Hollywood Reporter last week.
While he has not spoken out on issues concerning Israel, other than to call for the release of the hostages held by Hamas after October 7, when he was asked by The Hollywood Reporter about a boycott campaign proposed by left-wing activists against his movie and whether it was linked to antisemitism and anti-Israel sentiment:
“Well, I haven’t said anything about Israel … I think people are being portrayed as things that they are not on social media and it’s problematic. We are in a world where people can’t distinguish between facts and lies, and that’s something that I’ve spent a lot of the last few years trying to fix …
“So, I’m not surprised that prominent Jews are being targeted. I knew that this was going to happen. The level of organization is surprising, but this is a trend of Jews being portrayed in certain ways and trying to be silenced.”
In an essay he penned for Time Magazine, he wrote, “We are once again entering an age of ‘virtuous’ violence, where any atrocity – by racists, Jew haters, or Islamophobes, the Right or the Left – can be somehow justified. It is not a place any of us should want to live.”
Perhaps the biggest virtue of Ali G: Who Iz I? is that it shows that while we may not have much of a choice about living in such a world these days, the ideologues on both sides don’t have enough smarts or sense of humor to get Baron Cohen’s jokes. As such, Ali G’s creator has his pick of endless targets, and he can give us something to laugh at.

====================================================================================================

Behind the scenes on how IDF got its biggest ‘hasbara’ win of the war - exclusive
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
20:35:48 UTC
05:35:48 KST

It was the early evening of October 17, 2023, Israel time, and then IDF Chief Spokesman Daniel Hagari was on the way to make a daily statement about the state of the then 10-day-old war.
A female officer whispered to him that there were reports of a mass death incident at an attack on a hospital.
Hamas had fired a barrage of rockets at 6:15 p.m., Palestinian Islamic Jihad had fired its own barrage of around 10 rockets around 7:00 p., and shortly after that barrage there were reports of an explosion at the al-Ahli Hospital.
No reporters asked Hagari any questions about the incident because the reports were still fresh, which was good because no one within Israel's military or government apparatuses had a clue at that point of whether Israel was responsible or not.
Hamas claimed around 500 Palestinian civilians had been killed, and the news spread like wildfire across the planet from Al Jazeera to the BBC to The New York Times, and on to other secondary sites taking their information from those major outlets.
The IDF Spokesperson's Office went into high gear trying to connect the dots between videos and imagery of the alleged incident coming out from open sources compared to any inside special intelligence Israel might have.
There were several calls between senior IDF spokesperson's office officials and senior air force officials to ascertain what had really happened and to quickly decide how to probe the situation.
Top air force officials did not initially know about the incident.
Within a few hours, the initial reports and the beginnings of second-round reports started to present the incident as a more solid fact.
IDF Spokesperson's Office insisted on gathering facts first
There was already pressure from the political echelon to simply deny it as a ridiculous allegation, but the IDF Spokesperson's Office would insist on first gathering the facts.
This was no easy call. Simply the initial reports themselves, without even being validated, were already causing real-world riots in Amman, Turkey, and Cairo.
Also, then-US president Joe Biden had boarded his plane before the incident and was on his way to the Middle East for a summit with Arab leaders.
However, because of the unconfirmed reports, his summit was canceled by the Arab leaders who were alternating between fury at Israel and fear for their own populations if the incident were true.
But Biden was already on his plane, so he said he was still going to land in Israel to show solidarity with the Israeli people after Hamas's horrifying invasion.
The IDF Spokesperson's Office hoped that they would be able to resolve the issue before Biden landed, but there was still significant uncertainty.
But because of all of the unique momentous events happening at once, they understood the magnitude and gravity of the incident. It was an incident which could have stopped the entire war in its tracks. There would later be a few other major incidents of that magnitude that could have stopped the war, but this was the first one.
At a second stage, the air force's first review of battle damage assessments (BDA) in Gaza was that there was an air force bomb for which there still was no BDA.
It had been fired at a target that was a full kilometer away from the hospital in terms of the strike radius. But there were concerns that the proximity was close enough that a misfire could not be ruled out completely without probing further.
What if JDAM bomb had gone off course?
What if a JDAM bomb had gone off course? The IDF was carrying out a huge volume of airstrikes, and it was inevitable eventually that there would be errors, as with all wars.
Throughout the crisis, then-Defense Minister Yoav Gallant and then-IDF Chief of Staff Herzi Halevi were seeking and receiving debates about the incident, because it was viewed as having the potential power to prematurely end the war before Israel's counter-invasion of Gaza began (the full invasion only started on October 27).
In light of the second air force status update, it was decided to send a drone to the hospital perimeter to see if the hospital had been hit accidentally by an Israeli missile.
This process, including receiving footage and assessing the footage, would take a few precious hours, with much of the world continuing to boil over against Israel.
The IDF would later release a map showing the rocket launches of Hamas and the Islamic |Jihad against Israel.
As The Jerusalem Post would later report when visiting Israeli radars and interviewing Israeli LOTEM digital data-sharing commanders, IDF operations had tools that recorded every rocket launch from Gaza.
One could see from the vectors that there were launches fired from close proximity to the hospital and which passed over the hospital. The IDF spokesperson's office, the Intelligence Directorate, and the air force were working to connect that map to hitting the hospital.
IDF intercepts Hamas conversation about incident
After a few more hours, the IDF intelligence division intercepted astounding messages from two Hamas operatives. In these discussions, they admitted that they had misfired a rocket from a cemetery and that it hit the hospital.
Intercepted Hamas communications verified internally that this was what in fact happened, despite the fact that they continued to lie to the world externally.
The IDF spokesperson's office was buoyed and requested taking the almost unprecedented step of publishing the secretly intercepted information.
A deputy of IDF Intelligence Chief Aharon Haliva, at the rank of brigadier general, approved publishing the conversations. They said to paraphrase some of it to protect certain security considerations, but did not ask for too much in terms of editing.
Around 11:00 p.m., Hagari issued a statement in English – as opposed to his standard Hebrew statements - that the IDF had obtained intelligence proving that Palestinian Islamic Jihad had fired its missiles at the hospital.
Maybe this would turn the tide.
The IDF spokesperson's office was dismayed by the world and media reaction: there was almost no change.
The world was in such a frenzy of condemnation and anger, and the narrative was so extreme and important to maintain for critics of Israel that Hagari's words about having intelligence, without more, had zero impact.
Halevi asked the IDF spokesperson's office for recommendations.
Swiftly, the response came back that the discussions should be released.
It was one thing to have the approval of Haliva's top IDF intelligence deputy, and another to also have Halevi, who was the IDF chief and had previously headed IDF intelligence.
Haliva, Unit 8200 Chief Yossi Sariel, and others were also on board and invested massive efforts to prepare for the release of this highly classified intercepted conversation.
This required an extensive fast-forward process, but which still ensured not to harm Israeli intelligence sources. It was due to take 4-6 additional agonizing hours.
There was a debate among top IDF Spokesperson's Office officials about what else to do.
It was decided that the IDF would publish video footage from the air force of the attack and portions of information from Israeli radars.
Further, Hagari would carry out a major press conference live in English in the morning to give the disclosures more volume.
There was a third exchange with the air force.
Their drone, which had been sent hours earlier to probe the situation, had finally proven that Israel's missile had not hit the hospital.
It was unequivocally not a hit by an Israeli or American weapon.
Also, it clarified that what had been hit was not the hospital itself, but the parking lot, which had many evacuated refugees.
An analysis learned that the rocket had traveled such a short trajectory that it was still full of gas, and it was this gas and the sharp nails inside that caused dozens of deaths, around 50 - not 500.
Later, the IDF learned that Hamas always just rushed, without checking any facts, to claim around 500 were dead anytime it thought it had a chance at claiming a mass death incident.
A reservist from the international spokesperson team wrote the text of Hagari's speech the next morning. There was no time to rehearse.
IDF Col. and chief Arabic spokesperson Avichai Adraee personally translated the Gazan discussions to make sure they were worded correctly.
It started to seem possible that when Biden would check, he would be able to view the information as highly verified, and that it really would be released before he landed in Israel.
The next steps were coordinated not only with the air force and IDF intelligence, but also with Halevi, with Maj. Gen, Yaron Finkleman.
An entire operational probe which could take weeks or months was completed in a matter of several hours.
But much of this had been accomplished ad hoc.
Later, the IDF would build an improved apparatus for handling such crises.
Hagari's speech the morning after
Finally, it came time for Hagari's big morning speech.
The Post was present at the time, and there was an unusual air of excitement given that often such press conferences were just a rehash of news which had been disseminated throughout the day.
Hagari issued his list of dramatic statements, but that was only stage one.
Despite all the highly specific data points and astounding Hamas conversation transcripts, the first question showed there was still a major problem.
The angle of the first question was: the IDF lied to us about Shireen Abu Akleh; why should we believe you? In their understanding of the IDF's spokesperson's office, much of the foreign media viewed the IDF as having lost its credibility over two prior incidents: with a false denial of the IDF's mistaken killing of Al Jazeera Arab-American reporter Abu Akleh in the West Bank on May 11, 2022 (later the IDF admitted killing her) and with the false Gaza invasion and bombing of the "Gaza Metro" on May 14, 2021 (the IDF misled foreign media to say an invasion had started to try to trick Hamas into entering its tunnel network just before the IDF then bombed the network).
Hagari responded that he had been in his role only during 2023 and that before that he was the commander of Israel's navy commandos. He said he never spoke about Abu Akleh, but was presenting three facts about the current incident.
These facts were: 1) radar data on Gaza rockets; 2) telephone call intercepts; and 3) video provided by the air force. Hagari told reporters they could check with all of their local-home military officials: this was not a US or Israeli munition - 1000%.
After a few hours, BBC and The New York Times changed their coverage of the incident.
Biden saw the press conference while he was flying to Israel on Air Force One.
When he later commented on the incident, he completely adopted the Israeli version of events.
This incident rebuilt some IDF credibility, but it was still very hard to keep.
The IDF knew that it would not do as well in every crisis. Put simply: sometimes the IDF does not understand what happened in the fog of war.
Or the IDF figures out what happened, but it lacks the perfect video and phone calls.
Sometimes even if the IDF gets all of the data, it does not get all the relevant data until much later, when the media might have already moved on.
The longer a war goes, the harder it gets to impact the narrative and the curve of the coverage.
Later, there was the World Central Kitchen incident and the bakeries incident, and these were not always resolved well, and the government apparatus as a whole was often not ready.
There is also a difference between the mainstream media and social media. On social media, there were sites still falsely claiming that Israel had killed children at the al-Ahli hospital on a large scale even months later, because they can choose to ignore the facts.
How IDF disclosed information
How could Israel disclose classified sources and methods?
The Post has learned that disclosing eavesdropping on cellular communications is less complicated than some other instances.
In this case, the Post understands that the sources were intelligence operatives. In contrast, there are some sources which Israel cannot burn, as in the Eli Feldstein episode. But in this case, with different kinds of technology, the IDF could cope with the losses.
IDF sources believe Israel needs a diplomatic public relations mechanism, not just the IDF spokesperson's office.
Over three years, there were many crises, and there is a strategic price that Israel needs to take into account, according to the IDF.
The war over the narrative is complex, but it is profoundly important to combat disinformation with facts, data, and knowledge.

If you want to make the most of your day off on Election Day on October 27 and catch a movie or head for the great outdoors, there are some deals to sweeten these options, and some special programming.

The Jerusalem Cinematheque features the top three Israeli movies in its audience poll in honor of its 50th anniversary.
These include a serious, animated documentary about the First Lebanon War from the point of view of IDF soldiers – Ari Folman’s Waltz with Bashir; and two comedies about army life – Assi Dayan’s Halfon Hill Doesn’t Answer and Talya Lavie’s Zero Motivation. Tickets are just NIS 15 and are free for Jerusalem Cinematheque members.
Israel Nature and Parks Authority offers outdoor tours, activities

In the North, Kochav Hayarden National Park will offer bird migration tours, kite-making and flying workshops, and family activities. At Ein Afek Nature Reserve, visitors can explore the wetlands, join guided tours, and enjoy children’s crafts and face painting. Special tours at the Gamla Nature Reserve will focus on its vulture colony and conservation efforts, while Beit She’arim will offer tours of its burial caves, inscriptions, and reliefs.
At Beit Guvrin, couples and families can order picnic packages in advance for collection at the visitor service center. Farther south, visitors can try the cliffside Masada Challenge route or attend the evening “Masada: From Sunset to Sunrise” multimedia show on the mountain’s western side.
The authority advises visitors to check weather and trail conditions, bring sufficient water, and follow marked routes. Details about activities, reservations, and any additional charges are available at www.parks.org.il.
Also, ANU – Museum of the Jewish People will remain open on Election Day, offering permanent exhibits alongside interactive family activities like the Heroes gallery and the “Guardians of the Stories” quest.

Bulgaria's Presidential Election: Exit Poll Puts Gyurov Ahead of Yotova by 0.8%
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
20:34:25 UTC
05:34:25 KST

Bulgaria’s presidential election is heading for a runoff between Iliana Yotova and Andrey Gyurov on November 1, with completed parallel vote counts showing a narrow race and turnout of about 22%, according to polling agencies cited by BGNES and NOVA.
The final parallel count by the Market Links Agency put Gyurov and running mate Georgi Kandev in first place with 33.5%, ahead of Yotova and Kiril Valchev at 32.7%. Kostadin Kostadinov and Petar Volgin ranked third with 12.4%, followed by Radostin Vasilev and Krasimir Manov with 4.2%, Ivelin Mihaylov and Yuliana Mateeva with 3.4%, and Ivan Hristanov and Stoyanka Cherkezova with 2.8%. Market Links estimated turnout at 22.1%.
Myara Agency’s count, based on 100% of the sample, put Yotova and Valchev ahead with 35%, followed by Gyurov and Kandev at 31.9%. Kostadinov and Volgin received 12.4%, Vasilev and Manov 4.3%, Mihaylov and Mateeva 3.5%, and Hristanov and Cherkezova 2.2%. Myara reported turnout of 22.2% as of 8 p.m.
Alpha Research also placed Yotova and Valchev first, with 34.6%, while Gyurov and Kandev received 32.7%. Kostadinov and Volgin took 12.6%, Vasilev and Manov 4.1%, Mihaylov and Mateeva 3.8%, and Hristanov and Cherkezova 2.7%.
Earlier estimates showed similarly close competition, although the agencies differed on the size of the gap. Trend’s exit poll gave Yotova and Valchev 36.4%, compared with 32.1% for Gyurov and Kandev. Myara estimated their support at 35.6% and 32.5%, respectively. Both agencies placed Kostadinov and Volgin third, with between 13.5% and 14.1%, and reported turnout of 22.2%.
Initial parallel counts commissioned by NOVA also pointed to a runoff between the Yotova-Valchev and Gyurov-Kandev tickets. With 90% of the sample processed, Trend estimated 36% for Yotova and Valchev and 30.8% for Gyurov and Kandev, while Myara’s count based on 70% of the sample gave them 34% and 31.3%, respectively. Both agencies placed Kostadinov and Volgin third, at between 12.5% and 12.8%. Estimated turnout was 21.9% according to Trend and 20.8% according to Myara.
Interior Minister Ivan Demerdzhiev described election day as calm, saying authorities had not identified serious attempts at vote manipulation or buying. He said more than 17,000 police officers had been deployed to secure over 12,000 polling stations and pledged to maintain heightened vigilance throughout the week before the runoff.
Emil Stoimenov, co-chair of Yotova’s campaign team, called for an intensive campaign during the remaining seven days and urged voters from across the political spectrum to support her. “A full-scale mobilization is underway across the country. We will hold as many meetings as possible and urge people to turn out in large numbers to vote, so that we may fully restore the rule of law and statehood,” he said. Stoimenov declined to say whether the campaign would seek formal endorsements from other political parties, noting that it would first wait for the final parallel-count results.
GERB-SDS lawmaker and former Deputy Foreign Minister Georg Georgiev described the results as a sharp decline in support for Rumen Radev and Progressive Bulgaria. In a Facebook post, he questioned the earlier predictions of a decisive lead for Yotova and the political group backing her. “Where is the overwhelming lead that pollsters predicted for 'Progressive Bulgaria' and Yotova? The big question is: where did those 1.4 million-plus votes go?” Georgiev wrote, calling the outcome a verdict on Radev, his administration, his political faction and his candidate.
Revival leader Kostadinov said his party had improved on its 3.9% result in the presidential election five years ago. He thanked voters who had returned to the party and volunteers who took part in the campaign, while identifying low turnout and distrust of the political elite as its most serious negative features. “The outcome on November 1st will depend to a large extent on the voters of 'Vazrazhdane' as well. Our cause, for a peaceful, free, and independent Bulgaria, is not the cause of a single individual or a single political organization. It is the cause of every free Bulgarian,” he said.
Gyurov, speaking at the headquarters of the initiative committee supporting his candidacy, said the level of support for his ticket gave it a responsibility to continue its campaign. He thanked those who voted for him as well as those who chose other candidates, saying Bulgarians should not divide themselves into opposing camps. He said the country faced a choice between two people and two different paths, and argued that the next president should unite citizens rather than divide them.
Gyurov also invited Yotova to take part in a debate before the runoff, calling for an open discussion of their visions and how they would use presidential powers when Bulgaria faced difficult decisions.
MECH leader and presidential candidate Radostin Vassilev urged his supporters not to vote for Yotova in the runoff, presenting Gyurov as the alternative. Speaking at a post-election briefing, he said voters should follow their conscience but choose between backing Gyurov and staying home. He acknowledged that both options were difficult for his supporters but said he could not accept Yotova winning.
Vassilev said he had not yet decided how he would vote, although he intended to go to the polls to avoid setting a bad example despite his own ticket not advancing. According to the parallel count, Vassilev and running mate Krasimir Manov finished fourth with more than 4% of the vote, which he described as a significant result for an extra-parliamentary party competing against 27 presidential tickets.
Vassilev called the turnout the lowest since Bulgaria’s democratic changes began, interpreting it as evidence of deep public disappointment with the current administration. He predicted that Yotova’s defeat in the runoff would inevitably lead to snap parliamentary elections as early as the spring.
Slavi Vasilev, deputy chair of the Progressive Bulgaria parliamentary group, attributed the low turnout to the fact that the current prime minister was formerly president, arguing that many people believed the country was in safe hands regardless of who occupied the presidential office at Dondukov 2. In a Facebook post, he predicted that Yotova would win the runoff and turnout would rise the following Sunday.
He described the narrow margin between Yotova and Gyurov as a wake-up call, warning that what he called defeatism among the silent majority could undermine Progressive Bulgaria’s position. Slavi Vasilev also accused PP-DB of self-congratulatory rhetoric and claimed that Boyko Borissov and Delyan Peevski were preparing to support Gyurov in an effort to revive their political fortunes. He said all of them, along with PP and DB, would lose in the runoff.
In the comments below the post, GERB communications representative Nikola Nikolov responded with a countdown: “10, 9, 8, 7, 6, 5...” Most other comments were mocking or critical, with some users urging Slavi Vasilev to stop using artificial intelligence for his posts.
The Central Election Commission reported turnout of 16.04% at 4 p.m., compared with 24.12% at the same point in the 2021 presidential election. The country was electing its seventh president, with 6,590,000 eligible voters able to choose from 27 tickets. A total of 46,001 people were eligible to vote for the first time.
Within Bulgaria, 9,373 polling stations were equipped with voting machines. Of these, 2,249 had two machines each, bringing the total number of machines to 11,622.
For voting abroad, authorities established 613 polling stations in 60 countries. Voting machines were available at 242 of them, while 24 had two machines. The United Kingdom had the most polling stations abroad, with 82, followed by Turkey with 78, Germany with 70, Spain with 67 and the United States with 44.
Alexandrina Pendachanska, an opera singer and co-chair of the initiative committee that nominated Gyurov and Kandev, told BNT that the first-round result had been expected. Exit polls put Gyurov at about 32%, roughly three percentage points behind Yotova, although the final outcome remained uncertain pending the official count.
Pendachanska said she was optimistic about the runoff and expected the ticket to attract broader support. She urged voters to reject what she called the “ghosts of communism”, the past and those who looked toward the East, and instead support a Western-oriented ticket advocating a modern Bulgaria within a united Europe.

In an updated security alert, the US mission said the State Department had ordered non-emergency government employees and their families to leave Saudi Arabia, effective Oct. 23, citing growing safety risks.

The embassy said King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh partially reopened on Sunday for domestic flights and some international services operated by Saudi carriers.

US government personnel now require special authorization to use any airport in Saudi Arabia.
The Houthis have renewed threats against Riyadh's airport, warning that it remained a military target despite the partial reopening.
The airport had suspended operations following an Oct. 10 Houthi attack that killed 13 people and wounded hundreds.
Saudi Arabia also intercepted additional missiles and drones on Sunday as fighting with the Houthis continued.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on Sunday that Russian President Vladimir Putin’s stated readiness for peace talks could be a “political trick” to avoid escalating tensions with Washington ahead of US midterms.
In an interview with Ukrainian broadcaster TSN, Zelenskyy said the Kremlin’s intentions would become clear through its actions and readiness to reach agreements, and trilateral talks in November would show whether Putin’s stance was a “trick.”
Zelenskyy said Kyiv was ready for trilateral talks among technical groups in November, but stressed that they must produce concrete results.
If a full settlement is not possible in the forthcoming talks, Zelenskyy said he proposed an energy ceasefire, agreements on maritime security and grain shipments, an all-for-all prisoner exchange or a meeting between the leaders of Ukraine, the US and Russia.
“Energy, grain, people -- these are concrete things, while a meeting at the level of leaders is an opportunity to have something concrete after our trilateral. This is what we are asking for and proposing,” he said.
On the territorial issue, Zelenskyy said it could only be discussed at the leaders’ level, describing it as a “red line.” He also rejected restrictions on Ukraine’s armed forces and any requirement for the country to remain neutral.
“We are not exchanging anything for anything. We are ready for discussions,” he said, adding that other issues could be addressed by technical groups.
Zelenskyy said he did not want Ukraine to enter a trilateral meeting at leaders' level after sanctions against Moscow had been lifted.
“I do not want us to find ourselves at a meeting with Putin without tools -- without sanctions, without money, or without frozen assets. Because then, as Mr. Trump said, we really would not have too many cards in our deck,” he said.
On the localized ceasefire in the Russian-controlled Ukrainian city of Oleshky arranged by US first lady Melania Trump, Zelenskyy said the US proposed the truce starting Oct. 27 that would last several days to allow humanitarian missions to enter the area.
He said Russian forces would need to clear mined roads to facilitate access, expressing concern that Moscow could seek to direct evacuees toward its territories rather than allow them to leave freely.
“Of course, Russia will do everything to demine the roads in such a way that these people go to Russia and stay there. They are not going to simply set people free,” he said.
He added that some civilians would be evacuated to Ukrainian-controlled territory, stressing that the priority was to end the blockade and ensure residents could live safely.
“Ideally, they should be able to achieve their goal and evacuate here, to us, to Ukraine, which will provide them with everything they need and support them,” he said.

Democrats could gain control of the U.S. Senate – forecasts indicate the possibility of a substantial majority
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
22:29:56 EET
05:29:56 KST

Democrats could gain control of the U.S. Senate – forecasts indicate the possibility of a substantial majority
Kyiv • UNN
Forecasts give Democrats up to 55 seats in the Senate and a 66–71% chance of a majority. Experts consider a significant margin unlikely.
The U.S. Democratic Party could regain control of the Senate in the November 3 midterm elections. Some forecasting models suggest that the party could win up to 55 of the 100 seats, although experts consider such an outcome unlikely. Newsweek reports this, writes UNN.
Details
According to the Vote-Scope forecast, updated on October 23, Democrats could win 54 Senate seats. The model puts their chances of securing a majority at 71%, with a possible outcome ranging from 48 to 55 seats.
Another forecast, Fred Cornell, projects 52 seats for Democrats and estimates the probability of securing a majority at 66%. Meanwhile, the 270toWin consensus forecast assigns 49 seats to Democrats and considers another five uncertain.
Why a large majority remains unlikely
To gain control of the Senate, Democrats need to increase their representation by four seats—to 51. To reach 55 seats, the party would have to win eight additional seats without losing any of its current ones.
Marista Lee Miringoff, director of the Marist Institute for Public Opinion, considers such a scenario unlikely. Patrick Ruffini, a partner at Echelon Insights, estimated its probability at approximately 10%.
Elections in North Carolina, Maine, Ohio, and Texas could be crucial for Democrats. To secure a significantly larger advantage, the party would also need victories in traditionally Republican states, including Iowa and Kansas.
Experts also point to historical polling errors. According to Ruffini, in 73% of cases from 2018 to 2024, pollsters overestimated support for Democrats.
At the same time, the opposition party could benefit from the traditional decline in support for the incumbent president's political party during midterm elections.

Blanche defends Trump-ordered lawsuit over Alaska Senate election certification
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
20:28:55 UTC
05:28:55 KST

Attorney General Todd Blanche defended the Justice Department's lawsuit on Sunday seeking to block certification of Alaska's Senate election if Republican incumbent Sen. Dan Sullivan narrowly loses.
The lawsuit, filed last week, cites what it argues is likely voter confusion over the name Daniel J. Sullivan, a retired teacher also on the ballot. The DOJ said confusion over the two Sullivans could help former Alaska Democratic Rep. Mary Peltola, who is narrowly ahead in polls just over a week from Election Day, win the election.
"What we're asking the court to do is make sure that after the election, if it's clear that there was confusion, if it's clear, and that's for a court to decide at a later date if there's litigation ... and that confusion led to an unjust, improper result that is not the will of the Alaskan voter, we want to make sure that the Alaskan system and the Alaskan state courts and the Alaskan electoral process can understand that in a way that lets them do the right thing," Blanche said on CNN's "State of the Union."
"Never before have opponents gone to such lengths to try and thwart and cheat in an election as they're doing in this case," he said.
The DOJ's lawsuit says that the potential for voter confusion exists and Alaska should not certify the election if "(1) Senator Sullivan does not win the election; and (2) had all votes cast for Daniel J. Sullivan been cast instead for Senator Sullivan and Alaska's rank-choice process played out accordingly, Senator Sullivan would have won the election."
Alaska applies a top-four primary system to select candidates for the general election. The November general election uses ranked-choice voting.
Ranked-choice voting lets voters rank candidates in order of preference. If no candidate receives a majority of votes in the first round of counting, the candidate with the fewest votes is eliminated. Voters who ranked the eliminated candidate first then have their second choice counted and added to that candidate's total. This continues until a majority winner — or the candidate with more than half of the vote — wins.
Republicans have argued for months that Daniel J. Sullivan is a Democratic plant intended to confuse voters and have sought to remove him from the ballot. Democrats have maintained they have no connection to the candidate, and Sullivan himself has denied running to confuse voters.
The Alaska Division of Elections briefly removed Daniel J. Sullivan in June, before a state court ordered his name returned to the ballot. The state Supreme Court upheld that decision.
President Donald Trump, who has long made claims of voter fraud without evidence, said he ordered the DOJ's lawsuit himself.
Democratic groups and voting rights advocates, including Peltola's campaign, are seeking to join the lawsuit to stop the DOJ's effort to block certification of the election if Sen. Sullivan loses. The groups argue the executive branch lacks the legal authority to intervene in state-run elections and is attempting an unprecedented override of state election administration, with early voting already underway.
"In an unprecedented pre-emptive strike on democratic elections, the Department of Justice—acting on the President's personal orders—demands that this Court enjoin the certification of the ongoing U.S. Senate election, but only if the President's preferred candidate loses," the motion to intervene reads. "But the federal government has no power to impose that Hobson's choice on the people of this State."
Alaska is seen as one of the best chances for a Democratic flip in the Nov. 3 elections, which will determine control of Congress for the remainder of Trump's term. Trump has been barnstorming competitive states in recent weeks as the polls favor Democrats to win control of the House of Representatives and potentially flip the Senate.
Democrats and voting rights advocates have long feared that Trump — who denied his election loss to former President Joe Biden in 2020, leading to a violent riot at the U.S. Capitol on Jan. 6, 2021 — would attempt to meddle in the midterm contest to save narrow Republican majorities in Congress.
Blanche bristled on Sunday when asked whether the lawsuit aimed to sway the election in Alaska toward Republicans.
"That is crazy," Blanche said, pressed on CNN about whether the president is laying the groundwork for a "doomsday" scenario in which he tries to overturn election results.
"We're not laying any groundwork for the president to do that ... the groundwork that we are laying is for the state of Alaska, if it becomes an issue after the election, will have the ability to determine whether there was confusion that violates the law in determining who the senator should be."
