Algeria to send troops to Niger in first foreign deployment since 1973
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
21:26:35 CET
05:26:35 KST

ALGIERS, Oct 25 (Reuters) - Algeria’s parliament approved a resolution on Sunday authorising the deployment of army units to Niger, a parliamentary statement said, in what would mark Algeria’s first foreign troop deployment since it sent forces to support Egypt in the 1973 war.
Lawmakers unanimously backed the deployment of National Army units to Madama in northern Niger, near the Libyan border, at the site of a former French base used during Operation Barkhane, the statement said.
No troops have been officially deployed yet, according to a Niger security source. But Niger presidential chief of staff General Bacharou Ibro Amadou has been visiting the Kawar area in the Bilma department of Agadez region since October 19. He travelled to Madama for talks with local military commanders before returning to Dirkou to meet military and traditional authorities on plans for the base.
The move highlights a rapid improvement in ties between Algiers and Niamey after a period of strain.
Algeria opposed the 2023 coup that brought Niger’s current military leaders to power. Relations worsened last year, when Niger recalled its ambassador from Algiers after Algeria shot down a Malian drone near their border.
Niger, Mali and Burkina Faso are all ruled by military leaders who seized power in coups and later formed the Alliance of Sahel States.
Niger, like other countries in West Africa’s Sahel region, is battling insurgents linked to al Qaeda and Islamic State. Algeria, which shares a border with Niger, has traditionally regarded stability in the Sahel-Sahara as a key regional security priority.
Ties have improved this year. Niger President Abdourahamane Tiani visited Algiers in February, and Niger Defence Minister Salifou Mody travelled there on October 20 with a delegation of defence experts for talks on security cooperation.
Algeria has also deepened its economic interests in Niger. State energy company Sonatrach is working with Niger and Nigeria on the Trans-Saharan Gas Pipeline, which is intended to create a new export corridor for African gas to international markets, particularly Europe.
Sonatrach said in 2022 that it had signed a production-sharing agreement with Niger’s petroleum ministry for the Kafra region, where two exploration wells held proven reserves of 168 million barrels and 100 million barrels, respectively.
(Reporting by Abdelaziz Boumzar; Niger newsroom and David Lewis; Writing by Muhammad Al Gebaly and Menna Alaa El Din; Editing by Andrew Heavens and Bill Berkrot)

Kostadinov Says Revival Voters Could Decide the Runoff
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
20:18:33 UTC
05:18:33 KST

Revival leader and presidential candidate Kostadin Kostadinov said the October 25 election results were predictable given low turnout, adding that his party’s voters could play a decisive role in the November 1 runoff.
Speaking at a news briefing at the party’s headquarters in Sofia, Kostadinov said Revival had sought to bring as many people as possible to the polls, but that turnout reflected a broader problem with statehood in Bulgaria.
Kostadinov and his running mate Petar Volgin received between 12% and 15% of the vote, according to exit polls and parallel vote counts, placing them third in the race. The two leading candidates will face each other in a runoff on November 1.
Kostadinov said Revival’s performance exceeded its result in the parliamentary election six months earlier. He also said the party had won considerably more support than in the previous presidential election five years ago, when it received 3.9%, estimating that its current result would be at least four times higher.
“The outcome of the second round of the elections on November 1 will largely depend on Revival voters,” Kostadinov said.
Asked whether the party would endorse either candidate advancing to the runoff, he said it would decide after the final results were announced, provided its support was sought. “To give one's support, one needs to be asked for it,” he said.
When asked how Revival would respond if neither candidate requested its backing, Kostadinov said, “There is no way to remain neutral when it comes to our home.”
He also argued that the election had demonstrated the importance of his party’s electorate to other political forces. “Revival has demonstrated that all other parties will have to reckon with our voters, whether they like it or not,” he said.
Kostadinov thanked the party’s supporters, particularly those who had returned after backing another political force in the previous parliamentary election. He said some voters who had chosen Rumen Radev in that election had now come back to Revival, and expressed particular gratitude to them.
He said the low turnout could partly be explained by disappointment among Radev’s supporters, claiming that many had concluded within six months that their expectations of him had not been met.
Kostadinov said the decline in support was serious but should not be described as a catastrophic collapse. He warned that the country’s statehood was under threat and said Bulgarians no longer believed they could influence events in their own country.
“To overcome this crisis, we need statesmen - not merely politicians - who think generations ahead,” he said.
Kostadinov also said Revival had shown during the election campaign that it was willing to engage with people across political divides, respect differing views and maintain dialogue with those who disagreed with the party.

MPs to pay tribute to independent MP Helen Haines as parliament returns
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
20:15:46 UTC
05:15:46 KST

In brief
- Parliamentary business was suspended on Monday to pay tribute to independent MP Helen Haines.
- Haines remains in hospital a week after she was allegedly attacked outside her electorate office.
Prime Minister Anthony Albanese has led an emotional parliamentary tribute to Helen Haines, saying the shock caused by the alleged attack on the independent MP sits "like a stone in our hearts".
Federal parliamentarians returned to Canberra on Monday for the first sitting since Haines suffered catastrophic injuries after she was struck by a four-wheel drive outside her Wangaratta electorate office a week ago.
Albanese moved a motion to suspend parliamentary business for the day so colleagues could offer messages of support for Haines, who remains in hospital in Melbourne after both her legs were amputated.
The silhouette of a cockatoo was placed on Haines' chair by her friend and fellow crossbench MP Zali Steggall. Many MPs wore orange hearts on their lapels, while some held back tears as they paid tribute to Haines.
"Today, being back in this chamber on what should have been an ordinary day, looking across at the member for Indi's seat over there, and hoping and looking forward to the day in which she's back here," Albanese said.
News that makes sense
Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
"Right now our friend and colleague is in hospital, grievously injured. The shape of her life and her family's lives have changed forever."
The prime minister described Haines as a person with "decency, integrity, compassion, humour, and empathy" and who had "always embodied the truth that there is more that unites us than divides us".
Haines' husband, Phil, who was in the chamber for the speeches, was praised for showing a "level of grace that, for most of us, is simply beyond reckoning".
The bystanders who rushed to Haines' aid showed the "best of the Australian character".
While investigations continued into potential motives for the alleged attack, Albanese said "the very real rise in anger that distorts and corrodes our public discourse" could not be ignored.
"Enabled by the anonymity and speed afforded by social media, we are seeing rage and aggression increasing, not just in politics, but towards workers in hospitality and retail, in schools and in hospitals, towards police, paramedics, and other officials," he said.
"We are seeing a normalisation of the language of grievance and violence."
He said there had always been disagreement in Australia, but it could not be allowed to become a "full stop".
"We keep talking, we keep working towards something better," he said.
He said Haines embodied that spirit, as someone who believed disagreement only functioned when it didn't depart from respect and humanity.
"Right now, the member for Indi is on the hardest road of all," he said.
"As we pray for her, we console ourselves with this one solid truth. As Phil, who I've spoken to daily, keeps reminding me every day, Helen Haines is a fighter."
Angus Taylor says Haines 'epitomises civility'
Opposition leader Angus Taylor spoke after Albanese, saying Haines "epitomises civility".
"That's why the violent attack on her seems so unfathomable. In those horrific moments last Monday, and in the critical hours and days afterwards, one man's cruelty stood in stark contrast to the courage and decency of so many Australians," he said.
However, the Liberal Party rejected the suggestion there was a "causal connection between robust parliamentary debate and political violence".
Taylor said parliament debated "with adversarial vigour", but the debate could never be allowed to spill into violence.
"The choice to use violence is a rejection of robust debate, a refusal to accommodate difference and disagree. The antidote to violence isn't to compromise our system of robust debate, but to cherish, champion, and strengthen that system," he said.
Taylor said the government had made the right call to call out far-right extremism, but all extremism needed to be called out.
Australia also needed to celebrate its achievements more readily, he said, drawing a link between feelings of shame about the nation's history and growing hostility towards democratic institutions.
"Too many Australians have been taught to feel guilty and shame about our country and about our history. Is it any wonder that some feel deep animosity towards our democracy, our institutions, and our nation?" he said.
"Is it any wonder that we see war memorials graffitied and statues defaced?"
Zali Steggall 'struggling to process the shock'
Some of the most personal tributes came from Haines' crossbench colleagues.
Zali Steggall, who sits next to Haines in the lower house, became emotional as she addressed her "good friends", Helen and Phil, directly.
"Dear Helen and Phil, I've been going around in circles in my head, trying to express everything I want to say," she said, as she fought back tears.
"We are all struggling to process the shock and grief at what has happened. Our hearts go out to you both and your children and grandchildren."
Steggall said Haines was the "matriarch" of the crossbench and was "always a voice for respectful political debate".
Independent Kooyong MP Monique Ryan described Haines as a "woman of luminous generosity and kindness" who always acted with "integrity and respect".
The alleged attack sharpened the focus of the increasingly hostile political environment, she said.
"It's not all men, but most aggression is committed by men," she said.
"People say they don't recognise our country. I've been told that many times in the last week."
Ryan said she believed parliament bore some responsibility for the corrosion in public discourse.
"How we speak to each other is modelled by our communities, but the media also bears responsibility for turning anxiety into outrage and for amplifying grievance for more clicks, for fostering misogyny and disrespect of female leaders," she said.
"Our democracy depends on people being willing to serve their communities, as Helen has said herself, a woman's place is in every room where decisions are made."
Andrew Hastie urges an end to the 'nasty personal politics of MAGA'
Liberal frontbencher Andrew Hastie urged his colleagues to leave the "nasty personal politics of MAGA" to the United States.
He said the incident "forces us to pause and reflect".
"How can we do better? For me, how can I do better?" he said.
"I'll be the first to admit that I've overreached in my language during my 11 years in this house, and we've all erred in this way at some time.
"What we say here or online shapes the political culture. We can all do better and we should strive to do better. So let's play the ball, not the person, and leave the nasty personal politics of MAGA in the United States."
Fundraiser reaches more than $1.2 million
A fundraiser for Save the Children, set up in lieu of flowers by Haines' family, surpassed $1.2 million in donations by Monday morning.
Donations have poured in from across the country, including from Labor MP and fellow Victorian Jodie Belyea.
"To you and yours Helen. Stay strong. You are in our thoughts and prayers," Belyea said on behalf of her electorate of Dunkley.
Police are still investigating a potential motive for the alleged attack, but the suspect, Brendan Nugent, 43, posted online about political issues.
A wave of parliamentarians have spoken out about rising political tensions and an increase in threats, abuse and safety concerns in light of the alleged attack.
Labor's digital duty of care bill, aimed at curbing harmful content online and stamping out predatory behaviour from platforms, will be debated in the lower house later in the week.
The government aims to pass the legislation before the end of the year, but opponents argue it could result in political censorship.
The government has pointed to the alleged attack and rising threats toward leaders as examples of why greater action is needed against online harms.
On Sunday, Australian Federal Police commissioner Krissy Barrett acknowledged gaps in regional mental health care.
"There has been media reporting around his mental health, around some of the causes or issues that he has aligned himself with. That all remains part of the ongoing investigation," she told ABC's Insiders program.

But the option of withholding federal funds from jurisdictions that fail to act in line with the agreement has been raised multiple times.
McCarthy says she made changes to a funding agreement with the Northern Territory government, after it rejected an offer from the Commonwealth to buy the YiSSA short-stay accommodation centre in Darwin earlier this month, opting instead to close the facility.
"I have made adjustments to the Northern Territory remote area investment [NTRAI] as a result of it," McCarthy said.
"That's the first federal funding agreement, which I've incorporated changes in that through NIAA's negotiations."
McCarthy also said she and Finance Minister Katy Gallagher had flagged that further funding arrangement changes could be on the table if the NT government continued to act against the Closing the Gap agreement.
"In that meeting [we] expressed very clearly the financial concerns and the funding arrangements that were troubling the Commonwealth," McCarthy said.
"Also that we would start to seriously look at other avenues of funding, in particular direct funding, to Aboriginal organisations and/or local governments."

National Working with Children Check pilot system to begin operating early 2027
A national pilot system designed to check the criminal history of people applying for and already holding working with children checks will begin operating by early next year.
Officials from the Attorney-General's department have appeared at a Senate estimates hearing to provide an update on the system.
Late last year, the federal government committed $37 million dollars to create an IT system which continually updates records about people who've passed a Working with Children Check.
The Royal Commission into Institutional Responses to Child Sexual Abuse released a standalone report into working with children checks in August 2015 and recommended a national system to track the criminal histories of the 6 million Australians who hold a check.
Today, the department told Senate estimates that all Australian jurisdictions have now moved legislation to accommodate the new pilot system and will adopt the new system by early next year.
"Child safety remains an incredibly important priority for the government and the department," said Chris Collett, Acting Deputy Secretary for the Justice and Communities Group of the Attorney-General's department.
"It is a very complex area of policy, legislative and IT reform and it's a real example of commitment across all levels of government to shift that and improve safety and protections for children in Australia," he said.

Ombudsman issues scathing report into aged care algorithm
The Commonwealth Ombudsman has issued a damning report on the aged care algorithm, saying legislation should be introduced to allow assessors to override its decisions.
In a scathing report of more than 100 pages, the ombudsman says the Department of Health, Disability and Ageing put the classification algorithm in place "without any meaningful risk assessment, evaluation or analysis, despite the obvious risks that would arise with deterministic automated decision-making".
"In my view, the department did not, and may still not, understand key components of the legal framework it created, nor did it understand what legal framework it was meant to create," ombudsman Iain Anderson said.
The classification algorithm was launched on November 1 last year as part of the government's "once in a generation" reforms to aged care and is used to assign people a level of funding to stay at home with support rather than go into a nursing home.
But it has been mired in controversy since its introduction, with hundreds of people appealing its decision — a more than five-fold increase on appeals in the previous year.
Mr Anderson went further, saying "a reasonable person would, in my view, lack confidence that the system is in fact fair and consistent".
In a response to the draft report, the department said it "does not accept this characterisation" that it didn't test the algorithm or validate it.
Public servants told they can't request their evidence not to be shared on social media
Richard Pye, the outgoing clerk of the Senate, has said it was "profoundly unhelpful" for witnesses appearing before parliamentary inquiries and Senate estimates to say they didn't consent for their testimony to be clipped up and shared on social media.
During a parliamentary inquiry last month, Defence deputy secretary of security and estate Celia Perkins said that defence witnesses "do not consent to the reposting of our evidence to social media sites or the reproduction of our likenesses for purposes outside the framework of the parliament".
At the time, Greens senator David Shoebridge called that an "extraordinary" proposal and said there should not be a "blanket gag" on public hearings.
In response to a question from Liberal senator Jane Hume today, Pye said he recently provided advice, "simply that it's absolutely not something that a witness can do".
"This is not to minimise the fact that there are some people who have been very bruised by their experiences before Senate and House committee, and the treatment of footage that has come out of those," Pye said.
He said he observed some footage on social media — not posted by a senator — noting that the commentary was "horrendous" and "atrocious".
Snowy Hydro board strips bonus pay from chief executive Dennis Barnes
Snowy Hydro's chief executive Dennis Barnes will receive no bonus pay this financial year, after the company revealed last week another extraordinary blowout in cost and time to complete the Snowy 2.0 renewables expansion.
First estimated to cost $2 billion, and then revised to $12 billion after a project "reset" in 2023, Barnes warned last week it would now cost up to $25 billion, and won't be finished before 2029, eight years late.
The ABC reported in May that Snowy's executives were paid more than $1.2 million in bonus pay in 2025, including $323,000 to Barnes, just a month before ordering a "line by line" review of its spiralling costs.
The company's annual report has confirmed this year Barnes will receive $0 in "variable remuneration".
Three other executives at Snowy Hydro received $752,000 in bonus pay, with the company saying while it had missed targets on delivering Snowy 2.0, safety and the environment, it had met targets on the wider companies underlying financial performance, on customer satisfaction and corporate leadership.

"On behalf of the House, Helen, we are thinking of you. We are praying for your quick recovery and we look forward to the day you return to this place, and I get to say the following nine words: 'I give the call to the member for Indi.'"
Taylor disagrees with claim of link between 'robust' parliamentary debate and violence
Angus Taylor continues. He says today is a day to reflect on our democracy.
The opposition leader says he disagrees with the suggestion there is a causal connection between robust parliamentary debate and political violence.
"The choice to use violence is a rejection of robust debate, a refusal to accommodate difference and disagreement. The antidote to violence isn’t to compromise our system of robust debate, but to cherish, champion, and strengthen that system," he says.
Taylor says the antidote to violence isn't to compromise our system of robust debate.
"But to cherish, champion and strengthen that system. What we must do is call out and confront the actual sources of intolerance, intimidation of political violence in our country," he says.
Haines 'epitomizes civility': Taylor
Opposition Leader Angus Taylor has also thrown his support behind Helen Haines.

"That's why the violent [alleged] attack on Haines seems so unfathomable. In those horrific moments last Monday, and in the critical hours and days afterwards, one man’s cruelty stood in stark contrast to the courage and decency of so many Australians," he says.
Albanese says we can't shrug off 'very real rise in anger'
Prime Minister Anthony Albanese says we cannot shrug off the "very real rise in anger that distorts and corrodes our public discourse".
"We are seeing rage and aggression increasing, not just in politics, but towards workers in hospitality and retail, in schools and in hospitals, towards police, paramedics and other officials," he says.
"We are seeing a normalisation of the language of grievance and violence. We must not conflate the robustness of Australian democracy with this rising tide of rage.
"We've always had disagreement in Australia. It's part of our story, as is an unbroken democracy, and our continuous system of government shines as a beacon to the world.
"We cannot allow disagreement to become a full stop."
Albanese says he is praying for Haines as she is on the hardest road of all. But he says she is a "fighter".
📷 Parliament gathers to shares messages of support for Haines
Haines 'embodied the truth there is more that unites us than divides us': PM

"Right now our friend and colleague is in hospital, grievously injured. The shape of her life and her family's lives have changed forever."

Albanese says Haines has always "embodied the truth there is more that unites us than divides us".
"There is no stronger foundation than common ground. Her capacity to do it all with such heart and such unrelenting advocacy in its own way."
Key Event

Exit Poll: 39% of GERB Voters Back Gyurov for President of Bulgaria
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
20:14:25 UTC
05:14:25 KST

According to Alpha Research’s exit poll, 39% of GERB voters who participated in the presidential election chose Andrey Gyurov, while turnout among the party’s supporters exceeded 30%, representing approximately 130,000 votes.
Among these voters, 22% backed Iliana Yotova, 8% supported Kostadin Kostadinov, and 7% selected the “I do not support anyone” option.
Voters of Progressive Bulgaria largely supported Yotova, with 74% choosing her, compared with 9% who voted for Gyurov and 11% who backed Revival leader Kostadinov. Thus, three-quarters of Progressive Bulgaria supporters who went to the polls voted for its preferred candidate, while the remaining quarter divided their support between other options.
Turnout among DPS voters was just 15%, or around 40,000 people, marking a record low. Yotova received the largest share of their votes, at 39%, followed by Gyurov with 28%. Kostadinov won 3% of DPS voters, while Nikolay Nenchev received 3%, Radostin Vasilev 2%, and Hristanov 1%. Another 13% chose “I do not support anyone.”
Commenting on the arrests of mayors from the Movement, sociologist Boryana Dimitrova said, “Voters are not marched to the polls like soldiers.” She noted that some polling stations had not received a single ballot, reflecting the limited interest in the election among DPS supporters.
Former GERB MP Delyan Dobrev reacted to the pollsters’ presidential election results by posting on Facebook, “It’s a good thing we don’t have a candidate! There was a risk we might win!”
Earlier on election day, Dobrev had written on social media that he would not vote for the first time in three decades.
He had maintained the same position among GERB supporters since the start of the campaign. In late September, he told bTV, “I am a member of GERB, but I don’t even watch the news. I don’t like any of the presidential candidates, and for the first time in 30 years, I will not be voting.”
Within GERB, Dobrev is associated with one of two competing positions on whether the party should participate in the presidential election. He argued that GERB should nominate its own candidate, choosing a prominent figure to represent the party. At the party’s national meeting in late August, he identified Dimitar Nikolov, Tomislav Donchev, and Rosen Zhelyazkov as potential presidential candidates.
The alternative position was advocated by GERB MP Vladislav Goranov, who argued against putting forward a candidate to prevent what he called “fratricidal wars” within the political right.

Algeria to send troops to Niger in first foreign deployment since 1973
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
20:10:25 UTC
05:10:25 KST

Algeria to send troops to Niger in first foreign deployment since 1973
ALGIERS, Oct 25 - Algeria's parliament approved a resolution on Sunday authorising the deployment of army units to Niger, a parliamentary statement said, in what would mark Algeria's first foreign troop deployment since it sent forces to support Egypt in the 1973 war.
Lawmakers unanimously backed the deployment of National Army units to Madama in northern Niger, near the Libyan border, at the site of a former French base used during Operation Barkhane, the statement said.
No troops have been officially deployed yet, according to a Niger security source. But Niger presidential chief of staff General Bacharou Ibro Amadou has been visiting the Kawar area in the Bilma department of Agadez region since October 19. He travelled to Madama for talks with local military commanders before returning to Dirkou to meet military and traditional authorities on plans for the base.
The move highlights a rapid improvement in ties between Algiers and Niamey after a period of strain.
Algeria opposed the 2023 coup that brought Niger's current military leaders to power. Relations worsened last year, when Niger recalled its ambassador from Algiers after Algeria shot down a Malian drone near their border.
Niger, Mali and Burkina Faso are all ruled by military leaders who seized power in coups and later formed the Alliance of Sahel States.
Niger, like other countries in West Africa's Sahel region, is battling insurgents linked to al Qaeda and Islamic State. Algeria, which shares a border with Niger, has traditionally regarded stability in the Sahel-Sahara as a key regional security priority.
Ties have improved this year. Niger President Abdourahamane Tiani visited Algiers in February, and Niger Defence Minister Salifou Mody travelled there on October 20 with a delegation of defence experts for talks on security cooperation.
Algeria has also deepened its economic interests in Niger. State energy company Sonatrach is working with Niger and Nigeria on the Trans-Saharan Gas Pipeline, which is intended to create a new export corridor for African gas to international markets, particularly Europe.
Sonatrach said in 2022 that it had signed a production-sharing agreement with Niger's petroleum ministry for the Kafra region, where two exploration wells held proven reserves of 168 million barrels and 100 million barrels, respectively. REUTERS

Details

Oil prices could rise to $150 a barrel if war on Iran resumes
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
20:00:43 UTC
05:00:43 KST

Hojjatoleslam Mousa Ahmadi warned in an interview with local Iranian media on Sunday that a resumption of war and further disruptions to global oil supplies could push crude prices above $150 per barrel. Citing oil prices exceeding $117 per barrel and declining U.S. strategic petroleum reserves, he said a prolonged energy crisis could increase economic pressure on the United States and oil-importing countries.
He noted that higher oil prices would have consequences beyond energy markets, raising transportation, production, and energy costs while intensifying inflationary pressures in oil-consuming countries.
He said the U.S. government would face greater pressure to contain energy prices and protect domestic consumers. The longer the crisis continues, he added, the more difficult it would become to manage its economic and political consequences.
Ahmadi also said Iran intends to maintain long-term pressure on oil markets, drawing on its strategic position in the energy sector and the defensive capabilities of its armed forces. He argued that preventing prices from falling could prolong the energy crisis and increase the economic and political costs for Washington.
Concluding his remarks, Ahmadi pointed to energy-related challenges facing several European countries, including France, Portugal, Albania, and Italy. He warned that continued disruptions to oil supplies could pose further challenges to economic stability in both the United States and Europe.

Russia suspected of large-scale cyberattack on Jaguar Land Rover, causing losses of up to £2.1 billion
Kyiv • UNN
The attack halted Jaguar Land Rover’s production and affected 5,000 organizations. The British government has not yet named those responsible.
Former UK Defence Secretary Elphick Karns said that a foreign state supported the large-scale cyberattack on carmaker Jaguar Land Rover in 2025. Earlier, British media reported possible Russian involvement in the hack, which caused billions of pounds in damage. The Telegraph reports, writes UNN.
Details
According to estimates by the UK Centre for Cyber Monitoring, the total economic damage from the attack amounted to between £1.6 billion and £2.1 billion. It was called the most expensive cyberattack in the history of the United Kingdom.
Because of the hack, Jaguar Land Rover halted production for several weeks. The consequences were felt by around 5,000 organisations, including car dealerships, repair shops and component suppliers. Approximately 200,000 jobs were put at risk.
What is known about possible Russian involvement
Karns spoke about state support for the cyberattack in July during an event organised by the Chatham House think tank. However, his remarks became publicly known only now.
We know that the attack on Jaguar Land Rover was state-sponsored
At the same time, Karns clarified that his conclusions were not based on an official assessment by the UK Ministry of Defence. According to him, an attack of this scale could hardly have taken place without the knowledge of the state from whose territory the hackers operated.
Earlier, The New York Times, citing sources, reported that a group of Russian hackers might have been behind the hack.
The British government has not yet officially named those responsible for the attack, citing the ongoing investigation.

David Chau's chart of the day: NextDC hoping to avoid 'second strike' at AGM
Hello there! Every afternoon, I'll give you a sneak peek at what I'll be discussing on my 7pm News finance report.
Tonight we'll be taking at the extreme souring of the Australian 'AI trade' — NextDC's share price in particular.
Shares of the data centre operator were trading as high as $16.37 less than five months ago (on June 3).
NextDC has since plummeted 66% to its lowest level since January 2018.
It's also worth noting the company's annual general meeting (AGM) is happening on November 20.
The company received a "first strike" at last year's AGM as 72% of shareholder votes were cast against the board's remuneration report.
Essentially, a huge majority of shareholders were unhappy with the directors' plans to pay themselves hefty bonuses.
If NextDC cops a "second strike" at next month's AGM — which involves at least 25% of shareholder votes against its latest executive pay report — that could potentially trigger a board spill.

Key Event
Investors hang up on Tuas after Singapore investigation
The ASX-listed, Singapore-focussed telecom Tuas has crashed 40% after Singapore's communication regulator ramped up investigations about its Simba Telecom subsidiary alleged unauthorised network use.
Singapore's Infocomm Media Development Authority (IMDA) issued a show-cause notice to Simba Telecom, asking why the regulator should not make certain findings against it.
In May, Tuas scrapped its $SGD1.43 billion ($A1.60 billion) deal to buy a stake in mobile operator M1 through Simba after the Singaporean regulator halted the transaction, saying Simba may have used radio frequency spectrum that was not assigned to it to provide mobile services.
The regulator is investigating whether Simba had used of spectrum bandwidth in Singapore without authorisation at about 90 sites during intermittent periods between 2023 and 2026.
The regulator also asked Simba to respond to its use of the 2100 MHz band through dynamic sharing during intermittent periods in 2022 and 2023 for both 4G and 5G services, when it was authorised to use the spectrum only for 5G.
The "show cause" notice indicates that IMDA has yet to come to a conclusion about what, if any, action will be taken against Simba.
Shares of Tuas are down as much as 40% to $1.09 their lowest level since late June 2022.

Key Event
Vegetable wholesaler facing $12 million in fine for price fixing
The big national vegetable wholesaler Perfection Fresh is facing a $12 million fine after admitting to participating in a price-fixing operation with three other suppliers to the Aldi supermarket chain.
The action follows an investigation into the cartel by the ACCC, which started civil proceedings against Perfection in the Federal Court in 2025.
The ACCC alleged, and Perfection Fresh has admitted, that on eleven occasions between 2019 and 2020, Perfection Fresh engaged in cartel conduct by fixing the prices of broccoli, cauliflower and iceberg lettuce supplied to ALDI in New South Wales.
Perfection and the ACCC have made a joint submission to the Court that the wholesaler should pay $12 million in fines for nine contraventions and one attempted contravention of engaging in a cartel.
Perfection also agreed to establish a competition law compliance program.
The Court will determine whether the proposed penalty and other orders are appropriate at a later date.
"Cartel conduct undermines competition and can increase prices, harming consumers and raising the cost of doing business," ACCC Commissioner Luke Woodward said.
"Enforcing cartel laws and protecting competition in the supply of fresh food are ongoing priorities for the ACCC."
The ACCC's case against the other suppliers and individuals is ongoing.
Perfection Fresh is the second-largest fresh vegetable supplier in Australia, supplying a broad range of produce, including cauliflower, broccoli, iceberg lettuce, Brussels sprouts, broccolini and celery, to all states and territories.

Key Event
'Government spending is part of demand', says RBA chief economist
Despite a concerted effort from 60 Minutes's Adam Hegarty over several follow up questions, RBA chief economist Sarah Hunter declined to offer the federal and state governments any advice around their spending levels.
However, she did acknowledge that public spending in excess of revenues (i.e. deficit spending) does contribute demand to the economy at a time when the RBA is trying to take demand out.
"Government spending is definitely part of the picture, so we take quite a lot of time to understand what governments are planning to do," she said.
"You mentioned state and federal, and it is important that it's both because they both have a role to play.
"So we look at state budgets, announcements and things, and that's what we factor into our forecasts.
"And government spending is part of demand, and it's that imbalance between demand and supply that we're really trying to tackle right now.
"But what I would also say is that we are an independent central bank, we're unelected.
"It's really not our place to tell the country, politicians, individuals, anyone, what governments should or shouldn't spend money on, how much they should or shouldn't be spending.
"That's a conversation the country should have. We all get to have our say at the ballot box eventually when elections roll around."
You can read the full transcript of the interview on the RBA's website.

Key Event
RBA's chief economist reinforces expectations of one more rate hike
The Reserve Bank's chief economist Sarah Hunter has done an interview on 60 Minutes, recorded on October 21 and aired last night, which has backed up much of what was said by the RBA's deputy governor Andrew Hauser at the Citi Investment Conference last week.
"You see what's going on overseas, it's nothing to do with you, it's nothing to do with us," Hunter said.
"We can't stop that, but what we can do, and we must do, is make sure it doesn't become embedded.
"We don't want to live with high inflation for a long time. We want to get it out of the system.
"So we're still talking about inflation being high. Haven't we done enough?" Asked interviewer Adam Hegarty.
"It's tricky. It is hard. Unfortunately, not quite yet," responded Hunter.
"Obviously, the board have put through four rate hikes this year to keep on tackling the challenge.
"So not quite yet, but we I do think, and we do know from history and from looking at other countries too, high higher interest rates, higher rates will work. They do get through the system, they do bring inflation down, but it does take a bit of time, and that's the challenge at the moment.
"We're just stuck where we are today. We're just looking and need a bit more time. But the rates do work. Higher rates do work."
Financial markets are seeing that as reinforcement of Hauser's message last week, with market pricing on a November rate hike at around two-thirds, with a rate hike fully priced in by February next year.

Key Event
Why is gold losing its glitter?
As we noted earlier this morning, there is usually a positive correlation between rising oil prices and the price of gold.
So why with oil ripping higher to its highest level since April is gold now below $US4,000/ounce, its lowest level since July?
ANZ's commodities analyst Daniel Hynes points out the expectation of "tighter monetary policies" and rising interest rates is behind the move.
"A rotation out of AI-related stocks pushed investors toward the safety of US bonds…resulted in a rise in yields in US Treasuries, a headwind for non-yielding assets such as gold," Mr Hynes said.
Current market pricing points to the Fed leaving rates unchanged at this week's FOMC meeting, but a 78% chance of a December hike.
"Heightened inflation concerns suggest that major central banks of the world won't be able to ease monetary policies as quickly as they want to. All that's working against the gold and silver market bulls at present," American Gold Exchange analyst Jim Wyckoff told Reuters.
Mr Wyckoff also noted the selloff in technology stocks has also led to margin calls for equity traders and investors, prompting them to sell gold and silver assets.
Operation Jawbone's dislocation
"I guess I should warn you, if I turn out to be particularly clear, you've probably misunderstood what I said." Dr Alan Greenspan, former US Federal Reserve chair.
Oh, for the good old days of central banking, when every word was a lesson in obfuscation.
"Fedspeak" aka "Greenspeak", coined in honour of the good doctor, was a weapon of mass distraction to prevent financial markets overreacting, or indeed reacting at all, to public comments from Dr Greenspan.
One of his critics, former Princeton economics professor and Fed vice chair to Dr Greenspan for a while, Alan Binder called Fedspeak "a turgid dialect of English".
But that's a whole different story, which may not explain what Dr Greenspan was getting at, as much as Professor Binder's shorter-than-expected tenure at the Fed.
These days, central bankers have developed a bit of market moving clarity. It's deliberate.
It's also known as "jawboning", a process where central bankers' commentary works as a proxy for actually pulling interest rate levers.
However, central bank leaders can still simultaneously send the market in different directions, while trying to "keep on message".
To wit, RBA governor Michelle Bullock and her deputy, the loquacious Andrew Hauser seem to have sparked totally different reactions to their comments after the board's unanimous and "hawkish" 25 basis point hike to 4.60%.
The CBA's economic team has published an interesting minute-by-minute analysis of the market's reaction to recent speeches by governor Bullock and deputy governor Hauser.
On October 21, Dr Hauser sent the market's pricing for a November hike higher. On September 29, Ms Bullock sent the pricing lower.
"Governor Bullock's post-meeting press conference struck a softer tone, emphasising the long lags in monetary policy and the cumulative impact of the four hikes delivered this year," CBA economist Harry Ottley said.
"November pricing fell by around 4bp during the appearance."
"Deputy Governor Hauser's intervention (last week) moved expectations sharply in the opposite direction. He described the inflation outlook as 'materially worse' than projected in August, said upside inflation risks had crystallised and characterised the Board as facing "hard choices" between persistent inflation and weaker activity and employment
"Markets consequently priced around 3 — 4bp more tightening."
So, which is it? Who knows, but somewhere up there, Alan Greenspan is probably looking down at the RBA's jawboning efforts with an enigmatic smile.

Locally, the key event of the week will be the Q3 CPI from the ABS on Wednesday.
The market consensus is that the headline inflation rate will be 1.3% over the quarter, up from 0.6%, but will hold the annual pace flat at 3.9%.
The RBA's preferred Trimmed Mean measure is expected to come in at 0.6% over the quarter is forecast to edge up to around 1.o%, which would also see the annual hold at 3.6%.
"If realised, this would mark the fifth consecutive quarter in which trimmed mean inflation has increased by between 0.8% and 1.0%, highlighting the persistence of underlying inflation pressures," CBA's economics team wrote in a weekend note.
"The outcome would also be above the RBA's August forecast for trimmed mean inflation of around 0.8%/qtr, although the strength of the July and August monthly CPI prints means some deterioration in the inflation outlook is already well understood by the Board."
There will be another important insight into inflation with Friday's release of the Q3 Producers' Price Index.
"Final demand prices rose 1.3%/qtr and 3.6%/yr in Q2, the strongest quarterly increase since September 2023, with higher energy, freight and construction costs prominent," CBA said.
"The Q3 release will therefore be useful for assessing whether recent energy and supply chain pressures are continuing to lift upstream inflation."
Around the time the CPI figures drop on Wednesday, RBA Governor Michelle Bullock and her key lieutenants will be fronting the Senate Estimates Committee in Canberra, so we may get a real time reaction to the data.
Overseas, the focus will be on interest rate decisions from some of the biggest and most influential central banks.
The biggest and most influential, the US Federal Reserve makes its call on Thursday and is expected to keep its powder dry with a number of key voting members suggesting they are not in a hurry to lift rates again soon.
The Bank of Canada will follow soon after and it too is expected to be on hold, although a split decision is expected.
The European Central Bank and the Bank of Japan on Friday are also expected to be on hold, although the BoJ's guidance has not been that clear, and both are tipped to make another hike before the end of the year.
New Zealand's central bank is expected to lift its cash rate on Wednesday 25bp to 3.0%.
The big economies will also publish Q3 GDP numbers. Solid consumer spending and AI investment should see US GDP growth holding up at 3.4% (YoY).
The EU is expected to report a 0.3% jump in GDP over the quarter, following on from solid growth of 0.6% in Q2.
Another one to watch will the first UK budget brought down by new Prime Minister Andy Burham. His Chancellor John Healy has said that he will stick to the current fiscal rules and aims to deliver "a buffer also for uncertainty".
Key Event
Wall Street slips on oil, ASX to open lower
Wall Street's major indices all closed lower on Friday, although it wasn't AI stocks doing all the damage this time.
Global oil prices jumping another 3% to their highest level since April certainly helped fuel the general retreat.
- S&P 500: -0.5%
- Dow: -1.2%
- Nasdaq: -0.2%
Tech stocks were among the steadier performers amid widespread wobbles.
The Nasdaq's narrow loss was an improvement on Thursday's dump when the index endured is biggest fall since June as investors continued to fret about spending and investment returns in the sector.
Those anxieties remain, it's just that oil and inflation were the session's bigger worries
The S&P 500 energy sector, however, was resolute, gaining another 2.5% to another record high as key oil indices rose to levels last seen early in the US/Iran war.
- Brent futures: +3.1% to $US116.72/barrel
- WTI futures: +3.8% to $U103.27/barrel
That wave of worry will again likely wash up on our shores with futures trading pointing to a 0.5% decline on the ASX 200 this morning.
For the week, the S&P 500 fell 0.5% and the Nasdaq dropped 0.7%. The blue-chip Dow rose 0.4%, its third straight weekly gain.
Telecommunications stocks fell again on Friday, weighing on the communication services sector, after a report that SpaceX was seeking thousands of cell sites for a fourth wireless carrier.
Shares of AT&T and T-Mobile both sank nearly 8% while Verizon shed 1.2%. SpaceX shares rose 1.9%. US cell tower operators gained, with Crown Castle up 9% and American Tower up 4%.
Data from the University of Michigan showed US consumer sentiment edged down near a record low in October, as rising prices because of the Middle East conflict soured households' views of the economy.
Market focus remains on the earnings season, with robust corporate profit growth underpinning gains for major equity indexes this year.
S&P 500 companies are on track to have increased earnings by more than 32% in the third quarter, according to LSEG IBES data.
This week, about one-third of S&P 500 companies report quarterly results, including Alphabet, Microsoft and Amazon, three AI hyperscalers whose capital spending forecasts will be closely watched by investors.
US Treasury yields rose, a day after the benchmark 10-year yield saw its biggest one-day drop in nearly four years but remained around the 5% mark.
Gold fell to a three-month low as higher energy prices fuelled inflation concerns and reinforced US rate hike expectations ahead of next week's Federal Reserve meeting.
It gave up 4% over the week, and is now below $US4,000/ounce for the first time since July. The move also signalled a break from gold's usual positive correlation with oil.

Macron’s ‘vandals pay’ bill puts right to protest at risk
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
19:57:40 UTC
04:57:40 KST

Emmanuel Macron has been accused by trade unions of trying to curb the fundamental French right to protest as the government fast-tracks a bill to make protesters pay for damage caused by vandalism at street demonstrations even if they did not directly cause it themselves.
The French president, who leaves office next spring, has faced more than a month of protests in which high-school students have blockaded schools demanding a response to teacher absences, repairs to decrepit buildings and changes to the university applications platform.
Trade unions and gilets jaunes (yellow vest) anti-government protesters are now joining sustained street demonstrations in a growing social crisis over schools, as well as the cost of living and public services. Authorities have increased security measures and placed restrictions on demonstrating after France saw one of its worst days of violence in years earlier this month when largely peaceful demonstrations were marred by looting, fires and vandalism of state buildings.
The senate will this week debate the government’s proposed “vandals pay” law. The legislation would mean that a person protesting could be held liable to pay up to €10,000 for damage and vandalism even if they did not directly cause it themselves, if they were continuing to demonstrate nearby or as part of the same group as perpetrators. The bill also provides for greater use of drones over protests.
The prime minister, Sébastien Lecornu, said the bill, which was originally prepared in the wake of violent clashes after Paris Saint-Germain’s victory over Arsenal in the football Champions League in May, was “absolutely essential” after looting and burning during recent demonstrations across France.
The bill comes as the government struggles to contain the current crisis. Marine Le Pen, of the far-right, anti-immigration National Rally (RN), has seen her frontrunner status in next spring’s presidential election boosted as she seeks to reinforce her law-and-order credentials and back police.
Le Pen, who has lodged an appeal to France’s highest court over her conviction for embezzlement of European parliament funds, launched her presidential campaign on Sunday at a rally in Orléans, promising to “bring back order to France”.
The RN has claimed the “vandals pay” bill was originally its idea and Le Pen said she would ensure damage to property was paid for by rioters. Le Pen told a cheering crowd of more than 8,000 people at the rally: “Vandals will pay and if it takes their whole life to pay, then they will spend their whole life paying.”
She said: “We are going to restore the rule of law. Who can claim that there is rule of law when hordes come to ransack and burn our buildings?”
Éric Coquerel, from Jean-Luc Mélenchon’s radical left La France Insoumise, said on Sunday that the “vandals pay” law “would mean the end of street demonstrations” in France because people would not want to take the risk of being held responsible and made to pay up to €10,000 for vandalism they had not committed. The Communist senator Fabien Gay told the parliamentary TV channel Public Sénat: “No demonstration could take place again in our country.”
In an open letter to Le Monde, leftwing trade unions and France’s Human Rights League wrote: “This unfair law, which is a serious attack on the freedom to demonstrate, should be abandoned, or risk a major step back for the rule of law.”
At this weekend’s protests there was widespread anger at Macron for banning non-union demonstrations that his government deemed “illegitimate” and for keeping all protesters away from city centres.
Although Macron has not put in place a state of emergency, the government and local authorities have introduced limits on demonstrating, including bans on gatherings in front of schools and demonstrating in city centres, as well as curfews in some places and extended periods of police custody for the record number of people arrested.
At demonstrations this weekend, many said they had come out to defend the French right to protest in the street. Street protests in France, which are seen as a fundamental way for people to make themselves heard by a centralised state, have regularly been used to express criticism of changes to the law, from pension changes to same-sex marriage.
Serge Slama, a professor of public law at Université Grenoble Alpes, told Telerama magazine: “Although a state of emergency has been ruled out [by Emmanuel Macron] at this point, we have seen a number of decrees bringing a wide restriction on public liberties.”
He said this was “unprecedented” and would benefit the far right if they won elections next year, allowing them to put in place further crackdowns without changing the law.
Lecornu will meet representatives of protesting high-schoolers on Monday as the government comes under pressure to respond to their demands with funding and school repairs in order to avoid further school blockades.

Brazil votes in tense presidential runoff between Lula and Flávio Bolsonaro
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
19:52:43 UTC
04:52:43 KST

Lula wins fourth term as Brazil's president, beating Flávio Bolsonaro in runoff, but Bolsonaro rejects results
Brazil's President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, a vocal critic of President Trump, was reelected Sunday in a result that provides relief to critics of Mr. Trump and keeps some distance between Latin America's biggest economy and Washington.
With 100% of the vote counted, Brazil's electoral court announced that the soon to be 81-year-old Lula had a lead of nearly 4.4 million votes over opponent Flávio Bolsonaro, giving him 51.8% of the total vote. Bolsonaro quickly refused to concede defeat and asked for the election results to be annulled after an evening of chaos at some polling places that followed a last-minute decision to extend voting by two hours. That decision by a Supreme Court justice may trigger legal action by Bolsonaro.
Bolsonaro is the son of former President Jair Bolsonaro, whom Lula defeated to take the presidency in 2022.
Lula's triumph bucks a trend in Latin America, where increasing numbers of right-of-center presidential candidates allied with Mr. Trump have been winning, further extending the United States' influence in the region.
Lula's victory leaves Mexico and Brazil, Latin America's two most populous nations, with left-of-center leaders. It also means the nation with Latin America's largest economy, with a GDP of $2.6 trillion per year, will likely continue defying Mr. Trump's demands, despite the pressure of increased tariffs he imposed.
The announcement kicked off a celebration of supporters in and out of the Sao Paulo hotel where Lula watched the count with first lady Rosângela da Silva, allies, and friends.
Lula's victory, if confirmed by electoral authorities, will give him his non-consecutive fourth term as president. The next term begins on Jan. 5, 2027.
It is the first time since Brazil's military dictatorship ended in 1985 that the second-highest vote-getter in the first-round elections won the presidency. Bolsonaro had 47% of the vote in the first round to Lula's 45%, a difference of 2.2 million votes. However, more than 33 million voters out of nearly 160 million did not turn out in the first round.
A video published by Lula's campaign shows the veteran leader celebrating with first lady Rosângela da Silva and allies after his runoff victory was confirmed by Brazil's electoral court. Wearing star-shaped red glasses, he kissed his wife. Hundreds of his supporters began gathering on São Paulo's main artery to celebrate the victory.
In addressing supporters, Lula expressed his gratitude to the Brazilian people, and pledged to respect all Brazilians, regardless of gender or religion. He also attacked Bolsonaro."
"This was a defeat for denialism and lies. I must confess that every time I attended a debate, I felt embarrassed," he said.
He also doubled down on his commitment to Brazil's sovereignty.
"Either the homeland remains free, or we die for Brazil," he said. "This country will not accept being anyone's backyard."
In Rio de Janiero, cars beeped their horns and a woman dressed in red — the color of Lula supporters — shouted "You lost! Cry harder!" to four men in yellow and green sipping beers, Bolsonaro's signature colors. A huge roar echoed in the street as the result was confirmed.
Rodrigo Valentim, a 51-year-old businessman and supporter of Bolsonaro, said that another Lula government would harm the economy. He pointed to financial markets' positive reaction to the result of the first round, when Bolsonaro bested Lula.
"I don't understand how people can vote for Lula," he said. "The country is collapsing."
Sunday's victory will likely be the last of the veteran leader's political career. Lula began his political career in the 1970s as a union leader. He then helped found the Workers' Party, which he represented as a presidential candidate three times until he finally won it in 2002. He was reelected four years later and was succeeded by one of his cabinet ministers, Dilma Rousseff, in 2010. She was reelected in 2014.
Rousseff was impeached for accounting maneuvering in 2016 amid a sprawling corruption probe, which also ensnared Lula. He tried to run for president again in 2018 but was jailed in March after being convicted.
Lula was released from prison after 580 days and saw Brazil's Supreme Court annul his sentence after police found messages that showed the judge who convicted him was biased. He quickly became one of former President Jair Bolsonaro's biggest critics and narrowly beat him in 2022.
Lula admitted in 2024, two years into the job, that his administration had done little to earn the support of his voters.
Since he lost the first round, Lula reorganized his campaign, appealed to young voters, put millions of Brazilians on the streets to defend democratic values and his legacy, raised fears of another Bolsonaro administration and boosted several government initiatives.
Lula also defended Brazil's sovereignty and insisted that a Bolsonaro presidency would allow the U.S. to exert control over Brazil.
He joins Mr. Trump and Nicaragua's president, Daniel Ortega — all age 80 — as the oldest presidents in the Americas.
Judge ruled to extend voting by 2 hours
The electoral court's announcement ended an evening of confusion at polling places after Brazilian Supreme Court Justice Cristiano Zanin ruled three minutes before the scheduled end of voting to keep polls open for two more hours, following requests by both candidates. Lula's request came after issues with buses that provide transportation to polls in Sao Paulo and Salvador, two cities that tend to favor the incumbent. Bolsonaro's request was due to heavy rains in Brazil's south, where he was favored.
In Brasilia, volunteers who oversaw the vote count at a school debated whether they needed to stay after the announcement to extend voting, but most left 15 to 20 minutes after polls closed and they had given count information to electoral authorities. At a polling station in Rio de Janeiro, the voting machines had already been switched off minutes after polls were set to close and couldn't be turned back on.
The decision delayed tallying the votes by two hours. It was unclear how many polling stations stayed open after the scheduled closing time.
Bolsonaro ally Nikolas Ferreira noted that Zanin, who made the decision, is Lula's former lawyer.
Security and cost-of-living concerns
Lula, who first governed Brazil between 2003 and 2010, faced a tough reelection battle because of concerns about the cost of living and security. Bolsonaro made a tough-on-crime approach the cornerstone of his campaign and pledged to bring down food costs.
Both had been hit by corruption suspicions involving family members and allies, with Bolsonaro implicated in a sprawling scandal rocking Brazil. Lula previously spent more than a year in prison on corruption convictions that were eventually annulled.
Bolsonaro's admission that he accepted about $12 million from disgraced former banker Daniel Vorcaro to produce a film on his father's life has cast a shadow over his campaign. He is under investigation for corruption, money laundering and tax evasion in connection with the case.
As Bolsonaro voted at a school in Rio de Janeiro, his supporters shouted "Lula, thief, your place is in prison" while Lula's supporters chanted in his support.
"The time of real change has arrived," Bolsonaro said. "Brazil can't go on for another four years on its current trajectory."
In the lead-up to the vote, Lula frequently portrayed Bolsonaro, whose father is under house arrest for attempting a coup, as a threat to democracy. Bolsonaro has promised to seek an amnesty for his father if elected.
Lula, trying to lure undecided voters, has invested in costly incentives. His government endorsed a debt relief program for small businesses and promised free public transportation on weekends. A major win then came when the Senate backed a popular proposal to end the six-day workweek.
Lula thanked his voters for an outpouring of support while casting his ballot in the city of Sao Bernardo do Campo, where he began his political career as a union leader in the 1960s. "It is a lot of generosity, a lot of care, a lot of love. I will be forever grateful," Lula said.
Lula voters respect his past; Bolsonaro voters want change
Lula voters turned out Sunday driven by his history of supporting marginalized people and working to lift Brazilians out of poverty.
"Lula is a man of the people and he knows what it's like to be poor," Luzia da Souza, who runs a bar in Rio de Janeiro, said. "I find it impossible not to vote for him."
Anderson Falcão, a 43-year-old journalist in Brasilia who sported a red shirt in support of Lula, said he worried about Bolsonaro's long-term political vision, which he called "exclusionary."
"It's a project that harms the less fortunate, harms the worker, women, the forest, the Amazon," he said.
Bolsonaro voters, many of whom wore yellow and green Brazil jerseys in support of the senator, said they wanted change.
"Things are really expensive and taxes are too high," Fabianne Borges Santoro, a 45-year-old physiotherapist in Rio de Janeiro, said. She added that she once voted for Lula's party but now associates it with corruption.
Issues with public transportation affect the vote
In Bahia state, a stronghold for Lula, whose voters tend to live in areas that depend more heavily on buses, at least 75 public buses were prevented from leaving municipal garages during the presidential runoff vote, according to a state electoral judge. He ordered the arrest of the mobility secretary of the capital, Salvador, Pablo Souza, in relation to the case.
Mayor Bruno Reis, a Bolsonaro ally, blamed trade unionists for illegally sticking Workers' Party materials onto transit vehicles for the measure.
President of Brazil's Superior Electoral Court, Kassio Nunes Marques, confirmed that electoral authorities received a report on problems with buses in Bahia that is being analyzed. He did not confirm if voting would be extended, which Lula requested in Salvador and Sao Paulo, where issues with public transportation were also reported in the city with a mayor allied with Bolsonaro.
"We will not be robbed by mayors, governors or businessmen," Lula told the press. "These people need to respect democracy."
Bolsonaro did not immediately comment on the issue.
International observers earlier in the day said that voting was occurring peacefully and with transparency and did not immediately comment on the incident.
The Trump administration looms large
Lula criticized the U.S. president before Brazil's election, speaking about the risks of U.S. intervention in Brazilian elections after the Trump administration imposed high tariffs against Brazilian exports and classified drug-trafficking groups as foreign terrorist organizations. Experts say the moves may have been intended to make Lula look soft on crime.
Bolsonaro has touted his proximity to the White House and insisted that Brazil needs to strike better deals with the Trump administration, including in the rare minerals economy. Brazil estimates that its deposits hold up to 21 million tons, second only to China. He denies he's being helped by the U.S. government.
Mr. Trump said Sunday that he was watching the election but declined to endorse a candidate.
