Albanese faces stark choice if Trump escalates Iran war
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
18:00:00 UTC
03:00:00 KST

analysis
Disquiet among Labor MPs over Trump's Iran war a headache for Albanese
Twenty-three years ago, Anthony Albanese was a newish opposition frontbencher. That year was significant, not for the contribution he made as shadow minister for employment services and training (though he may argue otherwise), but for speaking out against a war he thought was wrong.
Albanese wasn't alone in his opposition; his colleague and longtime leadership rival Tanya Plibersek also said the Iraq war set a dangerous precedent for the world. Together they joined more than 40 senators and Labor MPs who signed an open letter to then US president George W Bush.
Admittedly these Labor MPs were in opposition, but it wasn't just one lone voice breaking ranks. It was 41 MPs. Imagine these same MPs and how they would respond if Donald Trump were around and said we "may do another little Epic Fury", as he did last week, as if it was a trivial game.
Blunting parts of the old brawler
Plibersek said at the time: "We wanted to let him know that there were many people in Australia, including the Labor Party, who didn't support the war in Iraq and we wanted him to know the reasons why."
The letter, which said the pre-emptive military action made the world more dangerous, rather than more secure, was not the only example of Albanese speaking out against the conflict.
In the first month of the conflict, in March 2003, Albanese delivered a speech in parliament that reflected his aggressive, left-wing pugilist style, earning him the nickname "the Marrickville Brawler".
"Our government is about to redefine us in the eyes of the world as willing backers of US militarism. The prime minister took a phone call and immediately said yes to President Bush, because we all know that that decision was made many months ago, before the pre-deployment of troops. We were not even at the meeting where the decision was made."
He went on to say: "We are, with this decision, supporting a pre-emptive strike, which changes forever the way that international politics works."
Albanese did acknowledge the need for regime change; it was the method that Labor opposed, not the sentiment.
Now Albanese is prime minister and a lot has changed. He begins this parliamentary sitting week with Trump saying the US may carry out another military operation against Iran at a time when the war is nearing its eighth month, and rising fuel prices dominate the US midterm elections.
"We may do another little Epic Fury," the president said at a rally in Florida last week as he spoke about the war. He did not elaborate. Operation Epic Fury is the name used by the US military for its war against Iran.
As John Maynard Keynes is often credited with saying: "When the facts change, I change my mind. What do you do, sir?"
Everyone grows up, grows older and learns in Canberra that the politics of passion give way to the business of governing and pragmatism.
Those around Albanese know the prime ministership is a job he has wanted for a long time, and one he almost never had after Bill Shorten defeated him in Labor's leadership ballot in 2013.
And while Albanese loves being PM, and loves reminding the media, the opposition and his own colleagues of the record 94-seat majority he secured at the last election, running a government has required him to blunt parts of the old brawler.
Now another American president is threatening to escalate a war that is smashing the economy, and this time Albanese has his phone number and doesn't have to sign a letter to get his views across.
The Labor backbench has been muted during the past eight months of this war, but will it remain muted if Trump escalates the war again?
Ongoing war Labor's next pinch point
In the past few weeks, the Labor backbench has become slightly more vocal, although this is coming off a low base. But a new escalation in this ongoing war is likely to be the next pinch point.
When Trump launched a joint offensive with Israel attacking Iran in February, Albanese, supported by Foreign Minister Penny Wong and Defence Minister Richard Marles, issued a statement supporting the action. The statement cited the need to prevent Iran from acquiring nuclear weapons and a need to protect Australians living in the region.
Back in February, the language was about a short, sharp attack. Like countless conflicts before it, this invasion has dragged on and even senior government figures admit to having no clue when it will end.
As it has dragged on, the cost hasn't just been felt in the Middle East. The closure of the Strait of Hormuz sent our government into a panic with low domestic fuel supplies and high bowser prices.
Some MPs will want Albanese to condemn Trump over Iran and get some distance from an unpopular president. Labor's strategy at the last election was a veiled signalling that it was the anti-Trump party, that Peter Dutton was a Trump-like figure.
But without stronger language and action, that case will be hard to argue twice. The world is becoming less safe, and Australians are angry about it.
Loading
Every sign we're in uncharted waters
A feeling that the world is spinning out of control is fuelled by a sense of being the recipients of chaos and rarely the decision-makers. A more forceful position on Iran and the US is something Labor MPs have increasingly been hoping for.
In the UK, the fallout from wars in Ukraine and Iran and cyber attacks have led the government to change its language and warn that the uncertainty abroad must be planned for at a household level. This messaging is about control and a sense of agency. People feel they have no control, and some governments are trying to lean into accepting that reality.
A new government "be ready" campaign in the UK is urging the public to prepare for the disruption of everyday services and to stockpile three days of key supplies.
The checklist advises stocking up on bottled water and non-perishable food, a battery or wind-up FM radio to receive updates during outages, and cash in case electronic payments or cash machines are disrupted.
Defence Secretary Wes Streeting told BBC One's Question Time that there was not a "specific thing" in mind when it came to potential emergency incidents, but said the advice might help during power cuts or if a local shop was subject to a cyber attack and was a matter of "everyday national resilience".
Put to him by an audience member that it could be "scaremongering" and push people towards panic buying like during the COVID-19 pandemic, he said: "We want people to be alert but not alarmed, and the truth is we looked around the rest of Europe, what are our friends doing across the continent? They are way ahead of us on some of this stuff."
If Europe is ahead, where are we? We may be geographically isolated but we are not immune to a more unsafe world both economically and strategically.
Our government hasn't told us to start stockpiling yet, but there is every sign that we are in uncharted waters.
Patricia Karvelas is host of ABC News Afternoon Briefing at 4pm weekdays on ABC News Channel, co-host of the weekly Party Room podcast with Fran Kelly, and host of politics and news podcast Politics Now.

Israeli bulldozing destroys olive groves in S. Syria
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
01:56:10 CST
02:56:10 KST

This photo taken on Oct. 25, 2026 shows a view of Jabata al-Khashab in the countryside of Quneitra province, Syria. (Str/Xinhua)
QUNEITRA, Syria, Oct. 25 (Xinhua) -- Israeli forces continued bulldozing agricultural land in Syria's southern province of Quneitra on Sunday, damaging olive groves that local farmers depend on for their livelihoods.
Syria's state news agency SANA reported that the operations were part of construction work on what Israel calls the "Sufa 53" line, involving a military road and a network of fortifications and observation positions along areas adjacent to the Israeli-occupied Golan Heights.
The route runs through or near several areas of Quneitra and lies within territory covered by the 1974 disengagement arrangements, which established a UN-monitored area of separation between Syrian and Israeli forces following the 1973 Arab-Israeli war, according to the SANA report.
SANA had earlier reported that Israeli forces bulldozed around 13 dunams of olive groves near Saida al-Hanout, a village close to the Israeli-occupied Golan Heights. Residents there have been collecting olives from severed trees piled in their courtyards.
"These olive trees are our livelihood. They support an entire family," Mohammad Ali al-Sawwar, a 60-year-old olive farmer, told Xinhua. "We are not employees who receive salaries every month. We earn our income only once a year."
Al-Sawwar said around 400 olive trees had been damaged or destroyed.
60-year-old farmer Awad al-Sawwar estimated that tanks had bulldozed around 20 dunams of productive olive groves, yet insisted residents would stay.
"We have no intention of leaving it, no matter what happens or how much pressure they put on us," he said.
In Jabata al-Khashab town, Hassan Ahmad, a 50-year-old farmer, said bulldozing operations had destroyed 10 dunams of his olive grove, or more than 400 olive trees, and a livestock shelter, depriving his family of an important source of income during the harvest season.
Ahmad also described continuing insecurity in Quneitra, saying residents still experienced the sounds of shelling, illuminating flares at night, and forest fires.
SANA also reported on Sunday that Israeli military vehicles entered northern Quneitra, setting up a temporary checkpoint and searching passersby before withdrawing.
The bulldozing comes amid continuing Israeli military activity in southern Syria following the collapse of the former Syrian government in December 2024. Syria has repeatedly condemned Israeli incursions on its territory as violations of its sovereignty and the 1974 disengagement agreement. ■

Israel Election 2026: What does Gadi Eisenkot’s Yashar stand for?

02:55:55 KST

Yashar, founded in September 2025, is one of many vying for citizens’ votes in the elections for the 26th Knesset, which will be held on October 27.
Led by Gadi Eisenkot, Yashar occupies the political center and currently leads the polls, making the former IDF chief of staff the top contender to lead the next government and replace Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.
Eisenkot entered politics in August 2022 through Benny Gantz’s National Unity alliance, which brought together Gantz’s Blue and White and Foreign Minister Gideon Sa’ar’s New Hope, taking third place on the list.
Although Eisenkot initially ruled out serving under Netanyahu, he and Gantz joined the emergency government after the October 7 massacre. Gantz became a member of the war cabinet, while Eisenkot served as an observer. Both left the government in June 2024, accusing Netanyahu’s leadership of failing to make the strategic decisions needed to achieve the war’s objectives.
In July 2025, Eisenkot left National Unity and resigned from the Knesset, citing the need for a transparent and democratic process for selecting the party's candidates. He said he wanted to build a broader leadership alternative capable of defeating the government, arguing that National Unity had failed to implement the internal reforms he sought.
Two months later, he founded Yashar alongside former politicians, senior security figures, and other public figures, presenting it as a broad alternative focused on Israel's security, national interests, and democratic character.
Yashar did not exist in the 25th Knesset, but the party has quickly risen through the ranks to become the leading party in the polls, which predict the party to win some 21-23 seats.
Confronting Iran, Hamas, and Hezbollah while opposing Palestinian statehood
Yashar places national security at the center of its platform, reflecting Eisenkot’s background as a former IDF chief. The party’s foreign policy focuses on confronting Iran, dismantling Hamas’s rule in Gaza, containing Hezbollah in Lebanon, and determining the future of Palestinian governance and security arrangements.
Yashar presents Iran as a continuing strategic threat. Eisenkot himself has favored a lasting, verifiable resolution of Iran’s nuclear threat.
If diplomacy fails, his proposals include US-enforced restrictions around remaining enriched-uranium sites and wider covert action against Iran’s missile capabilities.
On Gaza, the party’s stated approach combines replacing Hamas with retaining an Israeli security corridor. Eisenkot would also allow reconstruction to advance incrementally alongside partial disarmament. Earlier in October, Eisenkot pledged to destroy Hamas’s military wing and dismantle its leadership within 18 months.
In Lebanon, Eisenkot supports a security zone while seeking stronger American and French involvement in efforts to confront Hezbollah.
Regarding Palestinian statehood, Eisenkot has opposed establishing a Palestinian state, though he told The Jerusalem Post he would consider the Palestinian Authority preferable to continued Hamas rule if those are the alternatives.
On settlements, he told the Post he would return Civil Administration responsibilities to military coordination and restore military coordination of policing in the West Bank.
Eisenkot's goals: Ease cost of living, draft haredim, and reform Israel's economy
Yashar’s domestic platform focuses on reforming military-service obligations, easing the cost of living, and directing economic support toward working Israelis, young people, and those who serve the country.
Yashar’s clearest established position is its opposition to blanket haredi (ultra-Orthodox) exemptions from military service.
Eisenkot has proposed sanctions for evasion and benefits for those who serve, while allowing a limited Torah-study exemption for 3% of each annual haredi cohort. That allowance qualifies his universal-service message and has drawn criticism from opposition rivals demanding no exemptions.
Yashar also proposes expanding service obligations and giving servicemen greater priority in civilian benefits. Its September youth plan proposed raising compulsory-service soldiers’ pay by 15%, with a 50% increase for combat soldiers in their third year.
The party’s proposals place particular emphasis on those who contribute through military service and work.
Economist and Yashar candidate Shaul Meridor placed the “working middle class, young people, and service people” at the center of its economic policy.
Meridor outlined tax changes to reward those bearing the economic and security burden, together with priority in housing assistance and daycare subsidies. The reporting does not specify a full schedule of tax rates.
On living costs and competition, the party has advocated challenging exclusive import arrangements and reducing barriers in concentrated markets such as groceries and cosmetics.
The party’s September youth plan also outlined renter protections, paid internships, and practical financial guidance.
What a vote for this party is likely to produce
A vote for Yashar is most likely a vote to strengthen Eisenkot’s claim to the premiership and help build a coalition with former prime minister Naftali Bennett’s B’Yachad, Avigdor Liberman’s Yisrael Beytenu, and Yair Golan’s Democrats.
The four parties have agreed to coordinate campaigning and prepare principles for a future government, but have not settled how the bloc’s candidate for prime minister would be selected.
Eisenkot favors the leader of the largest party becoming the candidate for prime minister and has rejected a rotation arrangement. While that position still requires agreement from prospective partners, all four opposition leaders stressed in separate interviews during the election campaign that they would coalesce around an agreed-upon candidate following the election.
In a September interview with the Post, Eisenkot laid out his conditions for coalition eligibility, including accepting Israel’s Jewish and democratic identity, service obligations, and supporting the dismantling of Hamas.
His parameters exclude Arab parties Ra’am and the Joint List, and likely the haredi (ultra-Orthodox) parties Shas and United Torah Judaism as viable partners.
If the bloc falls short of 61 seats, it would need additional partners or support. Haredi parties accepting service reform represent a conditional opening in Eisenkot’s position, although his allies’ red lines could complicate it.
For voters, Yashar offers a path toward replacing Netanyahu, but the election result will determine how far that path goes.
Eisenkot must turn support for his leadership into a majority whose members agree on who should govern and what they are prepared to concede. The decisive test will be whether he can assemble those 61 seats while preserving the promises that brought voters to him.

As for what motivates people to vote, Marin Kachamakov identifies two main differences, largely along generational lines.

And let us not forget perhaps the most important thing: in a democracy, we can always vote for autocracy. In an autocracy, we cannot vote for democracy. People need to reflect on this, understand it and bear it in mind when they cast their ballots,” he stresses.

Important, fundamental issues are being overlooked, while other, more everyday matters receive far too much attention. This indirectly leads our compatriots to rely much more heavily on social media for information.”

Photo: Screen grab from Tsai's Sina Weibo

Another round of heavy showers and thunderstorms were expected to hit the south-west US on Sunday after the region endured days of rain that forced evacuations, water rescues and multi-million-dollar damage.
The National Weather Service issued a flood watch for much of the Four Corners – the meeting point of Arizona, Colorado, New Mexico and Utah – even as local officials forecast further receding of swollen rivers that surged since rains picked up on Wednesday.
About 4ft (1 meter) of water flooded the home of Shane Ferrari, the sheriff of San Juan county, New Mexico. He said the area’s situation was stable on Sunday, but he and other residents were trying to clean up and deal with damage.
The New Mexico governor, Michelle Lujan Grisham, said in a statement on Saturday that law enforcement had reported hundreds of water rescues between the cities of Farmington and Bloomfield.
“Families in Bloomfield and Farmington spent the night on rooftops watching the river flood their homes, and our national guard and state police crews have been bringing them to safety,” said Lujan Grisham. “Right now, our focus is saving lives. If you’re told to evacuate, go. Once the water recedes, the state will do everything in its power to help San Juan county families rebuild.”
“No deaths have been reported,” she added.
The San Juan River in Farmington on Friday ran 2 ft above its previous record set in 1909.
San Juan county spokesperson Devin Neeley said the county did not have official numbers on damage to homes or the number of people evacuated, but he was not aware of any loss of life.
Neeley said the flood waters were receding but left mud and silt, much of which has been contaminated with sewage because of failures at waste plants. There were still power outages affecting multiple areas, and it would probably be a few days until residents got their power back on.
“It’s a pretty active disaster zone,” he said. “We’re not on the downswing by any means.”
The flooding is just the latest from two months of on-and-off heavy rain caused by tropical moisture coming ashore from the Pacific. After months of drought, other recent deadly flooding struck the Grand Canyon and areas of New Mexico.
New Mexico has been hit with back-to-back weather events this weekend. A tornado struck Santa Fe on Saturday, damaging at least eight houses, including to roof collapses, according to a statement by the city of Santa Fe. No injuries were reported.

France’s far-right leader Marine Le Pen launches presidential bid as protests rattle the nation
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
17:45:56 UTC

France’s far-right leader Marine Le Pen launches presidential bid as protests rattle the nation
ORLEANS, France - Far-right leader Marine Le Pen, the frontrunner in the 2027 French presidential election, formally launched her campaign on Oct 25 with a promise to restore order and national confidence.
As France faces one of its most turbulent periods in years, Le Pen cast herself as the best placed to navigate what she described as mounting economic, social and security crises.
“We are not living through the end of the world but the end of a world, their world,” she said of her political opponents.
Le Pen chose to make her first campaign address in Orleans, home to Joan of Arc, the 15th-century warrior heroine revered by nationalists as a symbol of patriotism and sovereignty.
Addressing a crowd of cheering supporters, she promised “zero tolerance” policing and said restoring security was the state’s first duty.
Mass protests over living costs and inequality last weekend descended into looting and vandalism.
Opinion poll puts Le Pen in the lead
The street turmoil has given Le Pen a boost and an opinion poll published on Oct 25 put her on 32% to 33.5%, well ahead of her nearest rival, hard-left leader Jean-Luc Melenchon on 17%, as voters desert mainstream parties for the political extremes.
Surveys suggest she would easily defeat Melenchon in a run-off ballot, expected to be held in early May.
Seeking to project optimism, Le Pen built her speech around the theme of a national “Renaissance”. She said France was living through a period of upheaval but would emerge stronger if it embraced her vision of security, prosperity and renewal.
“We say: ‘Things were good before, they will be better tomorrow!’,” she said.
Le Pen promised a hard line on immigration, pledging to restore border controls, automatically expel foreign criminals and crack down on gangs and drug traffickers.
Le Pen herself could have to campaign wearing an ankle tag after she was convicted of embezzling European Parliament funds. She is appealing the court verdict.
On the economy, Le Pen pledged spending restraint, lower business taxes, reduced bureaucracy and support for industry, innovation and artificial intelligence. She rejected further increases in the retirement age.
The congress was designed to showcase unity at the top of the National Rally party, with Jordan Bardella re-elected party president and presented as Le Pen’s choice for prime minister.
Bardella’s speech was interrupted by activists from a Jewish student union, drawing attention to recent accusations he made antisemitic comments in his youth, which he denies.
Le Pen has spent more than a decade trying to transform the party she inherited from her father, Jean-Marie Le Pen, in 2011, softening its image and broadening its appeal beyond its traditional anti-immigration base.
On Europe, Le Pen stopped short of advocating a French exit from the European Union, but said she would roll back Brussels’ influence, restore national control over borders and laws, and put French interests first, including avoiding foreign wars.
“The future belongs to us,” she said, before leading the flag-waving crowd in singing the national anthem. REUTERS

Thousands protest Czech government’s public media overhaul after rushed vote

Thousands protest Czech government’s public media overhaul after rushed vote
PRAGUE - Thousands protested in Prague on Oct 25 after government lawmakers gave initial backing to public media funding changes in a rare overnight vote despite criticism the overhaul will damage media independence.
The proposal’s first reading was unexpectedly brought to the lower house floor outside the planned order of proceedings on Oct 23.
Opponents and media advocacy groups have objected to fast-tracking the legislation, which will abolish household fees that currently fund Czech public television and radio stations.
The populist government of billionaire Prime Minister Andrej Babis, backed by the far-right SPD party, has frequently clashed with public and private media.
It wants to move funding for Czech Television and Czech Radio to the state budget, which critics say will leave broadcasters vulnerable to political pressure.
Government has ‘gone too far’, protest leader says
Babis says it is a matter of funding transparency and not an attack on independence.
Smaller protests first broke out on Oct 23 at the Bill’s unexpected introduction. Speaker Tomio Okamura of the SPD limited debate and scheduled a vote for 4.36am local time on Oct 24.
The Bill is now at the committee stage before a later vote.
“Mr Babis ... Mr Okamura, nobody in this country believes that your intention was pure,” Mikulas Minar, a protest leader, said on Oct 25, criticising the overnight vote.
“(This protest) is a clear message to this government: you have really gone too far this time,” he told protesters who had filled Prague’s historic Old Town Square, amid chants of “Resignation” and “We’ve had enough”.
Organisers plan further protests.
Trust high in public media
Czech Television is the country’s most-watched broadcaster across major age groups. Public media are among the most trusted news sources in the country, according to a 2025 Reuters Institute survey.
The proposal would cut funding for Czech Television and Czech Radio by about 15%, possibly as early as 2027.
Opposition parties have compared the funding changes with reforms in Hungary under former Prime Minister Viktor Orban, who oversaw a major expansion of pro-government media.
On Oct 23, the European Broadcasting Union, along with 15 other groups including other public broadcasters as well as Reporters Without Borders, called for more debate and the removal of any measures threatening the broadcasters’ financial sustainability.
President Petr Pavel also called for more expert scrutiny.
“The Czech Republic is among the few countries in central and eastern Europe where the system of public service and private media works very well,” he said on X on Oct 24. REUTERS

Sri Lanka rescues 40 Iranian sailors, spokesman says
Italy
Unknown Publisher

18:40:44 CET
02:40:44 KST

By Uditha Jayasinghe
COLOMBO, Oct 25 (Reuters) - Sri Lanka coordinated the rescue of 40 Iranian sailors from multiple commercial ships in international waters off the coast of the country and supported their return to Iran, a spokesman for the island nation’s foreign ministry said on Sunday.
The ministry received a request from the Iranian embassy via diplomatic channels to rescue the sailors, Thushara Rodrigo, a spokesman for the ministry, said, adding they had been suffering unspecified medical emergencies.
The ministry didn’t give any further details of why they had to be rescued but local media including Indian national newspaper The Hindu reported they were on board vessels which were US-sanctioned oil tankers.
Washington has imposed a blockade on Iranian shipping as part of its war on Iran.
The sailors from 19 ships were brought ashore at Galle Harbour, about 126 km from commercial capital Colombo, and were given medical treatment before returning to Iran early on Sunday morning, the spokesman added.
Sri Lanka’s navy and coastguard typically provide support during humanitarian efforts, a government source with direct knowledge of the rescue told Reuters.
Earlier this year Sri Lanka rescued dozens of Iranian sailors on humanitarian grounds after the Iranian warship IRIS Dena was sunk by a torpedo from a U.S. submarine on March 4.
The bodies of more than 80 sailors who died in the attack were flown back to Iran in mid-March. Thirty-two survivors of the sunken ship, as well as 208 crew members from another vessel, were returned to Iran in April.
(Reporting by Uditha Jayasinghe; Editing by David Holmes)

Venezuela opposition leader Maria Corina Machado returns to Venezuela
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
18:40:42 CET
02:40:42 KST

By Vivian Sequera, Sarah Kinosian and Keren Torres
CARACAS/BARQUISIMETO, Oct 25 (Reuters) - Venezuelan opposition leader Maria Corina Machado was greeted by tens of thousands of cheering supporters as she made her way by car to Caracas on Sunday night, after she arrived home following several failed return attempts which have strained her ties with US President Donald Trump’s administration.
“This country is giving lessons to everyone,” she shouted as her convoy entered the capital, leaning out of the sunroof to shake hands and hug raucous supporters
Nobel Peace Prize laureate Machado, who was prevented from challenging deposed leader Nicolas Maduro for the presidency in 2024, has been out of the country for 10 months and spent the previous year in hiding following the disputed election.
On Sunday morning, Machado appeared at a church in western Lara state and was greeted by bystanders who sang the national anthem and shouted “liberty!” as she left in an SUV, a Reuters witness said.
She then traveled to the capital in a journey that took eight hours because of crowds. By the time she neared Caracas, festooned in rosaries handed to her by followers, the highway was all but blocked by cheering supporters.
“For the reunion of every family, for freedom of every political prisoner, for the freedom of Venezuela,” she wrote on social media.
Machado’s return was coordinated with the US, Panamanian and Colombian governments, according to a person briefed directly on her movements, who added Trump approved her return and was kept informed about it.
At the White House on Sunday, Trump said he did not know anything about Machado’s return and suggested the US would continue to back Venezuelan interim President Delcy Rodriguez.
“She’s a very nice woman,” he said, referring to Machado. “But we’re doing really well in Venezuela.”
The White House and the State Department did not respond to Reuters questions on the matter.
RETURN PREVIOUSLY DELAYED
Machado’s efforts to return have tested her relationship with the Trump administration, which she sought to cultivate as an ally even before it captured Maduro in January and took him to New York for trial.
Trump has repeatedly expressed support for Rodriguez, a former deputy to Maduro, and hailed deals on oil production and other business ventures by US companies in the South American country. Trump said in September it was too soon to consider democratic elections in Venezuela.
US officials have asked Machado at least once to delay her return, Reuters reported in June, and she has made several failed attempts to enter the country. Her team did not disclose details of how she returned.
Machado traveled in a private plane from Panama to Colombia and crossed overland on Sunday to Venezuela, four people familiar with her trip told Reuters.
One person briefed on her movements said the flight took place late last week and US security contractors guarded her during the journey. Rodriguez and the country’s authorities were warned by the US not to interfere or threaten her safety, the person said.
“The conditions allowing for the safe return of Ms. Machado to Venezuela are the direct result of the US-supported reconciliation talks which have already seen hundreds of political prisoners freed and hundreds of political opposition figures return from exile,” US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said in a statement on Sunday.
“We expect all political actors to support these talks which represent the best chance Venezuela has had in thirty years to peacefully achieve not just a free and fair election but an enduring democracy.”
A faction of the opposition and the interim government held a round of talks this month, with the aim of remaking the top court and electoral council, among other goals, ahead of eventual elections. The talks have not included Machado’s political movement.
The Venezuelan Communications Ministry, which handles all press queries for the government, did not immediately respond to requests for comment on Machado’s return.
SUPPORTERS CHEER MACHADO ON ROUTE
“Maria Corina Machado will achieve liberty and democracy in Venezuela,” said Hernan Adames, 69, as he celebrated with other supporters in Barquisimeto.
Zuleima Granadillo, 61, an employee at the Ministry of Education, waited for Machado at a point on the highway in Aragua state, closer to Caracas.
“What does Machado’s arrival mean? All paths are opening up for us, the future is opening up, we have a light, and we are going all the way to the end,” she said.
“This dictatorship is already over with the arrival of our leader.”
Machado plans to meet victims of the deadly earthquakes that struck Venezuela in June, as well as the families of political prisoners, the international community and various leaders from the democratic movement in Venezuela, David Smolansky, her top foreign affairs adviser, told Reuters.
“She will work proactively for a date for free and fair elections,” he added.
International energy firms committed last month to expanding projects in the country in a signing ceremony overseen by Rodriguez and US Energy Secretary Chris Wright.
Machado has said that only a “serious, democratic government” can provide the stability needed by investors.
She had been barred by Maduro’s government from exiting Venezuela but she secretly left in late 2025 to receive the Nobel Peace Prize, after spending more than a year living mostly in hiding.
Machado’s Vente Venezuela movement released an app on Saturday to collect voter registration information from Venezuelans abroad. The group hopes eventually to share data from the app, which was built by 15 staff over the last 18 months, with a reformed electoral council so users can be officially added to voter rolls.
Edmundo Gonzalez, a former presidential candidate for Machado’s movement who has been living in Spain, said on X he would soon join her in Venezuela.
(Reporting by Vivian Sequera and Sarah Kinosian in Caracas, Keren Torres in Barquisimeto, Mircely Guanipa in Aragua, and Matt Spetalnick and Trevor Hunnicutt in Washington; Editing by Julia Symmes Cobb, Laura Gottesdiener, Edmund Klamann and Kate Mayberry)

Bulgaria is electing a president – pro-Russian and pro-Ukrainian candidates are competing for the position
Kyiv • UNN
As of 4:00 p.m., 16.04% of Bulgarians had voted, compared with 24.12% in 2021. The main contest is between pro-Russian and pro-Ukrainian candidates.
Bulgaria is holding the first round of its presidential election on October 25, but voter turnout is significantly lower than five years ago. As of 4:00 p.m., only 16.04% of citizens had voted, compared with 24.12% in the 2021 election. This was reported by Bulgarian National Television, citing the Central Election Commission, writes UNN.
Details
Around 6.6 million citizens are eligible to vote, and polling stations will be open until 8:00 p.m. local time.
The main contenders are considered to be incumbent President Iliana Iotova, who is continuing Prime Minister Rumen Radev's political course, and former head of government Andrey Gyurov, who supports Ukraine and opposes rapprochement with Russia.
Will there be a second round?
To win in the first round, a candidate must receive more than 50% of the vote, provided that a majority of voters participate. Due to the low turnout, holding a second round is becoming practically inevitable.
If no candidate meets the necessary conditions, a runoff will take place on November 1.
The Central Election Commission of Bulgaria must announce the official results within 48 hours after voting ends.

On 24 October, at around 6 pm, a Russian drone struck civilian infrastructure in Synelnykove, Dnipropetrovsk region, some 80 kilometres from the frontline.

One patient told me he had just stepped out for a coffee, but ended up in hospital with serious injuriesKarina Ivanova, an MSF anaesthetist

UK and France Hold One of Their Largest Airborne Exercises in 20 Years
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
17:33:11 UTC
02:33:11 KST

The United Kingdom and France have conducted the large-scale Rhino Titan military exercise in Germany, involving more than 2,500 troops.
Sky News reported this, citing the UK Ministry of Defence.
The seven-week exercise took place at the Sennelager training area in Germany. Its purpose was to test British and French units’ readiness to deploy rapidly and defend NATO territory against a potential attack.
One of the key stages involved parachuting around 600 British and French troops from four Royal Air Force A400M Atlas transport aircraft.
According to the UK Ministry of Defence, this was one of the United Kingdom’s largest airborne operations in the past two decades.
During the exercise, troops practiced parachuting personnel and dropping specialized equipment from low altitudes on a scale not previously attempted in this way.
The main UK contingent was provided by the 16 Air Assault Brigade, which serves as the UK’s Global Response Force and maintains a high state of readiness.
Under the exercise scenario, troops faced a simulated adversary that made extensive use of drones and electronic warfare systems.
Three Royal Air Force Chinook transport helicopters also took part. Their crews practiced airlifting a casualty reception station.
Brig. Ed Cartwright, commander of the 16 Air Assault Brigade, said the exercise allowed troops to rehearse a realistic scenario involving the defense of NATO territory against an adversary using drones and electronic warfare.
UK Defense Secretary Wes Streeting emphasized that modern threats require new approaches to warfare.
“Alongside our French and German allies, this large-scale training exercise shows we can deliver rapid, large-scale airborne power anywhere it’s needed to defend NATO territory,” Streeting said.
British troops announced preparations for Rhino Titan in spring 2026. The Royal Artillery publication reported plans for a large-scale airborne operation in Germany as part of the Year of Air Manoeuvre program.
The exercise follows training conducted by the two countries on October 20-21, simulating a nuclear airstrike involving Rafale and Eurofighter Typhoon fighter jets.
Militarnyi previously reported on joint exercises involving British and French paratroopers during Exercise Orion 26, held in France from February 23 to March 3.

Most Poles want metal detectors in schools, poll shows
Following a spate of school violence, 52.4 percent of Poles backed installing metal detectors in schools in a new survey for Rzeczpospolita daily published on Friday.
According to the poll, 39.2 percent of respondents disagreed, while 8.3 percent held no opinion on the matter.
Support for the idea comes primarily from opposition voters (58 percent) and those who identify as right-wing (61 percent). Fifty-seven percent of women favour the changes, as do residents of large cities (60 percent) and those with primary education, also at 60 percent.
Konrad Ciesiolkiewicz, an information society expert, cited by the daily, acknowledged students' fears but added that detectors cannot replace educational activities.
Marek Plesniar of the National Association of Education Managers (OSKKO) said that Poland is not dealing with school shootings and noted that dangerous objects are not limited to knives.
"Experts, including those specialising in crisis management and terrorism, also advise against such extremes," he told the paper.
The poll was conducted by research firm IBRiS on a representative sample of 1,068 adult Poles between October 16 and 17.
The survey follows a series of unprecedented violent incidents in Polish schools in early October, including a fatal stabbing of a caretaker at a primary school in Leszczydol-Nowiny and a knife attack that injured several people at a vocational school in Ostroleka. Price overtakes quality as top criterion for Polish shoppers, report shows
Price has overtaken quality as the most important factor for Polish consumers when purchasing products, marking a significant shift in consumer sentiment compared to previous years, a new report shows.
According to a study by the Polish Promotional Emblem Foundation (Teraz Polska), 88.5 percent of Poles now name price as their top purchasing criterion, while 76.1 percent prioritise quality. This represents a reversal from 2024 and 2025, when quality consistently outranked price as the primary driver for shoppers.
The report also showed a growing gap in consumer spending power. While 82.8 percent of respondents agree they should choose Polish products, the actual country of origin remains the third most important daily purchasing factor for just 24.4 percent of shoppers, trailing far behind price and quality. Ecological features (12.7 percent) and packaging (5 percent) ranked lowest.
The willingness of consumers to pay extra for premium quality has also plummeted. This year, only 59.2 percent of respondents declared a readiness to pay more for a high-quality product, down drastically from 82.9 percent in 2024.
The study exposed a deep income gap regarding shopper priorities. Among those earning below PLN 2,000 (EUR 459) net monthly, price is a top factor for 90.2 percent compared to just 62.3 percent for quality. In the high-income bracket of over PLN 10,000 (EUR 2,296) per month, price and quality carry identical weight at 82.1 percent each.
The survey was conducted on September 16-19 on a representative sample of 1,010 adult Poles. (PAP)

The Guardian view on adult education: learning should be for all ages | Editorial
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
17:30:07 UTC
02:30:07 KST

The neglect of adults was, David Blunkett said in a recent interview, his biggest regret about education policy under New Labour. Spending on classroom-based adult learning in England has fallen steadily, from a high point of more than £5bn in 2003-04, to less than £2bn last year. We should not expect two decades of decline to be reversed quickly. But the upcoming report from Alan Milburn on young people who are not in education, employment or training is widely expected to result in a boost for colleges, as well as apprenticeship changes so that more are offered to new recruits rather than existing staff.
A timely report from MPs aims to ensure that older learners are included in these reforms. The all-party group for further education recognises the need to tackle the low level of labour market participation among young adults, which is particularly pronounced in smaller towns and cities. But the MPs take a longer view of the current system’s failings. Their report makes a persuasive case that an overall vision for adult education has been missing for a long time.
Economic and employment outcomes are important. If people are being trained in construction or IT or social care, their ability to find work afterwards matters. But adult education has a broader purpose that is harder to measure. Acquiring new skills, the MPs point out, can be a first step on a longer journey – a way to “begin to imagine different futures”. Learning can contribute to health and wellbeing, as well as income and productivity. One of the consistent themes from research was the importance of relationships – highlighting the role of education as a social glue, and of classrooms as a potential source of the people skills that employers want.
It is right for ministers to prioritise help for young adults who have yet to find their feet. But mid-career adults facing redundancy, or aiming to come off benefits, or to transition out of manual roles due to declining health, also need support. And while the promised modular alternative to maths and English GCSEs should be useful to future cohorts, the low literacy level of up to 8 million older people must also be addressed. In some areas, English language lesson providers urgently need more resources to meet demand. So does prison education, which has faced damaging cuts.
Adult education is not helped by the complicated administrative and funding arrangements that sit behind it. Overall responsibility for skills, including the £3.3bn apprenticeship budget, was transferred to the Department for Work and Pensions last year. But the Department of Education retains a role in further education, while the division of powers between Whitehall and the mayor-led regions is expected to be clarified in the budget.
This report proposes an England-wide minimum standard, which could then be developed by local partnerships. The lack of incentives for employers to invest in training is among the most serious problems at the moment. Uncompetitive pay is another, which makes recruitment of qualified instructors difficult. Careers advice is yet another gap.
Given these interlinked shortcomings, the proposed “renaissance” in adult education sounds optimistic. But at a time when the benefits of social and economic participation are being vigorously advocated, MPs are right to resist overly narrow prescriptions, and to champion the freedom to learn at any age.

Israel names former chief military prosecutor to lead October 7 massacre trials
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
17:29:42 UTC
02:29:42 KST

Former chief military prosecutor Zana Modzgvrishvili has been appointed to lead the prosecution of Hamas Nukhba terrorists accused of participating in the October 7, 2023, massacre, in what is expected to become one of the most complex and sensitive legal undertakings in the country's history.
The proceedings are expected to involve hundreds of suspects who infiltrated southern Israel during the Hamas-led attack, along with an extraordinary volume of evidence, witness testimony, victims' accounts and investigative materials.
Nukhba, Arabic for "elite," refers to Hamas' commando units, whose members played a central role in the October 7 assault on Israeli communities and military installations near the Gaza border.
The prosecution effort will be led by Modzgvrishvili, a veteran military attorney who served in the IDF for 22 years and held several senior positions in the Military Advocate General's Corps, including four years as chief military prosecutor.
After leaving the military in 2013, she was appointed to a Justice Ministry position responsible for examining complaints against interrogators from the Shin Bet domestic security agency.
More recently, she returned to military reserve duty and served as a prosecutor in the case against Aviad Frija, an Israeli soldier accused of causing the death of Yuval Castleman.
Castleman, an Israeli civilian, was shot after helping stop a terrorist attack at Jerusalem's Givat Shaul Junction in November 2023.
Modzgvrishvili will now be employed as a civilian IDF employee and oversee the extensive prosecution apparatus established to bring the October 7 suspects to trial.
The assignment carries significant implications both domestically and internationally. In Israel, the proceedings will unfold under intense scrutiny from bereaved families and a public still grappling with the trauma of the massacre. International legal observers are also expected to closely monitor the trials.
More than 400 suspects to face charges, with death penalty possible
The legal framework for the proceedings was established in May, when the Knesset approved legislation governing the prosecution of Nukhba operatives in its second and third readings by a vote of 93-0.
The law lays the groundwork for trials of a scale not seen in Israel since the prosecution of Nazi war criminal Adolf Eichmann, who was tried in Jerusalem in 1961 and executed the following year.
The legislation was initiated by Constitution, Law and Justice Committee Chairman Simcha Rothman of the Religious Zionist Party and lawmaker Yulia Malinovsky of Yisrael Beytenu.
It was developed through an unusual collaboration between Justice Minister Yariv Levin and Attorney General Gali Baharav-Miara, who have frequently been at odds over major legal and constitutional issues.
The law classifies acts committed by the attackers between Oct. 7 and Oct. 10, 2023, as crimes against the Jewish people, crimes against humanity and war crimes.
The offenses include murder, rape, kidnapping and looting.
Its provisions also extend to crimes committed after those dates against hostages held in the Gaza Strip, including those who were killed in captivity.
One of the law's most consequential provisions authorizes courts to impose the death penalty not only for murders committed during the October 7 attack, in which 1,164 civilians and soldiers were killed, but also for other serious offenses, including rape, under existing legislation such as the Prevention and Punishment of the Crime of Genocide Law and Counter-Terrorism Law.
Capital punishment is exceptionally rare in Israel. Eichmann remains the only person executed by the Israeli state following a civilian criminal conviction.
Under the new legislation, defendants sentenced to death, or indicted on offenses carrying a possible death sentence, would be ineligible for release under future prisoner exchange agreements.
Special military court to hear cases
The law provides for the establishment of a special military court in Jerusalem to hear the cases.
Indictments are expected against more than 400 suspects, although the final number will depend on the continuing investigative work of the Shin Bet and IDF in Gaza.
Rather than conducting a single mass trial, authorities plan to organize the proceedings according to the locations where the alleged crimes occurred.
Separate trials could focus on the October 7 attacks at Kibbutz Be'eri, Kibbutz Nir Oz and the Nova music festival, where hundreds of people were killed.
Each judicial panel will consist of three judges. At least one member must be either a president of a military court or a district court judge holding the rank of president or vice president who is called up for reserve duty to serve on the panel.
Convicted defendants will receive an automatic appeal, with a retired Supreme Court justice presiding over the appellate panel.
The structure is intended to accommodate an exceptionally large number of defendants while providing a formal mechanism for reviewing convictions and sentences.
Massive evidence collection, remote court appearances
Following the law's approval, prosecutors, led by the Southern District Attorney's Office, are expected to file indictments based on the extensive evidence collected since the massacre.
The evidence includes forensic findings from attack sites, transcripts of interrogations of detained Nukhba operatives and hundreds of videos documenting the atrocities.
A substantial portion of the material was gathered during combat operations by Israeli soldiers and Shin Bet personnel inside the Gaza Strip.
The collection and presentation of evidence will be among the most demanding aspects of the proceedings, given the number of suspects, victims and locations involved.
In most hearings, defendants will not be physically present in the courtroom. Instead, they will participate remotely through technological systems from detention facilities.
Families of those killed and other victims will be able to follow proceedings from a separate courtroom or through digital broadcasts.
The arrangements are designed to accommodate the scale and sensitivity of the trials while allowing families access to proceedings involving the deaths of their relatives.
First indictment could come in 2027
Despite the legislation's passage, the first indictments may still be months away.
During a special session of the Knesset's Constitution, Law and Justice Committee on Oct. 7, 2026, marking the third anniversary of the massacre, officials raised the possibility that the first indictment could be filed during the first half of 2027.
The timeline reflects the scale of the investigative and legal preparations required to prosecute hundreds of suspects for crimes committed across multiple locations over several days.
The proceedings will also require courts to address complex questions of criminal responsibility, evidence and sentencing in cases involving some of the deadliest attacks in Israel's history.

AI’s ‘opportunity divide’ could deepen global inequality, UN official warns
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
17:26:22 UTC
02:26:22 KST

AI’s ‘opportunity divide’ could deepen global inequality, UN official warns
The deputy secretary-general of the UN’s ICT agency tells Al Jazeera that unequal access to AI means poorer nations may be left behind.
Doha, Qatar – Artificial intelligence (AI) risks widening the gap between rich and poor countries, potentially deepening existing social and economic inequalities, a senior United Nations official has warned.
Developing countries face significant barriers to benefitting from the AI revolution, Tomas Lamanauskas, the deputy secretary-general of the International Telecommunication Union (ITU), a UN agency focused on information and communication technologies, told Al Jazeera.
“There is a risk … I think the AI divide is really the big concern because it’s really not just about the digital divide,” Lamanauskas said on the sidelines of the UN Conference on Trade and Development (UNCTAD) World Investment Forum in Doha, Qatar on Sunday.
“AI has the huge potential of powering health, education, public services, industries, agriculture, trade. So a great divide could really mean an opportunity divide, and really could deepen the socioeconomic divide,” he said.
“So that’s really the worrying part.”
Lamanauskas said the disparities are already evident in digital infrastructure, citing the examples of Africa and Latin America, which together account for just 3.3 percent of global data centre capacity.
“So you clearly see still a rather big infrastructure divide,” he said, adding that 2.2 billion people worldwide remain without internet access.
In a December 2025 report, the UN Development Programme (UNDP) cautioned that AI could trigger a new era of inequality between nations, reversing decades of progress in narrowing economic disparities between nations.
The UNDP warned that countries with unreliable power, limited connectivity, and a lack of technological skills risk missing out on the economic gains of AI.
Bridging the digital infrastructure gap would require an estimated $2.8 trillion in investment by 2030, UN official Lamanauskas said.
The divide between nations is also evident in the adoption of AI, he added. While approximately 29 percent of working-age people in developed countries use generative AI, that figure drops to 16 percent in developing nations.
“This actually affects your ability to be productive and to be part of job-market opportunities,” Lamanauskas said.
Loss of jobs
Lamanauskas acknowledged growing concerns about AI-driven job losses, citing estimates that the technology could displace 90 million jobs, but also create 170 million new ones.
However, he warned that even if there is a “net positive impact”, many people will personally experience disruption, as an estimated 40 percent of workplace skills could change by 2030.
He also pointed to language inequalities, revealing that only seven percent of African languages are represented in AI translation tools, limiting access for millions of potential users.
According to the 2026 International AI Safety Report released in February, about one billion people use AI for a variety of tasks, including seeking guidance on medical health and writing.
While no concrete data exists, the report estimated that about 60 percent of jobs in advanced economies and 40 percent in emerging economies could be exposed to AI-related impacts.
“The fears are real,” said Fazl Barez, a senior researcher at the University of Oxford specialising in AI safety and governance.
However, he cautioned that it was important to distinguish between AI “automating tasks and replacing entire jobs”.
“What are the types of jobs that could be lost? Those involving routine cognitive work are particularly exposed, but the scale remains uncertain,” Barez told Al Jazeera.
“AI-driven automation threatens to erode government tax bases, lower living standards, and disempower citizens.”
AI needs to benefit ‘everyone’
Despite concerns around the AI revolution, Lamanauskas said he did not believe there was a “possibility just to stop AI” or halt its rapid advancement.
“AI is here to stay, and AI is here to transform our lives,” he said, noting that 104 countries now have AI strategies, compared with just four a decade ago.
“AI is not a technology that can be controlled by one person or organisation or one company,” the UN official added.
Nevertheless, he called for greater investment in digital infrastructure, education and regulation to ensure developing countries can participate in helping shape the technology.
“The way forward is really to invest to make sure that the AI benefits everyone, to recognise and acknowledge the fears and anxieties that people feel,” he said.

The Guardian view on Oxford Street’s pedestrianisation: cities should be designed around people, not cars | Editorial
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
17:25:07 UTC
02:25:07 KST

Sadiq Khan has been trying to pedestrianise Oxford Street since he first became the mayor of London in 2016. On Monday, after numerous setbacks, his plan will finally come to fruition. The busiest stretch of the nation’s famous shopping street will be closed to traffic in a scheme designed to improve the area and make it more attractive to pedestrians. It should be an emblematic case study in making cities greener, less congested, more inviting places to live and visit.
The Greater London Authority hopes it will rejuvenate a high street fallen on hard times. Since the pandemic, the number of vacant shops on Oxford Street has more than quadrupled. It estimates that the scheme will generate £82m of value a year in the area by increasing footfall and encouraging visitors to linger. This impact remains to be seen, but research from other cities suggests that shops experience higher sales once an area is pedestrianised. Given the prime minister’s focus on rejuvenating British high streets, whose dilapidation is correlated with support for Reform UK, he should be watching with interest.
The benefits of pedestrianisation are far greater than increased shopping. Domestic transport remains the largest contributor to greenhouse-gas emissions in Britain. This sector’s emissions have fallen more slowly than others largely because too many people still rely on cars. Mr Khan’s city is an outlier: 59% of all journeys in Britain were made by car in 2024, while in London cars accounted for 34%. This is hardly surprising when the Treasury spends twice as much on London’s transport system as it does on other regions in England, and the capital’s bus fares are cheaper. In Leeds, which has no mass-transit system, nearly half of people drive to work. Car use cannot be reduced without simultaneously improving public transport.
The critics of pedestrianisation – including Westminster council – suggest it merely displaces traffic elsewhere. But the evidence on this is more nuanced. One study from the University of the West of England suggests the closure of strategic roads causes some traffic to disappear permanently, as people switch to public transport or walk. Low-traffic neighbourhoods (LTNs), the pedestrianisation schemes that were rushed through in the capital during Covid-19 and have since been introduced in Manchester and Birmingham, were fiercely criticised for causing a buildup of road traffic elsewhere. Yet one study of 46 LTNs in London suggested their impact on traffic elsewhere was minimal.
Car-free areas should be accompanied by other policies that reduce pollution on surrounding roads, such as the low-emissions zones introduced in London and Oxford. Mr Khan was criticised by the then leader of the opposition, Keir Starmer, for the expansion of Ulez in 2023, and also suffered racial abuse. He has since been vindicated by research from Imperial College suggesting Ulez has significantly improved the health of primary school children in the capital, whose lung growth had been stunted by pollution.
That Transport for London estimates the pedestrianisation of Oxford Street will have only a minimal impact on nitrogen dioxide emissions, which were already decreasing as a result of Ulez, is testimony to the policy’s success. In 2014, Oxford Street had the highest concentration of nitrogen dioxide pollution in the world. Its pedestrianisation should be an inspiration to other cities to embrace policies that work for people, not cars.

Asher Grunis steps down from leading Submarine Affair commission due to health concerns
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
17:19:45 UTC
02:19:45 KST

Retired Supreme Court justice Asher Grunis will not continue in his post heading the Submarine Affair commission, the Courts Administration announced on Sunday.
Supreme Court President Isaac Amit appointed retired Supreme Court justice Zvi Zylbertal to lead the commission on Sunday. Zylbertal was already one of the five members on it, so former Central District Court President Judge Ruth Lorch was appointed as a commission member.
Grunis, 81, informed Amit on Friday that he will not be able to continue due to medical circumstances that will affect him in the coming months, preventing him from participating in the hearings, which are scheduled throughout the months of November and December.
The commission was established in 2022 to examine how political and professional officials handled decisions concerning submarine and naval vessel purchases between 2009 and 2016. Its mandate also covers plans to privatize naval shipyards and Israel’s consent to Germany selling submarines to a third country.
In January, the commission published its report on systemic failures. This report examined flaws in decision-making and defense purchases – including the political leadership’s failure to set clear policy. It also proposed changes.
Netanyahu, Zamir due to testify in hearings
Now, the commission is due to begin hearing testimony on personal responsibility in the case on November 1. Grunis requested a replacement because postponing the hearings would harm the commission’s work, the announcement said.
The hearings will be behind closed doors and are set to focus on evidence relating to the personal warnings issued by the commission.
The panel includes economist Prof. Karnit Flug, who previously served as the governor of the Bank of Israel, Gideon Frank, a former director-general of the Israel Atomic Energy Commission, and Prof. Jacob Bortman, a professor of mechanical engineering at the Faculty of Engineering Sciences at Ben-Gurion University of the Negev (BGU).
Among those due to testify are Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, IDF chief of staff Lt.-Gen. Eyal Zamir, former president Reuven Rivlin, former defense minister Moshe “Bogi” Ya’alon, former Mossad chief Yossi Cohen, Navy commander V.-Adm. Eyal Harel, and former Navy commanders Eli Sharvit and Ram Rothberg.
The proceedings center on warnings issued in June 2024 to Netanyahu, Ya’alon, Cohen, Rothberg, and former National Security Council official Avner Simhoni.
The warnings notified them that the commission’s eventual findings could adversely affect them, allowing them to examine evidence and challenge the preliminary conclusions before personal responsibility is determined.
Being summoned as a witness does not mean an official received such a warning.
The hearings allow those facing possible adverse findings to question witnesses and present evidence in their defense; the commission has emphasized that its conclusions could change after that process.
Amit wished to “express deep appreciation” to Grunis “for his dedicated and professional work and important contribution” to the commission since its establishment.
A government decision established the commission on January 23, 2022. Appointments were made later that year, on February 20.
The commission of inquiry is separate from the criminal proceedings known as Case 3000. It examines decision-making and public responsibility surrounding the deals, while the criminal proceedings concern alleged corruption.

Cutting welfare to pay for work support is all wrong | Letters
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
17:14:58 UTC
02:14:58 KST

Alan Milburn correctly identifies that the nation’s 1 million young people not in education, employment, or training (Neet) represent a crisis of “youth detachment” deeply intertwined with mental ill health (Cut benefits to fund work support for young people, says Neet review author Alan Milburn, 18 October).
However, his proposal to cut welfare benefits to fund employment support both misdiagnoses the problem and points to a solution that will worsen it.
Framing welfare as something that is “plunging far too many young people into a life on benefits” ignores the fact that nearly half of Neet young people do not claim benefits.
The modern social security system is experienced as a regime of surveillance and scrutiny rather than a safety net. Paternalistic approaches that treat structural disadvantage as a personal failure actively drive vulnerable young people away from public institutions. Squeezing benefit safety nets further will deepen inequality, increase mistrust and worsen the problem, not alleviate it.
Rather than robbing Peter to pay Paul, we need the government to invest directly in reducing inequality. Creating the conditions for young people to thrive requires a fairer economic model that eradicates poverty and tackles gross disparities in income, wealth and power.
Health and employment support funding must come from progressive taxation on extreme wealth and corporate profits, not from threatening to withdraw support and further impoverishing already underresourced and vulnerable people.
We need government action that actively reduces inequality and builds security, giving every young person the structural foundation required to live a good life.
 
Priya Sahni-Nicholas
 
Co-executive director, Equality Trust
Thank you, Frances Ryan, for the call to arms in defence of our social security system (The right’s scrounger rhetoric dominates the benefits debate. Labour must fight back – and win, 16 October). But while it’s true that the right’s attack has been largely focused on disabled people’s benefits, the underlying hostility to social security and those reliant on it runs wider and deeper.
Fuelled by false claims that spending is out of control, the calls for cuts are relentless. And any attempt to start repairing the damage wreaked by the previous government’s cuts and restrictions – for instance, through the recent abolition of the two-child limit – are vilified with the kind of rhetoric she warns against. Cutting benefits to promote jobseeking is a false economy, as research suggests that impoverished people are ill-placed to seek and gain employment, and the costs are likely to fall elsewhere, including on the NHS.
The fightback needs to emphasise that social security, adequately financed, is both an essential weapon in combating poverty (including child poverty) and, as the name suggests, a key element in any strategy to promote the financial security of a wider population at a time of widespread insecurity.
 
Ruth Lister
 
Labour, House of Lords
Your article (Who exactly will be affected by the UK review of benefits for young people?, 20 October) again uses the term “Neets”. When I chaired the young people’s social inclusion charity Cities in Schools, we recognised that a new name was needed. Interbrand gave us Include, free of charge, with a modern logo: a lowercase “i” with a jagged line running through it, positive yet honest about the challenges our young people faced. The name mattered. It shaped how those young people saw themselves, and how others saw them.
Neet does the opposite. It defines young people by what they are not: in education, employment or training. Surely a government with all the resources at its command can find a less negative, less stigmatising term for the young people we need to help build a future.
 
Alan Coppin
 
Bourne End, Buckinghamshire

Donations for the Ukrainian Armed Forces’ daily needs have dropped sharply — Serhiy Prytula’s foundation named the reasons
Kyiv • UNN
In September, the foundation transferred more than UAH 440 million worth of equipment to the military, but only UAH 5–5.5 million was allocated for daily needs. Requests are increasing.
The amount of ongoing aid to the military from Serhii Prytula’s Charitable Foundation in September 2026 nearly halved compared with August and fell by approximately sixfold year-on-year. At the same time, the number of requests from units continues to grow. This was reported by Klym Khvostenko, deputy head of the foundation’s military department, according to UNN.
Details
According to him, in September the foundation delivered more than UAH 440 million worth of equipment, but most of the funds went toward large-scale projects. Only about UAH 5–5.5 million was allocated for the military’s daily needs.
Over the month, the foundation received 299 requests from 179 units. At the same time, the military increasingly needs vehicles, Starlink terminals, generators, charging stations, and laptops.
Why aid has declined
The foundation explains that Ukrainians are donating more actively to large-scale projects with visible results, particularly attack drones. By contrast, fundraisers for the military’s basic provisions receive significantly less attention.
Demand for vehicles, communications equipment, and energy equipment has increased by 1.5–3 times compared with last year.
At present, the foundation fulfills slightly more than 56% of requests, but within an individual request it provides, on average, only 20–25% of the equipment needed.
Khvostenko stressed that without stable funding for everyday needs, even the most modern military equipment will not be able to operate effectively at the front.

Plague risks in Russia and a dangerous delay on WHO pandemic agreement | Letters
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
17:13:58 UTC
02:13:58 KST

Your editorial on the silence from Siberia after a worker died at a plague research institute there is right that the lack of information is the real worry (The Guardian view on plague in Russia: what is most worrying is the lack of information, 18 October). But the deeper failure is not Russian. It is that, six years after Covid, we still have no agreed system for sharing pathogens, or for sharing what is made from them.
I spent three decades in Hong Kong, through bird flu, Sars and Covid, working on outbreak surveillance and sample-sharing between Hong Kong and the UK. It is also where this territorial argument began. In June 1894, two bacteriologists arrived to investigate the plague. Kitasato Shibasaburō was given lab space and immediate access to the bodies. Alexandre Yersin was refused access to the dead, and worked from a straw hut, having to appeal to the governor for his share of cadavers. Access to the material was allocated by favour, not by need. The organism carries the name of the man who was shut out: Yersinia pestis.
The pathogen access and benefit-sharing annexe to the World Health Organization pandemic agreement is the same argument in modern dress, and it has stalled on the same point. Poorer countries are asked to detect and share dangerous pathogens quickly. In return, they want a binding guarantee of what follows: 20% of real-time production of vaccines and treatments, half donated and half sold at cost. In article 13, the global supply chain and logistics network provides for a more equitable distribution of personal protective equipment. Richer countries prefer all that sharing to stay voluntary. The agreement cannot open for signature until this is settled, and it has now been deferred to 2027.
All pandemics start with a rumour. The next pandemic is likely to be something we have never seen before, and whoever first holds the samples will not be us. If we cannot agree what they get in return, we should not be surprised when they are slow to hand them over.
 
Dr Darren Mann
 
Former medical director, Cabinet Office Covid-19 PPE taskforce
Your editorial on plague in Russia is right that the system is fraying, but wrong to treat Moscow’s silence as an aberration. It is the predictable product of rules that member states built without teeth. The International Health Regulations oblige governments to notify the WHO within 24 hours, yet provide no verification, no sanctions and no independent monitoring. States mark their own homework through annual self-assessments. The amendments in force since last September add an implementation committee that is, by design, consultative only. Member states, Britain included, chose this. They then starved the WHO of assessed funding, leaving it dependent on the goodwill of the governments it is meant to hold to account.
Britain accepted the amended regulations in July 2025 and, with the United States gone, is among the WHO’s largest government funders. Ministers should raise Russia’s non-reporting formally within the WHO rather than leave Washington to make the only public request. The UK should table proposals for independent verification and a public compliance register when the pandemic agreement’s pathogen-sharing annex returns to the assembly, due by May 2027. And it should volunteer for the WHO’s Universal Health and Preparedness Review, a peer review that only 11 countries have joined and Britain has not. A government cannot demand transparency it declines to practise. The recent UN declaration on pandemics will mean little unless the governments that signed it are held to account.
 
Kent Buse
 
Co-CEO, Global 50/50

On dementia, we need to tell it how it is | Letter
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
17:12:58 UTC
02:12:58 KST

Sally Byers takes Polly Toynbee to task (Letters, 19 October) for using what she considers to be “deeply troubling language” about people with dementia, in particular the phrases “glazed stares or sleeping mouths agape” and “that terrible human vacancy” in Toynbee’s article (In Liverpool I saw the tough choices Louise Casey faces on social care – starting with who will pay?, 13 October).
I looked at the Dementia Engagement and Empowerment Project language guide for journalists highlighted in the letter. It gives a list of words and descriptions to avoid, including “dementia sufferer”, and lists alternative phrases to be used as “person/people with dementia”, “person/people living with dementia” or “person/people living well with dementia”.
I disagree. Toynbee described what she saw and wrote it, and her words had impact. In all the care homes I have been into to see elderly relatives, people with dementia weren’t “living well with dementia”; they were suffering. So why can’t we all tell it how it is rather than pretending otherwise?
 
David Lee
 
Staveley, Cumbria

Tech firms should pay the creators whose work they use | Letter
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
17:11:34 UTC
02:11:34 KST

Anthropic’s proposal (AI firm Anthropic to commit 5% of shares to fund for ‘public good’, 19 October) raises an important question: who should benefit from technological progress? Before pledging money for the public good, AI companies such as Anthropic should first pay the creators whose work they use.
Device manufacturers have a separate responsibility under the same principle: creators should share in the value their work generates. Smartphones, computers and other devices enable creative work to be copied and stored, yet UK creators receive no private-copying payments, unlike their counterparts in more than 40 other countries.
The proposed Smart Fund would require manufacturers and importers to make modest contributions on devices used to copy or store creative work. It could raise up to £300m a year, providing creators with additional income and supporting skills, cultural programmes and affordable workspaces.
For creators on persistently low and falling incomes, these payments would make a tangible difference. Visual artists’ median annual earnings are just £12,500 – 47% lower in real terms than in 2010. Authors earn a median of only £7,000 from writing, down from £11,300, according to surveys published in 2022 and 2018 respectively. Audiovisual performers report median annual earnings from performing of £17,500. Yet it is creators’ work that attracts people to technology, sustains their engagement and drives innovation. Those creators should share in the value their work helps generate, so they can continue creating and powering that cycle. The government should turn this principle into action by introducing the Smart Fund.
 
Barbara Hayes 
  
Chief executive, Authors’ Licensing and Collecting Society (ALCS) 
  
Tayyiba Nasser 
  
Chief executive, British Equity Collecting Society (BECS) 
  
Christian Zimmermann
 
Chief executive, Design and Artists Copyright Society (DACS)

Iran's Ghalibaf calls for cutting gas consumption by 10 percent as winter nears
Iran's parliament speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf on Sunday called for a campaign to cut gas consumption by at least 10 percent, with officials anticipating shortages as winter approaches.
While a major producer, Iran has long suffered shortages of natural gas, essential for powering heating systems, which have been exacerbated by war with the United States and Israel that began in February.
During the most intense phase of the fighting, which lasted nearly 40 days, the two countries struck key Iranian infrastructure including natural gas refineries, according to Tehran.
Winter in Iran often sees temperatures drop below freezing, especially in the country's north.
"To get through the approaching winter, a nationwide effort is essential ... to reduce gas consumption by at least 10 percent," said Ghalibaf in a video carried by Iranian media.
"Anyone who saves gas, regardless of the amount, will immediately receive the corresponding proceeds in their bank account, allowing everyone to see the tangible impact of those savings on their household budget."
Earlier in October, First Vice-President Mohammad Reza Aref said the government anticipated a daily "gas shortfall of 100 million to 250 million cubic metres during the cold season because of the damage caused by the war," according to the official IRNA news agency.
He added that he hoped to restore the supply of around 100 million cubic metres by the start of winter.
An April ceasefire brought an end to the initial phase of intense bombardment but the two sides have continued to vie for control over the Strait of Hormuz, through which around a fifth of the world's oil and liquefied natural gas used to travel.
Iran has claimed control over the strait since the outbreak of the war and has regularly targeted vessels that attempt crossings without its authorisation.
In response, Washington has imposed a counter-blockade on Iranian ports and in August announced what it called an "economic asphyxiation" campaign on Iran aimed at strangling its already battered economy.
