01:54:49 KST

Europe’s next crisis is already hiding behind the riots
These days, European headlines resemble reports from a war zone: from stormed city halls in Marseille and Lille, to looted boutiques along the French Riviera, burned tourist offices in Lyon, and clouds of tear gas enveloping the Élysée Palace. The ‘day of rage’ in France drew over 800,000 protesters onto the streets – an event that was dismissed by Paris and the European mainstream as merely the “spontaneous revolt of the outskirts” or a “raid by migrants.” However, a closer look at the ‘rebels’ reveals respectable, bourgeois-looking students and well-off citizens engaging in destruction and violence.
None of these people know what to expect from the future of mainstream European politics. In this shifting landscape, old institutions are losing their legitimacy, while right-wing political forces – whose ideas are increasingly seen as rational amid the chaos – are emerging on the broader European stage.
Portrait of the protesters: what happened?
French President Emmanuel Macron arrogantly advised the people to express their political will in six months during the forthcoming presidential elections; however, the streets responded to Macron’s proposal with looting and arson targeting government buildings. This reaction serves as a precise diagnosis of the French political system. The country’s civic framework can no longer hold society together and there is no confidence in a stable future.
Many believe that the current riots in France are a “spontaneous revolt of the outskirts.” However, as Fyodor Lukyanov, Research Director at the Valdai International Discussion Club writes, we are witnessing an inverted version of May 1968. Nearly 60 years ago, the nationwide wave of protests led by students and leftist intellectuals shaped the liberal framework that has dominated global and European politics ever since.
Today, it has reached the point of aggressive absurdity. The old narratives of ‘liberation’ have been successfully adopted by the bourgeois youth, whose behavior is more violent that of an uncivilized tribe, as HSE professor Alexander Filippov notes. But then, one may remember that, centuries ago, the Bastille wasn’t stormed by migrants either.
How did this happen? The liberal establishment in Paris and Brussels has become totally detached from ordinary citizens. Its agenda is completely irrelevant to society. Having imposed a rigid “confrontation with Russia” at the expense of the prosperity and development of its own people, the EU offers its citizens no viable ideas for survival.
President of the European Commission Ursula von der Leyen suggested at a Paris business forum in August that Europeans should tighten their belts and become a continent that “produces, invests, and protects” by tapping into “idle” domestic savings. Her logic implies using household savings to fund the real economy through the Capital Markets Union. Clearly, the proposal to dip into citizens’ savings while shifting the risks of factory bankruptcies onto them can only be met with outrage by the decent bourgeoisie brought up on ‘European ideals’.
The system has set a trap for itself: in order to retain its waning power, the left-liberal establishment is forced to close its eyes to the riots of anarchists and radical leftists. The authorities fear street protests far less than the rise of their right-wing opponents. The liberal mainstream would rather burn cities than allow rational thinkers with worldviews grounded in national interests to come to power.
Despite their passion for destruction, the rioters have no idea how to reconstruct the future of united Europe. Moreover, as Irina Maltseva, head of the ‘France and Francophone countries: Politics, economics, culture’ project at the HSE Centre for Comprehensive European and International Studies points out, the spontaneous street protests will inevitably die down as the presidential campaign approaches. Protests will wane, leaving us to wonder – what comes next?
The fight between left-wing and right-wing forces in Europe
The escalating competition between right and left-wing factions in Europe has transcended mere philosophical debate. It would be a mistake to view each new crisis as an isolated anomaly within the EU. Incidents like the riots in Paris, the brief unrest in Milan, the migration chaos in Ceuta, or the victory of the far-right in Germany’s Saxony-Anhalt state are all interconnected threads in the same narrative, best described as the collapse of the prevailing model.
Beneath the ideological clash between the right and left lies a harsh economic reality – the struggle over who will bear the costs of the sanctions crisis orchestrated by the European Commission. The establishment has attempted to persuade the world that a post-industrial economy – characterized by AI integration, cryptocurrency transactions, a shift toward green energy, Capital Markets Union speculations, and “normative” values – is more important than factories, raw materials, ports, and affordable energy. However, this is a path to economic self-destruction. The street protests in France and Italy vividly illustrate that Europe can no longer afford to uphold its previous social contract. Budget deficits are spiraling out of control and are becoming the EU’s economic curse.
Budapest serves as a prime example of this systemic failure. The Hungarian Parliament is currently reviewing the national budget proposal. Prime Minister Peter Magyar acknowledged that the country is grappling with a record-breaking, suffocating budget deficit of 7.5% to 8.3% of GDP. The economic strategies of past years, reliant on uninterrupted cheap energy from Russia and long-term loans from China, have collapsed under the pressure of the REPowerEU plan.
The Hungarian government’s only remaining support mechanism is the so-called ‘solidarity contribution’ tax imposed on excessive profits in opposition-led cities, but local governments can no longer afford to pay it amid the current crisis. To prevent Hungary from experiencing large-scale social upheavals similar to those in France, Magyar is urgently implementing a progressive tax system, cutting government contracts, imposing a wealth tax on billionaires, and escalating tensions with EU leadership by demanding the immediate unfreezing of €16 billion in EU grants, while threatening Orban with lifetime imprisonment if he pushes the opposition onto the streets.
The analysis of the internal dynamics of economic issues in the EU, however, should not boil down to a simplistic equation of ‘budget deficit = street protests’. For example, we may wonder why there are no protests in Poland and Romania, despite similar or even more severe budget deficits (7.3% and 7.9%, respectively), while Albania (a rather financially stable country and non-EU member) is engulfed in turmoil and the Flamingo Revolution.
The answer seems to lie in the differing nature of the deficit and the resilience of national institutions. In Poland and Romania, budget shortfalls are currently masked by rampant electoral populism and ‘social bribes’ – like Romania’s subsidies for farmers or Poland’s price caps at gas stations.
The government manages to mitigate discontent with funds extracted from big business. However, in France, the government has completely exhausted this option. The budget deficit has led to direct cuts in essential social commitments – from school funding to suburban support – quickly eroding its legitimacy.
For many Europeans, the right-wing agenda and national self-interest have become the only rational option. Right-wing pragmatists propose a clear audit and financial protection, while Brussels’ liberal framework advocates for insolvency for the sake of rather dubious dogmas.
The tactics of growing competition, or how to succeed in the ‘darkroom’
Contemporary global politics resembles a sort of ‘darkroom’ where old rules no longer apply, and new ones are still taking shape. The key revelation is that the ‘new right’ has learned to navigate this darkness by playing by Brussels’ own rules. There’s a growing understanding that to save the industrial base from stifling deficits, ideological romanticism must be abandoned.
A good example is Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni. Her approach has shown that it’s possible to dutifully follow external Euro-Atlantic rituals while negotiating exceptions from Brussels on crucial issues vital to the national economy – such as energy or migration.
Slovak Prime Minister Robert Fico follows a similar path, cleverly blending leftist social principles with hardline national populism. Bratislava is demanding official transitional periods and exemptions from the European Commission to continue receiving Russian gas, citing the need to protect the wallets of its voters.
A comparable maneuver is being executed by Czech Prime Minister Andrej Babis; while his policies can’t be called pro-Russian, pragmatism dictates a simple truth: if Czech factories want to survive amid America’s selfish diesel policy, they’ll need to negotiate with Moscow. Even Hungary has adeptly shifted the discussion to a language of tough bargaining. Budapest has formally agreed to comply with REPowerEU requirements and phase out Russian energy supplies by October 2027, but insists that the EU must provide compensation, or else Hungarian companies will face bankruptcy.
Poland’s stance is particularly notable. Rhetorically, Warsaw demands a complete sanctioning of Eurasian projects, presenting itself as Europe’s “primary eastern shield.” Yet this is merely an attempt to maintain appearances during a losing game. Internal realities compel Warsaw to negotiate with Beijing to preserve transit through the Malaszewicze hub and to impose a 60% windfall tax on its state-owned company Orlen to temporarily quell public dissatisfaction at gas stations ahead of elections.
Remarkably, this ‘trial by rage’ is unfolding not only within the EU, and it doesn't only affect Western capitalist giants. The trend is taking on a global scale.
In Albania, the ‘Flamingo Revolution’ is brewing. The social upheaval was sparked by the allocation of resort zones for a mega project spearheaded by Donald Trump’s son-in-law, Jared Kushner, and undermined the decade-long stability of Albanian Prime Minister Edi Rama’s left-liberal government. In a desperate attempt to cling to his dwindling legitimacy, Rama resorted to his usual tactics, accusing street protesters of links to the American Antifa political movement and “Moscow’s influence.”
The pendulum has swung even further in India, where a massive youth uprising led by the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) and Rahul Gandhi’s opposition alliance has paralyzed major cities from New Delhi to Mumbai. Although the immediate trigger was the Special Intensive Revision of electoral polls, the underlying issue is similar to the problem in France: the pro-American digital outsourcing model and liberal dogmas can no longer sustain the younger generation amidst a global crisis.
The issue isn’t capitalism per se, but rather the collapse of its specific, degenerate form: liberal globalization. In its place arises a rigid, sovereign capitalism rooted in national self-interest. The new right-wing pragmatists are not ‘Moscow’s friends’. They merely advocate for their own wallets in times of scarcity.
For Russia, this is an important signal: the West’s ‘unified’ sanctions policy has turned into an uncomfortable, but purely decorative facade; and behind it, we glimpse scenes of impressive but ultimately meaningless discontent. In this light, a critical question arises – will the political mainstream acknowledge its defeat and negotiate with its opponents, or will it continue to operate under the “apres nous, le deluge” (after us, the flood) principle? A key indicator will be the formation of a coalition between the ruling government and right-wing forces in Saxony-Anhalt, and their ability to govern effectively and maintain power in the long term.

Israeli-founded app Waze 'mapped sensitive areas of Malaysia': official
Israeli-founded navigation app Waze has mapped out sensitive locations not registered on public maps in Malaysia, the head of the country's National Cyber Security Agency (NACSA) has said.
The app, which is now owned by Google's parent company, has come under scrutiny from the Malaysian government in recent weeks over concerns about data being accessible to the state of Israel.
"We do not deny that the data is with them, including locations that may not have been placed on the map, sensitive areas," said NACSA head Megat Zuhairy Megat Tajuddin in a Malay-language statement carried by local media.
"If you remember, in the early stages of Waze's development, if we wanted to go back to our hometown, the directions given were not correct. However, after years of use, we Malaysians have provided the information the application needs."
He also said Malaysia had around 6.9 million Waze users in 2019, making it the app’s fifth-largest national user base at the time.
"Because of the input provided by us, Waze has a huge amount of information on locations and mapping in Malaysia," Megat said.
Earlier this week, Malaysia's government barred civil servants from using the app while on official duties, citing the need to "protect government information and users' personal data from the threat of misuse by the Israeli regime".
Several Malaysian officials have raised concerns over Waze’s terms of service, which state that the agreement is governed by Israeli law and disputes fall under the exclusive jurisdiction of courts in Israel’s Tel Aviv district.
Waze has rejected Malaysia’s claims, saying allegations that the platform collected sensitive information or allowed any entity to exploit users’ personal data were entirely false.
Earlier this month, Iraq banned the navigation app citing similar concerns.
Israel, which has no diplomatic ties with Malaysia, has previously been accused of conducting operations within Malaysia targeting Palestinians. This includes the 2018 assassination of engineer Fadi al-Batsh in Kuala Lumpur, and a failed attempt to kidnap a Palestinian computer engineer in 2022.

Thousands of sheep take over Madrid's streets for Transhumance Festival
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
16:52:23 UTC
01:52:23 KST

The flock of 1,250 sheep and 160 goats set off from Casa de Campo before crossing the Puente del Rey and making its way through the historic centre. Bells chimed and animals bleated as crowds of residents and tourists lined the streets to watch, take photographs and follow the procession.
Several shepherds wore traditional dress, while others carried young lambs or offered treats to their animals. Folk musicians added to the festive atmosphere as the flocks filled streets and squares normally dominated by traffic.
The event marks transhumance, the centuries-old practice of moving livestock between summer and winter pastures along vías pecuarias (drovers’ routes). At Plaza de la Villa, officials staged the traditional payment of 50 maravedís per thousand animals, a symbolic ceremony dating from 1418.
This year’s route was altered to avoid Puerta del Sol, where housing campaigners have set up a protest camp following the eviction and subsequent death of an 87-year-old local resident.
Beyond celebrating rural heritage, the festival highlights the environmental value of traditional grazing: by consuming vegetation, the animals help reduce flammable undergrowth and lower wildfire risks.

Algeria senate approves sending troops to Niger
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
16:50:07 UTC
01:50:07 KST

Breadcrumb
Algeria senate approves sending troops to Niger
Algeria's upper house of parliament on Sunday approved a proposal to deploy troops to neighbouring Niger to "protect energy facilities", a senator speaking on condition of anonymity told AFP.
Any overseas deployment would mark a first since Algiers sent troops to support Egypt during the 1973 Arab-Israeli war.
The legislator said 148 senators in the 174-seat body voted in favour of the move. The parliament's lower house is set to vote on the proposal later in the day, likely to approve it as well.
The rare measure from Algeria comes as Algiers and Niamey strengthen security ties after moving earlier this year to repair strained relations and following a thwarted mutiny in Niger in August.
Niger faces persistent attacks by armed groups, including in areas near the border with Algeria.
The neighbours, who share a 960-kilometre (600-mile) desert border, have agreed to deepen cooperation against jihadist violence, cross-border crime and trafficking.
"This decision marks a historic break with Algeria's doctrine of non-intervention in military conflicts beyond its borders," said Abdellah Akir, an international relations researcher.
"It's driven by the need to protect Algeria's strategic depth in the Sahel and to secure the future trans-Saharan gas pipeline," Akir told AFP.
The two countries have been working to build the Trans-Saharan Gas Pipeline (TSGP), a vast project to export natural gas to Europe from Nigeria via Niger.
'Strong signal'
Akir said the measure also sought to "send a strong signal to competing actors, including Morocco and the United Arab Emirates" - two countries with which Algiers no longer has diplomatic ties.
Geoff Porter, an analyst with the North Africa Risk Consulting group, said the move was "illustrative of a shift in Algerian policy".
Algeria "had tried to maintain its national interests and exert its regional influence through its customary means - dialogue, international law, multilateral forums," Porter told AFP.
"But in a multipolar and transactional world, those don't work anymore. Instead, Algeria moved toward more tangible means - actual physical presence."
"Algeria is still committed to its foreign policy principles," he added. "It's just demonstrating them in a new way."
Earlier this month, President Abdelmadjid Tebboune signalled the possibility of military involvement in the Sahel country.
"We will protect Niger no matter what," he said in a televised address on 3 October. "There are countries, which I will not name, that have conspired against (Niger). We stand by its side."
"Today, we have interests," Tebboune then said. "We have reached agreements (with Niger) in the oil, mining and other sectors, and some are seeking to destroy all of this overnight."
Algeria's highly unusual measure to deploy troops outside its territory requires the approval of two-thirds of its parliament, according to a constitutional amendment from 2020.
Gifted warplanes
The vote followed a visit last Wednesday by Niger's Defence Minister Salifou Modi to Algeria, where he met with Tebboune and army chief Said Chengriha.
A military cooperation protocol was signed by the two sides, according to Algerian reports, but no details were given at the time.
The move also comes months after Algiers gifted four military helicopters to Niamey.
The warplanes were deployed at the request of Nigerien authorities, the Algerian defence ministry said.
Additionally, Algeria inaugurated a 40-megawatt power plant in June intended to supply electricity to Niamey and surrounding areas.
Algeria and Niger's relations had been strained for months following Algeria's downing last year of a drone from Mali.
The incident triggered a diplomatic row, with Niger joining fellow junta-led allies Mali and Burkina Faso in recalling its ambassador from Algiers.
Algeria and Mali have since resumed diplomatic ties.
Niger has been run by General Tiani since a coup in July 2023 that toppled the elected president Mohamed Bazoum, who has been detained ever since.

“The legal claim is so absurdly thin, there’s essentially no likelihood of success,” said Derek Mueller, a law professor at the University of Notre Dame, in a blogpost.

Richard H Pildes, a law professor at New York University who focuses on elections, told the New York Times: “It is one of the weakest election lawsuits I’ve ever seen.”
“It should have no realistic chance of success in the courts,” Pildes said.

No Russian Navy Ships in Mediterranean for Two Months for First Time in Over a Decade
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
16:47:28 UTC
01:47:28 KST

For the first time in more than a decade, no Russian Navy vessels were in the Mediterranean Sea for two months this year.
Breaking Defense published the report, citing a NATO official.
According to the official, who spoke on condition of anonymity, the Russian Navy had no presence in the Mediterranean from early July to early September.
The source told the publication that the Russian Navy last had no ships in the region in 2016. Other assessments suggest this was the first such absence since 2013.
A NATO official and two analysts told Breaking Defense that several factors contributed to the absence, ranging from losing access to its key Mediterranean base in Tartus, Syria, to the need to protect shadow fleet vessels in other regions. At the same time, the Russian Navy lacks a sufficiently capable fleet of tankers and auxiliary vessels to sustain large deployed forces over an extended period.
“An example of this is that the Russian Navy has been positioning frigates in the English Channel continuously, and in order to keep those supplied, they have been relying on an Amur-class repair ship designed to deliver parts or fix things on the ship — not as a replenishment one. So they have been forced to do hull-to-hull transfers, which are really dangerous,” the NATO official said.
Basil Germond, a professor of international security at Lancaster University whom the publication approached for comment, agreed that Russia is increasingly redirecting its limited surface combatant force to protect strategically important commercial vessels. However, he cautioned against concluding that Russia would completely abandon critical Mediterranean maritime routes.

Google-backed Clear Sky honors teen suicide prevention app amid Israel's trauma crisis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
16:46:52 UTC
01:46:52 KST

In collaboration with Clear Sky
The mental health crisis that followed the October 7 attacks has exposed a major challenge for Israel: How can a healthcare system meet soaring demand for psychological treatment when the number of people seeking help far exceeds the available resources? One Israeli organization believes technology can help bridge that gap, not by replacing therapists, but by giving professionals and patients additional tools to cope with trauma and emotional distress.
Clear Sky, a nonprofit established in response to the October 7 attacks, marked a significant milestone this week with a technological innovation awards ceremony at Google's offices in Tel Aviv. The event highlighted initiatives designed to improve mental health care, including a digital tool intended to support teenagers at risk of suicide.
"We established Clear Sky right after October 7, with the idea and vision of bringing technology into the mental health field and trying to narrow the gap between supply and demand through the Israeli innovation we've trusted for so many years," said Adi Yoffe, a business futurist and co-founder of the organization.
According to Yoffe, the goal is to harness Israel's technological capabilities to address the country's growing emotional and psychological needs.
One of the main obstacles the organization's founders identified was the relatively conservative approach that has characterized medicine and mental health treatment for decades.
"Mental health is one of the most conservative fields in medicine," said Prof. Ehud Davidson, chairman of Clear Sky and former CEO of Clalit Health Services, Israel's largest health maintenance organization, who has also headed hospitals.
"We saw a field of medicine with almost no technologies capable of advancing or accelerating treatment, or allowing us to move beyond the traditional one-on-one model toward an entirely different approach."
The organization stresses that technology should not come at the expense of the human relationship between therapists and patients. Instead, it aims to strengthen that relationship by making practical, accessible tools available to more people.
"Technology and therapy can work wonderfully together if technology is introduced in the right places," said Clear Sky CEO Yael Aberman. "The human being is always part of the process. We're not removing people or the human connection. Quite the opposite. We want to empower people and give them tools."
An app designed to help teenagers at risk of suicide
The annual innovation awards ceremony brought together organizations involved in mental health care and technology, including the Defense Ministry, pharmaceutical company Teva and its Caring for the Mind initiative, Joint Israel and Google.
The event showcased technological projects aimed at strengthening mental resilience and improving access to mental health support.
Among the winners was Dr. Amit Shalev, a psychiatrist and head of child and adolescent psychiatry at Hadassah Medical Center in Jerusalem, who presented a digital tool already being used at the hospital.
"The app we submitted to the competition is a safety-planning program designed for teenagers with suicidal tendencies," Shalev explained.
"The app was developed in the United States and translated into Hebrew by our team. It helps identify triggers, cope with moments of intense impulses, regulate emotions and deal with distress. It also addresses the question: Who can I turn to when things get difficult?"
The application is intended to provide structured support during periods of emotional distress. Its recognition at the awards reflects the effort to incorporate digital tools into existing mental health services, rather than rely exclusively on traditional treatment methods.
"It's encouraging to have an organization that supports these processes, provides encouragement and accompanies them," Shalev said.
For Yoffe, the awards ceremony represented an opportunity to recognize organizations already bringing technology into mental health care. "We want to celebrate organizations in Israel that are implementing technologies in mental health and helping large numbers of people through technological innovation," she said.
Google's involvement is a central part of Clear Sky's effort to bring together the technology sector and mental health professionals. The awards initiative was supported by Google.org, the company's philanthropic arm, and the ceremony took place at Google's Tel Aviv offices.
Noa Elefant-Loffler, Google's director of public policy and government affairs in Israel, described the collaboration as an opportunity to address a pressing social challenge. "We see technology as an important tool for solving social problems, certainly in mental health, where there is so much need and so few solutions," she said.
"The collaboration between Google and Clear Sky gives us an opportunity to bring the power of technology together with entrepreneurs and people working on the ground to create positive change. From our perspective, this is an excellent model, and it's important that it continues."
The partnership reflects the organization's broader ambition to connect Israeli technological expertise with the people and institutions providing mental health care. Looking ahead, Aberman believes Israel's experience of turning urgent national challenges into technological innovation could offer a model for the mental health sector.
"When I look at Israel today, I see that we're leaders in technology, agriculture and cybersecurity because we faced existential needs," she said. "The same is true today of our need in mental health. We have to find ways to harness technology to serve that need."

HK agents risk losing Taiwan status

Any Hong Kongers who collaborate with China to carry out transnational repression in Taiwan would have their Taiwanese citizenship or residency revoked, an official familiar with the matter said yesterday.
The comment came after the Taipei District Prosecutors’ Office on Oct. 7 issued arrest warrants for two Hong Kongers, who allegedly in 2024 hired a Taiwanese private investigation agency to surveil Democratic Progressive Party (DPP) Legislator Puma Shen (沈伯洋).
Two Taiwanese private investigators, Cheng Yung-chin (鄭永津) and Hsieh Yi-chen (謝乙辰), were indicted on charges of illegally collecting and using personal data under the Personal Data Protection Act (個人資料保護法), alongside two employees, Chiang Wen-hsin (江文鑫) and Hou Kai-han (侯凱瀚), over the surveillance of Shen, the DPP’s Taipei mayoral candidate in next month’s local elections.
Photo: Reuters
Cheng was allegedly hired by Hong Kongers Kuk Kok-yin (鞠覺賢) and Lam Hing (林慶) on Sept. 5, 2024.
The suspects allegedly recorded Shen’s and his family’s movements from Oct. 1 to Nov. 8, 2024, and sent the footage via Telegram to Cheng, who forwarded it to Kuk, prosecutors said.
The suspects ran into difficulties tailing Shen because of his bodyguards, investigators found, adding that Kuk and Lam, flew to Taiwan to allegedly oversee the operation, and discuss surveillance tactics with the investigators.
Kuk and Lam entered Taiwan multiple times starting in September 2024, but are not currently in the country, prosecutors added.
The official, speaking on condition of anonymity, said the two Hong Kongers were not residing in Taiwan, but they allegedly committed a crime in the nation, which appeared to have been directed as part of a systematic campaign of transnational repression.
While arrest warrants have been issued for the two suspects, judicial cooperation between Taiwan and Hong Kong has almost frozen, making the case difficult to prosecute, they said, adding that the Hong Kong government is unlikely to extradite the suspects.
The priority is to quickly apprehend the suspects, they said, adding that securing arrests was crucial in cases of Chinese transnational repression.
The government aims to establish a system that would ensure swift arrest and severe sentences as a countermeasure, they said.
That would require rapid communication and coordination among government agencies to ensure a timely response to transnational repression, they said.
Close cooperation among police, prosecutors and judicial authorities is also required to quickly investigate crimes, track suspects and arrest them before they leave Taiwan, they added.
The Ministry of Justice is considering amendments to the Anti-Infiltration Act (反滲透法) to increase penalties, they said.
If acts of transnational repression orchestrated by the Chinese Communist Party continued to be prosecuted under ordinary laws, the penalties would be too lenient, the official said.
Citing the attack on Japanese political commentator Akio Yaita in July as an example, the official said the assailant, who allegedly punched Yaita in the face, was also a Hong Konger.
Prosecutors on Oct. 6 indicted Liao Gangfa (廖港發), 33, on charges of assault, public insult and participation in a criminal organization, seeking a five-year prison sentence.
The official also cited a case in which China allegedly dispatched a female real-estate agent to follow and collect information about President William Lai’s (賴清德) family members in the US.
While such offenses carry severe penalties in the US, Taiwan lacks a dedicated law targeting transnational repression, making legislative amendments necessary to deter such acts, the official said.
Transnational repression crimes should no longer be treated solely as contraventions of individual rights, but as offenses against national interests that warrant heavy sentences, they said.
Otherwise, suspects would face relatively minor charges, such as violations of the Personal Data Protection Act, they said.

BOOKMAN BILINGUAL 雙語書林：Chinglish or Natural English? 中式英語或道地英語？
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
16:46:48 UTC
01:46:48 KST

1. 有些國家由於接受別國的「經濟援助」而喪失了獨立自主。
ˇ A number of countries have lost their independence as a result of foreign “economic aid.”
χ A number of countries have lost their independence as a result of foreign “economical aid.”
Photo: AdobeStock 照片：AdobeStock
註：economical 是「節儉的」、「節約的」、「合算的」。economic 是「有關經濟方面的」，如 economic policies, economic history 等。
2. 他的實驗雖然失敗了，可是他的努力卻值得稱讚。
ˇ Though his experiment failed, his efforts are worthy of praise.
Photo: Adobe Stock 照片：Adobe Stock
ˇ Though his experiment failed, his efforts are worth praising.
χ Though his experiment failed, his efforts are worth praise.
註：to be worth 作「價值」解時，後面接金額；作「值得」解時，後面接動名詞。例如：
The pen is worth 8 dollars.
The book is well worth reading.
to be worthy of 作「值得」解，後面接名詞。
3. 這本書值得你看。
ˇ It is worth your while to read this book.
ˇ This book is worth reading.
χ It is worth to read this book.
註：worth 作「值得」解時，不能單獨在句中作補語形容詞用，在以先行詞 it 引導的句型中，應與 while 連用。例如：
It is worth while to see this film twice.
It is not worth while to bother about such trifles.
4. 首先，你們都必須用功讀書。
ˇ First, you all must study hard.
χ At first, you all must study hard.
註：at first 是「起初」、「當初」或「開始時」，等於 in the beginning，而不是「首先」或「第一」。例如：
At first I found French difficult, but I liked it from the start.
「首先」、「第一」是 first, in the first place 或 first of all。例如：
First, I will explain my topic. Next, I will give you some background material.。
5. 他努力學習日語。
ˇ He studies Japanese hard.
χ He studies Japanese hardly.
註：hard 和 hardly 都是副詞，但 hardly 作「幾乎不」解。例如：I could hardly understand him.（我幾乎不懂他的話）。hard 指「努力」、「用功」，兩者絕不可混淆。
Exercises
A. 起初我不喜歡英文，但現在卻喜歡。
__________ I didn’t like English but now I do.
1. Firstly 2. At first 3. First 4. In first
B. 這博物館很值得參觀。
This museum is well __________ visiting.
1. worthy 2. worth of 3. worth 4. worthy for
Answers: A. 2 B. 3

OpenAI resumes training AI, but without Internet
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
16:46:45 UTC
01:46:45 KST

OpenAI has begun cutting off Internet access for its most capable artificial intelligence (AI) models during the training process in response to prior incidents in which its systems breached other companies.
The company said in a blog post on Friday that, after a pause last month, it had resumed training its most advanced models, but intends to block Internet access until it feels it has adequate safeguards in place to mitigate the risk of unreleased models being able to take unapproved actions online during training.
“Based on the current state of alignment research, monitoring systems and the security of Internet infrastructure, we believe the responsible approach is to conduct frontier model training with no Internet access,” the company said.
Photo: Reuters
Late last month, the company said it would pause training its most advanced AI models after it discovered that one of its AI agent systems that was being trained in what was supposed to be a secured, Internet-free environment was able to gain access to the Web to reach an external, third-party chatbot.
At the time, OpenAI described the breakout as the first security incident of its kind since a combination of models gained Internet access during internal testing and inadvertently breached the system of the AI platform Hugging Face in July.
OpenAI said that after the Hugging Face incident, it reduced the connections through which its models might be able to reach the Internet during training and testing, but kept some for the purpose of metrics, logging and authentication. It also spent a vast amount of computing power on tasking agentic AI systems with identifying vulnerabilities in its training environments as part of a red-teaming effort, a phrase typically used to describe deliberate attempts to break into systems to uncover vulnerabilities before real attackers can.
“Our red-teaming agents found vulnerabilities in almost every one of these services that gave them limited forms of Internet access,” the firm said.
The company said it has since deployed software patches, imposed tighter network restrictions and disclosed the findings to vendors.
There have been a series of disclosures in the past few months from OpenAI and rivals including Anthropic PBC about incidents in which their models carried out self-directed attacks or unsanctioned actions on third-party Web sites and systems.
These cases, and a series of stark warnings from within the industry, have vaulted the safety debate into the mainstream. AI developers have warned that their systems could become too sophisticated for people to control, adding to concerns the technology could be used by malicious human actors.

Claims of meddling need facts, not hype
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
16:46:41 UTC
01:46:41 KST

Taiwan’s future must be determined by Taiwanese. No foreign power has the right to make that choice for them, nor should the Chinese Communist Party (CCP) be allowed to interfere in Taiwan’s elections through misinformation campaigns, political infiltration or other means.
The two sides of the Taiwan Strait are not subordinate to each other. Taiwanese exercise their sovereignty by electing public officials through democratic institutions.
The ballot represents the people’s right to determine the direction of their government and their country. If external forces are allowed to distort information, sow panic or fabricate public opinion, it is not merely an individual candidate who suffers, but also the rights of all citizens to choose their own representatives.
According to an operational report by the National Security Bureau, about 2.5 million pieces of potentially contentious information were recorded between January and September this year. That figure serves as a reminder that the Internet can be a battleground exploited by foreign forces.
However, the collection of information does not mean that every item has been verified as being manipulated by foreign actors. The government should clarify its findings and distinguish between confirmed, suspected and pending items of misinformation, and cases in which foreign involvement has been ruled out.
This would help the public understand the nature of the threats to democracy, while avoiding the blanket labeling of all political speech or election campaigning as cognitive warfare.
Countermeasures against foreign election interference require more than slogans; they must be supported by clear evidentiary standards. Coordinated activity by fake accounts, identity impersonation, foreign funding or chains of command and the spread of disinformation are all leads that warrant thorough investigation.
However, judgements should not be based solely on the volume of online activity, repetitive messaging or political affiliations. National security agencies should focus on identifying foreign interference and presenting evidence that can be independently scrutinized. Matters involving classified information can also be subject to oversight through closed-door sessions at the Legislative Yuan.
If intelligence is selectively cited, it can undermine public trust and the integrity of national security agencies. When senior government officials refer to directives from the CCP to interfere in Taiwan’s elections, they should explain the intelligence behind these claims and the extent to which they have been verified.
If the claims have not yet been substantiated, that should be made clear to prevent national security warnings from becoming ammunition used in election campaigns. Only through consistent standards and sufficient evidence can efforts to counter election interference build a broad public consensus rather than deepen political divisions.
In the face of foreign threats, Taiwan needs more sophisticated intelligence gathering, reliable cybersecurity protections and an electorate that can verify information and refuse to share suspicious content. Above all, Taiwan’s elections must be decided by Taiwanese.
Protecting electoral integrity means protecting democracy, and safeguarding people’s votes means safeguarding national sovereignty.
Chen Ching-yun is a former director of the Legislative Yuan’s Bureau of Legal Affairs.

The entries for “Formosa” and “Taiwan” chart an island’s journey from colonial fantasy to self-named reality. Names are rarely neutral; they are the first act of possession. Claims of vote-buying across Taiwan being probed
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
16:46:40 UTC
01:46:40 KST

Prosecutors have investigated more than 2,300 vote-buying cases ahead of next month’s nine-in-one local elections, involving a range of alleged vote-buying schemes, the Supreme Prosecutors’ Office said yesterday.
As of Oct. 19, prosecutors had received 2,302 reports of suspected vote-buying involving 2,593 people, the office said.
The cases accounted for about 35.9 percent of the 6,415 election-related offences reported to prosecutors, it said, adding that authorities also received 53 cases involving 54 people suspected of contravening the Anti-Infiltration Act (反滲透法).
Photo: Screen grab from the ministry’s Web site
Investigations have uncovered suspected vote-buying methods ranging from cash payments and banquets to gift boxes, as well as the use of charitable organizations and local groups to offer benefits in exchange for votes, it said.
The Ministry of Justice said prosecutors were following election investigation guidelines and would enforce the law objectively and impartially, regardless of political affiliation or the identities of candidates and others involved.
They would also follow due process, protect human rights and ensure fair elections, it said.
Among the cases being probed is suspected vote-buying involving Sioulin Township (秀林) Mayor Wang Mei-kuei (王玫瑰) and her husband, Hu Chih-min (胡智民), in Hualien County. Hu allegedly offered voters free meals at a birthday banquet. He also allegedly distributed cash gifts of NT$1,000 to NT$2,000 (US$31 to US$62) during exchange visits and used funds from a charitable organization to hold banquets.
Wang, Hu and a third person surnamed Hsu (徐) who heads a charitable organization have been detained and barred from receiving visitors by court order.
In Taichung, prosecutors are investigating a city council candidate surnamed Cheng (鄭) who allegedly used an intermediary to offer voters gift boxes. Investigators seized more than NT$15.26 million in cash and 69 gift boxes during a search on Sept. 21.
The intermediary, surnamed Yang (楊), was detained and barred from receiving visitors, while Cheng was released on NT$100,000 bail. Prosecutors are investigating the flow of funds and other aspects of the case.
Separately, prosecutors are investigating Changhua County Council Speaker Hsieh Dien-lin (謝典霖) over allegations that he used council funds to hold banquets as part of a vote-buying scheme. Investigators also uncovered alleged embezzlement of public funds.
Hsieh and his father, Hsieh Hsin-lung (謝新隆), were detained and barred from receiving visitors. Both appealed their detention orders, but the High Court’s Taichung branch rejected the appeals.
In Kaohsiung, prosecutors in Ciaotou District (橋頭) are investigating city council candidate Chang Chi-cheng (張騏晟) over suspected vote-buying. Chang allegedly gave voters gift boxes of pastries at a Mother’s Day banquet.
He is also suspected of using fishing association resources through his father, Chang Han-hsiung (張漢雄), a former director of the Kaohsiung City Government’s Marine Bureau, and his elder brother, Chang Chun-hua (張鈞華), to help voters obtain fishing-related qualifications and subsidies using false documents in exchange for votes.
The Supreme Prosecutors’ Office said Chang’s father and elder brother had been detained.
Investigations are ongoing, and the alleged offenses and criminal liability of the suspects remain subject to judicial proceedings.
The Supreme Prosecutors’ Office said that from the 2022 local elections to Sept. 21, it had paid a total of NT$161.44 million in rewards for reporting vote-buying.
The office previously proposed exempting the rewards from taxation and held discussions with agencies and officials. However, participants failed to reach a consensus, citing the principle of tax fairness. As a result, the rewards remain taxable.

France avoided a repeat of large-scale violence and looting that marred nationwide protests a week ago, suggesting the government’s decision to boost police numbers and contain marches paid off.
About 110,000 people on Saturday took part in a mostly peaceful demonstration confined to the edge of Paris, and another 300,000 turned out across the country, the French Ministry of the Interior said.
The CGT union put the figure at 800,000.
Photo: AFP
Some scuffles broke out, especially on the margins and at the end of processions, with hundreds of masked people dressed in black taking on security personnel, who used tear gas and water cannon to disperse crowds.
While the level of violence toward the police was again high, French Ministry of the Interior Laurent Nunez said authorities were able to prevent the looting of shops and damage to buildings seen on Oct. 17. He blamed the clashes on the ultra left, which he said was seeking to “start and finish the uprising.”
“All the warning signs were there so that we put in a place a significant presence,” he said late on Saturday. “We will of course remain fully focused in the days and weeks ahead to face up to this threat, because it is a threat.”
The government deployed about 70,000 security officials, including elite anti-terror forces, after being caught flat-footed a week ago, when nationwide demonstrations drew more than 500,000 people and descended into violence and looting.
Rioters attacked public buildings and broke into stores across the country, including in the capital, as well as fighting with police and setting fire to cars. French President Emmanuel Macron, the target of much of the anger, on Thursday acknowledged “planning failings and elements of surprise.”
For the latest protests, soldiers were brought in to guard sensitive buildings, and helicopters and armored vehicles known as Centaurs were made available on Saturday. Some cities banned protests and extended curfews.
Museums including Paris’s Louvre were closed, while many shops were boarded up. A soccer match between Paris Saint-Germain and Olympique Lyonnais in Paris was postponed.
The protest movement began last month with high schoolers blockading establishments, calling for more teachers, repairs to buildings and an end to Parcoursup, a computerized college admissions system.
Nathanael Combary, of the Renouveau Lyceen high-school union, which is due to meet with French Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu today, said students were ready to continue demonstrating in the absence of concrete measures.
“The period of dialogue has lasted long enough,” he told newspaper La Tribune Dimanche. “We now expect action.”

Starbucks’ new fee tests what consumers value
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
16:46:36 UTC
01:46:36 KST

Starbucks Taiwan’s decision to charge for drink customization, which had been free, has sparked consumer backlash, highlighting the challenge of raising prices without making customers feel they are losing value, experts said.
Since Oct. 12, customers who order drinks with less or no ice and ask to have the volume topped up with milk or other liquid have been charged an additional NT$15.
Topping off drinks without ice was previously free, and disgruntled customers posted photos on social media showing that iced drinks ordered without ice were only half full if the extra NT$15 was not paid.
Photo: CNA
The posts drew tens of thousands of reactions and comments, and consumers flooded Starbucks Taiwan’s Facebook page with complaints and calls for the company to reinstate its previous policy.
“How can they expect people to buy coffee like this?” one customer wrote on Threads. “They charge premium prices but are so stingy. They might as well go bankrupt and pull out of Taiwan, just like Carrefour.”
“It looks like someone’s drink that wasn’t finished,” said another poster of a partly empty cup.
One user suggested a way to beat the system: “You can bring your own reusable cup, put ice in it beforehand and order a hot drink! You can even get NT$10 off for the cup.”
Chinese Culture University College of Business assistant professor Cheng Kuei-i (鄭貴尹) said the key issue was whether customers viewed the fees as “paying for an additional option or losing a service they had come to expect.”
Businesses may set prices based on costs, but customers would judge them by the value they receive, he said.
Other businesses have tried changing pricing policies for supplementary services, with different outcomes, Cheng said.
For example, EVA Airways introduced fees for advance seat selection on some economy-class fares in 2019, and those have been maintained despite an initial backlash, Cheng said.
However, Japanese restaurant chain Yayoi stopped charging for rice refills at some outlets after the move drew criticism, he said.
Restaurant consultant Louis Lin (林剛羽), founder of Teamwork Consulting Service Firm, said charging NT$15 for customization would help improve profit margins without raising the base price of a drink.
However, Starbucks still faces rising labor, rent and utility costs, along with an expanding store network, which could put pressure on profitability, he said.
Starbucks Taiwan has more than 600 stores as of this year, up from 458 in September 2018, company disclosures showed.
Its operating margin fell from about 7.6 percent in 2018 to 6.3 percent in 2023, while net profit last year remained below its 2023 level.
The latest fee changes appear designed to bring in additional revenue without increasing standard drink prices, but their long-term impact would depend on whether customers consider the charges reasonable, Cheng said.
As of yesterday afternoon, Starbucks Taiwan had not responded to the Central News Agency’s request for comment on the policy change.

The CTBC Brothers took another step yesterday to overcoming a 3-0 deficit in the Taiwan Series with a dramatic 4-3 victory over the Wei Chuan Dragons at the Taipei Dome, extending the championship series to a Game 6.
The Brothers got strong performances from starting pitcher Nivaldo Rodriguez and shortstop Chiang Kun-yu, who scored the winning run in the top of the ninth to give CTBC its second straight win in the series.
With the score tied at 3-3, Brothers first baseman Huang Wei-sheng hit a sacrifice fly to drive home Chiang, who had reached base with his third hit of the game.
Photo: CNA
Brothers reliever Felix Pena then retired the Dragons in order in the bottom of the ninth to seal the victory.
After losing the first three games of the best-of-seven series, the Brothers have now won two straight to narrow the Dragons’ lead to 3-2.
No team in Chinese Professional Baseball League (CPBL) Taiwan Series history has overcome a 3-0 deficit to win the championship, nor had any team even won two games in a row after losing three straight until now.
Game 6 is scheduled for 3:05pm today at the Taipei Dome.
In yesterday’s Game 5, Rodriguez won the pitching duel against Dragons ace John Gant.
The Venezuelan right-hander pitched 6.1 innings, allowing two runs on three hits, including a solo home run by Dragons cleanup hitter Liu Ji-hong in the bottom of the fourth.
Trailing 3-1 in the bottom of the seventh, the Dragons capitalized after the Brothers pulled Rodriguez from the mound with Liu on second base.

The US Federal Reserve and its peers in the eurozone and Japan would probably keep interest rates steady this week, opting to bide their time before potential further hikes.

New laws needed to fight repression: activist
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
16:46:32 UTC
01:46:32 KST

Taiwan should adopt a strict foreign agent registration law, human rights activist Lee Ming-che (李明哲) said yesterday, while warning that low-profile cases of transnational repression pose a great threat to Taiwan.
The government should consider legislation inspired by the US Foreign Agents Registration Act, which requires certain agents of foreign principals to register with the government, but go further by establishing a presumption that people suspected of carrying out crimes in Taiwan on behalf of the Chinese government are agents of China unless they could demonstrate otherwise, Lee said in an interview with the Chinese-language Liberty Times (the Taipei Times’ sister paper).
The Anti-Infiltration Act (反滲透法) makes it difficult to convict local collaborators who assist in suspected acts of transnational repression, Lee said.
Photo: Reuters
Although Beijing uses people in Taiwan to carry out such acts, proving that they were directed by the Chinese government can be difficult, he said.
“I would use the concept of a presumption of guilt,” Lee said.
The Chinese Communist Party exercises extensive control over Chinese society, making it difficult to distinguish between independent organizations and those acting on behalf of the government, he said.
The party maintains influence over businesses and other organizations through state ownership and party organizations within them, he added.
Meanwhile, Beijing has issued arrest warrants for several Taiwanese prosecutors responsible for investigating national security cases, threatening judicial independence and seeking to undermine Taiwan’s democratic system, he said.
Statistics compiled by the Mainland Affairs Council showed that from January 2024 to Thursday, 461 Taiwanese had been reported missing, detained for questioning or otherwise suspected of having their freedom of movement restricted in China.
Opposition lawmakers have questioned the figures, saying the government was using them to fuel political divisions under the banner of resisting China and protecting Taiwan, Lee said.
The government has struggled to clarify the claims because many victims’ families are reluctant to speak publicly and cases are often subject to rumor and disinformation, he said.
In one incident, two Taiwanese police officers traveling in China as tourists were taken away by national security personnel for questioning, he said.
At the time, rumors were circulating that the officers had been caught soliciting prostitutes at a hotel, he said.
Families of people detained after traveling to China for religious activities have received threatening messages from Chinese authorities warning them not to disclose their relatives’ arrests, Lee said.
Such threats can discourage families from reporting cases to the Mainland Affairs Council because they fear repercussions, he said.
Such behind-the-scene cases pose an even greater danger to Taiwan, he said.
Beyond legislation, the government should raise public awareness of China’s activities, while non-governmental organizations should help victims of repression rebuild their ties to Taiwanese society, Lee said.
Public awareness is particularly important because victims of repression are often ostracized, he said.
Helping them reconnect with their communities could help counter Chinese repression efforts, he said.
Lee cited the case of Hong Kong Human Rights Front founder Henry Tong (湯偉雄), whose martial arts gym in Taiwan was vandalized with paint.
Alarmed by the incident, Tong’s neighbors shunned him, further isolating him and allowing China to achieve its repression goal, Lee said.
By contrast, if Taiwanese welcomed and supported victims, China’s efforts to isolate and intimidate them would be less effective, he said.

MODA working on better social media AI disclosure
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
16:46:31 UTC
01:46:31 KST

Given the proliferation of deepfake content on social media platforms, the Ministry of Digital Affairs (MODA) said it is pushing platforms such as Meta and Google to disclose artificial intelligence (AI)-generated content through a three-layer system.
Clearly labeling posts as AI-generated content would help build a trustworthy digital environment and prevent deepfake content from misleading people, the ministry said.
The digital ministry has over the year met with Meta, Google, Line, industry associations and experts to discuss ways to ensure that AI-generated content is appropriately labeled so people can easily identify it, Department of Digital Strategy Director Tsai Shou-chuan (蔡壽?) said yesterday.
Photo: Reuters
It is requiring platforms to make AI content labels prominent, he added.
For example, YouTube’s label for AI-generated content is not visible enough, because people have to click “more” in the video description to see it, so the ministry is pushing YouTube to put the label right below videos, Tsai said.
The ministry’s proposed labeling system has three layers, he said.
First, creators would have to disclose AI-generated content by checking a box when uploading it, Tsai said.
Second, platforms should automatically label content as AI generated if there are signs that the tech was used, but the post was not labeled properly during upload, he said, adding that the right system can detect AI content.
Third is establishing channels for the government and people to report unlabeled AI-generated content, he said.
Some posts might slip through the first two layers if creators remove embedded AI markers or platforms have too much content to sort through, Tsai said, adding that reporting channels could help platforms add labels as needed and take action against content that contravene its rules.
If AI-generated content is used in scams or infringes on people’s rights, the ministry would coordinate with platforms to determine appropriate measures, such as adding labels or removing the content, he said.
Google is making fast progress while Meta is still making technical adjustments, Tsai said.
As Line mostly involves private communication, labeling would initially focus on publicly available content, he said.
The ministry would also promote education on AI literacy so people can recognize AI-generated content, he added.

Notes from Central Taiwan: Taiwan’s welcome has limits
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
16:46:30 UTC
01:46:30 KST

In 1986 I entered the US Peace Corps in Kenya. As a US government volunteer we had a special US government ID for use in Kenya. Because of our position, we received extensive training in how to behave. This had special urgency for my group of volunteers: we had originally been slated for Nepal, but a US Peace Corps volunteer in another country had criticized that nation’s authoritarian president in public, and all of the Peace Corps volunteers were kicked out. As a result, the next group for that nation got sent to Nepal, and we got bumped to Kenya.
The simple fact of the matter is that visas come with speech restrictions. Even people like myself, nearly 40 years in Taiwan, face these restrictions. Though thankfully I can speak loudly in the newspaper, I cannot, for example, get up on a stage at a political event and make a speech. Others on different visas face differing restrictions. There is nothing interesting or unusual about that, almost every nation places limits on the speech of foreigners within its borders.
FREE SPEECH VIOLATION?
Photo: Peter Lo, Taipei Times
We were reminded of that last week when a student surnamed Wang (王) from the People’s Republic of China (PRC), in Taiwan on a temporary exchange program, was deported for making derogatory and even threatening remarks about Taiwan and President William Lai (賴清德). He posted his remarks on Douyin, saying: “Is this the only chance you’ll ever get?” “Take down ‘little Lai’” and “Say no to Taiwan independence secessionist actions.”
The usual bad faith actors presented the deportation of this unfortunate student as a free speech violation. What is the harm, they cried, in this satirical presentation? Doesn’t this make Taiwan’s democracy ring hollow? Well, not exactly. His visa specifically forbids him from engaging in speech of this nature. The bad faith crowd might argue that the regulation is vague. Quite true. Were it specific, people would immediately start gaming it (and bad faith actors on social media would lustily defend them). By keeping it vague, the government forces people to consider their behavior and its limits, and err on the side of caution.
Note that this determination is made by the government. The speaker doesn’t get to decide whether his speech is a violation. Another nation I hold residency in does not permit foreigners to speak in public, on politics, period. This may seem clear, but it is actually quite vague. For example, if I criticized the food of a popular restaurant chain currently engaged in overseas expansion, is that a political act? How do I know? I don’t, and so I don’t discuss that nation in public. At all.
Photo: Screengrab from Threads
The failure in Wang’s case was twofold. First, the university failed to explain to these kids that their visas preclude certain behaviors and that if they test those limits they will be deported. This is actually an example of a greater failure: in my experience, universities do a poor job orientating foreign students. Someone needed to explain to Wang that while local citizens can say what they want, he can’t. Apparently, nobody did.
Second, there is a democracy violation, but it does not involve speech. Rather, it is the lack of due process. There is no appeal, and the government is the sole determiner of when the lines are crossed. It would have looked better for Taiwan if there were an appeals process. Due process makes democracy real.
PRC THREATS TO TAIWAN
Screenshot from Huang Yihao’s Facebook page, “Comedy First”
It must be emphasized: Wang’s remarks were not “satire” in any meaningful sense of the word. They have force only because they both reference, and forward, the vast, insensate campaign of hate and violence that the PRC has aimed at Taiwan. Those comments were comprehensible only in that context.
As if in reminder of this, last week the government indicted five people in connection with a car attack on Taiwanese comedian Huang Yi-hao (黃逸豪). They had been paid by an individual in the PRC, who ironically refused part of the payment because Huang had not suffered enough. Huang had mocked PRC dictator Xi Jinping (習近平) and was scheduled for a performance at the Taipei Comedy Club, which the men were determined to stop. Two other men were already under indictment for throwing paint and feces at the same club in May.
The deported student was simply feeling his way along the outskirts of that violence and hate, exploiting it for clicks. His comments were a manifestation of the same violence that drove those men to engage in transnational repression. Had it been in the American South in the 1930s, and he had made a negative comment about the intelligence of black people or put on blackface to mock African-Americans, it would be obvious that he was part of the same miasma of violence and hate that got thousands of black Americans lynched. No one would be explaining this actions by saying they were “satire.”
Hence, any separation of the deported student from the PRC campaign against Taiwan is an artificial act intended to whitewash his actions and downplay PRC threats. It is precisely through constructing an atmosphere of hate and violence that its citizens learn to forward that the PRC enables acts like the violent attack on Huang Yi-hao.
Moreover, President Lai is an especial target of PRC ire and of racist constructions of Taiwan independence as something stimulated by “Japanese blood” in the veins of independence activists. The deported student was reflecting some of that as well.
Also last week the Mainland Affairs Council (MAC) and the PRC’s Taiwan Affairs Office (TAO) exchanged insults over Taiwan’s refusal to grant PRC actor Zhang Linghe (張凌赫) an entry application to enter the nation. MAC’s reasoning was that Zhang had attacked Taiwan’s sovereignty on social media and was a guest speaker at the Straits Forum, a united front platform.
Good news, that Taiwan is standing up for itself in this way. People might argue that such exchanges are important, but that is nonsense. In the first 8 months of this year, the government reported recently, Taiwanese made 2.492 million trips to China, up 19.63 percent year on year. Taiwanese do business there, marry locals, watch PRC shows and other entertainment and make purchases on its shopping sites. None of these copious exchanges has had the slightest effect on PRC attitudes towards Taiwan. Nor have we witnessed any great changes in Taiwanese attitudes toward the PRC. High profile exchanges like student trips and entertainer visits may make great newspaper copy, but they have no effect in the greater scheme of things.
Very obviously, the government and institutions carrying out these exchanges need to do a better job explaining where the lines are. Clearly, some kind of appeals process might be useful in some cases. But as long as people forward programs of hate and violence against Taiwan, they can and should be deported.
Notes from Central Taiwan is a column written by long-term resident Michael Turton, who provides incisive commentary informed by three decades of living in and writing about his adoptive country. The views expressed here are his own.

Huang pledged to continue writing and performing, and refused to tone down his act for a show in Taipei next month.
Photo: Screen grab from Huang’s Facebook page
Five Taiwanese men were on Wednesday charged with hitting Huang with a car on Sept. 11 in what investigators said was a staged traffic accident.
The New Taipei District Prosecutors’ Office said in their indictment that a Chinese person allegedly offered NT$450,000 to seriously injure Huang so he could not perform on Sept. 20, following the comedian’s previous comments critical of the Chinese Communist Party (CCP).

However, he is concerned about the effect it would have on his family, who worry he would lose his job and have to ask them for money, he said.
The comedian said he always thought that art and politics are closely intertwined.
Art strives to breaks free of politics, but politics keeps clinging to art, he said, adding that he never expected he would be caught in the crosshairs.
Huang said he first began listening to xiangsheng (相聲, also known as “cross talk”), a traditional Chinese comedy act, in junior-high school, before he studied history at Chinese Culture University.
He then worked as a part-time kitchen assistant at a cross talk club after struggling to find work, he said.
He did not begin performing until he was 25, after completing his military service.
He relied on his natural talent and experience gained from immersing himself in the art, Huang said.
He integrated Internet subculture, popular culture and current affairs into his routines to attract younger audiences, although his sharp and vulgar style made him less popular with more traditional audiences, he said.
The routine that criticized Xi was a take on a traditional routine called Bamagua (扒馬褂, Taking Off the Mandarin Jacket), which has been performed for more than a century, Huang said.
“I am the only cross talk performer in the world who would use the art form to deliver an extended, uninterrupted criticism of Xi. I am the only one who would do it, and it is only possible in free Taiwan,” he said.
Next month, he is set to perform an adaptation of the traditional piece Shumeiye (樹沒葉, A Tree Without Leaves) at the Red House in Taipei’s Ximending (西門町) shopping area.
Huang said he hoped audiences would continue to support cross talk, which he described as his “core mission.”

Former US president Barack Obama on Saturday delivered scathing criticisms of his successor, US President Donald Trump, at rallies in Ohio and Michigan to support Democratic candidates ahead of the Nov. 3 midterm elections.
Democrats are attempting to wrest back control of one or both chambers of the US Congress, which are currently controlled by Trump’s Republican Party.
The former president retains considerable popularity among the Democratic base, which he is keen to leverage to support his party’s candidates.
Photo: AP
In both states, the 65-year-old former president blamed the Trump administration for the rising cost of living, a top voter concern amid soaring fuel prices.
“The current president chose to make a series of bad decisions,” Obama said in Ohio, where he rallied in support of former Democratic senator Sherrod Brown.

In Ohio, Brown will attempt a comeback against incumbent Republican Senator Jon Husted, while the race for governor will be contested between Democrat Amy Acton and Republican Vivek Ramaswamy, a former presidential candidate in 2024.
Polls for Ohio give Democrats a slight lead in both those races, but the results are expected to be close.
Obama also took digs at Trump’s renovation projects across the US capital, including his botched renovation of the National Mall’s Reflecting Pool, his construction of a massive White House ballroom and the gilded decorations he has adorned the Oval Office with during his second tenure.
“He’s got the White House looking like Saddam Hussein opened a Cheesecake Factory,” Obama said, referring to popular, but indulgent US restaurant chain.
Nationally, polls also suggest that Democrats could regain control of the US House of Representatives, but face a much more competitive contest for the Senate.

Richard D. Fisher, Jr. On Taiwan: Winning the two space races
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
16:46:26 UTC
01:46:26 KST

There are two space races that the democracies must win: one to deter military campaigns near Earth, and the other to secure positional deterrence on the Moon and beyond.
The good news is that the US is engaged in both races, which will also benefit US allies and partners in Asia, including Taiwan.
On Sept. 14, US Air Force Secretary Troy Meink disclosed, “...the US now has on-orbit space control weapons capable of defending the Joint Force against hostile adversary action.”
No details about these “space control weapons” have yet been disclosed. However, a graphic apparently issued by French Space Command and posted on Sept. 16 on the “X” platform notes that the US, China and Russia possess anti-satellite (ASAT) weapons, jamming capabilities, and satellites capable of proximity operations.
China and Russia understand that the US relies heavily on space-based surveillance, intelligence and communications to ensure its military success on Earth, including in the Taiwan Strait. Now they know that the US can defend those assets and retaliate, which could help deter war in space and on Earth.
On Sept. 15, Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesman Guo Jiakun (郭嘉昆) stated, “We urge the US to stop expanding its military presence and preparing for war in outer space.”
State-run newspaper the Global Times that same day added, “China has no intention of initiating a space arms race and remains committed to the peaceful use and exploration of outer space.”
Yet during an Oct. 8 debate in the United Nations General Assembly’s First Committee, Dr. Christopher Yeaw, US Assistant Secretary of State for the Bureau of Arms Control and Nonproliferation, noted:
“China’s hypocrisy on weapons in space is also noteworthy, since China has counter-space weapons in orbit today and has been placing them in orbit for many years. The US was just the first to be transparent about our deployment as a responsible military power...”
The Chinese Communist Party’s (CCP) People’s Liberation Army (PLA) began demonstrating military space-combat capabilities with ground-based laser ASAT weapons in 2006, followed by its January 2007 destruction of a weather satellite with an ASAT rocket.
Subsequent demonstrations included satellite rendezvous and maneuvering (2010), robotic-arm grappling (2013), advanced maneuvering in geostationary Earth orbit (2016), and satellite capture and relocation (2022).
China could send modules equipped for attack or defense to its Tiangong space station and will send more weapons into Earth orbit as it advances development of a national missile defense system.
In 2021, China tested an orbital, potentially nuclear-armed Fractional Orbital Bombardment system, while since 2024 the US has suspected that Russia has placed a nuclear weapon in space to threaten US satellite mega-constellations.
Potential US space-combat operations will involve the US Space Command, assisted by the US Space Force, both established in 2019.
US President Donald Trump’s 2025 plan to build a “Golden Dome” national missile defense system will also include space-based antimissile and sensor systems that could also be used to help defend US allies and partners in Asia.
In 2022, US allies Japan, South Korea and Australia established military “space commands” that are potential partners in deterring conflict in space.
The second space race is for the Moon and beyond. China and the US are competing to establish positional deterrence in the Earth-Moon system, while the military character of China’s space expansion is illustrated by its astronauts’ membership in the “PLA Astronaut Brigade.”
In 2021, China and Russia formed the International Lunar Research Station (ILRS), a largely China-dominated lunar coalition that now has 13 member nations. The CCP’s influence was strengthened by the 2023 formation of the International Lunar Research Station Cooperation Organization (ILRSCO), which has 60 percent membership overlap with the China-dominated Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO).
This matters because the legal regime governing the Moon remains largely unsettled. ILRSCO could be expected to defend Chinese actions that appear to conflict with the 1967 Outer Space Treaty, which China signed in 1983, or the 1979 Moon Agreement, which prohibits “military bases” and “military maneuvers” on the Moon but which China has not signed.
As early as 2016, the South China Morning Post reported China was funding research into a large, 50-meter lunar radar that could monitor cislunar space between Earth and the Moon.
Other Chinese academics have proposed space stations at the cislunar Earth-Moon L-1 Lagrange point, suggesting the potential for a PLA “toll booth” controlling access to the Moon.
China is also using its space program to cultivate partners and advance its goal of “unification.”
It is training two Pakistani astronaut candidates, one of whom is expected to visit its Tiangong space station. Two European astronauts completed Chinese astronaut survival training in 2017, although the program was halted in 2023 for lack of funding.
In October 2022, China opened astronaut candidacy to citizens of Macau, and former Hong Kong police officer Lai Ka-ying (黎家盈) boarded Tiangong in May 2026.
Earlier, in February 2013, Taiwanese former vice president Lien Chan (連戰), a two-time Chinese Nationalist Party (KMT) presidential candidate, visited China and met three astronauts from its Shenzhou-9 mission. Although China did not publicly invite astronaut candidates from Taiwan, the meeting could be interpreted as an implicit invitation.
China may begin sending astronauts to the Moon in 2029 or 2030 as it tests its Long March-10 manned lunar launch vehicle and Lanyue manned lunar lander. An initial crewed ILRS lunar base, including a nuclear power plant, is planned for the mid-2030s.
But in August 2023, a symposium hosted by the China Aerospace Science and Technology Corporation (CASC) revealed that CASC had spent three years developing a 100-year plan to extend China’s presence throughout the solar system — in effect, extending CCP power.
Fortunately for the free world, Trump revived the US crewed lunar program in December 2017, following former US president Barack Obama’s 2010 cancellation of former US president George W. Bush’s “Constellation” lunar program.
Obama explained that day, “We are no longer racing against an adversary.”
In 2020, the Trump administration formulated the Artemis Accords, under which signatories commit to principles including peaceful and transparent exploration, rendering assistance to others, avoiding harmful interference, and protecting historic sites.
The accords began with eight signatories and attracted a total of 76 by the end of September 2026.
This is a significant diplomatic achievement: nearly 40 percent of the world’s countries now agree on basic principles for lunar behavior, creating a powerful political incentive for China and Russia to respect them.
But the Moon lacks a formal, enforceable legal regime; building a presence will therefore be necessary to establish lunar precedents.
This helps explain why Trump directed NASA in early 2026 to accelerate its lunar program to return Americans to the Moon before he leaves office.
On March 24, NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman announced NASA’s “Ignition” program, a US$30 billion initiative encompassing 79 launches for lunar missions, 72 lunar landings, up to 24 crewed lunar landings, lunar nuclear power plants, a 10-satellite lunar constellation, two large crewed launch vehicles, and two crewed lunar landing vehicles.
Japan is funding a large pressurized lunar rover that could enable two Japanese astronauts to reach the Moon as early as 2033. Italy’s US$5 billion investment in a multipurpose habitat could enable two Italian astronauts to arrive by 2033 or 2034.
India, another important Artemis Accords signatory, is also pursuing independent lunar capabilities. Its Chandrayaan-3 probe landed on the Moon in August 2023, and it aspires to send astronauts there in the 2040s.
Taiwan is already a US space partner. The US launched Taiwan’s first satellite in 1999, and eight of Taiwan’s current nine satellites have been launched aboard SpaceX rockets.
It is in the US’ interest for Taiwan to develop its next generation of high-resolution optical and radar surveillance satellites. Washington should also help Taiwan develop a larger, more survivable satellite communications capability to strengthen deterrence against PLA attacks and reduce vulnerability to attacks on undersea communications cables.
Taiwan helped develop a computer used on the International Space Station, was selected by NASA in 2016 to help develop an uncrewed lunar probe that was never funded, and developed electronics used in NASA’s 2021 Perseverance Mars rover.
Taiwan, therefore, is able to contribute to future lunar programs through private-sector partnerships or cooperation with the US government.
Finally, Trump’s August 28, 2026, executive order calling for a United States Space Academy aims to “prepare the next generation of astronauts, scientists, engineers, operators, entrepreneurs, civil servants and warfighters.”
The academy should eventually welcome personnel from US allies and partners, including Taiwan, helping develop the skilled cadre needed for their future space programs.
Winning both space races will require more than American military capabilities and lunar missions. It will require a coalition of democracies able to deter aggression near Earth, establish a sustained presence on the Moon, and prevent China from translating its growing space capabilities into strategic dominance.
Richard D. Fisher, Jr. is a senior fellow with the International Assessment and Strategy Center.

Skeptics counter that much of this manufacturing is mere final assembly — screwdriver work that adds little value.
