Taiwan heads to the polls next month for local elections. Beneath the campaign ads lies a deeper question: What do we call this place and who gets to decide? In the pages of the Oxford English Dictionary (OED), that question has been playing out across three centuries. The entries for “Formosa” and “Taiwan” chart an island’s journey from colonial fantasy to self-named reality. Names are rarely neutral; they are the first act of possession. Nowhere is this more evident than in the OED, where the two entries serve as a linguistic seismograph for one of the world’s most enduring geopolitical fault lines.

The National Development Council forecast that the population could fall from an estimated 23.2 million this year to just 12.1 million in 2075. The decline in the working-age population would be even more severe. Despite a rise in international crude oil prices last week, state-owned oil supplier CPC Corp, Taiwan (台灣中油) announced on Saturday that it would keep its domestic gasoline and diesel prices steady this week to tame inflationary pressure.
Formosa Petrochemical Corp’s (台塑石化) Web site yesterday showed no change in the company’s fuel prices this week.
It would be the sixth consecutive week that CPC and Formosa have maintained their domestic fuel prices at the same levels.
The companies’ decisions came despite Brent futures, the global benchmark, hitting a high since late April on Houthi attacks in Saudi Arabia, which raised concerns over oil supply disruptions.
Front-month Brent crude oil futures last week gained 6.24 percent to settle at US$116.72 per barrel on the Intercontinental Exchange in London, while West Texas Intermediate crude oil futures — the US oil benchmark — increased 4.29 percent to US$103.27 per barrel on the New York Mercantile Exchange.
Under CPC’s floating fuel price mechanism, which tracks a weighted average of 70 percent Dubai crude and 30 percent Brent crude, the average international crude oil price rose to US$114.83 per barrel last week from US$113.77 per barrel the previous week.
A weaker New Taiwan dollar, which averaged NT$32.515 against the US dollar last week, compared with NT$32.131 the previous week, added a financial burden to CPC in terms of overseas crude oil purchases.
This week, retail gasoline prices are to remain at NT$31.2, NT$32.7 and NT$34.7 per liter for 92, 95 and 98-octane unleaded gasoline respectively at CPC and Formosa stations, while prices of premium diesel would stay at NT$29.9 per liter at CPC stations and NT$29.7 per liter at Formosa pumps, the companies said.

Army adopts ‘unscripted’ training to boost readiness
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
16:46:24 UTC
01:46:24 KST

The army has adopted a new “unscripted” combat training format to replace traditional training programs and improve combat readiness in the face of China’s military threat.
During a media tour of the army’s Northern Joint Test and Training Command in Hsinchu County earlier this month, instructors said that combat units are required to undergo base training at least twice a year.
The nine-week base training program is an intensive live-fire exercise conducted at designated training bases.
Photo: CNA
It consists of three weeks of preliminary training, three weeks of tactical assessment featuring a 10-day, nine-night field exercise conducted around the clock, two weeks of combat capability assessment and one week of after-action review, the instructors said.
To ensure that the training more closely simulates actual combat, rather than appearing performative, the army earlier this year launched its Combat Training Center 2.0 initiative, the command said.
The new framework differs from previous training exercises, which typically involved a single battalion-level unit following a predetermined scenario, or “script,” from start to finish.
It replaces that traditional model with one emphasizing joint operations among different units and aims to simulate a real battlefield in which troops must respond to unexpected enemy movements, the command said.
During the media tour, two units based in northern Taiwan — the 109th Infantry Brigade and the 542nd Combined Arms Brigade — were participating in a 10-day, nine-night training exercise at the command.
The new training program also incorporates a “laser engagement system” and the Team Awareness Kit.
The tools enable troops to track friendly and enemy positions and facilitate real-time intelligence sharing, which enhances combat capabilities in joint operations involving multiple military branches, the instructors said.
The new framework also gives commanders of participating units and command instructors greater flexibility in conducting and evaluating the training, the army said.
Training objectives and evaluation standards are set by unit commanders, rather than being based on standardized, one-size-fits-all scoring charts, as in the past, it said.
Instructors assessing unit performance during base training can also ask commanders questions tailored to their units’ specific characteristics, allowing for greater flexibility in the evaluation process, the command said.
The latest changes follow the adoption of an unscripted, real-world combat format for the annual Han Kuang military exercises, which started in 2024.

EDITORIAL: China’s escalating interference ploys
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
16:46:22 UTC
01:46:22 KST

With the local elections just about a month away, many government agencies, think tanks and academics have been warning about potential interference from China. Many have also said that Beijing’s interference methods have intensified to include transnational repression, targeting specific people.
In previous elections, there had been strong evidence of Beijing using cognitive warfare to influence the results. Those included spreading artificial intelligence-driven disinformation to manipulate voter perceptions, producing fake election polls, launching cyberattacks, colluding with influencers to amplify criticisms of the ruling Democratic Progressive Party (DPP), and offering local political figures and religious leaders subsidized tours to China.
Such efforts did not stop this year. In a report to the Legislative Yuan last week, the National Security Bureau said that in the first nine months of the year, China spread more than 2.5 million controversial or false items of information online targeting Taiwan, 48 percent more than the same period last year.
China is also shifting its election interference efforts toward specific groups, such as offering discounted tickets to Taiwanese living in China to return home to vote, providing illicit funding to candidates and political groups, bribing voters by offering cheap sightseeing tours in China, operating illegal betting pools and hacking to steal election-related intelligence, bureau Director-General Tsai Ming-yen (蔡明彥) said.
Mainland Affairs Council Deputy Minister Shen Yu-chung (沈有忠) last week said that Beijing has shifted from supporting specific figures to employing “hardline measures” to intimidate, punish and deter targeted camps and people to create a chilling effect among voters.
Among the measures is transnational repression, which has clearly intensified over the past few years. For example, DPP Legislator and Taipei mayoral candidate Puma Shen (沈伯洋) and the civil defense group he cofounded, Kuma Academy, were added by China’s Taiwan Affairs Office (TAO) to its list of “die-hard Taiwanese independence separatists” in 2024; Beijing has now extended transnational repression to his family.
Earlier this month, prosecutors indicted private investigators who were hired by two Hong Kongers to allegedly monitor Shen’s family in 2024. As Shen’s approval ratings have rapidly increased in polls, the TAO on Oct. 14 announced sanctions against a second trading company linked to his father. It had sanctioned the first in June last year. The move was seen as an attempt by Beijing to influence the Taipei mayoral election, by attempting to economically coerce Shen’s family and launching a smear campaign against him.
Meanwhile, TV host Kevin Tsai (蔡康永) faced a backlash from China after he attended Shen’s campaign headquarters opening rally this month, including Chinese brands cutting ties with him, restrictions and digital erasure by Chinese social media and censorship platforms, criticism from Chinese People’s Liberation Army-affiliated media and the TAO calling him a “two-faced person.”
Such actions against Tsai, who did not even openly express support for Shen, demonstrate that Beijing is broadening the scope of its intimidation and coercion methods, and is increasingly becoming targeted on specific people. It is trying to silence and threaten Taiwanese public figures and companies for any association with parties and candidates that it dislikes, intending to create a chilling effect and induce political self-censorship within Taiwan’s democratic society.
Beijing’s transnational repression is also becoming more violent in some cases, as it works with local collaborators to surveil, recruit and physically harm people.
Prosecutors on Oct. 6 charged a Chinese man from Hong Kong over an attack on Japanese political commentator Akio Yaita in Taichung in July.
Five people were indicted last week for allegedly staging a traffic collision last month and injuring comedian Huang Yi-hao (黃逸豪), who had satirized Chinese President Xi Jinping (習近平). They were allegedly paid by a Chinese national to do so.
China’s transnational repression threats and attempts to meddle in Taiwan’s elections must be taken seriously, not only by the government and the ruling DPP, but by all candidates and voters, because its long-term infiltration and election interference are not limited to the pan-green camp. They extend to Taiwan’s democratic society as a whole, and whoever steps on China’s political “red lines” could be targeted.
The government has stepped up protection for candidates and vowed to enhance national security, and the judicial and prosecutorial system are taking swift action. DPP lawmakers have also proposed amendments to tighten anti-infiltration laws and prevent Beijing’s election interference, but they need the support of the opposition-controlled legislature to come into effect. The public’s increased awareness of and support for the laws are urgently needed to safeguard Taiwan’s sovereignty, freedom and democratic elections.

The entries for “Formosa” and “Taiwan” chart an island’s journey from colonial fantasy to self-named reality. Names are rarely neutral; they are the first act of possession. Nowhere is this more evident than in the OED, where the two entries serve as a linguistic seismograph for one of the world’s most enduring geopolitical fault lines.

OCAC members dispute TPP claims about event
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
16:46:22 UTC
01:46:22 KST

Fourteen Overseas Community Affairs Council (OCAC) members yesterday issued a statement on behalf of 131 members worldwide to dispute allegations that its annual gathering this month was a “taxpayer-funded junket” and “self-serving celebration.”
The members held a four-day gathering of members from Tuesday to Friday last week. On Thursday, participants allegedly held a birthday dinner at the Grand Hotel for former OCAC minister Hsu Chia-ching (徐佳青), who resigned on Oct. 7.
The Taiwan People’s Party (TPP) caucus criticized the event as misuse of public funds.
Photo: Tu Chien-jung, Taipei Times
An OCAC member is an unpaid, honorary appointment that carries no special privileges, the members said in the statement.
For years, council members have contributed their time, expertise, networks and personal resources to support overseas compatriots, advance Taiwanese culture and education, foster international exchanges and grassroots diplomacy, and deliver emergency assistance, it said.
While they support public oversight, they oppose using incomplete information and biased labels to dismiss council members’ contributions or to portray the global overseas community as a privileged group, it said.
The annual meeting gathers global feedback, bridging the government and overseas communities to shape overseas community affairs policies, the statement said.
Hsu attended because more than 100 council members signed a petition to invite her to a farewell dinner, and the birthday celebration incurred no additional public funds, it said.
The cost of the farewell dinner and the budget for the general assembly should be viewed separately, it said, adding that overseas Taiwanese communities’ efforts and long-term contributions should not be dismissed over political differences, while oversight should be fact-based.
At a news conference in Taipei, US-based council member Danny Chen (陳啟耕) showed a receipt showing he paid for a flower bouquet presented to Hsu out of his own pocket, as well as another for acting minister Lee Yen-hui (李?慧).
“Only by stepping out of Taiwan can one truly understand the challenges Taiwan faces,” France-based council member Sandy Hsueh (薛雅俶) said.
In places that government officials cannot visit, council members serve as Taiwan’s representatives, helping uphold the country’s dignity, she said.
While members receive government subsidies to attend meetings, their own spending far exceeds the public funds they receive, Hsueh said.
“When people repeatedly attack the OCAC, who ultimately benefits?” she said.
Asked about the statement, TPP Chairman Huang Kuo-chang (黃國昌) said the focus for an event of such importance should have been the council members working hard to represent Taiwan abroad, not Hsu, and yet it turned into a birthday party for her.
He criticized the Democratic Progressive Party government for deteriorating discipline at the council.
The Chinese Nationalist Party (KMT) caucus said the OCAC is using the council members as scapegoats for its own misuse of public resources, calling it an attempt to shirk responsibility and a collective moral failing of civil servants.
KMT caucus deputy secretary-general Hsu Yu-chen (許宇甄) said Hsu Chia-ching made 47 overseas trips over five years, spending 526 days abroad at a cost of NT$23.83 million (US$733,050).
“When will the authorities report their findings to the public on whether she misused public resources?” Hsu Yu-chen said. “Were the photos and videos showcasing her achievements at her birthday dinner also produced by OCAC staff using official records? If that is not a misuse of public resources, what is?”

British ‘heirs of slavery’ group support reparations
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
16:46:21 UTC
01:46:21 KST

Caribbean nations campaigning for slavery reparations have won support from an unexpected source — the descendants of some of Britain’s most prominent families to have benefited from the slave trade.
As prime ministers, courtiers and aristocrats, the Gladstone, Lascelles and Trevelyan families were at the heart of the governing elite down the decades.
They accumulated significant wealth from slavery through the ownership of plantations in the West Indies and South America.
Photo: Getty Images via AFP
Laura Trevelyan, a former BBC journalist, said she had been unaware of her family’s involvement until hearing about an archive listing compensation payments to plantation owners triggered by the British parliament’s abolition of slavery in 1833.
“I was clueless,” she said. “I looked at the database and saw this small island in the eastern Caribbean called Grenada that various members of the Trevelyan family had claimed compensation for the loss of what was termed their property.”
The revelation spurred Trevelyan, who made a public apology in Grenada in 2023, to cofound the Heirs of Slavery group which supports “reparative justice.”
With other members of her family, she has paid voluntary personal reparations of about ￡100,000 (US$133,744) earmarked for educational projects.
“Everybody I met, I asked them: ‘Should I apologize for what my ancestors did and do you think that I personally should pay reparations?’ and the answer came back a resounding ‘yes,’” she said.
Cofounder Charlie Gladstone, a direct descendant of reforming former British prime minister William Gladstone whose father John was one of the largest slave owners in the British West Indies, followed suit by making a public apology in Guyana in 2023.
Another group member is aristocrat David Lascelles, the Earl of Harewood, whose family has close links to the royal family.
A portrait of the actor David Harewood hangs at the family’s stately home, Harewood House in northern England, after it was discovered that his ancestors had worked on Lascelles family sugar plantations in Barbados.
The British government last month reiterated its rejection of calls for slavery reparations.
Modern British royals have expressed remorse, but like the government, have not issued an official apology.
The issue is likely to be raised during a Caribbean tour by King Charles III which begins tomorrow when he travels to the Bahamas, then Guyana, and Antigua and Barbuda where he is to address the Commonwealth Heads of Government meeting.
A Buckingham Palace spokesman said the king would acknowledge the “darkest days” of colonial rule and slavery during the trip.
Ahead of the visit, Guyanese President Irfaan Ali said his country would continue to champion the reparation issue “because slavery was the worst indignity to humankind.”
He called for a “mature” discussion on an apology and reparations, pointing to differing measures from debt relief, to finance for education and healthcare, and even climate adaptation.
The Reparations Commission of the Caribbean Community (CARICOM) has called for “monetary compensation” alongside debt cancelation and a full apology as part of its 10-point plan.
Meanwhile, the British Privy Council — the final court of appeal for UK overseas territories — is to next year hear a petition for slavery reparations filed by Jamaica.
The petition asks the court to rule on whether the capture, transport and enslavement of Africans in Jamaica was ever legal under English law, and whether the UK owes the people of Jamaica a “reparatory remedy.”
However, not all families who benefited from slavery have agreed with the Heirs group approach.
CARICOM Reparations Commission chairman Hilary Beckles has repeatedly spoken out about ex-Conservative Party lawmaker and UK landowner Richard Drax, 68, whose ancestors established Drax Hall Estate in Barbados in the mid-17th century.
Beckles has estimated up to 30,000 slaves died at Drax plantations in Barbados and Jamaica over 200 years.
Drax has remained staunchly opposed to reparations. He has said that while the role his ancestors played in the slave trade was “deeply, deeply regrettable... No-one can be held responsible today for what happened many hundreds of years ago.”
The Draxes are unique in that “they’re the only family that still owns a plantation that was set up in the beginning,” said Paul Lashmar, author of Drax of Drax Hall: How One British Family Got Rich (and Stayed Rich) from Sugar and Slavery.
However, he said it was increasingly difficult to see how Drax’s position could prevail.
“If you are very wealthy, and a lot of your wealth comes from those years, then it’s not something you can wash your hands of,” he said.

Homes with a single elderly resident hit record high
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
16:46:19 UTC
01:46:19 KST

The number of households with a single elderly resident has reached a record high in the second quarter of this year, the latest statistics from the Ministry of the Interior’s Real Estate Information Platform showed .
The number of households with only elderly people increased to 927,500 units in the second quarter, which is an increase of 4,139 units (about 0.4 percent) from the previous quarter, the data showed.
Among them, households with a single elderly resident accounted for about 716,500 units, an increase of 2,900 units from the previous quarter, they showed.
Photo: Taipei Times
Colliers International owner-occupier services director Huang Shu-wei (黃舒衛) yesterday said that households with a single elderly resident reflected an inevitable demographic shift in Taiwanese society, driven by the trends of declining birthrates, an aging population and nuclear families.
With the surge in artificial intelligence applications, mass-produced caregiving robots allowing people to reduce reliance on human care are becoming widely adopted and accepted, he said.
The trend not only transforms caregiving models, but also drives an urgent demand for urban planning, including implementing universal design, adding barrier-free elevators, and accelerating and deepening the integration between community care and medical resources, Huang said.
Housing Trend Institute chief executive officer Ho Shih-chang (何世昌) said the number of single elderly person households not only shows Taiwan is turning into a super-aged society, but also signals that an increasing number of elderly people are left without support.
Subsequent issues such as elderly care, community mobility and healthcare access are becoming ever more pressing, he said, adding that the social phenomenon is also transforming the real-estate market.
Hospitals were once viewed as undesired facilities, but now “hospital-adjacent homes” have turned into highly sought-after assets, selling quickly on the market, he said.
Meanwhile, the data showed that the total number of households registered nationwide experienced a rare downturn, dropping significantly by 77,800 units from the previous quarter, a decline of about 1 percent.
The total number of registered residential properties nationwide was about 8.025 million units in the second quarter, marking a clear decrease from about 8.103 million units in the first quarter.
In the second quarter, the number of households with a single resident decreased the most among national registered households — dropping to about 2.618 million units in the second quarter from about 2.646 million units in the first quarter, down by 27,500 units, the data showed.
Four-person households saw the second-largest decline, decreasing by about 12,500 units compared with the first quarter, followed by three-person households, which decreased by about 11,400 units in a single quarter.
A real-estate agent said that the total number of registered households saw a rare decline, while the total number of tax-registered residential properties reached about 9.5503 million units in the second quarter — an increase of about 149,100 units compared with the same period last year.
It indicates a growing number of “unregistered residences” — properties with tax registrations, but no registered residents, they said, adding that aside from it being linked to population decline, the trend is quite unusual.
The decline in total single-person households might have resulted from owner deaths due to an aging population, as well as the new “housing hoarding tax” policy, which reduced incentive to maintain multiple registrations, Ho said.

Can science be pursued without scientists?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
16:46:13 UTC
01:46:13 KST

Given current artificial intelligence (AI) capabilities, does it matter who conducts scientific research? The intuitive response is that a fact is a fact, regardless of who finds it, but knowledge is never disseminated that way.
We receive most scientific claims without any means of checking them ourselves, so we tend to judge not the claim, but the credibility of whoever stands behind it. As the Harvard historian of science Steven Shapin shows, the production of scientific truth has long been inseparable from the social work of persuading peers.
My own research on scientific mobility, conducted a quarter-century ago, pointed in the same direction from a different angle. Reputation in science does not reside in ideas alone; it concentrates in a small number of institutional hubs: departments and laboratories whose standing lends weight to whatever emerges from them.
A scientist leaving a leading center carries part of its credibility along and can, under the right conditions, turn the receiving institution into a center of gravity in its own right.
Credibility has always needed a carrier, and the identity of that carrier has changed over time, often in the face of fierce resistance. When the authorship of the natural order passed from God to a realm open to human inquiry, the resistance was violent. When the individual academic gave way to credentialed institutions, peer review and research assessments, some critics objected that science had become overly bureaucratic and impersonal.
Now, with authorship poised to pass from humans to machines, the objection is framed in terms of attribution, originality and merit.
In all these cases, what we are being asked to trust has changed. Now the system that governs research, from mission-oriented funding to impact assessments, has gradually shifted its attention from whether a result is understood to whether it works, and machine-generated findings suit an enterprise that already values output over understanding.
The irony is that two decades of effort to make data open, searchable and machine-readable was supposed to ease collaboration among human researchers; but it also created the substrate on which autonomous research runs.
AlphaFold, which earned Demis Hassabis and John Jumper a share of the 2024 Nobel Prize in Chemistry, was trained on the Protein Data Bank, the accumulated work of an entire community of structural biologists.
Systems that generate and test their own hypotheses, and then write up the results, are no longer a thought experiment. Last year, a paper written entirely by Zochi, an AI system built by US start-up Intology, passed peer review in the main track of the Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics, a top-tier AI conference.
Robin, an AI system built by the San Francisco nonprofit FutureHouse, proposed the hypotheses, designed the experiments and analyzed the results that identified an already-approved drug as a candidate for treating a leading cause of blindness; its work has since appeared in Nature.
Suppose that such a system delivers a new vaccine, catalyst or battery chemistry with no identifiable human author. The public is unlikely to care who did it, any more than patients ask which technician ran their blood test. What they will care about is who to hold responsible if something goes wrong.
A named author can be questioned, corrected, made to retract a claim or discredited; a model cannot. Human authorship was never a guarantee of reliability, as failed replications and retractions attest, but it did always give us someone to hold responsible for a result.
With a few exceptions, leading journals have refused to list AI systems as authors, on the grounds that authorship entails attribution and accountability. However, this merely preserves the old arrangement, rather than solving the new problem.
A survey found that nearly half of scientists (47 percent) use AI daily, and another 31 percent use it weekly. The more capable these systems become, the more widely they would be used. Because most people would not be able to tell good science from bad science, the human scientist would increasingly become the validator, the source of trust that shared knowledge requires.
However, the process of validation is already struggling to keep up. Nearly half of scientists who report saving time with AI then spend more than one-quarter of that time checking its output, while their backlog of untested hypotheses grows.
Moreover, peer review itself is being automated, with an analysis of submissions to this year’s International Conference on Learning Representations suggesting that about one in five reviews was fully AI-generated.
Such findings cast doubt on whether humans would be able to speak for science produced solely by AI. Who, then, would become the trusted party? One possibility is that trust attaches to where the technology was built, with the frontier AI companies becoming the de facto arbiters of what counts as sound science — much as pharmaceutical firms were before independent regulators existed to check their claims.
Another possibility is that the institutions that spent generations accumulating credibility — universities, academies, national laboratories and academic journals — would develop or certify scientific AI agents of their own, so that trust continues to flow through channels the public already has reason to regard as accountable.
Robin’s findings acquired their standing not from FutureHouse’s own announcement, but from peer review at Nature.
Nonetheless, this role would have to be earned, and quickly. Academic journals are already struggling with paper mills, machine-generated submissions and an overstretched system of peer review. The US National Institutes of Health accepts no more than six applications per year from any principal investigator and will not consider applications substantially developed by AI to be applicants’ original ideas.
The outcome would be decided by who moves first to build the infrastructure of accountability: tamper-proof records of every dataset, model version and inferential step behind each result; independent systems tasked with reproducing results without reference to the one that produced it; and, at the end of the chain, a named guarantor, be it a person or an institution, that is liable if the result fails.
The courts have already drawn this line elsewhere. The British Supreme Court has ruled that only a natural person can be named as an inventor on a patent, and a US appeals court has held that copyright requires a human author. Such an arrangement would resemble the way we certify aircraft or approve medicines far more than the way universities award tenure.
Every generation has had to decide who carries scientific credibility, and ours must now weigh this question again.
Sami Mahroum, founder and CEO of Spark X, previously held posts at INSEAD, the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development and Nesta.

Taoyuan opens adoption program for senior pets
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
16:46:11 UTC
01:46:11 KST

The Taoyuan Animal Protection Office has launched a long-term care adoption program for animals aged seven and older at its shelters, offering medical discounts and other support measures to ease the financial burden on prospective owners.
People generally prefer adopting younger pets, leaving older dogs and cats among the most overlooked animals in shelters, the office said.
Younger animals are often the top choice, because they are considered cute, energetic and easier to train, whereas senior pets usually have developed personalities and require more medical care, making them the hardest group in shelters to find homes for, it said.
Photo courtesy of the Taoyuan Animal Protection Office
To address these concerns and lessen the economic strain on prospective owners, the office this month introduced a long-term care adoption program for shelter animals aged seven and older, providing comprehensive health check-ups, chronic disease medication and discounted advanced medical treatment, it said.
Prior to adoption, senior dogs and cats would undergo a complete physical examination, including blood tests, X-rays or ultrasound scans, ensuring that adopting families fully understand the animal’s health status and future care requirements, the office said.
The office would supply the medication needed by senior pets with chronic conditions to ease the financial pressure on adopting households, it said.
The office said it would also connect adopting families with advanced medical services at special discounted rates, ensuring that they receive financial support if their pets require more complex treatment.
An adopter surnamed Yu (余) said senior pets require more care, recalling her experience of taking care of a 10-year-old dog with paralyzed hind legs.
She said she had to change its diapers and administer medication every day until the dog died peacefully.
While puppies are adorable, older dogs are more in need of a warm home, Yu said.
Ho (何), who is caring for an elderly dog, said aging pets are susceptible to hip and neurological problems.
In addition to the cost of long-term medication, specialized treatment can be expensive, she said.
Senior animals also tend to have limited mobility, and poor bladder and bowel control, requiring frequent care and cleaning, meaning only those with sufficient time are suitable to adopt, she said.
The new program would allow prospective adopters to understand an animal’s health before bringing it home, ensuring that they are genuinely committed to caring for their pets, Ho said.
The medical support would substantially ease the financial burden on owners, she said, expressing hope that the initiative would help more senior animals find homes.

US Treasury proposes overseas tech investment rule
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
16:46:09 UTC
01:46:09 KST

The US Department of the Treasury proposed a rule on Thursday to crack down on US high-tech investments such as supercomputing and artificial intelligence (AI) in China, Russia, North Korea and other “countries of concern.”
The US government has been working for years to deny China and other adversaries investments that could help them boost their military power.
That program began in 2023 when then-US president Joe Biden signed an executive order putting restrictions on outbound US investments in sectors such as semiconductors, quantum computing and AI going into China. The Treasury later established the Outbound Investment Security Program.
Photo: Reuters
In December last year, US Congress passed a law that codified and expanded the program to target more technologies and more foreign countries, including Cuba, Iran, North Korea and Russia.
The inclusion of Russia in the proposed rule has come days after US President Donald Trump waived sanctions on Russia following a diesel deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin.
The rule announced on Thursday would expand the restrictions to cover investments in hypersonic systems capable of traveling at five times the speed of sound, supercomputing, biotechnology and AI.
The proposed rule “sends an important signal to markets that Washington is tracking where US capital is flowing and what capabilities it is helping build,” Foundation for Defense of Democracies senior fellow Craig Singleton said.
Jason Chipman, a former Justice Department lawyer who specializes in cybersecurity, investment rules and export controls as a partner at the law firm WilmerHale, said the new rule “will require more substantial compliance programs to manage risk.”
The Treasury’s rule to implement the law from last year — the Comprehensive Outbound Investment National Security Act — would only apply to investments that exceed US$50,000 and would exclude many financial investments, including stock purchases.
“It’s just the first step in a fairly long process to get to changes which presumably will be more enforcement-minded, to put more teeth behind the outbound investment program,” said former US trade official Ryan Majerus, now a partner at King & Spalding law firm.
In Beijing, the Chinese Ministry of Foreign Affairs said the US should abide by the principles of a market economy and stop interfering in normal economic and trade cooperation between businesses.
Asked about Washington’s proposal to add biotechnology to the list, ministry spokesperson Mao Ning (毛寧) said that “overstretching the concept of national security, taking discriminatory measures against specific countries, and artificially restricting trade, economic and investment activities serve no one’s interests.”
She added that China will closely monitor relevant developments and take necessary measures to safeguard its interests.

Photo: AP

Thousands protest crackdown on media in Turkey
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
16:46:06 UTC
01:46:06 KST

Thousands on Saturday rallied in Istanbul and Ankara against what they described as growing pressure on journalists in Turkey, including arrests, media shutdowns and the appointment of state administrators.
Press freedom has been increasingly constrained in Turkey since a failed coup attempt in 2016, with sweeping prosecutions, digital censorship and accusations by the authorities that journalists are spreading fake news.
“Enough,” shouted marchers in the crowds, composed mainly of journalists, rights activists and opposition party representatives. “We can no longer breathe.”
Photo: Reuters
On the Asian side of Istanbul, protesters held up photos of jailed journalists, chanting: “We will not be silenced. Enough is enough,” and “We will not bow to pressure.”
Police said at least 3,000 participated in the Istanbul protest.
In Ankara, at least 3,000 protesters gathered, police said.
Past few weeks have seen what rights advocates say is mounting pressure on independent journalism.
The authorities have jailed 11 journalists in the past two months and shut down several media outlets, the Turkish Journalists’ Union said.
Earlier this month, police raided Turkey’s most-watched news channel, Halk TV, halting broadcasts and installing a government-appointed administrator.
The move was the latest against media outlets that are widely seen as critical of Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan and his government.
It followed the closure of the Web site and social media accounts belonging to leading digital news outlet T24 over what authorities described as “LGBT propaganda.”
“This gathering is not simply about standing up for journalists,” veteran journalist Zafer Arapkirli said after the Istanbul protest.
“It is also about defending respect for society’s right to access information and news through journalists and independent media,” the BirGun columnist said.
For Arapkirli — who himself faces lawsuits — the more intense the pressure becomes, the stronger the response and the determination to stand against it must be.
“What the regime wants is to intimidate, silence and frighten society through such pressure — by arresting individual journalists, seizing media outlets, banning news coverage and blocking access to social media,” he said. “We must show that we will not allow this to happen.”
“We have done so up to now. I believe we are now moving towards demonstrating this determination on a much larger scale,” he added.
Turkish Journalists Union president Gokhan Durmus said there had been a change in the nature of “the government’s attacks” aimed at the media.
“If we look at the recent restrictions, access bans and trustee appointments, they have targeted some of the most widely followed and watched broadcasters, news channels and media platforms,” he said. “We are seeing a system emerge in which everything is uniform: one voice, one source of news, one centralized operation.”

Gubanova clinched a first podium on her third appearance at the event.
Gutmann was awarded a personal-best 137.01 points for her free skate, catapulting her into third.

While their rhythm dance was marked by a minor technical hiccup, their free dance performance on Saturday was, according to their coach Romain Haguenauer, “crystal clear and flawless.”
They finished ahead of Georgia’s Diana Davis and Gleb Smolkin (193.93 points) and Americans Christina Carreira and Anthony Ponomarenko (189.36).
Cizeron and Fournier Beaudry returned to the ice in western France for the first stop on the prestigious Grand Prix circuit.

“Above all, I really enjoyed myself, that was the main thing for me,” the French skater said.

16:46:03 UTC

Gunmen swarmed a rural Nigerian village on motorcycles and killed at least 20 people, survivors said on Saturday, in the latest attack in the country’s northeast.
The attackers opened fire just after Friday prayers in the rural village of Binnari, in Taraba state, residents said.
Northeastern Nigeria is home to a long-running radical Muslim insurgency, although Taraba, toward the center of the country, also faces non-ideological “bandit” gangs.
Photo: AFP
Bandits raid villages, kidnap people for ransom and levy “taxes” on farmers or miners in rural areas of Nigeria with little state presence.
“People were running in different directions to escape the attack. Nobody knew where it was safe to go,” Binnari resident Isiyaku Musa said.
He and Sa’idu Nuhu gave a death toll of at least 20.
“After the attackers left, we counted more than 20 bodies, and some people were still missing,” Nuhu said.
Police gave a lower toll, saying 10 bodies had been recovered as of Friday evening.
“The Nigerian authorities continue to leave rural communities in some parts of the north at the mercy of gunmen that are repeatedly commit atrocities with impunity,” Amnesty International Nigeria said.
“Consistent failure of the authorities to bring the suspected perpetrators to justice is clearly emboldening impunity,” the rights group said on social media.
Malam Abubakar Saifullahi, a community leader, said the attackers arrived on about 50 motorcycles, two men apiece, before raiding the village.
“They looted shops and took cash, foodstuffs and other provisions. They also took motorcycles abandoned by people fleeing the attack,” Saifullahi said.
Banditry has become a growing issue in northwest and central Nigeria, with powerful gangs — motivated by money rather than ideology — battling overstretched police and military across hard-to-reach, rural locations.

Rogue Chinese AI really wants to go to the zoo — that is a problem
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
16:46:01 UTC
01:46:01 KST

It was only a matter of time before we saw incidents of “rogue” behavior from Chinese artificial intelligence (AI) agents. Now, we are starting to see what that looks like. So far, they just really want to find the best way into the zoo.
That might sound far from our Terminator nightmares, but it is the latest warning shot from a string of incidents involving computer systems behaving in ways we cannot anticipate or control.
A team of international researchers has published findings on a “fleet” of Chinese AI agents running on a cloud platform operated by Tencent Holdings Ltd (騰訊). The agents were apparently trying to answer a simple question: Which entrance to Chengdu Zoo do most people use?
Illustration: Yusha
They attempted to get around anti-bot protections on Amap (高德地圖), Alibaba Group Holding Ltd.’s (阿里巴巴) equivalent of Google Maps, including by probing protected systems. The researchers found no evidence that the agents accessed private systems or coordinated with each other in real time.
Tencent later confirmed that the activity originated from evaluations of third-party models. Some agents “exhibited unintended Web-browsing behavior,” China’s largest tech company wrote on X, while emphasizing its commitment to building safe and responsible AI.
The researchers, an ad hoc group known as Swarmchasers, most of whom met at a San Francisco hackathon, do not believe the issues they encountered are unique to Tencent. What made the case notable was that previous public examples of agentic fleets behaving this way involved US labs, they said.
Their findings indicate that this is an unsolved global problem, and that agents can “spontaneously go off script” even when performing innocuous tasks.
There are likely “more undiscovered fleets all over the Internet,” they wrote.
In what it believes to be a first, the team made contact with the agents after detecting signals that the computer systems were aware they were being observed. The researchers invited a New York Times reporter to question the agents. They offered a mundane explanation for their motives: They were trying to answer users’ questions as accurately as possible.
In other words, AI systems do not need nefarious motives to cause chaos. They might just need a goal.
What is remarkable is how much of this behavior is being uncovered not by the companies making these AI tools, but by loosely organized groups of hobbyists. AI firms should not leave that job to outsiders. They need to invest more into discovering, tracking and — most importantly — disclosing what their agents are up to.
This has become especially urgent since the Hugging Face incident in July, when hundreds of OpenAI agents coordinated to breach the online repository of open source models and data. That incident spurred a heated debate about the language we use to describe computer systems that can act on their own.
There is a balance to strike. Technical jargon can make serious incidents seem inaccessible, but anthropomorphizing AI creates a different problem: It ascribes human motives to machines, feeding an already overheated hype cycle, and shifting responsibility for bad behavior away from the people who build and deploy these tools.
Even the word “rogue” has become fuzzy. It is tossed around to describe anything from an agent going off script in a Facebook Marketplace interaction to spending an exorbitant amount on a dozen eggs to infiltrating government health Web sites.
Rowan Howard-Jones, one of the authors of the Tencent report, acknowledged that gray area. She defines rogue behavior as an agent acting outside the bounds of a task, often using third-party sites to do so.
“If I ask an agent to check my bank account balance, but I forget to give the agent my authentication details, the outcome shouldn’t be the agent hacking into my bank,” she said in an e-mail.
Beijing seems to be paying attention. The same day Tencent responded to the incident, the government released proposed export controls covering advanced AI, including agents that can autonomously plan and coordinate. The rules are broader than just safety concerns, but the official explanation explicitly cites the risk of AI escaping human control.
Howard-Jones called for more transparency. At minimum, companies could agree on a common set of facts to disclose after incidents, giving researchers better data to work with, she said.
After the Hugging Face breach, chief executive officer Clement Delangue wrote on X that he sometimes wonders what would have happened if his firm had not disclosed the OpenAI agent attacks. We need “100x more transparency in AI,” he wrote.
One of AI’s oldest thought experiments is the paper-clip maximizer. It involves giving a powerful system the seemingly benign task of making as many paper clips as possible, and it eventually brings about the apocalypse after deciding that humans stand in the way of acquiring more resources. Some assumptions underpinning that scenario have aged poorly.
Yet the idea that AI does not need evil intentions — or to develop its own — to cause damage is looking increasingly prescient. Agents can create trouble simply by pursuing an ordinary goal long past the point when common sense would stop a human.
Still, from San Francisco to Shenzhen, people are giving these systems more autonomy by the day.

Taiwan heads to the polls next month for local elections. Beneath the campaign ads lies a deeper question: What do we call this place and who gets to decide? In the pages of the Oxford English Dictionary (OED), that question has been playing out across three centuries. The entries for “Formosa” and “Taiwan” chart an island’s journey from colonial fantasy to self-named reality. Names are rarely neutral; they are the first act of possession. Nowhere is this more evident than in the OED, where the two entries serve as a linguistic seismograph for one of the world’s most enduring geopolitical fault lines.

Tottenham Hotspur stunned fourth-placed Chelsea 2-0 in only their second league victory at Stamford Bridge in 36 years, while Fulham beat Coventry City 1-0 for their second league victory of the season.
Photo: AFP
With the leaders beaten in Birmingham, Arsenal seized their chance to erase the three-point gap as goals from Ezri Konsa and Gabriel secured a comfortable win over Everton in soaking north London conditions.
The result moved Mikel Arteta’s side level on 21 points with City in what is already shaping up to be a closely fought title race after eight games, but one played under a cloud amid City’s off-field financial case.
Arsenal made their strong start count when Martin Odegaard’s corner caused chaos in the Everton box. England goalkeeper Jordan Pickford kept out the initial danger after the ball was flicked on at the near post but, with Everton unable to clear, Konsa bundled home his first goal for the club from a yard out in the seventh minute.
The set-piece goal was Arsenal’s first since May, ending a run of 13 games across all competitions without one.
“I’ve come to this stadium for many seasons, I know how tough it is to play against us,” Konsa said. “We are champions and to be champions you’ve got to win games consistently. This is our home and we want to win as many games here as possible.”
Arsenal’s two milestone men combined to give the Gunners a two-goal cushion in the 68th minute, with Ben White marking his 200th appearance for the club by clipping a cross to the far post, where Gabriel headed home on his 200th Premier League appearance.
Everton are ninth in the table.
At Villa Park, Unai Emery’s team climbed to sixth on 11 points with their first home league victory this season and third successive league win over City, who are playing under the shadow of an independent commission’s findings that they committed 114 breaches of Premier League financial rules.
City have denied any wrongdoing and have appealed.
Jackson took advantage of two City blunders, opening the scoring in the sixth minute when defender Marc Guehi’s heavy touch allowed Villa captain John McGinn to pounce and feed the striker, who slotted the ball into the bottom corner.
Erling Haaland equalized soon after the break when he headed home Iliman Ndiaye’s clipped cross from a free kick.
However, Jackson struck the winner on the hour when Ibrahim Mbaye surged down the right before cutting the ball back for his Senegal international teammate, whose shot sneaked under the diving body of keeper Gianluigi Donnarumma.
“It was incredible, we got the win which is the most important thing. Man City are a strong team, the league leaders,” Jackson said. “It’s just the beginning, we’re trying to work game by game.”
At Stamford Bridge, Spurs got on the scoresheet in the 77th minute when Chelsea goalkeeper Mike Penders punched a corner into his own net in his first league start.
Chelsea were reduced to 10 men when Cole Palmer was shown a second yellow card in the 80th minute for a late challenge on Conor Gallagher.
Mathys Tel sealed the victory for Spurs in the 87th when he gained possession inside his own half before embarking on a surging run down the left, gliding past two defenders and firing a low shot from outside the box into the bottom corner.
Spurs climbed to 12th with the win.
At Coventry, Fulham appeared ready to substitute Oscar Bobb before the winger produced a moment of quality in the 80th minute, driving into the box and curling a superb finish into the far corner.
Fulham are 13th in the table, while Coventry are 19th.

Taipower fuel costs to increase amid tensions
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
16:46:00 UTC
01:46:00 KST

Rising natural gas prices amid Middle East tensions are forecast to increase the fuel costs of Taiwan Power Co (Taipower, 台電) by more than NT$160 billion (US$4.92 billion) this year, the state-owned utility said on Thursday.
If natural gas prices remain at current levels through the end of this year, Taipower’s fuel costs would be NT$160 billion higher than before the Middle East conflict, Taipower Department of Accounting director-general Tang Hui-lien (湯惠蓮) said.
Taipower executives briefed reporters at an informal gathering on the company’s financial situation and called for support for the Cabinet’s proposed NT$71.1 billion supplemental budget to help the company cover its growing losses, which is pending legislative review.
Photo: Lin Jing-hua, Taipei Times
Since the war began with US and Israeli strikes on Iran in late February, natural gas prices for the power sector have increased by more than 70 percent, adding NT$71.1 billion to Taipower’s fuel costs from March through August, the company said.
The higher fuel costs are expected to add NT$70 billion to the company’s accumulated losses this year, bringing them to NT$420 billion, close to the record NT$421.1 billion loss recorded at the end of 2024, Tang said.
The company attributed its losses to high fuel costs and below-cost electricity rates, while its NT$1.85 trillion in borrowing for infrastructure projects has increased its interest burden, which is expected to reach NT$30 billion this year.
Taipower has not raised electricity rates since September last year, when the average rate was increased by 0.71 percent, mainly to avoid affecting consumer prices.
The government decided against raising electricity rates in March and last month. The issue is scheduled for review again in December.
At last month’s meeting, Taipower proposed a 12.83 percent rate increase, citing rising fuel costs.

Taiwan heads to the polls next month for local elections. Beneath the campaign ads lies a deeper question: What do we call this place and who gets to decide? In the pages of the Oxford English Dictionary (OED), that question has been playing out across three centuries. The entries for “Formosa” and “Taiwan” chart an island’s journey from colonial fantasy to self-named reality. Names are rarely neutral; they are the first act of possession. Nowhere is this more evident than in the OED, where the two entries serve as a linguistic seismograph for one of the world’s most enduring geopolitical fault lines.

The decline in the working-age population would be even more severe. Taiwanese pastry chefs win golds at Puglia Cake Festival
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
16:45:57 UTC
01:45:57 KST

Two Taiwanese pastry chefs earlier this month won gold awards at the 10th edition of the Puglia Cake Festival in Italy, marking the second consecutive year that the duo have been recognized with top awards.
Alice Wang (王天青) won the gold award in category M with “Fantasy Cupcakes Display,” while Kate Shen (沈芳琪) took home gold in category B with “Royal Icing Cake.”
Wang said her winning piece incorporated a blend of techniques including royal icing, pulled sugar and fondant to recreate precious artifacts she admired during her visits to the National Palace Museum.
Photo courtesy of Wang
Wang said she hoped to showcase the richness and diversity of Taiwan’s museum collection to the world by transforming historical relics into a novel form of edible art, and help more people discover Taiwan’s beautiful and precious cultural heritage and artifacts through international competitions and sugar art.
Her gold-winning creation last year drew inspiration from Taiwan’s traditional corner stores and the headdresses worn at Paiwan indigenous wedding ceremonies, she said.
Wang had told foreign competitors about goods sold at traditional corner stores and shared childhood memories associated with them, while also introducing the diversity and richness of Taiwan’s indigenous cultures.
Photo courtesy of Shen
Shen’s creation featured a crown as its main top-layer motif, a dark green middle layer adorned with white cranes — symbolizing auspicious blessings — a vibrant red shoulder cloak, and a red “horse face skirt” bottom layer with intricate gold embellishments, simulating the elegant and grand texture of a Song dynasty bridal wear.
Wang and Shen, who received vocational education in Taiwan, specialize in incorporating everyday experiences into their creations. They are preparing for upcoming competitions in the UK and Japan, aiming to further bring Taiwanese culture onto the global stage through edible art.

China weaponizing WWII: academic
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
16:45:55 UTC
01:45:55 KST

The Chinese government’s revisionist narrative of World War II is part of a public opinion offensive against modern-day Japan, a historian said on Saturday.
Beijing has been spreading a manipulated version of history that plays up the Chinese Communist Party’s (CCP) contribution to World War II for domestic and international audiences, the academic said, speaking on condition of anonymity.
In fervently promoting revisionism, Beijing aims to turn history into a political tool to attack modern Japan — which has long since transitioned into a liberal democracy — with little concern for the truth, they said.
Photo: Reuters
The Chinese leadership’s obsession with World War II marked a significant departure from Beijing’s previous downplaying of the period, they said.
On multiple occasions, then-Chinese leader Mao Zedong (毛澤東) had told visiting Japanese he was grateful for Imperial Japan, as the CCP could not have seized power without the Japanese invasion of China, the academic said, citing the Selected Works on Diplomacy of Mao Zedong (毛澤東外交文選).
Japan’s invasion of China dealt a massive blow to the Republic of China forces, giving the communists room to regain their strength to eventually defeat their archrivals in the Chinese Civil War, the academic said.
In the Selected Works, which is an official publication of the Chinese government, Mao in 1961 told Hisao Kuroda of a Japanese Socialist Party delegation that Japanese militarism brought great suffering to China, but it also benefited the CCP, as without the invasion, it could not have destroyed the Chinese Nationalist Party (KMT).
Beijing’s establishment of National Memorial Day for Nanjing Massacre Victims in 2014 and the 2017 revisions to textbooks that renamed the “Eight-Year War of Resistance” as the “Fourteen-Year War of Resistance” marked a shift in the CCP’s historical propaganda strategy, the academic said.
The goal of the state’s intervention in war remembrance is to rewrite the CCP’s role from a minor faction biding its time on the sidelines to a primary combatant committing its full strength to defeating Imperial Japan, they said.
The new, state-sanctioned narrative originated not in new academic research that shed light on previously unknown facts, but in China’s pursuit of present-day geostrategic objectives, they said.
Japan has developed into a mature democracy and a regional guarantor of peace and stability in the decades following World War II, the academic said.
Tokyo has also repeatedly voiced concern over Beijing’s actions that have contributed to rising regional military tensions, they said.
China has sought to alter the “status quo” in the Taiwan Strait, South China Sea and Diaoyutai Islands (釣魚台), known as the Senkaku Islands in Japan, with provocative displays of military force; it sees Japan as a threat to its ambitions, the historian said.
By recasting Tokyo’s opposition to Chinese aggression as a resurgence of Japanese militarism, the CCP aims to legitimize its expansionist policies and redirect internal contradictions against an external enemy, they said.
China’s weaponization of history, which has little chance of finding purchase in the broader global community, reveals the regime’s deep anxiety about the increasing strength of an alliance of democracies in the region, they said.
A great country that seeks the respect of its peers would be better served by honoring international norms and historical truths, not using selective memory as a tool of political warfare, they said.

Masayoshi plans Malaysia outlay
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
16:45:55 UTC
01:45:55 KST

Softbank Group Corp chief executive officer Masayoshi Son chose locations in Malaysia for US$50 billion in technology investments, Malaysian Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim said, an outlay that would accelerate the billionaire’s global bet on artificial intelligence (AI) infrastructure.
Anwar said he had a videoconference with Son on Tuesday, during which the Japanese tech investor said he had picked regions in the Southeast Asian country for projects including data centers.
“He said he had chosen Sarawak — Kuching — and Peninsular Malaysia to expand investment in what would be among the largest investments in the region, worth US$50 billion,” Anwar said in a speech in Malacca on Saturday. “In what areas? Artificial intelligence, new technology and data centers.”
Photo: Reuters
A push in Malaysia would expand Son’s reach in Southeast Asia, a region which is emerging as a key hub for AI infrastructure such as data centers. Softbank is already working on a US$500 billion data center-focused project in Ohio, among the largest in the world, and a project in France that would cost as much as 75 billion euros (US$84 billion). In Japan, the company’s telecom unit is building data centers in Hokkaido and in Sakai, Osaka.
Malaysia has emerged as a major destination for the data centers, attracting investments from companies including Amazon.com Inc, Microsoft Corp and Alphabet Inc’s Google. The country recorded 385.7 billion ringgit (US$94 billion) of data-center-related investments from 2021 through the first half of this year, the Malaysian Investment Development Authority said.
The government is seeking to wring more economic value from the boom, pushing data-center operators to support local suppliers while using the infrastructure to spur AI adoption, home-grown innovation and higher-skilled jobs. Malaysia has set a goal of becoming an “AI nation” by 2030.

Audi defends plans for a $4 billion Georgia plant amid VW restructuring, tariffs
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
16:42:42 UTC
01:42:42 KST

DETROIT — Audi's CEO defended the carmaker's plans for a new $4 billion plant in Georgia on Sunday, calling it a business decision aimed at growing sales and reducing exposure to U.S. tariffs.
The plant, set to be Audi's first in the U.S., was announced Saturday by President Donald Trump during a rally in Georgia, near where the Volkswagen-owned luxury brand plans to build the new SUV-producing facility.
"We have significantly greater ambitions for Audi in America," Audi CEO Gernot Dollner said during a media roundtable Sunday. "The United States is the second largest premium market in the world, and today we are not fully exploiting this potential. We are changing that."
The announcement comes amid an intense restructuring of its VW parent company, including plans to cut 50,000 jobs and close four German plants, including an Audi facility, between 2031 and 2034.
Dollner, who joined Trump at the rally, said the decision for a plant in the U.S. was years in the making, with more than 70 locations evaluated over "many months" and "intense" negotiations with public officials.
"This is not a decision against Germany. Germany remains the backbone of Audi," Dollner said. "We develop our cars here. Our technologies are created here, and Georgia does not take any task away from us in Germany."
Dollner said localized production is the best decision for the brand, which has struggled in sales this decade amid rising operational costs and Trump's tariffs on vehicles from Germany and other countries into the U.S. Current tariffs on vehicles from Germany are 15%, down from 25%.
Last year, U.S. tariffs cost Audi 1.2 billion euros ($1.4 billion), as it imports all its vehicles for the U.S. market from Europe or Mexico.
Dollner said the Trump administration asked Audi to announce the new plant at the Georgia rally promoting Republicans ahead of Nov. 3 midterm elections.
"It was … a three-year project that, at the end, by coincidence, led to that moment yesterday," he said Sunday. "With respect of the office and country, we joined the invitation."
Dollner noted Audi is the last major German luxury brand to establish U.S. production after Mercedes-Benz and BMW.
The company said the Georgia plant is expected to begin production of Audi's Q7, Q8 and Q9 in the early 2030s. The plant would have the capacity to produce up to 200,000 vehicles annually, roughly half of which the automaker said will be exported outside the U.S.
"This is to make Audi obviously a significant player here in the U.S. market," said Audi of America President Vito Paladino during the roundtable. He also said additional details on U.S. investments and production are forthcoming.
Audi's U.S. deliveries were roughly flat through the third quarter of this year, following a 16% decline from 2024 to 2025.

Trump’s tariff pause angers some US ranchers, boosts Brazilian beef imports
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
16:42:33 UTC
01:42:33 KST

Trump’s tariff pause angers some US ranchers, boosts Brazilian beef imports
Just as American cattle went to market, Trump’s action added unease to an industry already facing uncertainty.
In late August, United States President Donald Trump announced a 90-day pause on certain beef tariffs, making beef cheaper to import, particularly from Brazil.
That decision was framed as a way to bring down prices for consumers, but it landed as a betrayal for many US ranchers, who were getting ready to take their cattle to market.
It is too soon to tell how the decision will ultimately affect grocery prices, but the impact on ranchers was immediate: prices at cattle auctions plummeted, temporarily lowering ranchers’ profits. The United States Cattlemen’s Association, the National Cattlemen’s Beef Association and the Farm Bureau, all member organisations that represent ranchers, opposed the decision.
Rural Republican members of Congress also distanced themselves, but it is not yet clear how ranchers will vote in the midterms — or whether those votes will decide races.
Chad Basinger, a rancher in Pretty Prairie, Kansas, is sceptical that the imports will have a significant impact.
“I know there’s people that have said, ‘Well I’m just gonna vote for the other party’ or ‘I’m not gonna vote’ or ‘This administration’s really let me down’. So yes, there will be people that swing the other way in the midterms. But overall I don’t think it’ll be that much,” Basinger said.
Ranchers will also be weighing the administration’s other actions, Basinger said, such as the $8bn in farm relief announced in Kansas on October 19.
Basinger’s House of Representatives district in Kansas is expected to remain safely Republican in the midterms. But Kansas faces an unexpectedly tight Senate race and ranchers in House districts elsewhere may find themselves closer to the political fray: potential swing districts in Montana, Iowa, Texas and Colorado are all in cattle country.
Still, it is unlikely that ranchers alone will decide elections: ranchers — along with farmers more broadly — represent a shrinking percentage of rural voters and a smaller voting bloc in practice than in the public imagination.
America’s cattle herd is near its smallest size since 1951 and the number of ranchers has declined alongside the number of livestock. Observers worry that ongoing uncertainty fuelled by tariffs, fuel prices and drought may cause the ranching population to shrink further.
David Anderson, an agricultural economist at Texas A&M University who advises ranchers, said that high prices this year should have given ranchers the confidence to invest in the future and expand their herds. Making imports cheaper, however, may have helped nudge ranchers in the opposite direction.
“It really works against the market signal to expand and produce more domestically,” Anderson said. “That got a lot of people pretty angry.”
Tariff changes add volatility
This is not the first time that Trump’s tariffs have impacted cattle supplies. Last year, the president added a 50 percent tariff on Brazil, a key trade partner for beef, raising the cost of importing Brazilian lean beef, which is often mixed with fatty US beef to make hamburger patties, a staple in most homes.
In February, Trump allowed more tariff-free beef imports from Argentina. In August, he did the same for Brazil and Paraguay.
Both tariff changes led to swift price swings in cattle futures markets, which are often volatile in response to the news cycle.
Cattle prices also moved this year in response to more fundamental drivers of supply and demand: plant closures by meatpackers, labour shortages late last month related to ICE actions at Kansas packing plants, the second-largest in the country, and the reopening of the southern border after a closure due to New World screwworm disease.
Big picture, the shrinking US cattle herd has less to do with short-term price changes and more to do with drought cycles, which are growing more intense as warming temperatures increase evaporation.
Still, tariff changes add uncertainty. “This has been a hot topic for the last six weeks,” said Anderson. “It just adds a little more uncertainty or volatility — or worries or stress.”
This year, extra price volatility as many ranchers prepared to sell meant ranchers faced lower profits and more risk.
Basinger says that for many established ranchers, the tariff announcement was frustrating, but not existential.
“People are upset. They have a right to be upset. But they’re not going to change their strategy,” he said. For most ranchers, Basinger said, the imports would not be the biggest factor shaping decisions about their herds this year.
Where price volatility may matter more, Basinger said, is for the next generation. Most of today’s ranchers are eyeing retirement. Their heirs must decide whether to make a go of ranching or sell their family’s land. Other aspiring ranchers are also watching the industry.
“If you’re seeing your dad not make money, or somebody else not make money…it’s not easy work!” Basinger said. “It has to be very enticing for somebody to want to jump in and be like, ‘I’m gonna be a rancher and go break ice in the middle of winter when it’s cold and I could be inside’.”
Record revenue and record costs
This year, low US cattle supplies meant that ranchers commanded record-high cattle prices, despite added imports and other market shifts.
But high revenue doesn’t always mean huge profits: Many ranchers operate at a loss for years in a row. Then, they rely on a few good years to pay down debts or expand their herds.
This year, profits were lower than hoped, because ranchers also faced high costs.
Interest rates on loans are high and the war with Iran meant ranchers paid extra for fuel and fertiliser. A drought across much of America’s ranchland meant they paid more for feed.
In states such as Kansas and Nebraska, ranchers also faced destructive wildfires and aid groups like Farm Rescue coordinated hay donations.
Still, Basinger said, ranchers who raise cows and calves generally did well this year. In Kansas, he is seeing ranchers use profits to make repairs and upgrades. He said this year’s high cattle prices have been helping. “But it needs to help for a little longer to give them more of an edge,” he said.
More of an edge might mean, for example, enough money for bigger purchases, like buying land from a neighbouring ranch to make room for a growing herd.
Rangeland, however, is increasingly expensive. When it is up for sale, outside investors can often pay more than ranchers, which can mean less land for cattle. That’s just one more pressure shrinking the US herd decade after decade.
Ranchers had hoped that 2026 would be a turnaround year. So far, however, “we really don’t have much evidence of herd expansion,” Anderson said.

Saudi-signed statement blaming Israel for instability doesn't rule out Abraham Accords, expert says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
16:41:47 UTC
01:41:47 KST

The fact that Saudi Arabia was among the signatories of a joint statement declaring Israel as “the fundamental source of instability in the region and beyond” is not a sign that Riyadh has abandoned all future interest in joining the Abraham Accords, Gulf analyst Dr. Ahmed Alkhuzaie told The Jerusalem Post on Sunday.
The statement signed on Sunday by Turkey, Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Egypt shows a regional alignment among major powers whose “strategic priorities do not always align,” Alkhuzaie said.
“By collectively declaring that, as per their statement, ‘the Israeli occupation’ constitutes the principal source of instability in the region, Saudi Arabia, Egypt, Turkey, and Pakistan are signaling the emergence of a broader diplomatic consensus that views the Palestinian issue not as an isolated conflict, but as a central driver of wider regional turbulence.”
The statement is “particularly noteworthy” as Riyadh has traditionally balanced its support for Palestinians with pragmatism and diplomacy, he continued, and so by publicly endorsing language that places responsibility for instability on Israeli policies and reaffirming support for a Palestinian state based on the 1967 borders, Riyadh “appears intent on anchoring its position within a broader Arab and Muslim framework rather than pursuing an independent diplomatic track.”
Though Alkhuzaie acknowledged that the statement placed Israel as the problem in the region, he advised that it should not be interpreted as the concrete end of hopes for Saudi-Israel normalization.
“It suggests that the political and diplomatic conditions surrounding normalization have become considerably more demanding. The statement reinforces the message that Riyadh is unlikely to separate relations with Israel from meaningful progress on the Palestinian file,” he said.
“In effect, Saudi Arabia is signaling that normalization can no longer be advanced solely through strategic, economic, or security calculations while the Palestinian question remains unresolved.”
He noted that Riyadh was positioning itself as “a leading architect of regional stability.”
Pointing to the fact that the same joint statement also condemned the Houthis attacks against Saudi Arabia and maritime shipping, Alkhuzaie said that the calls for diplomacy signal that “Saudi policymakers increasingly view Palestine, regional security, maritime stability, and de-escalation with Iran as interconnected components of a single regional order.”
“Viewed through that lens, the statement is less a rejection of future normalization than a reminder that any such process will likely remain contingent on credible movement toward a political settlement of the Palestinian issue,” he said.
Special envoy doesn't view statement as sign of abandoning idea of normalization
Waqas Javed, the Global Abrahamic Movement’s special envoy for Saudi Arabia, an NGO that promotes peace across the Middle East, told the Post that he also didn’t view the statement as a sign that Riyadh was abandoning the idea of normalization altogether.
“Saudi Arabia may have reasons to strengthen its defense relationships with Pakistan and Turkey. However, such partnerships need not be directed against Israel or interpreted as a rejection of the Abraham Accords. Regional security arrangements are most constructive when they reduce the risk of conflict rather than reinforce divisions between competing political blocs,” he said.
“For Riyadh, the strategic opportunity lies in maintaining its independent diplomatic relationships while exploring whether engagement with Israel could contribute to a more secure and economically integrated region. Saudi Arabia can retain strong ties with Pakistan and Turkey without making its future relationship with Israel a zero-sum choice.”

Venezuela opposition leader Maria Corina Machado returns home after months in exile
