Venezuela opposition leader Maria Corina Machado returns home after months in exile
CARACAS – Venezuelan opposition leader María Corina Machado returned to Caracas in a surprise move that could pose the biggest test yet to acting President Delcy Rodriguez’s political opening and the Trump administration’s strategy for a post-Maduro Venezuela.
“I’m here, with you,” Machado posted on X on Oct 25, confirming her return after months abroad.
She gave no details on how she entered Venezuela, but her party shared photos and videos of her arriving at a church in Lara state, where emotional supporters embraced her and said “she will be the next president of Venezuela”.
Machado’s team earlier thanked US President Donald Trump and Secretary of State Marco Rubio for their support, signalling an effort to underscore her ties with Washington even as her return risks complicating the administration’s Venezuela strategy.
Trump, speaking to reporters as he left the White House, said he did not know about Machado’s return. Other US officials, including her long-time ally, Representative Maria Elvira Salazar of Florida, celebrated the move, with Salazar calling it “the beginning of a new chapter”.
Rubio said Machado’s return is the “direct result of the US-supported reconciliation talks”.
“The United States expects the freedoms of all sectors of Venezuelan politics to continue to be respected,” Rubio said on X.
“Likewise, we expect all political actors to support these talks which represent the best chance Venezuela has had in 30 years to peacefully achieve not just a free and fair election, but also an enduring democracy.”
The move confronts Rodriguez with a difficult choice over how much political space to give her most formidable rival.
Her government has allowed politicians, activists and journalists who spent years in exile to return, including some of Machado’s closest allies.
Allowing Machado to organise and campaign freely would mark the most consequential expansion yet of that opening.
Detaining her or restricting her activities, meanwhile, could put pressure on Washington to respond.
Machado’s ability to mobilise supporters “adds a new layer of complexity” for the interim government, said David Smilde, a sociology professor and Venezuela expert at Tulane University in New Orleans.
“The big absent voice so far this year has been the voice of the Venezuelan people,” Smilde said.
Machado’s return, he added, could spur greater public mobilisation and demands for a return to democracy.
An official from Venezuela’s Information Ministry did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Signs of Machado’s impact quickly emerged. Her party called on supporters to gather in Caracas later on Oct 25 to welcome her as she made her way from western Venezuela towards the capital in a caravan escorted by motorcycles.
People gathered along the route, singing the national anthem, chanting and reaching out to touch Machado as she greeted them from the window of the sport utility vehicle carrying her.
In Caracas, supporters carrying Venezuelan flags gathered in Altamira, an area in the city’s east long associated with the opposition.
Some chanted “the leader has arrived”, while passing drivers honked their horns amid music and the blare of vuvuzelas.
Machado had a 61% positive rating in the latest AtlasIntel survey for Bloomberg News. The same poll showed her leading Rodriguez 52% to 19% in a hypothetical presidential election.
Washington has prioritised economic stability and rebuilding Venezuela’s oil industry alongside a gradual political transition, while relying on Rodriguez to maintain order and negotiate changes to the country’s political institutions.
The approach has culminated in a major energy agreement giving the US access to as much as 65 billion barrels of Venezuela’s crude reserves.
The political process has largely advanced without Machado. US-backed talks between Rodriguez’s government and a faction of the opposition ended their latest round this week with agreements to begin reviewing laws governing political disqualifications, political parties and public demonstrations, among other measures.
Opposition negotiator Dinorah Figuera also met Rodriguez at the Miraflores presidential palace following the talks, a striking image of engagement between the government and some of its political opponents even as Machado remained outside the process.
Figuera celebrated Machado’s return in a social post, saying the opposition will continue “without interruption in the conversation process until achieving a real and sustainable democracy in Venezuela”.
Machado had been signalling that her return was imminent. In a recent interview with the New York Times, she suggested she intended to mobilise Venezuelans ahead of eventual elections.
She has also criticised parts of Washington’s transition strategy, including the energy deal with businessman Alejandro Betancourt, potentially complicating an agreement that has become central to the administration’s plans for Venezuela.
The timing may also be significant. She has returned less than two weeks before US midterm elections that could shift control of Congress and subject the administration’s Venezuela policy to greater scrutiny.
Machado’s arrival follows fresh opposition protests in several Venezuelan cities demanding a presidential election date.
The authorities briefly detained at least seven people and blocked a route ahead of demonstrations in Caracas, testing the limits of the government’s political opening.
Machado went into hiding shortly after the disputed 2024 presidential election, saying she feared for her life as Nicolas Maduro’s government targeted opposition leaders.
She left Venezuela in late 2025 in a clandestine operation to collect her Nobel Peace Prize. BLOOMBERG

Off the Record: Yalta 2.0 spells bad news for Europe in desperate need of a plan
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
16:39:10 UTC
01:39:10 KST

In this week’s newsletter Euronews’ Chief Europe Editor Maria Tadeo examines an “unfortunate triumvirate” facing Europe: Trump, Xi and Putin.
Welcome back to Off the Record, coming to you from Brussels.
This week, a story made my jaw hit the floor.
Russian President Vladimir Putin has floated a three-way meeting with Donald Trump and China’s Xi Jinping to discuss a way out of the war in Ukraine, which he started. Trump seemed to confirm the pitch, without putting a date on it, suggesting it could be good for the world if it included denuclearisation.
If you’re not alarmed by this, you should be.
Putin wants a Yalta 2.0 moment. One that would restore his international stature and present Russia as a great power, much like the three-way summit that helped shape the post-WWII order 81 years ago in the resort city of Yalta.
In 1945, as victory over Nazi Germany drew closer, Roosevelt, Churchill and Stalin gathered in Yalta to divvy up the post-war world. The conference helped lay the groundwork for spheres of influence across Europe, with the Soviets subsequently cementing their control over practically all of Eastern Europe.
Churchill was an imperfect man, but nonetheless the war hero Great Britain needed at the time. He walked away from the whole affair disenchanted.
He knew the Soviets would engulf half of Europe, leaving the continent divided by an Iron Curtain for decades to come. In the midst of it all, Poland would be sacrificed, alongside the Baltic states, much of Central Europe and parts of the Balkans. And he was right. But he still had to accept the deal.
Yalta dictated the terms of a new world order, but also set the stage for the Cold War. Of course, the echoes of history can be cruel: Yalta has been under Russian occupation since 2014, following Moscow’s illegal annexation of Crimea.
If you follow that logic, the modern-day triumvirate of Trump, Xi and Putin would get together and split up the world for the next 100 years. One piece for you, another for me — you get the gist of it.
Presumably, the talks would focus on Ukraine and Taiwan. If Yalta 2.0 works anything like the 1945 conference, the three would cut a backroom deal and the rest of the world would have no choice but to go along with it. Putin would emerge as the winner, which explains why he’s pitching it in the first place.
Russia is a nuclear power, but it is no longer a great power. Putin, who once called the collapse of the Soviet Union “the greatest geopolitical catastrophe of the century” for Russia, has long sought to restore Moscow’s lost sphere of influence.
If Trump joins that meeting, he would be handing the Russian leader his biggest strategic victory since the Soviet Union’s collapse.
Along the way, the US President would alienate America’s friends. Trump may not think much of his allies, but they are crucial. Policing the world has brought Washington lucrative deals, enormous influence and military bases that it needs for its own security, whether Trump likes to admit it or not.
A new Yalta without his allies would certify the death of the West as we know it.
The Europeans should be very concerned, as they too are on the chopping board in this dangerous ménage à trois. A backroom deal over Kyiv’s head would also spell the end of the transatlantic relationship and erode NATO’s deterrence.
Brussels may insist it is in the game, but it’s clear that much is happening behind its back already. The Europeans need their own peace plan and a clear definition of what a good outcome truly entails — for Ukraine and for Europe.
Inevitably, this will force the EU to confront uncomfortable questions it has long avoided, from the territories Ukraine may not get back to the security guarantees it will need to provide in exchange for a US backstop. That means boots on the ground to ensure peace, and it can’t just be France and the UK.
The EU will also need to ring-fence funding for Ukraine as the political cycle turns against continued support. Let’s face it: it is expensive, and it’s becoming unpopular as protests over the cost of living mount.
Our politicians need to do a much better job of explaining that our security is at stake too, with more than 4,000 kilometres of Europe’s eastern flank at play. It is in Europe’s interest to reach a fair deal in Ukraine. The opposite will come back to haunt us.
Europe needs its own peace plan, starting with the appointment of an envoy who can secure a seat at the negotiating table, set out a clear negotiating position and report back. This should have been done a year ago. Enough with the Trump whisperer strategy. It doesn’t work. It is futile as long as Europe is not represented by someone who can speak with a political mandate.
If you’re not at the table, you’re on the menu. Serve it while it’s hot.
Thank you for reading Off The Record make sure to subscribe here.

Despite his early fame, he had to start all over again and earn a living through other work. PEOPLE reports this in an interview dated October 24, UNN writes.
Details
Mathews played Ritchie Petrie in the popular American sitcom, which ended in 1966. The actor was only 10 years old at the time. After filming ended, he returned to school and later earned a theater degree from the University of California, Los Angeles.
However, returning to the screen proved far more difficult than he had expected. Even his experience working on a successful television series did not guarantee him new roles, and the competition at auditions made him doubt his own prospects.
From television fame to odd jobs
After unsuccessful attempts to revive his acting career, Mathews moved behind the scenes in the film industry. He initially worked as a production assistant and later handled post-production for television projects.
When steady work was scarce, the actor accepted temporary jobs, including in the audiovisual field. He later worked in sales and post-production services management.
Now 71, Mathews has ended his professional career. After nearly 60 years in the entertainment industry, he devotes his time to his personal life and his wife, Jennifer, with whom he will soon celebrate their 40th wedding anniversary.

Mass rally against Netanyahu government just ahead of elections
Three days before Israel’s first general election since the genocidal war on Gaza began, thousands of Israelis protested against the Netanyahu government late on Saturday in Tel Aviv demanding an independent inquiry into the security failures that led to the October 7, 2023 attacks.
The protest was organised by the October Council, a group founded by the families of captives taken to Gaza three years ago, to demand accountability for the government’s failure to prevent the Hamas attack that preceded the war.
“Three days before the election, we will hold the culminating event marking three years of struggle to uncover the truth, demand accountability and establish a state commission of inquiry,” the October Council wrote on X ahead of the rally.

Lubinets asks people to report residents of Oleshky who need assistance
Kyiv • UNN
The Ombudsman’s Office is preparing a humanitarian mission to the temporarily occupied city of Oleshky. Information about those who need assistance can be submitted online or by phone.
Ukrainian Parliament Commissioner for Human Rights Dmytro Lubinets called on Ukrainians to provide information about residents of the temporarily occupied city of Oleshky in Kherson region who need assistance. The Ombudsman's Office is collecting such information to prepare a humanitarian mission in the city. Lubinets himself reported this, UNN writes.
Details
According to the ombudsman, a humanitarian mission to support people remaining in Oleshky is planned to be organized in the near future. It is currently important to collect as much information as possible about their situation and needs.
Particular attention is being paid to elderly people, people with reduced mobility, and those who cannot care for themselves independently. Lubinets called on the relatives and acquaintances of such people to contact his Office.
Where to report residents of Oleshky who need assistance
Information can be provided via WhatsApp, Viber, or Telegram at the following numbers:
- +38 067 717 51 70
- +38 073 719 81 34
- +38 067 182 55 04
The Ombudsman's Office also accepts inquiries by email at hotline\@ombudsman.gov.ua and through the institution's electronic office.
We are ready to process every inquiry and do everything possible to help our citizens
The ombudsman added that the humanitarian mission is being prepared in cooperation with Russia's Commissioner for Human Rights Yana Lantratova, mediated by U.S. First Lady Melania Trump. Lubinets himself maintains regular contact with the parties involved, government bodies, and local authorities.

Women founders are building India's social startups, their representation in nonprofits outpaces corporate leadership by a big margin, shows study
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
16:30:25 UTC
01:30:25 KST

Women founders are building India's social startups
NEW DELHI: A survey of more than 145 organisations working in the social impact space shows that over 57% of non-profits have at least one female founder – more than three times the 18% share reported among Indian startups. Moreover, female representation in the nonprofit sector outpaces corporate leadership, where women hold just 1.8% of CEO positions, 4.4% of CFO positions, and 29% of executive director roles.These findings are part of accelerator for non-profits Change Engine’s ‘East of Doing Good’ report - “Access to flexible funding: a Gender Lens”. The survey covers small organisations (annual budgets less than Rs 1 crore), medium (annual budgets between Rs 1 crore -5 crore) and large organisations (Rs 5 crore and more). The study sample also had an almost equal split between organisations eligible for foreign funding (with FCRA or US 501(c)) and those that were not.Out of the 145 plus organisations surveyed, nearly 31% have only female founders, while around 27% have both male and female founders.The research also shows that women are not only founding more nonprofits, but women founded organisations are better funded and hold more long term flexible funding.
The study found that non-profits with atleast one female founder also had bigger budgets. The data shows that 70% of organisations with at least one female founder have an annual budget of over Rs 1 crore, compared to 43.5% of organisations with only-male founders.Also around 21% of organisations with at least one female founder have more than 25% of their budget in flexible unrestricted funding, compared to just about 13% of organisations with only male founders. Flexible funding is the non-programmatic funding that nonprofits can use to invest in talent, technology, research and strengthening the organisation.As far as long-term grants are concerned it turns out that over 65% of organisations with at least one female founder have access to multi-year funding (three years or more), compared to around 56% of organisations with only male founders. Among these, around 27% of organisations with at least one female founder have received multi-year grants above Rs 1 crore, compared to just about 11% of only male founder organisations.The report highlights that when asked to rate (on a scale of 1-5) how easy it was to raise unrestricted funds from corporate social responsibility (CSR), high net-worth individuals (HNIs), domestic foundations, foreign foundations, and crowdfunding/retail, organisations with at least one female founder scored consistently scored higher across every category with an average score of 2.41 in comparison with 2.06 of organisations with only male founders.However, challenges remain. The study shows that cheque sizes remain small for everyone: “A staggering 82% of organisations with at least one female founder and 83% of only male founded organisations said typical unrestricted cheque sizes in India are less than Rs 25 lakh, showing that the small-cheque problem cuts across gender lines,” the study highlights.
Varun Aggarwal and Shubham Bansal, co-founders, Change Engine highlighted that the findings show that women are leading India’s social sector and building bigger and better resourced organisations. We need to encourage more women to come into this sector," Aggarwal asserted. “In our accelerator, we meet women founders who are building strong, ambitious institutions to tackle some of India’s biggest social challenges. It’s encouraging to see that what we’ve been observing on the ground is now backed by data. Six in ten nonprofits in our survey were founded by a woman founder,” Bansal added.However, the Change Engine founders highlight that the access to unrestricted flexible funding remains consistently low across the board with 80% of the surveyed founders reporting that they struggle to scale their work due to the lack of unrestricted funding. “This funding rigidity forces organisations to spend disproportionate time on fundraising, rather than focusing on innovation and impact,” they added.

Netanyahu postpones Gaza security, administrative arrangements until after Israeli election
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
16:23:33 UTC
01:23:33 KST

Zein Khalil and Rania Abushamala
25 October 2026•Update: 25 October 2026
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has postponed security and administrative arrangements regarding the future of the Gaza Strip until after the Oct. 27 election, including the deployment of an international force and the arrival of a committee to administer the territory, according to Israeli media on Sunday.
Israel’s public broadcaster KAN said Netanyahu has ordered a delay in the travel of about 7,000 Palestinians from Gaza to Egypt for police training, despite being approved by Israel’s Shin Bet domestic security agency.
The outlet said the decision was part of “a series of steps concerning the future of the Gaza Strip that the Israeli political leadership has postponed until after the election.”
The delayed measures also include preparations to build a new city in Rafah, the deployment of an international stabilization force in Gaza and the arrival of the National Committee for the Administration of Gaza.
The Hebrew-language newspaper Israel Hayom reported that the Shin Bet had given security clearance to between 5,000 and 7,000 Palestinians being considered for police training in Egypt.
The agency’s role was limited to vetting names submitted to it by US President Donald Trump’s Board of Peace, the newspaper said, adding that it had no authority to decide whether the candidates could travel.
The paper cited informed sources as saying that instructions to delay Gaza reconstruction measures had been issued by Israeli political leaders in stages over recent weeks, rather than through a single explicit order to halt the process.
The instructions included general indications that the measures should be implemented after the election, the sources said.
They suggested the delays may reflect concerns that Gaza reconstruction efforts and the training of Palestinian police officers in Egypt “do not serve Netanyahu’s political interests at this time.”
In August, Netanyahu denied approving the deployment of an international stabilization force in Gaza, although its deployment is part of Trump’s plan to end Israel’s war on the territory.
The force is expected to comprise troops from several countries and be led by a US general, according to the Board of Peace.
Last July, the Board of Peace announced a roadmap for implementing the next phases of the Gaza ceasefire agreement. Hamas later announced its acceptance of the plan and called for Israel to be compelled to implement it.
The roadmap calls for transferring administration of Gaza to the national committee under international supervision, deploying the international stabilization force, placing Hamas’ weapons under the committee’s responsibility, and carrying out a phased Israeli withdrawal alongside reconstruction.
Netanyahu, however, announced in August that he rejected the understandings, insisting that Hamas disarm before any Israeli withdrawal.
Despite a ceasefire that took effect on Oct. 10, 2025, the Israeli army has killed 1,551 Palestinians and injured 5,573 others, according to Gaza’s Health Ministry.
Since October 2023, Israel's war in Gaza has killed more than 74,000 Palestinians and wounded over 175,000, while causing widespread destruction to about 90% of the territory's civilian infrastructure.

Egypt's water security cannot be compromised -- president
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
00:14:09 CST
01:14:09 KST

CAIRO, Oct. 25 (Xinhua) -- Egyptian President Abdel Fattah El-Sisi said here on Sunday that Egypt faces a unique water challenge due to its geographic nature and reliance on the Nile River, warning that the country's water security cannot be compromised.
In a recorded address opening the ninth Cairo Water Week, Sisi noted that the Nile provides Egypt with more than 98 percent of its renewable water resources, reiterating his country's willingness to cooperate with other basin states based on international law, consultation, coordination, good neighborliness, and the principle of causing no harm.
The Egyptian president noted that Egypt has consciously chosen the path of cooperation and dialogue, saying "Egypt respects and supports the right of all Nile Basin states to development."
Highlighting cooperation with southern Nile Basin countries on proposed projects in energy, agriculture and irrigation, Sisi said Egypt looks forward to reinforcing cooperation in the Eastern Nile Basin as well "in a manner that serves the interests of Egypt, Sudan, and Ethiopia."
Meanwhile, Sisi emphasized, "Any wager that Egypt will accept a fait accompli or compromise its water security is a losing wager," stressing that the state will not neglect its responsibility to protect the interests of the Egyptian people.
The president called for turning the potential of the Nile Basin into partnerships that maximize shared benefits, safeguard the rights of all nations, and ensure that the Nile remains a source of development, prosperity, and stability for all peoples of the Basin.
Downstream countries, Egypt and Sudan, have repeatedly voiced concern over their water shares following the construction of the Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam (GERD) by upstream Ethiopia. Years of trilateral negotiations have failed to produce a binding legal agreement on the rules governing the filling and operation of the dam.
Ethiopia officially inaugurated the dam in September 2025, saying the hydropower project would boost electricity generation and economic development without harming downstream countries.
Held under the theme "Water as a Catalyst for Peace, Shared Prosperity and a Sustainable Planet," the five-day Ninth Cairo Water Week runs until Thursday. More than 130 sessions are scheduled on water security, capacity building, and preparations for the 2026 UN Water Conference to be convened in the UAE in December. ■

China Focus: China marks anniversary of Taiwan's recovery with events across Taiwan Strait
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
00:13:46 CST
01:13:46 KST

This photo shows a commemorative stamp issued by China Post to mark Taiwan Recovery Day. China Post issued a commemorative stamp marking Taiwan Recovery Day on Sunday. Featuring the Great Wall, Alishan and Sun Moon Lake, the stamp attracted strong interest from collectors at postal outlets and online platforms across the mainland. (Xinhua)
BEIJING/TAIPEI, Oct. 25 (Xinhua) -- China on Sunday marked the 81st anniversary of its recovery of Taiwan and observed Taiwan Recovery Day, with commemorative events held across the Taiwan Strait to honor the shared history of resistance against Japanese aggression and reaffirm calls for national reunification.
A symposium in Fuzhou, capital of east China's Fujian Province, brought together about 200 participants, including descendants of Taiwan's anti-Japanese resistance fighters and revolutionary martyrs, young people from both sides of the Strait, representatives from Hong Kong, Macao and overseas communities, and experts and scholars.
Song Tao, head of both the Taiwan Work Office of the Communist Party of China Central Committee and the Taiwan Affairs Office of the State Council, said at the symposium that the establishment of Taiwan Recovery Day underscored China's firm resolve to safeguard its sovereignty and territorial integrity and helped consolidate the international consensus on upholding the one-China principle.
Song urged people on both sides of the Strait to carry forward the spirit of the Chinese people's resistance against Japanese aggression and resolutely oppose "Taiwan independence" secessionism and foreign interference. He pledged firm support for patriots in Taiwan who support reunification and reaffirmed the mainland's commitment to advancing national reunification.
Hung Hsiu-chu, former chairwoman of the Chinese Kuomintang party and chairwoman of the Taiwan-based Chinese Cyan Geese Peace Education Foundation, said people on both sides of the Strait should carry forward the spirit of those who defended the country's territory and work toward peaceful reunification.
Following its war against China in 1894, Japan seized Taiwan and the Penghu Islands in 1895, subjecting Taiwan to five decades of colonial rule. Taiwan's recovery in 1945 marked a hard-won victory in the Chinese people's resistance against Japanese aggression during World War II and a defining moment in the nation's efforts to safeguard its sovereignty and territorial integrity.
In October 2025, China's national legislature designated Oct. 25 as Taiwan Recovery Day.
In Beijing, the Central Committee of the Taiwan Democratic Self-Government League held a commemorative event on Saturday at a memorial square in the city's western suburbs. Participants observed a moment of silence, sang songs and laid flowers before a monument measuring 14 meters long and 4 meters high, paying tribute to those who sacrificed their lives for national reunification.
Xu Yunchu, granddaughter of revolutionary martyr Zhu Feng, said the history of Taiwan's recovery demonstrated that Taiwan is an inalienable part of China.
"Our territory must remain undivided, and our nation must remain united. Chinese on both sides of the Strait should work together to safeguard the common homeland of the Chinese nation," she said.
Chen Wen-cheng, a young participant from Taiwan, said establishing Taiwan Recovery Day was significant in strengthening historical awareness among people in Taiwan and deepening emotional ties across the Strait. He called on younger generations to preserve their shared historical memory and carry forward the aspirations of their predecessors.
Other commemorative activities included the release in Beijing of a music video about Taiwan's recovery, an exhibition in Shanghai featuring historical materials on Taiwan people's resistance against Japanese aggression, and a seminar in Jinhua, Zhejiang Province, on the history and legacy of the Taiwan volunteer corps, a force formed by patriotic Taiwan residents to resist Japanese aggression during WWII.
China Post also issued a commemorative stamp marking Taiwan Recovery Day on Sunday. Featuring the Great Wall, Alishan and Sun Moon Lake, the stamp attracted strong interest from collectors at postal outlets and online platforms across the mainland.
In Taiwan, representatives from more than 20 groups gathered on Sunday at the Taipei Zhongshan Hall, where a ceremony to accept Japan's surrender in Taiwan Province of the China war theater of the Allied powers was held in 1945, marking the end of five decades of Japanese colonial rule.
Participants sang a song commemorating Taiwan's recovery and paid tribute to those who fought against Japanese aggression before a stone monument in the square outside the hall.
The commemorative event took place as the secessionist-minded Democratic Progressive Party authorities in Taiwan have conspicuously avoided mentioning China's victory in the War of Resistance Against Japanese Aggression and China's recovery of Taiwan, and repeatedly downplayed or whitewashed Japan's colonial rule over the island.
Hsiung Yi, deputy secretary-general of the Reunification Alliance Party in Taiwan, said Taiwan's recovery is a shared historical memory of all Chinese people.
"History must not be forgotten. We must never erase the crimes committed by the aggressors. I hope more people in Taiwan will remember this day and the profound significance it carries," Hsiung said.
A Taipei resident surnamed Yu, whose family originated in east China's Shandong Province, said her father had often reminded the family that "we are Chinese." She attended the ceremony because she was concerned about insufficient media coverage of the anniversary and wanted to support efforts to preserve historical truth.
Chi Hsing, who works with Taiwan-based magazine The Observer, said the joint commemorations on both sides of the Strait underscored that both sides of the Strait belong to an inseparable community with a shared future.
The ceremony concluded with representatives reading a joint statement calling for remembrance of history, opposition to Japanese militarism, the preservation of peace and the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. ■

'Putin's paranoia' — New air defenses appear around Russian president's Valdai residence, analysis shows
Russia has built an additional ring of air defense towers within 50 kilometers (30 miles) of Russian President Vladimir Putin's residence in Valdai, Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty (RFE/RL) and OSINT analyst Jembob reported on Oct. 25.
Valdai is a small town in Russia's northwestern Novgorod Oblast. The town had a population of around 13,600 in 2025, according to Russia's Federal State Statistics Service (Rosstat).
The defensive perimeter extends to the Khotilovo military base, which serves as an alternate landing site, and a secret biological laboratory on Lisiy Island, according to RFE/RL.
Satellite images indicate that the new perimeter encompasses both the military airfield in Khotilovo and the laboratory complex on Lisiy Island.
By October, air defense systems believed to be Pantsir or Tor units had been positioned south of Putin's residence, within the 50-kilometer (30-mile) zone.
No positions have yet been identified along the northern section of the perimeter, though additional sites could be established in the coming months, the report said.
One of the towers forming the outer defensive line was already in place by March 2026, on the grounds of the Khotilovo military air base. Putin reportedly uses the base regularly. A dedicated railway branch connects it to his Valdai residence, providing a direct train route, according to RFE/RL.
Other air defense sites have been established along the shores of the Vyshny Volochyok Reservoir.
RFE/RL published an investigation into the secret laboratory on the island on Sept. 3, around the same time construction began on two new air defense towers in the area.
The Kremlin accused Ukraine of attacking Putin's residence in Valdai with more than 90 drones on Dec. 29, 2025. Russian officials claimed the drones were carrying 6-kilogram (13-pound) high-explosive warheads, but claimed that air defenses had allegedly intercepted them all, with no casualties or damage reported.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky and the Foreign Ministry denied the allegations, calling them a "lie." Kyiv also accused Moscow of fabricating the claims to undermine Ukraine's standing with U.S. President Donald Trump's administration and derail ongoing peace efforts.
In early January 2026, the U.S. Central Intelligence Agency (CIA) informed Trump that Ukraine had not targeted Putin's Valdai residence. U.S. intelligence assessed that Ukrainian forces had struck a military facility in the same region that night, but far from the Russian president's residence.

====================================================================================================

Protein shakes for teenagers: Good or bad idea?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
16:12:00 UTC
01:12:00 KST

Protein shakes for teenagers: Good or bad idea?
October 25, 2026
You can take it as a powdered drink, or in a snack bar. Puddings and certain breads are also promoted as "sources of protein," and protein-enriched products like Kindershake and Teen Balance are specifically designed to appeal to a young people — and it appears to be working.
In a representative survey of almost 1,000 parents by the University of Michigan in 2024, just under half said their children, who were aged 13 to 17, had consumed protein products over the previous year. The survey found that boys were more likely to do so than girls, especially in connection with sport, or to build muscle. Girls took them to balance their diet, and to lose weight.
According to the statistics portal Statista, between March 2024 and March 2025 the fitness protein product market in Germany recorded a huge jump of around 25% in retail revenue.
How much protein do we actually need?
Proteins are key building blocks for our metabolism. They play an important role in building up and repairing tissue in our muscles, skin and organs. Proteins are the basis for the formation of enzymes that regulate chemical reactions in the body, and of antibodies that are vital for our immune system.
According to the German Nutrition Society (DGE), healthy adults should consume 0.8 grams of protein daily per kilogram of body weight. A woman weighing 65 kilos should eat 52 grams of protein per day, for example.
But they can do this without special protein products. A portion of oat flakes with an almond drink for breakfast, a baked potato with curd cheese for lunch, and two slices of wholemeal bread with peanut butter in the evening — objective achieved.
Young people should consume a little more, as they are still growing. For them, the formula is 0.9 grams of protein per kilo of body weight. A teenager weighing 45 kilos should therefore eat 40.5 grams of protein per day. People over 65 and children aged one to four should have a little more: one gram of protein per kilo of body weight.
Older people tend to eat too little protein, often because their appetite decreases. But a study done in Germany between 2015 and 2017 showed that children and young people there often consume too much. Around half of six- to 17-year-olds ate more than double the recommended daily amount of protein.
Can too much protein be dangerous?
Too much protein can be harmful in the long term, according to the DGE. Various studies show that children who eat too much protein, particularly animal protein, often become overweight. Some enter puberty early.
Above all, too much protein can put excessive strain on the kidneys, causing damage. The kidneys have to convert the amino acids that constitute the building blocks of proteins into urea before they are excreted in urine. Damage is particularly likely if a person doesn't drink enough fluids, or has pre-existing kidney damage — but adolescents are also at greater risk.
Protein helps build muscle and shed weight
A person's protein requirement is greater if they are very physically active. Among other things, according to a DGE position paper, proteins can help maintain or build up muscular mass and strength, and support recovery after strain.
The paper states that, depending on physical condition and what they are training for, sportspeople should consume between 1.2 and 2 grams of protein per kilo of body weight, divided into several portions throughout the day. These recommendations only apply to people who train for more than five hours a day.
Proteins are of interest to people who want to lose weight because they are good at satisfying hunger. People usually lose more weight by following a protein-rich diet rather than another. Long-term, though, the most important thing to look at is: How many calories am I consuming, and how many am I burning?
Is animal protein better than plant protein?
Overall, plant proteins usually contain somewhat fewer essential amino acids than animal protein. "Essential" because the body cannot make them by itself – it has to take them in as food.
However, wholegrain products, pulses, or nuts are also higher in fiber, vitamins, and unsaturated fats – all of which are healthy. The DGE therefore advises that protein intake should be increased primarily with sources of plant protein.
What is the criticism leveled against protein products?
Protein powders and bars are often enriched not only with vitamins and minerals but also with unhelpful ingredients like sweeteners, sugar, additives and flavorings. The German Sport University in Cologne even found doping substances in protein products that were praised for building muscle.
Adolescents in particular might experience an unpleasant side-effect of consuming protein powders. These usually consist of milk proteins. There are various ways in which milk proteins can increase the skin's production of sebum, and this can trigger or exacerbate acne, although a direct link between milk protein products and acne has not been definitively proven.
Specialists are also skeptical about protein shakes, fearing that they could lead to young people eating fewer normal meals, and thus consuming less fiber, micronutrients, and healthy fats.
'High protein content' = higher price
Protein-enriched foods are usually expensive. In a 2022 study, consumer organizations also found that foods that are naturally high in protein, such as cheese, curds, or soya drinks, often cost more if the protein content has been highlighted by the manufacturer.
Not even sportspeople with a high protein requirement need to supplement their diet with special protein products. The DGE advises that they should aim to satisfy their requirements by optimizing their diet, and says there is no scientific evidence that our bodies require protein-enriched food supplements when put under strain.
However, the experts do say that it may make sense for people to use protein preparations if they have allergies, problems with digestion, chewing, or swallowing, or if their appetite is very low.

Why is the Middle East waiting out the Trump presidency?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
16:08:54 UTC
01:08:54 KST

There appears to be little prospect of lasting peace between Iran and the United States while Donald Trump remains in the White House. This is a view that an increasing number of serious actors across the region now seem to share. Eight months into Iran war, Washington has neither broken Tehran’s resolve nor found a clear path out. The president’s own remarks point to a narrowing set of options. Trump told TIME he does not believe peace with Iran is ever possible, a striking admission from the leader still expected to negotiate one.
Tehran, for its part, has set conditions it knows this administration cannot meet, insisting that sanctions and threats be lifted before talks resume and that not a single gram of enriched uranium leaves the country. Neither side is bargaining towards a settlement. Each is waiting for the political ground beneath the other to shift.
Trump’s problem is that the ground is shifting under him first, as the 3rd November midterms approach with his approval rating near 39 per cent and crude trading above 110 dollars a barrel. The House has voted three times to restrict his war powers in Iran, with Republican candidates in competitive seats now campaigning openly on ending the war to lower petrol prices. Facing a likely defeat, the president has promised no strikes before polling day while Central Command has reportedly been told to prepare for resuming major combat operations. Therefore, it is quite likely that Trump may order striking Iran even before the mid-term day.
Analysts have noted that a Republican defeat could strengthen this incentive, as a president with little left to lose at the ballot box faces fewer costs for escalation. Yet such strikes would do little damage control, since a Politico survey found 46 per cent of voters said ending the war before the election would not change their vote at all. Iran has meanwhile fortified its nuclear sites and warned that regional energy infrastructure would be targeted, so any parting blow risks sending oil prices even higher.
The president’s own inner circle appears to have read the same numbers and is quietly positioning itself for the aftermath. Vice President JD Vance, reportedly sceptical from the outset, has kept his distance and this week declined to endorse Benjamin Netanyahu ahead of Israel’s election.
Secretary of State Marco Rubio, his chief rival for 2028, spent the same week in India on a trip devoted largely to trade rather than Iran.
Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth, by contrast, made an unannounced visit to Israel a day after Trump endorsed Netanyahu, keeping himself firmly in the frame. Commentators suggested as early as April that Hegseth was being set up as the fall guy should the war end badly. His visibility since has only reinforced that impression.
The Gulf states have reached the same conclusion. They are hedging accordingly against an American policy they no longer trust to last. The UAE joined the campaign against Iran in February, yet they opened a backchannel with Iranians lately after the realization that it is better to deal directly instead of relying on the US. Moreover, the UAE, by the virtue of being in support of the Saudis vis-à-vis Yemen, is trying to find a diplomatic way to lower tensions. It signals a striking reversal in barely eight months. Having absorbed thousands of Iranian missiles and drones, Abu Dhabi appears to be securing its own understandings before Washington’s next round begins.
Yemen shows how the burden is being shifted, since the United States has twice rebuffed Saudi requests for airstrikes against the Houthis and says it will not take kinetic action for now. Instead, the UAE has reportedly agreed to resume funding anti-Houthi forces in southern Yemen. This is an arrangement that lets Washington stay out while a partner carries the fight on its behalf.
Iran’s strategy rests on patience and its leaders appear confident they can absorb another year or so of American pressure before the political weather in Washington changes. Its posture towards Saudi Arabia fits this reading more closely than the images of burning airports suggest. Houthi strikes have killed at least 19 people at Saudi airports, and the Wall Street Journal has reported Revolutionary Guard officers helping to direct them. Yet within days of the deadliest attack, Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi called Riyadh to offer mediation with the Houthis and insist the crisis had no military solution.
The aim is not to destroy Saudi infrastructure but to convince the kingdom that American protection is unreliable and that any opening to Israel will carry a heavy price. Riyadh has begun to absorb that lesson, but the pressure is unlikely to ease while Trump remains in office and Tehran sees no reason to settle.
The real question is how Israel reacts to all this, both during the remainder of Netanyahu’s tenure and after it. Trump has endorsed Netanyahu so he can help “finish the job” against Iran, and Israel has reportedly asked that any renewed strikes wait until after its 27 October vote. Polls give Netanyahu’s coalition fewer than 50 of the 61 seats needed to govern, raising the prospect of a weakened caretaker with every reason to keep the Iran file burning.
A successor led by Gadi Eisenkot would hardly soften Israel’s line on the Iranian nuclear programme, but it might be less willing to tie national strategy to American president’s fortunes. Should Israel strike alone after an American exit, Gulf hedging would only accelerate and normalisation with Riyadh would recede further from view.
Tehran and the Gulf have made their calculations. Both now wait for a different figure in the Oval Office.
The views expressed in this article belong to the author and do not necessarily reflect the editorial policy of Middle East Monitor.

The health and wellbeing of around 1200 Palestinian civilians in the West Bank is being put at risk by the forced displacement being carried out in response to a terror attack carried out by two terrorists last week, multiple Israeli human rights organizations told The Jerusalem Post on Sunday.
The IDF announced that its operation in the Al-Jaladah and Ein Deir Baha neighborhoods near the military checkpoint at the entrance to Hebron was aimed at locating terrorists and weapons and would include demolitions.
The Palestinian Authority condemned the operation as “collective punishment,” while Palestinian officials warned that it would have a significant impact on civilian life. Yousef Zouhair Al-Jabari, head of Hebron’s municipality, told Reuters that around 1,300 additional people faced losing their homes, on top of the 1,200 already displaced.
Al-Jabari alleged that the military had demolished shops, factories, homes, and roads in Hebron.
Milena Ansari, director of Physicians for Human Rights Israel’s Palestinian Territory Department, told the Post that the effects of the latest operation were already being felt by sick and vulnerable residents.
Palestinians fear displacement could be more long-term
Citing the testimony of Osama Abu Sbeih, a Palestinian ambulance driver with the private Al-Salam Ambulance service in Hebron, PHRI reported multiple incidents in which patients were unable to reach critical medical care promptly, including a six-month-old baby suffering from a lung infection who had to wait two days to be transferred from a hospital in Ramallah to Hebron.
“Crews are relying on passing patients from one ambulance to another at checkpoints. Even our mobile clinic that usually goes across the West Bank to provide medical treatment couldn’t reach Msafaryatta for a scheduled medical day,” Ansari said. “But it’s the long-term damage, which is a bit less visible but is as serious as what we’re seeing right now on the ground.”
Ansari shared her fears that the temporary displacement would become more long-term, and warned that the Palestinians housed in temporary shelters or in the crowded homes of relatives would be at risk. Noting that many of the shelters lack proper heating, entering the winter months without proper housing could drive respiratory infections.
For those with chronic conditions, she continued, the disruption to routine can create emergencies. Patients with hypertension, diabetes and on dialysis might particularly struggle should these disruptions become long-term, she warned.
“The psychological toll of being forced out of your home in the middle of the night, especially for the children…These psychological hardships last longer even after an operation ends,” Ansari shared.
Israeli rights group tells IDF there's no link between demolitions and terror attack
The Association for Civil Rights in Israel, in a letter addressed to senior officials in the IDF, including IDF Central Command chief Maj. Gen. Avi Bluth, seen by the Post, complained that there was no evidence of links between the houses being destroyed and the terrorists who carried out last week’s attacks.
ACRI also shared concern in response to the Palestinian claim that some of the displaced were removed from their home at night and left without shelter, that worshipers had been cut off from accessing the Ibrahimi mosque and that thousands were cut off from reaching work and school.
“No attack, however grave, gives the military license to punish an entire city. Families who had nothing to do with the attack are being driven out and their homes demolished, while ministers present this to voters, a few days before the election, as the price Palestinians must pay. That is collective punishment. The military must stop it and let these families return home now, and ACRI will use every legal means available to make sure it does,” said Noa Sattath, Executive Director of ACRI.

Enforce the draft, but don't punish haredi kids for their fathers refusal to serve - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
16:07:35 UTC
01:07:35 KST

“If they don’t serve, they shouldn’t get a shekel.” This line has become a staple of the High Court of Justice rulings, attorney-general opinions, Knesset speeches, and WhatsApp groups. It is no longer rhetoric. Since the High Court ruled in June 2024 that there is no legal basis for exempting yeshiva students from the draft, the sanctions have only grown.
Yeshivas lose funding for draft-age students, and the Labor Ministry’s daycare criteria now deny the subsidy to any family whose father is classified as a draft evader, even if he is employed. Draft bills go further: National Insurance benefits, housing programs, property tax discounts, driver’s licenses, and travel abroad.
For a kollel family of six, “benefits” is a bureaucrat’s word for groceries. Stripped of euphemism, the proposal is that the state will help feed a haredi (ultra-Orthodox) father’s children if he serves, and not if he doesn’t.
Whether haredim must serve (many already do, in the Hashmonaim Brigade) is a hard argument between citizens. Settling it by controlling who eats is not an argument at all. It is a tactic, and it has a history.
Lenin made “He who does not work, neither shall he eat” a principle of state in May 1918, calling it the “root principle of socialism” in a letter about seizing grain. Within months, Petrograd (now Saint Petersburg) was rationing bread by class.
Stalin wrote the slogan into his 1936 constitution; Mao’s 1975 constitution adopted it too. Each makes the same move: the state decides what counts as work, then feeds those who comply. Trotsky saw where that leads: where the state is the sole employer, the principle becomes, “Who does not obey shall not eat.”
The slogan has been used on Jews before. The 1918 Soviet constitution disenfranchised clergy, creating the lishentsy. Rabbis, kosher slaughterers, and cantors were counted as non-laborers; from 1929 they were denied ration cards, evicted from state housing, and their children barred from universities.
The Yevsektsiya shut cheders (schoolrooms) and yeshivas on precisely the grounds now heard in Jerusalem: that men who sit and learn produce nothing.
The Nazis followed the same path, stripping Jews of their professions, their children’s schooling, and public welfare before reaching for anything worse. Every clause of the argument is now being said, in Hebrew, by people who would be horrified to hear its Russian original.
A democracy enforces its laws on individuals; it does not ration bread to communities. If the Knesset passes a draft law, the state may summon, try, fine, or jail each man who refuses, as it would any secular evader. Sanctions on the evader himself – a fine, his license, his passport – are ordinary tools of law. But the state may not make children answer for their fathers.
A three-year-old in Bnei Brak did not dodge the draft. Cutting her daycare subsidy enlists no one; it punishes her. A sanction that falls on a child is a child’s lunch withheld until her father complies.
Israel should reconsider its tactics with the Haredi draft
Jewish law refuses to condition food. The Talmud (Bava Batra 9a) and Shulchan Aruch (Yoreh De’ah 251:10) rule that one who asks for food is fed at once, without investigation.
The Torah’s model of the citizen who does not fight is not the parasite but the Levi, whom the Rambam (Hilchot Shmita v’Yovel 13:12-13) described as set apart for God’s service and fed by the nation, a “standing open” to anyone whose spirit moves him. The vocabulary of “parasites” is not Jewish. We borrowed it.
Welfare states condition benefits on need and income; the Soviet way was conditioning them on obedience, and on a father’s obedience for his child’s food. The daycare rule, applied even when the father works, shows what Israel is doing.
Israel should also consider who it is pulling the lever on.
There are about 1.4 million haredim, with a birth rate near six and a half, and a quarter of Jewish first-graders – on CBS projections, a third of Israel’s Jews within a generation. Squeezing a 10th of the country’s consumers is not a policy but a recession. And they are the keepers of what held the Jewish people to this land through two thousand years of exile.
Nor are they unwilling to fight: Hashmonaim soldiers have fought and fallen in Gaza, not because their children’s daycare was threatened, but because the state built a framework that kept their kashrut, prayer, and rabbis intact. Israel can have the Hashmonaim or the ration book. It cannot have both.
Coercion does not integrate; it disintegrates. Stalin’s Gulag, where rations were graded by output, should have produced perfect compliance. Solzhenitsyn records the opposite: the special camps forged a solidarity that erupted in strikes and revolts, culminating in the 40 Days of Kengir uprising. A sanction felt at the kitchen table binds families to their community.
Every lost daycare place becomes evidence for those who call the state an enemy of Torah, and the young man who might have enlisted must now do so as a defection from his besieged neighbors. The Talmud (Sotah 47a) teaches that the left hand pushes away while the right draws near.
Integration succeeds by making membership worth having: units like Hashmonaim whose soldiers leave as observant as they entered; respect for those diligently learning; career tracks that honor the beit midrash; and a public language that treats Torah as a shared treasure rather than a debt.
The High Court has never affirmed the haredim’s right to serve in such a unit. If it will not, its call for integration is not sincere; it is an attempt to uproot haredi values. Alienation produces radicals; belonging produces citizens.
“Her ways are ways of pleasantness.” A Jewish state that wants its most devout citizens beside it should try those ways first.
The writer is an attorney in Jerusalem and principal of David Page Law, a full-service law firm with an emphasis on real estate, wills, trusts, and estates. He has taught law at the Hebrew University at the Faculty of Law and made aliyah after a judicial clerkship and a year in Washington DC’s largest law firm. He is also a member of R’ Daniel Belsky’s Kollel and the author of Rav Gustman, on the Rosh Yeshiva who was the last Dayan of Vilna, and the creator of the podcast The Kings of Israel.

====================================================================================================

Israel must confront double standards in Hebron security, accountability - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
16:07:29 UTC
01:07:29 KST

I reject all armed attacks, and I believe that security for Israelis and dignity for Palestinians must form the foundation of any shared future. That position also compels me to ask: Why does an entire Palestinian city become the target of sweeping military measures after a single attack, while we see no equally determined response to protect Palestinians from repeated settler attacks?
Events in Hebron following the October 23 attack make this question urgent. Reports of closures, families forced to leave their homes, raids and demolitions describe measures whose impact extends beyond the perpetrators, affecting large sections of the population and their daily lives.
In my assessment, the speed and scale of this response reveal a political template ready for implementation, activated after Friday’s attack: expanding responsibility from the perpetrator to those around him, then to the neighborhood and the city, and turning civilian life into an instrument of pressure.
This is a political interpretation of the pattern of response, rather than a claim to possess a document proving that the operation’s details were prepared in advance. The question this pattern raises is whether the objective is to pursue those responsible for the attack or to subjugate an entire community by making it bear the consequences.
A double standard in responding to attacks on Palestinian civilians
That question becomes even more pressing when we compare this response with the treatment of settler violence.
When Palestinian civilians are killed in attacks, their property is burned, or their communities are assaulted, where is the mobilization to ensure their protection? Where are the effective, sustained measures to prevent further attacks and bring those responsible to trial?
I reject collective punishment, whether directed at Hebron’s residents or at the residents of settlements from which attackers targeting Palestinians emerge. I demand one standard: Pursue the perpetrator, protect the victim, and do not hold civilians responsible for crimes they did not commit.
The fact that some settlers have been arrested does not, by itself, answer this question. The measure of a law enforcement system is its ability to prevent attacks, investigate them, and hold perpetrators accountable. The problem lies in the persistent gap between the scale of the violence and the effectiveness of deterrence and accountability.
In its reports, the Israeli organization Yesh Din has linked settler violence against Palestinians to the settlement expansion project and described the support this violence receives from state institutions. These findings deserve serious scrutiny and accountability.
In my view, this disparity reflects a deliberate political approach that has become entrenched in practice: tolerance of settler violence that pressures Palestinians to leave, alongside the use of extensive force and measures affecting entire communities when violence comes from the Palestinian side.
The political consequence of this tolerance is clear: Remaining on their land becomes more difficult for Palestinians, while the settlement presence expands. When this pattern repeats itself, it becomes difficult to treat it as a series of security failures disconnected from politics.
The result is two systems of protection and accountability operating on the same land, with their effectiveness varying according to the identity of the perpetrator and the victim.
Protecting lives in the West Bank
Another aspect of this contradiction appears in the way the West Bank is presented within Israel’s statistical framework. Israeli tables covering the population of Israeli localities there count settlers, who number roughly half a million, while the millions of Palestinians living on the same land fall outside that population category.
This statistical distinction reflects the scope of those tables. It does not mean that Palestinians are not counted by other bodies, nor does it establish, on its own, the existence of a discriminatory security policy.
But it raises a deeper question about the exercise of authority: Do the Israeli military and security institutions regard Palestinians as residents whose rights and needs require protection, or primarily as subjects of surveillance and control?
Palestinians exist, and they have a clear legal status and rights. Under the law of occupation, Israel has obligations toward them, such as protecting them from violence, including settler violence, and maintaining public order and civilian life. Those obligations do not disappear because Palestinians lack Israeli citizenship.
The issue, therefore, is the responsibility of an authority legally obliged to provide protection, and the need to hold it accountable when it fails to fulfill that duty or applies it selectively.
Any system that exercises military control over land, roads, and people’s movement, while providing effective protection to one population and leaving another exposed to attack, creates a crisis that goes beyond an isolated security failure. It makes identity a decisive factor in determining who enjoys safety and whose life is restricted in the name of someone else’s security.
As a Palestinian who advocates dialogue and a democratic, demilitarized Palestinian state alongside Israel, I see this reality as a danger to the future of both peoples. We ask young Palestinians to believe in peaceful political action. That choice needs tangible results and confidence that the rights, lives, and property of those who embrace it will be protected.
When a peaceful Palestinian cannot protect his home from an attack or reach his workplace because of a measure imposed on him despite his having no connection to any attack, the credibility of the path we urge him to follow is weakened.
In Masar Jadid – New Path – our guiding message is “From confrontation to dialogue.” We work for politics that improve people’s lives, institutions that protect them, and accountability for perpetrators, whoever they may be.
The people of Hebron deserve protection, freedom of movement, and a life of dignity. So do Palestinians exposed to settler attacks throughout the West Bank.
The true test of any policy claiming to deliver security is its ability to protect civilians and hold those responsible for violence accountable under one standard. Security for Israelis will not be sustainable as long as Palestinians living under Israeli control are denied effective and equal protection.

Transcript: Attorney General Todd Blanche on "Face the Nation with Margaret Brennan," Oct. 25, 2026
The following is the transcript of the interview with Attorney General Todd Blance that aired on "Face the Nation with Margaret Brennan" on Oct. 25, 2026.
MARGARET BRENNAN: And we begin with U.S. Attorney General Todd Blanche. Good morning to you, sir.
ATTORNEY GENERAL TODD BLANCHE: Good morning.
MARGARET BRENNAN: So we're nine days out. Your colleague Harmeet Dhillon, whose office would oversee election integrity cases, told my colleagues over at 60 Minutes that, quote, "absent some shocking contingency that's unexpected, there should be no interruption in the usual course of counting and certifying the results in the states." Do you share that view?
AG BLANCHE: Well, yes, of course. Absent- absent some facts that require us to do otherwise, there's President Trump, the Department of Justice- we don't want to have to get a law involved in elections, of course not. But that doesn't mean that at times any Justice Department doesn't do that and shouldn't do that if the facts and the law require it.
MARGARET BRENNAN: Well, it seems you already are taking action up in Alaska. Just for our audience to understand, there are two Dan Sullivans on the ballot there. There's the incumbent senator, a Republican, Dan S. Sullivan, and then there's a challenger there, Dan J. Sullivan. The Justice Department is suing Alaska preemptively to block the certification of the results if Senator Sullivan loses. Now, President Trump was asked about this lawsuit. He said quote, "I'm the one that said do it." Who did he tell to do this? Did he tell you to do this?
AG BLANCHE: Well, first of all, let me correct you, okay. You describe facts that were just simply either at best misleading, but really a lie to your viewers. Russians attacked a minibus in Kherson – one passenger was killed and five others were injured
Kyiv • UNN
In Kherson, a Russian drone attacked a minibus: one passenger was killed and five were injured. A woman was also injured, and houses and cars were damaged.
On October 25, Russian forces attacked a route bus in Kherson using a drone. One passenger was killed and five others were injured. This was reported by the Kherson Regional Prosecutor's Office, writes UNN.
Details
According to the investigation, the occupiers struck the minibus at around 3:20 p.m. One of the injured people was taken to hospital, but medics were unable to save his life. Five other passengers are receiving the necessary medical assistance.
In total, during the day, Russian forces shelled populated areas in the Kherson region with rocket and tube artillery, and also attacked with drones of various types. As of 5:30 p.m., one person had been killed and six civilians injured in the region.
A woman was injured in a morning drone attack in Kherson
In addition to the strike on the minibus, Russian forces attacked the regional capital with a drone in the morning. As a result, a woman was injured.
Enemy shelling also damaged private homes, a store building and cars.
Based on the attacks, law enforcement officers launched pretrial investigations under Parts 1 and 2 of Article 438 of the Criminal Code of Ukraine — violation of the laws and customs of war.

Fresh protests in Tirana, despite new measures to curb unrest

Unknown Publisher

01:05:35 KST

Fresh protests in Tirana, despite new measures to curb unrest
TIRANA, Oct 25 - Protesters poured onto the streets of Tirana on Sunday hours after Prime Minister Edi Rama announced new measures to stem a wave of anti-government demonstrations.
On a rainy afternoon, protesters gathered in front of the Education Ministry and then walked to Rama's office, setting on fire chairs he had placed in front of it as an invitation to a dialogue with the government.
Student-led demonstrations, fuelled by anger over perceived government corruption, a lack of jobs and poor education standards, have engulfed central Tirana and spread to other cities this month.
Demonstrators demanding Rama's resignation have set fire to government buildings and banks, smashed shop windows and pulled up paving stones to throw at police.
"I believe that those who demand my resignation are mistaken if they think they can impose it through violence or any other means, but I do not believe that everything they say or demand is wrong," Rama said in a video address.
The unrest, which followed months of largely peaceful summer protests against a luxury coastal development backed by US President Donald Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner, poses the biggest challenge yet to Rama, who has governed since 2013 and won a fourth term in office last year.
Earlier on Sunday, Rama introduced new measures to curb violence including fines of 500,000 lek ($6,188) for everyone who participates in a protest that turns violent even if he or she does not commit acts of violence. REUTERS

Musk urged people to pity the “poor Russian conscripts” fighting against Ukraine
Kyiv • UNN
Elon Musk called Russian conscripts “children with no choice” who are fighting and dying from drones. He did not mention the Kremlin’s responsibility.
American billionaire Elon Musk called for sympathy for Russian conscripts taking part in the war against Ukraine. He called them "children" who allegedly have no choice but to fight and die in drone strikes, UNN reports.
Details
We should sympathize with the poor Russian conscripts. These children have no choice but to fight and die in drone strikes
Notably, in his call for sympathy, the billionaire focused specifically on Russian troops. At the same time, Russia launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine, and its army continues to conduct combat operations on Ukrainian territory.
Sympathy for the troops of an army that invaded Ukraine
Musk's words create a revealing contrast: in his statement, Russian troops who are on the territory of another state as part of an invading army are presented primarily as victims of the war.
At the same time, Musk's statement did not raise the issue of the responsibility of the Russian leadership for starting the full-scale invasion.
Thus, the billionaire's call to sympathize with Russian conscripts overlooks a key circumstance: they are not fighting to defend Russia against an invasion, but on the territory of Ukraine, which is defending itself against Russian aggression.

Dutch Army Plans to Replace Kodiak Engineer Vehicles After Just 12 Years in Service
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
16:02:32 UTC
01:02:32 KST

The Dutch Ministry of Defense plans to replace its Kodiak engineer vehicles and, in cooperation with Germany, acquire additional Leguan tank-launched bridges.
The Dutch Ministry of Defense outlined the plans in an official letter to parliament dated October 22, 2026.
The Dutch Army has operated Kodiak engineer vehicles since 2014. They are designed for engineering tasks, mine clearance, breaching obstacles, and creating passages for military vehicles.
However, the Ministry of Defense considers the vehicles outdated because their protection no longer meets today’s battlefield threats. The vehicles also have low operational availability because individual systems and components malfunction.
The military initially considered upgrading the Kodiaks under a Midlife Update (MLU) program but abandoned the option because of its technical complexity and lengthy implementation timeline.
The ministry emphasized that the war in Ukraine has shown the need for modern capabilities to overcome engineering obstacles directly in combat.
The replacement and expansion program has been allocated a budget range of €250 million to €1 billion in 2026 prices, including a risk reserve.
The Ministry of Defense plans to complete the study and procurement preparation phase in the first half of 2028, after which it will present further plans to parliament. The type of replacement engineer vehicle has not yet been determined.
In October, Militarnyi reported the start of trials of two Pionierpanzer 3 Kodiak engineer vehicles in Germany. German troops received them without the Natter remotely operated weapon stations originally planned for installation.
The AEV 3 Kodiak is an armored engineer vehicle developed by Germany’s Rheinmetall in cooperation with Switzerland’s RUAG, based on the Leopard 2 tank chassis.
It is designed to clear paths through minefields, breach engineering obstacles, prepare defensive positions, and perform earthmoving tasks. In 2014, the Netherlands received 10 vehicles for its engineer units.
The Kodiak weighs about 62 tons and is equipped with a front-mounted excavator arm, a bulldozer blade, and two winches.
The blade can be replaced with a specialized mine plow to clear paths through minefields.
The Dutch Ministry of Defense also plans to procure additional Leguan tank-launched bridges to strengthen its engineer units.
To do so, the Netherlands intends to join Germany’s contract for modernized Leguan bridge-layers. Germany is expected to sign the relevant agreement with a German supplier in the first quarter of 2027.
The additional bridge-layers have been allocated a budget range of €50 million to €250 million in 2026 prices, including a risk reserve. The exact number of vehicles has not been disclosed.
The Leguan, manufactured by KNDS, is designed to rapidly deploy bridges across water obstacles and dry gaps. The system, mounted on a Leopard 2 chassis, can deploy either a single 26-meter bridge or two 14-meter bridges.
In January, Belgium signed a contract with KNDS to order eight wheeled Leguan bridge-layers worth approximately €80 million.
In February, it was also reported that the Netherlands planned to acquire WiSENT 2 armored recovery vehicles to equip new units.

Polls close in Serbia as strongman Vučić faces challenge to 12-year rule – Europe live

Updated projection: Student List wins with 52.9% vote, 141 seats in new parliament
The latest version of the Ipsos/CeSID poll, updated with the partial results, gives the Student List 141 out of 250 seats in the new parliament with 52.9% of the vote share.
That’s well clear of the 126 required for majority.
Vučić’s list will have 103 seats in the new parliament, with 38.8% of the vote share.

Student opposition movement ends strongman Vučić's rule in Serbia - summary
Jakub Krupa
And, on that note, we will be closing the blog for tonight as the clocks strike half past midnight in Belgrade.
The opposition grassroots movement Student List has won a landslide in the Serbian parliamentary election, ousting the country’s authoritarian leader Aleksandar Vučić.
The leaderless student movement, which started less than a year ago in protest against alleged widespread state corruption (17:42), is projected to have a clear majority in the new parliament (21:43, 22:22, 00:37).
The result appears to have been driven primarily by unprecedented mobilisation across the country, with the final turnout projected to be just below 70%, the highest since the first election in 1990.
“It is clear that we have lost these elections,” Vučić conceded (21:35), prompting wild scenes of celebrations in Belgrade and other Serbian cities (21:45, 22:01, 22:08, 22:19, 22:38, 22:42, 22:45, 23:21).
Vučić rose to prominence in the 1990s as a radical nationalist, who supported the policies of Serbian expansion and ethnic cleansing led by Slobodan Milošević, and has been the country’s leading government figure for more than a decade (17:14).
A prominent Student List candidateRadomir Saičić hailed the result as “a victory of courage over fear, of hope over indifference,” as he stressed “the great responsibility” facing the movement. “Tonight, we celebrate … Tomorrow, the work begins,” he said (22:34).
The result was warmly welcomed by EU leaders,Ursula von der Leyen and António Costa, as they expressed their hopes for a new start in the bloc’s relationship with Serbia (23:39, 23:54), despite the movement’s ambiguous positioning on the EU (16:48).
Hungary’s prime minister Péter Magyar was the first national EU leader to offer congratulations, drawing parallels with his victory over Viktor Orbán earlier this year (22:48, 23:09).
In a likely further embarrassment to the ousted strongman Vučić, Serbia will have to hold presidential elections in the coming months to choose his successoras the head of state (23:34).
Thousands of diaspora voters joined in lengthy queues to cast their votes around the world (20:41), with up to three hours wait in London (18:58, 19:09).
For now, that’s all from me, Jakub Krupa, with contributions from Ana Milosavljevic on the ground in Belgrade. Thank you for joining us tonight.
Updated projection: Student List wins with 52.9% vote, 141 seats in new parliament
The latest version of the Ipsos/CeSID poll, updated with the partial results, gives the Student List 141 out of 250 seats in the new parliament with 52.9% of the vote share.
That’s well clear of the 126 required for majority.
Vučić’s list will have 103 seats in the new parliament, with 38.8% of the vote share.

The change of government in Serbia could indeed significantly shift the dynamic in the western Balkans, although again we should not necessarily expect an immediate move against Russia (17:54).

'We stand ready to support reforms ... and work to advance Serbia's future in the EU,' von der Leyen and Costa say
European Commission chief Ursula von der Leyen and European Council president António Costa have congratulated the Student List on their victory in tonight’s election in Serbia.
