We stand ready to support reforms on the rule of law, media freedom, the fight against corruption and strong democratic institutions, and to work together to advance Serbia’s future in the European Union.”
As explained earlier, it may not be quite that straightforward when it comes to the EU… (16:48).
Vučić’s gambit backfires as Serbia will need to host second elections to choose his presidential successor
Jakub Krupa
By the way, Vučić’s decision to step down as president to contest this election now puts him in a very awkward position.
Because, erm,the Serbian people will now have to choose his successor as the head of state, and looking at the results tonight, he may not like the outcome of that process either.
After his resignation, a close Vučić ally – the outgoing speaker of the parliament and former prime minister Ana Brnabić – has temporarily stepped into the role as acting president.
But once the new parliament forms, the new speaker will have to decide the next steps for recruiting the full-time replacement.
The process is complicated and CRTA has a good explanation on all possible dates here, but essentially the vote needs to take place before the end of the year.
Despite some similarities, Student List's win in Serbia is slightly different than Tisza's in Hungary – snap analysis
Jakub Krupa
When thinking about today’s opposition win in Serbia, there is an understandable temptation to compare it to Hungary and the fall of Viktor Orbán in April – and Magyar clearly plays on that in his reaction, too (22:48).
And there are some undeniable similarities in how the two countries visibly grew tired of their increasingly authoritarian leaders.
The opposition forces in both countries – Tisza in Hungary and the Student List in Serbia – have some things in common, for example their sort of catch-all character as they formulate their demands in the broadest possible terms to attract all sorts of voters, while relentlessly focusing on corruption and demands of accountability for political leaders.
On a technical level, they both focused on a door to door campaign, making a point of covering thousands of kilometres across the country, and reaching out to voters directly, instead of being a sort of talking shop with ideas. They also both adopted elements of national folks and symbolism for their campaigns.
But there are also very substantial differences.
The Serbian Student List does not have a single strong leader figure in sharp contrast to Péter Magyar’s strong position in Tisza. It is based on a grassroots group of people with little prior experience of frontline politics, and not on a former insider who switched sides, with all sorts of upsides and downsides that come with that. For one, we do not even know who could be their PM.
The Student List’s path to a parliamentary majority was also technically more complicated or, put it simply, required a larger win. That is largely down to the mechanics of the Serbian electoral system, which – unlike the setup Viktor Orbán had tailored in Hungary with the intention of helping his own party, not the opposition – does not offer the same disproportionate winner’s bonus.
Finally, the underlying issues demanding immediate attention are possibly much bigger and more complicated to resolve in Serbia than in Hungary, particularly without the option of getting some EU funds flowing quickly after the vote to buy you some good will and time. Hungary’s Tisza is much more openly pro-European than the Student List.
But Magyar clearly and, at least to an extent, rightly sees the two movements and their victories as linked: earlier this morning, he even posted a slightly cheesy post reminiscing the times he and his parents spent at an unnamed Serbian restaurant in Budapest, “which has since closed down.”
“Fortunately, you can still find great ćevapi in plenty of places, whether Sarajevo-style or Serbian-style,” he added, posting a picture of himself with the said ćevapi.
(There are some sensational Serbian places in London, too. Just saying.)
Hungary's Magyar congratulates the Student List on election win
Hungary’s prime minister Péter Magyar – who came to power ousting Viktor Orbán after 16 years in power – is among the very first European leaders to offer his congratulations to the Student List.
In a post on X, he says:
“I have just spoken by phone with the leaders of the Students’ List @studentblokade, who won the elections in Serbia, to congratulate them on their victory. I assured them of Hungary’s support.
I was delighted to hear how much strength our victory in April had given them during this difficult struggle.”
Earlier tonight, he cheekily said:
“In Serbia, @avucic has conceded defeat. The Students’ List has won an absolute majority in the elections. Celebrations have begun in the streets across Serbia. Sound familiar?”
'We will remember this moment for the rest of our lives'
Ana Milosavljevic
in Belgrade

A Sierra Leone-flagged vessel carrying grain from the Ukrainian port of Reni to Egypt was sailing off the Bulgarian coast on 24 October with its tracking transponder switched off. The vessel’s name has not been disclosed for security reasons, Maritime.bg reports.

How the menstrual cycle might alter ADHD symptoms in women taking stimulant medication
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
16:00:43 UTC
01:00:43 KST

The menstrual cycle appears to modulate the severity of attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) traits in women taking common stimulant medications. A new small study suggests that these traits peak in severity during menstruation and ease soon after, pointing toward a need for hormone-aware treatment plans. The research was published in the Journal of Attention Disorders.
ADHD is a neurodevelopmental condition characterized by distraction, impulsivity, and hyperactive behavior. Medical professionals historically viewed the condition as something that primarily affected young boys. That diagnostic gap is rapidly closing, and women now make up nearly half of the adult ADHD population in the United States. Women often present with different behavioral patterns than men, leaning toward severe inattention and internalizing behaviors rather than disruptive hyperactivity.
Despite facing daily impairments in their careers and social lives, women remain largely underrepresented in ADHD research. One distinct biological variable separating women from men is the constant fluctuation of ovarian hormones. During the follicular phase of the menstrual cycle, estrogen levels rise and peak near ovulation. The subsequent luteal phase features elevated estrogen and progesterone, which then drop rapidly shortly before menstruation begins.
Researchers suspect these hormones play a direct role in brain chemistry. Low estrogen levels are thought to decrease dopamine signaling in the brain. Because dopamine is the primary neurotransmitter involved in focus and attention, these natural hormonal drops could theoretically worsen ADHD symptoms.
Researchers Rebecca Zaritsky, Stephanie C. Reed, and Suzette M. Evans wanted to understand how these hormonal variations interact with ADHD treatments. Prior laboratory work demonstrated that amphetamines, the most commonly prescribed class of ADHD medications, can be less effective during the luteal phase of the cycle. Case reports from clinical settings also hinted that some women experience worsening moods and fading concentration right before their periods.
The research team designed a study to track these daily changes prospectively. The investigators recruited participants through online advertisements to monitor their daily experiences. They screened for individuals between the ages of 18 and 40 who experienced regular menstrual cycles lasting between 21 and 35 days.
To join the study, participants had to report an ADHD diagnosis and currently use amphetamine salts (commonly known by brand names like Adderall) for treatment on at least five days of the week. The team excluded anyone taking hormonal birth control, as well as individuals using other psychiatric medications. After exclusions and dropouts, the researchers ended up with a small study of 30 participants who completed the required long-term tracking.
Each individual filled out an initial survey detailing their medical history, baseline mood, and general impulsive behaviors. Following this baseline assessment, participants completed a daily online survey for 35 consecutive days. This extended timeline ensured the researchers could capture data from one full menstrual cycle for every participant.
The daily questionnaires asked participants to rate their current ADHD symptoms on a standardized four-point scale. They evaluated 18 distinct symptoms, splitting them equally between inattentive traits and hyperactive-impulsive traits. Participants also rated their daily mood variations on a six-point scale measuring 17 distinct emotional states, and reported their exact medication dosage for the day. Finally, they noted whether they were actively menstruating or spotting.
The researchers averaged the daily survey responses and grouped them into three specific biological windows. These windows included the first five days of menstruation, the mid-follicular phase shortly after bleeding ends, and the late luteal phase just before the next period begins. Participants reported their most severe ADHD symptoms during the active menstruation phase. In contrast, they experienced comparatively milder symptoms during the mid-follicular phase.
When researchers separated the specific types of ADHD traits, hyperactive and impulsive behaviors showed variation across the cycle phases, but after adjusting for multiple comparisons this amounted only to a trend rather than a statistically significant difference. Inattentive symptoms also fluctuated, but the differences were not statistically significant. Participants did not report any differences in how much their symptoms generally impaired their daily lives across the different phases.
Mood tracking revealed a correlation between negative emotions and ADHD symptoms. Participants reported elevated negative moods during both the late luteal and menstruation phases compared to the mid-follicular phase. The individuals who experienced the largest drops in mood during menstruation also reported the greatest increases in ADHD symptoms. This correlation held true for both inattentive and hyperactive traits.
Daily amphetamine doses remained remarkably steady across the entire cycle. Participants did not instinctively take more medication to compensate for feeling more distracted or hyperactive during their periods. The research team had hypothesized that some participants using flexible dosing regimens might attempt to counteract their worsening symptoms with higher doses. This lack of adjustment might reflect strict prescribing practices, as many doctors do not encourage patients to alter their daily stimulant intake based on their menstrual cycles.
This research relied entirely on self-reported surveys. The investigators did not measure hormone levels in a laboratory to perfectly confirm each biological phase, opting instead to estimate phases based on reported bleeding days. The small sample size also limited the statistical power of the analysis, meaning the results require verification in larger populations. Because participants taking other psychiatric medications were excluded, the results might not represent individuals managing ADHD alongside conditions such as mood disorders or premenstrual dysphoric disorder.
The study design carried a few distinct demographic and methodological limitations. The researchers did not explicitly gather information on gender identity, meaning the relationship between gender identity, hormone cycles, and ADHD remains untested in this specific context. The standardized survey tool used to track daily symptoms was also based on older diagnostic criteria. This older framework lacks recent diagnostic updates designed to capture how ADHD presents in adults.
The research team also looked at baseline mental health using standardized questionnaires for depression and anxiety. They found a trend suggesting that individuals with higher baseline depression and anxiety scores might experience slightly smaller shifts in ADHD symptoms across their cycles. However, having a higher overall symptom count on average consistently predicted a lower ADHD-related quality of life.
Future studies will need to incorporate direct hormone sampling to precisely map biological changes to behavioral shifts. Researchers might also explore how oral contraceptives or specific antidepressants impact this hormonal cycle in neurodivergent populations. Some clinics have already begun testing symptom-based dosing regimens, where patients take slightly more medication during the specific weeks when their natural hormones work against them. Tracking these targeted interventions could eventually help doctors provide highly individualized care for women navigating adult ADHD.
The study, “Changes in ADHD Symptoms and Mood Across the Menstrual Cycle in Females Treated With Stimulants: A Pilot Study,” was authored by Rebecca Zaritsky, Stephanie C. Reed, and Suzette M. Evans.

Returnee from Czechia: Apathy on election day is surprising
Unknown

Gergana Mancheva
News
Returnee from Czechia: Apathy on election day is surprising
Sasho Vakashinski: The first thing i did today was vote
Sunday 25 October 2026 17:06
Sunday, 25 October 2026, 17:06
PHOTO Reuters
Font size
One of the few Bulgarian compatriots who voted early this morning was Sasho Vakashinski, who recently returned to Bulgaria. He is from the village of Pokrovnik, near the town of Blagoevgrad (Southwestern Bulgaria).
“The first thing my family and I did today was go and vote. This is an obligation of every Bulgarian citizen, a right guaranteed by our Constitution. However, I see that many people do not exercise this right, both in Bulgaria and abroad”, Sasho Vakashinski said in an interview with Radio Bulgaria.
In previous elections, he voted in the Czech Republic. He says that the problem with polling stations abroad is logistical: people have to travel long distances because polling stations are located only in Prague, at the Bulgarian Embassy. Meanwhile, more than 50,000 Bulgarians live in the Czech Republic, spread across various cities throughout the country.
Sasho Vakashinski has been living in Bulgaria for over a year now and today he is surprised to see such apathy among his fellow Bulgarians on election day, even in their own homeland.
PHOTO BGNES
“I don’t know why people in Bulgaria make excuses and don’t go out to vote. Even if they were undecided in the first round and didn’t know whom to vote for, I don’t think voter turnout would be particularly high even in a runoff election. I’ve been back in Bulgaria for a little over a year now, and I can see people’s attitude toward elections. There is a complete indifference here. People no longer care about what will happen to Bulgaria. Everyone is clinging to some job that pays very little, with no concern for the country’s future. And the country’s future is the future of our children and grandchildren. What are we going to leave these children? A country that has fallen apart?”
“Unfortunately, Bulgarians living abroad are much more active in elections and think more about Bulgaria than those who live here”, our compatriot adds sadly.
PHOTO mfa.bg
“Many people are returning to Bulgaria, not only from the Czech Republic, but also from the UK, Italy and Germany. Quite a few of them are young people who were not even born in Bulgaria. I hope that these people, who did not grow up in the country but hold Bulgarian citizenship, will be the ones to bring about change. You simply cannot have a minimum wage of just EUR 620 in Bulgaria! In the Czech Republic, for example, the minimum wage in Czech koruna is equivalent to EUR 800. But hardly anyone there actually works for the minimum wage, it is just a formal baseline. Starting salaries are higher. Recently, some friends of mine from the Czech Republic came to visit, and they were surprised to find that many products in Bulgarian shops were more expensive. And I am not even talking about restaurant prices. Everything that was priced in leva last year is now priced in euros, while wages here are half what they are in other countries. That is the reality. If someone had told me years ago that I would return to Bulgaria, I would have laughed at them. But here I am today, living in Bulgaria with my whole family. We now live in a village near Blagoevgrad. But even here in the city, there are no jobs. Most people work in Sofia, and to avoid paying rent there, they commute every day. The tragic thing about Bulgaria is the lack of employment opportunities. There are a few shops and perhaps a small workshop employing 10 to 20 people. For a regional city, that is practically nothing.”
After spending more than 15 years in the Czech Republic, Sasho Vakashinski has returned to Bulgaria only to find that, in his homeland, little seems to have changed.
“If you have no money here, you simply end up dying on the street. A minimum wage of just EUR 620 would be enough to bring people out onto the streets in protest in a country like France, for example. But we are a nation that has fallen asleep, despite our glorious past. Still, I hope we will have a glorious future, too! We Bulgarians may be slow to wake up, but once we do, nothing can stop us. That is what I’m hoping for”, said Sasho Vakashinski.

Glaciers are melting and revealing millennia-old secrets: what archaeologists find beneath the ice
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
18:00:01 EET
01:00:01 KST

Glaciers are melting and revealing millennia-old secrets: what archaeologists find beneath the ice
Kyiv • UNN
The melting of glaciers is revealing mummies, weapons and clothing to archaeologists, including the 5,300-year-old body of Ötzi. Moisture and air threaten the finds.
Due to global warming, glaciers around the world are rapidly melting, revealing unique finds to archaeologists that had remained hidden beneath the ice for millennia. Among them are mummified human remains, ancient weapons, clothing, and other household items. BBC reports, UNN writes.
Details
One of the most famous finds was Ötzi the “Iceman,” whose body was accidentally discovered by German tourists in the Alps in 1991 at an altitude of about 3,200 meters. At first, they thought they had come across a victim of a recent accident.
However, radiocarbon analysis showed that the man lived approximately 5,300 years ago, before the construction of the Egyptian pyramids. His body was so well preserved that researchers were able to make out tattoos, determine the composition of his last meal, and discover an arrowhead lodged in his shoulder, indicating a violent death.
Thousands of ancient artifacts are emerging from beneath the ice
According to a 2025 study, from 2000 to 2023, the world's glaciers, excluding the Greenland and Antarctic ice sheets, lost an average of about 270 billion tonnes of ice each year. The fastest melting occurred during the last decade.
Norwegian archaeologist Espen Finstad said that over the past 20 years alone, researchers had found thousands of items that had previously been concealed by the ice.
It is a huge historical freezer that no longer works. That is why these artifacts are reappearing in the world, and many of them have been preserved just as well as they were thousands of years ago
Archaeologist Andreas Putzer emphasizes that such discoveries are particularly valuable because they make it possible to study the daily lives of ancient people. Unlike burials, where objects were often placed deliberately, finds such as Ötzi preserve the items a person used directly before their death.
At the same time, melting glaciers are creating a new problem for archaeologists: once ancient objects emerge from beneath the ice, they are exposed to moisture, air, and temperature fluctuations, which can cause them to deteriorate rapidly.

By Steven Scheer and Alexander Cornwell
JERUSALEM, Oct 25 (Reuters) - Billionaire American investor Bill Ackman on Sunday said that Itamar Ben-Gvir and Bezalel Smotrich should not serve in Israel’s next government, saying the two far-right politicians had caused enormous damage to the country’s reputation.
The public intervention by the prominent hedge fund manager, who is Jewish, comes just two days before Israel’s general election, in which polls show a tight race between Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s coalition and the opposition.
Ackman wrote on X that from the perspective of someone who had an understanding of how Israel was perceived in the United States, “Ben-Gvir and Smotrich have caused Israel enormous reputational damage with their statements and actions.”
BOTH MINISTERS HAVE FACED SANCTIONS
The founder of Pershing Square Capital Management, who praised Netanyahu last week, said a government without the two ministers would send a message that Israel was “turning a new page.”
“This will allow Israel to rebuild lost credibility, increase the opportunity for an expansion of the Abraham Accords, and enjoy a better relationship with Democrats and Republicans and Americans at large,” he said.
The Abraham Accords are the 2020 agreement, mediated by President Donald Trump’s first administration, that saw Israel establish relations with the United Arab Emirates and Bahrain. It later reestablished official ties with Morocco.
Representatives for Ben-Gvir and Smotrich did not immediately respond to requests for comment.
As ministers in Netanyahu’s religious-nationalist coalition, Ben-Gvir and Smotrich have overseen policies widely perceived as discriminatory against Israel’s minority Arab population and Palestinians living in the occupied West Bank.
Several countries, including Britain, Canada and Australia, have imposed sanctions on the two ministers over accusations that they have incited violence against Palestinians in the West Bank.
Ben-Gvir’s Jewish Power party is projected to win around 10 parliamentary seats at Tuesday’s election, up from 6, while Smotrich’s Religious Zionism is projected to win 8, up from 7.
Ackman, who was visiting Israel last week, and who along with his wife Neri Oxman owns 5% of the Tel Aviv Stock Exchange, supported Donald Trump’s candidacy for president in 2024. Trump last week publicly endorsed Netanyahu for prime minister.
Nimrod Goren, the president of Israeli think tank Mitvim, said Ackman’s statement appeared to reflect a desire among Trump’s circles for Netanyahu to drop his far-right allies after the vote to form a ‘unity government’ with opposition parties.
However, Gadi Eisenkot, the leading challenger to Netanyahu, and other opposition party leaders have ruled out forming a government with Israel’s longest-serving prime minister.
Speaking at a Tel Aviv conference on Thursday, Ackman praised Netanyahu, who he said had done a good job in protecting and defending Israel since the October 7, 2023, Hamas attack.
Thousands of Israelis rallied in Tel Aviv on Saturday calling for an independent inquiry into the attack that killed around 1,200 people.
(Reporting by Steven Scheer, Alexander Cornwell; writing by Alexander Cornwell; editing by Andrew Heavens)

At least 128 people were arrested following violent riots in central Barcelona, Spain, on Saturday, with more than half of those detained being minors, public broadcaster RTVE reported Sunday.
The riots left 14 officers injured, four of them seriously, while a municipal police officer was also injured.
Police said 72 of those arrested were minors.
Authorities also identified around 450 people during an operation to contain the unrest.
The violence erupted around Placa Catalunya after some 500 young people gathered for a protest promoted through social media by an anonymous platform, which had called for demonstrations in major Spanish cities in support of better educational conditions.
The demonstration was promoted mainly through TikTok and messaging platforms, including Telegram and WhatsApp.

At least 23 businesses were vandalized or looted, while street furniture and vehicles were also damaged.
The Barcelona City Council estimated that damage to public street furniture alone would cost at least €36,000 ($40,330).
Emergency services received around 450 calls related to the disturbances, while firefighters responded to 33 incidents involving fires in public areas.
Police also issued 68 administrative reports following the confiscation of bladed weapons, sprays, balaclavas, pyrotechnics and other objects.
Silvia Cata, chief commissioner of Catalonia’s regional police, the Mossos d’Esquadra, said officers had been surprised by the “extreme violence” displayed by the participants, describing them as a disorganized group of very young individuals who gathered in small groups to commit acts of vandalism and looting.
She said some participants were under the age of 14 and therefore below the age of criminal responsibility in Spain.
Cata added that police were monitoring social media platforms and cooperating with other European law enforcement agencies to investigate the spread of calls for demonstrations and identify those responsible.

Fifty British peers have called on Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood to bar US rapper Macklemore from entering the UK ahead of a pro-Palestine concert in London, citing his plans to raise money for the Palestinian Youth Movement (PYM).
The letter, organised by Lord Walney, a former chairman of Labour Friends of Israel, urges Mahmood to revoke the artist’s electronic travel authorisation before his scheduled performance at the OVO Arena Wembley on 30 October. The peers argue that his presence would not be "conducive to the public good".
Macklemore, whose real name is Benjamin Haggerty, has pledged proceeds from his "Free Palestine Tour" to PYM. Shows in London, Dublin and Paris reportedly sold out shortly after tickets went on sale.
The intervention by the unelected lords seeks to use immigration powers to prevent a fundraising performance by one of the most prominent musicians supporting the Palestinian cause. The peers’ objections centre on PYM’s political campaigning and statements about the Hamas-led attacks of 7 October 2023.
"A foreign national proposes to come to Britain to raise money, from a British audience, for an organisation whose record of glorifying terrorism and of intimidating elected representatives should concern any government," the letter alleges, according to The Telegraph. PYM denies allegations that it celebrates terrorism or has links to terrorist organisations.
Several named signatories have established links to pro-Israel advocacy organisations. Alongside Walney, they include Lord Eric Pickles, whose parliamentary biography records his leadership of Conservative Friends of Israel in the Lords, and Lord David Pannick, a patron of UK Lawyers for Israel. The latter organisation campaigns against the boycott, divestment and sanctions movement and describes its mission as countering Israel’s "delegitimisation".
Other named signatories include former Northern Ireland first minister Arlene Foster, former Conservative 1922 Committee chairman Graham Brady, former minister Zac Goldsmith, and historian Andrew Roberts.
Walney, a former government adviser on political violence, also criticised PYM’s "siege on Labour" campaign, which sets out tactics for protests targeting party offices and elected representatives. He characterised such demonstrations as an attempt to coerce MPs "through fear".
The dispute follows Macklemore’s removal from Ed Sheeran’s US tour after he led pro-Palestinian chants at two New Jersey concerts in September. Several other supporting acts subsequently withdrew in solidarity.

Demonstrators wounded as police break up Lisbon and Porto housing protest camps

15:52:16 UTC

The ongoing confrontation between police and protesters demanding affordable housing turned violent overnight. Police again moved in against protest camps in Lisbon and Porto in the early hours of Sunday, with several arrests and injuries reported.
Protesters chanted "smells like a dictatorship" overnight into Sunday as police hit desmonstrators with batons in both the capital Lisbon and and the city of Porto, in an operation to dismantle tents set up to protest against skyrocketing housing prices.
In a message posted on X, the police said officers had "intervened early this morning... to put an end to these illegal encampments".
"Once dialogue ended, the operation led to 31 arrests for disobedience," the police added.
A spokeswoman for the protest camp in Porto told the Portuguese news agency Lusa there were 37 minor injuries and two arrests.
"It is the third night in which we are being repressed with a method of total intimidation that one would never expect in a democratic country governed by the rule of law," said Catarina dos Santos, speaking to reporters.
The Public Security Police (PSP) had warned earlier in the afternoon that it would not allow tents to remain overnight in Rossio.
Protest camps in main public squares a point of friction for weeks
The presence of tents in Rossio Square and Praça D. João I (in Porto) have been the main points of friction with the police during the past weeks of protest. As night fell, the demonstrators decided by majority to put up tents and stay overnight.
Around 130 tents were erected in Rossio Square in Lisbon.
The operation to remove the tents began at around 1 am in both cities, after protesters started to notice what they called "disproportionate" police reinforcement, with canine units gathering in the squares in both locations.
"There were at least 20 crowd-control dogs, clearly agitated, and and a number of weapons pointed at us, and if this is not intimidating and serious, I don't know what is," lamented Catarina Santos, quoted by Lusa.
Shortly before 2 am on Sunday, the police contingent had both squares cordoned off and began moving in against the demonstrators, who had formed a human chain. Police used batons, while firecrackers were heard causing considerable confusion. In Praça D. João I, bystanders criticised the PSP's conduct and began to sing "Grândola Vila Morena", a song associated with the revolution of the 25 April that ended decades of dictatorship in 1974.
The "clean-up" operation in the squares was swift: the tents were removed immediately by the authorities and the protesters, who say they will return, dispersed to nearby squares.
Protesters demand changes in new tenancy law and a cap on rents
The Lisbon and Porto camp movements are calling for measures such as the reversal of the tenancy law, an end to evictions of people with no housing alternative, limits on the purchase of property by real-estate funds, the rehabilitation of vacant buildings and a ceiling on rents.
Large crowds had turned out the previous day for peaceful demonstrations, accusing the government of failing to act to tackle Portugal's housing crisis

128 arrested in Barcelona riots as Italy detains activist who praised Hamas' October 7 massacre
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
15:51:08 UTC
00:51:08 KST

Spanish police arrested 128 people during a night of looting, vandalism and violent unrest in Barcelona, authorities announced Sunday, as a wave of youth-led protests continued to sweep across European cities. Meanwhile, Italian police detained a 30-year-old pro-Palestinian activist suspected of encouraging further unrest through social media, with local reports revealing his history of praising Hamas' October 7 attack on Israel.
The disturbances in Barcelona began Saturday evening, when hundreds of young people gathered around Plaça de Catalunya, one of the city's busiest central squares, following calls circulated on social media. The gathering had not been authorized by local authorities and quickly descended into violence.
Video footage shared online showed groups of young people, many dressed entirely in black and wearing masks, running through the streets, smashing store windows and carrying away stolen merchandise. Clothing, footwear and electronics stores were among the businesses targeted.
According to the Catalan regional police, known as the Mossos d'Esquadra, 23 businesses were vandalized or looted, while firefighters responded to 33 fires involving street furniture, garbage containers and other property.
More than half of those arrested were minors, according to authorities. Catalan police chief Sílvia Catà said 73 detainees were under 18, while other police summaries put the figure at 72. Only two of those arrested had previous records for public disorder offenses. Fifteen police officers were injured during the disturbances, four of them seriously.
Some of the most alarming scenes unfolded inside shopping establishments. Videos showed customers trapped inside stores, including the El Corte Inglés department store, after security shutters were lowered to prevent looters from entering.
Other footage showed masked rioters kicking through shop windows before fleeing with merchandise. In several cases, participants broadcast their actions live on social media, where viewers could be seen encouraging them.
Barcelona Mayor Jaume Collboni condemned the violence and warned that those responsible would face legal consequences, including potential action against the guardians of minors involved.
Catà described the disturbances as violence for its own sake, saying investigators were working to establish the backgrounds of those detained and determine how the unrest had been organized.
Although the participants did not appear to belong to a single organization, police said they had coordinated their activities through social media. Online posts encouraged young people to join an anti-establishment movement, sometimes using the slogan Instituts Indignats, a reference to the French Lycéens Indignés, or "Angry High School Students," movement that has mobilized demonstrators in France in recent weeks.
The incidents come amid a broader wave of demonstrations across Europe, although the protests have varied significantly in their demands and levels of violence.
Soldiers deployed in Milan, protesters enter Rome's Colosseum
Italy has become another focal point of the unrest, particularly Milan, where violent clashes and looting the previous weekend involved approximately 2,000 young demonstrators, according to police. Many were teenagers from working-class suburbs, including children of immigrant families.
Italian authorities responded to fears of renewed violence Saturday by deploying large numbers of police officers and soldiers to major cities.
In Milan, Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni's government sent an additional 500 soldiers to reinforce the security presence, alongside thousands of police and other law enforcement personnel. Authorities also conducted preventive checks and tightened security around transport hubs and shopping districts.
Businesses prepared for the worst. Luxury retailers in Milan's famous fashion district, including Omega, Tiffany and Gucci, covered their windows with wooden boards to protect them from potential attacks.
Thousands of demonstrators nevertheless gathered in the city, chanting slogans against Meloni and displaying banners reading "No to the lies of the state." One group dumped waste outside the offices of Italy's energy regulator and burned a symbolic oversized electricity bill in protest against rising costs.
Despite fears of another violent outbreak, the main demonstration in Milan ended largely peacefully, in contrast to the previous weekend's destruction. A separate group of about 30 far-right activists, described as soccer hooligans associated with Inter Milan, appeared briefly and shouted anti-immigrant and anti-Muslim slogans before being isolated by police.
Rome also saw heightened security, with authorities restricting access to luxury shopping streets and major landmarks. A small group of protesters attempted to force its way into the Colosseum, and some entered the ancient amphitheater before being escorted out by security personnel.
Elsewhere in the capital, an anti-war march turned tense despite organizers' efforts to prevent violence. Participants had been urged to keep their faces uncovered and their hands visible to demonstrate that they had no intention of attacking police.
Nevertheless, brief confrontations broke out near Piazza della Repubblica, where officers used batons, tear gas and water cannons to disperse demonstrators. Similar tensions were reported in other Italian cities, including Turin, as protests continued over economic hardship, government policies and international conflicts.
The Moroccan-origin activist suspected of inciting unrest
As Italian authorities investigated the violence in Milan, attention turned to Youssef Siher, a 30-year-old Italian citizen of Moroccan descent who had become prominent in pro-Palestinian activist circles.
Police detained Siher on Saturday following an investigation into a social media movement called Movimento 17 ottobre, or "October 17 Movement," which promoted demonstrations across several Italian cities.
According to Italian reports, Siher created an Instagram page and Telegram group after the initial outbreak of violence in Milan, using the platforms to encourage further demonstrations and urge followers to take control of public squares.
Investigators suspect that the online campaign sought to capitalize on anger among young Italians, particularly those from immigrant backgrounds, toward the authorities.
Following searches of properties associated with Siher, investigators reportedly recovered electronic files containing proposed gathering points and organizational details for demonstrations planned for Saturday. At least one of those locations was subsequently used by pro-Palestinian protesters.
Siher was detained on orders from Milan prosecutors and is under investigation for alleged criminal incitement, organized violence at public demonstrations and terrorism-related offenses. He has not been convicted. Italian authorities also placed his wife under investigation in connection with the same alleged offenses, although she remained free.
There is an important distinction between the allegations against Siher and his possible responsibility for the earlier unrest. His online movement emerged after the initial disturbances in Milan, and Italian reporting has cautioned that investigators have not established whether he exercised actual command over the original rioters.
The investigation has nevertheless brought renewed scrutiny to Siher's background and his previous activities.
Siher, who grew up in the Brescia area in northern Italy, pursued higher education in communications and political science at the University of Milan. He also studied political Islam, Middle Eastern politics and geopolitical affairs.
His academic background included research experience at the Italian Institute for International Political Studies, known as ISPI. He also worked as a freelance journalist, contributing to Italian publications including Il Fatto Quotidiano and Il Foglio. Although he had no previous criminal record, Siher had become increasingly active in pro-Palestinian organizations and demonstrations in Italy.
According to Corriere della Sera, Italian intelligence agencies had taken an interest in him in 2024 after he established an organization called Alba Nascente, or "Rising Dawn." The group reportedly promoted demonstrations against Israel and disseminated material sympathetic to Hamas and the Popular Front for the Liberation of Palestine.
Italian media also reported that Siher had collaborated with a satellite television channel described as close to Hezbollah. The nature and extent of that alleged relationship have not been independently established.
His past statements about the October 7, 2023, Hamas attack on Israel have attracted particular attention. On the day of the attack, Siher responded to a social media message by Italian Deputy Prime Minister Matteo Salvini expressing solidarity with Israel by writing "Allahu Akbar," meaning "God is greatest."
In a subsequent article published by the online magazine Miccia, Siher argued that few people in the West had understood the true meaning of Hamas' October 7 operation, known by the organization as Al-Aqsa Flood.
He described it as "a revolutionary act of decolonization," portraying the assault through an ideological framework of resistance to colonialism. The statement has since resurfaced in Italian media coverage of his detention.
Siher continued publishing criticism of Israel and the Italian government in recent months. In some writings, he sought to connect separate incidents involving the deaths of young men from immigrant backgrounds during encounters with law enforcement, presenting them as examples of wider institutional discrimination.
Investigators are now examining whether his online activity went beyond political advocacy and crossed the legal threshold into criminal incitement or the organization of violence.
The case comes as European authorities confront the growing role of social media in mobilizing demonstrations, including gatherings that begin with political demands but escalate into coordinated attacks on property and confrontations with police.

The dollar has hit an all-time record in Ukraine: what is happening with the exchange rate

The dollar has hit an all-time record in Ukraine: what is happening with the exchange rate
Kyiv • UNN
The NBU set the dollar exchange rate for October 26 at UAH 45.2021 — a new all-time record. Cash exchange rates may differ.
The National Bank of Ukraine set the official exchange rate of the dollar for Monday, October 26, at UAH 45.2021. The U.S. currency reached a new all-time high against the hryvnia. UNN reports this, citing NBU data.
Details
The previous record was recorded on October 14, when the official dollar exchange rate stood at UAH 45.0802. Thus, the new figure exceeded the previous high by approximately 12 kopecks.
At the same time, the euro also remains near record levels. However, the exact exchange rate of the European currency for October 26 is not provided in the data cited.
What the new dollar record means
The NBU’s official exchange rate is used for accounting and other calculations stipulated by law. At the same time, cash exchange rates at banks and exchange offices may differ from the rate set by the regulator.
The new dollar high indicates a further nominal weakening of the hryvnia against the U.S. currency. At the same time, the official exchange-rate record alone does not mean a sharp jump in the dollar’s value on the cash market.

BEIJING (Reuters) -- The Chinese commerce ministry urged the United States on Saturday to stop expanding restrictions on American investments in China, saying a proposed rule on sensitive technologies would disrupt trade ties.
The U.S. Treasury Department issued proposals on Thursday to update its outbound-investment security program, adding biotechnology to restricted sectors and expanding coverage of high-performance computing and hypersonic systems.
Beijing's commerce ministry said in a statement that the proposal "discriminatorily" widened China-related investment restrictions and intensified curbs.

The U.S. Treasury has said the measures, which do not only cover China, are intended to stop U.S. capital from supporting foreign adversaries' development of dual-use strategic technologies that could threaten U.S. national security.
The U.S. program had already restricted certain U.S. investments involving China in semiconductors, quantum technologies and artificial intelligence.

Breadcrumb
Netanyahu rebuked for plan to use crypto to bypass economic sanctions
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who faces re-election this week, is drawing criticism from economists and political rivals after suggesting Israel could use cryptocurrency to help shield its economy from potential international sanctions.
In an interview with Israel's Channel 10 on Friday, Netanyahu said he was preparing for a scenario in which broader sanctions were imposed on Israel.
Last month, Britain, France and Canada said they would block imports from Israeli settlements in the West Bank in what was the latest in a series of actions targeting Israel's settlement policy, underscoring its growing diplomatic isolation among some of its traditional allies.
"There could be sanctions, and sanctions on banks so you need to set up a bypass economy," Netanyahu said. "You know, there are currencies that can bypass (sanctions). We are also working on that."
Asked whether he was referring to cryptocurrency, Netanyahu replied: "Very true, very true," adding that blockchain technology was another possibility.
The comments drew a rare rebuke by the Bank of Israel, which said cryptocurrencies cannot serve as a route to bypass sanctions and that political leaders should focus on policy that would render such measures unnecessary.
"The right course for Israel's economy is to preserve our economic relations with our main trading partners, and to focus on preventing sanctions and their negative impact on the economy," it said.
Netanyahu on Sunday continued to defend his record, urging voters to back him and saying he and US President Donald Trump had two years left to work together to topple Iran's rulers.
Plan draws criticism
On Sunday, more than 100 economists, including former Bank of Israel officials, ex-central bank governor Jacob Frenkel and several Nobel laureates, signed a letter expressing alarm over Netanyahu's proposal. They said it would lead to higher unemployment, a fall in foreign investment and the collapse of Israel's economic standing in the world.
"As we have seen in countries that have suffered similar sanctions, such as South Africa, Iran, and Russia, the living standards of Israeli citizens would plummet dramatically, and the state's ability to finance its security and defend itself against its enemies would be severely damaged," the letter read.
"Netanyahu is knowingly leading the State of Israel toward boycott and international economic isolation, and all he has to offer the Israeli economy is a puzzling solution, one accepted in criminal organisations, that will not help in the slightest."
Netanyahu's main rival in Tuesday's election, Gadi Eisenkot, called the crypto plan "madness" and said he feared that the "BibiCoin policy" would drive companies abroad and undermine national security.
Opposition leader Yair Lapid said: "Netanyahu has gone off the rails ... He promises the citizens of Israel before these elections that they'll be standing in line for an hour and a half for bread, like in Russia and Iran."
Opinion polls point to a potential stalemate in the election with neither Netanyahu's ruling coalition nor an opposition alliance securing a governing majority in parliament.

Russia failed to create its own strategic silicon: the multimillion-ruble contract was terminated
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
17:41:05 EET
00:41:05 KST

Russia failed to create its own strategic silicon: the multimillion-ruble contract was terminated
Kyiv • UNN
Russia terminated a 400 million ruble contract due to the failure to carry out work on producing silicon for power electronics. The launch may be postponed until 2028.
The Ministry of Industry and Trade of the Russian Federation terminated a RUB 400 million contract with a Rosatom enterprise that was supposed to develop technology for producing special silicon for power electronics. UNN reports this, citing the Foreign Intelligence Service of Ukraine.
Details
Due to the failure to fulfill its obligations, the launch of domestic production of the strategically important material in Russia may be postponed until at least 2028.
The contract was with JSC Research Institute of Instruments, which is part of the Rosatom structure. The enterprise was supposed to develop technology for manufacturing 150 mm-diameter silicon wafers needed to produce high-power electronic components.
The agreement was concluded in December 2024, and the work was scheduled to be completed by the end of 2026. However, the contractor was unable to fulfill its obligations even under the first stage of the project, which involved manufacturing pilot batches of the material and conducting preliminary tests. The deadline for completing the first stage expired on May 15, 2026. At the same time, the institute failed to provide the required reporting documentation and documents for accepting the work. Due to the breach of the contract terms, the Russian ministry imposed a fine of RUB 1.5 million on the enterprise, which remained unpaid at the time the agreement was terminated.
The project envisaged mastering the production of ingots and polished wafers of neutron-transmutation-doped single-crystal silicon. This material is used to manufacture power thyristors, IGBT transistors, and high-speed diodes, which are used in electric transport, power equipment, as well as the defense and space industries. However, Russia currently has no domestic production of this type of silicon, while the procurement of foreign counterparts is complicated by the material's strategic purpose. That is why the development was supposed to become one of the elements of Russia's import-substitution program in the field of high-tech electronics.
The enterprise was expected to prepare the technological foundation for creating production with a capacity of at least 100,000 silicon wafers per year. The transition to mass production was planned for 2027. However, following the termination of the contract, these deadlines have been called into question. According to Oleksandr Tymoshenko, head of Troichni Technologies, the development of production of the strategic material in Russia may now be postponed until 2028 or later.
Recall
In March 2026, the Armed Forces of Ukraine attacked the Kremniy El Group plant in the Russian Federation, which manufactures chips for missile systems and unmanned aerial vehicles. The plant produces components for Iskanders and S-400s.

Additionally, the Israeli military said most Palestinian workers with permits will not be allowed to enter Israeli settlements for work on Sunday and Monday, and crossings into Israel will remain closed until after Tuesday's Israeli elections.
The election is largely seen as a referendum on Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's leadership and security policies during the past three years of war.
Six Israelis have been killed this year in attacks in the West Bank, which is experiencing a surge of violence. During the same period, 112 Palestinians have been killed, according to the Ramallah-based Palestinian Health Ministry.
Friday's attack sparked outrage in Israel, with Netanyahu and three members of his right-wing government giving statements from the site of the attack on Friday afternoon, vowing to respond forcefully.
"We warned a few weeks ago about attempts by our enemies to harm us, our citizens and our soldiers ahead of the election," Netanyahu said. "We will act to destroy this place."
Netanyahu, who is running for reelection in next week's elections and has received President Trump's endorsement, is under pressure to demonstrate a strong show of force against Palestinian attackers to bolster his image for Israelis concerned with security.
Roughly 3 million Palestinians and 540,000 Israeli settlers live in the West Bank, which Israel occupied in the 1967 Mideast war. Hebron is one of its most tense cities and the only place where Jewish settlers live in the heart of a densely populated Palestinian area under Israeli military protection.

The public intervention by the prominent hedge fund manager, who is Jewish, comes just two days before Israel's general election, in which polls show a tight race between Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's coalition and the opposition.
Ackman wrote on X that from the perspective of someone who had an understanding of how Israel was perceived in the United States, "Ben-Gvir and Smotrich have caused Israel enormous reputational damage with their statements and actions."
BOTH MINISTERS HAVE FACED SANCTIONS
The founder of Pershing Square Capital Management, who praised Netanyahu last week, said a government without the two ministers would send a message that Israel was "turning a new page."
"This will allow Israel to rebuild lost credibility, increase the opportunity for an expansion of the Abraham Accords, and enjoy a better relationship with Democrats and Republicans and Americans at large," he said.
The Abraham Accords are the 2020 agreement, mediated by President Donald Trump's first administration, that saw Israel establish relations with the United Arab Emirates and Bahrain. It later reestablished official ties with Morocco.
Representatives for Ben-Gvir and Smotrich did not immediately respond to requests for comment.
As ministers in Netanyahu's religious-nationalist coalition, Ben-Gvir and Smotrich have overseen policies widely perceived as discriminatory against Israel's minority Arab population and Palestinians living in the occupied West Bank.
Several countries, including Britain, Canada and Australia, have imposed sanctions on the two ministers over accusations that they have incited violence against Palestinians in the West Bank.
Ben-Gvir's Jewish Power party is projected to win around 10 parliamentary seats at Tuesday's election, up from 6, while Smotrich's Religious Zionism is projected to win 8, up from 7.
Ackman, who was visiting Israel last week, and who along with his wife Neri Oxman owns 5% of the Tel Aviv Stock Exchange, supported Donald Trump's candidacy for president in 2024. Trump last week publicly endorsed Netanyahu for prime minister.
Nimrod Goren, the president of Israeli think tank Mitvim, said Ackman's statement appeared to reflect a desire among Trump's circles for Netanyahu to drop his far-right allies after the vote to form a 'unity government' with opposition parties.
However, Gadi Eisenkot, the leading challenger to Netanyahu, and other opposition party leaders have ruled out forming a government with Israel's longest-serving prime minister.

AI generated
Saudi Arabia said its main airport resumed operations at two terminals on Oct 25 even as Yemen’s Iran-aligned Houthis vowed to keep striking the facility, which they called a “military target”.

The Houthis said they had launched attacks on the air hub among other sites in the kingdom, including in Khamis Mushait and Jazan. It was not immediately clear if those were the strikes the kingdom said it had blocked.

The renewed fighting in Yemen has shattered a UN-brokered truce that had largely held since 2022.

Suspect in deadly Paris suburb shooting sent for psychiatric observation
- Published
A man suspected of a deadly gun attack near Paris has left custody and been placed under psychiatric observation, French anti-terrorism officials have said.
One person was killed and five others injured on Friday when an attacker opened fire from his car - first in Trappes, and then in nearby La Verrière - appearing to target people of migrant origin.
The suspect, named in French media as 39-year-old Kevin T, will be observed to evaluate whether his "psychiatric health is compatible with pursuing his interrogation", the National Anti-Terrorist Prosecutor's Office (PNAT) said.
President Emmanuel Macron called it a "racist terrorist attack", adding that people had been targeted over their skin colour or religion.
It marked a "turning point in the life of our Republic and our nation", the French president said.
PNAT said the move to place the suspect under psychiatric evaluation followed guidance from a psychiatric expert.
The evaluation will determine whether the suspect should remain in police custody and is "likely to last 48 hours", PNAT added.
PNAT said the suspect was also found to have cannabis and cocaine in his bloodstream.
French newspaper Le Monde, external and news agency AFP report that a Bible, a Quran and a copy of Adolf Hitler's Mein Kampf were found at the suspect's home, citing a source close to the investigation.
The lawyer for Pengo Bossio Wangi, the one person killed during the attack, told French media the move to place the suspect under observation was "very rare".
He alleged that it was being used to portray the suspect as criminally irresponsible rather than having acted deliberately.
Wangi, a 26-year-old French-Congolese martial artist, was named as the one fatality on Saturday.
The mixed martial arts club where he trained paid tribute to him, saying: "On the mats as off them, he was one of those who lead by example: present, respectful, always ready to lift others up.

Three of those injured in the attack were taken to hospital in a serious condition - including a 12-year-old girl who remains in a critical condition.

Another injured resident was recovering while a third remained in a critical condition, he said.
The suspect had been known to police prior to the attack but not to France's intelligence services, local media report. PNAT previously said he had four previous convictions that had been "automatically expunged".
He is thought to have used an old semi-automatic weapon during the attack, firing in bursts from his car window.

Algeria moves to send troops to Niger to protect energy assets in historic policy shift
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
15:32:23 UTC
00:32:23 KST

Algeria’s upper house of parliament on Sunday approved a proposal to deploy troops to neighbouring Niger to protect energy facilities, marking a potential turning point in the country’s long-standing policy of military non-intervention beyond its borders.
A senator, speaking to AFP on condition of anonymity, said 148 members of the 174-seat Council of the Nation voted in favour of the measure. The lower house was expected to vote on the proposal later on Sunday.
Any overseas deployment would mark Algeria’s first such military operation since it sent troops to support Egypt during the 1973 Arab-Israeli war.
The move comes as Algeria and Niger strengthen security cooperation following efforts to repair strained relations earlier this year, amid persistent attacks by armed groups in Niger and concerns over regional stability.
Energy security at the heart of the deployment
Algeria and Niger share a 960-kilometre (600-mile) desert border and have pledged to deepen cooperation against jihadist violence, cross-border crime and trafficking.
The proposed deployment is also linked to strategic economic interests, particularly the Trans-Saharan Gas Pipeline (TSGP), a major project designed to transport natural gas from Nigeria through Niger and Algeria towards European markets.
International relations researcher Abdellah Akir described the proposal as a historic departure from Algeria’s traditional reluctance to intervene militarily beyond its borders.
He told AFP that the move reflected a desire to protect Algeria’s strategic interests in the Sahel and secure the future of the planned pipeline.
Akir also said the decision was intended to send a strong signal to regional competitors, including Morocco and the United Arab Emirates, with which Algeria has severed diplomatic relations.
Algiers adopts a more direct regional role
Geoff Porter, an analyst with North Africa Risk Consulting, said the proposal illustrated a shift in Algerian foreign policy towards a more direct physical presence in the region.
Algeria had traditionally pursued its interests through dialogue, international law and multilateral institutions, Porter told AFP, but was increasingly turning to more tangible measures to protect its regional influence.
He added that Algeria remained committed to its foreign policy principles while demonstrating them in a different way.
Earlier this month, Algerian President Abdelmadjid Tebboune signalled his country’s willingness to support Niger during a televised address.
“We will protect Niger no matter what,” Tebboune said on October 3, accusing unnamed countries of conspiring against the West African nation.
He also pointed to agreements between the two countries covering oil, mining and other sectors, warning that Algeria’s interests were at stake.
Under a constitutional amendment adopted in 2020, deploying Algerian troops abroad requires approval from two-thirds of parliament.
Military and economic ties gather pace
The parliamentary vote followed a visit to Algeria last Wednesday by Nigerien Defence Minister Salifou Modi, who met Tebboune and Algerian army chief Said Chengriha.
Algerian reports said the two sides signed a military cooperation protocol, although details were not disclosed.
The latest move follows other forms of support from Algiers. Algeria previously supplied Niger with four military helicopters at the request of Nigerien authorities, according to the Algerian Defence Ministry.
In June, Algeria also inaugurated a 40-megawatt power plant intended to provide electricity to Niger’s capital, Niamey, and surrounding areas.
Relations between the neighbours had deteriorated after Algeria shot down a drone from Mali last year, triggering a diplomatic dispute. Niger joined Mali and Burkina Faso in recalling its ambassador from Algiers. Algeria and Mali have since restored diplomatic relations.

Police in Portugal ‘use dogs and batons’ to dismantle housing protest camps
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
15:32:20 UTC
00:32:20 KST

Police in Portugal have dismantled housing protest camps in Lisbon and Porto, baton-charging campaigners in the early hours of Sunday and arresting more than 30 people.
The raids were the latest incident in days of clashes between police and campaigners who – inspired by similar camps in Spain – had sought to pitch tents in central squares to protest against the country’s deepening housing crisis.
Dozens of officers, some with dogs, moved shortly after 2am on Sunday to clear out the more than 100 tents that had sprung up in Lisbon’s Rossio Square. Police said they had also taken down a smaller camp of about 50 tents in Porto’s Dom João I Square.
The camp in the heart of Lisbon had been set up after thousands of people marched along one of the Portuguese capital’s main thoroughfares to rail against housing prices that have soared past average incomes in the country.
Police described their actions on Sunday as proportionate and said they had earlier urged people to leave the camps of their own accord. The operations in the two cities led to the arrests of 31 people for disobedience and 171 structures were removed, police said on social media. Eleven people were injured, including three police officers.
Reuters reported that 25 people detained in Lisbon had been released with orders to appear in court on Monday.
The group Casa Para Viver (A Home to Live In) contested the police figures, saying the raids had left more than 20 people injured as police moved into the camps with batons, dogs and rubber bullets.
“Choosing the early morning to deploy police dogs and fire rubber bullets at people who were sleeping or peacefully protesting is a political decision,” the group said in a statement as it called for further protests on Wednesday. “It shows that this government would rather crack down on those who speak out against the housing crisis than solve the crisis itself.”
Fabian Figueiredo, an MP with the Left Bloc, described the police action as a “wound that had been inflicted” on the country’s democracy. “Fighting for a home is a right. So is peaceful protest. The constitution guarantees both,” he said on social media. “Let’s keep going – for the sake of our future.”
The housing protest camps in Portugal trace back to early October when campaigners began pitching tents in Porto, prompting police to clear them out. Similar actions soon began sprouting up in Lisbon, leading to dozens of arrests and reports of injuries as police repeatedly clashed with campaigners.
As European cities grapple with a wave of discontent, much of the focus in Spain and Portugal has been on housing costs that have priced many local people out of the market.
House prices in Portugal have more than doubled since 2017, while those seeking to rent have struggled with prices that have nearly doubled, fuelling one of Europe’s most acute home affordability crises.
Residents have long told of bearing the brunt of a market that has surged as a result of liberalisation, the issuing of so-called golden visas, digital nomad schemes and the proliferation of short-term rentals.
Campaigners have called on the centre-right government to scrap proposed legislation that would make evictions easier and end rent caps on new leases. The legislation recently passed a first parliamentary reading.
In Spain, the sprawling housing camp in the centre of Madrid marked its fourth week on Saturday, becoming one of the most tangible symbols of a widespread protest movement that has led to early general elections on 29 November.

Modgavrishvili spent a little over two decades in the military, serving as a military judge and in other legal positions, and eventually, in her last four years of service, as chief military prosecutor.

Netanyahu shows 'political desperation' in push for Trump backing, US sources tell 'Post'

00:30:58 KST

Two days before Israel’s elections, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu is intensifying his efforts to secure additional support from US President Donald Trump, who already gave him an extraordinary public endorsement last week.
Two American sources confirmed to The Jerusalem Post that Trump is facing particularly intense pressure from Netanyahu himself and several of the prime minister’s supporters within the president’s inner circle, who are seeking to generate additional political momentum through new statements of support.
According to the sources, some figures close to Trump have been repeatedly raising Netanyahu and the Israeli elections with the president, seeking to ensure that he continues to publicly back the prime minister during the final days of the campaign.
American sources with extensive knowledge of Israeli public sentiment described to the Post the intensity of Netanyahu’s efforts to secure American support.
“We have never seen Netanyahu like this before. He is showing signs of political desperation,” they said.
State Department signals readiness to work with Israel's next government
Meanwhile, a senior US State Department official told the Post that the administration maintains contact with a broad range of Israeli stakeholders and looks forward to continuing its cooperation with the government formed following the elections.
“As part of our regular diplomatic work, US officials engage with a broad range of Israeli stakeholders,” the official said. “We do not speak to private diplomatic conversations.”
The official added: “We look forward to continuing our close partnership with Israel’s post-election government on shared priorities. Normalization between Israel and its neighbors remains a priority of this Administration.”
The remarks underscore that the State Department is preparing to continue working with Israel’s elected leadership, even if it differs from the current government.
Netanyahu asked Trump to increase his support
The developments follow a report published Sunday by Axios, according to which Netanyahu spoke with Trump twice over the past three days and asked him to issue additional statements of support.
According to the report, Netanyahu even suggested possible wording for new endorsements. An Israeli source briefed on the efforts told Axios that the prime minister proposed having Trump speak with Israeli journalists to reiterate his support.
Last week, after months of refraining from an explicit endorsement, Trump posted a statement on Truth Social giving Netanyahu his “complete and total endorsement,” describing him as a “great warrior prime minister” and a key partner in the struggle against Iran.
Trump also suggested that the election of another candidate could have consequences for relations with the United States.
“If Israel has the wrong leader, meaning anyone other than Bibi, America will have to do this job itself, and I’m not inclined to do that,” he wrote, referring to the confrontation with Iran.
Not everyone in the administration is enthusiastic about Netanyahu’s endorsement
Despite Trump’s public support, other senior administration officials have declined to join him.
Vice President JD Vance made clear last week that he does not intend to endorse Netanyahu or intervene in Israel’s elections.
“I’m not attacking Bibi Netanyahu. I’m not endorsing Bibi Netanyahu,” Vance said. “I think the president’s endorsement is ultimately what matters.”
Vance noted that the only foreign candidate he had ever endorsed was former Hungarian prime minister Viktor Orbán, who lost the election in April.
He said he intends to focus on the US midterm elections and will not endorse any more foreign candidates.
And Vance is not the only one expressing reservations. Senior Trump advisers believe that a different Israeli government could actually make it easier to advance the president’s diplomatic objectives in the Middle East.
Trump’s envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner have expressed frustration over difficulties implementing the president’s Gaza plan, while US envoy Tom Barrack has reservations about some of Israel’s actions in Syria.
Within the State Department, officials believe Israel could do more to strengthen the Lebanese government and curb settler violence in the West Bank.
Some American officials also believe that a government without Netanyahu’s far-right coalition partners could give Washington greater flexibility in advancing regional agreements.
Similar views are being expressed outside the administration.
Jewish-American investor Bill Ackman, a prominent voice in the American public debate over Israel, called Sunday for the formation of a government without Itamar Ben-Gvir and Bezalel Smotrich.
According to Ackman, the two ministers have caused significant damage to Israel’s international reputation, and a government without them could help restore international credibility, expand the Abraham Accords, and improve Israel’s relations with both American political parties.
The election test and the day after
From the White House’s perspective, the elections could affect not only the identity of Israel’s next prime minister but also the continuation of American initiatives across the Middle East, particularly the war with Iran, the reconstruction and demilitarization plan for Gaza, and the potential expansion of the Abraham Accords.
Against this backdrop, the senior State Department official’s comments to the Post make clear that while Trump continues to offer Netanyahu his personal political backing, the US administration is maintaining channels of communication with other Israeli stakeholders and intends to continue advancing its regional agenda following the elections.
Netanyahu, for his part, continues his efforts to ensure that the American president’s voice is heard in Israel during the final stretch of the election campaign.
If Netanyahu remains in power, Trump could claim credit for saving the prime minister’s political future and press him for retribution. If he loses, whoever wins on Tuesday would still have every incentive to cultivate a good relationship with the president.
Currently, Israeli polls show that Gadi Eisenkot is projected to secure an average of 23 seats, while Netanyahu’s Likud secured 20.
Notably, Likud’s projected numbers for the 2026 election show it losing as many as 17 seats. The party currently holds 32 seats in the Knesset.

Moscow will host the 2030 World Weightlifting Championships, the International Weightlifting Federation (IWF) announced on Sunday.
No world championships in an Olympic sport, summer or winter, have been held in Russia since the start of the war in Ukraine. The 2025 World Aquatics Championships, originally awarded to the Russian city of Kazan, were later moved to Singapore.
“Concerning the IWF Senior World Championships, Ahmedabad (India) will host the 2029 edition and Moscow (Russia) will host the 2030 edition,” the IWF said in a statement.
It will be the first time since 1983 that Moscow has hosted the World Weightlifting Championships.
“All the bids we received were excellent and we are sure that the Championships in your respective countries will be a huge success,” said IWF General Secretary Jose Quinones.
Russian and Belarusian weightlifters have been eligible to compete in IWF events since the International Olympic Committee provisionally lifted its suspension of the Russian Olympic Committee in July, a step seen as advancing Russia's gradual return to international sport.
The IOC Executive Board, when it lifted the suspension, said athletes should not be held responsible for the actions of their governments. No decision has yet been taken on whether Russian athletes will compete under their national flag, colors and anthem at the Olympic Games.
The National Olympic Committee of Ukraine has appealed to the Court of Arbitration for Sport against the IOC's decision.
The ROC was suspended in October 2023 after recognizing regional Olympic councils in the Russian-occupied Ukrainian territories of Luhansk, Donetsk, Kherson and Zaporizhzhia, following Russia's invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.
Russia's return to international competition also comes against the backdrop of one of the biggest doping scandals in Olympic sport.
The country has been under scrutiny since a 2015 World Anti-Doping Agency-commissioned report found evidence of systematic doping in Russian athletics, while subsequent investigations uncovered a state-backed cover-up linked to the 2014 Sochi Winter Olympics.
The IOC said all Russian athletes now returning to international competition would have to meet relevant anti-doping requirements.

Netanyahu's final campaign strategy: Fear - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
15:30:39 UTC
00:30:39 KST

Benjamin Netanyahu has entered the scorched-earth phase of his election campaign. It is a familiar ritual for Israelis, one that almost always comes in the final days before an election. And the message is always the same: I am the only person who can protect Israel. Without me, the country will fall apart. Without me, Israel will be destroyed. You need me.
The talk last week about a possible new military operation against Iran was just the preview. The real campaign began on Friday.
In an interview on Channel 10, Netanyahu warned that Israel could soon face unprecedented international banking sanctions and that he was already working on ways to circumvent them using blockchain technology and cryptocurrency.
The comments sent shock waves through Israel’s financial establishment. Even the Bank of Israel issued an unusually harsh statement, rejecting the idea that cryptocurrency could provide a way around sanctions. The central bank made an obvious point: The best way to deal with sanctions is to prevent them in the first place, not to look for ways to bypass them.
But Netanyahu was just getting started.
On Saturday night, he released a video warning that Iran had resumed its nuclear program, wanted to destroy Israel, and that the country’s very survival was at stake in Tuesday’s election. If Israelis wanted to stop Iran, he said, they needed to listen to US President Donald Trump and vote for Netanyahu.
Netanyahu's message: If you want Israel to survive, vote Bibi
Then came Sunday afternoon. Netanyahu shared an AI-generated image of a mushroom cloud rising over Tel Aviv after a nuclear explosion, accompanied by a warning that if Iran obtains a nuclear weapon, nothing else will matter.
The message could not be clearer. If you want Israel to survive, vote Netanyahu. If you are willing to risk the country’s destruction, whether through financial collapse brought on by international sanctions or a nuclear explosion over Tel Aviv, then go ahead and vote for someone else.
This is Netanyahu’s election strategy in its most naked form: Fear.
Let’s be clear. Iran poses a genuine and serious threat to Israel. The danger of international sanctions is also real. These are challenges that any Israeli government will have to confront. But there is a difference between confronting threats and exploiting them, between preparing the public for difficult decisions and deliberately frightening people into believing that the survival of their country depends on one man.
And that is precisely what Netanyahu is doing.
This is electioneering at its worst. It is fear-mongering dressed up as national security. It is the familiar Netanyahu playbook of trying to scare Israelis into submission, convincing them to vote not out of confidence in his leadership or support for his policies, but out of fear of what might happen without him.
The tragedy is that this strategy has worked before. Netanyahu knows it, which is why he keeps returning to it.
But Israelis should know better by now. After October 7, after everything this country has endured, the idea that any one politician has a monopoly on protecting Israel should be dismissed.
Israel existed before this prime minister, and it will exist after him. Its survival does not depend on one politician, one party, or one election.
