Kyiv plans to add more than 1.5 GW of thermal generation capacity
According to Ukrinform, Minister for Restoration, Infrastructure and Transport Mykola Kalashnyk reported this on Telegram.
Kalashnyk inspected construction work on protective structures for critical infrastructure facilities and backup boiler houses in Kyiv. Together with representatives of the city authorities, the project owner and contractors, he reviewed the actual progress of the work.
"Overall, the capital plans to bring more than 1.5 GW of additional thermal generation capacity online. Part of this effort involves setting up backup boiler houses, and we inspected their construction progress today," Kalashnyk said.
He noted that a substantial amount of construction work remained to be completed, along with grid connections, equipment installation and commissioning.
"Based on current estimates, the work will take approximately two months to complete, while equipment installation at some sites is scheduled to be finished by the end of December. These facilities will therefore strengthen the capital's heat supply during the heating season," Kalashnyk said.
He noted that, since the start of the project, his ministry's team had been in constant coordination with the project owner, city authorities and contractors on every facility. The team was helping resolve issues related to grid connections, approval of design solutions and equipment supplies wherever work could be expedited. At the same time, amendments to the regulatory framework were being developed to speed up the implementation of similar projects across the country.
The project owners are the Service for Restoration and Infrastructure Development in Kyiv Region and the Kyiv City State Administration. Issues falling under the responsibility of the ministry and the State Agency for Restoration and Infrastructure Development are being addressed jointly with the city authorities and the gas distribution company.
"We have explored ways to speed up work at the sites, including alternative connection points to gas networks, carrying out construction and gas-related work in parallel, reinforcing crews and working multiple shifts. It is important to complete every stage through to commissioning, so that the equipment can reliably supply heat," Kalashnyk said.
The team also inspected a facility transferred from state to municipal ownership. It is expected to become an additional source of power for part of the city in the near future.
"Protecting infrastructure and creating backup capacity are key components of Kyiv's resilience plan. A difficult winter lies ahead, and the capital needs these solutions now. Responsibility for this work is shared, and the outcome is tangible: equipment that operates and provides people with heat and electricity," Kalashnyk said.

Libya opens gas field with output capacity of 50 million cubic feet per day
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
15:25:32 UTC
00:25:32 KST

Mohammed Ertima and Rania Abushamala
25 October 2026•Update: 25 October 2026
Libya opened the Al-Rashad gas field south of the eastern city of Brega on Sunday, with a production capacity of up to 50 million cubic feet per day, in a move aimed at boosting gas supplies to power plants and industrial sectors.
The National Oil Corporation (NOC) said in a statement that its chairman, Masoud Suleiman, announced the opening during a ceremony marking the 65th anniversary of Libya’s first crude oil shipment.
Suleiman said the field’s production capacity reaches 50 million cubic feet of gas per day.
“Bringing this field into production is an important addition to the oil and gas sector, strengthens gas supplies and meets the needs of power plants and industrial sectors,” he added.
Libya exported its first crude oil shipment through the Brega oil terminal on Oct. 25, 1961, marking the beginning of its crude oil exports to international markets.
Libya produces about 2.4 billion cubic feet of natural gas per day, while estimates of its proven reserves range from 53 trillion to 80 trillion cubic feet, according to the NOC.
Libya exports natural gas to Europe through pipelines and relies on it domestically to generate electricity and meet the needs of industrial sectors.

Instead of earning money—war against Ukraine: three countries demand that the Russian Federation return their citizens
Kyiv • UNN
Citizens of Kazakhstan, Kenya, and Kyrgyzstan were recruited into the Russian army through deception or coercion. The countries' governments are seeking their return and investigating cases of human trafficking.
Kyrgyzstan, Kazakhstan and Kenya report cases of their citizens being recruited into the Russian army through deception or coercion. The authorities of these countries are seeking to secure the return of their fellow citizens home, while the issue of recruiting foreigners to participate in the war against Ukraine is increasingly becoming a subject of diplomatic negotiations. The Foreign Intelligence Service of Ukraine reported this, according to UNN.
Details
Kyrgyzstan’s Minister of Foreign Affairs Jeenbek Kulubayev confirmed that the diplomatic service is receiving information about cases of the country’s citizens being forced to sign contracts with Russia’s Ministry of Defense. According to him, such cases are being recorded, in particular, at Russian military enlistment offices and pretrial detention centers. If information about forced recruitment is received in a timely manner, Kyrgyz diplomats attempt to intervene and prevent their citizens from being sent to the front.
Kazakhstan is also negotiating with the Russian side over the return of citizens who ended up in the combat zone in Ukraine. According to Kazakh diplomats, the ministry responds to appeals from fellow citizens seeking to return home. Some of these cases involve men who initially traveled to Russia for work but later ended up serving in the Russian military. In particular, relatives of one Kazakh citizen said that after he complained about working conditions, he and other men were taken to a military enlistment office, where they were forced to sign military contracts.
Kenya has also reported a similar problem. The authorities of the African country are seeking the return of its citizens who fought on Russia’s side and were captured by Ukraine. Kenya’s Foreign Minister Musalia Mudavadi said that the recruited men had been promised civilian employment in Russia. In particular, the jobs involved working as drivers, security guards or cooks. Instead, after arriving, they ended up serving in the Russian occupying army.
Cases of foreigners being drawn into the war against Ukraine through deception or coercion are causing growing concern among the governments of other countries. Some countries are considering such situations as possible cases of human trafficking.
Previously mentioned
Earlier, UNN reported that Russia had begun recruiting residents of Thailand into its army, promising "safe" service far from Ukraine.

‘He had so many dreams’: Israel mourns soldier killed in West Bank shooting attack
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
15:23:42 UTC
00:23:42 KST

Hundreds of mourners gathered Sunday at the Neve Hadar military cemetery in Hod Hasharon, central Israel, to bid farewell to Sgt. Yuval Shai Svilem, 20, who was killed Friday in a shooting attack near the West Bank city of Hebron.
Svilem, a soldier in the 755th Battalion of the Home Front Command Search and Rescue Brigade, was killed alongside Staff Sgt. Ron Yonatan Roytman, 23, of Ashkelon, a squad commander in the same battalion. Roytman was laid to rest earlier Sunday.
Svilem was the eldest of three children born to Amnon and Sivan Svilem and the older brother of Shira and Itamar. Family members and friends described him as a quiet, kindhearted and beloved young man who was always willing to help others.
Capt. Or, commander of the battalion's Eitan Company, praised Svilem's actions during the attack, saying he had helped prevent a much larger assault.
"Terrorists arrived at the scene, and the force thwarted the attack," Or said in his eulogy. "Yuval was an outstanding and energetic soldier. He fought the terrorists, returned fire and prevented a major and significant attack. He fell in heroic combat."
"Yuval was someone you could always turn to," he added.
'We thought he would have so much more time'
Svilem's parents, Amnon and Sivan, delivered emotional eulogies, recalling their son's ambitions and the future they had imagined for him.
"Our boy was only 20 years old," his father said, thanking those who had come to accompany his son on his final journey.
"He had so many dreams. We thought he would have so much more time. We wanted to see him build a life, and now we are left with longing and pain, with everything we will never get to experience."
Amnon referred to the weekly Torah portion, Lech Lecha, which recounts God's command to Abraham to leave his homeland.
"He died during the week of Lech Lecha, and he went to a high and good place, a place everyone would want to reach, just as you did. You reached the very highest heights," he said.
But his grief also turned to anger as he demanded answers from the military and the government about the circumstances of his son's death.
"Our home has fallen apart. We are not living. They took our souls," he said.
"Yuval wanted to save his friend. He was hit, and his weapon jammed. We will not give up. We want to know how we reached this situation."
Amnon called for the families of the Palestinian terrorists to be expelled from Israel before the end of the seven-day Jewish mourning period, known as shiva.
"We will not forget, and we will not remain silent. We hope the government and the judiciary will take this into account," he said. "The terrorists shattered several families and took everything from us."
"Just as they destroyed our families, I demand that the state expel them from the country before the end of the shiva," he continued.
"If the state does not do its job, we will take matters into our own hands. The military should have been prepared, and if the state does not act, we will take the law into our own hands. That is my final pledge to Yuval."
His sister, Shira, spoke of the private bond they had shared.
"Only you and I know the secret language we had between us," she said. "Don't worry. The terrorists will not tarnish what you were to me."
Svilem's cousin Linoy recalled the milestones he would never experience.
"You were only 20. You hadn't had the chance to do anything — not to travel, not to get married," she said.
"You were brutally murdered by a criminal. You were clearing a jam in your weapon, and in an instant, a bullet struck you. Now you're no longer here."
Linoy described her cousin as generous, sensitive and funny, a devoted older brother who always looked out for his siblings.
"Yuval was a child who gave to others, a sensitive and funny person, a good brother who always protected his siblings," she said.
"A wonderful young man was murdered in cold blood, and he will never return. Nothing will ever fill the hole left here."
"We hope you weren't afraid or in pain. Send us strength, and rest in peace, our hero."
Another cousin, Ben, said he had always imagined speaking about Svilem at his wedding, never at his funeral.
"I imagined I would speak about you only at your wedding, not under these circumstances," he said.
"He took command and prevented civilians from being harmed. He went beyond his capabilities and did everything to protect the people of Israel."
Ben recalled a conversation before Svilem enlisted in the military.
"Before he joined the army, he told me he wanted to go as far as possible in the military because he knew there was nobody else to protect us," he said.
"It seems you reached the place you wanted, the unit that goes deep into enemy territory. Yuval Shai was the pillar of our family."
'You were a hero who saved lives'
National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir attended the funeral and delivered a eulogy.
Hod Hasharon Mayor Amir Kochavi was the final speaker, recalling Svilem's devotion to his family and the small gestures that had defined his character.
"I looked into your eyes, the eyes of a good soul," Kochavi said.
"Since Friday, I have been hearing about you, about the wonderful boy you were. The boy who looked after his mother and grandmother, whether near or far, who performed Havdalah with his father, Amnon, and who kept in touch with his childhood caregiver."
Havdalah is the Jewish ceremony marking the end of the Sabbath.
"You were not just a boy, not just a soldier. You were a hero who saved lives," Kochavi said.
"In recent years, we have known far too much pain. May we find a way to end this cycle of bereavement and suffering."
Deadly gunbattle near Hebron
The attack occurred Friday at approximately 7:10 a.m. at the Yehuda Junction near Hebron, a major Palestinian city in the southern West Bank.
According to the IDF, two Palestinian gunmen arrived at the junction in a vehicle, got out and opened fire on Israeli troops stationed in the area.
Svilem and Roytman were killed in the ensuing exchange of fire, while three other soldiers sustained minor injuries.
The gunbattle lasted more than 20 minutes before additional Israeli forces arrived, maneuvered around the attackers and shot them dead.
Security forces subsequently discovered a large quantity of ammunition inside the attackers' vehicle.
Security officials believe the two terrorists had been preparing to carry out a larger attack against civilians and that the soldiers' response prevented potentially more extensive casualties.
Following the shooting, the IDF launched a large-scale counterterrorism operation in the Hebron area.
Svilem and Roytman were the first two soldiers from the 755th Battalion to be killed in action since the unit was established within the past year.
The battalion is part of the Home Front Command's Search and Rescue Brigade, whose soldiers are trained for rescue operations and combat missions.
Military seals attackers' homes ahead of demolition
Overnight Saturday into Sunday, Israeli forces operating under the Yehuda Brigade sealed the homes of the two Palestinian terrorists in preparation for their demolition.
The military said the measures followed the shooting that killed Svilem and Roytman and wounded three other soldiers.
Israel has long used punitive home demolitions against Palestinians who carried out deadly attacks, describing the policy as a deterrent against future violence.
The two attackers were killed in the gunbattle with Israeli security forces.

Fredrick Nyasani, an administrator at XCMG Kenya office, noted that the company mobilized the machinery immediately after learning of the collapse.
Nyasani added that the excavator and crane work in tandem, clearing rubble and hoisting concrete slabs, to help rescuers reach those trapped beneath the wreckage.
The multi-story building collapsed in Eastleigh, a high-density commercial and residential suburb in Nairobi, on Friday, raising fears that construction workers and bystanders could be trapped beneath the rubble.
Authorities are coordinating rescue efforts as teams work to determine if more people remain in the debris.
Kenya has seen several building collapses in recent years, with experts pointing to lax regulatory enforcement and a lack of routine safety inspections by government officials. ■

Ukraine’s FP-1 Drones Fly 2,500 Kilometers Deep Into Russia, Set Major Chemical Plant Ablaze
Unknown

- Category

Ukraine’s FP-1 Drones Fly 2,500 Kilometers Deep Into Russia, Set Major Chemical Plant Ablaze
Ukrainian FP-1 long-range attack drones struck two facilities in the Russian city of Omsk on October 24, targeting a major petrochemical plant and a logistics warehouse operated by Russian e-commerce company Ozon, more than 2,500 kilometers from Ukraine’s border.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to Ukrainian drone manufacturer Fire Point on October 24, its FP-1 drones traveled more than 2,500 kilometers before striking the Omsky Kauchuk chemical plant and an Ozon logistics complex.
Omsky Kauchuk, part of Russia’s Titan Group, is one of the country’s largest producers of synthetic rubber. The facility accounted for approximately 25% of Russia’s production of butadiene-methylstyrene rubber during the first nine months of 2024.
Synthetic rubber is used in various industrial applications, including the production of solid rocket propellants. The plant also manufactures methyl tert-butyl ether (MTBE), a gasoline additive used to increase octane ratings, as well as phenol and acetone.
Footage circulated by the OSINT community Exilenova+ showed a large fire at the chemical facility following the drone attack. The extent of the damage and its potential impact on production have not been independently verified.
Omsk regional governor Vitaly Khotsenko confirmed that drones had reached the city’s northern industrial district, where emergency services were responding to the incident.
Khotsenko subsequently acknowledged that an Ozon logistics facility had also been struck. According to the regional authorities, personnel were evacuated from the warehouse, while emergency crews continued working at the site.
Ozon operates one of Russia’s largest online marketplaces, with logistics centers responsible for receiving, storing, processing, and distributing goods across the country.
The Omsk attack followed another Ukrainian drone strike earlier on October 24 against the Tolyattikauchuk petrochemical plant in Tolyatti, Russia’s Samara region. Both facilities manufacture chemical products used in industrial production, including materials associated with fuel manufacturing.

The reported strike targeted a facility that supplies components for Russia’s military-industrial complex as Moscow continues its war against Ukraine.

The Energiya plant is located in Yelets, approximately 250 km (150 miles) from the Ukrainian border.
Plant produces components for Russian weapons
According to Dnipro OSINT, Energiya specializes in developing and manufacturing chemical power sources. Its products are used in several Russian weapons systems, including Iskander-K and Iskander-M missiles, Kh-47M2 Kinzhal air-launched ballistic missiles, Zircon missiles, and Pantsir air defense systems. The plant also supplies power sources for UMPB D-30SN guided aerial bombs.
Many of these weapons are used in Russian strikes on Ukrainian cities, killing civilians and destroying residential buildings and civilian infrastructure.

Daily Update: Russia Loses 1,850 Troops, 417 Vehicles, and 49 Artillery Systems in One Day
Russia lost an estimated 1,850 troops and hundreds of pieces of military equipment over the past 24 hours, bringing its total personnel losses since the start of the full-scale invasion to approximately 1,578,450, Ukraine’s General Staff reported on October 25.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to the General Staff’s latest figures, Russian forces also lost three tanks and five armored combat vehicles, bringing cumulative losses in those categories to 12,447 and 25,605, respectively.
Another 49 artillery systems were added to the tally, raising the total to 51,614, while five multiple-launch rocket systems and three air defense systems brought those figures to 2,237 and 1,725, respectively.
Ukraine also reported six ground robotic systems lost, bringing the cumulative total to 3,017. Another 1,738 operational-tactical UAVs were recorded, pushing estimated losses in that category to 580,802.
Russia’s aviation losses remained unchanged at 449 aircraft and 356 helicopters, while cruise missile losses stayed at 5,138. Naval losses remained at 35 ships and boats and two submarines.
Another 417 vehicles and fuel tankers were recorded as lost over the past day, bringing cumulative losses to 166,918. Four additional pieces of special equipment raised that total to 4,856.
Ukrainian and Russian forces clashed 193 times across the front during the latest reporting period, with particularly intense fighting in the Pokrovsk, Kostiantynivka, and Huliaipole sectors, where Ukrainian forces recorded 16, 13, and 13 Russian attacks, respectively.
Earlier, Ukrainian drone operators struck a Russian tank camouflaged with branches near Vovchansk in the Kharkiv region. The operation also targeted Russian infantry, military vehicles, and a supply depot, according to footage released by Ukraine’s 16th Army Corps on October 23.

Thousands mourn victims of deadly Jordan church attack
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
15:21:26 UTC
00:21:26 KST

Thousands mourn victims of deadly Jordan church attack
Jordan’s prime minister represents king at funeral for eight of the church attack victims as hunt for gunmen continues.
Thousands of mourners have gathered for the funerals of eight of the victims of a deadly attack on a church in southern Jordan, with Prime Minister Jafar Hassan also in attendance.
The burials on Sunday were beside St George’s Greek Orthodox Church in the village of Hamoud, southwest of the capital, Amman, two days after attackers opened fire during another funeral there.
Nine people were killed and dozens wounded in a rare attack on Jordan’s Christian minority, prompting three days of national mourning.
The ninth victim, Mohammed al-Qasous, is due to be buried on Monday, his family told the AFP news agency.
Coffins wrapped in Jordanian flags were carried through crowds gathered around the church in Karak province, as priests led prayers and security personnel stood guard.
Prime Minister Hassan attended the service alongside government ministers and senior military and civilian officials, according to Jordan’s state news agency, Petra.
Thousands of citizens also participated in the funeral procession, Petra said.
Among those caught in Friday’s shooting was Sahar al-Halsa, who told the Reuters news agency from her nearby home that she sheltered behind a pillar as gunfire erupted and people screamed.
When she rushed outside, she found her cousin Assem lying wounded.
“Assem, Assem, my darling, answer me,” she recalled calling to him. He briefly opened his eyes before dying, she said.
Father Yohanna Hamati told AFP that about 170 to 200 people were at the church for Friday’s funeral when firing began outside.
The mourners initially struggled to understand what was happening, he said, before people began rushing into the church to escape.
By Saturday, bullet holes remained in the walls and wooden pews, and windows had been shattered.
Church workers were cleaning away blood as villagers prepared to bury the dead. Jordanian authorities have described the attack as “extremist terrorism”.
King Abdullah, who visited some of the wounded in hospital on Friday, has promised a forceful response and the assailants are still being sought.
Officials say they have not established whether the attackers were connected to an armed group and no organisation has claimed responsibility.
The violence has also drawn expressions of solidarity across religious lines. Christians account for about 3 percent of Jordan’s largely Muslim population and AFP reported that Muslims were among those wounded.
Young volunteers visited a hospital in Karak with flowers and a message reading, “Our loss is one”.
The mourning reached Washington, DC, on Sunday, where members of the Jordanian community lit candles outside their country’s embassy.
Jordan’s ambassador to the US, Dina Kawar, told those gathered that efforts to stir religious division were “bound to fail”. Back in Hamoud, Father Hamati appealed for unity, stressing that Muslims had also suffered in the attack.
“We make no distinction between Muslim and Christian,” he told AFP.

That took a billion dollars from our neighborhood public schools to take and put into unaccountable private schools. And so, school districts are really struggling. Our schools are shutting down. They are Friday Night Lights, and so there is bipartisan anger about what Greg Abbott has done to our public schools. And listen, I'm running my broad agendas to secure the American Dream, and public schools are essential- are an essential part of the American dream because they provide the gateway and the opportunity to the American dream. So saving Texas public schools is a key part of my agenda, and that's why this campaign has resonated amongst Texans.
MARGARET BRENNAN: You've been campaigning on the issue of Texas having the highest uninsured rate and the highest number of uninsured children in this country. We're one of the few states that hasn't expanded Medicaid. Expanding Medicaid is one way to get there. Democrats of the past have run on expanding Medicaid, I am not because most people don't understand what that means. They know what it means to provide quality healthcare to our children. There's also a big problem in Texas with those of us who have insurance paying more, and it's harder to see the doctors we need, getting- and getting the medication we need. HINOJOSA: Yes, but we're not running on that. That is just the process. It's kind of a geeky way to talk about insuring people. MARGARET BRENNAN: Okay, so Governor Abbott gave hyperscale data centers, which you mentioned, a 20-year tax break, and wanted to make your state the epicenter, he said, of AI development. MARGARET BRENNAN: Yeah.

MARGARET BRENNAN: We'll see what you get. We'll watch your campaign. Thank you for your time today. We'll be back in a moment.

thinking with animals in the sicilian village of santo pietro explores the human-animal divide
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
15:15:23 UTC
00:15:23 KST

thinking with animals in the sicilian village of santo pietro explores the human-animal divide
co-director marco navarra discusses the ecological regeneration project connecting community life, the post-anthropocene, and design.
prefer designboom on google
[FEATURED]
bosco colto campus co-director marco navarra
In and around the forests of Santo Pietro, near Caltagirone in southeastern Sicily, is Bosco Colto, the ecological regeneration project established in 2022 by Makramè APS. Through interdisciplinary programming, the organization explores the Bosco di Santo Pietro area and develops new ways of inhabiting and caring for the territory. In the summer of 2026, it invited guests and community members to participate in its annual Bosco Colto Campus, a summer session of workshops and activations that takes place across the village of Santo Pietro.
Titled Thinking with Animals, this year’s edition welcomed the likes of Yoshiharu Tsukamoto of Atelier Bow-Wow, Food Hack Lab, and other practitioners in academia, design, and architecture. Through experiments in architecture, agroecology, ceramics, sound, and spatial practices, the program explored environmental justice through a nonhuman lens. In conversation with designboom, Marco Navarra, who co-directs the program with Dario Felice, Beatrice Fontana, and Antonio Scarponi, talks about the organization’s growth and what was cultivated—both literally and philosophically—during Thinking with Animals.
Thinking with Animals and a New Approach to Architecture
From the end of July through the first week of August, Bosco Colto Campus featured Fabio Ciaravella’s workshop Order of the Oaks of Santo Pietro, which focused on the study of the ancient relationship between the forest and the city. It also brought to life a hybrid train kiln, a wood-fired kiln for experimental ceramics. Additionally, the program engaged with audio, digital, and culinary modalities for interacting with the world around Santo Pietro.
Navarra comments on how the framework of Thinking with Animals unified these activities by ‘[providing] an opportunity to experiment in practice with a shift in perspective away from the anthropocentric framework that has characterized traditional approaches to architecture.’ He remarks that the Campus, a nearly ten-day event, ‘became a living research tool, where design was transformed from a mere formal exercise into a situated practice, capable of embracing the unexpected, other presences and the logics of the non-human world as an integral part of the process.’
on designing spaces shared with other species
The name of its governing organization, Bosco Colto, plays on the Italian words bosco (woodland or forest) and colto (cultivated or cultured). These fundamental principles were further manifested in Thinking with Animals, with Navarra emphasizing that ‘Designing spaces shared with other species means, on the one hand, recognizing one’s own limits—the limits of humankind—and establishing them as the starting point for the design; on the other hand, it means simultaneously exercising a great capacity for listening and imagination.’
Sicilian Satoyama with Yoshiharu Tsukamoto
A standout workshop during the late-summer program was Yoshiharu Tsukamoto’s Sicilian Satoyama, in which the group participated in the collective construction of the Zucca Gazebo and Mulberry Canopy, two permanent installations on the site. Navarra explains the concept: ‘Satoyama is the traditional Japanese agricultural landscape, where different forms of land use coexist, within a mosaic-like structure that brings together woodland and rice paddies. This balance is made possible by a social system that ensures its care and management over time.’ Reflecting on the workshop, he adds that ‘Tsukamoto’s team experimented with a different way of applying these materials in construction, to create more opportunities for utilizing local resources and to build something within this network of elements that make up a Sicilian Satoyama.’
Navarra remarks on the success of adapting this concept to the Sicilian landscape, saying that ‘the Satoyama model can be replicated and adapted to the Boschi di Santo Pietro area, which also features a mosaic structure composed of agricultural landscapes and edges of an ancient forest…. Of course, Sicily has historically developed certain agricultural practices similar to Satoyama, but it has been particularly valuable to link Bosco Colto’s activities to the Satoyama revitalization actions that Tsukamoto is carrying out in Japan.’
A Space to Practice at Casa Bosco Colto
Alongside the Campus, Casa Bosco Colto is the project’s developing permanent infrastructure, conceived as a network of buildings and outdoor spaces in Santo Pietro. In summer 2026, the Campus inaugurated a wood-fired ceramic kiln in the village, a permanent addition to the Casa project. The broader plan to redevelop four public buildings into a connected cultural infrastructure is underway. Navarra describes the space as ‘an independent research center that will serve as a facility (with laboratories and guest accommodation) dedicated to field research in architecture, art and nature, with the local community involved in all daily activities.’
On the importance of continually engaging with the Sicilian region through Bosco Colto’s program and spaces, Navarra remarks: ‘Foundations bloom seeds buried in the past like a regenerating fire that brings them back to light and makes them blossom again. The actions and small architecture of Bosco Colto work with time to build the future through a self-regeneration of places.’
project info:
name: Bosco Colto, a project by Makramè APS
program: Bosco Colto Campus 2026, Thinking with Animals
dates: July 30 – August 9, 2026
location: Caltagirone, southeastern Sicily
directors: Marco Navarra, Dario Felice, Beatrice Fontana, and Antonio Scarponi

Iran's Araghchi doubles down on national positions amid war threat
Iran's Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said on Sunday that a potential resumption of war with Israel and the United States would not change his country's positions.
The remarks come amid mounting US and Israeli threats of renewed attacks on Iran, as President Donald Trump said on Friday that Washington "may do another little Epic Fury," referring to the US-Israeli campaign on Iran that began on 28 February.
"Recently, there has been talk of a new war, but I am already thinking about the post-war period. Whether there is war or not, our policies remain the same," said Araghchi during a televised event in Tehran.
"They have already done so twice and have seen the results. If they want to try again, they know they will achieve no different outcome from those of the past."
An April 8 ceasefire between Iran and the United States put an end to the most intense fighting, apart from sporadic exchanges of fire in and around the strategic Strait of Hormuz, a key route for global energy supplies.
These military flare-ups have lulled in recent weeks.
Iran has claimed control over the strait since the outbreak of the war and has regularly targeted vessels that attempt crossing without its authorisation - moves strongly opposed by Washington and countries in the region.
In response, the US has been maintaining a naval counter-blockade on Iranian ports.
In June, Iran agreed with the United States to a memorandum of understanding laying out a pathway to a permanent settlement of the conflict, only for the deal to later unravel as each side accused the other of violating it.
Tehran has since called for a return to the accord to end the conflict.
"The current war has changed everything. We must accept that new realities are taking hold. Shipping routes through the Strait of Hormuz will no longer be the same, and the management of the strait will no longer be the same," said Araghchi.
"To achieve peace and stability, our region must move towards the complete absence of foreign forces."

Early reports suggest record high turnout in Serbia elections
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
15:07:00 GMT
00:07:00 KST

Early reports suggest record high turnout in Serbia elections
- Published
Early reports suggest Serbian voters turned out in droves for its parliamentary election, as a student protest movement attempts to end the rule of the country's right-wing populist leader.
Preliminary figures provided by Serbia's election commission suggested a record high turnout, with 64.9% having cast their vote by 18:00 local time (17:00 GMT), two hours before polls were set to close.
The apparent high participation is fuelling the hopes of opposition party Student List that they can oust Aleksandar Vučić and his Serbian Progressive Party (SNS), who have been in power since 2012.
The snap elections called by Vučić follow two years of student protests triggered by the 2024 collapse of a train station canopy, which killed 16 and was seen as emblematic of corruption and negligence in Serbia.
Anti-corruption movement Student List are running on a manifesto including purging officials who broke rules cracking down on protesters, stopping party loyalists heading public enterprises, and freeing the public broadcaster of political control.
Vučić and the SNS party deny corruption and seeking to influence the media.
- What you need to know about Serbia's pivotal election 
  - Published2 days ago
- Student movement takes Serbia's Vučić to the wire in neck-and-neck election 
  - Published2 days ago
Most commentators have suggested that a high final turnout, 65% or above, would favour the students.
Long queues formed outside polling stations in larger cities and smaller towns alike in Serbia, and at polling stations abroad - including Slovenia's capital Ljubljana, Munich, Los Angeles and Chicago. In Paris, Serbian voters waited in line in heavy rain.
Tensions are high across Serbia. In Belgrade, police have closed streets around the Republic Electoral Commission (RIK).
Independent watchdog CRTA reported a "large number of irregularities" and an increasing number of "violent incidents" outside polling stations. AFP news agency reported that police had not confirmed any major election-related violence.
In the street nearby, cars at the traffic lights lowered their windows to blast one of the students' anthems from loudspeakers, 'I want three kisses' - a folk song favoured because the Students' List is number three on the ballot paper. Young people on the pavement nearby started dancing.
Vučić and his SNS party are number one on the ballot paper. He has spent two terms as president and cannot seek a third term, so he is now leading his party with the aim of returning to the post of prime minister, which he left in 2017.
The 56-year-old retains strong support among a significant section of Serbia's population. They view him as a strong leader who stands up for the country's interests. He can also point to significant economic growth over the past decade and numerous improvements in infrastructure.
Vučić, who backs Serbia's candidacy for the European Union while refusing to impose sanctions on Russia over its war in Ukraine, has pledged higher pensions and public sector salaries, and investment in state healthcare.
SNS posters plastered around cities show two hands clasped together in solidarity: the hands of doctors and nurses, farmers, construction workers, teachers and parents.
"These are the hands that hold Serbia in their palms," says Vučić in his campaign video. "And with these hands, calmly and with dignity, we shall finish what we started."
That is question of this election, continuity or change.
Amid fears of electoral fraud by the SNS, the students have delegated at least two observers to each of Serbia's 8,210 voting stations.
Videos circulating on social media on Sunday morning show a cafe in the southern city of Nis, where ballot papers were allegedly filled out in advance in a practice known as 'chain voting'. Signs in the window read "private party". When they realise that they are being filmed, the papers are quickly hidden.
There have also been reports of attacks on election monitors and journalists at several polling stations.
"We are witnessing a unique experiment in European contemporary history," Žarko Korać, a former deputy prime minister and long-term opponent of nationalist parties in Serbia including the SNS, told the BBC.
Instead of running for office themselves, student-led assemblies at the country's university faculties have chosen 250 candidates to stand in the parliamentary election, with Ilija Srdanović, professor at Novi Sad University, heading the list.
The Student List of candidates for the 250-member parliament also includes doctors, actors, academics and sports personalities. Several opposition parties have opted not to run, urging their supporters to back students.
"These are people that don't know each other, you have no idea what their political beliefs are, and we now expect them to create a functioning government. So it's anybody's guess what happens after they win," Korać says.
"On the other hand, if Vučić declares victory this evening, probably late in the evening, I don't think the students will accept that."
Korać suggests that many former Vučić loyalists in high office could change sides at the last moment, if the students win. A close result, however, with both sides claiming victory, could result in weeks or months of political instability.
The electorate is 6.45 million in a population of 6.53 million, raising concerns about the reliability of the electoral register. Serbs from Kosovo, and dual Serbian citizens from neighbouring Bosnia also have the right to vote.
Katarina, 29, told the BBC she had travelled from the Netherlands back home to Serbia to vote for Student List, even though she could have cast her ballot remotely.
"I wanted to be a part of this, and I wanted to be part of a movement," she told the BBC outside a polling station in the capital's Zvezdara district.
"I think they have a chance of winning," she said, but expressed doubt about whether such a result would be respected by Vučić.
Asked whether the party's selection of candidates from different walks of life might hinder its ability to govern, she responded: "Just because they're politically inexperienced, they are experts in their own fields, which we have not seen thus far."

Gugging Museum: How Art Changes Our View of Humanity
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
15:04:00 UTC
00:04:00 KST

Near Vienna, in Lower Austria, there is a museum whose history challenges conventional ideas about art, mental health, and human dignity. Here, works by people long regarded primarily as psychiatric patients, have become part of the international art scene.
The Gugging Museum, located in Maria Gugging near Klosterneuburg, is dedicated to artists associated with a former psychiatric institution. Their drawings, paintings, and distinctive visual worlds have attracted the attention of curators, collectors, and researchers, becoming an important part of the history of art beyond academic traditions.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
                                                                                                                                                                         Gugging Museum (Photo by Myroslava Makarevych)                             
In 2026, the museum marks its 20th anniversary. The jubilee exhibition “museum gugging.! 20 jahre kUNSt” runs from March 15, 2026, to January 17, 2027. It presents the work of artists from different generations. Yet Gugging’s history encompasses more than artistic recognition: it also includes Nazi crimes against the hospital’s patients. This combination makes the museum an important setting for conversations about culture, human rights, and historical responsibility.
From psychiatric hospital to international art center
Gugging’s history began in 1885, when a psychiatric hospital was established in Maria Gugging. A turning point came in the 1950s, when psychiatrist Leo Navratil began using drawing as part of his diagnostic work. He noticed the unusual expressiveness and originality of works produced by some of his patients.
Zoom Versus The Hague: Anatomy of a Russian Sleight of Hand
                                                                                                                                                                         Gugging Museum (Photo by Myroslava Makarevych)                             
In 1965, Navratil published “Schizophrenia and Art.” He later corresponded with French artist Jean Dubuffet, who developed the concept of “Art Brut” – art created outside established academic conventions and traditional systems of artistic education.
Dubuffet was interested in creative expression that did not conform to the expectations of the art establishment. The work produced by Gugging’s artists reflected this vision. During the 1970s, they began attracting recognition beyond the walls of the psychiatric institution.
In 1981, Navratil founded the Center for Art and Psychotherapy, providing 18 patients with a dedicated place to live and work. In 1983, psychiatrist and sculptor Johann Feilacher joined the project, encouraging the artists to transform not only sheets of paper but also their surroundings into works of art.
In 1986, the center became “Haus der Künstler” – the House of Artists. The focus gradually shifted from residents’ diagnoses to their creative work and identities as artists.
In September 1994, British rock singer and songwriter David Bowie and music producer Brian Eno visited the artists at Gugging. The encounter inspired Bowie while he was working on his album 1. Outside (1995) and later became the subject of special exhibitions, including “gugging inspires.! from bowie to roth.”
                                                                                                                                                                         Gugging Museum (Photo by Myroslava Makarevych)                             
Transformations
A broader cultural infrastructure subsequently emerged, including a gallery, studios, and a museum that opened in 2006. The psychiatric hospital closed in 2007, but the site continued to develop as a center for art, research, and cultural dialogue.
                                                                                                                                                                         Gugging Museum (Photo by Myroslava Makarevych)                             
Gugging’s history shows how perceptions of people can change when they are no longer defined exclusively by a medical diagnosis. At the same time, artistic recognition alone does not resolve every issue involving human rights, personal autonomy, and the quality of medical care. These are distinct, though interconnected, aspects of human dignity.
Among Gugging’s best-known artists are Johann Hauser, August Walla, and Oswald Tschirtner. Their works demonstrate the diversity of artistic languages that emerged beyond academic traditions.
                                                                                                                                                                         Gugging Museum (Photo by Myroslava Makarevych)                             
Works by Gugging artists are held in international art collections, including specialized Art Brut collections. Their creativity has attracted attention beyond Austria, and Gugging has become an important reference point in discussions about art that develops outside conventional systems of professional training, establishing criteria of artistic skill, with its own imagery, symbols, and ways of seeing the world.
Nazi crimes – history that must not be silenced
Gugging’s history also contains a tragic chapter. Under the Nazi regime, the psychiatric hospital became a site associated with the systematic persecution and killing of people with mental health conditions.
According to a historical study commissioned by the Institute of Science and Technology Austria, 675 people were deported from the hospital to the killing center at Hartheim Castle between November 1940 and May 1941. They were murdered. Among the victims were 116 children and adolescents aged four to 17. In the following years, patients also fell victim to violence, deprivation of adequate care, and denial of necessary treatment.
These events formed part of Nazi policy, which classified people according to supposedly measurable social worth and declared certain lives unworthy of existence. Dehumanization became a justification for state violence, while institutions intended to protect people were turned into instruments of persecution.
This context is essential to understanding Gugging. The history of a place where the creative abilities of people often overlooked by society were later recognized also preserves the memory of those who were denied the right to live.
Honoring the art, therefore, cannot be separated from remembering the victims. Without that memory, the story of Gugging would remain incomplete. The museum is located at Am Campus 2 in Maria Gugging, near Vienna. A memorial to the victims of Nazi medical crimes stands near the campus of the Institute of Science and Technology Austria. Their proximity is a reminder that cultural heritage cannot be separated from historical memory.
The museum’s anniversary and the significance of its history
The jubilee exhibition “museum gugging.! 20 jahre kUNSt” presents the work of 20 artists from different generations, bringing historical and contemporary works together.
                                                                                                                                                                         In the museum’s anniversary exhibition. (Photo by Myroslava Makarevych)                             
Gugging offers an important lesson: human dignity does not depend on a diagnosis, social status, or conformity to generally accepted norms. Ensuring that people whose voices are often pushed to the margins are heard requires more than good intentions. It requires institutions, professional support, and access to culture.
                                                                                                                                                                         Gugging Museum (Photo by Myroslava Makarevych)                             
Today, as far-right movements gain strength in various countries and intolerance and exclusionary rhetoric spread, Gugging’s history takes on particular relevance. Cruelty does not emerge overnight. It is preceded by a habit of failing to recognize another person as an equal human being.
That is why such museums, memorials, and cultural institutions also remind us what can happen when a society forgets the lessons of history.

French far-right leader Le Pen seeks to leverage unrest in presidential campaign kick-off
Marine Le Pen, leader of France’s far-right National Rally, addressed some 10,000 supporters on Sunday in the city of Orleans as she kicked off her presidential campaign, a day after nationwide cost-of-living protests flared again into violence. Le Pen, the frontrunner, is seen to be benefiting in the polls from the weeks of unrest.
Marine Le Pen, France's far-right candidate in the next national election to succeed President Emmanuel Macron in six months, gave her first campaign speech on Sunday, a day after protests sweeping the country again flared into violence.
Le Pen on Sunday vowed to "restore the rule of law" if she won the election next year.
"We are going to restore the rule of law," she said, after the looting of shops and burning of buildings on the sidelines of cost-of-living protests last weekend.
The frontrunner according to surveys, Le Pen is seen to be benefiting in the polls from the convulsions France has been going through for weeks, punctuated by mass rallies and violent clashes on Saturday and a week earlier.
More than 400,000 people marched in major French cities on Saturday to protest against the rising cost of living, with clashes erupting after groups of masked protesters broke away from the demonstrations.
Police made more than 1,300 arrests and Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez blamed much of the violence on "ultra-left" extremists.

Similar nationwide protests a week earlier also descended into unrest, following four weeks of student demonstrations over the poor state of France's schools.
Unions and Yellow Vest protesters have vowed to keep up their street marches in the weeks ahead, pointing to a febrile period as the elections draw near.

Anger at Macron
Le Pen, who addressed 10,000 members of her National Rally (RN) party in the city of Orleans, has accused Macron's centrist government of being soft on violent protesters and lacking authority.
Police were on Sunday filtering traffic going into Orleans, after thousands of counter-protesters opposed to Le Pen and her anti-immigration, nationalist RN marched in the city on Saturday chanting anti-fascist slogans.
Police put their numbers at 13,000, while organisers estimated the turnout at twice that.
One protester on Saturday, 35-year-old yoga teacher Antonine Rochet, said: "One of the risks of the National Rally coming to power, beyond the implementation of its policies, is the atmosphere it could create."
"If the far right comes to power, we fear things will become much worse," she added.

Another anti-fascist rally was called for Sunday on the southern outskirts of Orleans.
If Le Pen wins the two-stage presidential elections in April and May, she has vowed to cut the cost of living through capped household energy bills, reduced taxes and trimming France's contribution to the European Union.
She is also critical of NATO and of France's support of Ukraine against Russia's invasion.
The RN has sought to reinforce its law-and-order credentials by backing police during the unrest.
French voters, angry over Macron's perceived detachment over his two terms and his recent orders to curb the protests, are turning to more extremist politics, polling shows.
An Ipsos survey published Saturday suggested Le Pen would win 32-34 percent of first-round votes. The poll also found widespread anger over the unrest, with a majority believing that the government bears responsibility for the crisis.
No money
Whoever wins the presidency will face limited room for additional spending, with France's debt and budget deficit already above EU limits and Macron's government struggling to push through a cost-cutting budget.

As Macron enters the final months of his presidency, he faces pressure to restore order while maintaining dialogue with unions and student groups.
Protesters and rights groups accuse the government of restricting the right to demonstrate, while unions and Yellow Vest activists are planning further action in the coming weeks.
The Yellow Vest movement, which challenged Macron eight years ago with street disruptions, has called for another day of protests next Saturday.
And the powerful CGT union, prominent in the demonstrations – and one of the official organisers – is urging a campaign of strikes starting from November 5.

‘They paved paradise’: fighting back over the loss of green spaces in Cameroon’s capital
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
15:00:05 UTC
00:00:05 KST

A little piece of paradise is buried under the asphalt that is now lined with parked cars. The romantic spot where Sosthène Hugues Ngono used to bring his first dates had been green and beautiful. “It wasn’t just a park,” he says, standing at the edge of what is now a private car park in Cameroon’s capital, Yaoundé.
“It was where I came to clear my head when things felt confused,” he says. “Where I met people; where I fell in love, more than once.”
Ngono, 36, a mathematics teacher, watched in dismay as the public park in Essos, a densely populated neighbourhood of Yaoundé, was razed in February last year, but his loss was only a small, personal version of a larger one playing out across the city.
Green space in Yaoundé is under mounting pressure from unregulated urban expansion. Yaoundé covered nearly 33 sq miles (85 sq km) in 1984. By 2024 it had spread to cover 181 sq miles, according to a study by the University of Yaoundé.
Over the same period, the share of wooded areas in the city’s land cover dropped from 28.6% to just 5.4%.
Yaoundé’s rapid development reflects growing demand for housing and infrastructure as its population expands. The UN put the capital’s population at 5.1 million in 2025. Cameroon’s housing ministry estimated a national housing deficit of 2.5m units in 2020, most acutely felt in the city.
With formal housing supply falling far short of demand, much of Yaoundé’s growth has taken the form of informal settlements and slums, often built without permits over the valleys, wetlands and hillsides of its green belt.
However, its disappearance has given rise to a quiet counter-movement. Jean-Baptiste Tchengang, a 34-year-old self-taught gardener, grows mostly ornamental plants, decorative foliage and small shrubs suited to Yaoundé’s climate, chosen because they multiply easily and fit into small yards.
“Their value is as much practical as it is beautiful,” he says. “They bring colour and coolness, but they also give people a simple way to rebuild small green spaces where the big gardens are disappearing.”
Since 2022, Tchengang has run community workshops on composting and preserving local plant species from his own plot in Nkolbisson, a district on Yaoundé’s outskirts that researchers identify as one of the city’s historic areas of urban expansion, dating from 1984.
“I have trained or helped about 300 people since I started,” he says. Ten of his trainees have gone on to build their own gardens on abandoned plots, providing vegetables, medicinal plants and social spaces.
“Getting access to land is the hardest part,” Tchengang says. “There’s no funding, plants get stolen, and the ones you can buy are scarce and expensive. But somehow, I make it work.”
When funds allow, Yaoundé city council buys shrubs and gets him to plant and maintain them, but it is not regular work. In July, Tchengang brought together about 50 young nature conservation volunteers who wanted to learn his methods to make their own case to the authorities. Trees especially have been suffering, disappearing from the urban landscape.
“Trees are not there simply to make Yaoundé more beautiful,” says Jean-Marie Essoh, a climate specialist in the city. “They absorb rainwater, slow runoff and help hold the soil together.
“They also cool a city where concrete keeps spreading,” he says. “When they disappear, it weakens far more than the landscape.”
As trees are carbon sinks, absorbing CO2, their disappearance makes climate adaptation harder in a city regularly hit by heavy rains and flooding; when they are felled, that carbon is released back into the atmosphere.
A 2023 report on urban forests by the UN’s Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) found that trees and green spaces play a vital role in climate resilience and warned that their benefits are increasingly under threat as cities expand.
Knowing where those benefits are being lost is the starting point for Mireille Nonga’s work. A 33-year-old urban-planning student at the University of Yaoundé I, she has mapped the city’s green spaces with 20 classmates since 2023, identifying 10 potential sites for reforestation.
“There are several criteria,” says Nonga. “First, the position of the plot in relation to urban development in the area, its availability and its land status, whether it belongs to the state.
Other points to consider, she says, are “accessibility, access to water and the flow of people around it”.
Today, the Sainte-Anastasie wood and the nearby garden at Place Charles Atangana are among the few green spaces remaining in Yaoundé. According to Nonga, even these central spaces are inconsistently maintained.
Yaoundé’s authorities do recognise the problem. The MoVe Yaoundé project, launched in January 2024, includes a four-year urban renewal plan for the city centre, with about 1,000 sq metres (10,800 sq ft) of green space planned, including tree-lined avenues.
In September, the council published a call for tenders that included landscaping works, new parks, tree-lined avenues and permeable paving.
But until the green spaces promised under MoVe Yaoundé take shape, the work of preserving what is left falls to people such as Nonga. “If we don’t know what we’re losing, we can’t defend it,” she says.
The Guardian contacted the Yaoundé urban council about the loss of Essos park and the authorisation of the private car park. The council referred the questions to the official in charge of the MoVe Yaoundé project, who did not respond to requests for comment.

This is reported by the BBC, according to UNN.
Details
According to the Israeli military, the restrictions will be introduced in stages. On October 25–26, Palestinian workers will be prohibited from entering Israeli settlements in the West Bank and the Jordan Valley, with the exception of certain industrial zones.
On Tuesday, October 27, when parliamentary elections will be held in Israel, all land crossings between the country and the West Bank will be closed. The restrictions will also apply to industrial zones.
The Israeli authorities explain the decision as necessary to strengthen security measures during the vote. The restrictions are expected to be lifted after the elections. The decision was made following an attack near Hebron on October 23, in which two Israeli servicemen were killed and three others were wounded. According to the Israel Defense Forces (IDF), two attackers were killed by return fire.
Following the incident, Israeli forces launched a large-scale operation in the West Bank. According to the military, from October 23–24, security forces conducted raids in approximately 40 areas, searched about 400 sites, and detained around 40 suspects. The main operations are taking place in Hebron and nearby communities. The military blocked roads, restricted residents' movement, and began demolishing a number of buildings that the Israeli side considers illegal or a security threat.
According to local authorities, as cited by the Associated Press, more than 2,600 Palestinians were forced to leave their homes because of the military operation. The restrictions also disrupted the work of educational institutions and businesses and made it more difficult for residents to access medical care.
Israeli Defense Minister Israel Katz said that residents of certain areas would not be able to return to their homes until the operation against Hamas infrastructure was completed.
Context
At the same time, the Palestinian authorities condemned the actions of the Israeli military, accusing them of forcibly displacing civilians and destroying residential buildings. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu promised a tough response after the attack in Hebron and emphasized the need to prevent further attacks.
The escalation is taking place ahead of the parliamentary elections scheduled for October 27. Security issues and the Palestinian-Israeli conflict remain among the key topics of the election campaign.
It is currently unknown how long the military operation in Hebron will last and when all displaced residents will be able to return to their homes.
Reminder
The U.S. and Israeli militaries developed specific plans to resume strikes against Iran after the midterm elections to the U.S. Congress.

Ex-Mossad chief Barnea intended for Iran to see Israel's operations to overwhelm IRGC
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

14:58:01 UTC
23:58:01 KST

When the Mossad took the stunning move of publishing multiple videos in real time of its agents acting against the regime within Iran in June 2025, one of the main reasons was to overwhelm and confuse the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), former Mossad chief David Barnea has revealed.
Leaked on Sunday from comments he made to a closed audience at the Priority Summit this past Thursday.
On June 13, 2025, the Mossad released sensational and rare video footage of its co-lead role with the air force in Israel’s preemptive strike on Iran’s ballistic missiles and air defenses.
Three videos showed the Mossad targeting ballistic missile targets, air defense targets, and general preparations for the attacks (with the agents’ faces covered up).
From the perspective of the videos, it appeared that the Mossad used drones from inside Iran to attack various targets.
Iran had previously accused the Mossad of using drones to attack the Karaj facility in June 2021 as well as other operations.
Mossad's warehouse of drones used to sabotage Iran
It was later confirmed that the Mossad used an entire warehouse of drones to attack and sabotage Iran, along with helping with a large number of remote-controlled vehicles attacking regime targets, and a significant number of human agents on the ground also assisting in assassinations.
Although far more information was quickly publicized about the IDF’s actions, these videos gave readers a rare front-row and real-time seat into what normally were entirely clandestine operations which the Mossad would not even admit to.
Barnea said at the Priority Summit that the video was deliberately published to trigger mass arrests and make it more difficult for the IRGC to identify actual Israeli agents.
“One of the reasons we immediately released an official video on the morning of Operation Rising Lion, with the Mossad logo, was to protect the agents who were there,” Barnea said in a video which Yediot Ahronot shared, and regarding which the Jerusalem Post confirmed the authenticity. “We wanted to make sure they arrested so many people in Iran that they wouldn’t be able to distinguish the wheat from the chaff and would eventually release everyone,” adding that Iran did release all of the detainees.
IRGC arrested over 20,000 people on second day of war
The former Mossad chief said that the IRGC arrested 21,000 people on the second day of the fighting.
“You have to imagine that when you arrest 21,000 people, even if you’ve caught an agent or two, eventually you have to release them because everyone’s story will be the same: I was walking down the street, I was driving a car, they arrested me,” he said, emphasizing that the IRGC would have no way of knowing who was a real agent with such a vast number of detainees,
Barnea added that many of those arrested or executed by the IRGC as “Mossad agents” had nothing to do with the agency.
In addition, he said that nearly all of the Mossad agents were never caught, and at the end of the June 2025 operation, he even publicly taunted the IRGC, issuing a statement, “We will [continue to] be there, like we have been there.”
His explanation may close the book on the unexplained mystery of why the Mossad would have risked broadcasting some of its agents’ actions in real time during the June 2025 operation.
In September 2025, the Post reported exclusively that dozens of Mossad women penetrated Iran and were on the ground performing a variety of kinds of operations during Israel’s attacks on Tehran’s nuclear and ballistic missile programs in June 2025.
While the Mossad does not want to bring too much attention to any one sub-group of potential spies, the Post’s impression was that the Mossad women of 2025 were doing more of every kind of spy role as compared to their sisters of yesterday.
In that same September report, the Post noted that Barnea sent hundreds of Mossad agents, or individuals being run by agents, into operations in Iran simultaneously. All of the varying groups of staff were highly coordinated.
The spy chief directed a project leading to a diverse spectrum of all of the different kinds of agents and backgrounds of those agents one could imagine.
On top of actual Israeli Mossad agents, the spy service has reached new levels in recruiting and training local dissident Iranian agents to act against the ayatollahs’ regime, the Post reported at the time.
While the early 2026 war with Iran is viewed by many as a mixed bag, the June 2025 war was viewed as the most successful Israeli operation of the last three years, along with the exploding beepers used against Hezbollah.

Ahead of the US midterms in nine days, Democrats are hopeful for a blue wave to flip several Senate seats, as US President Donald Trump’s approval ratings hit an all-time low of 31%, according to a Reuters/Ipsos poll from last week.
According to CNN, the most likely Senate seats to flip include several Republican strongholds, including states that Trump won by double digits in the 2024 election.
In order, CNN analysts believe that the most likely seats to flip are: North Carolina, Ohio, Alaska, Maine, Texas, Michigan, Iowa, Kansas, New Hampshire, and Georgia.
Democrats would need to win seven of these 10 seats to gain a 51-seat majority in the Senate. However, it is rare for a party to take control of the House and the Senate in one singular election.
Of the Senate seats listed, Georgia is the only state where the seat could flip from blue back to red. However, a recent Atlanta Journal-Constitution found that Sen. John Ossoff (D-Georgia) has an eight-point lead over his challenger, Republican Rep. Mike Collins.
Will Democrats be able to take the House?
Cook Political Report found that the Democrats would only need to take one or two seats out of 435 in the House of Representatives to regain a majority. Cook labeled 21 seats in races across the US as “toss-ups”; 16 of them are held by Republicans, and five are held by Democrats.
Ten Republican-held seats could flip blue, while eight Democratic seats could flip red, Cook reported.
A separate Reuters/Ipsos poll earlier this month showed Democrats leading Republicans by 7 points, 44% to 37%.
Much of the drop in support for Republican congressional candidates was due to a larger share of women saying they would pick Democrats. Some 50% of female voters said they would vote Democratic, compared to 32% eyeing Republican candidates. Men also favored Democrats, but by a smaller margin.
While the data collected shows potential for a series of wins for the Democrats, CNN noted that the House and the Senate rarely change control in the same year. The last time the Democrats took control of both chambers was in 2006 as part of the Blue Wave against the war in Iraq.
What have Republicans done to strengthen their chances of winning?
The president’s party historically loses House seats in the midterms. The Trump administration and Republicans have stressed to their base for months the importance of voting, and have resorted to unorthodox ways of trying to boost turnout.
At the beginning of October, Trump promised voters that if Republicans win big in the midterms, he will send US adults $5,000.
It is unclear how the president will get the money to Americans, and where the money would come from.
NBC reported that the endeavor would cost at least $1.3 trillion.
Trump told Republicans earlier this month that he will be blamed if the GOP loses several seats in the midterms.
“If we don’t win the midterms, they’re going to blame me,” Trump told crowds in Tennessee earlier this month. “You know that. And if we do win them, I will get no credit whatsoever. It’s true. I won’t get any.”
“But I’m working my ass off. You better get out there and vote,” he added.
Sources close to Trump told NBC that he is in “grind it out mode” ahead of the midterms and is prepared for the worst-case scenario.
How many Americans have voted so far?
Notably, at least 26 million Americans have already cast their ballots in early voting ahead of November 3 midterms, according to data from NBC News updated on Sunday.
Of them, 47% are registered Democrats, 35% are registered Republicans, and 18% are registered as other, according to NBC.
According to data from NBC, 14.3 million voters have sent in mail-in ballots, while at least another 12.6 million have voted in person at early in-person voting locations.

News from occupied Ukraine: Former Oleshky resident warns people 'won't survive this winter'

News from occupied Ukraine: Former Oleshky resident warns people 'won't survive this winter'
This weekly update from the Kyiv Independent aims to shed light on the situation facing Ukrainians living under Russian occupation and the ever-tightening control of information imposed by the Kremlin.
Key news as of Oct. 25:
- Oleshky native warns residents may not survive winter as evacuation hopes rise
- Russian-occupied Crimea imposes power and water restrictions after drone attack
- Russia sentences 77-year-old Crimean activist to 18 years over alleged plot against Moscow's proxy
- At least 34 Ukrainians were brought back from occupied territories, including over 20 children
- Russia intensifies pressure on occupied Ukrainians without Russian passports, military intelligence says
- Data center in occupied Donetsk destroyed following Ukraine's strikes
A woman who fled Russian-occupied Oleshky in Kherson Oblast has warned that residents remaining in the town may not survive the winter, as hopes grow for a possible evacuation mission.
Oleshky has been under Russian occupation since the early days of the full-scale invasion. Residents face severe shortages of food, water, and electricity, while mined roads and constant drone attacks make safe evacuation virtually impossible.
"If the evacuation goes ahead, it will be a lifeline for those who remain. People won't survive the winter," a woman who left Oleshky in recent months told the Kyiv Independent on Oct. 24. She declined to reveal her name for security reasons.
The woman pointed to severe food shortages and a lack of fuel for heating and cooking. She said residents had already burned much of the available wood during the previous winter, leaving few options to keep their homes warm as temperatures fall.
"There is almost no chance of survival," she added.
U.S. First Lady Melania Trump mediated a localized ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine in and around Oleshky to allow the safe evacuation of civilians and delivery of humanitarian aid, Ukrainian human rights ombudsman Dmytro Lubinets confirmed on Oct. 23.
Under the agreement, a ceasefire will be implemented, humanitarian cargo will be delivered to Oleshky, and civilians will be allowed to leave the city freely, according to Lubinets.
President Volodymyr Zelensky said on Oct. 24 that Ukraine will fulfill its part of the "extremely difficult" humanitarian operation in Oleshky.
The move came amid increased attention to the worsening humanitarian crisis in the city, which over the past weeks has gained international attention, including from Pope Leo XIV.
Despite hoping the evacuation would proceed, the woman expressed concern that Russian authorities could prevent it from going ahead.
"I'd like to believe that this mission will go ahead, but you can expect anything from the Russian Federation," she said, adding that she believed civilians were being kept in the area as human shields.
Stefan Vorontsov, a volunteer coordinator with the NGO Humanity, which helps evacuate civilians from occupied territories, told the Kyiv Independent that while he hoped that people would be saved, he expects Russian provocations, blackmail, and propaganda surrounding those who manage to get out.
"God willing, we will be able to set a precedent where Russia admits what they did in the occupied territories, and we will be able to organize the first official evacuation from there, then maybe the rest of us will be able to do it too. But again, I have little faith," Vorontsov said.
In spring 2026, evacuation volunteers still managed to help Oleshky residents leave for other occupied settlements in Kherson Oblast or Ukraine-controlled areas in exhausting multi-day trips through Russia and Belarus. Now, they said, the risk of Russian attacks and mines has made organized evacuation impossible.
In recent months, some residents have started walking out of Oleshky to the neighboring village of Radensk alone or in pairs, on roads mined by Russian forces. At the end of September, four people were attempting to leave the town when they stepped on a mine and were injured, while a man collecting nuts was killed by another mine.
Ukraine's Foreign Ministry said that around 2,000 people, including nearly 50 children, remained in the occupied town with severely limited access to food, drinking water, electricity, and other basic services.

Russian-occupied Crimea imposes power and water restrictions after drone attack
Russian-installed authorities in occupied Crimea introduced electricity and water restrictions on Oct. 24 following a reported Ukrainian drone attack on energy infrastructure outside the peninsula, the Russian proxy governor of occupied Crimea, Sergei Aksyonov, said.
The restrictions came after Ukrainian strikes on energy infrastructure in southern Russia on Oct. 23-24, including damage to the Taman substation in Krasnodar Krai, which supplies electricity to occupied Crimea.
Major cities, including Sevastopol and Yalta, were left without electricity following the hit on the key power station.
Aksyonov said repairs were underway while rolling power cuts were implemented.
In Sevastopol, Russian-installed governor Mikhail Razvozhaev said on Oct. 25 that renewed strain on the power grid had prompted rolling blackouts on a "three hours on, three hours off" schedule.
Razvozhaev added that electricity supply to industrial sites and shopping centers will be restricted "as much as possible" to reduce the load on the grid.
"The capacity freed up must be channeled first and foremost to residential properties. This is our top priority," Razvozhaev said.
Ukrainian Telegram channel Exilenova+ reported on the evening of Oct. 23 that "the entire peninsula" was without electricity.
Crimea, which was occupied and illegally annexed by Russian forces in 2014, has been hit with widespread power outages before. This summer, Ukrainian forces reportedly hit 16 power stations across Crimea in 48 hours, in an effort to hinder Moscow in its war effort.

Russia sentences 77-year-old Crimean activist to 18 years over alleged plot against Moscow's proxy
A Russian court in Rostov-on-Don said on Oct. 22 it had sentenced 77-year-old Crimean political prisoner Volodymyr Ananiev to 18 years in prison over an alleged plot to assassinate Sergey Aksyonov, the Russian proxy governor.
"Volodymyr Ananiev is the oldest Crimean political prisoner. He suffers from vision problems and issues with his spine, muscles, kidneys, and legs, and walks with a cane," The NGO Crimean Tatar Resource Center said.
Ananiev was detained in the Russian-occupied city of Simferopol in February 2024. Russian investigators claimed Ananiev was part of a group that tracked Aksyonov's car and prepared an explosive device to blow it up.
Moscow has continued to repress Crimean Tatars and other residents, including journalists and activists, of the peninsula since its occupation in 2014. Around 300 people, including journalists and activists, were being held on politically motivated charges as of spring, more than 150 of them Crimean Tatars, Ukraine's Foreign Ministry said.

At least 34 Ukrainians brought back from occupied territories, including over 20 children
Over the past week, Ukraine brought back at least 34 citizens who were forced to stay in Russian-occupied territories, including 23 children, Ukraine's human rights ombudsman Dmytro Lubinets and the presidential initiative Bring Kids Back UA said.
On Oct. 22, Lubinets said that 11 Ukrainian citizens returned to government-controlled territory. Some of those who returned faced additional challenges due to health conditions, the need for medical care, and difficulties arranging a safe way back.
Among them was a married couple whose return journey involved two attempts. The woman had previously managed to leave occupied territory, but returned after her husband became seriously ill and was admitted to intensive care. After his condition improved, she arranged for them to leave together.
Separately, Bring Kids Back UA announced on Oct. 19 that it brought home 23 more children from Russian-occupied territory.
Among the children returned to Ukrainian-controlled territory was 9-year-old Stefan, who was forced to undergo military training at a school under Russian occupation, including instruction in handling grenades and firearms, the statement said.
The Ukrainian ombudsman's office coordinates returns through the humanitarian route connecting Mokrany in Belarus with Domanove in Ukraine's northwestern Volyn Oblast. Lubinets said the office is effectively the only Ukrainian state institution systematically organizing returns from occupied territories through this route, assisting people who cannot leave independently.
The Volyn humanitarian corridor is the main working checkpoint between Ukraine and Belarus. There are currently no functioning checkpoints between Ukraine and Russia.
According to Lubinets, 24,953 people, including 2,054 children, returned to Ukraine through this humanitarian corridor between May 24, 2024, and Oct. 15, 2026. Of these, 11,815 people, including 802 children, returned in 2026 alone.
