The Israeli elections have become a fight over October 7, but only Zionist opinions are allowed
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
13:00:00 UTC
22:00:00 KST

The elections in the apartheid, genocidal state of Israel are nearing on October 27, 2026, but it is October 7 of three years ago that continues to dominate the political conversation. In fact, it can be said that these elections are about the very question of what lessons Zionist society should take from October 7. But what this means for Israeli politics is that the voters are solely deciding who can best manage Israel’s expansion and massacre of the Palestinians. What this means for the rest of the world is that any change to Israeli society will need to be enforced from outside.
The Zionist fight over October 7
I recently returned from a visit to Israel, and here are a few small snapshots that help illustrate the overall atmosphere:
- The kibbutz I grew up in, where most of my close family lives, aligns with the Labor-Zionist movement like most other kibbutzim and is generally associated with the Zionist left-wing. The entrance to the communal dining hall has a big sticker on it, with an Israeli flag, saying ‘Elections 27.10. We will not forget’. The digits 7.10 are marked in bold.
- At the airport electronic passport control, an ad has been put on the screen, which normally just contains instructions for placing your passport on the scanner. It now says: “7.10 – REMEMBERING EVERYONE.” My exit date was October 18. This will apparently be running the whole month.
Israeli society is obsessed with the fight over how to ‘remember’ October 7, 2023, and this question is now appearing to be a critical issue in the elections. Any analysis of that day in any way that explains its logic other than “terror” is considered subversive. This is the precise background for the disqualification of Palestinian Knesset member Sami Abu Shehadeh of the Balad party (part of the Joint List). This fight over how to remember October 7 has extended to all Zionist parties during this election.
The kibbutz society, which is representative of the Zionist left, bore the brunt of the attack on October 7, and has become increasingly and explicitly genocidal in the last three years. For them, the purpose of remembering October 7 is to blame Netanyahu for the security failure that day and for putting Jews at risk. Before October 7, this same sector was leading the protests against the government’s judicial reform/overhaul, which reduced democratic trappings of the “Jewish and democratic” state. But now, October 7 overshadows all that. Even back then, the protests featured a sea of Israeli flags while generally excluding Palestinians in an effort to preserve Israeli ‘Democracy,’ which in liberal Israeli terms is synonymous and compatible with Jewish supremacy and apartheid. As Palestinian lawmaker Ahmad Tibi, who holds Israeli citizenship, quipped in 2009, and remains blatantly true today, what the “Jewish and democratic” state means in practice is that it is “democratic toward Jews, and Jewish toward Arabs.”
The Zionist right-wing, on the other hand, just wants to use October 7 as a means of further dehumanization of Palestinians. It is the supposed cause, backdrop, and rationale for all of Israel’s expansions and aggression since, for the sake of Israel’s security.
Across Zionist society, the general thinking about October 7 has become the justification for rampant militarism, and the agreed upon solution to Israel’s own settler-colonialist problems. Thus, even in the kibbutz society, it is now common to see more right-wing banners than Labor-Zionist ones at election time. The liberals have responded by trying to one-up the right at its own game. The Labor party merged with slightly more left-Zionist Meretz to create The Democrats, led by Yair Golan, the general who advocated the starvation of Gaza, and expressed that “we’d all like to wake up one spring morning and find that 7 million Palestinians who live between the sea and the river have simply disappeared.” And during my visit, there are just as many banners at the kibbutz promoting Gadi Eisenkot, the mastermind of the genocidal Dahiya Doctrine, and his centrist party Yashar (meaning ‘straight’ and ‘honest’), as there are anyone further to his left.
While the debate over October 7 has played a central role in this election, none of that discourse has focused on the Palestinians who have been the victims of Israeli genocide for the last three years. They are a topic that doesn’t even bear mentioning, as there are no meaningful differences to discuss.
Apartheid above all
In the final days of the election, Eisenkot and his party appear to be potential winners and are leading in many polls with a plurality of about 22 seats (out of 120), above Netanyahu’s Likud, which in most polls is around 20.
A recent poll (Oct. 18) of the public broadcaster Kan11, appears quite representative, where the current governing coalition polls at about 51 (with Likud at 21 seats) and opposition stands at 69 (with Yashar at 23 seats).
It would thus appear that the opposition easily clears the 61-seat majority threshold. But one must not be fooled by the number 69, which would seem to indicate an opposition win. This is because that number includes 13 seats representing Palestinian parties, 8 from the Joint List (Hadash, Ta’al, Balad) and 5 from Ra’am. And as we know in the Jewish apartheid state of Israel, Palestinian political representation is never a clear-cut issue.
In fact, several opposition parties that would be central to this potential new governing coalition have already said partnering with ‘non-Zionist’ parties like the ‘Arab parties’ is out of the question. This is the case for the Together party (polling at 12 seats), led by religious-nationalist Naftali Bennett and centrist (opposition leader) Yair Lapid, as well as for Avigdor Lieberman and his Jewish Home right-wing party (polling at 8 seats).
Lieberman wrote on social media on October 19 that:
“at the principle level, it is not possible to lean upon MK’s (Members of Knesset] from Ra’am and the Joint List, who after the massacre of October 7, the worst catastrophe since the establishment of the state, define Hamas as a charity organization and accuse IDF soldiers of genocide and crimes against humanity.”
Netanyahu’s Likud have long sought to exploit the racism of Israeli society and use the political reality as a cudgel to beat opposition parties. Likud has chided the opposition bloc for potentially depending upon Ra’am and its leader Mansour Abbas, like in the mocking AI video featuring Abbas driving Bennet and Lapid who appear as children seated in the back of a car. Bennett and Lapid did in fact have Ra’am and Abbas in their short-lived government in 2021 and 2022, and the idea for doing so was actually first pitched by Netanyahu himself in 2019 (and again in 2021), but the whole issue of involving Palestinians remains politically contentious among Jewish Israelis, and it’s only become worse since 2023.
If anything, there is one issue that Lieberman and the rest of the Zionist opposition have been uniting around, and that is increasing militarism: more conscription into the Israeli military. Netanyahu’s right-wing coalition is largely based on the Jewish ultra-Orthodox parties Shas (8 seats) and United Torah Judaism (7 seats), which demand maintaining military exemption for Yeshiva (religious academy) students. The Zionist opposition bloc agrees that this exemption should be canceled. Thus, Lieberman, who constantly chides Netanyahu for allowing the exemption to continue, proceeds in his tweet:
“In order to win in the elections, 4-5 mandates must be moved from the draft-dodgers’ bloc to the bloc of those who serve [in the military]. All the talks about a minority government are transmitting weakness and defeat”.
Another issue at the center of the opposition bloc’s concerns again relates to October 7: an investigation into the day’s events. Such a committee will no doubt paint Netanyahu badly, but it is doubtful that Eisenkot would have handled the event differently. And it is clear that matters other than “military intelligence failure” are of no great interest. The Hannibal Directive enacted by Israel, which entailed indiscriminate fire also at its own soldiers and civilians, is ostensibly claimed by the Israeli army to be subject to a later investigation. “Questions of this kind will be looked into at a later stage”, the Israeli military told Australia’s ABC News, because “the IDF is currently focused on eliminating the threat from the terrorist organization Hamas.” But probes have already cleared soldiers of wrongdoing, and the IDF previously said that “it would not be morally sound to investigate these incidents.” “Morally sound” means that it could implicate Israeli soldiers in killing a considerable amount of Israelis, soldiers as well as civilians.
So everything in this election seems to circle back to October 7, although there are several realities around that day you are not allowed to confront. Within Israeli society, October 7 has become a way to engulf oneself in a national narrative of victimhood, which serves as a means to deny the genocide that Israel continues to carry out. This ethos is serving to create a nationalist Zionist sense of unity where the political competition among the parties is solely about how to be more Zionist and more militaristic. Everything else has become ancillary. Stopping the genocide in Gaza is not even in question – over three out of four Jewish Israelis believe there are “no innocents in Gaza,” while they deny the genocide. So there is no horizon indicating substantial change, with or without Netanyahu. If one is looking for change, its agency is to be found outside Israel, in external pressure through Boycotts, Divestment, and Sanctions.

According to Ukrinform, this was reported by The Moscow Times.
Perm Krai Governor Dmitry Makhonin stated that, as a result of the drone attack, “an industrial facility in the north of the region sustained minor damage and continues to operate normally.”
According to preliminary information, five employees of the plant were injured, three of whom were taken to the hospital for examination,
According to the Ukrainian monitoring channel Exilenova+, the chemical and metallurgical plant “Avisma” in Berezniki was targeted.
Its products are used in the manufacture of military aircraft, aircraft engines, and rocket and space technology. Local residents in online chat rooms confirm the attack on the facility.
The plant is owned by the VSMPO-Avisma Corporation—the world’s largest titanium producer and a key supplier of this metal to Russian defense industry enterprises.
According to publicly available data, the facility produces sponge titanium (with a capacity of 44,000 metric tons per year), metallic magnesium (60,000 metric tons per year), and magnesium-based alloys. The company employs over 7,100 people.
As reported by Ukrinform, on Saturday in Omsk, Russia—located more than 2,500 km from Ukraine—drones attacked a local industrial complex.

China Flexes Its Naval Muscles Near Japan With Ukraine-Built Aircraft Carrier
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
12:56:45 UTC
21:56:45 KST

- Category
- War in Ukraine
China Flexes Its Naval Muscles Near Japan With Ukraine-Built Aircraft Carrier
China has deployed its first aircraft carrier, Liaoning, originally built at a shipyard in Ukraine, to waters near Japan as part of a major naval training operation in the Western Pacific, prompting Japanese fighter jets to scramble in response to Chinese carrier-based aviation activity.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The deployment marks another milestone in the transformation of the former Soviet aircraft carrier Varyag, constructed in Mykolaiv, Ukraine, from an unfinished Cold War-era warship into a centerpiece of China’s growing naval power.
According to Defence Blog on October 24, citing Chinese state broadcaster CCTV and Japan’s Joint Staff, the Liaoning carrier group completed its second Western Pacific training deployment of 2026, a decade after its first such voyage in 2016.
Japanese forces initially detected the carrier on October 13, accompanied by two Renhai-class destroyers, hull numbers 103 and 104, and a Luyang III-class destroyer, hull number 123.
The following day, the Chinese naval group sailed southeast between Okinawa and Miyako-jima into the Pacific Ocean. Japanese maritime forces subsequently observed fighter aircraft taking off and landing aboard Liaoning approximately 250 kilometers (155 miles) south of Ishigaki Island.
Japan’s Air Self-Defense Force scrambled fighter jets in response to the Chinese aircraft activity, according to the Japanese Joint Staff. By October 15, all four Chinese vessels had been observed heading toward the South China Sea.
Liaoning’s origins trace back to Ukraine’s major shipbuilding industry. Originally named Varyag, the Soviet-era aircraft carrier was constructed at the Black Sea Shipyard in the Ukrainian city of Mykolaiv, one of the Soviet Union’s most important naval shipbuilding centers.
Following Ukraine’s independence in 1991, the unfinished carrier came under Ukrainian ownership before being sold to Chinese buyers. Beijing subsequently completed and modernized the vessel, commissioning it into its navy as Liaoning in 2012.
The Ukrainian-built hull became the foundation of China’s first aircraft carrier, helping Beijing establish its own carrier program. According to Chinese military commentator Du Wenlong, the reconstruction process allowed Chinese engineers to acquire essential aircraft carrier design and construction expertise.
Over the following decade, Liaoning evolved from a training platform into a combat-capable warship and flagship of its carrier group, equipped with upgraded weapons, aviation, and command systems.
Earlier, China deployed naval and air forces near the disputed Scarborough Shoal in the South China Sea as the US, the Philippines, and regional allies conducted major joint military exercises. Beijing described the operation as a combat readiness patrol, while Philippine officials accused China of using military activity claims to project control over contested waters.

Photo exhibition held in South Africa to mark 81st anniversary of Taiwan's restoration
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
20:49:57 CST
21:49:57 KST

JOHANNESBURG, Oct. 25 (Xinhua) -- A photo exhibition marking the 81st anniversary of Taiwan's restoration to China was held on Saturday in South Africa's Johannesburg, under the theme "Remembering Taiwan's Restoration, Advancing National Reunification."
Chinese Ambassador to South Africa Wu Peng said at the event that Taiwan's restoration is a great victory won through the fearless struggle and bloodshed of the Chinese people, including the compatriots in Taiwan. He noted that Taiwan's restoration to China is a victorious outcome of World War II and an integral part of the postwar international order.
He stressed that a series of instruments with legal effect under international law, including the Cairo Declaration and the Potsdam Proclamation, have all affirmed China's sovereignty over Taiwan. The historical and legal fact therein brooks no challenge. And the authority of United Nations General Assembly Resolution 2758 brooks no challenge.
Wu said the photo exhibition once again demonstrates that the victory of Taiwan's restoration cannot be denied, nor can the historical fact and legal chain that Taiwan is an integral part of China be challenged.
The one-China principle is a basic norm governing international relations and a prevailing consensus of the international community, he said, noting that 183 countries, including South Africa, have established and developed diplomatic relations with China on the basis of the one-China principle.
China appreciates the South African government's long-standing adherence to the one-China policy, Wu added.
Zheng Xingli, president of the All-Africa Association for Peaceful Reunification of China, said that history is the best textbook, noting that the exhibition revisits the history of Taiwan's restoration through a collection of precious historical photos and pays tribute to those who made sacrifices and contributions to national independence and reunification.
The association will continue to unite overseas Chinese in Africa, firmly uphold the one-China principle, resolutely oppose separatist activities seeking "Taiwan independence," and remain committed to promoting national reunification, Zheng added.
Featuring four thematic sections with more than 30 photos, the event was organized by China's Xinhua News Agency Africa Regional Bureau in partnership with the All-Africa Association for Peaceful Reunification of China and several other organizations.
The event brought together about 150 people, including Wu, Chinese Consul General in Johannesburg Pan Qingjiang and representatives of the Chinese community, Chinese enterprises and media organizations in South Africa. ■

Youth gathering in Barcelona turns violent, 128 arrested
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
20:49:49 CST
21:49:49 KST

MADRID, Oct. 25 (Xinhua) -- A total of 128 people, including 72 minors, were arrested after a social media-organized gathering of young people in central Barcelona, Spain, turned violent on Saturday, according to figures released Sunday by the Mossos d'Esquadra, Catalonia's regional police force.
The violence left 15 police officers injured, including 14 Mossos officers and one Barcelona municipal police officer. Four officers were seriously injured. Shops were damaged, street furniture was set on fire and participants clashed with police.
The gathering, which had not been notified to the authorities in advance, took place at Placa de Catalunya on Saturday evening, Spanish news agency EFE reported.
Most of the several hundred young people attending the event were dressed in black. The event followed calls circulating on TikTok and other social media and resembled recent protests in other European cities, particularly in France, some of which also turned violent.
Mossos chief commissioner Silvia Cata said in an interview with local media on Sunday that police had been monitoring the social media calls for several days but were still surprised by the participants' "gratuitous violence," particularly toward officers.
She described the participants as "completely disorganized," saying they gathered at Placa de Catalunya and then split into groups of four to six, without putting forward any specific demands.
The Mossos said officers made "selective" use of foam projectile launchers during the unrest, citing the force of the attacks and the need to restore public order. The violent incidents continued until 10 p.m. (2000 GMT) on Saturday, when the remaining fires on streets were extinguished. ■

With 1,500 kg of dumplings, restaurant owner heads to quake-hit Baqen
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
20:49:36 CST
21:49:36 KST

A rescuer thanks Du Guoping (R) at a temporary shelter in Maru Township of Baqen County, Nagqu City, southwest China's Xizang Autonomous Region, Oct. 24, 2026. After a 7.0-magnitude earthquake struck Baqen County in Nagqu, southwest China's Xizang Autonomous Region, on Thursday, Du Guoping, owner of a dumpling restaurant in Xigaze, postponed the opening of his two new restaurants and headed to the disaster zone with his staff.
"It took only about 10 minutes to make the decision that we would go to Baqen and cook dumplings for earthquake-affected residents," Du said.
The team loaded more than 1,500 kilograms of dumplings onto vehicles and set off from Xigaze at midnight on the night of the earthquake.
Upon arrival, Du and his staff set up cooking equipment and prepared dumplings for rescue workers and affected residents.
"Make sure everyone gets enough dumplings, and give children a couple more," Du kept telling his staff.
Du and his staff did not eat any of the dumplings themselves. After a full day of cooking, they had some instant noodles -- their only meal of the day. At night, the six team members of Du squeezed into two vehicles to rest.
"We will cook all the dumplings we brought," Du said. "We feel honored to be able to contribute in our own way." (Xinhua/Tenzin Nyida)

21:49:35 KST

BELGRADE, Oct. 25 (Xinhua) -- Former Serbian President Aleksandar Vucic said Sunday that his camp would act responsibly and respect voters' will in the country's snap parliamentary elections.
Speaking to reporters after casting his ballot in Belgrade, Vucic said, "If we lose, we will recognize the electoral will; if we win, no one will take it away."
He added that he expected a high turnout and the Serbian people to express their will democratically.
"Whatever the outcome, we will remain courteous and polite," Vucic said. Unlike some who had never congratulated their opponents, his camp would give no one cause for concern, he added.
"As for the result, let's wait and see tonight," he said. He expected preliminary results to emerge between 10 p.m. (2100 GMT) and midnight local time.
Serbia is holding snap parliamentary elections on Sunday to elect the 250 members of its National Assembly. The ruling Serbian Progressive Party (SNS) previously endorsed Vucic as the lead candidate on its electoral list and as its candidate for prime minister.
Vucic dissolved parliament on Sept. 9 and called elections for Oct. 25 before resigning as president on Sept. 27.
Under Serbia's constitution, a nominee for prime minister must present a government program and a proposed cabinet to parliament and secure the support of a majority of all lawmakers to take office and form a government. ■

US President Donald Trump said that Washington plans to conduct commercial business with both Ukraine and Russia once the war between the two nations concludes.

Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“I think that after this war ends, we’ll do business with Ukraine and with Russia, I would think,” Trump told reporters.
The remarks reflect Trump’s transactional approach toward foreign policy and international economic engagement, positioning post-war trade reconciliation as an element of future bilateral ties.
Trump on Ukraine:
We'll do business with Ukraine and with Russia after this war ends, I would think. pic.twitter.com/bjxgf4l8cw
— Clash Report (@clashreport) October 24, 2026
Tariff threats and bilateral trade limitations
Trump’s statements arrive shortly after comments delivered at a campaign rally in Florida on Friday, Oct. 23, in which the US president suggested that imposing 200 percent import tariffs on Ukraine and Russia could theoretically pressure both parties toward a diplomatic settlement.
However, Trump conceded that direct trade measures would likely have minimal impact due to limited bilateral trade volumes.
“We ended five wars thanks to tariffs. I said, ‘If you continue to fight, we’re going to put a 200 percent tariff on you,’ and they stopped,” Trump told supporters in Florida.
“We should probably immediately do it with Ukraine and Russia. Never thought of it. But we don’t buy enough to do it to them, so it doesn’t work.”
‘Trump Is Cooked’: Republicans Clash Over Ukraine as Midterms Loom
The administration has increasingly utilized trade restrictions, tariff waivers, and commercial agreements as central instruments in its diplomatic maneuvering ahead of the Nov. 3 US midterm elections.
Disputed economic leverage
Trump’s focus on future commercial engagement with Moscow and Kyiv unfolds amid continuing friction regarding Washington’s economic tools to influence the conflict.
President Volodymyr Zelensky previously stated that the US president possesses statutory leverage to compel Russian President Vladimir Putin to negotiate, emphasizing that bipartisan sanctions approved by the US Congress remain unenacted at the White House.
“Trump could very easily bring Putin to the negotiating table, because he has the means to do so. The way he speaks about me – President Trump should speak about Putin in the same way,” Zelensky said.
“Sanctions are sitting on his desk. He didn’t vote for them – Congress voted for strong sanctions. He has the power to act.”
Ukraine’s head of state also rejected assertions by the Trump administration linking retail fuel price increases in the United States to Ukrainian long-range drone interdiction strikes on Russian oil refineries.
While Trump justified a bilateral commercial arrangement to facilitate Russian diesel sales on global markets to lower consumer costs, Zelensky stated that domestic US diesel benchmarks operate independently of Russian export volumes.
Sanctions waivers
The debate over commercial relations arrives after Trump’s recent decision to suspend statutory sanctions and trade duties codified under the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026.
On Oct. 16, Trump signed an executive order invoking Section 115 of the Graham Act to waive mandatory 500 percent tariffs on Russian imports and 100 percent secondary duties targeting global buyers of Russian hydrocarbons, just 48 hours before the measures were scheduled to take statutory effect.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio defended the suspension as a 60-day pause to assess the broader economic fallout of tariffs on both the US and international economies, citing third-party dependencies such as India’s reliance on Russian crude.

Voting under way across Brazil in tight presidential run-off between Lula and Flavio Bolsonaro
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
12:46:02 UTC
21:46:02 KST

Lula thanks voters for his victory, Flavio Bolsonaro does not recognize the results
It is the first time in the country’s history since the return of democracy that a candidate who lost in the first round manages to come back and win in the runoff. The left-wing president obtained 51.7% of the votes, compared with the 48.2% received by right-wing Senator Flavio Bolsonaro.
Veteran pro-union President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva suddenly found himself the underdog after right-wing challenger Flavio Bolsonaro took 47% compared to 45% for the incumbent in the October 4 first round.
A combative, three-week run-off campaign turned the political atmosphere electric. The left threw all its energy into securing a comeback, taking to the streets and mobilising on social media – notably with a WhatsApp channel dubbed "Lula’s Army" that now boasts 8.5 million subscribers. Finally, Lula, a former labor leader, sought and won a fourth (non-consecutive) term in what he has framed as his final battle.
Thank you to all our readers who followed our live coverage of Brazil’s presidential election. This live blog was coordinated first by our team in Paris and then by María Clara Calle and Léa Hurel from our Spanish-speaking newsroom in Bogotá.
Lula’s victory reverses the trend of the right’s rise in Latin America
For more than a year, right-wing candidates had won every election held in the region, as happened in Chile with Jose Antonio Kast, in Peru with Keiko Fujimori, in Ecuador with Daniel Noboa, and in Colombia with Abelardo de la Espriella. Once in office, these countries also joined the U.S. military cooperation initiative known as the Shield of the Americas.
In this way, Washington has been consolidating a bloc favorable to Donald Trump’s policies. Nevertheless, Brazil’s elections represent a setback for the U.S. president, after the Republican supported the Bolsonaro family and the victory of Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva breaks this streak.
In his speech, he defended his country’s sovereignty and stressed that Brazil needs to develop its own artificial intelligence so as not to depend on the United States. “We had to overcome the external interference of digital platforms, which we are going to have to regulate,” he said.
Thus, he continues as one of the few left-wing leaders in the region, alongside Claudia Sheinbaum in Mexico.
Even so, Brazil remains split in two: those who support Lula’s progressive ideas and those who want change with the Bolsonaros.
“It is impossible to recognize this election; we are going to request its annulment”: Bolsonaro
Brazilian presidential candidate Flavio Bolsonaro of the Liberal Party (PL) arrives to speak after losing the presidential runoff election, in Brasilia, Brazil October 25, 2026. REUTERS/Agustin Marcarian
From Brasilia, candidate Flavio Bolsonaro delivered his speech after the results were announced. He spoke briefly and said it was difficult to acknowledge the results given the current context.
The Supreme Court ordered the voting period to be extended by two more hours after Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva’s campaign filed an appeal alleging delays in voter transportation.
“This country will not accept being anyone’s backyard”: Lula
He also stood up for Brazil’s sovereignty. Donald Trump has supported several candidates in Latin America, as he did with Abelardo de la Espriella in Colombia and Daniel Noboa in Ecuador. The Republican also backed the Bolsonaro family during the campaign.
The Workers' Party candidate also said “I am going to deliver the best term that any president has ever had in this country” and he added that he will govern for all Brazilians, despite the polarization.
Lula delivers his first victory speech after reelection
Brazil's President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva, the Workers' Party (PT) candidate for re-election, smiles as he gathers with supporters after winning the presidential runoff in Sao Paulo, Brazil, October 25, 2026. REUTERS/Amanda Perobelli
“Thanks to the Brazilian people for their generosity, to the youth who took to the streets to defend democracy.” This is what Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva said in his victory speech from São Paulo. He also thanked those who helped convince others that “voting was very important to protect the country’s democracy.”
He referred as well to the controversy involving Meta that reached the courts. “We had to overcome the external interference of digital platforms, which we are going to have to regulate,” Lula said. And he added that digital communications will be very important in his government—an essential point, since during the reelection campaign he doubled down on his efforts on social media.
Leftist former presidents congratulate Lula on his victory
Contrary to the trend set by recent elections in Latin America, the right did not win in Brazil. Various leftist former presidents from the region celebrated the victory of Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva.
"Thank you, dear old friend, for never stopping the fight, for upholding the hope of a world," said Gabriel Boric of Chile. Meanwhile, Bolivian leader Evo Morales posted: "Your triumph renews the hope of the peoples who fight for social justice, dignity, and sovereignty."
Former Colombian president also congratulated Lula.
Abstention decreased in Brazil’s second round
Lula’s campaign focused over the last three weeks on winning new votes in order to come back from Flavio Bolsonaro’s first-round victory.
In that effort, securing votes from those who had abstained was essential. In the end, abstention was three million votes lower than in the first round. Although not all of those can be attributed directly to Lula, the difference between the president and Flavio Bolsonaro was just over four million votes in the runoff.
According to the Superior Electoral Court, 33.4 million people abstained from voting on October 4, compared with 30.4 million abstentions in the runoff.
Lula surprises in the runoff and wins Brazil’s presidential election
Supporters of Brazil's President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva, the Workers' Party (PT) candidate for re-election, react to early result during the presidential runoff election, in Sao Paulo, Brazil, October 25, 2026. REUTERS/Amanda Perobell
President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva went from losing in the first round with 45.16% of the votes to winning the runoff with a total of 51.79%, while right-wing Senator Flavio Bolsonaro obtained 48.21%, according to the official count from the Superior Electoral Court.
It is the first time in Brazil’s history since the return of democracy that a candidate who lost in the first round manages to win the runoff and become president.
Lula widens his lead over Bolsonaro with 70% of the votes counted
Supporters of Brazilian President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva, the Workers' Party (PT) candidate for presidential re-election, gather to wait for the results of the presidential runoff election, on the outskirts of Brasilia, Brazil, October 25, 2026. REUTERS/Diego Herculano
At this point, President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva has 50.92% of the votes, while Flavio Bolsonaro has 49.08%.
During the count, the difference between both candidates did not exceed one percentage point, but that gap has now been surpassed and continues to grow in favor of the left-wing president.
This is how Lula’s surge in the vote count was experienced in Rio de Janeiro
Lula retakes the lead in the vote count with a minimal difference
When half of the votes have been tallied, President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva has 50.14% of the vote. Senator Flavio Bolsonaro has 49.86%, according to the Superior Electoral Court.
The difference between both candidates has not exceeded one percentage point during the count.
Lula to win Brazil election runoff, AtlasIntel CEO says
Although in the vote count President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva is trailing by a narrow margin, the CEO of pollster AtlasIntel, Andrei Roman, predicts that Lula will be re-elected.
Roman spoke to Reuters and made his predictions based on the ongoing vote count in the presidential runoff against Senator Flavio Bolsonaro.
A slight lead for Flavio Bolsonaro with 20% of the votes counted
The senator has 50.41% compared to Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva’s 49.59%, as the TSE reports 20% of the votes counted. It is a difference of less than one percentage point.
As in the first round, the states in northern Brazil support the outgoing left-wing president, while those in the south back the far-right candidate.
Flavio overturns the results and takes the lead over Lula
Opposition presidential candidate Sen. Flávio Bolsonaro waves as he arrives in Brasilia, Brazil, on the day of the presidential runoff election, Sunday, Oct. 25, 2026. (AP Photo/Eraldo Peres)
Although President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva began ahead in the Superior Electoral Court’s count, Senator Flavio Bolsonaro now has 50.04% of the votes.
He began to lead the count from 13% of the votes tallied.
Lula holds a slight lead with 5% of the votes counted
Incumbent President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva has 51.16% of the votes, which is just over two percentage points more than his runoff rival Flavio Bolsonaro.
The Superior Electoral Court begins by counting votes cast abroad, where Lula won in the first round.
Voting officially ends in Brazil and the counting resumes
At 7:00 p.m. Brasilia time (10:00 p.m. GMT), the polling stations that were still operating closed.
Now, the Superior Electoral Court is resuming the vote count that it had suspended after the Supreme Court ordered voting to be extended by two more hours.
The extension of voting in Brazil causes confusion at the polls
The Supreme Court’s decision came at around 5:00 p.m. Brasilia time (8:00 p.m. GMT), when the polls were supposed to close. Local media report that several polling stations had already shut down.
In response, the Superior Electoral Court stated that “the election continues in progress only in the locations where voting had not been concluded by 5 p.m.” Meanwhile, the Workers’ Party (PT) and the Liberal Party called on its supporters to keep voting.
Supreme Court approves extending voting by two hours across Brazil
Cristiano Zanin is the Supreme Court justice who decided to extend voting in Brazil’s runoff on October 25. (AP Photo/Eraldo Peres)
At the last minute, Brazilian Supreme Court Justice Cristiano Zanin ordered that voting in the country’s presidential runoff on Sunday be extended by two hours, until 7:00 p.m. Brasilia time (10:00 p.m. GMT).
The decision grants a request from President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva’s campaign. A similar petition was sent to the Superior Electoral Court, but it has not made any decision.
Meanwhile, the Superior Electoral Court has paused the counting of votes following the Supreme Court’s decision.
Flavio Bolsonaro’s campaign also asked to extend the closing of the ballot boxes
Their request is to extend the voting period by two hours, so that it ends at 7:00 p.m. Brasilia time. The appeal was submitted to the president of the Superior Electoral Court, Kassio Nunes Marques, and they are asking for the extension to apply in 17 municipalities in the states of São Paulo, Paraná, and Santa Catarina.
Just like Lula’s Workers’ Party, the Liberal Party that supports Bolsonaro denounced delays in transportation. However, Flavio Bolsonaro’s campaign says that the transportation delays are due to the rains and flooding affecting those states.

Drones Strike Russian Titanium Producer Avisma in Urals
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
12:45:00 UTC
21:45:00 KST

Long-range strike drones struck the “Avisma” titanium and chemical-metallurgical plant in the city of Berezniki in Russia’s Perm region overnight into Sunday, Oct. 25, targeting one of the world’s largest titanium production facilities, The Moscow Times and independent monitoring groups reported.
The enterprise operates as a subsidiary production division of VSMPO-Avisma Corporation, the world’s leading manufacturer of titanium sponge, specialized titanium alloys, and raw magnesium.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Perm Region Governor Dmitry Makhonin acknowledged the aerial incursion on Sunday, stating that an industrial enterprise situated in the northern sector of the province sustained “minor damage” following an attack by unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs).
Makhonin claimed that the damaged facility continues to operate under standard routines and reported no casualties.
However, Ukrainian open-source intelligence (OSINT) monitoring channel Exilenova+ reported that the drone strikes engaged the production grounds of the Avisma chemical-metallurgical facility in Berezniki.
Local residents similarly reported hearing multiple drone engines followed by detonations and the sound of air defense engagements in the vicinity of the plant’s industrial perimeter.
Strategic defense metallurgy and aerospace components
The Berezniki metallurgical complex functions as an irreplaceable industrial node within the Russian Federation’s defense-industrial supply chain.
Trump Eyes Post-War Business Ties With Both Ukraine and Russia
Avisma specializes in the chemical processing of ilmenite ore into titanium tetrachloride and the subsequent thermal reduction of titanium sponge, alongside refining metallic magnesium and magnesium-based master alloys.
The refined titanium sponge and intermediate billets produced at Berezniki are transported to VSMPO’s primary smelting and mechanical processing facilities in Verkhnyaya Salda, Sverdlovsk region, to manufacture high-strength forgings, rolled sheets, and structural sub-assemblies.
The enterprise’s titanium alloys are critical structural materials utilized across Russian aerospace manufacturing, combat aviation, jet engine production, and missile systems.
Components fabricated from Avisma’s metals are integrated into fuselage airframes and turbine components for Su-35 and Su-57 fighter aircraft, fuselage mountings for tactical bombers, heavy armor assemblies, and missile airframes for cruise and ballistic platforms.
Beyond conventional defense hardware, specialized titanium castings and corrosion-resistant alloys from VSMPO-Avisma are supplied directly to Roscosmos for space rocket propulsion casings and to naval shipyards constructing nuclear-powered submarines.
Deep-tier asymmetric campaign against defense suppliers
The strike in Berezniki – located approximately 1,500 kilometers (930 miles) from Ukrainian borders in the Ural Mountains – forms part of an expanding Ukrainian asymmetric campaign systematically targeting Russia’s deep-rear defense metallurgy and strategic chemical supply lines.
The incident in Perm region coincides with long-range drone strikes conducted across Siberia on Saturday, where unmanned platforms struck the Omsky Kauchuk chemical enterprise in Omsk – over 2,500 kilometers from Ukraine – igniting a large-scale blaze at a facility supplying synthetic rubbers and chemical binders used in solid rocket propellant for Iskander-M and intercontinental ballistic missile platforms.
Concurrently overnight into Sunday, Ukrainian strike drones engaged industrial and logistics infrastructure in central Belgorod, damaging the closed MegaGRINN commercial facility, while previous precision missile and drone interdictions hit the Proton defense microelectronics plant in Oryol and the Tolyattikauchuk petrochemical plant in Samara region.

Houthis fire missiles at Saudi Arabia as Riyadh airport reopens
Yemen's Houthis launched wide-ranging strikes across swathes of southern Saudi Arabia on Sunday, as the kingdom announced the partial reopening of Riyadh's international airport despite repeated attacks by the group.
Alerts warning of possible attacks were activated across the kingdom's south throughout the day, with the Saudi-led military coalition fighting the Houthis saying at least 10 ballistic missiles were intercepted.
Saudi Arabia, which leads a military coalition fighting the Iran-backed Houthis, has faced a barrage of strikes from the group in recent weeks.
The fighting erupted after a years-long truce between the Houthis and Yemen's Riyadh-backed government fell apart.
"The bombardment has been very heavy since this morning - may God keep us safe. Everything is shaking because of the explosions," one resident in Khamis Mushait told AFP Sunday on condition of anonymity.
Further north, Riyadh's international airport said flights would resume on Sunday after a two-week closure following the Houthi strikes.
However it remained unclear to what extent the airport was operational.
The Houthi fighters have carried out waves of strikes on the airport, including an attack this month that killed 13 people and wounded more than 300, the deadliest in the kingdom in more than a decade.
The group has also targeted oil infrastructure and other sites.
Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree warned that Riyadh airport was still "unsafe" and a "military target".
"The Yemeni Armed Forces warn all international, regional and local airlines - as well as staff and travellers - against using King Khalid Airport in Riyadh, as it is unsafe and serves as a military target for our forces," he said.
"The Saudi regime shall bear the consequences of any operations at the airport."
Attack warning
As the airport prepared to open, AFP journalists in Riyadh heard three explosions in the early hours of Sunday, with residents receiving alert messages for a "hostile aerial threat" urging them to stay in a safe place.
The warning came as the Saudi-led coalition fighting the Houthis said it had downed a ballistic missile launched by the group towards the capital, as well as two drones in the capital area.
"Air defences intercepted and destroyed a ballistic missile launched by the terrorist Houthi militia toward Riyadh," the coalition posted on X.
Later Sunday morning, the coalition said its forces intercepted a cruise missile fired by the Houthis at the kingdom's southern city of Khamis Mushait.
Attacks appeared to target areas across the south, with warnings also issued for Abha city along with areas in Taif, Namas and Jazan.
The attacks came after the Houthi fighters said that - in the space of 24 hours - they targeted three Saudi airports, including in Riyadh, energy installations, a pipeline and an air base.
The Saudi civil defence agency said it had also responded to falling debris in the Mecca and Medina regions on Saturday after intercepting two Houthi missiles.
The Houthis denied targeting the cities, the two holiest in Islam, calling the Saudi claim a "huge lie".
The Houthis also fired at the southern Yemeni city of Aden, the interim seat of the Saudi-backed government, saying they targeted a naval base and military camp overseen by Saudi forces.
The flare-up in Yemen, with the Houthis taking control of the entire Red Sea coast in a lightning offensive last month, has further destabilised the region and disrupted oil markets.
The Houthi attacks have dealt a blow to Saudi Arabia, the world's biggest exporter of crude, disrupting businesses, airlines and residents, and rattling its drive to shift its international image.

– Warning against economic isolation

He also questioned how international acquisitions of Israeli companies could proceed if the economy moved toward isolation from the global financial system.

“This is not an imagined nightmare scenario, but Netanyahu’s plan for Israel if he is reelected” on Tuesday, he said.
“This is a real warning. Israel will not withstand another four years like these.”
-Controversial remarks

The exchanges also come ahead of Tuesday’s Knesset elections, in which Netanyahu and Eisenkot are competing to lead the next government.
In his post, Eisenkot urged Israelis to vote for “a better shared future.”
The former military chief is one of Netanyahu’s leading rivals, with the two sharply divided on security and economic policies, the country’s leadership, and its foreign relations.
Israeli politics also remains deeply divided on responsibility for the failures surrounding the October 2023 attack, the conduct of subsequent wars, military conscription, the economy, and relations with the US and other Western countries.

Long queues in Zurich ahead of the Brazil and Serbia elections
Long queues have formed outside the Serbian Consulate and the Kongresshaus in Zurich ahead of Sunday’s upcoming elections in Serbia and Brazil. Initial results for both countries are expected late this evening and overnight.
Many Brazilians living in Switzerland wanted to cast their votes in Sunday’s presidential election. Hundreds of people queued up on Sunday morning outside Zurich’s Kongresshaus, for example, despite the persistent rain.
The presidential run-off in South America’s largest country pits the incumbent, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, against his challenger, Flávio Bolsonaro. Both candidates face considerable scepticism. Bolsonaro, however, is heading into the run-off with momentum on his side.

Jameh Mosque of Fahraj: A timeless architectural treasure near Yazd
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
12:42:12 UTC
21:42:12 KST

Jameh Mosque of Fahraj: A timeless architectural treasure near Yazd
TEHRAN - Located near the historic city of Yazd in central Iran, the Jameh Mosque of Fahraj, also known as Masjid-i Jami of Fahraj, is a remarkable destination for travelers interested in history, architecture and Iran’s Islamic heritage. Distinguished by its simple earthen construction, ancient vaults and historic minaret, the mosque offers a glimpse into an important period in the evolution of Iranian religious architecture.
The mosque stands in Fahraj, approximately 25 to 30 kilometers southeast of Yazd, along the historic route connecting Yazd with Bafq. Situated in an arid landscape near the edge of the desert, the village reflects the region’s long-standing adaptation to dry conditions and traditional water systems, including qanats and deep wells.
A landmark of early Islamic architecture
The Jameh Mosque of Fahraj is widely recognized as one of the oldest surviving mosques in Iran. Historical accounts associate its construction with the early Islamic period, following the conquest of Yazd by Muslim armies in the first century AH. However, its exact construction date, original patron and earliest building history have not been conclusively established. The possibility of an earlier origin has also been raised, partly because of the region’s pre-Islamic heritage and the historical practice of adapting existing sacred sites for new religious purposes.
The mosque holds particular architectural significance because it preserves features associated with the transition from early post-and-lintel building systems to more developed vaulted structures. Alongside the Tarikhaneh Mosque in Damghan, Semnan province, it illustrates an important stage in the development of Iranian mosque architecture, when substantial piers increasingly replaced columns as primary structural supports.
Built largely from mud bricks and sun-dried clay materials, the mosque demonstrates how local construction techniques were adapted to religious architecture in a challenging desert environment. Its restrained appearance, with little decorative ornamentation, distinguishes it from many of Iran’s later monumental mosques.
A courtyard framed by ancient arches
The mosque’s architectural composition centers on an enclosed courtyard surrounded by arcades and a vaulted prayer hall. The courtyard, lined with clay tiles, contains a central ablution tank that is now dry. Thick rectangular piers divide the arcades into arched bays, creating a balanced rhythm across the interior façades.
The prayer hall features traditional Iranian barrel vaults, supported by sturdy brick piers. These vaults, together with the building’s oval-shaped arches and pointed arches above the entrances, reflect a combination of structural ingenuity and architectural traditions associated with the transition from the Sassanid era to the Islamic period.
The prayer hall has three entrances, with the central entrance wider than the two side entrances. This arrangement reflects the importance of the main axis leading toward the qibla, the direction of prayer. The building also contains two mihrabs, or prayer niches, positioned close to one another. The larger, principal mihrab is made of plaster and measures approximately 2.32 meters wide and 3.24 meters high.
Unlike many famous Iranian mosques, the Jameh Mosque of Fahraj has no prominent dome, elaborate tilework or extensive inscriptions. Its architectural interest lies instead in its proportions, construction methods and preservation of early building forms.
An early example of the Iranian minaret
One of the mosque’s most notable features is its clay minaret, which is believed to have been added later, possibly during the 10th century. Together with the early minaret at the ancient city of Na’in, it represents an important surviving example of the development of the Iranian minaret.
The structure takes the form of a tapering cylinder, with an internal spiral staircase illuminated by narrow openings in its exterior walls. A projecting balcony and triangular crenellations emphasize its vertical profile, creating a striking contrast with the mosque’s low, horizontal roofline.
The minaret is significant beyond its immediate setting. The development of the cylindrical minaret became an influential feature of Islamic architecture, with related forms spreading across regions including Iraq, Syria, Anatolia, Afghanistan and India over subsequent centuries.
A rewarding stop for cultural travelers
For visitors exploring Yazd and its surrounding historic settlements, the Jameh Mosque of Fahraj offers an opportunity to discover a lesser-known architectural landmark away from the region’s more elaborate monuments. Its understated appearance invites closer attention to the details of early Islamic construction, from the arrangement of its arches and piers to the geometry of its vaulted prayer hall.
The mosque is particularly appealing to travelers interested in architectural history, archaeology and the cultural connections between pre-Islamic Persia and the Islamic period. Its location in Fahraj also makes it a potential stop on a journey through the villages and desert landscapes southeast of Yazd.
The mosque’s simplicity, however, has contributed to its receiving less public attention than some of Iran’s more decorative historic buildings. Its historical importance rests precisely in the architectural innovations it preserves, features that were gradually overshadowed by later mosque designs, including the four-iwan plan that became prominent under the Seljuks.
For those seeking to understand Iran beyond its celebrated tiled domes and monumental courtyards, the Jameh Mosque of Fahraj provides a compelling encounter with the foundations of the country’s Islamic architectural heritage. It is a reminder that some of the most significant historic places are not necessarily the most ornate, but those that preserve traces of how architectural traditions evolved across centuries.

Burnham says Britain should have an ‘honest discussion’ about how immigration to the UK has changed since Brexit.
Prime Minister Andy Burnham says he wants to discuss Britain returning to the European Union’s freedom of movement rules for workers, a key issue in the 2016 Brexit referendum which led to the United Kingdom leaving the bloc.
Addressing the need to rethink ties with Brussels, Burnham told The Sunday Times newspaper that the influx of EU workers into Britain before Brexit had posed significant challenges.
“But, at the same time, it was a type of immigration that perhaps wasn’t as difficult [as now],” he said in a report released on Sunday.
“Revolving door migration where people would come and then go back is different. The balance of migration has changed, hasn’t it, since then? I think we’ve just got to have an honest discussion about those things,” he said.
The issue of immigration was a key factor in the 2016 Brexit referendum campaign that ended with Britons narrowly voting to leave the EU.
A decade later, Burnham, who has even touted the possibility of Britain applying to rejoin the EU one day, said the country should have an “honest discussion” about how immigration to Britain has changed since Brexit.
Long-term net migration to the UK nearly halved in 2025, according to the Office for National Statistics (ONS), falling to 171,000 in 2025 from 331,000 a year earlier. This drop had not been seen since before the post-Brexit immigration system was introduced, as tougher government measures have restricted arrivals.
In his October 19 interview with The Sunday Times, Burnham said the issue of freedom of movement could be considered as part of a broader reset of the UK’s relationship with the EU, including on data sharing and migration.
“Consider what we’ve lost, which was the ability to be part of Eurodac and all the data collaboration around migration. You’ve got to see it in the round, rather than just looking at freedom of movement on its own,” he told The Sunday Times.
Nigel Farage, leader of the anti-immigration Reform UK party, called Burnham’s comments on free movement a “total betrayal of Brexit Britain”.
In his speech to the Labour Party conference last month, Burnham said Brexit had done “more harm than good” and called for Britain to consider its “long-term relationship” with the EU.
The prime minister, who is trying to find ways to speed up the UK economy, is due to meet top EU officials for a summit on November 20.

Restoration of Sassanid reliefs at Naqsh-e Rostam nears completion after three decades
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
12:38:22 UTC
21:38:22 KST

Restoration of Sassanid reliefs at Naqsh-e Rostam nears completion after three decades
TEHRAN – The restoration of Sassanid-era bas-reliefs at Naqsh-e Rostam, one of Iran’s most significant archaeological sites, is approaching completion after a conservation effort that began in the 1990s, with work continuing on a relief depicting Shapur II, a site official said.
Mostafa Rakhshandehkhoo, head of the Naqsh-e Rostam complex and supervisor of its conservation and restoration workshops, told the Iranian Students’ News Agency (ISNA) that restoration work on more than eight Sassanid bas-reliefs had been pursued over several decades to preserve their historical and artistic value.
The ongoing work on the relief of Shapur II represents a decisive stage in the long-running effort, bringing the restoration program close to its final phase, he said.
Rakhshandehkhoo stressed that conserving historical monuments involves more than physical intervention. It requires detailed studies, expert assessments, informed decision-making and the careful application of appropriate conservation methods.
“The primary objective is to preserve the authenticity of the monument, control damaging factors and create conditions that will help ensure its long-term survival,” he said, according to ISNA.
He added that preparing a restoration plan suited to the condition of the Shapur II relief, as well as reviewing and approving it through the relevant authorities, was particularly important. Work based on an approved plan and carried out in accordance with professional conservation standards helps ensure that interventions are appropriate to the monument’s specific circumstances.
The official said the experience gained over decades at Naqsh-e Rostam demonstrated the importance of sustained conservation efforts, technical expertise and careful monitoring in protecting archaeological remains.
Historical monuments are exposed to various damaging factors over time, he said, making long-term planning essential to preserving them for future generations. He added that the value of the project lay not only in bringing restoration work to an end but also in the methods used, adherence to scientific principles and responsibility toward cultural heritage.
Rakhshandehkhoo added that the experience could serve as a model for other conservation projects, emphasizing that understanding the characteristics and condition of each monument and selecting suitable techniques were essential to avoiding unnecessary interventions and improving the durability of restoration work.
A record of Sassanid power and artistry
Naqsh-e Rostam, located in Fars province near Persepolis, contains monuments from several periods of ancient Iranian history. The site is particularly notable for its Achaemenid royal rock-cut tombs and Sassanid bas-reliefs carved into the cliff face.
The Sassanid Empire, which ruled Iran from 224 to 651, left an extensive artistic and archaeological legacy. The reliefs at Naqsh-e Rostam depict royal ceremonies, military victories and scenes associated with the authority of Sassanid rulers, providing important evidence for understanding the period’s political history and artistic traditions.
The site’s rock-cut monuments stand alongside the tombs attributed to Achaemenid kings, making Naqsh-e Rostam an important archaeological landscape spanning different eras of ancient Iranian civilization.
Its reliefs are more than works of art; they are historical records that help researchers investigate royal representation, political power and the cultural traditions of the Sassanid period.
The site’s proximity to Persepolis, the ceremonial capital of the Achaemenid Empire and a UNESCO World Heritage property, further underscores its significance within Iran’s archaeological heritage.

Secrets of Presidential Protocol: Who shakes hands first and why hugs are inappropriate
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
12:37:46 UTC
21:37:46 KST

Who should shake the president's hand first? Why is there a red carpet for one visit and not another? And can an overly cordial hug turn into a diplomatic blunder?
Behind the seemingly natural behavior of state leaders lies a complex system of rules that determine almost every detail of their official meetings. State and diplomatic protocol is a kind of invisible framework of international relations - a language through which respect, equality and political messages are expressed.
Unlike ordinary good manners, protocol has not only symbolic, but also political and legal significance.
How this system works was explained by the international consultant on corporate etiquette and protocol , Kristina Kruncheva, in the special election studio "New Chapter" on Bulgaria ON AIR.
Who decides when the president will lend a hand?
The preparation of the head of state's meetings is entrusted to professionals who specify in advance even details that go unnoticed by the public.
"The protocol at the president's office, depending on the various activities, is managed either by the State Protocol Directorate, which is part of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, or by the protocol of the presidency," explained Krancheva.
According to her, the most important thing is how official events take place and what impression they leave.
Mistakes are relatively rare because almost every action is coordinated in advance – when the head of state will arrive, who will greet him, who he will shake hands with, and who will be the first to extend a hand.
Even official correspondence is subject to special rules.
Behind natural behavior lie hours of preparation
One of the biggest challenges of diplomatic protocol is making everything seem casual.
"There is nothing accidental. In order to create the impression that everything is going smoothly and everyone knows what to do, as if they have been taught this since childhood, a lot of preliminary work is actually needed before each meeting," the specialist emphasized.
She explained that every activity of the presidential institution follows a clearly established sequence - what is done, how, and at what time.
It is this organization that allows state leaders to focus on conversations instead of thinking about ceremonial details.
Why is there sometimes a red carpet and other times not?
Not all international visits are organized in the same way.
Kristina Kruncheva drew attention to the difference between an official and a working visit.
"Before we know that there will be a visit from another head of state, a lot of work is done. Depending on whether the meeting will be an official visit or a working visit, there are different rules," she explained.
During official visits, the ceremony is significantly more solemn. Among the characteristic elements is the red carpet, which may begin at the plane of the visiting president.
Such formality is not necessary in business meetings.
The difference is not an expression of more or less respect, but stems from the nature and predetermined status of the visit.
The president also needs to learn etiquette
After being elected, the head of state must be familiar with the basic rules that will accompany the fulfillment of his duties.
This includes behavior at official meetings, manner of greeting, ceremonial order, and the specifics of communicating with foreign representatives.
Krancheva pointed out that excessive familiarity is not always appropriate.
"Hugs are avoided, hands are not shaken, as if we have known each other since we were little," she explained.
According to the expert, some presidents demonstratively ignore established rules. Sometimes this is perceived as part of their personal style or an attempt to show that they are above formalities.
However, such behavior does not always leave a good impression.
First ladies have their own agenda
A curious detail from the world of diplomatic etiquette is that the wives of heads of state usually have a separate program during official visits.
While presidents engage in political conversations, their partners may attend cultural, social, or charitable events.
And here everything is organized in advance, including clothing.
What does the dress code say?
Formal invitations contain instructions on appropriate attire for guests.
"The invitations mention the men's dress code because it is assumed that women know how to dress. When it is very formal, women wear long dresses," explained Kristina Kruncheva.
She also paid attention to a seemingly small detail - the jacket.
According to the consultant, the jacket is the garment that gives structure to the body and creates a more formal appearance.
In a diplomatic environment, clothing is part of the overall presence and can emphasize both respect for the event and the attitude towards the hosts.
That's why, in the world of high diplomacy, even the most ordinary greeting, choice of attire, or a few steps on the red carpet have their place in a carefully prepared scenario.

Wallhack M-001 Review: When Fun Overrides Specs
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
12:30:00 UTC
21:30:00 KST

With a tactile dongle for on-the-fly customization and a metal chassis, the Wallhack M-001 is the most fun I've had reviewing a gaming mouse in a long time.
Magnesium shell. Hot-swappable, rechargeable batteries. 52-gram weight. Functional and innovative dongle. Satisfying tactile experience. Great styling and design language.
TIRED
High price point. Slightly outdated sensor. Only 2.4G wireless connectivity with dongle; no Bluetooth or USB-C connectivity on mouse.
Batteries. They're not typically thought of as a significant source of innovation. Most companies have spent the last few years removing mice in favor of more lightweight designs.
That's what's made the return of the replaceable and rechargeable battery surprising—something I once thought to be a lost technology from a bygone era. A few companies have recently realized that the ability to pop out and replace your battery in seconds is a great way to extend mouse life without needing to increase battery size or efficiency.
From the handful of mice I’ve tested with hot-swappable batteries so far, Wallhack does it best. The mouse is designed around the function’s ease-of-use, and everything else comes together to make a mouse that feels not only competitive for gaming, but also well thought-out and satisfying to use in everyday life.
Effective Shape
The M-001’s shape is a standard right-handed, symmetrical design. This means the mouse’s left and right sides are shaped identically, but only the left side has thumb buttons. There are two main buttons, two side buttons, a standard ratcheting scroll wheel, and a power switch on the underside.
With a length of 120 mm, the M-001 is slightly shorter than contemporaries like the Razer Viper V4 Pro (125 mm) and Logitech Pro Superstrike X2 (127 mm). The overall width and height are comparable, at 63.5-mm tall and a 39-mm wide. The largest difference is the profile of the mouse: The front end sits significantly lower than other mice, and the rear has a more significant hump, which creates a more angled shape overall. When using a palm grip, this puts your hand at a slightly more aggressive forwards angle, with your palm sitting higher and your fingers pointing more downwards. It’s a slight difference, but I found this angle to be better for quick movements compared to a more “flat” design. However, like most shape-related choices, this is ultimately down to individual preference. (To compare mouse sizes, I typically use a website like eloshapes)
The two main buttons are lightly sculpted, with subtle concavity for fingers to comfortably rest in. Similarly, there is a subtle taper at the bottom center of the mouse which makes lifting and moving easier. The side buttons use a simple, rounded shape placed just above the taper, making it easy to rock your thumb upwards to press them without getting in the way. They’re just elevated enough that the buttons don’t recess into the shell when pressed. The only shape-related issue I had was the scroll wheel, which is a good bit more elevated than other mice. This isn’t a huge issue, and I adapted to it after a few hours of use, but it’s something I could see being off-putting for users accustomed to a lower-profile scroll wheel.
(Not) Heavy Metal
The most important part of this mouse’s construction is the magnesium shell, which provides significantly more rigidity than the plastic shells used on most mice. Because of this, the mouse feels incredibly sturdy and solid. The metal shell also gives the mouse a cool, slick feeling underneath your fingertips, which I prefer to the matte plastic feeling that most mice have.
Despite using metal, it only weighs 53.6 grams, making the M-001 quite light by most standards, It still falls slightly behind the Viper V4 Pro’s 50.3 grams and lags way behind Corsair’s superlight, 36-gram Sabre V2 Pro Ultralight. But the M-001 is incredibly solid, with none of the flexibility or flimsiness that most plastic mice have. When compared to other magnesium mice like the AngryMiao Infinity .97 or Corsair’s magnesium-shelled Sabre, the M-001 has an entirely solid upper shell without any cutouts or holes, which feels much better for regular use with a multitude of grip styles (plus, it’s much less likely to have dust, dead skin, or anything else build up inside of it). While the full magnesium shell increases weight, it’s a worthwhile trade-off for a smooth and rigid shape.
It’s also worth noting that some of Wallhack’s promotional material depicts the mouse as being a solid black color, but this isn’t quite the case. The unit I received is much closer to a gunmetal color, with a significant amount of metallic flake across the finish. The color looks fantastic in person, but it's difficult to properly capture in images.
Flipping over this mouse reveals one of the more atypical design decisions being made: the lack of a bottom shell. Instead of an entire underside, there is a thin frame around the circumference of the mouse that holds six feet in place. Between them is a chasm that reveals the entire PCB and battery.
Of particular note is the PCB’s function inside the mouse: Instead of simply sitting inside of the shell, the PCB works as a primary structural component. Similar techniques have been used in designing supercars and sport bikes, with the Ferrari F50 using the engine block as a stressed member that provides rigidity to the entire car, a technology borrowed from Ferrari’s F1 team. This provides some obvious benefits to rigidity and weight-savings, but it’s also just undeniably cool to be able to flip over your mouse and see the entire circuit board.
Right behind the PCB is the star of the show, a hot-swappable battery. While I’ve tested quite a few mice with this technology, none of them have managed to make the battery-swapping so satisfying. Instead of being attached with magnets or a rotating locking mechanism, the batteries use a custom-made -spring-loaded ejector similar to an SD card or a Nintendo Switch cartridge. To insert the battery, simply press until you feel a click, and it will lock into place. To remove it, do the same: press until you feel a click, and it will pop out slightly. Of all the mice I’ve tested with removable batteries, this is by far my favorite mechanism to use: It’s intuitive, fun, and feels sturdy.
This battery system does come with a trade-off. Because hot-swappable batteries means an effectively-infinite battery life (as long as you remember to plug the old one into the dongle when you swap), Wallhack has decided to entirely remove the USB-C port on the mouse. This means it only functions as a 2.4G wireless mouse and cannot be plugged or charged in directly. This isn’t a huge issue (it never inconvenienced me, since there was always a fully charged battery ready to swap in), and it theoretically means the connection quality will be better, since there’s fewer components between the antenna and the receiver. But it is worth noting that, if a battery dies or your dongle craps out, there’s no other way to use this mouse.
The Perfect Dongle
In every high-polling mouse I’ve reviewed, the dongle has been a bit of a pain point. A high polling rate necessitates proximity, which in turn requires in a small thing sitting on your desk. In most cases, these things have only one or two functions: They connect to the mouse, and they maybe have a small number of LED indicators (between 1 and 3) that can display battery life, connection quality, or some other setting. Almost every time, they’re small and light enough to slide around on your desk and will inevitably end up falling behind it once or twice due to the weight of the cable pulling it back.
With the M-001, nearly all of these issues are resolved: The dongle is given purpose, function, and I’d even argue dignity. Instead of the small, existing-by-necessity designs that most manufacturers ship with their mice, Wallhack has managed to make a beautiful piece of industrial design. The dongle is a medium-sized metal wedge sporting a gunmetal gray finish identical to the mouse. It has two camera-like dials up front, a button, and a slot for a rechargeable battery. The DPI dial features numbering from 400 to 25,600, and the polling dial goes from 125 Hz to 8,000 Hz.
The dials both have LED indicators next to them, which illuminate alongside the mouse to indicate a setting being changed. When rotated, they both have a satisfying ratcheting mechanism that’s stiff enough to avoid accidental inputs, without being difficult to turn using a single finger.
While I loved these dials from the moment I saw them, I really didn’t expect to use them much. I’ve always been more of a set-and-forget type of person. But after testing this mouse for a while, I regularly found myself using both of the dials: On-the-fly DPI adjustments were great for games like Marvel Rivals. I tended to prefer, for example, a higher DPI for Thing and a lower for Thor. Polling adjustments, too, were useful in situations where older games (like Destiny 2) got grumpy when I was using a mouse above 1,000 Hz.
Performance and Software
Like many mice today, the M-001 uses an in-browser customization client. Wallhack’s web client, Wallhack Terminal, takes a unique stylistic approach, relying on a black-and-white, text-based system that resembles Command Prompt more than a typical gaming software. This is both a breath of fresh air stylistically, and much more straightforward than some of the software I’ve used in the past.
The configurator has an extensive feature set, including adjustments for mouse rotation, acceleration, and lift-off distance, which is adjustable by millimeters instead of the vague Low/Medium/High that some softwares use. The sensor can also be pushed to scan faster than the mouse’s 8,000 Hz polling rate, which can potentially improve the accuracy of the sensor, but limits battery life.
Along with adjusting DPI and polling with the dials on the dongle, switching them to the red “DPI” And “Hz” text allows for more granular adjustments within the configurator.
The sensor inside the mouse is a Pixart PAW3950. For anyone who doesn’t have an exhaustive list of mouse sensors floating around their head, this is the same type of sensor used in the 2022 Razer Viper V2 Pro (branded as the Razer Focus Pro 30k). That's four years old at this point. It’s not quite a cutting-edge sensor anymore. But unless you're in the top-tier of competitive play, the sensor will feel consistent and reliable enough, being able to easily track and manage direction changes during fast-paced shootouts. My personal daily driver is a Viper V2 Pro with the exact same sensor (I prefer the shape to the V3 and V4), and it’s still perfectly serviceable after four years of use.
The main buttons inside this mouse use Omron Optical switches, while the side buttons opt for low-profile Omron blue-dot mechanical switches. The scroll wheel’s encoder is a mechanical unit as well, which means it doesn’t have quite the same longevity as the optical units some mice are beginning to use. However, they are easier to replace or fix if something does go wrong.
The internal design of this mouse is impressively simple: There are six feet on the underside, and the outer four all have screws underneath. When you remove these four screws, the bottom half of the shell comes off cleanly (no flimsy plastic clips!), and a few more screws separate the internals from the top shell.
Mice Should Be Fun
I’ve said many times that, when it comes to peripherals, technical specs are only one part of the story. More than that, it’s important to have a device you enjoy using. Of all the mice I’ve tested, the M-001 is by far one of the most enjoyable. The shape is comfortable and natural for multiple grip styles, and the material ensures that the mouse feels rigid and stable despite its light weight. The dongle is a brilliant design that elevates itself from a sad desk tchotchke to a practical and functional device. And the battery mechanism is one of the most clever and fun designs I’ve seen in ages.
Everything about this mouse is deeply satisfying, and I found myself excited to use it every time I sat down. Of course, this mouse isn’t at the cutting edge of sensors or switches, and because of this, I can’t exactly recommend this mouse to someone looking for an ultra-cost-effective option with min-maxed specs. But in using the mouse on the daily, I didn't find that it mattered as much as you might think. 8,000 Hz polling and a 25,600 DPI sensor are enough for all but the pros. Instead, it uses tried-and-true internals that function perfectly well and, more importantly, have crisp and precise tactile responses.
