Iran to add 3,800 MW of thermal power capacity to national grid
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
11:29:29 UTC
20:29:29 KST

Iran to add 3,800 MW of thermal power capacity to national grid
TEHRAN – Iran plans to add 3,800 megawatts of new thermal power generation capacity to its national grid in the next Iranian calendar year (begins late March 2027), as the electricity sector faces financial pressures that threaten investment in infrastructure, a deputy energy minister said.
Mostafa Rajabi-Mashhadi, deputy energy minister for electricity and energy affairs, said the gap between regulated electricity tariffs and the actual cost of supply was increasing the sector’s outstanding receivables and debts while reducing its capacity to finance infrastructure development.
Without sustainable funding to offset the shortfall, the situation could further weaken investment, while covering the gap through the public budget could put additional pressure on government finances and widen the budget deficit, he said, according to IRIB.
Rajabi-Mashhadi said gradual electricity pricing reform, targeted support for vulnerable households and expansion of competitive electricity markets were among the measures needed to improve the sector’s financial sustainability and encourage new investment.
Industries to play a growing role in power generation
Of the 3,800 MW of thermal power capacity expected to come online next year, the capacity being developed by industries for their own electricity needs will be about twice that of new power units being built by the Energy Ministry, Rajabi-Mashhadi said.
The figures reflect the growing role of industrial companies in investing in electricity generation to meet domestic demand, he added.
He also highlighted the expansion of electricity trading on the Energy Exchange as a way to improve price transparency, facilitate transactions and strengthen incentives for investment and consumption management. Deepening the market could help bring electricity supply and demand into closer balance, he said.
Smart meters to support demand management
Rajabi-Mashhadi said the rollout of smart electricity meters was another key element of demand management, allowing more accurate monitoring of consumption and more effective implementation of tariff policies.
The meters also enable authorities to control the power consumption of high-use customers within established regulations, a measure that could help curb excessive demand and ease pressure on the grid during peak hours.
The Energy Ministry aims to encourage public participation in managing electricity consumption, he said. Customers who keep consumption within prescribed limits will benefit from incentives, while high-use customers are encouraged to adjust their consumption patterns and pay for electricity consumed above the prescribed level at rates reflecting its supply cost.
Power sector prepares for winter supply pressures
Rajabi-Mashhadi said fuel supplies for power plants were entering a critical period ahead of winter. Although stocks of liquid fuel at power plant storage facilities were at satisfactory levels, constraints on natural gas supplies and rising seasonal demand could make it more difficult to secure enough gas for power generation.
He said the electricity sector needed to be fully prepared for the critical 100-day winter period to ensure reliable energy supplies.
Achieving that goal would require coordination among the relevant sectors to secure fuel supplies, keep power plants operational and encourage all consumers to manage electricity and gas use, he added. The aim is to get through the period with minimal disruption to the country's energy network.

Energy Ministry implements 60 measures to secure electricity supplies during winter
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
11:29:17 UTC
20:29:17 KST

Energy Ministry implements 60 measures to secure electricity supplies during winter
TEHRAN – Iranian Energy Ministry is implementing 60 operational measures to ensure stable electricity supplies during the winter and mitigate the potential impact of fuel shortages, while power plants’ liquid fuel reserves remain at satisfactory levels, the country's electricity industry spokesman said.
Ehsan Zabihzadeh said more than 80 percent of the fuel consumed by thermal power plants comes from natural gas, with most facilities designed to operate primarily on gas. Liquid fuels serve as a backup to improve grid reliability and help offset potential gas supply constraints, he added, according to IRIB.
Gas supplies to power plants and their liquid fuel inventories are currently in a favourable position, Zabihzadeh said. Liquid fuel stocks are roughly at the same level as a year earlier, when reserves were particularly strong, and the trend this year has also been positive so far.
Some storage capacity remains to be filled, but the remaining tanks are expected to reach capacity in the coming days and weeks as winter approaches, with the help of the Oil Ministry, he said.
However, maintaining reliable electricity supplies throughout the winter will depend not only on initial preparedness but also on continued gas allocations and the timely delivery of liquid fuels, Zabihzadeh said.
Authorities have designated a roughly 100-day period, beginning in mid-December, as the main window for winter preparedness and have coordinated plans to secure power plant fuel supplies with the Oil Ministry, he added.
60 measures to manage winter constraints
Zabihzadeh said attacks attributed by Iranian officials to Israel and the United States had damaged gas supply infrastructure, reducing part of the country's gas supply capacity compared with last year, according to statements by Oil Ministry officials.
The electricity sector has therefore drawn up 60 operational measures to get through the 100-day winter period with minimal disruption. Implementation of the measures is progressing satisfactorily, he said.
The main steps include completing essential power plant maintenance on schedule, accelerating renewable energy development to increase electricity generation without fuel consumption, advancing maintenance at the country's nuclear power plant so it can return to service at the beginning of the cold season, and optimizing hydropower generation.
Improving the efficiency of thermal power generation is also a priority, Zabihzadeh said. Authorities aim to maximize the use of high-efficiency generating units and reduce diesel consumption, particularly in northern Iran, where power plants face a greater risk of fuel supply constraints.
Maintenance of the electricity grid and major energy transmission corridors is receiving greater attention than in previous years, he added, as authorities seek to minimize transmission bottlenecks that could restrict electricity supplies during winter.
Energy conservation remains a priority
Zabihzadeh said coordination among different sectors was essential to managing energy consumption and maintaining reliable electricity supplies throughout the cold season.
Government agencies and public institutions should lead by example in conserving energy, while all electricity and gas consumers should help manage demand, he said.
Reducing energy consumption can lessen the impact of potential fuel shortages, Zabihzadeh added, stressing that conservation should extend beyond winter. Even small savings can have a meaningful effect if sustained and adopted as a long-term practice.

Next year’s budget bill to be submitted to parliament in a month
TEHRAN – Iranian government plans to finalize the budget bill for the next Iranian calendar year (starts in late March 2027) within a month and submit it to parliament in December, the head of the Plan and Budget Organization (PBO) said.
Hamid Pourmohammadi said the budget circular for the Iranian year 1406, which begins in March 2027, had been drafted and approved by the Economic Council and sent to the president for issuance.
“Our plan is to complete the process of preparing and finalizing the budget bill in the government within a month and, God willing, submit it to the Islamic Consultative Assembly in December,” Pourmohammadi was quoted as saying by ISNA.
He said the government had already held talks with lawmakers on how to prepare next year’s budget, noting that the country’s current economic circumstances made the process different from that of the previous year.
Despite the impact of war, blockade and military confrontations, the country’s financial and budgetary systems must continue operating on schedule, Pourmohammadi said. He added that budget payments had so far faced minimal disruption, although some expenditures could be given lower priority at certain times.
Pourmohammadi said the government would place greater emphasis on improving the living conditions of civil servants and retirees, many of whom are struggling with inflation. It would also seek to address disparities in public-sector pay, he added.
He said recent developments could also prompt changes in the composition of government revenue, potentially reducing the budget’s reliance on oil income and shifting some of the burden toward other sources.
Improving household livelihoods, narrowing pay inequalities among government employees and reviewing the balance of revenue sources are among the issues expected to be considered in drafting the next year’s budget, Pourmohammadi said.

Iran seeks to expand gas trade with GECF members
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
11:28:11 UTC
20:28:11 KST

Iran seeks to expand gas trade with GECF members
TEHRAN – Iran is seeking to expand gas trade with members of the Gas Exporting Countries Forum (GECF), develop a common gas market and strengthen energy cooperation, the country's acting oil minister said ahead of the group's eighth summit in Russia.
Hamid Bovard said Iran would hold bilateral talks with oil and energy ministers from member countries on the sidelines of the summit to discuss expanding cooperation and bilateral activities.
Iran, a founding member of the GECF, would outline its positions through President Masoud Pezeshkian at the leaders' summit and through the acting oil minister at the group's ministerial meeting, Bovard said, according to Shana.
Key issues on the agenda include protecting energy infrastructure during wars and crises, expanding gas trade among exporting countries and identifying ways to increase exchanges, he said.
Bovard added that Iran would also push for the establishment of a common gas market and closer coordination among exporting countries to develop common policies on gas exports.
On relations with Russia, Bovard said the two countries had established cooperation in the energy sector, with Russian companies holding contracts to develop several Iranian oil and gas fields. Negotiations on gas exchanges between the two countries are also under way, he added.
"We hope to achieve positive results during this trip and further pave the way for strengthening cooperation and expanding energy exchanges between Iran and Russia," Bovard said.
Bovard travelled to Moscow on Sunday to accompany Pezeshkian at the eighth GECF summit and attend the forum's 28th ministerial meeting.
The ministerial meeting is scheduled for Monday, a day before the leaders' summit. An extraordinary meeting of the GECF Executive Board, chaired by Seyed Ali-Mohammad Mousavi, Iran's deputy oil minister for international affairs and commerce, and a meeting of the Ad Hoc High-Level Committee were also scheduled for Sunday.
The meetings are expected to review and finalize key documents, including the summit's final declaration.
The GECF provides a framework for dialogue and coordination among natural gas-producing and exporting countries. Its meetings address developments in gas markets, supply and demand outlooks, energy security and the role of natural gas in the global energy mix.
Other areas of focus include developing natural gas markets, monitoring trends in the liquefied natural gas (LNG) industry and assessing investment needs to meet future demand.
The forum's leaders' summit is held every two years. Previous summits took place in Doha in 2011, Moscow in 2013, Tehran in 2015, Santa Cruz de la Sierra in Bolivia in 2017, Malabo in Equatorial Guinea in 2019, Doha in 2022 and Algiers in 2024.
The GECF has 12 full members: Algeria, Bolivia, Egypt, Equatorial Guinea, Iran, Libya, Nigeria, Qatar, Russia, Trinidad and Tobago, the United Arab Emirates and Venezuela. Angola, Azerbaijan, Iraq, Malaysia, Mauritania, Mozambique, Peru and Senegal participate as observer countries.
According to figures cited by the forum, its members collectively hold about 70 percent of the world's proven natural gas reserves, account for 38 percent of global marketed gas production and 42 percent of global gas exports. Their share of global LNG exports is estimated at around 47 percent.

The Kremlin would support the appointment of a EU diplomatic envoy to participate in negotiations, provided that the designated representative demonstrates a genuine commitment to facilitating a peaceful settlement, Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov stated on Sunday, Oct. 25.

“If the European Union puts forward a negotiator who genuinely wants to contribute to a peaceful settlement, we would support it,” Peskov said.
The Kremlin spokesperson criticized European leaders for procedural delays in establishing a diplomatic track with Moscow, claiming that the EU has long expressed an interest in appointing an interlocutor but lacks the institutional resolve to finalize a mandate.
Peskov alleged that the bloc “has wanted to do this for a very long time, but either cannot or does not dare to” designate a representative.
European deliberations over leadership candidates
Peskov’s comments arrive as European capitals actively debate appointing a high-level envoy to secure direct European representation in prospective settlement talks, amid concerns that bilateral engagements between Washington and Moscow could sideline European and Ukrainian security interests.
According to diplomatic sources cited by The Telegraph, five European leaders are under consideration to represent the continent in discussions with Russian President Vladimir Putin.
North Korea Expands Missiles and Drones With Russian Help
The candidates include Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni, Finnish President Alexander Stubb, Czech President Petr Pavel, Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen, and Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre.
European diplomats have reportedly initiated exploratory contacts with prospective candidates to evaluate their willingness to assume the role.
“There first needs to be a consensus that we need to negotiate with the Russians,” a source familiar with internal deliberations told the British newspaper. “Secondly, there needs to be a consensus on what that position is.”
The diplomatic initiative follows apprehension across European capitals regarding the Trump administration’s unilateral diplomacy with Moscow, which has included backchannel discussions on post-war economic ties alongside the bilateral commercial diesel agreement and executive sanctions waivers under the Lindsey O. Graham Act.
Institutional hurdles and envoy models
Reaching internal consensus across European institutions has proven complex. German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul previously faced resistance over a proposal to lead European diplomatic efforts, while European Council President António Costa declined to undertake the envoy role during a recent meeting of European Union heads of state.
Diplomatic sources suggested that appointing a collective delegation of European leaders could prove more viable than selecting a single envoy, mitigating inter-state friction and reducing the likelihood of individual national vetoes.
The concept of a European negotiating representative has circulated for several months. In June, Meloni endorsed Stubb as a viable candidate to conduct dialogue between Kyiv and Moscow.
Stubb has maintained an active role in European coordination, participating alongside President Volodymyr Zelensky and US special presidential envoy Steve Witkoff in consultations in Oslo on Oct. 20.
Stubb has also maintained regular communication with US President Donald Trump, while asserting that asymmetric military pressure – including Ukrainian long-range strikes against Russian territory – remains essential to forcing Moscow into substantive negotiations.
Preparations for trilateral consultations
The Kremlin’s conditional opening toward a European negotiator coincides with diplomatic preparations for prospective trilateral talks between delegations from the US, Ukraine, and Russia.
Following an Oct. 21 meeting in St. Petersburg between Putin and Witkoff, the Kremlin confirmed that Moscow is prepared in principle to resume trilateral consultations in early November, with Abu Dhabi and Switzerland identified by diplomatic sources as prospective venues.
Zelensky has affirmed Kyiv’s readiness to engage in trilateral consultations provided that an enforceable ceasefire and binding security guarantees serve as baseline conditions, while warning that economic accommodations granted to Moscow without verified de-escalation merely prolong the conflict.

Brazil votes in closely contested presidential runoff
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
11:25:13 UTC
20:25:13 KST

Polls opened across Brazil at 8 am local time on Sunday as voters began casting ballots in a closely contested presidential runoff between incumbent Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva and conservative Senator Flavio Bolsonaro.
The election pits 80-year-old Lula of the Workers' Party against 45-year-old Bolsonaro, the eldest son and political heir of former President Jair Bolsonaro.
The runoff follows a competitive first-round vote on October 4, when Bolsonaro led with 47 percent of valid votes against Lula's 45 percent. Neither candidate secured an outright majority.
The contest enters election day in a statistical dead heat, with a Datafolha poll showing both candidates tied at 50 percent of valid votes.
The election has centred on the rising cost of living, public insecurity and persistent corruption concerns affecting Brazilians' daily lives.
Lula, who governed Brazil from 2003 to 2010, returned to power after defeating Jair Bolsonaro in the 2022 presidential election by less than two percentage points.
The victory marked the narrowest presidential margin in modern Brazilian history. Lula is now seeking a fourth nonconsecutive term.
Flavio Bolsonaro entered the race after his father was barred from holding public office and sentenced to 27 years in prison following investigations into a planned military coup after his 2022 defeat.
The former president's political base remains strong, with his wife, Michelle Bolsonaro, securing a seat in the Federal Senate during first-round voting.
A victory for Flavio Bolsonaro would mark a return of the right in Brazil and align the country with a broader conservative shift across the region linked to the Trump administration in the US.
More than 150 million registered voters are expected to cast their ballots electronically across Brazil's 26 states and the Federal District.
Preliminary results are expected shortly after polls close at 5 pm Brasilia time.

An April 8 ceasefire between Iran and the United States put an end to the most intense fighting, apart from sporadic exchanges of fire in and around the strategic Strait of Hormuz, a key route for global energy supplies.
At the same time, Washington is reinforcing its military presence in the region. Ukraine Strikes AVISMA Plant, Which Produces 96% of Russia’s Titanium Sponge
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
11:24:14 UTC
20:24:14 KST

The Ukrainian Defense Forces attacked the AVISMA chemical and metallurgical plant, Russia’s largest producer of titanium sponge, used to make alloys for Su-34 and Su-35 fighter jets, as well as cruise and ballistic missiles.
The Exilenova+ community published footage of the attack.
Local authorities confirmed the attack. Perm Krai Governor Dmitry Makhonin stated that Russian air defenses had shot down 11 drones and that an unnamed industrial facility in the northern part of the region had sustained “minor damage.” According to preliminary information, five employees of the facility were injured.
The AVISMA chemical and metallurgical plant in Berezniki, Perm Krai, is one of the world’s largest producers of titanium sponge – a primary form of metallic titanium used to manufacture titanium alloys, ingots, and semi-finished products. The facility is part of the VSMPO-AVISMA Corporation, which, according to the OSINT VARTA project, is the world’s largest titanium producer with a fully integrated production cycle, from raw material processing to finished products at its plant in Verkhnyaya Salda, Sverdlovsk Oblast.
Berezniki. Explosions are being heard deep inside Russia.
Facilities in Perm Krai are under attack. https://t.co/cbltsqMJFf
— Exilenova+ (@Exilenova_plus) October 25, 2026
According to the U.S. Geological Survey (USGS), VSMPO-AVISMA Corporation produced about 33,500 tonnes of titanium sponge in 2024, accounting for about 96% of Russia’s total titanium sponge production.
Until 2021, the corporation exported about 70% of its titanium products, supplying companies including Boeing, Airbus, Embraer, Rolls-Royce, and Safran. According to the U.S. Geological Survey (USGS), the corporation’s products accounted for approximately 35% of Boeing’s titanium requirements, 65% of Airbus’s, and 100% of Embraer’s.
In July 2023, the independent Russian media outlet Proekt published an investigative report on supplies from major industrial companies to Russia’s military industry. Journalists identified dozens of contracts between VSMPO-AVISMA and defense industry enterprises, including manufacturers of ballistic missiles, military aircraft, armored vehicles, and naval vessels.
One of VSMPO-AVISMA Corporation’s largest missile-industry customers is the Votkinsk Plant, which manufactures ballistic missiles for Iskander tactical ballistic missile systems, as well as the Yars and Topol-M intercontinental ballistic missiles. Titanium raw materials supplied through entities linked to the corporation are also known to have been used to produce Kalibr cruise missiles.
In the aviation sector, the corporation supplies titanium alloys to Sukhoi and Irkut, which manufacture Su-30, Su-34, and Su-35S combat aircraft, as well as to the Tupolev design bureau, which manufactures and modernizes the Tu-95MS and Tu-160 strategic bombers and the Tu-22M3 long-range bomber. The corporation’s materials are used in the airframes and engines of Russian military aircraft.
Ukraine’s Defense Intelligence has documented the use of the corporation’s titanium products in the manufacture of Su-34 fighter-bombers and Su-35S fighter jets.
Other customers include Aviastar-SP, which manufactures Il-76 military transport aircraft and Il-78 aerial refueling tankers; the Voronezh Joint-Stock Aircraft Manufacturing Company; and the Kamensk-Uralsky Foundry.
In the shipbuilding sector, the Admiralty Shipyards, the Amur Shipbuilding Plant, and the Zvezdochka Ship Repair Center purchase VSMPO-AVISMA products. These enterprises build, repair, and modernize military ships and submarines. In particular, the Admiralty Shipyards builds Project 636.3 diesel-electric submarines equipped with Kalibr-family cruise missiles.
In the armored vehicle sector, the corporation works with Uralvagonzavod, a manufacturer of Russia’s T-72B3 and T-90M tanks. The company purchases metal forgings, stamped components, hatch covers, and other products from VSMPO-AVISMA.

In a statement, the Israel Defense Forces (IDF) announced a "ban on the entry and exit of Palestinian workers to and from all of Judea, Samaria, and the Jordan Valley, including industrial zones, as well as the closure of all land crossings throughout election day."
It added that from Sunday through Monday, Palestinian workers would also not be permitted to enter Judea, Samaria or the Jordan Valley to work, "with the exception of industrial zones and a few other approved areas."
The move comes as part of a wider clampdown in the occupied West Bank after two Israeli soldiers were killed by Palestinian gunmen in the city of Hebron earlier this week.
Following the shooting, the IDF said its forces were surrounding Hebron as soldiers conducted search operations. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said he had instructed the military to "cordon off the city" and take "additional security measures" in the area.
Israel has since begun demolishing buildings as residents have been removed from the region.
The Palestinian News Agency (Wafa) reported on Sunday that more than 200 families have been displaced in Hebron over the past three days, with around 2,500 people forcibly removed from their homes in the al-Jilda and Ain Deir Baha areas.
Israeli forces also detained 20 people across the wider Hebron Governorate on Sunday as part of the crackdown, the report said.
The IDF said it had launched a "targeted operation" around Hebron that aimed to dismantle "terrorist infrastructure" and prevent future attacks.
"To reduce the risk to civilians, civilians were permitted to temporarily leave the area through designated screening points. No civilians were forced to evacuate," it said in a statement.
The military also confirmed that a number of structures in Hebron had been demolished, saying they had posed a "security threat."
"All other structures demolished in the area were also built illegally, and their demolition was carried out in accordance with international law in order to enforce law and order and remove potential security threats," the IDF said.
B'Tselem, an Israeli human rights group, has condemned Israeli "plans to forcibly displace Palestinian residents from their homes and carry out widespread destruction in the area."
The group has also called on the international community to "act immediately" to put a stop to Israel's campaign in Hebron.
Anti-government protests

Demonstrators reportedly marched from Rabin Square in the city centre towards Hostages Square, renamed in the wake of Hamas' 7 October 2023 attacks on Israel.
The rally was organised by the October Council, a group set up by families of victims and hostages taken by militants during the attacks.

Jared Kushner, the Bank of Israel, and the difference between allegations and facts - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
11:18:09 UTC
20:18:09 KST

I know Jared Kushner. I have spoken with him personally on several occasions. I know that he worked hand in hand with Steve Witkoff to bring the Israeli hostages home from captivity in Gaza. I know that Kushner cares deeply about the future of the State of Israel. I also believe that he is one of the few people with real influence in the Trump administration who genuinely cares about the future and welfare of the Palestinian people.
I cannot speak about Kushner’s private business dealings, his financial affairs, or every aspect of his work in the Middle East. I have no firsthand knowledge of those matters, and I will not pretend otherwise.
I can speak to his involvement in efforts to help Israelis and Palestinians. I have witnessed an evolution in his thinking, and in my judgment, that evolution has been for the better. I believe he increasingly understands that Israel’s future cannot be separated from the future of the Palestinian people.
That is why I read with particular interest the extraordinary allegations published in Vanity Fair on October 22, in an article by Matthew Cole concerning Kushner’s alleged secret financial arrangements in the Middle East.
One allegation immediately caught my attention. The article claims that approximately $1 billion was transferred into an account at the Bank of Israel, supposedly connected to Kushner and, according to one source, intended for his personal benefit.
This story has a fundamental problem.
The Bank of Israel is not a commercial bank. It is Israel’s central bank. Private individuals cannot simply open accounts there.
This is not a matter of opinion. It is how the Israeli banking system operates. The Bank of Israel maintains accounts for the government, banking institutions, certain financial entities, and authorized foreign central banks and financial institutions. It does not offer private banking services to individuals, whether they are Israeli citizens, American businessmen, or presidential advisers.
Allegations of private Kushner account incompatible with bank rules
If the allegation is that Kushner personally opened or controlled a private account at the Bank of Israel, it is incompatible with the bank’s published rules.
Could money have moved through an institutional account? That is a different question and would require specific evidence. But the published allegation raises an obvious question that should have been answered before publication: Who was the legal account holder, and how could Kushner supposedly control the funds?
I do not know whether the other financial allegations in the article are true or false. But when an investigation makes an extraordinary claim involving a central bank without adequately explaining how such an arrangement could exist, it raises serious questions about the reliability of its reporting.
Extraordinary allegations require extraordinary scrutiny. They should not be accepted simply because they make sensational headlines.
My defense of Kushner is not based on political loyalty. I have disagreed with American administrations, including this one, on fundamental questions concerning Israel and Palestine. I judge people by what I know of their actions and by whether they contribute to a better future.
In Kushner’s case, I have seen someone willing to engage with difficult realities and to reconsider positions. I have seen someone who understands that diplomacy requires more than repeating established formulas. Most importantly, I believe he recognizes that a sustainable future for Israel must also offer Palestinians dignity, opportunity, and hope.
After decades of working for Israeli-Palestinian peace, I have learned to recognize the difference between people who speak about peace and people who may actually help make it possible.
Kushner increasingly an ally of those seeking peace between Israelis, Palestinians
In my personal judgment, Kushner is increasingly an ally of those of us who have devoted our lives to achieving Israeli-Palestinian peace.
That does not place him above criticism or scrutiny. No one should be above either. But criticism must be grounded in facts, and serious journalism must distinguish between evidence and speculation.
The claim about a private account at the Bank of Israel deserves a clear explanation. Until one is provided, I see no reason to accept it – and every reason to question the credibility of that part of the story.
The writer is the Middle East director of the International Communities Organization and the co-head of the Alliance for Two States.

Türkiye urges Greece to respect minority’s choice of muftis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
11:18:00 UTC
20:18:00 KST

AA Photo
Türkiye on Oct. 24 called on Greece to recognize Muslim religious leaders elected by the Turkish minority in Western Thrace, accusing Athens of disregarding religious freedom by appointing its own muftis in the region.
“We call on the Greek authorities to recognize the legitimate muftis elected by the minority and to refrain from attempts to impose appointed muftis,” the Turkish Foreign Ministry said in a statement.
The statement came after the Greek government appointed muftis for five-year terms in the cities of Komotini and Xanthi, following an earlier appointment to the Didymoteicho mufti office in January.
The Turkish minority in Western Thrace has elected İbrahim Şerif as mufti of Komotini and Mustafa Trampa as mufti of Xanthi.
Turkish Parliament Speaker Numan Kurtulmuş also urged Greece to comply with the 1923 Treaty of Lausanne, which established the framework for the protection of minority rights in the region.
“Attempting to determine a community’s religious practices and representatives through state intervention is incompatible with both the law and the fundamental principles of democracy,” Kurtulmuş said in a statement.
Western Thrace, in northeastern Greece, includes the cities of Komotini, Xanthi and Alexandroupoli and is home to a Muslim minority estimated at around 150,000 people.
The appointment of muftis has long been a point of contention between Türkiye and Greece. Ankara argues that Muslim religious leaders in the region should be elected by the members of the community they serve, citing international agreements, including the Treaty of Lausanne.
Greece, which maintained an election system for muftis until 1985, subsequently shifted to government appointments.
Athens does not officially recognize the Muslim minority in Western Thrace as a Turkish minority, instead identifying it by its religious affiliation.

Miri Regev's unfulfilled promises: Eight transportation reforms that never happened
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
11:17:49 UTC
20:17:49 KST

Miri Regev returned to the Transportation and Road Safety Ministry on December 29, 2022, and her second term has so far failed to reduce road-accident fatalities.
In 2024 and 2025, road deaths hit a two-decade high, and 2026 shows no sign of change except a slight decline, driven only by a sharp drop in March, when the country was in shelters and safe rooms during Operation Roaring Lion.
Evidence of the minister’s major failure came from the European Transport Safety Council (ETSC). At the end of 2025, the council announced it was suspending Israel over government measures that, the organization said, were incompatible with its basic commitment to saving lives. The organization formally ended Israel’s participation in its Road Safety Performance Index (PIN) program, with no clear path back.
The ETSC decided to suspend Israel’s National Road Safety Authority (RSA) from the program until further notice: “The recent actions of the current Israeli government are not consistent with the fundamental commitment of ETSC and the PIN program to protecting human life.”
Israel’s Transportation Ministry claimed the move was political, but the surge in the number of people killed and injured on Israel’s roads, in contrast to most European countries, Regev’s lack of interest in road safety, and the departure of key figures in the field, such as Avi Naor, who served as chairman of the RSA, and Erez Kita, who served as the authority’s director general, suggest otherwise.
Despite the poor results and scant action, the transportation and road safety minister delivered a stream of media statements meant to benefit Israel’s citizens and the road safety community. A comprehensive check by Walla Cars and the Or Yarok road safety association reveals the minister's main statements and promises during her term, and how much of them were carried out.
Ride-sharing in Israel: Didn’t happen
“Uber will be in Israel. Period.”
That was Regev’s reply on October 22, 2025, to a parliamentary question from MK Eitan Ginzburg on advancing shared transportation.
The approval was meant to allow private drivers to carry paying passengers in their own cars, aiming to increase competition in the passenger transport market and lower prices for consumers. The bill initiated by Ginzburg (Blue and White, Beyachad) passed a preliminary reading in the Knesset and even a first reading, but went no further.
As of October 2026, ride-sharing is not legal in Israel, but the Transportation Ministry rarely acts against private drivers who pick up paying passengers, mainly in the Haredi (ultra-Orthodox) community, where they are known as “drivers.”
They are not subject to the high insurance costs and licensing fees charged to legal cab drivers, or to the other regulatory requirements the state imposes on official taxis, such as buying a “green number” taxi license for more than 200,000 shekels, or leasing one.
Higher fines for a range of offenses, especially cellphone use: Didn’t happen
Regev supplied the quote and announced the move at the Yedioth Ahronoth transportation conference: “Police will catch someone texting, and they’ll immediately give him a 10,000-shekel fine the first time. He won’t go to court. The second time, it will be confiscation of the vehicle.”
On December 2, 2025, the minister declared on her Facebook account and on X that she would raise the fines.
As of October 2026, the stiffer fines have not yet materialized.
Scrapping the internal driving test: Didn’t happen
In another attempt to present itself as fighting the cost of living, the Transportation Ministry promoted abolishing the internal test, which pre-test driving instructors administer before the official exam and costs learners and their parents between 150 and 400 shekels. The move was even formally included in the 2026 state budget agreements, and an official circular stated that the abolition would take effect on June 18, 2026.
The move was never completed because of protests by driving instructors and technical problems and failures, leading the ministry to announce, just one day before implementation, that it had decided to postpone the amendment’s entry into force for an in-depth reexamination.
No new date was set.
Approval for Tesla full self-driving: Didn’t happen
Regev addressed the issue after Tesla drivers in Israel submitted a petition, posting the following on her official accounts. On October 29, 2025, she wrote on her Facebook page and on X: “I’ve received the many appeals from Tesla drivers in Israel! Tesla drivers? Soon you won’t have to hold the wheel.”
In a conversation with Tesla CEO Elon Musk at the Smart Mobility conference, Regev also promised to speed up approval in Israel for FSD and equivalent systems from other carmakers.
Since then, a long list of European countries, from the Netherlands to Belgium, Denmark and the Czech Republic, have approved its use. But in Israel, the Transportation Ministry has not yet updated the regulation requiring drivers to keep their hands on the wheel throughout the drive, nor has it worked with the Commissioner of Insurance to settle liability for an accident that occurs while the vehicle is in autonomous mode.
Multi-year national road safety plan for 2026–2030: Didn’t happen
Government Resolution 3491 of November 16, 2025, states that “with the aim of reducing the rate of road accident casualties, reducing the economic damage caused by road accidents and strengthening the government’s commitment to improving road safety,” the government approved a multi-year national road safety plan for 2026–2030.
Under the plan, the rate of road accident casualties is to be cut by 25% within five years of the resolution’s approval and funding, compared with the 2021–2025 average, a lower target than had been set in the past. The ministry also set a goal for Israel to rank among the seven leading countries in road safety, measured by casualties relative to population size.
On December 14, 2025, the ministry declared: “Stopping the carnage on the roads: 350 million shekels a year have been budgeted for saving lives and restoring road safety in Israel. The most dramatic road safety move in a decade: a comprehensive, budgeted and measurable national plan will get underway as early as 2026.”
“We are launching a dramatic national move to save lives. This is a significant moment of taking national responsibility, in which the State of Israel is changing direction and putting the safety of road users at the top of its priorities,” Regev boasted in a press release at the time. “After years in which road safety received no systemic, comprehensive response, we are bringing a comprehensive, budgeted and focused plan to save lives, which means fewer families receiving the terrible news at the door. The state is taking responsibility.”
As of October 2026, the money has not been transferred to fund the plan.
Fewer required driving lessons: Didn’t happen
In August 2024, Regev proposed a new procedure that would dramatically reduce the minimum number of driving lessons required before taking the road test, from 28 lessons to just 22 for automatic vehicles, to lower the cost of getting a driver’s license.
Or Yarok opposed it, as did the ETSC, which issued a formal warning that cutting initial training would harm the safety of young drivers, who are defined as a high-risk group. Professionals at the RSA, to whom the initiative was referred to assess its implications, also objected.
The move never went ahead.
Annual vehicle inspections at garages: Didn’t happen
On June 6, 2023, the minister posted on her page on X (formerly Twitter): “ONE STOP SHOP – who doesn’t know the hassle when it’s time for the annual vehicle inspection. You clear half a day, if not more, going to a licensed testing center; if the car fails, you drive to a garage to fix the faults, then back to the center, and so on. Wasting time, fuel, workdays, and more.
“I have instructed the relevant parties in my ministry to put an end to this, and they are now working on it, setting professional standards, with supervision and oversight and preserving the safety and consumer aspects, so that licensed garages will be qualified to carry out the annual vehicle inspection. Quickly and efficiently, and all this as part of my plan to fight the cost of living in Israel.”
The following day, the ministry released a statement reading: “This is a historic move that will significantly shorten the long lines and reduce the load on testing centers, encourage inspections to be carried out on time, accessibly and close to drivers’ homes or workplaces, alongside lower costs as part of the fight against the cost of living in Israel.”
Regev claimed the move was based on a professional opinion that she refused to disclose, and ignored the fact that the law had once allowed inspections at garages but was changed because of the garages’ conflict of interest: a single body that looks for faults in a vehicle on behalf of the state and can immediately offer to fix them for the customer on the premises.
Such an arrangement could also lead to vehicles that are not fully roadworthy being approved in return for the customer having other, non-safety maintenance work done there.
As of October 2026, the plan is stuck in the legislative process and under review by professional staff. Drivers in Israel must still go in person to official licensed testing centers for the annual inspection.
Shorter waits for medical exams: Didn’t happen
Regev pledged to shorten long waiting times at the Medical Institute for Road Safety (MIRS) by outsourcing the institute’s services and decentralizing its powers to private bodies.
As of October 2026, the move has not been completed, and the institute still operates at a sluggish pace, to the detriment of tens of thousands of drivers a year whose licenses are revoked on medical grounds and who are forced to wait months for an examination at the only institute authorized to restore their licenses.
Ministerial committee on road safety: Met three times in two years
On November 24, 2024, Regev announced the formation of a ministerial committee on road safety. Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu was appointed chairman, and the committee includes the government’s most senior ministers.
The committee held its first meeting on May 4, 2025, about six months after the government announced its establishment. The second was held on October 26, 2025, and the third on February 8, 2026.
Netanyahu did not attend a single session.
The committee’s deliberations led to no significant road-safety decisions.
Attorney Yaniv Yaakov, CEO of Or Yarok: “The Israeli public deserves a road safety minister who understands the weight of the responsibility and the purpose for which he works every day — to save lives. Minister Regev made many promises, but at the end of her term, only a small portion of them served road safety, as the grim figures also show. The minister’s biggest failure is her refusal to approve a multi-year national plan, even though she requested it and it already exists.
"The wrong priorities have led us to the worst figures in two decades and to our removal from the European Transport Safety Council’s annual performance report. Inaction costs human lives. The next transportation and road safety minister will have to change the priorities and put saving lives first. That is his duty and his privilege.”

A group of 109 economists, business leaders, high-tech entrepreneurs, and former senior public officials issued a strongly worded statement expressing "deep anxiety and concern" over Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's conduct, warning of irreversible damage to Israel's economy if international sanctions are imposed.

B'Yachad party chairman Naftali Bennett said he was appalled by Netanyahu's vision. "This means the destruction of Israeli high-tech, the loss of livelihoods for hundreds of thousands of families, poverty for millions of Israelis, and a threat to security. Netanyahu is placing Israel in the same category as Iran, North Korea, and Russia."

Fourteen years after genocide, Yazidis may see stability in Iraq - analysis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
11:17:28 UTC
20:17:28 KST

Fourteen years after ISIS invaded the Sinjar region of Iraq and targeted the Yazidi minority in a genocidal campaign, the group may finally see some stability in northern Iraq.
Yazidis are one of several minority groups in Iraq, and most live in the Sinjar region of northern Iraq and in some towns in the Kurdistan Regional Government’s governorates. In August 2014, ISIS invaded Sinjar and massacred thousands of Yazidis. ISIS also kidnapped thousands and sold them into slavery. It was one of the most horrific crimes that ISIS committed.
Sinjar, which Yazidis also call Shingal, was liberated in November of 2015. Sinjar refers to the entire region, including a long mountain and a city with the same name. Numerous Yazidi villages and towns to the north and south of the mountain.
During the genocide, many Yazidis fled to the mountain, and many were also saved by the Kurdish People’s Protection Units (YPG) in Syria, who helped open a corridor for them to flee. Since then, many of the group have lived in IDP camps in the Kurdistan region or slowly made their way back to poverty-stricken livelihoods in Sinjar.
The Yazidi region was largely abandoned by Iraq. In 2017, the Kurdish Peshmerga, who had helped liberate the area from ISIS, were pushed out by Iraqi federal troops and by Iranian-backed militias of the Popular Mobilization Forces. The Yazidis remained, but they were divided.
Some Yazidis targeted by Turkey after joining PKK-linked group
Some Yazidis had joined the Shingal Protection Units (YBS), a group that is linked to the Kurdistan Workers’ Party (PKK). As such, the Yazidis found themselves in the crosshairs of Turkey, which views the PKK as a terrorist group.
Now things are changing again. Rudaw, a Kurdish media outlet, noted on October 24 that Murad Ismael, a Yazidi activist and Iraqi lawmaker who has spent many years seeking to help his community, said on Saturday that members of the Shingal Protection Units (YBS) would be integrated into several Iraqi security institutions, including the police, rejecting suggestions that all fighters would join the Shiite-dominated Popular Mobilization Forces (PMF).
This matters because, for several weeks, there has been talk of a deal between Baghdad and the YBS to integrate the group into the security forces. The goal of Iraq is to rein in all the independent militias in Iraq. This also includes disarming the Iranian-backed militias. However, those groups are stronger and more influential. The Yazidis are a group that Iraq feels it can work with and possibly have a model for integrating an independent armed group into the security forces.
However, there is some controversy about how the group might be integrated. If it is integrated as a brigade within the PMF, concerns remain about how it might operate. The report indicates that the YBS integration will be more multi-layered.
Ismael's remarks followed Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi's Friday interview with state media, where the leader said the YBS would be integrated into the PMF as part of an agreement to restore federal control over Shingal (Sinjar), Rudaw reported.
“The integration process is not limited to the PMF, only a portion of it, with part of it being integrated into the police and part of it into other security structures,” said Ismael of the plan.
It now remains to be seen how quickly the integration process will happen. Ismael appeared to indicate that it will begin in the next several days. Iraq has said it wants the other militias integrated by June 2027. According to Rudaw, Ismael said he expected members of the YBS's all-female force to be integrated into the Iraqi Interior Ministry's Community Police.
This matters because it mirrors a similar process on the other side of the border with the Syrian Democratic Forces. This mostly Kurdish group is integrating into the Syrian security forces. As a result, a swath of Iraq and Syria is now changing. This will allow stability and investment on both sides of the border.
Region in dire need of investment
The region is badly in need of investment. This includes basic infrastructure, as well as schools and other facilities. It has been badly neglected for many years. Part of the neglect has been due to the uncertainty of what might come next. Yazidis have been wary of returning in the past unless they feel that ISIS and its supporters will be prevented from returning.
At the same time, the different armed groups, such as the YBS and also Iranian-backed militias, make it impossible for investment to flow into the area, or for people to feel that stability will return.
The decision by Baghdad to seek to normalize the situation in Sinjar and work on security is important. The issue now will be whether the details of the agreement lead to change. Iraq has successfully revived Mosul, which is between Sinjar and the Kurdistan Region. That large city of 2 million people was once occupied by ISIS until it was liberated in 2017. Now, it’s possible that the stability in Mosul might radiate out to Sinjar.

Iran unlikely to change position even if US, Israel resume war
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
11:16:00 UTC
20:16:00 KST

Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said Sunday that a potential resumption of war with Israel and the United States would not change Tehran’s position.
The remarks come amid mounting U.S. and Israeli threats of renewed attacks on Iran, as U.S. President Donald Trump said Friday that Washington "may do another little Epic Fury," referring to the U.S.-Israeli campaign on Iran that began Feb. 28.
"Recently, there has been talk of a new war, but I am already thinking about the post-war period. Whether there is war or not, our policies remain the same," Araghchi said during a televised event in Tehran.
"They have already done so twice and have seen the results. If they want to try again, they know they will achieve no different outcome from those of the past."
An April 8 cease-fire between Iran and the U.S. ended the most intense fighting, apart from sporadic exchanges of fire in and around the strategic Strait of Hormuz, a key route for global energy supplies.
These military flare-ups have subsided in recent weeks.
Iran has claimed control over the strait since the war began, regularly targeting vessels that attempt crossing without its authorization. Washington and countries in the region strongly oppose these moves.
In response, the U.S. maintains a naval counterblockade on Iranian ports.
In June, Iran agreed with the U.S. to a memorandum of understanding outlining a path to permanent conflict settlement, but the deal later unraveled as each side accused the other of violating it.
Tehran has since called for a return to the accord to end the conflict.
"The current war has changed everything. We must accept that new realities are taking hold. Shipping routes through the Strait of Hormuz will no longer be the same, and the management of the strait will no longer be the same," Araghchi said.
"To achieve peace and stability, our region must move towards the complete absence of foreign forces."

Democrats need a net gain of four seats in both the US Senate and US House of Representatives to overturn Republicans' narrow 53-47 and 218-214 majorities.

Serbia election: Main players, voter concerns and what is at stake

Unknown Publisher

Serbia election: Main players, voter concerns and what is at stake
Oct 25 - Serbia is holding parliamentary elections on Sunday, in which a popular student movement is seeking to end the rule of longtime leader Aleksandar Vucic.
Here are the main players, issues and stakes in the vote.
WHO ARE THE MAJOR PLAYERS AND WHAT DO THEY STAND FOR?
Aleksandar Vucic – United Serbia: The Serbian Progressive Party (SNS)-led electoral list is campaigning on economic growth, higher wages and pensions, infrastructure investment and political stability. SNS leader Milos Vucevic has pledged 4% economic growth in 2027. Vucic, who resigned as president on September 27, is running to become prime minister.
Students Win: Emerging from protests over the November 2024 Novi Sad railway station canopy collapse that killed 16 people, the anti-corruption movement has campaigned for accountability and transparent public procurement. The Democratic Party and Kreni Promeni movement have backed it rather than fielding their own lists.
Socialist Party of Serbia (SPS) – Ivica Dacic – Factor of Stability: A longstanding ally of the SNS, the pro-Russian SPS leads a coalition with Unified Serbia, the Social Democratic Party of Serbia and the Greens of Serbia. It campaigns on social justice, workers' rights and welfare, political stability, and national interests.
European Serbia: A pro-European opposition alliance led by Marinika Tepic and Zdravko Ponos, bringing together the Party of Freedom and Justice, Serbia Centre, and the Solidarity, Self-Defence and Liberation movement. It advocates closer European integration, sanctions against Russia and democratic reforms.
WHAT ARE PARTY LISTS AND HOW DO THEY WORK?
Political parties, party coalitions, movements and other groups can submit party lists, or electoral lists comprising no more than 250 candidates.
The election commission has approved a total of 18 lists.
On election day, voters vote for one electoral list on the ballot, rather than individual candidates.
WHAT ARE THE MAIN ISSUES FOR VOTERS?
Corruption and government accountability have dominated the campaign since the Novi Sad disaster. Protesters accuse Vucic and his allies of corruption, controlling the media and mistreating demonstrators, allegations the authorities deny.
Living standards, economic development and the fairness of the electoral process are also campaign issues.
HOW WILL A VICTORY OR LOSS FOR VUCIC IMPACT SERBIA AT HOME AND ABROAD?
A victory allowing Vucic to become prime minister would extend his political leadership and could preserve Serbia's balancing act between its ambition to join the European Union and maintain Belgrade's close ties with Russia and China.
A defeat could pave the way for sweeping domestic reforms, including stronger institutions and measures against corruption. REUTERS

Brazil has not given up yet

====================================================================================================

Brazil has not given up yet
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
11:06:27 UTC
20:06:27 KST

On Sunday 25 October, Brazilians will decide between Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva and Flávio Bolsonaro, in an election with consequences for the entire continent. After coming first in the first round of the presidential election on 4 October, the third son of the far-right former president has seen his lead shrink. On the eve of the vote, the two candidates were neck and neck in the polls.
On the streets, Lula’s supporters are mobilising to bring about a comeback for the incumbent president: students, labor unions, grassroots activists and artists are holding a growing number of rallies against Flávio Bolsonaro. In São Paulo, gig-economy delivery workers have even led their own versions of the motorbike caravans popularised by Jair Bolsonaro and taken up by his son as part of his signature campaign style. They support Lula while demanding that his administration provide the social protections for which they are still waiting.
Four years after Jair Bolsonaro’s defeat, ‘Bolsonarism’ still has powerful means to reclaim the presidency. Despite Bolsonaro’s conviction for an attempted coup d’état, the alliances that fuelled his initial rise have not been broken. The agribusiness sector, evangelical churches and sections of the security forces remain key pillars of support — structures that the change in government in 2022 failed to eliminate.
In a country where nearly 60% of the population relies exclusively on social media for news, the Brazilian far right is highly organised. Its opponents accuse US tech platforms — most notably Meta (Facebook, Instagram and WhatsApp) — of using their algorithms to favour Bolsonaro’s camp. Following a petition from Lula’s campaign team, the Supreme Federal Court demanded explanations from the company, as well as from Elon Musk’s X.
In the US, Bolsonarism relies on the support of the Donald Trump administration. During the 18 October debate, Lula denounced Eduardo Bolsonaro’s overtures to the US, which contributed to Washington imposing sanctions on Brazil intended to put pressure on its judicial system. This demonstrates a curious interpretation of ‘sovereignty’, a concept that the Brazilian far-right claims to champion.
The issue of sovereignty also plays out within national borders. In Brazil, 1% of landowners hold nearly half of all agricultural land. The landless movement continues its struggle for agrarian reform — a process that remains incomplete, largely due to resistance from major landowners. The economic weight of these landowners translates into political influence, most notably within Congress. Beneath the rhetoric surrounding national independence lies a fundamental question: who gets to decide how land is used, how resources are exploited and how wealth is distributed? Regardless of who wins on Sunday, those who control these assets will retain significant means to defend their own interests.
There remains one final question about this election: will the US administration recognise the results on Sunday night, should Lula secure a narrow victory?

(AA Photo)
Opposition Republican People’s Party (CHP) leader Kemal Kılıçdaroğlu has stated his party will vote in favor of a defense agreement between Türkiye, Pakistan and Saudi Arabia when it comes before parliament for ratification.
“My first thought when I heard about the Mecca Agreement was whether it could pave the way for a future conflict with Iran. But Iran later issued a statement saying that the Mecca Agreement was appropriate,” Kılıçdaroğlu told reporters during a visit to the southeastern province of Gaziantep on Oct. 24.
The three countries signed the agreement on Aug. 7. Under Türkiye’s constitution, the deal must be ratified by parliament, with a simple majority sufficient for approval.
The agreement will first be reviewed by the parliamentary Foreign Affairs Commission before being submitted to the General Assembly for a vote.
Although he said he had no direct information on the matter, Kılıçdaroğlu said he believed Türkiye had assured Iran that the agreement did not mean Ankara intended to engage in any conflict with Tehran.
“The agreement has been submitted. Its rationale has been provided, and explanations have been made. We have our criticisms, but we will vote in favor of the Mecca Agreement,” he said.
The agreement contains 16 articles, according to the text submitted to the parliament.
Under the agreement, a threat to the territorial integrity, sovereignty or internationally recognized borders of any signatory would require the parties to use all necessary means to eliminate the threat or danger.
An externally originating armed attack against any of the three countries would be considered an attack against all parties.
If one country faces an armed attack or military aggression by another country or group of countries, the others would be required to provide immediate assistance, making full use of the means of mutual assistance available to them.

The latest tragedy comes as the National Police Service and the National Transport and Safety Authority (NTSA) intensify nationwide public awareness campaigns targeting road users ahead of the December festive season.
According to the NTSA, roughly 4,000 Kenyans lose their lives in road accidents each year, despite ongoing safety initiatives led by both government and private-sector stakeholders. ■

PARIS – A man suspected of a gun attack in the Paris suburbs that killed one person and wounded five has left custody and been placed in a psychiatric unit for observation, French anti-terror prosecutors said on Oct 25.
The 39-year-old suspect, partly identified as Kevin T, was arrested on Oct 23 in possession of a submachine gun and tear-gas grenades in his car, shortly after the victims were shot as a vehicle drove through the working-class town of Trappes and neighbouring La Verriere.
President Emmanuel Macron had branded the shooting a “racist terrorist attack”, as most of the victims were from foreign backgrounds.
The French National Anti-Terrorism Prosecutor’s Office (PNAT), which is handling the case, on Oct 24 extended the suspect’s time in detention to pursue its interrogation.
But a day later, the PNAT said: “After a psychiatric examination of Kevin T carried out in the evening (of Saturday), his custody has been lifted.”
It said that, in line with conclusions from a psychiatric expert, he “was transferred to the police psychiatric unit to be subjected to a psychiatric observation period likely to last 48 hours”.
That observation period “should allow us to evaluate whether his state of psychiatric health is compatible with pursuing interrogation sessions”.
The PNAT added that traces of cannabis and cocaine were found in the suspect’s blood.
Police have searched his home in the town of Plaisir outside of Paris.
According to a source close to the investigation on Oct 24, they found a Bible, a Quran and a copy of Adolf Hitler’s Mein Kampf.
The person killed in the Oct 23 shooting was a 26-year-old man of Congolese origin, Pengo Bossio Wangi.
One of those wounded was a 12-year-old girl who was hit by bullets eight times. She remains in a critical condition.
The shooting comes at a moment of deep divisions in France, which is heading for elections in six months with far-right candidate Marine le Pen leading in the polls.
Political and social tensions boiled over a week ago into riots that have marred the country’s image ahead of the vote to choose Macron’s successor. AFP

Türkiye is stepping up security measures ahead of the U.N.’s annual climate summit, COP31, which will be held in Antalya next month, with 26,000 security personnel expected to be deployed on the ground, Interior Minister Mustafa Çiftçi has said.
“Nearly 100 heads of state and government, 200 to 300 ministers and around 20,000 delegates are expected to attend. In addition, daily visitor numbers are projected to reach 100,000. We therefore need to plan and assess security arrangements for each of these groups separately,” Çiftçi said in a televised interview on Oct. 24.
COP31 will take place from Nov. 9 to 20 in Antalya, a Mediterranean coastal city.
Security arrangements will involve not only police and gendarmerie forces but also the coast guard, Çiftçi said.
“We will have 26,000 personnel deployed on the ground. We have security plans and measures in place for land, sea and air,” he said.
Çiftçi added that Türkiye would implement security measures in Antalya similar to those introduced for the NATO leaders’ summit held in the capital Ankara in July.
“We have divided the areas where leaders, heads of government, ministers and delegations will stay into five zones. Around 1,500 special operations personnel will be deployed at the summit venue,” he said.
“All routes have been planned, from the moment leaders arrive at the airport to their transfer to hotels, as well as the routes they will use to travel from their hotels to the venue of the climate summit,” Çiftçi added.
The venue includes a Green Zone open to the public, while official negotiations will take place in the Blue Zone, accessible only to registered participants.
Transport arrangements will include low-emission buses and electric shuttles, with 630 additional vehicles being deployed.
Authorities estimated that COP31 would generate about $2 billion in direct economic activity for Antalya, benefiting businesses in accommodation, transport, retail, construction and event production.

Humanitarian crisis in the left-bank enclave
The drone delivery underscores the desperate conditions in Oleshky, situated approximately five kilometers southeast of liberated Kherson on the east bank of the Dnipro River.
The municipality has remained under Russian military control since the opening days of the full-scale invasion in February 2022 and has been entirely severed from authorized overland cargo deliveries and international humanitarian missions since late May.
Roughly 1,700 civilians remain trapped in the municipal center amid destroyed municipal heating networks, severed running water, and intermittent electrical supply ahead of freezing winter temperatures.
Ukrainian officials have repeatedly described the municipality as under virtual siege, noting that exit roads and river transit points are heavily mined and subjected to continuous loitering drone reconnaissance.
Ukrainian defense units have intermittently utilized heavy multi-rotor transport drones to air-drop rations and pharmaceuticals into residential yards as diplomatic negotiations to secure an overland corridor continue.
Pending localized ceasefire
The aerial relief mission coincides with preparations for a synchronized, localized ceasefire framework scheduled to take effect across Oleshky on Tuesday, Oct. 27, at 3:00 a.m. Kyiv time (4:00 a.m. Moscow time).
Finalized during bilateral consultations between Ukrainian Parliament Commissioner for Human Rights Dmytro Lubinets and Russian negotiating lead Yana Lantratova – mediated with assistance from US First Lady Melania Trump – the framework establishes a phased humanitarian operation to deliver larger medical and food consignments and begin civilian evacuations.
President Volodymyr Zelensky affirmed that Kyiv will adhere strictly to operational commitments to unblock the city, emphasizing that opening humanitarian access to Oleshky remains vital to preventing catastrophic civilian loss ahead of winter.

Türkiye advances joint restoration project of historic bridge on Armenian border
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
11:01:00 UTC
20:01:00 KST

Türkiye has completed the tender process for the reconstruction of the historic Ani Bridge on the Turkish-Armenian border, Transport and Infrastructure Minister Abdulkadir Uraloğlu said on Oct. 25.
Estimated to date back to the 10th century, the bridge, of which only its piers remain today, has emerged as a symbol of normalization efforts between Türkiye and Armenia, which have no diplomatic relations and have kept their land border closed for decades.
The agreement, signed in Yerevan on May 4, outlines the scope and methods of the reconstruction work.
Under the protocol, restoration work will be coordinated by a joint commission involving Türkiye’s Transport and Infrastructure Ministry and the General Directorate of Highways (KGM), Uraloğlu said.
The General Directorate of Highways held a tender for the bridge’s restoration works on Sept. 16, Uraloğlu said, adding that the process was completed with the signing of a contract on Sept. 28.
“With the reconstruction of the historic bridge, we aim to preserve one of the important cultural heritage sites along the Silk Road and pass it on to future generations,” he said.
Uraloğlu said the bridge originally measured 80 meters in length and 8 meters in width. It was built at the narrowest point of the Arpaçay River, where the riverbed narrows to 36 meters.
The bridge’s circular arch, which spanned 31 meters, collapsed on Oct. 16, 1807, he said, noting that the structure had once served as an important crossing point along the Silk Road.
The Ani archaeological site, which includes the bridge, was added to UNESCO’s World Heritage List in 2016 alongside 20 other cultural assets.
Türkiye and Armenia have had no diplomatic relations since 1991, while their shared land border has remained closed since 1993 amid tensions related to the Nagorno-Karabakh conflict and disagreements over the events of 1915.
The normalization process gained momentum in late 2021 with the appointment of special envoys by both countries.
Since then, the two sides have taken several confidence-building steps, including launching direct cargo flights, discussing the opening of the land border to third-country nationals and diplomats, and advancing projects such as the Gyumri-Kars railway and the restoration of the historic Ani Bridge.

Romantic breakups correspond with changes in sexual identity during adulthood
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
11:00:48 UTC
20:00:48 KST

Ending a committed relationship can prompt people to fundamentally reevaluate who they are, and a recent study suggests this process may extend to a person’s sexual orientation. Research published in The Journal of Sex Research indicates that individuals who experience highly disruptive material changes after a breakup report higher levels of ambiguity regarding their sexual identity. These findings highlight how major life transitions might correspond with shifts in sexual development throughout adulthood.
To understand these findings, it helps to look at how social scientists view human development. Life course theory suggests that human development is a lifelong process shaped by both expected milestones and unexpected events. Major life disruptions often act as turning points that influence a person’s future trajectory and sense of self.
Identity process theory builds on this idea by proposing that people constantly evaluate and adjust their identities to fit their environments. When a person’s social context changes rapidly, they often enter a processing period. During this time, they might assimilate new identity traits or discard old ones to maintain a coherent sense of self.
For many people, a romantic breakup is one of the most jarring transitions they will experience. Exiting a relationship requires a person to untangle their individual identity from their former partnership.
This untangling process can affect many facets of a person’s life, including their sexuality. Sexual orientation is not a single, unchangeable trait. It encompasses a person’s attractions, behaviors, and internal identity labels.
Sometimes, these different components do not perfectly align. Sexual orientation ambiguity refers to a period where a person feels their sexual identity is incongruent, unpredictable, or in a state of flux. While adolescence is frequently viewed as the primary time for sexual exploration, adults can experience changes in their sexual orientation at any point in their lives.
Grace A. O’Toole and her colleagues at Kansas State University conducted the study to explore these lifespan changes. The research team included O’Toole, Peyton Woods, Kristin M. Anders, Jared Durtschi, and Anthony J. Ferraro. They wanted to see if the end of a committed romantic relationship corresponded with periods of sexual ambiguity.
The researchers were particularly interested in differentiating between two types of relationship fallout. They wanted to separate the psychological toll of a breakup from its material consequences.
To investigate this, the researchers recruited 493 adults living in the United States through an online survey platform. Every participant had experienced the end of a committed romantic relationship within the past two years. The group included a wide age range, spanning from 18 to 76 years old.
Participants completed questionnaires assessing how the breakup impacted their lives. The survey split these impacts into two distinct categories. Psychological impacts measured changes in a person’s thoughts, emotions, and attitudes following the split.
Material impacts measured concrete lifestyle changes. This category included tangible disruptions like having to move to a new home, losing shared friend groups, or facing altered financial circumstances.
The participants also answered questions designed to measure sexual orientation ambiguity and sexual orientation uncertainty. Ambiguity questions assessed whether a person viewed their sexual orientation as changing rapidly. Uncertainty questions asked if participants felt a general sense of doubt about their sexual identity.
The researchers used statistical models to look for associations between the severity of the breakup’s impact and the participant’s reported levels of sexual ambiguity. They accounted for variables like gender, race, sexual orientation, and the seriousness of the past relationship.
The results revealed a link between the material consequences of a breakup and an individual’s sexual identity. Participants who reported higher levels of material impact from their relationship dissolution also reported higher levels of sexual orientation ambiguity. Those who faced greater concrete lifestyle disruptions were more likely to feel that their sexual orientation was in a state of flux.
The psychological impact of the breakup did not show the same relationship. The statistical models revealed that changes in a person’s emotional or mental state following the breakup were not statistically significant predictors of sexual orientation ambiguity.
The study also revealed notable differences across various demographic groups. People who identified as bisexual reported higher levels of sexual ambiguity compared to those who identified as heterosexual. This aligns with past research suggesting that bisexual individuals often navigate social environments that question the legitimacy of their orientation, which can prompt feelings of incongruence.
Participants who identified as genderqueer reported higher ambiguity than those who identified as cisgender men. Racial identity also correlated with these feelings of ambiguity. Black participants reported higher levels of sexual orientation ambiguity than White participants.
The nature of the ended relationship played a role in the findings as well. Participants who had been cohabitating with their former partners reported lower sexual ambiguity than those who had only been seriously dating.
The authors suggest that these findings point to a need for broader public education regarding sexual development. Recognizing that sexuality can be fluid across the entire lifespan could help individuals navigate periods of uncertainty. The researchers suggest that therapists and counselors should be attuned to how material disruptions might trigger identity shifts in their clients.
The study relies on cross-sectional data, meaning the researchers collected all the information at a single point in time. Because of this design, the results can only show correlations rather than cause and effect. It is possible that navigating the material fallout of a breakup leads to sexual ambiguity, but it is equally possible that existing sexual ambiguity contributed to the end of the relationship.
The participant pool was predominantly heterosexual, cisgender, and White. This demographic makeup limits how broadly the conclusions can be applied to other groups. The experiences of individuals with diverse sexual and gender identities might differ substantially from the patterns observed in this specific sample.
The survey measures used to assess sexual ambiguity have primarily been tested on young adults in past research. Applying these measures across a broader age range provides a useful first step, but the questionnaires may need further testing to ensure they capture the nuances of older adults’ experiences accurately.
Future research could track individuals over time to better understand the sequence of these identity shifts. Tracking participants over several years would help clarify whether the material disruption of a breakup directly prompts people to reevaluate their sexual orientation. Examining a more diverse group of participants could also reveal how different cultural and social backgrounds influence identity development after a major life transition.
The study, “Understanding Sexual Orientation Ambiguity: Perceptions of Transitional Impacts in the Context of a Relationship Dissolution,” was authored by Grace A. O’Toole, Peyton Woods, Kristin M. Anders, Jared Durtschi, and Anthony J. Ferraro.

Uganda to impose 21-day quarantine on returning citizens with Congo travel history
KAMPALA, Oct 25 - Ugandan citizens returning to the country with a history of travel to Democratic Republic of Congo will be quarantined for 21 days, Health Minister Chris Baryomunsi said on Sunday as Uganda tightened Ebola precautions despite saying it remained Ebola-free.
Uganda has been investigating a Nigerian Ebola case involving a woman who had travelled from Uganda. Officials said they were reviewing genomic sequencing, travel information, interactions and movements in coordination with Nigerian authorities and international partners.
Baryomunsi said on Sunday that all 60 contacts linked to a Kenyan Ebola case had completed their 21-day monitoring period and been discharged. The contacts were traced across points of entry and exit, hotels and transport operators linked to travellers' movements through Uganda.
"The ministry has intensified traveller screening at Entebbe International Airport and all land border crossings. All travellers intending to enter Uganda by air, land or water must complete the passenger locator form," he said.
Genomic analysis of Nigeria's only confirmed Ebola case showed the virus was closely related to the strain detected in Kenya's index case, though Nigerian authorities said there was no evidence that the Kenya case travelled to Nigeria or had a direct connection.
