Thousands march across Italy as protests bring isolated clashes with police
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
09:32:06 UTC
18:32:06 KST

Demonstrations took place in Italy on Saturday over the rising cost of living. No serious clashes were reported, with nine people arrested nationwide.
Thousands of people took to the streets on Saturday across Italy's main cities to protest over a range of issues, including the rising cost of living, Giorgia Meloni's government and the wars in the Middle East.
The protests were mostly peaceful, although some moments of tension were reported towards the evening in Turin, Florence, Bologna and Rome.
After last weekend's violence, the government enacted a significant new security operation, with police officers and soldiers patrolling city centres.
In Milan, 500 soldiers were also deployed in response to attacks on shops last Saturday.
In Florence, as in Turin, Milan and Rome, protesters did not organise a single main march, but instead small groups gathered in different parts of the city and later joined up. They repeatedly tried to reach the city centres but were blocked by security forces.
Protesters enter the Colosseum
In Rome, tensions flared when a small group of protesters broke away from the main march on Via Cavour and headed for the Colosseum.
There, they managed to enter the Flavian Amphitheatre, chanting slogans and holding up placards. The authorities later escorted them out of the historical site as the march continued through the streets of the city.
Later on, a young demonstrator also stood in front of a police water cannon truck, which continued for a couple of metres before the young man almost ended up beneath it. Officers then forcefully dragged him away, videos circulating on social media show.
In Florence, tensions also spiked when demonstrators tried to cross the Santa Trìnita bridge, but officers maintained the security cordon and used batons as protesters pushed to break through the barrier.
In Bologna, a march was prevented from continuing towards Via Marconi and Via Reno, with bottles and other objects hurled at security forces, who responded with a water cannon and tear gas.
One person was taken to hospital after being struck by police officers.
In Milan, the situation was calmer on Saturday; at least three marches joined together and moved through the streets around the city centre. There were verbal clashes between protesters and some far-right activists.
Nine arrests made
By the end of the day, nine people had been arrested and 87 were reported to the authorities, according to the Department of Public Security. A further 371 people were taken to police stations for checks, including 110 minors and 69 foreign nationals.
In Milan, 30-year-old Youssef Siher was also detained and placed under investigation on suspicion of aggravated incitement to commit a crime. He is alleged to have been behind the "17 October Movement," a group through which thousands of people are said to have shared information about taking part in last weekend's protests.
Meloni praises security operation
In a post on social media on Saturday evening, Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni praised those involved in the efforts to manage the demonstrations.
"The right to demonstrate must always be guaranteed, just as the right of citizens to live in their cities in safety," Meloni said.
"Safety must be guaranteed for everyone. For those who want to protest peacefully, for those who work and for those who want to live in their city without fear. Without leaving room for those who seek only confrontation and violence," she added.

Terrorists in the West Bank: Settler violence and the excusing hand
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
09:31:56 UTC
18:31:56 KST

The persistent violence from Israeli settlers against Palestinians in the occupied territories of the West Bank has become such common fare it risks becoming banal. Unfortunately, it takes events such as those befalling veteran photojournalist Heidi Levine of The Washington Post and European diplomats to return the attention to something that is not only grotesque but programmatic.
On 16th October, while covering the annual olive harvest in the West Bank Levine, fellow journalists and a group of Palestinians became the ripe targets of Israeli settlers. The auguries of violence were already present: over the course of 24 days since the season commenced, 125 physical attacks on Palestinian olive harvesters had been reported. After an initial gathering at a hilltop in the proximity of Abu Falah, the numbers of the assailants ominously swelled. They approached the group menacingly, burning olive trees on route. Then came tear gas and shots. A Palestinian was wounded in the leg.
Levine, in her description, was forced to the ground. “They just kept kicking me and hitting me with sticks, and it just kept going on and on. And then I actually thought, okay, maybe I’ll just play dead and pretend I’m dead, and they’ll stop and they’ll leave me alone.” The decision failed to yield the desired result.
Her camera bag, lenses, pouch filled with her US passport, credit cards, documents and relevant items were seized. She was hauled to her feet.
Eventually, a group of Palestinian men intervened to stand “in front of me to protect us, me and my rescuers from being attacked again.” Without that involvement, the group “would have been in the same situation as me.” In that encounter, Levine suffered a broken rib, a broken vertebra and a severe finger injury needing surgery.
In a separate attack on 17th October, French, Belgian and Polish diplomats and dignitaries of the Catholic Church found themselves targets at the mostly Christian village of Taybeh near Ramallah.
The window of a car from the Belgian consulate was smashed. Bernard Baudoux, mayor of the northern French town of Aulnoye-Aymeries, was beaten
The response from the Israeli government was, as to be expected, guarded, qualified and, in the end, light on the egregious conduct of the assailants. Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Sa’ar merely called the attacks on the European officials the cavalier work of “Israeli rioters”, blaming those who had organised the convoy for not coordinating “with the IDF in advance. Such coordination could have helped safeguard the visitors’ security.” Presumably, irresponsible Palestinian olive pickers do not coordinate with the IDF sufficiently to prevent settler attacks they invite upon themselves for simply being there.
A new sanctions regime: Targeting Israel’s West Bank settlements
An official statement from Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s office suggested that “serious questions” remained unanswered regarding the attack on Levine, a neat way of suggesting that non-settler accounts were to be treated as mendacious, self-interested and ultimately, unreliable. “Reports indicate some 200 Arabs and far-left activists confronted approximately 40 Israeli youths.” Those Arabs, those leftists, in a struggle against unblemished Israeli youth. The violence that ensued had a certain equivalence – so the PM’s office seemed to imply. “Footage shows masked individuals on both sides hurling objects, amid reports of fireworks fired at Jewish youths.”
As for Levine, was she to be trusted? After all, “footage appears to show Levine knocked down and immediately helped to her feet by the same unidentified individual.” Not so, rebutted Levine.
The attackers “only stood me up because they couldn’t manage to get everything off my shoulders to rob me, including ripping off my gold necklace that my daughter gave me for my birthday.”
The statement went on to reveal the whole rationale of such parrying responses. “We will not allow disputed incidents to be exploited to demonize the hundreds of thousands of law-abiding Jewish residents of Judea and Samaria.” Hard to be law abiding if one’s entire presence is premised on illegal occupation.
Stung into modest, cosmetic action, the Israeli authorities detained ten suspects regarding the two attacks on 19th October. On 21st October, nine of them were ordered by a Jerusalem court to be released to house arrest. “In the vast majority of attacks against Palestinians, no arrests are made at all,” explained Yonatan Kanonich, head of research at the Israeli rights outfit Yesh Din. “In cases that receive media coverage … the police arrest several settlers and release most of them shortly afterward.” Assaf Gonen of the legal aid organisation Honenu, bluntly claimed that such arrests were only “for show” with the intention of satisfying “media pressure and foreign interests.”
Interest has now shifted to the latest spate of bloodletting, with the 23rd October shooting deaths of two IDF soldiers at a checkpoint in Hebron giving Netanyahu the pretext to dig in, condemn and authorise acts of collective punishment. The IDF describes its avenging operation as “focused and limited to the area from which the terrorists operated”, which suggest that the area in question is likely to be flattened. Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich is unreserved in justifying the demolition orders against “illegal structures” to “create deterrence and exact a price for the serious attack”.
Dreams about Gaza: Israel’s ethnic cleansing proposals
The PM has an election to win, and the security and military forces have become his electioneering playthings. As for the terrorising settlers, Netanyahu only has warm words of praise. They were “heroic” emissaries of Israel’s broader project of settlement. “You are standing in the breach. You are a role model for the people of Israel, you are role model for the State of Israel. We are going to destroy the terror infrastructures, and we are going to build the settlement infrastructures.”
Levine acknowledges the asymmetrical interest shown for Palestinian residents relative to the tenacious, gluttonous coverage given notable foreign visitors who have suffered injury at the hands of the same assailants. “What hurts me most is I can now really understand what others have gone through, what Palestinian women, children, men have gone through,” she reflected in an 22nd October interview with CNN’s Jake Tapper.
“I’m an American, I work for The Washington Post, my story is getting a lot of attention around the world, everyone wants to talk to me – but I can’t imagine what it’s like for all the victims that have gone through the same ordeal and are living with the threat of this violence on a daily basis.”
The response from Democratic Congresswoman Rosa DeLauro from Connecticut to the attack had the good sense to note that the Palestinian “farmers in the grove had no flak jackets and no helmets. They had no major American newspaper behind them. If the settlers will do this to an American journalist on camera, in broad daylight, imagine what Palestinian families face when no one is watching.” Heroic deeds, according to Netanyahu, with more to come.

World leaders congratulate Kassym-Jomart Tokayev on Republic Day
President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev has received congratulatory messages from heads of foreign states and leaders of international organizations on the occasion of Kazakhstan’s national holiday, Republic Day, Qazinform News Agency cites the Akorda press service.
In his message, Russian President Vladimir Putin highlighted Kazakhstan’s achievements in the economic and social spheres, noting the country’s significant and constructive role in international affairs and its well-deserved standing on the world stage.
“Relations between Russia and Kazakhstan are successfully developing in the spirit of strategic partnership and alliance. I am confident that we will continue to consistently strengthen mutually beneficial Russian-Kazakh ties across all areas, for the benefit of our friendly peoples and in the interests of enhancing security and stability across the Eurasian region,” Vladimir Putin wrote.
President of the People’s Republic of China Xi Jinping noted that Kazakhstan is consistently implementing large-scale political reforms, maintaining social stability, sustaining steady economic growth, improving the well-being of its population, and strengthening its regional and international standing.
“I attach particular importance to the development of Kazakh-Chinese relations. I stand ready to continue our joint efforts to further deepen bilateral cooperation and make it more substantive for the benefit of the peoples of our two countries,” Xi Jinping stated.
Earlier, U.S. President Donald Trump sent a congratulatory message to our Head of State.
“I am grateful for the Enhanced Strategic Partnership between our nations and I look forward to continuing the great relationship that you and I have built during both of my Presidencies. I am proud to join in celebrating this important milestone,” Donald Trump emphasized.
President of Uzbekistan Shavkat Mirziyoyev expressed satisfaction that, in recent years, through the joint efforts of the two leaders, the strategic partnership and alliance between Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan, founded on the principles of good-neighborliness and close friendship, have continued to grow stronger.
President of Kyrgyzstan Sadyr Japarov noted that the adoption of the Declaration of State Sovereignty on October 25, 1990, paved the way for the emergence of an independent Kazakhstan, reflecting the country’s commitment to its historical heritage and the people’s firm determination to shape their nation’s future independently.
President of Tajikistan Emomali Rahmon spoke highly of the relations of friendship and cooperation with Kazakhstan, rooted in historical traditions and the principles of mutual respect and trust.
In his congratulatory message, President of Turkmenistan Serdar Berdimuhamedov emphasized that, over the years of sovereign development, Kazakhstan has made significant progress in strengthening its statehood, improving the well-being of its people and enhancing its standing on the international stage.
President of Türkiye Recep Tayyip Erdoğan expressed confidence that the special relations between the two countries, rooted in deep historical and cultural ties, would continue to develop in the spirit of an enhanced strategic partnership for the benefit of both peoples.
“The sixth meeting of the High-Level Strategic Cooperation Council between Kazakhstan and Türkiye, held in Astana on May 14, 2026, followed by the informal summit of the Organization of Turkic States in Turkistan, served as clear evidence of the strength of our strategic partnership,” Recep Tayyip Erdoğan emphasized.
President of Azerbaijan Ilham Aliyev noted that Azerbaijan, as a brotherly nation, sincerely rejoices in Kazakhstan’s significant successes and achievements.
“Our regular reciprocal visits, meetings and active dialogue at the highest level play an important role in further accelerating the development of our bilateral relations, strengthening our strategic partnership and alliance, and enriching them with new substance. I highly appreciate your recent visit to Azerbaijan to participate in the seventh CICA Summit,” Ilham Aliyev wrote.

Israeli forces turn Hebron homes into military posts amid lockdown
Evictions, raids and outpost expansion continue across the occupied West Bank amid heightened tensions.
Israeli forces have turned Palestinian homes in the city of Hebron into barracks and observation posts after forcing residents to leave, as a military operation in the southern occupied West Bank continues, the Palestinian news agency Wafa has reported.
They took over homes in the Khallat Manna and Dahiyat al-Zaytoun areas of southern Hebron to use them as barracks, and forced residents from homes in other neighbourhoods to use the properties as observation posts, Wafa said on Sunday, citing sources.
The Israeli military has imposed a lockdown in Hebron and conducted hundreds of raids since two armed Palestinian men allegedly carried out an attack on an Israeli army reserve base on Friday, killing two soldiers. The two suspects were also killed.
Since then, Israel has also forcibly displaced hundreds of families amid extensive raids, road closures and tight restrictions on movement.
“More than 2,670 Palestinians have been forcibly displaced from their homes in Hebron by Israeli occupation forces,” the office of Palestinian Prime Minister Mohammad Mustafa said on Sunday.
The statement, citing data from Hebron Municipality, added that the majority of those displaced were “women, children, and elderly people”.
According to the Palestinian Prisoner’s Society, those displaced from Hebron include 127 infants, 81 pregnant women and 26 people with disabilities.
Some 134 Palestinians with chronic illnesses and 265 elderly people over the age of 60 were also forced from their homes, the NGO told Al Jazeera.
The Palestinian Prisoner’s Society also said Israeli forces had detained at least 47 Palestinians across Hebron since Friday. Troops have conducted hundreds of field interrogations, subjecting Palestinians to detention and abuse, the group said.
New settler outposts
Meanwhile, Israeli settlers began establishing two new outposts on Palestinian-owned land in the town of Yatta, south of Hebron, Wafa reported.
Activist Osama Makhamra told Wafa that settlers began setting up an outpost in the Khallet al-Fara area, west of Yatta, where they pitched a tent, brought in bulldozers and excavation machinery, and started levelling and digging the land in preparation for construction.
He added that another outpost was established in the Yatta desert area, on Palestinian-owned land between the villages of az-Zuweidin and Umm Qussa, where settlers pitched several tents and began installing infrastructure, including water and electricity networks.
Near Bethlehem, Israeli forces continued to close roads and entrances across the governorate for the third consecutive day on Sunday, affecting several towns and villages, Wafa reported.
On Saturday, Israeli forces shut down dirt roads leading to Tuqu to block access, firing tear gas canisters and stun grenades towards Palestinian vehicles travelling along rough alternative routes near the town.
The latest attacks and closures come days before Israel’s general elections and as tensions remain high across the occupied Palestinian territory, where settlers, backed by the military, have carried out a wave of pogroms targeting olive harvesters.

Nepal's power export rises despite devastating floods
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
17:26:47 CST
18:26:47 KST

KATHMANDU, Oct. 25 (Xinhua) -- Nepal earned 5.93 billion Nepalese rupees from electricity exports to India in the third month of fiscal year 2026/27, which began in mid-July, the Nepal Electricity Authority (NEA) said on Sunday.
Revenue from electricity exports in the month increased by 962 million rupees compared with the same month last year, according to data from the state-owned power utility. Nepal earned 4.96 billion rupees from electricity exports to India during the same period last year.
The NEA reported an increase in export earnings despite damage to several hydropower projects caused by the devastating floods of Aug. 26, which forced some plants authorized to export electricity to suspend generation.
Nepal had suspended electricity exports to Bangladesh following the floods, but shipments resumed on Friday, according to the NEA. The country has been authorized to export up to 40MW of electricity as per the tripartite agreement between Nepal, India and Bangladesh.
During the first three months of the current fiscal year, from mid-July to mid-October, Nepal recorded electricity export transactions worth a total of 16.15 billion rupees.
The Aug. 26 floods severely damaged seven operational hydropower plants, three of which had received approval to export electricity. A total of 12 hydropower projects, including operational plants and those under construction, were damaged by the floods, according to the Nepal Development Update released by the World Bank earlier this month. (1 Nepalese rupee equals to 0.0066 U.S. dollar) ■

Western Sydney Int'l Airport launches passenger services
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
17:26:28 CST
18:26:28 KST

Passengers queue for security check at Western Sydney International Airport in Australia on Oct. 25, 2026. Western Sydney International Airport officially launched passenger operations on Sunday, with Jetstar flight JQ362 departing for the Gold Coast as the airport's first commercial passenger flight. Located about 45 km west of central Sydney, the airport began cargo operations in July after seven years of construction. Unlike Sydney's existing Kingsford Smith Airport, which is subject to a night-time curfew, the new airport can operate 24 hours a day. (Xinhua/Gong Bing)
SYDNEY, Oct. 25 (Xinhua) - Western Sydney International Airport officially launched passenger operations on Sunday, with Jetstar flight JQ362 departing for the Gold Coast as the airport's first commercial passenger flight.
The fully booked inaugural flight opened for check-in at 8 a.m. local time and took off around 11:20 a.m., Xinhua reporters learned at the airport.
Jetstar flight JQ363 from the Gold Coast landed at the new airport at around 3:10 p.m. The day's schedule also included Jetstar flight JQ375 to Melbourne.
"I'm so excited to see this airport. I just want to be part of history," Francis, a passenger on the inaugural flight, told Xinhua.
Francis, who lives in Strathfield in Sydney's west, said he took a train to St Marys before transferring to a bus to reach the airport, with the journey taking about one hour and 20 minutes.
Although the airport is not yet directly connected to the rail network, Francis said its round-the-clock operations would be particularly convenient for frequent travelers and that he would consider using the airport again.
Western Sydney International Airport CEO Simon Hickey told the Australian Broadcasting Corporation (ABC) that the opening marked a significant milestone and a generational change for Australia's aviation industry.
Hickey said the airport had been designed with future growth in mind, with annual passenger traffic expected to approach 10 million by the early to mid-2030s.
Located about 45 km west of central Sydney, the airport began cargo operations in July after seven years of construction.
Unlike Sydney's existing Kingsford Smith Airport, which is subject to a night-time curfew, the new airport can operate 24 hours a day.
Under the announced flight plans, the airport will serve domestic destinations including the Gold Coast, Melbourne and Brisbane. Its first international passenger service, connecting Western Sydney with Auckland, New Zealand, is scheduled to begin on Monday, with more international routes planned for the future. ■

Arab Israeli voters are essential to Israel’s democratic future - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
09:26:04 UTC
18:26:04 KST

I remember it well. In the 2015 Knesset elections, I came out of the voting booth in my kibbutz in the Galilee, Hanaton, and read on the news: Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, the prime minister of the State of Israel (yes, then too), announced to the public: “The Arabs are flocking to the voting booths! Go out and vote!”
I was stunned and horrified. I had moved to Israel 20 years before, from the US. Back then, 10 years ago, before President Donald Trump’s rise to power, I could not imagine a US president saying something like, “The blacks are flocking to the voting booths! Go out and vote!” Even if a president was thinking that, he would not have dared to say it back in 2015. Maybe before then or after then, but not then.
What shocked me was that the prime minister, who is supposed to be the prime minister of all citizens of the state, would blatantly and unabashedly address one portion of the state and pit them against another, as if Arab Israelis were not citizens, too.
Moreover, it was clear that the country’s prime minister was upset they were exercising their democratic right to vote! I was truly shocked.
Since then, I have been participating in a state-wide group (with smaller groups across the country) that does voter encouragement work in Arab Israeli towns and cities before national elections. We are not affiliated with a specific party, nor do we encourage people to vote for one.
The idea is to encourage people to exercise their democratic right to vote – especially in Arab Israeli society, where the voting percentages in the national elections are so low.
In the 2022 Knesset elections, only 52% of Arab Israelis came out to vote. I admit that I feel extremely invested in defeating this government. I find our current coalition terrifyingly dangerous on many levels. And yes, if the Arab population comes out en masse to vote, that will help democratically remove this government from power.
But my involvement in this work began before this particular election, and it is only one example of my activism to create a shared society among Arab and Jewish Israelis in this country. In the Galilee, where the population is 50-50 Arab-Jewish, this is our way of life. Despite Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich and MK Zvi Sukkot’s campaigns to create conflict among us, we live in peace, and often even friendship.
My children went to a Hand in Hand bilingual Arab-Jewish school, and I am heavily involved in my local chapter of the grassroots Arab-Jewish movement Standing Together, as well as in an interfaith group of spiritual leaders in the Galilee called Spirit of the Galilee. (To my delight, both groups are starting a youth program this year.)
Life in the Galilee could (and should) be much more integrated, and there is a lot of work to be done. But the work should be done in the direction of building more connections and bridges, not breaking those that have already been built and pitting our communities against each other.
I see in the news gangs of Jewish youth attacking Arab bus drivers in Jerusalem and Beit Shemesh, and it shatters my heart. Or adults – police officers – beating up Arab security guard Qais Haddad outside Teddy Stadium a year ago.
I wept when I read of a gang of Jewish youth in my area, in Haifa’s bayside suburbs, who beat up high school senior Khalil Sabach from Shefa-Amr, an Arab town I frequent, only 15 minutes from my home.
I went with a group from Tag Meir to visit him. What a lovely and impressive young man he is. He told us this incident did not break his spirit or his belief in Arab-Jewish partnership and let me hug him.
Government failure on crime in Arab Israeli society
Since this government came into power, the homicide rate from organized crime in Arab Israeli society has skyrocketed. It was bad before, but at least the previous government, the Yair Lapid-Naftali Bennett “Government of Change,” had a plan in place to combat this crisis – and it was working!
In fact, Yoav Segalovitz, who is running alongside MK Mansour Abbas in the Ra’am party, was instrumental in applying this plan. He worked under Omer Bar Lev, the public security minister at the time.
When Itamar Ben-Gvir took over this position (and its title was changed to national security minister), he stopped the program, and the problem has intensified to the point that there is on average about one person killed every day in Arab (and mixed) cities and towns.
This is intolerable, and if not stopped, the next generation of Arab Israelis who can manage to leave will do so – which is, of course, Ben-Gvir’s goal. That, and to have them kill one another.
This goal of ethnic cleansing in the Galilee, just like Smotrich and Sukkot are doing, mimicking the flags at the entrances of Jewish settlements in the West Bank, trying to scare away Arab residents by recruiting Jewish youth to hang swarms of Israeli flags at the entrances to Jewish villages and along main roads in areas heavily populated by Arab Israelis – is meant to intimidate them and send the message: We are the landlords here!
I know because this happened in my own village of Hanaton, where youth hung two long rows of Israeli flags all along the road leading up to our front gate. And I see it in other areas – including the area around Karmiel, where a group of young men were planted on Keren Kayemeth LeIsrael-Jewish National Fund land bordering on agricultural land of residents of the Muslim town of Majd el-Kurum, to intimidate farmers from the town going to work their land.
The Jewish youth were supposed to be shepherding, to keep the weeds under control; yet, they had no sheep. I know because I went there to protest until KKL-JNF said they would move them to a nearby location and make sure they do have sheep and are actually shepherding. Let’s see if they keep to their word.
Arab Israeli society has suffered terribly since October 7, when they, too, suffered. Thirty-four Arab Israelis (mostly, but not only, Bedouin) were killed on October 7, and more after (as soldiers and as victims of missiles from Gaza, Iran, the Houthis, and Hezbollah). There were also nine taken hostage to Gaza.
Hamas tried on October 7 to incite Arab Israelis to rise up against Israel from within, but they did not. Instead, they helped clean out shelters, treat the wounded in hospitals, collect supplies for and house the displaced, like the rest of us. They proved their loyalty to the state.
And when some did speak out against the war in Gaza – which is their democratic right – they were arrested, humiliated, and released with no charges (because there was no legal case against them). This was done to intimidate, silence, and frighten a big section of the population into either leaving or becoming passive citizens.
But we must not let the government get away with this. I understand why so many Arab Israelis are despairing. But when I go out into the streets of Nazareth, Shefa-Amr, Kafr Manda, Bir al-Maksur, and other Arab towns and cities around my kibbutz, I urge them not to give up hope, not to squander their democratic right to influence the direction of our shared country.
Being loyal but passive citizens is not enough. In order to put the country back on track, Arab Israelis must overcome their fear, anger, and depression, and come out and vote. If not out of a love for the country (although some do love the country, despite their complicated relationship with it), then out of self-interest – for the sake of their futures and the futures of their children and grandchildren.
Some can leave, but not all. And some will choose not to, even if they can. Like my own children. In the end, there will always be Arabs (some who identify as Palestinian and some who don’t) and Jews living in this country. I personally prefer it that way.
But even those who don’t, like most in the current coalition, must wake up to that reality and understand that for life here to be tolerable – let alone thriving, which is, ideally, what anyone sane wants – we must work to make it good for us all.
Organized crime, bigotry, never-ending war, Jewish terror in the West Bank – these are not our fate. If we get rid of this government, we could salvage our chances of living together here in peace and harmony.
Therefore, we all – proud Jewish Zionist Israelis included – must encourage this part of the population – full citizens of the Jewish State of Israel – to exercise not only their lawful right to vote but their lawful right to sit in the Knesset, be in the governing coalition, and serve as government ministers. And we must accept them with open arms when they “flock” to do so.
This is the only viable, sustainable, and livable future for this country.

Arab world hopes for an Israel without Netanyahu, but doubts it will change - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
09:25:35 UTC
18:25:35 KST

The Arab media are following Israel’s upcoming elections with considerable interest, recognizing that their outcome could have significant implications for Israel’s regional policies and its approach toward the Palestinians.
One striking feature of Arab media coverage is the in-depth familiarity many Arab commentators display with Israel’s political system, including the differences between and within its political parties – a level of understanding that is not always matched by Israeli coverage of politics in Arab countries.
The term “Arab media” encompasses a broad and diverse range of outlets, including satellite television networks, print and online newspapers, and social media platforms across numerous countries in the region and beyond. It is therefore difficult to present a comprehensive and reliable picture of the various voices and perspectives expressed within this vast media landscape.
But, at the risk of oversimplification, Arab discourse on the Israeli elections can be divided into two main trends.
The pessimistic view: a prominent perspective within this camp regards Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu not as the problem itself but rather as a manifestation of deeper trends within Israeli society and politics, which have shifted sharply to the Right since October 7 and embraced a hardline security doctrine.
Accordingly, even if Yashar party leader Gadi Eisenkot becomes prime minister, the change would primarily be reflected in a different tone, improved relations with Washington, and greater diplomatic pragmatism, rather than any fundamental shift in policy toward the Palestinians. This perspective is particularly prominent in the coverage of Qatar’s Al Jazeera network, although it is also reflected in other Arab media outlets.
For example, Jordanian journalist Osama al-Sharif published an article on a Saudi website with a title that speaks for itself: “Netanyahu, Eisenkot, Lapid: Three Names, One Anti-Palestinian Policy.”
In his view, the elections offer no genuine alternative for Palestinians or the wider Arab world, since all the leading candidates share similar security-oriented positions and offer no new approach to resolving the Palestinian question.
Although Israel’s endless wars have failed to bury the Palestinian cause, he argued, there is little reason to expect any meaningful change in Israeli policy toward it. This assessment is shared by numerous Palestinian observers and journalists.
Supporters of this view emphasize the historical processes and sociological transformations that have reshaped Jewish Israeli society, both ideologically and politically, creating formidable obstacles to any significant change in Israeli policy following the elections.
From this perspective, the identity of the prime minister matters relatively little, since any government would be constrained by coalition politics and compelled to respond to an electorate that is predominantly right-wing.
Arab skepticism stems not only from assessments of the political balance of power within Israel but also from the deep scars left by the wars since October 7 – scars that will not necessarily disappear with a change of government.
The optimistic view: commentators representing this perspective believe that a new Israeli government could create fresh diplomatic opportunities for dialogue, potentially leading to an expansion of the Abraham Accords.
This approach can be found in several Gulf media outlets. Yet the optimism it expresses is cautious and conditional, and does not necessarily reflect the official positions of the governments concerned.
For example, Egyptian columnist Sobhi Shabana wrote in the Saudi newspaper Al Jazirah that Eisenkot’s election could open a window of opportunity for change. Unlike Netanyahu, who remains beholden to the far Right, Eisenkot views military force not as an end in itself but as a means of achieving political objectives.
In the same newspaper, columnist Ahmed Adam argued that a new Israeli government could make it easier for countries that have signed the Abraham Accords to expand their public relations with Israel, facilitate the resumption of high-level political dialogue between Israel and Egypt and Jordan, remove a major political and psychological obstacle to improving regional relations, and create conditions for renewed negotiations with Saudi Arabia – provided that the new government offers tangible progress on the Palestinian issue.
The tension between these two schools of thought is well illustrated by Omar Raddad, a Jordanian political and security analyst. On the one hand, he argued that various regional actors view the Israeli elections as an opportunity to reshape Israeli policy in ways that could open a new window for peace and normalization processes that have stalled because of the policies of the far Right.
On the other hand, he cautioned that the elections may merely replace political figures without altering the fundamental principles of Israeli policy, which remain rooted in security doctrines that have become more entrenched since October 7.
Beyond the question of whether a new government would change Israeli policy, Arab commentators are also examining who might bring such a government to power.
Role of Arab Israelis in the election
In this context, considerable attention has been devoted to the role of Arab citizens of Israel in the elections. Many observers suggest that a high voter turnout among Arab citizens could determine Netanyahu’s political fate, with particular attention focused on Mansour Abbas and his Ra’am party.
Yet alongside recognition of the Arab electorate’s potential political influence, there is considerable skepticism about the willingness of Jewish opposition parties to rely on Arab parties in forming the next government.
This creates a paradox: Arab citizens could play a decisive role in bringing about a change of government without necessarily becoming partners in shaping its policies.
Perhaps the most revealing finding emerging from Arab media discourse is the gap between hopes for a change of government in Israel and skepticism about whether such a change would produce a meaningful shift in Israeli policy.
For some commentators, a new government could open a window of opportunity for improving regional relations and perhaps even reviving the normalization process. Yet even the optimists do not anticipate a fundamental change in Israel’s approach toward the Palestinians.
In this sense, Arab discourse can largely be described as “pessoptimistic,” to borrow the term coined by Palestinian writer Emile Habibi: it combines hope for political change with pessimism about the prospects for strategic transformation. The Arab world, it seems, longs for an Israel without Netanyahu, but doubts that an Israel without Netanyahu would necessarily be a different Israel.
Prof. Elie Podeh teaches in the Department of Islamic and Middle Eastern Studies at the Hebrew University of Jerusalem and is a board member of Mitvim – The Israeli Institute for Regional Foreign Policies.

Israel braces for rainy Election Day, but can bad weather affect voter turnout?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
09:25:28 UTC
18:25:28 KST

Election day in Israel is expected to bring cooler temperatures and rain in southern and eastern Israel, raising the question: Will Dreary weather keep Israelis away from the polls?
The expected rain will intensify at midday, mainly in the south and east, with thunderstorms, gusty winds, and hail. Significant flash flooding is also possible in the Negev and Arava streambeds, and in the Dead Sea area.
Is there any real basis for this fear? The data show the answer is an unequivocal no.
Looking back, Israel has no proven link between rain and voter turnout. In fact, the all-time turnout record of 87% was set in the First Knesset elections in January 1949, on an especially stormy winter day. By contrast, the Second Knesset elections were held on an ordinary summer day in July 1951 and recorded just 75%, lower than any election held in the country until 2003.
The all-time low was recorded in the 2006 elections (the 17th Knesset), when only 63.5% of Israelis voted. That election was held on March 28, a spring day, but clouds and rain covered parts of the country. The media at the time rushed to blame the weather, but an in-depth review by the Israel Meteorological Service showed that rain has no real connection to voter participation; political and social factors drive it.
The paradox is simple: rain supposedly keeps people at home under the covers, while pleasant sunshine sends them to the beach, parks, and malls, supposed “enemies of the ballot box.” In practice, polling stations stay open for a full 15 hours, rain in Israel mostly falls in short bursts, and no outing lasts all day.
First Israeli election on schedule in three decades
Israel’s lawmakers actually considered the weather in advance. A 1959 amendment to Basic Law: The Knesset set the Hebrew month of Cheshvan as the fixed election date, and 2006 documents from the Knesset Constitution Committee explain that it is a comfortable month, falling right after the Tishrei holidays and before the peak of winter. The assumption was that mild weather would make it easy to get to the polls, and that early sunsets, especially in winter, like the switch that took effect this week, would send day-trippers from the beaches straight to the polling stations well before closing.
But political reality in Israel rarely goes by the book. Since 1988, every election has been moved up (though the November 2022 election was held in Cheshvan because the Knesset dissolved itself). If the election on Tuesday, October 27, goes ahead as planned, it will be the first time Israelis vote on the original date set by law in 38 years.
A statistical look at the 25 elections held since the state's founding, along with this week’s election for the 26th Knesset, shows an almost even seasonal spread: seven in winter, seven in summer, six in spring, and six in fall. Most elections, 14 of them, were in fact held in the “hard” seasons (winter and summer), and 12 in the “comfortable” ones (fall and spring).
The bottom line: turnout shows no real difference between summer and winter, partly because the July–August elections took place long before Israelis began flying abroad en masse for vacation.
But what about the rest of the world?
How weather impacts elections worldwide
An American study of 14 presidential elections found that roughly 25 mm (about an inch) of rain lowered turnout by about one percentage point. In the Netherlands (13 elections between 1971 and 2010), researchers found a similar result: pleasant sunshine encourages people to go out and vote. In Sweden, by contrast, researchers found no significant effect of rain.
Rather than settling on a single country, researchers at the University of Copenhagen combined data from 34 studies worldwide, published in the journal Electoral Studies.
The conclusion: every centimeter of rain lowers turnout by about 0.95%, with young people and undecided voters six times more sensitive to the weather than others. Even so, applying this to Israel is hard; here, Election Day is a public holiday, unlike in many countries where people vote on a regular workday.
An International IDEA institute report this past April, together with King’s College and Griffith University, found that between 2006 and 2025 at least 94 elections and referendums in 52 countries were disrupted by natural disasters (in 26 of those cases the vote was postponed; in 2024 alone, 23 elections in 18 countries were disrupted).
But don't worry, that study focuses on typhoons, hurricanes, massive wildfires, and devastating floods that paralyze infrastructure, events irrelevant to Israel's climate.
A local autumn shower may mean grabbing an umbrella on the way to the polls, but Israeli history shows it won't stop voters from having their say.

Dimona's former Netanyahu loyalists turn to Eisenkot as battle for final undecided voters heats up
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
09:25:22 UTC
18:25:22 KST

Former supporters of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu in the once Likud party hub of Dimona are campaigning for rival candidate Gadi Eisenkot in the days leading up to Tuesday's election.
The ballot is Israel's first since Hamas' October 7, 2023 attack that shook the country and plunged the region into turmoil, as Israel went to war on the terrorist group in Gaza and its allies in Lebanon and Iran.
The October 7 security breach saw Likud's popularity plummet. Opinion polls have predicted for months that Netanyahu's coalition will lose its majority. But his top rival, Yashar's Eisenkot, has no clear path to power either, and the race has become tighter as the election nears.
Dimona, where an Iranian missile wounded dozens in March, has become a political battleground.
"We must have change. Bibi has to go," said Yossi Assayag, 74, who says he has supported Likud most of his life. "Bibi has brought disaster to Israel."
Eisenkot's Yashar party targets Likud Loyalists
Assayag is part of a group of town residents trying to convince their community to vote for Eisenkot's party, which is neck and neck with Likud in the polls.
It's a tough task in Dimona, where half the voters in the 2022 election voted for Likud.
"I will never betray Likud," said Ruti Ohana, a pensioner, who says she has voted Likud ever since immigrating to Israel from North Africa more than 60 years ago. She said Netanyahu was a cut above his rivals, and that detractors unfairly blamed him for October 7.
Likud long ago formed a core voter base among Jews of Middle Eastern and North African descent, known as Mizrahis, who felt neglected by the European-influenced Labor Party that dominated Israel for generations.
Labor has since dwindled to a rump as Israeli politics have shifted rightward, and around half a dozen other parties now court Likud voters, from the center to the far right. But the link to the party among its past supporters remains strong.
"Most people here vote for Likud just because that's how they were raised," said Oria Asaf, 25, a past Likud voter now backing Yashar. "The change will come when people start to think about their children's future rather than their parents' past."
The Dimona battle for wavering 'Likudniks'
While Netanyahu has a substantial base of supporters that can't be won over, the prize is undecided voters who "understand that we are in a state of crisis" and are open to persuasion, said Michal Elmalem Abu, elected as a member of the city council from Likud and now leading Eisenkot's Dimona campaign.
Some 13% of Israeli voters still haven't decided how they will vote, according to data collected by the Viterbi Family Center for Public Opinion and Policy Research at the Israel Democracy Institute.
Of those who voted for Likud in 2022, just 55% now say they will vote for the party again on Tuesday. Fifteen percent will support parties aligned against Netanyahu, including 8% for Yashar. Another 14% will vote for alternative right-wing parties, and 9% are undecided.
In places like Dimona, Eisenkot could take a chunk out of Likud's base, said Amotz Asa-El, a columnist for The Jerusalem Post and political scientist at the Hartman Institute.
A child of Moroccan immigrants who rose through the ranks to become military chief of staff, Eisenkot, 66, has a personal story of humble origins in the Mizrahi community that "appeals to a big swath of the Israeli electorate, particularly Likud's traditional electorate," Asa-El said.
In an electoral field crowded with ex-soldiers, his peerless security credentials are an asset. The loss of his son, killed in combat in Gaza in December 2023, resonates with voters.
At a town hall in Dimona in July, residents said they were excited about the prospect of a Mizrahi leader. Others approached him with hugs and tearful condolences for the loss of his son.
But a week later Netanyahu held his own event, demonstrating his powerful appeal in the hardscrabble Negev, where Likud governments have long boasted of bringing development funds.
"Look around you, look at your community, look at what was here then and what is here now, and ask yourselves which governments invested in this monumental effort. And I do this out of immense love," he said.
Lior Katzav, a Likud former mayor of Kiryat Malachi, another small-town stronghold, said party surveys show voters who had abandoned Likud are returning as the election nears.
But even some who sympathize with Netanyahu say it may be time for a change. Israel's youngest prime minister when he was first elected 30 years ago, he has since become its longest-serving, now 77, having governed for 18 years over six terms.
"It's time for him to go," said Dimona software engineer David Iskali. "He's done a lot for Israel, but it can't go on. I won't give my vote to someone almost 80 years old."

The military said the financial transfers had recently supported Hamas' efforts to restore its military infrastructure and advance attacks against Israeli forces and civilians.
In a separate operation last week, the IDF and Shin Bet security agency carried out an airstrike in central Gaza, destroying a weapons depot used by Hamas to store military equipment. The facility contained Kalashnikov rifles, a launcher and rockets, according to the military.
Additional terrorists killed in Gaza strikes
The announcement follows an IDF statement last week confirming the deaths of two additional terrorists in separate strikes.
One was Akram Bassam Shaaban Yassin, a senior member of Hamas' General Security apparatus in the Gaza Strip. The other was Tamer Mohammed Ibrahim al-Sabbagh, whom the military identified as a member of the terrorist cell responsible for abducting and murdering German-Israeli citizen Shani Louk during the October 7, 2023, Hamas-led attack on Israel.

Taiwan pushes social media platforms to label deepfake and AI images
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
09:18:06 UTC
18:18:06 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — The Ministry of Digital Affairs is urging social media platforms to make AI-generated images clearly identifiable, proposing a three-layer labeling system to help users distinguish authentic content.
The proposed system would combine voluntary disclosures by content creators, automated detection, and reporting channels for suspected violations. The ministry said the initiative aims to build a trustworthy digital environment and prioritize high-risk deepfakes that could mislead the public, per CNA.
Tsai Shou-chuan (蔡壽洤), director of MODA's Department of Digital Strategy, said the ministry has held meetings with Meta, Google, Line, and industry associations since the beginning of the year to discuss ways to improve labeling of AI-generated images.
The ministry is not currently requiring platforms to adopt a uniform labeling format but wants disclosures to be prominent and easy for users to notice, Tsai said.
He cited YouTube as an example, saying its existing disclosure that content was generated using AI appears beneath the video description and requires users to click “More” to see it. MODA wants the platform to display a more visible AI label below videos.
The first layer of the proposed system would require platforms to give creators a way to identify and disclose AI-generated images when uploading content.
The second would involve automated detection. AI-generated images may contain embedded or otherwise hidden provenance information that software can read even when it is not visible to users, Tsai said. MODA wants platforms to detect these signals and add labels when appropriate, including when uploaders have not disclosed the use of AI, he said.
Tsai acknowledged that both measures could have gaps. Users may deliberately remove or damage embedded identifiers, while platforms may struggle to detect every instance of AI-generated content because of the volume of material uploaded.
The third layer would establish channels for government notifications, public reports, and privacy-related complaints. Platforms would then assess individual cases involving potentially misleading, infringing, or otherwise prohibited content.
Where AI-generated images are connected to fraud or violations of others' rights, MODA would coordinate with platforms on appropriate responses, including adding labels or removing content, depending on the applicable regulations and circumstances, Tsai said.
Regarding implementation, Tsai said Google was making the fastest progress, while Meta was continuing technical adjustments. Line would initially focus on public-facing material, such as advertisements, because private one-on-one conversations and group messages raise privacy concerns, per CNA.
The initiative follows broader efforts to develop guidance for AI-generated content and deepfakes. In March, MODA said it would consult industry representatives, experts, and other stakeholders on AI governance to develop initial policy principles or a framework by the end of the year, per CNA.
In September, MODA fined Meta a combined NT$10 million (US$306,000) in two cases involving disclosure of AI-generated or deepfake images in advertisements and the handling of suspected scam advertisements. The cases underscore the challenges regulators face in ensuring platforms adequately disclose synthetic content and respond to harmful material.

A survey confirms interest in a direct train service between Switzerland and London
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
09:17:37 UTC
18:17:37 KST

A survey confirms interest in a direct train service between Switzerland and London
The Swiss are overwhelmingly in favour of a direct train service to London. A survey confirms widespread support for this rail link, which is seen as essential for competing with air travel and reducing the impact on the climate.
The introduction of direct trains to the United Kingdom is generating considerable interest in Switzerland. A YouGov poll found that 58% of those surveyed are in favour, whilst only 8% are against. The survey, conducted amongst 1,048 people and published on Saturday, was commissioned by the organisations T&E, actif-trafiC and ATE.
Those surveyed favour flying because of its speed (79%). To encourage them to choose rail, lower fares (61%), direct connections (37%) and shorter journey times (37%) would be key factors.
The choice to travel by train is driven by its appeal (58%), its low environmental impact (55%) and the location of stations in city centres (45%). “By removing the stopover in Paris, the journey time between Geneva and London would be reduced from over seven hours to around five hours 30 minutes,” emphasised Victor Thévenet of the T&E association.
SBB has signed a memorandum of understanding with SNCF and Eurostar. Obstacles remain, and implementation is not expected until the 2030s.

Audi heads to US: Trump hopes to score at the polls with German carmaker
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
09:15:55 UTC
18:15:55 KST

Audi is planning its first car factory in the United States, with the Ingolstadt-based manufacturer set to invest billions in a new plant in Georgia.
Audi is taking a major step into the United States: the premium carmaker from Ingolstadt plans to invest around four billion US dollars in its first own US car plant in the state of Georgia.
The announcement was made on Saturday, 24 October 2026, at a campaign rally by US President Donald Trump in Perry, Georgia. Trump appeared alongside Döllner and stressed in his speech that his trade policy was prompting companies to move their production to the United States. The announcement is likely to play well in the battle for the midterm elections on 3 November.
Audi CEO Gernot Döllner justified the investment in his address by pointing to the company’s long-term ambitions in the US: the American market is one of the world’s most important premium car markets, but Audi has not yet fully tapped its potential there.
Production scheduled to start in the early 2030s
The plan is for an annual capacity of up to 200,000 vehicles and around 4,500 jobs. The plant is to be built at the Middle Georgia Megasite in Peach County, near the city of Macon. According to the state authorities, Georgia won out as a location partly because of its existing supplier base, its transport links and its pool of skilled workers. The option to expand the facility at a later date also played a role in the choice.
According to the company, preparatory work is due to begin in 2027, with series production to start in the early 2030s. The government of Georgia is naming 2031 as the target date for full-scale production.
With around 4,500 planned jobs, the project would be a major industrial development for the region. Additional posts at suppliers, logistics firms and service providers would come on top.
Large SUVs for the American market
The new plant will mainly build large, high-end sport utility vehicles. Reuters reports, citing a US government official, that the Audi Q7, Q8 and Q9 models are planned. Audi itself speaks of particularly large and upmarket SUVs tailored to the needs of North American customers.
For Audi, the move is strategically significant, as until now the company has imported its vehicles for the US market from Europe or Mexico. Local production would reduce its dependence on international supply chains and exchange-rate fluctuations. At the same time, Audi would be producing closer to its American customers and strengthening its competitive position against manufacturers with their own US plants, as the carmaker stresses in an official statement.
Trump claims the move as a success for his tariff policy
Trump imposed additional tariffs on imports of cars and car parts and repeatedly called on foreign manufacturers to produce more in the United States. For companies such as Audi, this policy increases the cost of imports, making local manufacturing more economically attractive. According to Reuters, Trump’s tariffs cost Audi around 1.2 billion euros last year.
However, this does not mean that the tariffs alone explain the choice of location: Audi also points to the long-term expansion of its US business, access to the sales market, the existing infrastructure and the regional supplier base.
What does this mean for Germany?
The decision raises questions for the German sites of the Volkswagen Group. Additional production in the US does not automatically mean job losses in Germany, but it does alter the geographical distribution of future investment and increase the importance of North America.
Audi emphasises that Germany and Europe are to remain the company’s industrial backbone; the existing expertise in development, engineering and production is merely to be complemented by the new site.
According to Tagesschau, the IG Metall union broadly welcomes the stronger push into the US market, but at the same time is calling for firm long-term prospects for employees at the German sites. The union also says that the final decision is still subject to approval by the relevant Volkswagen bodies.
Georgia: an industrial hub with a car-making tradition
Georgia has long been a centre of the American car industry. South Korean carmaker Kia has been producing in West Point since 2009, while Hyundai, also from South Korea, has built a multibillion-dollar plant for electrified vehicles near Savannah. Added to this are the powerful ports of Savannah and Brunswick, through which vehicles and components can be shipped internationally.
For Trump, the investment would be another trump card in his strategy of bringing more industrial production back to the United States. For Audi, it marks a step closer to one of the world’s most important car markets.

Italy Orders KF51 Panther-Based Tanks and Lynx Armored Vehicles Worth €3.7 Billion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
09:15:36 UTC
18:15:36 KST

A joint venture between Italy’s Leonardo and Germany’s Rheinmetall has secured two contracts to supply armored vehicles to the Italian Army.
According to German defense news outlet Hartpunkt, citing Italian newspaper Milano Finanza, the contracts are worth about €3.7 billion in total.
According to the media, the order includes 30 next-generation main battle tanks and 48 tracked armored vehicles as part of Italy’s military modernization programs.
The new tank, designated the NMBT (New Main Battle Tank), is being developed based on Rheinmetall’s KF51 Panther technology demonstrator. It is intended to replace Italy’s Ariete tanks.
The second part of the order concerns the A2CS (Army Armoured Combat System) program, under which Italy is procuring new tracked combat vehicles based on Germany’s KF41 Lynx platform.
The vehicles are intended to replace the outdated Dardo infantry fighting vehicles and supplement the Italian Army’s existing armored fleet.
The Leonardo Rheinmetall Military Vehicles (LRMV) joint venture, established by the two companies in 2024, is carrying out the NMBT tank program.
In September 2026, Militarnyi reported that Italy’s Ministry of Defense published a procurement procedure for new tanks and specialized vehicles based on the tank platform, with an estimated total value of €5.14 billion.
Italy plans to complete the program by 2038, with the country’s total requirement previously estimated at approximately132 new main battle tanks.
In January 2026, the Italian military received the first four vehicles of this type. In November 2025, LRMV signed an initial contract to deliver 21 KF41 Lynx infantry fighting vehicles. The agreement also included an option to purchase an additional 30 vehicles.
In the longer term, Italy plans to procure 1,050 Lynx-family armored vehicles across ten versions, including 649 infantry fighting vehicles. The A2CS program also covers command, reconnaissance, medical, and recovery vehicles.
Italy’s defense industry will play a significant role in manufacturing the vehicles. Under preliminary plans, Italian companies will handle final assembly, testing, and subsequent maintenance. Domestic production is expected to account for about 60% of the program.

Ukraine's General Staff reports strikes on Russian radars in Belgorod Oblast and command posts
Ukrainian forces struck radar stations in Russia's Belgorod Oblast and Russian forces' command posts in Zaporizhzhia and Kherson oblasts on 24 October and on the night of 24-25 October.
Source: General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine
Details: The General Staff reported that Ukrainian forces struck Russian radar stations near the settlements of Gostishchevo and Kurgannoye in Belgorod Oblast.
They also struck a Russian unit command post near Tarasivka in Zaporizhzhia Oblast and a command and observation post near the occupied town of Hola Prystan in Kherson Oblast.
Ukrainian forces also attacked clusters of Russian troops near Mykolaiivka and Novoukraiinka in Donetsk Oblast, as well as Berdiansk, Okhrimivka and Tarasivka in Zaporizhzhia Oblast.
The extent of the damage to the targeted facilities has not been specified.
Background: Russia lost 1,850 soldiers killed and wounded over the past day, bringing its total number of personnel losses to 1,578,450.

Borr Drilling rig sinks off Gabon, one person dead and four missing
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
09:10:20 UTC
18:10:20 KST

Borr Drilling rig sinks off Gabon, one person dead and four missing
Oct 25 - Borr Drilling's Prospector 5 rig sank late on Saturday off the coast of Mayumba, Gabon, killing one employee and leaving four others missing among the 115 people on board, three sources familiar with the matter said on Sunday.
An Indian national, one of the five initially unaccounted for, has been found dead. The remaining four missing include three Gabonese nationals and one other expatriate, the sources said.
The government has not confirmed the death, instead saying that five people remain missing and that search efforts were ongoing.
"Preliminary information indicates that the rig experienced a punch-through event during preload activities, resulting in loss of stability and the subsequent sinking of the rig," the offshore drilling contractor said.
The Prospector 5 oil and gas rig, owned and operated by Borr, is contracted to support BW Energy's drilling operations off Gabon. The rig had not yet begun drilling.
Prospector 5 is located at the Dussafu Marin permit, a licence off the Gabon coast. BW Energy holds a 73.5% working interest in the licence, with Panoro Energy holding 17.5%.
Gabon's Ministry of Petroleum and Gas said it had activated a crisis unit and ordered the navy to reinforce search and rescue operations at sea. The ministry also ordered a technical investigation, Petroleum and Gas Minister Clotaire Kondja said in a statement.
The crisis unit brings together the ministry, the navy, state oil company Gabon Oil, BW Energy and Borr Drilling, Kondja said.
The accident occurred at approximately 9:40 p.m. (2040 GMT) on Saturday in the Dussafu Marin permit area near the Mabomont production facility, the ministry said.
"We are deeply concerned for those who remain unaccounted for and everyone affected by this incident," said Borr Drilling Chief Executive Bruno Morand.
"Our immediate priority is supporting the ongoing search and rescue efforts and the welfare of all personnel involved."
Panoro Energy said production had been halted, adding that there were no reports of damage or accidental discharges.
No discharge of harmful substances has been observed, the ministry said, adding that pollution-response resources remained deployed to protect the coastline and nearby Mayumba National Park. REUTERS

Watch: IAF’s Tejas steals the show at ‘Wings over Ganges’ aerial display in Varanasi
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
09:08:12 UTC
18:08:12 KST

Varanasi city hosted the 94th Indian Air Force Day celebrations.
NEW DELHI: Prime Minister Narendra Modi and defence minister Rajnath Singh witnessed the Indian Air Force’s aerial display at the ‘Wings over Ganges’ event in Varanasi on October 25, as the city hosted the 94th Indian Air Force Day celebrations.The display featured the IAF’s LCA Tejas, Sukhoi-30MKI, Rafale and Light Combat Helicopter (LCH) Prachand, alongside the Sarang Helicopter Display Team. Aircraft from the Indian Navy and the Army also participated, showcasing coordination among the three services.Uttar Pradesh governor Anandiben Patel and Chief minister Yogi Adityanath were also present at the event.
The event came amid the IAF’s emphasis on jointness and integration as the armed forces prepare for future multi-domain conflicts. IAF chief Air Chief Marshal AP Singh has said the three services would need to operate more closely and that theatreisation should focus on employing air power effectively within an integrated structure.“We are not viewing theaterisation as an exercise to permanently divide fighter assets geographically,” Singh told news agency PTI. He said future conflicts would be multi-domain by nature and require closer coordination among the three services.
During his visit to his parliamentary constituency, PM Modi also inaugurated a new garment manufacturing facility at Arvind Mills. He travelled to the facility by Army helicopter after arriving in Varanasi.His roadshow passed through Police Lines, the Cultural Complex and Chowkaghat before reaching Namo Ghat for the aerial display.
Priyanka Jaiswal has four years of experience in digital journalism, news agency reporting and video production. Currently with The Times of India, she covers public policy, politics and global affairs. She is particularly drawn to human-interest stories that put people at the heart of an issue, spark awareness , and contribute to meaningful conversations.

We have switched to winter astronomical time
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
09:07:42 UTC
18:07:42 KST

How Long Does It Take to Learn Poker? Plus Three Card Games That Can Be Learned Quickly
Poker chips, playing cards and laptop
Bulgaria switched to astronomical time last night, after clocks were set back one hour to 3:00 a.m. at exactly 4:00 a.m., BGNES reports. The change marks the beginning of the so-called winter time, which will remain in effect until the last Sunday of March next year. This fall, the clock change provides an extra hour of sleep on the very day millions of Bulgarian citizens head to the polls for the country's presidential election.
Astronomical time is the natural time for our geographical zone (UTC+2), which we use every year from the end of October to the end of March. The mechanism is strictly fixed throughout the European Union: on the night of the last Sunday in October, the clocks are moved back one hour, and on the last Sunday in March, they are moved forward one hour for the transition to summer time.
The main economic and social goal of the summer shift is to achieve a better match between the daylight hours and the active hours of workers and students. With the return to the standard astronomical rhythm in the fall, mornings will become brighter, but at the expense of this, evenings will begin to get dark significantly earlier. While modern mobile phones, computers and smart watches make the correction automatically, mechanical devices and some household appliances require manual adjustment - a detail of particular importance for adhering to the schedule on today's election day, when the sections opened their doors at 07:00 and will accept voters until 20:00.
From Franklin's joke to the war economy
The concept of artificially adjusting working hours to the sun was born in the eighteenth century. Its author was the American scientist, diplomat and statesman Benjamin Franklin. In 1784, he sent his famous essay in the form of a letter to the editor of the newspaper "Paris Journal", in which he suggested that the inhabitants of the French capital get up and go to bed earlier in order to save candles and take advantage of the morning sunlight.
Although the idea initially sounded like satire, it found real government application more than a century later under the pressure of wartime shortages. During World War I, the German government first introduced daylight saving time from April 30 to October 1, 1916, as an emergency measure to save coal and fuel. Just a few weeks later, Great Britain became the second country to adopt the practice between May 21 and October 1, 1916, and the United States followed suit in 1918.
In modern Europe, the coordinated movement of clocks began in 1976 at the insistence of France amid the oil crisis of the 1970s. In Bulgaria, the practice was officially introduced by Decree No. 6 of the Council of Ministers of January 26, 1979. Today's order in our country is regulated by Decree No. 94 of March 13, 1997 and its subsequent synchronization with European directives, according to which daylight saving time comes into effect at 03:00 on the last Sunday in March and ends at 04:00 on the last Sunday in October.
The blocked reform in Brussels
Although the original energy-saving idea has long been questioned by economists and doctors, about 70 countries around the world, covering a third of the planet's population, still continue to change their clocks twice a year. Within the European Union, the issue has remained in institutional limbo for seven years.
Back in 2018, a large-scale public opinion poll among European citizens showed that 84 percent of respondents wanted to abolish the seasonal clock change. In response to public pressure, the European Parliament voted officially to abolish the practice in March 2019, with the idea that each capital would choose whether to remain permanently on summer or winter time.
However, the reform remained blocked in the negotiation phase between individual governments in the Council of the European Union. In order for a final decision to be adopted, a qualified majority is needed - support from at least 15 member states, representing at least 65 percent of the union's population. Fears of a chaotic mosaic of time zones within the single market and the lack of consensus between the northern and southern countries have stalled the process. In 2026, the European Commission commissioned a new in-depth study on the consequences of ending the seasonal change, which would help member states make a common decision. Brussels has not yet committed to specific deadlines for when the results will be ready and when the debates will return to the agenda of European leaders, and the next time the clocks will move forward is set for spring 2027.

Poland has ended a six-day search for an unidentified flying object that may have entered its airspace near Lublin on October 18.
According to RMF24, the military and other services found no evidence of the object.
More than 30 members of Poland’s Territorial Defense Forces participated in the operation each day. They searched the area around a reservoir and locations south of Lublin, including the municipality of Niedrzwica Duża near the S19 expressway.
During the first few days of the search, the military also deployed a helicopter.
Polish authorities analyzed radar data and local residents’ statements to determine the nature of the unidentified object.
Possible explanations included meteorological phenomena, smuggling activity, or a provocation.
Lieutenant Colonel Jacek Goryszewski, spokesperson for the Polish Armed Forces Operational Command, said the military had no evidence confirming that the country’s airspace had been violated.
The search operation ended on Friday, October 23.
According to Captain Marta Haborek, spokesperson for the 2nd Lublin Territorial Defense Brigade, the military found neither the object itself nor any debris or other traces that could confirm local residents’ reports.
At around 2:00 a.m. on October 18, 2026, police received two reports from local residents who had heard a loud noise from an unidentified object flying over the area near the Zemborzyce Reservoir.
At the time, the Polish Armed Forces Operational Command said it was investigating a radar signal and local residents’ reports.
