Disenchanted Netanyahu supporters are prize of Israel election campaign
DIMONA, Oct 25 - In the remote Negev Desert town of Dimona, long a bastion of Benjamin Netanyahu's Likud party, disenchanted voters are going door-to-door campaigning for his top rival, hoping to bring down the veteran prime minister in Israel's election on Tuesday.
The ballot is Israel's first since Hamas' October 7, 2023, surprise attack that shook the country and plunged the region into turmoil, as Israel went to war on the militant group in Gaza and its allies in Lebanon and Iran.
The October 7 security breach saw Likud's popularity plummet. Opinion polls for months have predicted Netanyahu's coalition of right-wing, far-right and ultra-Orthodox parties losing its majority. But his top rival, centrist Gadi Eisenkot, has no clear path to power either, and the race has become tighter as the election nears.
Dimona, where an Iranian missile wounded dozens in March, has become a political battleground.
"We must have change. Bibi has to go," said Yossi Assayag, 74, who says he has supported Likud most his life. "Bibi has brought disaster to Israel."
LIKUD LOYALISTS
Assayag is part of a cohort of town residents trying to convince their community to vote for Eisenkot's party Yashar, which is neck-and-neck with Likud in the polls.
It's a tough task in Dimona, where half the voters in the previous 2022 election cast a ballot for Likud.
"I will never betray Likud," said Ruti Ohana, a pensioner, who says she has voted Likud ever since immigrating to Israel from North Africa more than 60 years ago. She said Netanyahu was a cut above his rivals, and the blame he receives from detractors for October 7 was unfair.
Right-wing Likud long ago formed a core voter base among Jews of Middle Eastern and North African descent, known as Mizrahis, who felt neglected by the European-influenced centre-left Labor Party that dominated Israel for generations.
Labor has since dwindled to a rump as Israeli politics have shifted rightwards, and there are now around half a dozen other parties courting Likud voters, from the centre to the far right. But the link to the party among its past supporters remains strong.
"Most people here vote for Likud just because that's how they were raised," said Oria Asaf, 25, a past Likud voter now backing Yashar. "The change will come when people start to think about their children's future rather than their parents' past."
BATTLE FOR WAVERING LIKUDNIKS
While Netanyahu has a hard core of supporters that can't be won over, the prize is undecided voters who "understand that we are in a state of crisis" and are open to persuasion, said Michal Elmalem Abu, elected as a member of the city council from Likud and now leading Eisenkot's Dimona campaign.
Some 13% of Israeli voters have yet to decide how they will vote, according to data collected by the Viterbi Family Center for Public Opinion and Policy Research at the Israel Democracy Institute.
Of those who voted for Likud in 2022, just 55% now say they will vote for the party again on Tuesday. Fifteen percent will support parties aligned against Netanyahu, including 8% for Yashar. Another 14% will vote for alternative right-wing parties, and 9% are undecided.
It is in places just like Dimona where Eisenkot stands a chance to bite a chunk out of Likud's base, said Amotz Asa-El, a political scientist at the Hartman Institute.
A child of Moroccan immigrants who rose through the ranks to become military chief of staff, Eisenkot, 66, has a personal story of humble origins from the Mizrahi community that "appeals to a big swath of the Israeli electorate, particularly Likud's traditional electorate", said Asa-El.
In an electoral field crowded with ex-soldiers, his peerless security credentials are an asset. The loss of his son, killed in combat in Gaza in December 2023, resonates with voters.
At a town hall during a visit to Dimona in July, residents said they were excited about the prospect of a leader of Mizrahi descent. Others approached him with hugs and tearful condolences for the loss of his son.
But a week later Netanyahu held his own event, demonstrating his powerful appeal in the hardscrabble Negev, where Likud governments have long boasted of bringing development funds.
"Look around you, look at your community, look at what was here then and what is here now, and ask yourselves which governments invested in this monumental effort. And I do this out of immense love," he said.
Lior Katzav, a Likud former mayor of Kiryat Malachi, another small-town stronghold, said party surveys show voters who had abandoned Likud are returning as the election nears.
But even some who are sympathetic to Netanyahu say it may be time for a change. Israel's youngest prime minister when he was first elected 30 years ago, he has since become its longest-serving, now 77, having governed for 18 years over six terms.
"It's time for him to go," said Dimona software engineer David Iskali. "He's done a lot for Israel but it can't go on. I won't give my vote to someone almost 80 years old." REUTERS

Who Are the Presidents of Bulgaria?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
07:06:35 UTC
16:06:35 KST

Today, Bulgaria is voting for president and vice president. This provides an opportunity to look back at the history of the country’s presidential institution, from Zhelyu Zhelev, the first head of state elected by direct popular vote, to Rumen Radev, who resigned before completing his second term.
Following Radev’s resignation, Iliana Iotova assumed the presidency as the incumbent vice president, without having been directly elected by the public as head of state.
Who have been Bulgaria’s presidents to date, who is eligible to hold the office, and how is the head of state elected?
Zhelyu Zhelev was elected president by the Grand National Assembly on August 1, 1990. In January 1992, he won Bulgaria’s first direct presidential election. He remained in office until 1997, with Blaga Dimitrova serving as his vice president.
Petar Stoyanov won the 1996 presidential election as the candidate of the United Democratic Forces. He took office on January 22, 1997, and served as president until January 2002.
Georgi Parvanov was elected president in 2001 and took office in January 2002. In 2006, he won a second term and remained head of state until January 2012. He was the first Bulgarian president to be re-elected for a second consecutive term through direct elections.
Rosen Plevneliev won the 2011 presidential election alongside vice-presidential candidate Margarita Popova. They took office in January 2012 and remained in their positions until January 2017.
Rumen Radev was elected president in November 2016, with Iliana Iotova as vice president. In 2021, the two won a second term. On January 19, 2026, Radev announced that he was resigning. Three days later, the Constitutional Court established the early termination of his presidential powers. He thus became the first president of Bulgaria to leave office voluntarily before the end of his term.
Iliana Iotova assumed the presidency following the termination of Radev’s powers. Before that, she had served as vice president for two consecutive terms.
How Is the President Elected?
Under the Constitution of the Republic of Bulgaria, the president is elected directly by voters for a five-year term. The election is conducted in accordance with the procedures set out in the Electoral Code.
The president and vice president are elected simultaneously on a joint ticket. This means that voters cast their ballots for a presidential pair rather than electing the two candidates separately.
To win in the first round, a presidential ticket must receive more than half of the valid votes, provided that more than half of the voters registered on the electoral rolls have participated in the election.
If these conditions are not met, a second round is held within seven days. It features the two presidential tickets that received the highest number of votes in the first round. The candidates who receive more votes in the runoff are declared elected.
The Constitution allows the president and vice president to be re-elected to the same offices for only one additional term. Consequently, an individual may serve a maximum of two consecutive terms.
Who Can Become President of Bulgaria?
The eligibility requirements for candidates for head of state are set out in Article 93 of the Constitution.
A person may be elected president if they are a Bulgarian citizen by birth and meet the following conditions:
They must be at least 40 years old.
They must not hold any other citizenship.
They must not have been placed under legal guardianship due to incapacity.
They must not be serving a prison sentence.
They must have resided in Bulgaria during the five years preceding the election.
These requirements apply to presidential candidates. The vice president is elected simultaneously with the president and must also meet the constitutional eligibility criteria for the office.
The Constitution further stipulates that the president and vice president may not serve as members of parliament, engage in other state, public or commercial activities, or participate in the leadership of political parties.
What Are the President’s Powers?
The president is the head of state and represents Bulgaria in international relations. The president is also the supreme commander of the armed forces and exercises powers relating to national defence and security.
The president’s main functions include appointing and dismissing senior military commanders in accordance with the applicable constitutional procedures, conferring senior military ranks, and chairing the Consultative Council for National Security.
The head of state issues decrees within the scope of their constitutional powers, may return legislation to the National Assembly for reconsideration, and participates in the process of forming a government.
Caretaker Government
Following the constitutional amendments, the president may select a candidate for caretaker prime minister from a list of officials specified in the Constitution. These include the Speaker of the National Assembly, the governor or a deputy governor of the Bulgarian National Bank, the chairperson or a deputy chairperson of the National Audit Office, and the ombudsman or a deputy ombudsman.
The caretaker government is appointed by the president on the proposal of the designated caretaker prime minister.
Why Is the Presidential Election Important?
Presidential elections give citizens the opportunity to decide directly who will represent the country over the following five years. The vote determines not only the identity of the head of state but also the vice president, who will work alongside the president throughout the term.
Today, October 25, voters will exercise their right to vote in an election that will shape the next chapter in the development of Bulgaria’s presidential institution.

Feature: A butterfly in Yerevan highlights common ground on biodiversity
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
14:39:27 CST
15:39:27 KST

YEREVAN, Oct. 25 (Xinhua) -- A ribbon blending 23 colors forms a butterfly, with each hue representing one of the 23 targets of the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework (KMGBF), adopted in 2022.
At the ongoing 17th meeting of the Conference of the Parties to the United Nations (UN) Convention on Biological Diversity (COP17) in Yerevan, the emblem appears on conference walls, delegates' lapel pins and the accreditation badges.
Yet the real butterfly is nowhere to be seen.
Polyommatus eriwanensis, a butterfly species endemic to Armenia, produces a single generation each year, with adults flying from mid-June to mid-July before disappearing from the country's limestone grasslands at elevations of 1,200-2,200 meters.
By October, when representatives of the Convention on Biological Diversity's 196 Parties gather in the Armenian capital for COP17, its brief flying season is long over. But the little-known insect has become a fitting symbol for a conference grappling with difficult questions about protecting nature -- who has the resources to do it, how to measure progress, and how to act when so much about nature remains unknown.
Disagreements are part of the negotiations. At the opening plenary, Senegal, speaking for the African Group, called on developed countries to honor their financial commitments, while Jamaica stressed the importance of mobilizing adequate resources.
Fewer than half of the national targets assessed by the parties are on track. Yet the same butterfly appears across delegations, serving as a visual reminder of a shared commitment that transcends national boundaries and needs no negotiation.
Its 23 blended colors represent the KMGBF's 23 targets, which are grouped into three thematic areas: reducing threats to biodiversity, meeting people's needs through sustainable use and benefit-sharing, and providing tools and solutions for implementation.
Its designers also drew on the butterfly's metamorphosis as a symbol of the transformation needed to protect nature.
The butterfly spends only about a month each year as a flying adult. For the rest of its life cycle, it develops through less visible stages as an egg, caterpillar and chrysalis.
Biodiversity diplomacy follows a similar pattern. A COP meeting brings two weeks of speeches, photographs and declarations. The work that determines whether those promises lead to change takes place largely out of the spotlight -- passing laws, allocating budgets, reforming harmful subsidies and enforcing conservation measures.
With four years remaining before the framework's 2030 deadline, governments are conducting the first global review of collective progress, drawing on national reports, targets and indicators to assess what has been achieved and where more action is needed.
Yet this process depends on reliable monitoring data, which remain difficult to obtain. The butterfly illustrates the challenge -- despite its prominence at COP17, scientists still do not know which plant its caterpillars feed on.
Difficult to identify in the wild, the butterfly is also hard to monitor, leaving scientists with limited information about its population trends and the threats it faces.
If tracking a single species presents such challenges, monitoring biodiversity across vast, remote forests, deep oceans and wetlands is an even greater undertaking.
The butterfly also brings to mind the butterfly effect. In 1972, meteorologist Edward Lorenz posed a now-famous question: Could the flap of a butterfly's wings in Brazil set off a tornado in Texas?
His point was that even tiny disturbances in complex systems can change the course of events, sometimes with consequences that are difficult to predict.
Though Lorenz was discussing the atmosphere, not ecosystems, the limits of prediction offer a useful parallel with nature.
Species and habitats are connected in ways scientists do not yet fully understand. For Polyommatus eriwanensis, whose caterpillars' host plant remains unknown, what consequences might follow if the butterfly disappears from Armenia's limestone grasslands?
There may be no reliable way to know in advance.
That uncertainty is not a reason to delay conservation. Rather, it strengthens the case for protecting ecosystems before the damage becomes irreversible.
As Lorenz noted, if the flap of a butterfly's wings can help trigger a tornado, it can just as well help prevent one.
Perhaps that offers another way to understand the butterfly at COP17: The delegates cannot know precisely what consequences their decisions will have for nature in the years ahead, but they can still take action to reduce further biodiversity loss. ■

This mysterious mushroom makes people see hundreds of tiny humans
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
06:36:10 UTC
15:36:10 KST

This mysterious mushroom makes people see hundreds of tiny humans
- Date:
- October 25, 2026
- Source:
- University of Utah
- Summary:
- For nearly a century, people in distant parts of the world have reported a bizarre experience after eating certain wild mushrooms: seeing dozens or even hundreds of tiny, colorful humans moving through the real world. Now, scientists have identified a mushroom species, Lanmaoa asiatica, responsible for these extraordinary hallucinations in China and the Philippines.
- Share:
People living thousands of miles apart have reported an extraordinarily strange experience after eating certain wild mushrooms. They begin seeing tiny human figures that appear to move through the real world, walking around objects, climbing over surfaces, and interacting with their surroundings.
These visions are known as Lilliputian hallucinations, named after the miniature inhabitants of "Gulliver's Travels," who stand just 6 inches tall. For decades, researchers suspected that cultural beliefs and folklore might explain why people in different regions described such similar experiences.
Now, a new study provides evidence that the phenomenon has a biological explanation.
Researchers at the University of Utah (U) used DNA sequencing to identify Lanmaoa asiatica as the mushroom responsible for these unusual hallucinations in Southwest China and the northern Philippines. Surprisingly, their investigation found no evidence of any known psychoactive mushroom compounds, including psilocybin.
The findings suggest that the mushroom may produce an entirely unfamiliar hallucinogenic substance. Identifying that chemical could help scientists better understand neurological disorders, unusual visual experiences, and the processes through which the brain creates our perception of reality.
The research was conducted by Colin Domnauer, a doctoral student at the U, and Bryn Dentinger, a mycologist affiliated with the university and the Natural History Museum of Utah. Their findings were published in the journal Mycologia.
In an interview with @theU, Domnauer explained how researchers traced the mushroom's identity, what makes its effects so unusual, and why the discovery could have implications far beyond the study of fungi.
A Century-Old Mystery of Tiny Human Hallucinations
The scientific mystery dates back to 1934, when Western researchers learned that people in Papua New Guinea sometimes experienced vivid visions of miniature humans after eating wild mushrooms. The bizarre effect became known as "mushroom madness."
During the 1950s and 1960s, anthropologists and mushroom specialists traveled to Papua New Guinea to investigate. Their work pointed toward several possible species belonging to the Boletaceae (bolete) family.
However, chemical testing failed to reveal any substances that could explain the hallucinations. Samples were even examined by Albert Hofmann, the scientist who first isolated psilocybin and discovered LSD. He, too, was unable to identify an active ingredient.
With no chemical explanation available, some researchers began questioning whether the mushrooms were responsible at all. They suggested that the visions might instead arise from cultural expectations or traditional beliefs. By the end of the 1960s, scientific investigation of the phenomenon had largely stopped.
The mystery resurfaced during the 1990s, when people in Yunnan, Southwest China, reported similar hallucinations after eating bolete mushrooms. Although the precise species remained uncertain, researchers suspected a recently described mushroom called Lanmaoa asiatica.
Scientists Identify the Mushroom Behind the Strange Visions
Another important clue appeared in 2024, when Domnauer learned of comparable experiences among an Indigenous community in the remote Northern Cordillera region of the Philippines.
Community members described a wild edible mushroom called "Sedesdem" that could sometimes cause people to see miniature human figures. Similar mushrooms were known locally as "Nonda" in Papua New Guinea and "Jian shou qing" in Yunnan.
These mushrooms have an important place in local food traditions, but consuming them without thoroughly cooking them can trigger the unusual hallucinations.
The Philippine accounts represented a third independent report of wild mushrooms causing remarkably similar visions of tiny people.
To investigate, Domnauer traveled to Yunnan and the Philippines, interviewed local residents, and collected specimens of L. asiatica along with other mushrooms belonging to the Lanmaoa genus.
The fieldwork included the first scientific survey of fungi in the northern Philippines. Researchers then analyzed DNA from the collected mushrooms to establish their identities and evolutionary relationships.
The results revealed that the mushrooms called Jian shou qing in China and Sedesdem in the Philippines were both L. asiatica.
This was an unexpected finding because scientists had previously believed the species occurred only in China.
Dentinger also visited Papua New Guinea in hopes of collecting specimens from the location where the mystery originally began. Unfortunately, unusually dry weather made it impossible to obtain samples for genetic comparison.
Although the Papua New Guinea mushroom remains unverified, the evidence from China and the Philippines provides a compelling connection. Three geographically separated cultures have described the same highly specific hallucinations, and DNA testing has linked two of those cases to a single mushroom species.
That consistency strongly suggests a shared chemical and neurological explanation rather than unrelated cultural influences.
Hallucinations of Tiny Humans That Seem Remarkably Real
What makes these hallucinations especially unusual is their striking similarity across different accounts.
People typically describe seeing dozens or even hundreds of miniature figures, generally measuring between 3 and 30 centimeters tall. The figures appear with extraordinary clarity, often seeming as solid and convincing as actual people.
According to Domnauer, approximately 90% of those experiencing the visions describe figures resembling elves, clowns, or other fairy-like characters, often wearing brightly colored clothing.
Even more surprising is the way these imaginary figures seem to behave.
Rather than floating through walls or ignoring their surroundings, they appear to follow familiar physical rules. They walk around obstacles, move across ordinary objects, and sometimes tumble from the edges of tables.
Domnauer recalled one particularly unusual account involving someone eating soup. The person reported seeing tiny humans leap from a spoon into the bowl, where they began swimming. When the person took another spoonful, the miniature figures reportedly remained visible inside their mouth.
Such detailed interactions distinguish these visions from many other forms of drug-induced hallucination.
A Mysterious Psychedelic Compound Unlike Any Known Drug
Scientists also investigated whether L. asiatica contains any of the chemicals already known to cause psychedelic experiences.
Using both chemical testing and genetic analysis, the researchers searched for established psychoactive compounds found in other mushroom species.
They found no trace of them.
The absence of familiar hallucinogens was particularly intriguing because the mushroom's effects differ so dramatically from those associated with known psychedelic drugs.
Researchers now suspect that L. asiatica produces an unidentified psychoactive substance responsible for the tiny human hallucinations.
The compound has not yet been isolated or chemically identified, so its exact nature and mechanism remain unknown.
Discovering it could open an entirely new avenue of research into how certain chemicals alter visual perception.
What the Mushroom Could Reveal About the Human Brain
Although L. asiatica provides an unusually consistent trigger for Lilliputian hallucinations, the phenomenon is not limited to mushroom consumption.
Stories involving miniature humanlike beings appear throughout folklore around the world. Similar hallucinations have also been documented in people experiencing alcohol withdrawal, dementia, macular degeneration, and other neurological conditions.
These connections suggest that the visions may arise from a fundamental feature of the way the human brain processes visual information.
However, scientists still do not fully understand the neurological mechanisms responsible for these experiences or how best to treat them when they occur in medical settings.
This is where the mysterious mushroom could become especially valuable.
Unlike the neurological and medical conditions in which Lilliputian hallucinations occur relatively rarely, L. asiatica can produce the phenomenon in a more consistent and recognizable way.
If researchers can isolate the chemical responsible, they may gain a useful tool for investigating the brain circuits and processes that create these unusually detailed visual experiences.
Such research could eventually improve scientific understanding of hallucinations associated with neurological diseases.
The research team's next major objective is to isolate and identify the suspected psychedelic compound.
DNA Sequencing Reveals Four Previously Unknown Mushroom Species
The investigation also produced important discoveries about fungal biodiversity.
Rather than studying L. asiatica alone, Domnauer and Dentinger conducted the first comprehensive genomic analysis of the Lanmaoa genus.
They examined 53 mushroom specimens collected from natural habitats and preserved in fungarium collections around the world.
Genetic sequencing revealed 17 species within the group, including four species previously unknown to science.
Remarkably, two of those newly identified species had already been preserved in existing collections in the United States. Their distinct identities had gone unrecognized until researchers examined their DNA.
The analysis also indicated that L. asiatica is the only species in the genus currently known to produce psychoactive effects.
Scientists are now working to reconstruct the group's evolutionary history. They hope to determine how the unusual chemical trait developed and whether closely related mushrooms might produce comparable substances.
The findings also demonstrate the scientific value of museum collections. Specimens preserved for years can contain biological discoveries that become apparent only when newer analytical techniques are applied.
For Domnauer, the hidden diversity found in these collections is a reminder that many species and potentially important biological characteristics remain undiscovered, even among organisms that scientists have already collected.
Exploring Fungi Could Lead to New Medicines and Discoveries
The broader implications extend well beyond unusual hallucinations.
Fungi remain one of the least thoroughly explored groups of organisms, and researchers believe their chemical diversity could provide valuable clues about biology, medicine, and the nervous system.
One of the most famous examples is penicillin, the antibiotic originally obtained from a fungus that transformed the treatment of bacterial infections and became one of the most consequential medical discoveries of the last century.
Scientists hope continued exploration of fungal biodiversity could reveal other medically useful compounds and previously unknown biological processes.
The mysterious effects of L. asiatica illustrate just how much remains to be learned about the fungal kingdom. A mushroom long consumed by communities in Asia may contain a substance capable of revealing new information about the human brain and how it creates conscious experience.
The research received funding from the National Science Foundation (award #DEB-2114785).

The U.K. government has outlined plans to expand funding for artificial intelligence safety amid growing concerns over the cyber risks posed by the increasingly advanced technology.
"The economic opportunities from AI will only be realised if our critical infrastructure, public services and businesses are resilient to cyber, biological and emerging AI-enabled threats," the government said in a statement on Oct. 23 ahead of its annual budget update on Oct. 28.

"As AI becomes more powerful, Britain must have the capabilities to protect its people and shape its own future," said AI minister Kanishka Narayan.
"That means staying ahead of emerging threats, from cyberattacks to biological risks, while building more of the critical technology our security depends on," he added.
The plans include investment in AI tools to identify cyber vulnerabilities across critical infrastructure.

Fed expected to hold rates steady days ahead of US midterms
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
06:23:00 UTC
15:23:00 KST

AP Photo
The U.S. Federal Reserve appears set to hold interest rates steady at its meeting next week, analysts say, despite stubbornly high inflation and with markets pricing in at least one rate hike before year-end.
The central bank's Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) will meet over two days, announcing its decision on Oct. 28.
The Fed has missed its long-term 2 percent target for inflation for more than five years, and at its last meeting in September the FOMC voted to raise the key federal funds rate for the first time in three years, lifting the target range to 3.75 percent to 4 percent.
The Fed's meeting comes days ahead of key midterm elections in the United States on Nov. 3, with the Democratic Party seeking to wrest control of both houses of Congress from U.S. President Donald Trump's Republicans.
Trump frequently berated and criticized Fed Chair Kevin Warsh's predecessor Jerome Powell over interest rates, which he deems to be too high, but has so far refrained from targeting the man he appointed to replace him over the issue.
The Fed's preferred gauge for inflation, the Personal Consumption Expenditures (PCE) price index, hit a pandemic-era peak of 7.2 percent in 2022, before a series of interest-rate hikes tamed it to around 2.2 percent by late 2024.
Trump's economic policies, including his upending of the global trade order using tariffs and his war on Iran, fueled it once more, and it hit a three-year high of 3.9 percent in May.
Since the United States and Israel attacked Iran in late February, global energy prices have skyrocketed, with Tehran's retaliatory actions sharply curtailing oil and gas supplies through the Gulf.
Higher energy prices have begun to cascade through into other goods and services, fuelling inflation in the United States, with prices a key issue for voters as they head to the polls.
Loretta Mester, former regional head of the Cleveland Fed, told AFP that the timing of the meeting just days ahead of the election would not be a factor for policymakers.
"The Fed doesn't take into account any kind of political issues in that FOMC room," she said. "It really is based on the economics."
Mester argued that the fundamentals call for continuing to raise interest rates.
"The data that's come in continue to show a stable labor market and continue to show inflation above target," she said, adding that there was no evidence that it was on a path downwards towards the target.
"The economics would suggest then you need to continue raising rates."
Still, she thought that most policymakers seemed keen to avoid moving too quickly, and may hold rates at this meeting, waiting to tighten the screws until the following meeting in early December.
Wendy Edelberg, a senior fellow at the Brookings Institution, believes central bankers would rather not put themselves in the middle of the political debate ahead of the midterms.
"It's unhelpful for everyone if the Fed gets wrapped up in all the political discourse right before an election," she told AFP.
Edelberg said that "there wouldn't be huge economic implications" if policymakers raised rates in December as opposed to October.
She saw such a decision less as a "nod to Trump", who has aggressively demanded lower rates to spur economic activity, and more a way to avoid being the potential target of political barbs.
Since returning to power last year, the U.S. president has waged an unprecedented assault on the Fed's independence, launching a criminal probe against Powell and attempting to unseat Fed Governor Lisa Cook.
The probe against Powell was dropped to smooth the way for Warsh's Senate confirmation, but the battle to fire Cook continues despite a Supreme Court decision nullifying an earlier attempt to do so.
Last week, Cook declined to attend a hearing in the White House's probe into mortgage fraud allegations, which she denies.

Opposition from local communities

Beijing has said its project will have no "negative impact" downstream.
China claims Arunachal Pradesh as part of southern Tibet. India says the state is an integral part of its territory.
India's proposed dam, which would be by far its largest hydropower project, has drawn fierce opposition from local communities who fear the loss of their homes and land.
The project underscores tensions between the two most populous countries, which share a disputed Himalayan border patrolled by tens of thousands of troops.

1 million Hong Kong employees to get ‘full portability’ of MPF funds in December
Roll-out from December 21 allows eligible members to transfer both employer and employee contributions to preferred providers once a year
About 1 million employees in Hong Kong will be allowed to move their entire Mandatory Provident Fund (MPF) savings to a different provider once a year, starting December 21.
The Mandatory Provident Fund Schemes Authority, which regulates the mandatory pension plans, said on Sunday that the “full portability” arrangement would be carried out in two phases to ensure a smooth implementation.
In a blog post, authority chairwoman Ayesha Macpherson Lau said the arrangement would allow eligible members to transfer both the employer and employee contribution portions to their preferred MPF scheme once per calendar year.

Remember to pay attention to your attention. Allow it to be open and free, so that your awareness will expand, your suffering will shrink, and your joy will grow. Open it by letting go of anything that could restrict it from going where it needs to go. Free it by unshackling it from control and by allowing it to move when it needs to move.
Notice your attachments to your intentions — to your strongest desires, aversions, and beliefs. Notice how your attention returns to these same intentions over and over again. Notice also the kinds of suffering that you experience — persistent feelings of regret, stress, anxiety, frustration, anger, despair, grief, and many more.
Recognize the connection between your suffering and your attachments, and how the former arises when your attention is controlled by the latter. Set your attention free from all of the thoughts, feelings, memories, and imaginings that arise in you again and again. Notice how often your attention settles on thoughts about your intentions and how difficult it can be to set it free again.

What’s next for Hong Kong developers in mainland China?
The city’s developers are turning to other sources of income amid a prolonged housing downturn on the mainland
Hong Kong’s major property developers are shifting investment in mainland China from residential projects to commercial assets, including hospitality, as weak home sales and fewer attractive investment opportunities prompt them to focus on existing properties, recurring income and debt reduction.
“In recent years, after we recycled the capital from our projects, we haven’t really found many good opportunities on the mainland,” Stephen Ng, chairman and managing director of Wharf Holdings, said at its interim results press conference in August.
Wharf’s experience reflects a broader change in how Hong Kong developers are approaching assets in the world’s second-largest economy.

Collectible furniture meets cultural critique at Dutch Design Week’s Table of Power
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
06:00:00 UTC
15:00:00 KST

Collectible furniture meets cultural critique at Dutch Design Week’s Table of Power
Show Not Show has put a twist on a classic project documenting the echelons of power with an exhibition of the design collective’s furniture at Dutch Design Week.
Held at the Kruisruimte exhibition space in Eindhoven, The Table of Power exhibition takes inspiration from Jacqueline Hassink’s 1990s photo series of the same name.
This saw the photographer document the boardrooms of Fortune 500 companies, empty of people.
As in those photographs, The Table of Power has a long table at its centre as a symbol of institutional authority.
In this case, the table seems to stretch eternally into the horizon, thanks to the mirror placed at the far end.
Designed especially for the exhibition by collective members Frank Penders and Luuk van Laarhoven, the table is made from sheet metal, cut and bent into a brutalist form, with brushed textures and chromatic gradients adding allure.
Around it, collectible furniture, lighting and textile pieces from fellow members Lucas Zito, Marc Meeuwissen, Mokko and Studio Fabius Clovis as well as guest exhibitors Aleksandra Adamchyk, Kilian Vos and Pablo Octavio fill the room with a mix of raw wood, glossy lacquer, sculptural metal and translucent glowing bioplastic.
The idea for the exhibition came after Show Not Show were invited to host Dutch Design Week’s official press dinner.
“Our exhibition space isn’t that big,” said Penders. “So we decided to do something quite simple: instead of fitting a dinner into our exhibition, we made the dinner the starting point for the exhibition.”
In Show Not Show’s vision, the press represents a site of power in the design industry, influencing what gets seen, discussed and remembered, and their presence completes the exhibition’s concept.
Guests at the dinner were encouraged to get up from the table from time to time to “share the power”, but Dezeen observed that few journalists ever got up.
Penders told Dezeen that The Table of Power continues Show Not Show’s practice of using exhibitions to explore aspects of the design world that are not commonly seen.
“Each exhibition offers a glimpse into our world as designers, revealing something that visitors might not normally see or consider,” Penders told Dezeen. “In 2024, we showed our experiments and prototypes. In 2025, we focused on the ideas and concepts behind our work.”
“This year, the subject is visibility. Being seen, becoming known and finding recognition for what you create. It is about the relationship between designers, their work and the media that bring it to a wider audience.”
In addition to the table, Octavio’s curtain-like brushed aluminium room dividers are given a symbolic role to play in the exhibition. Their height allows those sitting down greater oversight of the room than their standing peers, adding to the sense of power imbalance.
Key pieces in the exhibition include a new series of angular wooden stools called Barricada, designed by Meewissen to match the dining table seating. Like all of his works, they are made with just one tool and one material.
There is also characterful plywood furniture by Studio Fabius Clovis, its uneven surface highlighted with high-gloss lacquer, and totemic pendant lights by Lucas Zito, 3D printed from bioplastic and playing with the spatial effects of unexpected scale.
Guest exhibitors Adamchyk, Vos and Octavio continue the elemental mood, bringing their sculptural zigzagging Waveform drawer, geological Future Fossils rugs and stone-like but squishy Lapis lounge chair respectively.
Show Not Show launched in 2024 and has exhibited at the Kruisruimte each year since. It has also taken its shows abroad with presentations at the Design Biennale Rotterdam, Collectible Brussels and Milan design week.
Elsewhere at Dutch Design Week, Boris Acket and Maison the Faux have staged the moody and maximalist installation Everything Moist Seems Alive at the MU Hybrid Art House, complete with performances from the Dutch National Opera and Ballet.
Dutch Design Week 2026 takes place from 17 to 25 October 2026 at various locations across Eindhoven, the Netherlands. See Dezeen Events Guide for more architecture and design events around the world.
Photography by Show Not Show

DPP urges vigilance against Chinese election meddling
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
05:57:41 UTC
14:57:41 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — The DPP China Affairs Department warned that the rise of Puma Shen’s (沈伯洋) mayoral campaign has drawn significant attention from China, which it warned is covertly and overtly interfering with Taiwan’s elections.
The DPP said the public must be particularly vigilant against two types of election interference, including disinformation and political intimidation, according to a party Facebook post.
Disinformation may range from fake opinion polls with unknown sources and audio or video clips taken out of context to fabricated scandals, romantic rumors, and false deepfake reports of candidates withdrawing from races, the DPP said. Such content may be disseminated en masse shortly before voting, when there is little time to verify its accuracy. The more sensational a claim is, and the more urgently it urges people to “share immediately,” the more important it is to pause and check the facts first, the party said.
Political intimidation includes threats, surveillance, and attacks targeting candidates, their relatives, and their supporters, the DPP said. These attacks can restrict people’s ability to participate freely in politics, it added.
The party said Taiwan's law enforcement should investigate the masterminds and funding sources behind such cases. The public must be aware of attempts to incite retaliation using unverified information, which could further escalate tensions, it said.
The DPP stressed that Beijing accuses Taiwan of democratic disorder while simultaneously manipulating information and applying political pressure. Its aim is to undermine mutual trust within society and weaken public confidence in the democratic system, the party said.
Elections must be decided by the Taiwanese alone, the DPP said, adding that Beijing must not be allowed to influence their choices through disinformation and intimidation.

Prices Keep Bulgaria’s Public Tension High Despite Gradual Decline
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
05:57:00 UTC
14:57:00 KST

Bulgaria’s Public Tension Index edged down to 6.10 points in the third quarter of 2026 from 6.22 in the previous quarter, continuing its decline at a slower pace, the Centre for Analysis and Crisis Communications reported.
Despite the improvement, the index remained in the high-risk category, reflecting tensions and risks that are difficult to manage.
Compiled quarterly by the Centre for Analysis and Crisis Communications and sociological agency Myara, with support from the Sensika monitoring platform, the index tracks public calm and anxiety and assesses their potential impact on political and economic developments.
The scale runs from zero to 10. Scores below 4 indicate low tension and fully manageable risks, while readings from 4 to 5.99 represent moderate tension and manageable risks. Values between 6 and 7.99 fall into the high-tension category, with risks that are difficult to manage, while scores of 8 or higher signal very high tension and an almost unmanageable situation.
Alexander Hristov, chairman of the Centre for Analysis and Crisis Communications, said the easing of tension was continuing but had slowed, with prices and perceptions of the country’s overall economic situation keeping the index elevated.
He said the impact of the presidential election campaign and developments elsewhere in Europe on public anxiety remained unclear. Pointing to protests in several Western countries, Hristov warned that Bulgaria could also see what he called an “import of tension.”
Myara founder Parvan Simeonov said recent attacks in the Black Sea, the election campaign and its outcome could also affect public sentiment, but their impact would become measurable only in the next quarter.
The Centre said the latest data had been collected before Thursday’s incident involving a National Service for Protection officer and journalist Sonia Koltuklieva. Any effect of that incident would therefore appear in later measurements.
The report found that expectations for the government to provide quick solutions remained high, while indicators linked to the wider social and economic environment had changed little, reflecting their slower rate of change.
Among crimes and other incidents, researchers singled out a murder in Plovdiv as having a particularly strong effect on public sentiment. Otherwise, the period was relatively calm in terms of crime and incidents.
Public confidence in institutions showed signs of stabilizing, although attitudes toward Parliament remained as critical as they traditionally are in Bulgaria.
Current prices, especially expectations about how prices will develop in the future, continued to be among the main drivers of public tension.
For the first time since the index was launched, positive and neutral media coverage exceeded negative reporting, which researchers viewed as an indication of improving public sentiment. Negative material on social media, however, remained widespread.
Sensika continuously monitors Bulgarian news outlets and social media channels to identify signs of public dissatisfaction, protest activity and shifts in sentiment.
The index had reached 6.88 in the first quarter of 2026, slightly above the 6.76 recorded in the preceding quarter. It has fallen for two consecutive quarters since then but remains in the high-tension category.

Houthi militia targets Riyadh airport, Saudi-led coalition strikes Sanaa missile launchers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
05:31:49 UTC
14:31:49 KST

Yemen’s Houthi militia said they targeted Riyadh airport and pumping stations along Saudi Arabia’s East-West oil pipeline, while the Saudi-led coalition said it destroyed two Houthi militia ballistic missile launchers in Sanaa.
Houthi militia spokesman Yahya Saree said on X that the group targeted the airport with a ballistic missile. Saree also said the Houthi militia carried out drone attacks on crude oil pumping stations along the East-West Pipeline.
Saudi Arabia’s Civil Defence Directorate earlier announced that its early warning system had issued a danger alert for Riyadh. Major General Turki al-Maliki, spokesman for the Saudi-led coalition, said a Houthi militia ballistic missile targeting the capital had been intercepted.
The East-West Pipeline is one of Saudi Arabia’s most important crude oil transportation routes. Operated by state-owned oil giant Saudi Aramco, it stretches approximately 1,200 kilometres (745 miles) from the Abqaiq area in eastern Saudi Arabia to Yanbu on the Red Sea coast.
The pipeline transports crude oil from production and processing facilities in the east to refineries and export terminals along the Red Sea, providing an overland alternative to maritime shipments through the Strait of Hormuz.
The Saudi-led coalition has supported Yemen’s internationally recognised government since March 2015. Clashes between government forces and the Houthi militia have intensified in recent months. The group has targeted Saudi Arabia with ballistic missiles and drones, accusing the kingdom of responsibility for attacks against it.
Striking missile launchers
Meanwhile, the Saudi-led coalition fighting in Yemen launched strikes on the capital, Sanaa, early on Monday, claiming to have destroyed two Houthi militia ballistic missile launchers.
Al-Maliki said one of the launchers had been used in a Houthi militia attack on Riyadh in recent hours. In a post on X, he said the coalition was continuing operations to dismantle the group’s ballistic missile network.
The Yemeni army said on Sunday that its forces had “neutralised” around 218 Houthi militias and field commanders in 753 operations over the previous 24 hours, destroying or damaging 78 military vehicles and weapons.
The army said the operations, part of Operation ‘Dawn of Yemen’, targeted forward command centres, fortifications, firing positions, troop concentrations, reinforcements and supply vehicles. It added that the attacks disrupted Houthi militia reinforcements heading to front lines and supported raids and ground assaults by government forces.
The army did not specify how many of those it said had been “neutralised” were killed or wounded. The Houthi militias did not immediately comment.
Yemen has been engulfed in conflict since the Houthi militias seized Sanaa and several provinces in 2014, prompting a Saudi-led coalition to intervene the following year in support of the internationally recognised government.
The Houthis control much of northern and western Yemen, including Sanaa, while the government and allied forces retain Aden and substantial areas of southern and eastern Yemen. Renewed fighting has shifted front lines, particularly along the Red Sea coast, and control of some areas remains contested.

King Abdullah II bin al Hussein, who met with victims after the attack, said during a National Security Council meeting on Saturday that "the security and safety of Jordanians are a red line", adding that "the hand of justice will reach every terrorist".
He said on Friday that the shooting would be met with the "harshest retaliation" possible.
Prime Minister Jafar Hassan ordered a three-day period of national mourning from Friday, with flags to be flown at half-mast over government and public institutions.
On Sunday, eight of the nine victims were laid to rest next to the church, in a funeral that drew a huge crowd.
Their flag-draped coffins were carried through the gathered masses, which included numerous religious figures and a large security presence, AFP images showed.

Taiwan Railway bento sales hit record NT$876 million in 2025
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
05:43:24 UTC
14:43:24 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Taiwan Railway Corp. generated a record NT$876 million (US$26.89 million) in bento sales revenue in 2025, up 9.07% from a year earlier.
TR sold an average of about 25,800 bentos a day last year, although total sales volume remained below the record of 10.54 million set in 2019, per CNA.
Pork chop bentos, a longtime staple dating back to the railway’s early meal offerings, remained the clear favorite. They accounted for 7.18 million sales, far ahead of chicken leg bentos at 560,000 and the “Kaohsiung Double Happiness Bento” at 260,000.
Taipei Main Station led sales with 2.65 million bentos sold in 2025, followed by Xinzuoying Station with 800,000 and Banqiao Station with 680,000.
TR’s bento production is handled by six catering units in Taipei, Qidu, Taichung, Kaohsiung, Hualien, and Taitung. The Taipei unit is the largest, producing 3.5 million bentos last year.
TR said it was cautiously optimistic about sales this year and plans to maintain food quality while introducing special bentos featuring holiday themes and local ingredients. Its bento business began in 1949 and has since expanded to include options such as braised pork and fish.

Newsletters & Email Marketing Manager

Today, the team consists of over 90 people, mostly based in Kyiv. Publishing in English, we serve as Ukraine's voice in the world and the world's window into Ukraine.
The Role
We are seeking an experienced and strategic Newsletters & Email Marketing Manager to join our growing Marketing team. In this role, you will own the growth and performance of our editorial newsletters and email marketing, from growing our contactable base to designing new formats, automated journeys, and experiments that turn readers into engaged subscribers and members. You will work closely with the editorial, reader revenue, audience, and product teams, and report to the Head of Marketing.
The ideal candidate combines a product mindset with hands-on email marketing expertise, is comfortable with data and A/B testing, and understands how newsletters can serve both great journalism and sustainable reader revenue. Within your first months, you will audit our newsletters and emails, establish baseline KPIs, and present a six-month growth roadmap to leadership.

- Support the launch of new editorial newsletter products with clear target metrics.
- Work with the editorial team to ensure newsletters stay aligned with our journalism and editorial standards.
Audience Growth:
- Own organic subscriber growth and the overall growth of our newsletters.
- Own and grow the email marketing contactable base.
- Audit and optimize sign-up and conversion paths across the website in collaboration with the Audience and Product teams.
- Plan and run product, marketing, and communications initiatives to grow the contactable base, including cross-channel campaigns to extend reach.
Reader Revenue & Experimentation:
- Drive reader revenue growth from editorial newsletters and email marketing through A/B testing and new initiatives, in collaboration with the Reader Revenue team.
- Build and run an A/B testing pipeline: define KPIs, run tests, and report on impact to retention, engagement, and sign-up rates.

Strategy & Collaboration:

- Mentor and support team members involved in newsletter and campaign execution to ensure operational stability.

Experience & Technical Skills:
- 3+ years of experience in newsletter, email marketing, or CRM roles, ideally in digital media, publishing, or a subscription business.
- Proven track record of growing an email subscriber base and improving engagement and conversion metrics.
- Hands-on experience with email service providers (e.g., Mailchimp or similar), including automation, segmentation, and list hygiene.
- Strong experience designing and analyzing A/B tests, with confidence in setting KPIs and reporting on results.

Soft Skills:

Parents urged to check children’s electric scooters after illegal riding cases
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
05:27:03 UTC
14:27:03 KST

Denmark’s power grid operator will answer hundreds of connection requests in November while big data centers face long delays.
Energinet, the Danish state-owned electricity transmission company, has now mapped out the capacity needs on the country’s strained electricity grid, the company said in a press release on Wednesday.
With this overview finished, the company will be able to answer applications from several hundred electricity consumers and power producers in November about whether they can connect to the grid.
“In a time of sharply rising demand for electricity, we unfortunately cannot give connection to everyone at the pace they desire,” said Soren Dupont Kristensen, the acting chief executive officer of Energinet.
“But there is room in the transmission grid to cover the electricity needs of ordinary households, smaller businesses, and critical societal functions such as healthcare, defense, and emergency preparedness, both now and in the years to come,” Kristensen said.
Customers will be sorted into four priority categories that were recently passed by a broad political majority as part of an emergency plan for the power network.
Projects placed in Category 1 and Category 2 will get their answers first. These two groups include critical public services, as well as green transition and electrification projects.
Category 3 includes energy storage systems, such as large battery facilities. Category 4 covers major electricity users, including data centers.
“We do not have all the results in place, but it looks difficult to give full grid access to projects in categories 3 and 4,” Kristensen said in Wednesday’s statement.
The political emergency plan was designed to let Energinet and local electricity companies choose who gets hooked up to the power lines. Under this plan, large data centers are pushed to the back of the line because the grid does not have room for huge new projects.
Energinet has faced heavy criticism for expanding the Danish electricity network too slowly. This criticism has come from several groups, including Rigsrevisionen, the National Audit Office of Denmark.
In March, the state company stopped connecting new projects. At that time, Energinet announced that no new connection contracts would be signed until the autumn.
In May, the company stated that very large connection projects could face waiting times of five to ten years. At that point, Energinet also admitted that demand for power had grown at an unexpectedly rapid speed.
Several business groups say it is good news that applicants will soon get answers, but they stress that Denmark still has a real shortage of space on its power grid.
This warning came from DI, Dansk Industri, the Confederation of Danish Industry, which is the main employers’ and business association in Denmark; Dansk Erhverv, the Danish Chamber of Commerce, an employers’ organization representing businesses; and Green Power Denmark, the business and trade group for the green energy sector.
Ulrich Bang, the deputy director for climate, energy, environment, and building at Dansk Erhverv, said the likely lack of space for Category 3 and Category 4 projects shows how serious the situation is.
“Denmark cannot build the industries, business community, and jobs of the future in a waiting room,” Bang said.
“Therefore, action must be taken now, and we look forward to dialogue with authorities and grid companies on how room can be made for more on the electricity grid in the very short term,” Bang said.

How Material Choices Shape Contemporary Additions to Historic Buildings
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
01:30:00 UTC
10:30:00 KST

Adding new floors on top of a historic building presents a challenge beyond accommodating additional space: how can a contemporary intervention respond to the character of an existing structure? Material selection plays an important role in establishing a relationship between different construction periods, whether the aim is to complement the existing building or create a more distinct architectural expression. The LH Residence in Varna, Bulgaria, designed by STARH, offers an example of how fiber cement can help relate a contemporary addition to a historic building.
As a composite material made from cement, water, reinforcing fibers, and other additives, fiber cement combines relative lightness with strength and durability. Its range of colors, textures, panel dimensions, and installation methods gives architects different options for designing contemporary building envelopes that respond to their historic context. Materials such as Swisspearl's fiber cement panels offer variations in surface finish that can support this approach.
Understanding Fiber Cement
For centuries, clay slates and roof tiles were among the most common roofing materials across much of Europe. The Industrial Revolution brought changes to their production and introduced new alternatives, including cement-based roofing products. As production processes were refined toward the end of the 19th century, cement sheets became more widely available. Their relatively low cost, water and frost resistance, and suitability for shallow roof pitches contributed to their popularity.
A further development came with the introduction of fibers into cement, improving properties such as bending strength and fire resistance. In the late 19th century, Austrian industrialist Ludwig Hatschek developed and patented a process for manufacturing thin fiber-reinforced cement sheets. Marketed as Eternit, the material became widely used for roofing as production methods improved and sheets became more readily available. Since then, fiber cement has also been adapted for applications such as facade cladding and interior finishes.
As facade cladding, fiber cement can be installed as part of a rear-ventilated system. In this arrangement, panels are attached to a supporting substructure, leaving a cavity between the cladding and the wall behind it. The panels form an outer layer that screens most rainwater, while the ventilated cavity helps moisture that enters the space to evaporate. These technical characteristics, combined with the material's range of finishes, make fiber cement suitable for both new construction and the renovation of existing buildings.
LH Residence: Integrating Contemporary Architecture in Varna
Located in Varna's historic center, LH Residence retains a two-story structure dating from 1923 and integrates it into a new five-story composition. The original facade features limestone ornamentation and sculptural details, including figures of two children above the corner pediment, created by local artist Kiril Shivarov. For the new facade, STARH designed a minimal grid and set the cladding slightly back from the original facade, allowing the addition to relate to the existing architecture without dominating it. The choice of material was closely tied to the architects' approach to the existing facade. As STARH founder Svetoslav Stanislavov explains:
 From the very beginning, we had a clear vision of the look and finish we wanted to achieve, harmonizing with the original plaster facade.
The suspended cladding system uses two Swisspearl finishes on the new facades: Carat Ivory 8090 and Gravial Ivory 3090. The roof surfaces facing the streets are clad in Nobilis panels in custom colors, selected to match the light tone of the original plastered facade. Treating the roof as a visible part of the composition extends the material approach beyond the vertical facades. The two facade finishes introduce variation within the restrained ivory palette. Swisspearl Carat has a smooth, translucent, lightly pigmented surface, while Gravial features a linearly milled texture that creates patterns of light and shadow as viewing angles and lighting conditions change. Together, they add surface variation without relying on strong color contrast. Large windows wrapping around the building's corner further distinguish the new floors from the ornamented historic structure. As Stanislavov describes:
 We view LH as a complete organism without a defined beginning or end, seamlessly integrating elements from two different time periods into a unified structure.
Although the existing building did not have formal protected-monument status, it was recognized for its importance to the surrounding architectural ensemble. The original structure and decorative facade were preserved, with degraded or missing elements reconstructed and the facade finished in smooth plaster with a natural white tone. Retaining the existing building also avoided demolishing its original structure, illustrating how adaptive reuse can preserve existing building fabric while accommodating additional space. STARH reorganized the interior layout and program and added three additional floors to accommodate residential spaces. The ground floor includes a public space and café, connecting the building to street-level activity.
Contemporary additions to historic buildings can take different approaches to the relationship between old and new. A design may follow the existing building's proportions, colors, and materials to create a more discreet addition, or reinterpret elements such as facade rhythms and window proportions without replicating historic details. A more contrasting intervention may use distinct materials, geometries, or colors to make the difference between construction periods explicit. The appropriate approach depends on the existing building's character, its surroundings, and the role of the new intervention. At LH Residence, STARH uses fiber cement to connect the new floors to the original building while keeping its ornamental facade intact.

====================================================================================================

Indonesia Seizes More Than 2 Tons of Narcotics in Major Anti-drug Operations
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
00:58:00 UTC
09:58:00 KST

Indonesian authorities have made two major drug busts in Sumatra that led to the seizure of more than 2 tons of ketamine and methamphetamine, authorities said on Friday.
National Police Chief Gen. Suyudi Ario Seto told a press conference that police and customs officers intercepted a ship carrying 1.1 tons of ketamine in the waters off Sumatra on October 20, the AFP news agency reported.
The tanker MT Global 168 was intercepted after intelligence officers detected irregularities in its route through the Malacca Strait and the Andaman Sea. It was then taken to Belawan Port in North Sumatra for inspection.
“From this search operation, the joint team managed to seize illicit drugs in the form of ketamine HCL (hydrochloride). The evidence was found in 58 sacks with a total weight reaching 1.16 tonnes,” Suyudi said, adding that the shipment had an estimated value of 3.48 trillion rupiah ($210 million).
The police chief added that the MT Global 168 flew the Mongolian flag but is owned by a company based in Johor Bahru, Malaysia.
The following day, Suyudi added, in what the National Narcotics Board (BNN) described as a joint operation with the National Narcotics Control Commission of China, Indonesian authorities raided a clandestine drug laboratory in Aceh province’s Pidie regency. There, they seized around 1.2 tons of liquid and crystal methamphetamine, assorted equipment for converting liquid into crystal meth, and arrested 11 suspects, including two Chinese nationals. Authorities put the value of the drugs at around 2.16 trillion rupiah ($119 million).
“The back-to-back operations underscore how Indonesia remains a major target for international drug trafficking organizations,” Suyudi said, as per the Associated Press.
The AP added that Indonesian authorities are investigating possible connections between the meth lab and drug syndicates in China, Malaysia, and Indonesia, as well as criminal groups in the Golden Triangle – the tri-border region between Myanmar, Thailand, and Laos – a region long associated with large-scale narcotics production and trafficking.
The two drug operations, which come after the seizure in August of 1.3 tons of ketamine from a ship near the Riau Islands, reflect the booming state of the illicit drug trade in Southeast Asia.
In its most recent annual report on the Asian synthetic drug market, released in June, the U.N. Office on Drugs and Crime (UNODC) reported that methamphetamine seizures spiked to a record 349 tons in East and Southeast Asia in 2025, a 48 percent increase over last year’s record of 236 tons. Last year was also notable for a surge in ketamine seizures, which rose to 52.5 tons, a whopping 185 percent increase on 2024’s total.
The majority of last year’s methamphetamine seizures – around 94 percent – occurred in Southeast Asia. As The Diplomat explored in a video last week, most of these narcotics are produced in areas of Myanmar controlled by rebel groups and militias of various stripes. While drug production in Myanmar is nothing new, production and trafficking have spiked since the military coup of 2021.
The resulting conflict, chaos, and economic dysfunction have created lucrative opportunities for criminal syndicates. The civil war has weakened the state’s hold on outlying regions of the country, where most drug production has historically been concentrated, while disrupting law enforcement efforts and heightening the nation’s reliance on drug-related proceeds.
As a result, flows of narcotics from Myanmar have increased in all directions. In its June report, the UNODC noted the increasing trafficking of drugs via maritime routes, for the purposes of “both domestic distribution and transit trafficking to third countries.”
In addition to Indonesia, last year saw record seizures in Thailand, Malaysia, Myanmar, and the Philippines, including numerous multi-ton seizures.
